I'm huge fan of the franchise and played Dishonored 1 countless times when I had it on the Xbox 360 back in the day.
Dishonored 2 does a great job at sticking to an already, great fromula.
Stealth is possible and challenging while combat is intense and exciting.
However, my GTX 1070 shouldn't be having such a hard time running this game at 60FPS on almost-ultra settings.
Framerate can't stay steady. It likes to jump and dip in the high 50s, and when parts of the map move (especially in the clockwork mansion) framerate almost immediately plummets to 30.
Come on, Arkane Studios, that's some console-peasant crap.
I also found that on my second run through the game, (when I decided to play as Emily) framrate drops were even more noticable.
For a game that's trying to incorperate more female characters into its gameplay and plot, you guys aren't making it easy to enjoy playing as the girl...
With the poor optimization aside, this game offers hours of gameplay with multiple endings and endless ways to play each mission.
So I would recomend this game if you apply to any of the following:
-The game is on sale
-Your computer is a beast
-You're from the future and my GPU is obsolete/garbage
-You love Dishonored so much you wouldn't mind jittering your way through the clockwork mansion like a console peasant.

Ok, here the review:
I can't recommend this game. Alot of stuff in this game is really really cool, like the environment graphics and the lighting or
the looks of the spells, but there are sooo many things that should be fixed:
1. you are going to run/ride/click unnecessary often - the transport system feels like they actually want you to waste your time going from point a to point b. It's possible to go directly to points on the map without using a wayshrine, but that costs gold, which I don't understand at all. Forcing players to use those crappy wayshrines that lead to load screens makes the playing experience ridiculous grindy.
Also not having all together, like you are in town and only have to go into a menu to visit different institutions like banks, guild traders, taverns, etc makes the game unnecessary time-consuming. The first 20 hours it may be cool to explore towns, but i am getting really annoyed being forced to manually run to all institutions without the possibility of a shortcut. If they would drop this fee for going directly to points on the map and make towns less tedious the game would be 200% better instantly, especially for players like me that don't want to spend 6 hours everyday on a game only to have a shot at levelling up.
At first i wanted to stop here, to i want to explain this detailed, because this annoys me the most:
you are in a town, you want to go to a banker, you hit M for map, you find the banker, you walk in front of the bank door, you hit key E, load screen, you are in the bank. Takes up to 4 minutes, just to make a single action in the game.
This should be way, way easier, like:
you are in a town, you want to go to a banker, you hit M for map, you click on the bank building on the map, short load screen, bam - you are inside the bank. Takes 2 seconds. Of course this shouldn't be possible if you have stolen or are in a town filled with enemies.
Also I don't understand how there are so many doors and obstacles. Is it really that difficult to implement going through doors without load-screens in 2016? Especially if the room you are going in is like 10 squaremeters with 6 objects and two persons. This is not a clever game design at all.
2. alot of elements in this game are not skill oriented. While the quests aren't bad in any way, i don't like being forced to do them in order to gain more experience than if i had moved freely. That contradicts the open-world character the game has. I find myself just going from person A to person B, clicking alot on the E key and searching on the compass/map for person C, only to get send back to person A, which takes no skill, just the ability to stay awake. This is what you seem to get the most experience points from.
3. the controls could be improved. The map could be an overlay instead of covering my screen. Inventory should be searchable and sortable, also grid view without installing addons would be nice. Climbing and diving are practically impossible. Funny to imagine that our hero isn't able to climb over a 3 meter wall or get on a dock which is 1 meter over the water. Again, alot of unnecessary wasted time for the player just to get from point a to point b in a lot of situations.
4. pay-to-win or grind-to-win are the only options. If you buy the basic game, you are basically getting ripped off, because sooner or later you are going to pay for the ESO-plus membership, because of stuff like crafting bags, horses, DLCs and so on. I don't think a monthly subscription is bad at all and i don't think buying expansions is bad at all, but putting players that just have the basic game into a drastic disadvantage to those who have bought the imperial edition or have the eso-plus is not right in my opinion. They shouldn't sell the basic game at all, to make it fair. If you buy the basic game, you will want to buy either a dlc or the subscription sooner or later, if you take it serious. I think there are games out there that give you alot more bang for your buck than ESO. The way the pricing is and the way they try to make money off the players makes me personally mistrust the developers.

This is a great game to have running in the background, while watching a movie, or relaxing.  However, it might not be for everyone.
It can be tedious at times, especially in the beginning.  You can't place many sources of vegetation at once, and it can take a while if you want to add a lot of vegetation.  The game itself runs slowly- I've had it running while watching TV for around two or three hours and only got through six months.  And that's on the fastest speed setting.
You can speed up time, but it costs precious resources (Tyto Coins) that are gained by achievements (few and far between) or 'weekly' in the game (maybe about every 15/20 minutes?).   And you only get around 5-10 for the first couple 'months.'  Oh yeah; if you want new animals, decomposers or providers?  Yep, they cost Tyto Coins too.  It takes a while to get a good cache of unlocked organisms.
The other currency, Energy, regerates steadily.  You need energy to put unlocked organisms in your biome.
Things I wish were in the game:
- Slightly faster breeding times
- A third speed setting
- Seeing exactly how a population declines or increases- I often question if they're being eaten, dying, or starving.
- Other ways to gain Tyto Coins, even if it's a small amounts.
- More statistics!  I would love seeing which animals are eating what.
Overall, I'm enjoying it, but it's definitely not a game that I can play without doing anything else :)

This is one of the most realistic ecology simulators I have ever played. It teaches players about looking ahead to see the consequences of their actions. Right now, the game is just a seed with so much potential to grow. The more people that play this game, report bugs, and share their screenshots, the more that seed grows into a beautiful tree. So what are you waiting for? Become a part of the Tyto Ecology community today.

Some shortcomings i have found so far (all of which can be easily rectified) is the lacck if animals, and the lack of biomes, other than that I think it has a lot of potential and well worht the 10 dollars i spent on it (dlc included).

A fun and clever way to learn about the meaning of animal life.
Game Details:
In Tyto Ecology, you have the power to create your own biodome and fill it with life!
Start with an empty biodome as your canvas, then create a rich, diverse ecosystem by balancing producers, consumers, and decomposers. You’re in control as you work to create a functioning ecosystem from the ground up, problem solving to learn life science principles. Tyto Ecology, an ecology simulation game, teaches Next Generation Science Standards to learners in a fun and innovative way!
This is a calm, slow-paced game (at least until things start going wrong) that encourages learning through experimentation as you work to sustain, or destroy, life. Up to three months of time can pass while you are away, so you come back to changes in your ecosystem and potentially several problems to handle each time you return to the game.

Not impressed so far.
The game has three speeds.
1. Realtime.  Uh....
2. 'fast forward' which is?  Maybe 2x realtime.  Lol
3. Skip ahead days/weeks or a month, which you pay from limited funds.
I put down some rabbits, bobcats and moths.  The rabbits spread out, the bob cats lolled around, and the moths just sat in one place refusing to migrate over to the plants I needed pollinated.  That's where it sat, for an hour while I watched.  I threw the bobcats in out of boredom.  They come in 100% fed, I guess it takes a long time for them to get hungry.  I'd already skipped ahead a week so had no T points available to skip ahead more.  Maybe someday if I leave the program running unattended I'll get more.  But then, how will I play my other steam games that are fun?
The graphics are lackluster.  They start out on minimum settings.  I cranked everything up to maximum, the only change I could see is the textures got fuzzy due to the anti-aliasing.  It appears none of the creatures make sound on their own, but the bobcats growl if you click on them.   I may be wrong about that though.
To make this game better it needs more ambiance, more sound effects, MORE ACTION, ability to fast forward without dumb restrictions.
Edit:  I read in another review that time can pass when the app is closed.  The default is time does not pass when app is closed.  I changed that to 'easy', one week passes when app is closed.  I left the app and came back in 15 minutes.  Four days had passed in game.  My rabbit population went from 12 to 8.  At this rate they will be long gone before the ~70 days to reproduce happens.  Not sure HOW they died.  It would be nice to get a log of what is going on when the door is closed.  "Bobcat ate rabbit", "Rabbit died of old age", "Rabbit died of starvation".......

I'm a huge alien fan, but not a huge fan of sneaking and hiding. I was afraid that i might not like it but It's what the game is for the most parts. The alien itself is there just to slow you down in parts of the game. It didn't give me horror, more like agony of waiting for it to go away and frustration. I enjoyed so much on the parts where i didn't have to worry about the alien - at all.
The game has few flaws too that make you really frustrated. You make a sound, like hit an enemy with a wrench or run around, the alien will appear suddenly from the closest ceiling vent and will take you out immediately unless you can hide within 2 seconds. But if someone else, like other human sees you and shoots at you, it doesn't care. You shoot one bullet at the dude and the alien will kill you.
Then there are facehugger eggs. You get your flamethrower, clear the area from active non-hatched facehugger eggs and still a facehugger will spawn behind you from thin air and tries to take you out. From the place where you already looked for and it was clear. You can torch all the eggs and still in one spot that thing will come for you, just because it's scripted into the game as event. Frustration continues.
The synthetic humans. They burn and will not die from it. You would think that burning flame would kill them but no. It doesn't even make their skin black. Killing them is more harder than keeping the alien from getting you. They are tough as hell. You can explode them, use shotgun or pistol to finish them off but burning doesn't do a god damn thing. Very unlogical to me.
The humans. You are supposed to hide from them and they will shoot you on sight. Everyone has a gun. EVERY ONE OF THEM. But if you still don't have the gun, if  you manage to kill them, you cannot pick their gun up from the ground. Because you haven't found the pistol yet, that you need to find before you can pick their guns up. Ridiculous.
The game has it's hook. You can investigate what happened there, find personnel ID cards, read their mail, access the station logs and read on about different things. The levels are well made, look awesome and the gameplay is solid. If only it had more action and less frustration with the alien. I get that it's ment to cause horror but in the current form, it just causes frustration more than horror.
If you are going to get this, get it from sale. I did, and i'm glad i did though. Worth a play through, if you exclude all the bad things.

Slime Rancher is nice at first sight, and its mix of farming and FPS is both intriguing and enjoyable. Alas, there is no incentive to play and the game is mostly purposeless. Exploration is not that rewarding and new locations are just the same as before, with new colors. It would have been better with secrets, side quests, and small objectives.
Slime Rancher is a farming game mixed with an FPS. You own a ranch, where you raise slimes, harmless bubble-like creatures, which produces a magical brighly-colored poo called 'plort' which, for some reason, is worth a good deal of money. You can also grow vegetables and chickens to feed the slimes according to their preferences. That's about all for the farming part, though you must take care to provide good living conditions for the different slimes (e.g. fireflies slimes cannot stand daylight so you must protect them).
The interest of the game lies in the exploration part. To capture new kind of slimes, you must go into the wild armed with some kind of a vacuum cleaner which can absorb slimes and all sorts of objects (chickens, vegetables, plorts). As the capacity of your vacuum cleaner is drastically reduced (you can only carry four different kinds of items, all in limited quantities), it means a lot of backtracking since you constantly have to go back to your ranch to bring back your loot.
To unlock new locations, you must find a key which is given by the bursting of a giant slime thanks to your overfeeding it. It's a bit cruel, but fine. New locations mean new kind of graphical textures, and new slimes. A teleporter can bring you back to the ranch, but it's one-way only for most of them (actually the teleportation system is extremely confusing).
When you die, you loose everything you carry and you get to sleep for hours (in the meanwhile slimes can escape their corral and wreak havoc in your farm by eating all the chickens). As the jumping system is not that great, it means that you can waste all your loot just for falling into the water. It seems a bit cheap.
The money you get by selling plorts can be used to improve your ranch (e.g. unlocking new parts of it) and the living conditions of your slimes, or to upgrade your staff (jetpack, carrying capacity, health).
Additionnally, you have daily objectives. They are trade offers from other slime ranchers (that you will never get to meet in real). Usually it's not that interesting and not worth the trouble.
Also, you find treasure spheres during your explorations. Unfortunately, you cannot open them unless you are in the late game. Which means, until then, exploring carefully all the caves and places is basically pointless. It's a bit disappointing that exploration is not rewarded to begin with.
And that's about it. I think this little description fairly covers all the main aspects of the game. In my opinion, it's not enough to provide a good reason to play. I enjoyed the few hours I spent with the game but I cannot be certain I will keep playing it in the future. Due to an overall lack of small objectives, there is no "one more thing to do and I quit" effect and you can lose interest pretty fast. Without story, without purpose except making good money, without special fun in the FPS part (I mean, you just collect the slimes, there is no fight of any kind), the game certainly feels a bit bland.

//    This review is based on a first experience with the franchise and focuses exclusively on PVE!    //
Dark Souls II was a pleasant suprise after I finished the game, despite it leaving a sour taste in my mouth the first time when I started playing it. No wonder, this was my first time playing with the franchise and the learning curve was a bit huge.
But as I explored the world of Drangleic and fought more enemies, I slowly learnt the game's mechanics, and I got hooked up into the game. Yes, Dark Souls II is hard and it will punish you for every mistakes, but if you put enough time and effort into it, you will eventually finish the game. And nothing feels better than finally beating a boss, that has been murdering you over and over again.
The concept of the Dark Souls II is simple, yet extremely addictive:
You play as a cursed undead and set on a journey in Drangleic to save yourself and lift the curse. As you travel you defeat enemies and absorb their souls.
Souls serve as both EXP and currency to purchase new items or upgrade your current loadout.
But here's the catch: if you die you will lose your unspent souls. All of them. If you can go back to the location where you have died, you can reclaim them, but if you get killed again before you can do so, your souls are lost permanently.
Furthermore, each time you die your maximum HP will decrease a bit and you become a hollow. This HP punishment keeps going on with each death till your max HP is 50% of the original. This might sound extremely harsh, but that's the way of the game communicating with you and teaching the error of your ways. The process can be reversed by using a Human Effigy. This item restores you back to max HP and gives you back your humanity. As a human you can summon NPC-s and fellow players to aid you on your journey, while you can't do that when you are hollow (basicly zombie mode).
As you discover new areas you will come across bonfires, these will be your checkpoints and your fast travel stations.
As you get deeper into the game the curiosity will lead you further and pushes you to progress:
- Can I survive the next area?
- What's behind that gate?
- How to get THAT treasure over there?
- This didn't work, but what if I try something else?
I often just started up the game to make a small progress in the game and ended up spending hours, so believe me when I say it's addictive.
The multiplayer is also an essential part of Dark Souls. There's no exact multiplayer mode, but it's nicely integrated into the singleplayer: as you travel you will see the spirits of fellow players, who are still in the same area, but in their own game session. Players can communicate with each other by leaving messages to help or hinder others, and if someone dies during the game they will leave a bloodstain behind. Interacting with the bloodstain will show the last few seconds of the player before he passes away, sometimes it helps alot as it warns of the surrounding danger and sometimes it's just hillarious to watch how others die. During the gameplay other players can invade you and kill you, while others can be summoned to help you.
Graphics wise the game is average, it doesn't look bad, but it's far from looking great too.
However the level design is extremely well done, there are plenty of secrets to discover, and the every section is well connected to another.
Not much to say about the sound design. The game doesn't have any music most of the time, only in boss battles. However the ambient sounds, the voice acting and the creatures' sounds are very well done.
Overall, I have to say I really enjoyed the game, and would highly recommend it to anyone, who's looking for a challanging game.
- Hard, but fair game: if you die, it's your fault.....well most of the time. But when you make a huge progress int the game, it feels rewarding.
- Dark atmosphere and the constant pressure the game puts on you.
- High number of story and optional boss fights.
- Interesting story and lore.
- Satisfaction and freedom of exploration: the game doesn't tell you much. No waypoints, no map, you discover everything on your own.
- Solid voice acting and sound design.
- Performance wise the game is well optimized. It runs well on weaker computers too with solid 50-60FPS.
- High replay value.
- Hitboxes can be a bit off.
- Graphics are average. Not bad, but far from amazing too.
- Control-wise it's a lazy port. Can you play it with keyboard and mouse? Yes, you can. But you will need to remap many keys, as the mouse doesn't really work as intended for many actions such as jump attack and parry.
- Some bosses are too easy.

Ok, here the review:
I can't recommend this game. Alot of stuff in this game is really really cool, like the environment graphics and the lighting or
the looks of the spells, but there are sooo many things that should be fixed:
1. you are going to run/ride/click unnecessary often - the transport system feels like they actually want you to waste your time going from point a to point b. It's possible to go directly to points on the map without using a wayshrine, but that costs gold, which I don't understand at all. Forcing players to use those crappy wayshrines that lead to load screens makes the playing experience ridiculous grindy.
Also not having all together, like you are in town and only have to go into a menu to visit different institutions like banks, guild traders, taverns, etc makes the game unnecessary time-consuming. The first 20 hours it may be cool to explore towns, but i am getting really annoyed being forced to manually run to all institutions without the possibility of a shortcut. If they would drop this fee for going directly to points on the map and make towns less tedious the game would be 200% better instantly, especially for players like me that don't want to spend 6 hours everyday on a game only to have a shot at levelling up.
At first i wanted to stop here, to i want to explain this detailed, because this annoys me the most:
you are in a town, you want to go to a banker, you hit M for map, you find the banker, you walk in front of the bank door, you hit key E, load screen, you are in the bank. Takes up to 4 minutes, just to make a single action in the game.
This should be way, way easier, like:
you are in a town, you want to go to a banker, you hit M for map, you click on the bank building on the map, short load screen, bam - you are inside the bank. Takes 2 seconds. Of course this shouldn't be possible if you have stolen or are in a town filled with enemies.
Also I don't understand how there are so many doors and obstacles. Is it really that difficult to implement going through doors without load-screens in 2016? Especially if the room you are going in is like 10 squaremeters with 6 objects and two persons. This is not a clever game design at all.
2. alot of elements in this game are not skill oriented. While the quests aren't bad in any way, i don't like being forced to do them in order to gain more experience than if i had moved freely. That contradicts the open-world character the game has. I find myself just going from person A to person B, clicking alot on the E key and searching on the compass/map for person C, only to get send back to person A, which takes no skill, just the ability to stay awake. This is what you seem to get the most experience points from.
3. the controls could be improved. The map could be an overlay instead of covering my screen. Inventory should be searchable and sortable, also grid view without installing addons would be nice. Climbing and diving are practically impossible. Funny to imagine that our hero isn't able to climb over a 3 meter wall or get on a dock which is 1 meter over the water. Again, alot of unnecessary wasted time for the player just to get from point a to point b in a lot of situations.
4. pay-to-win or grind-to-win are the only options. If you buy the basic game, you are basically getting ripped off, because sooner or later you are going to pay for the ESO-plus membership, because of stuff like crafting bags, horses, DLCs and so on. I don't think a monthly subscription is bad at all and i don't think buying expansions is bad at all, but putting players that just have the basic game into a drastic disadvantage to those who have bought the imperial edition or have the eso-plus is not right in my opinion. They shouldn't sell the basic game at all, to make it fair. If you buy the basic game, you will want to buy either a dlc or the subscription sooner or later, if you take it serious. I think there are games out there that give you alot more bang for your buck than ESO. The way the pricing is and the way they try to make money off the players makes me personally mistrust the developers.

When the game originally came out I was 16 years old, and I quite liked it.  The original Deus Ex was (and probably still is) my favourite game, period, so I was really pumped to revist the world.  I remember being really impressed by the visuals, as the real-time lighting system was very impressive for the time, and the ragdoll physics were also lots of fun to play with.  The shooting also felt like an improvement over the original.  However even in my overhyped state of optimism, it was clear to me that some major concessions had been made on the level design.  The levels were far smaller than anything from the original Deus Ex, and felt claustrophobic in comparison.  The storyline also had no sense of pace, jumping straight into the twists far too soon, and the tone just seemed off in the dialogue.  I revisted the game recently when doing a playthrough of all the Deus Ex games, and now that the graphics are no longer impressive and the physics seem positively ropey, the problems with the levels stood out much more.  I would actually say this game has aged a lot worse than the original.  Invisible War still has some interesting hub areas and some cool side-quests, and it does consistently give you choice about how you approach missions.  However the choice is more a narrative choice about which faction to support, rather than the sneak/shoot/hack approach of the other Deus Ex games.  There is a little of that too, but not separated to the degree seen in the other games.  I'll still recommend playing the game for historical interest, and there are some interesting ideas in here both narratively and mechanically (universal ammo, for instance, was probably a mistake but nonethless a novel idea).  There's also some rather poignant moments revisiting some former locations from the original game.  So whilst I don't claim this as a good game, it's still something you should play if you haven't.  And if you only played it back in 2003, it's worth revisiting for it's curiosity value.  Ideally, though, pick it up on sale.

I've owned this game since it came out, and despite its age and some well-deserved criticisms, I still now and then go on a binge and play it through a few times in a row. The game has enough depth that you can do that and still find new ways of doing things.
When this game came out, there was a lot of negative press about it. Even once you filter through the hyperbole, there are some disappointments and flaws. The three major criticisms of any substance that you hear most often are:
One warning: Windows 10 (and I think 8) don't play nice with the game. If you check the message boards for tips, everyone will recommend VisibleTweaker and for good reason. It was the only way I could get it going after I upgraded, plus it incorporates various higher resolution texture mods. After I upgraded to Windows 10, I couldn't reinstall because the original disks and some horrible content protection, so I re-purchased on Steam, so I do know that VisibleTweaker will work with a Steam version.
Like the original and the prequels, Invisible War has enough richness that you can pick biomods and weapons to suit (or challenge) your play style; there are enough side quests and alternative paths to suit your mood, sense of humor, or sense of ethics. Pacifist, non-lethal, or unnecessarily lethal are all legitimate options. Myself, I tend to either sneak past or knock unconscious clock-punching security guards and frustrated working-class stiffs. deal with soldiers pragmatically, but when it comes to the Templars (uniform-loving purists), I like to set them on fire and watch them run around screaming. If that's not your style, then there is an exclusive boarding school for girls, and you can kill everyone inside if you'd like.
There are male and female versions of the protagonist, Alex D. (Skin tone can also be adjusted). Gender doesn't make a huge difference, but a side-quest or two have different possibilities depending on which you choose.
The dialog is solid and has the same attitude that the series is known for. The voice actor for the male Alex D is good, but personally, I think the voice actor for the female Alex D nails the delivery perfectly. She is probably a big part of why I keep replaying it; her verbal smackdowns are that good.
Overall, I think it has aged quite well. I've forgotten most of the other games from its generation, and of the ones that I can remember without going back and looking through what I own, this is the only one I still play. With the one caveat that you might have to do some tweaking before it will work, I think it is worth it. Maybe it's just nostalgia talking, but I think it is fun enough that I paid for it twice.

System Shock 2 has a unique Sci-fi RPG layout, but it is also kind of horror.
System Shock 2 was made before there was too much of a quota for exactly what a game needed to be, so it is fun discovering what is different. I was 4 when this game came out, and played it for the first time maybe 3 years ago. The game aged very well. The rpg aspect of System Shock 2 is different from a lot of rpg's today in that it is very hard to get to max level in anything. You level up skills from 1-5 and they get exponentially more expensive to level up. Therefore, you could get level 5 heavy machine guns, but at that point you are sacrificing leveling up so many other things once or twice. The skill system is very fresh. In fantasy rpgs everyone knows that fighters use strength and constitution while wizards use intelligence. But skills here range from physical traits to handling machinery to using psy magic.
Overall a well fleshed out and interesting environment backed up by adaptable gameplay options. You should probably get this game

I'm a huge alien fan, but not a huge fan of sneaking and hiding. I was afraid that i might not like it but It's what the game is for the most parts. The alien itself is there just to slow you down in parts of the game. It didn't give me horror, more like agony of waiting for it to go away and frustration. I enjoyed so much on the parts where i didn't have to worry about the alien - at all.
The game has few flaws too that make you really frustrated. You make a sound, like hit an enemy with a wrench or run around, the alien will appear suddenly from the closest ceiling vent and will take you out immediately unless you can hide within 2 seconds. But if someone else, like other human sees you and shoots at you, it doesn't care. You shoot one bullet at the dude and the alien will kill you.
Then there are facehugger eggs. You get your flamethrower, clear the area from active non-hatched facehugger eggs and still a facehugger will spawn behind you from thin air and tries to take you out. From the place where you already looked for and it was clear. You can torch all the eggs and still in one spot that thing will come for you, just because it's scripted into the game as event. Frustration continues.
The synthetic humans. They burn and will not die from it. You would think that burning flame would kill them but no. It doesn't even make their skin black. Killing them is more harder than keeping the alien from getting you. They are tough as hell. You can explode them, use shotgun or pistol to finish them off but burning doesn't do a god damn thing. Very unlogical to me.
The humans. You are supposed to hide from them and they will shoot you on sight. Everyone has a gun. EVERY ONE OF THEM. But if you still don't have the gun, if  you manage to kill them, you cannot pick their gun up from the ground. Because you haven't found the pistol yet, that you need to find before you can pick their guns up. Ridiculous.
The game has it's hook. You can investigate what happened there, find personnel ID cards, read their mail, access the station logs and read on about different things. The levels are well made, look awesome and the gameplay is solid. If only it had more action and less frustration with the alien. I get that it's ment to cause horror but in the current form, it just causes frustration more than horror.
If you are going to get this, get it from sale. I did, and i'm glad i did though. Worth a play through, if you exclude all the bad things.

Overall the game is really good. I didn’t expect much from a free steam RPG, but Holy God was I impressed. The people who made this game put a lot of love into it. I look forward to the sequel.

The series as a whole before the individual game
The series is great. However, their is a warning, the set of games, especially the last one, are harder than most of these type of games. The writing is great, the stats carry over between games, different events can happen based on the stats you have or what classes you choose. However, for your first run, expect to fail. However, there is a lot of replay value in these games and they are very enjoyable.
This last game is the climactic conclusion to the story. Your character will learn about the demons and search for an artifact to fight them before the big final battle. Once again, more classes, bringing the total amount of classes your character can be to a whopping 35 classes. The mechanic of managing the ship, which helps bring you to the artifact, is not as fun or as extensive as managing the army in the previous game. There is however, a major plot thing that can be fun at the end.

As I write this (18 Nov 2017), the reviews of "Deus Ex: Invisible War" (the 2003 sequel to the original "Deus Ex" (2000)) are running 335 to 501, or about 40% negative.  Oddly, as an individual, that group divide pretty much summarizes my feelings toward the game.  Just before playing this game, I re-played the original "Deus Ex."  As I played it, the overriding emotion for the game was awe.  On the other hand, for "Invisible War," my overriding emotion was disappointment.  Why?  In a nutshell, it's because the developers dumbed the game down.  Since this was written for the consoles of the time and ported over to the PC, I can understand the reduced gameplay:
- Small levels,
- Long loading times (15 seconds),
- Fewer Biomod upgrades (I fully upgraded about half way through the game and ended up with 14 standard and 8 black market upgrade canisters sitting unused in my inventory),
- No exploration points (heck, no points at all),
- No skills to apply for each upgrade,
- Very restricted weapon mod ability (as with Biomod canisters, I finished the game with 25 unused weapon mods sitting in my inventory),
- Ridiculously tiny inventory.
But, the big problem is the dumbing down of the philosophical, social, and political thought in the game.  I guess I can understand that, too:  there are probably far more people who want to just play a game than those who enjoy thinking about the philosophical underpinnings of the game.
Another problem is that this game seems to target a much younger audience than did the original game.  That's especially noticable at the beginning where all the characters behave pretty simplistically.  But, that does get better by the end.
So, why am I recommending the game?  Because about 14 hours through, I realized I was still playing.  As a sequel to "Deus Ex," yes, this game is disappointing.  But, on its own, it's actually pretty good.  Again, it's no "Deus Ex."  But, a list price of about $7 (and I paid a whole lot less for the total "Deus Ex Collection" bundle) for 27.5 hours of reasonable game play justifies it.

After playing through the whole game, I honestly don't get the hate or denial of this game's existence. It has areas that are inferior to both Deus Ex 1 (DX1) and DX: HR, but also many areas that are just as good or simply different. Sadly, that widespread opinion is one of the reasons why I waited longer to play this than I should have. Although, in this case I guess it's fitting, because Deus Ex are about global AI's with their own opinions/agendas and the Internet can seem like that at times, although with a major case of split personality and other mental issues.
IW has lots of things that I associate with Deus Ex and other games like it, e.g. Knights of the Old Republic, The Witcher and VtM:Bloodlines. The mentioned games are all personal favorites of mine, because they give you quest/gameplay/dialogue options and let's you roleplay a character or attitude, which says something about how I view IW.
There's quite a lot of voice acting, something I look for in every game. Even most no-name NPC's say 5-6 lines of dialogues before they start repeating themselves. This helps with immersing you into the game world, makes the whole gaming experience more interesting, encourages you to explore and, above all, pester everyone until they've run out of dialogue lines, even if they tell you to go away, heh heh. On that account, IW is every bit as good as DX1 and it also has several references to the first game, both small and large.
The story and world created through that voice acting is intricate like in DX1. I play Deus Ex games for the gameplay options, but I enjoyed the story. You have several different companies/factions/people to keep track of. with several story twists along the way. The characters themselves aren't as memorable (or amusingly stereotypical) as those from DX1, but I wouldn't say they are one-dimensional or boring.
The level design is also very Deus Ex-y, with the vents and being able to approach an objective/mission area in different ways. Perhaps not entirely as well made as DX1, but it's nothing that made me stop and think that I wanted to play DX1 instead.
The biomod and tools/weapons are great and I was able to get most of what I wanted early on for my non-lethal stealth playstyle. However, it's here that I first realized what people had against IW, since like in DX1, you have to choose between 3 options in five categories. For some reason, hacking and invisibilty is in the same category, which didn't bother me at first, because I rarely found the need for either. At the end of the game, I wished I could have had both at the same time.
The end stages are where you encounter heavily armed/armored troops that you can't knock out via tranquilizing darts/gas and can't backstab like in DX1 (DX1 had the Dragon's Tooth nano blade, IW has an energy blade that is much less effective). It's possible that I could have just sneaked/run away from them and I did at one point, because I didn't have enough ammo or desire to to take them all out. I had switched from invisibility to hacking by then and even when crouching, enemies hear you very well and are able to locate you. It was much easier to ghost my way around in DX1, while IW practically requires the "soft feet" and invisibility biomod for successful sneaking (not many large spaces because it had to work on the Xbox as well), which means you can't use the hacking or jumping biomod at the same time.
Exploring the area by jumping up on stuff and hacking were two of my favorite activities in DX1. They don't work as well in IW. The jumping mechanic is odd, seems like you jump higher if you jump up on a small ledge and then jump again. It's imprecise and unintuitive and you most often push away boxes when trying to jump up on them. DX1 had excellent box stacking mechanics, something I really miss in IW. Hacking might be more useful than it seemed, but money is quickly a non-issue and there were too few (well placed) security terminals to hack, so you could turn the tables on your enemies or simply turn off cameras.
A large source of hate for IW is perhaps because one of the factions wants you to kill certain people. Being loyal to one faction all throughout the game doesn't make you feel good, they both want you to do stuff at times that doesn't rhyme well with how I want to roleplay my character (a good-natured hero). The Witcher 1 was better at making factions be both good and bad, I didn't feel at home with either of IW's factions, because of the things they asked me to do.
Most of my complaints are from the end stages. It made it much harder to sneak/knock out people and I found my health/ ammo reserves depleted, couldn't keep on playing like I had before. I was ready to say "it's been great, but now it's over, time to start a new game from the backlog" like five hours before the actual ending revealed itself. It has good moment-to-moment gameplay, I never felt like I wanted to quit, but I sometimes felt like it didn't matter if I continued playing or not. Each point in the game felt as good as any to stop playing or to continue.
Then again, it was at the end that I realized how I could have done some things better, things that would have nullified some of my complaints and annoyances. This is a game best played twice to get the most out of it and I'll do so one day (will choose the female protagonist then, to hear a new voice do all the hero's voice acting), but the backlog beckons and I have had my fill of IW for now.

tl;dr game is great, aged very well, runs in 1920x1080. Pay attention to tutorial messages found on walls. Build for both psi and regular guns or you will be out of ammo.
Do you want to play the game that inspired many recent AAA titles, such as Bioshock 1 & 2, Deus Ex, and Prey, but is better than all of them? System Shock 2 is your game.
Almost everything about this game really shines in my opinion, so I won't waste time describing how the level design is great or how well the game rewards exploration.
+Graphics are still serviceable. While definitely not up to today's standards, they are immersive, and you get used to them fast
+1920x1080 (16:9) support. No idea if it supports anything higher
+Fully rebindable keys, which is good, because the game has TERRIBLE default bindings
+Full mouse support. This seems silly to point out but I've played 20 yr old games with no mouselook
+You can change the settings to make it control just like FPS games that come out today
+Great positional audio (Play this game with headphones, it's really helpful)
+Really good voice acting
+Atmosphere is still pretty tense and dark
-Gunplay is meh (I was debating putting this one in the "aged well" category. All the bullets that seem like the should connect, do connect. My main issue is using corners as cover is sort of unreliable due to very slow walk speed in any direction but forward)
-Animations are pretty good, you can tell they are old. Better than some games of similar age (Thief 2)
-Hitboxes on small monkey enemies are really annoying, and they are super hard to hit with the wrench
-Too few autosaves (fortunately, you can save/load the game whenever you want)
-A lot of VERY useful info about game mechanics is on display boards throughout the early stages of the game. They are almost always placed right next to the thing they are referring to. Make sure to inspect (right click) all of these and read everything they have to say. Make sure to savor and cherish these moments. Don't just skim over the tutorial messages or ignore them because you don't
it. The game is constantly testing you, and if you miss out on too many mechanincs, you're going to have a hard time.
-Important, mission-crucial information is on audio logs found as loot throughout the game. Make sure to listen to all of them. If you don't think you have the patience to do this and the previous thing on this list, this isn't the game for you, and not just because of that.
-Try not to use internet guides in this game. When the game came out, there was no internet, and is best played
blind. If playing it completely blind was a good idea, this entire section wouldn't exist. That being said, if you really get lost, and have already gone over your audio logs and notes (which are basically mission objectives), and you feel like you have explored everywhere, looking things up is fine. Just try not to get too wrapped up in it.
-The tutorial about the map glosses over a really useful feature that I wish i'd discovered sooner. You can press "M" to open the map, and there is a minimap button you can press. I recommend always having this on, but don't fall into the trap of having your eyes glued to the minimap. Lots of loot, environmental signs (like an arrow on the ground that says "medical"), security cameras, etc. are present throughout the entire game, and you don't want to miss them.
-Another thing the map tutorial glosses over is that you can click on points of interest, such as shops and upgrade stations, then type something and it will appear on your map. You can also press "N" to create one of these points of interest at your current location. This is incredibly useful for marking keypads you don't know the code to, storerooms for supplies that you don't want to carry around due to inventory constraints, etc.
It's very possible that you could get 75% through the game and be stuck because your build wasn't good. The most important skills in the game are Hack and Maintainence. Make sure to level them both a few times. Beyond that, the best build is one that can make use of everything you pick up. If you only spec into Psi, and can't use any guns, you will always have too few psi hypos and too many bullets. You will end up having to use the wrench, and no one wants to try to wrestle with the sh*tty monkey hitboxes.
Holy sh*t, I didn't expect this review to be so long. If you read to the end, you probably enjoyed it, so make sure to give this review a helpful rating or leave a comment about something I can change!

I picked up
recently because I like trying out classic games.  Although I had fun with it, it's certainly a game that has aged poorly.  A combination of advances in technology and design, plus many of its ideas being copied by other games, weaken the appeal.  That doesn't make this a bad game, rather one that's not for everyone.
The most obvious sign of age is the graphics.  I usually say that gameplay is more important, but
is from the age of 3D where people look really weird.  While that kind of works for the corrupted monstrosities, the ordinary characters seen in flashbacks suffer the same problem, and this hinders immersion.  This is something you have to be able to accept to properly experience the game.
A more serious obstacle is the interface.  It's a bad sign when any decent walkthrough will start by telling you to open the options menu and rebind movement controls to something less ridiculous.  You need to remember a lot of keyboard shortcuts to avoid having to use the clunky inventory screen in the middle of combat, without pausing.  Part of the problem is that the game gives you a lot of options, with different healing items, weapons, ammunition, stat boosts and so on.  Those who feel modern games are too simple might appreciate the depth, but I still think there's room to streamline things.
One gameplay weakness that can't be attributed to its age is the balance.
is an action RPG, where you can't hit enemies with a stick without the right skills.  Unfortunately, the different options are unbalanced; for example,
are vastly superior to the alternative weapon types.  On Normal difficulty, you just about have enough cyber modules to correct a mistake, but it's the sort of game where reading a guide on character builds is highly recommended.
Despite the above three paragraphs, I do still recommend
.  I've hinted already that the gameplay, while fiddly, offers depth and realism.  There's a curious mix of action and strategy in the need to plan ahead to your next encounter, which you don't find very often.  Not only must you make sure you have the right items, you must ensure they are all either bound to suitable shortcuts or easily arranged in your inventory.  The ability to anticipate the nature of threats also helps.
The exploration of the
is also well done, albeit according to a now-familiar pattern.  The unlocking of different areas gradually is a classic example of gameplay serving the narrative.  The need to access the next area keeps a clear goal at all times, allows a sensible difficulty curve, generally makes sense in-game and also slowly reveals the backstory explaining what has happened.  This has been done in countless games since 1998, but it's still done well here.
The story in general holds up okay.  There are some flaws, such as weak voice acting and "twists" that can be seen a mile off.  But I found the contrast between organic and machine that runs through
well-done, with some really unsettling imagery and implementation.
There's a steep entry price for
, in the sense of the issues you must overlook to fully appreciate it.  Not everyone will be able to willing to do that.  But if you think you might, I'd certainly encourage checking this out.

Alien Isolation is one of the first mainstream games to come out in quite a while that is actually true survival horror instead of action horror. Crafting items and using distractions and other tactics is key to survival instead of just aiming a gun at  the scary monster and pulling the trigger until it dies (though there is a bit of that.) The game is amazingly optomized and runs well on my low-mid end PC at 60 FPS. The game DOES seem to have a lot of buggy issues with crashing frequently, always during a reload though whether this is on my PCs end or not I don't know. The game is lengthy and that us both a good and bad thing. More gameplay is always good but the games story drags on and on and on much like dead space, making you repair things all the time to keep the story going. By no means am I criticizing the game for too long, I am simply saying the games story wasn't crafted around that length. Instead the game extends its length through many points where you think "This is the end right" often with a new thing on the space station to fix. Be that as it may, the game never feels boring. It's tense and only gets more tense as the game goes on and consistently raises the stakes and danger on you.
Danger is key here: You ALWAYS feel vulnerable, but sometimes it feels as if the game is trying just a bit too hard. There's numerous pointless jump scares involving the androids; there will be a dead one on the floor that grabs you when you walk buy. The game does this multiple times from start to finish and I truly wonder if the developers thought they'd get anyone with this; even I didn't fall for it because all the jumpscare androids have glowing white eyes, the really dead ones don't. Another part where the game tries to hard is that the alien constantly stalks you in somewhat obvious ways to create tension, almost ALWAYS running up to where you're hiding to scare you, even if he was far away when you hid. The game sounds AMAZING, I'd say the sound is more important than the graphics in this and I fully suggest playing this game with all sounds turned up while wearing headphones. I truly cannot gush about the sound enough, the music is terrifying and keeps you on edge and every creak and squeak on the station causes you to feel tense and uneasy, as if death is right behind you. The graphics are also nice, and the station itself looks right out of Alien. However the NPC character faces tend to look really...off and plastic, creepy to look at.
The story is pretty good and though it drags on, is still pretty solid and keeps you pretty invested in the characters. You want to see what happens to Ripley and the other people aboard the sevastapol station. However, without spoiling anything, I feel like the games ending is a depressing letdown and it feels like there's no real closure.
Overall Alien Isolation is a true return to survival horror, and seriously one of the most suspensful and scary games I've played in a long time, and I've played quite a bit of survival horror but Alien Isolation still manages to scare the crap out of me.

Even after a year they haven't fixed the design problems.  All they've done is patch the bugs and (slightly) finish the political/civil war system.  Even the best modders out there can't fix the way buildings and provinces interact.  The main problem is that if you don't have all the regions in a province your buildings are *much* less efficient because all buildings provide their bonuses on a province-wide basis.  This results in you declaring war on your allies when they take the wrong province in a war.
Why declare war on them?  Because there's no way to diplomatically deal with it.  You can't trade provinces or even give them to your client state.  You can't threaten to intervene in a war between your client state and another.  The diplomacy boils down to: "Want a trade route?" or "Declare war?"
These fundimental issues are unmoddable, and every time I come back hoping to see improvement it never is there.  I simply cannot recommend this game to anyone.

If you are reading this, Mike Walter (the Author): please consider the 'fun vs function' dichotomy when you are writing your next story game.
Too much of the former, and it is hard to take the story seriously.
Too much of the latter, and it becomes difficult to enjoy said story.
I know how hard it is to write: you drive yourself crazy scrapping idea after idea until you 'finally' come up with something that you are satisfied with. The problem is that, far too often , what the author likes will not necessarily be to the audiences' liking, and, unfortunately, there is no formula to help you guess what that is until after you have released your story.
All that aside: i did experience moments of enjoyment in TLH3, but they were overshadowed by the instances of function overpowering fun, and said function, i'm sorry to say, wasn't very well implemented.

In general this game looks great... as long as you don't stray of the path the game wants you to take. This was very noticable during the area leading up to Sebastian's arrival in Union where leaving the road caused me to discover a lot of unnatural looking terrain and stupidly placed invisible walls. Unlike first game, this one isn't overloaded with gore. Instead they used gore effectively in Stefano's "art" and during fights. I'm also a huge fan of the atmosphere in Stefano's Mansion and Union. However, the other areas in the game (especially the Marrow and everything in the last 3 chapters) fail to build up tension, fail to terrify me in the slightest mostly because many of them are either uninspired/boring or way too bright.
In terms of performance this game is a bit flawed. Playing on 1440p with max settings (on a 1080ti) my average FPS were somewhere between 70 and 80. While this isn't bad, the problems start to arise when trying to play on a 144Hz monitor, because (at least in my experience) lowering settings barely increased to framerate (85FPS on medium settings).
Sebastian's animations in this game often look hilariously bad. For example, when climbing onto a box, on several occasions, Sebastian grabbed the air in front of him instead of the box he should climb on. Attacking with the knife was extremely frustrating because it sometimes didn't damage enemies despite touching them. The knife also can only destroy one box/object per attack, making it incredibly frustrating to gather resources while not having an axe. Lip sync during conversations is a bit off sometimes.
Mobius (the organization, that's responsible for the beacon incident in the first game) uses Sebastian Castellanos' daughter as the core in their hive mind called STEM. After the core goes missing and STEM starts falling apart, they contact Sebastian and force him to enter STEM to find his daughter. During the second half the story changes from "find your daughter" to
and the game starts to feel a bit like Resident Evil 5 and 6. Just like Far Cry 3, this game also gets rid of the best part of it's story halfway through the game, which almost led me to discontinue my playthrough. On a more positive note, I appreciate the lack of meaningless jumpscares. There was only one that felt forced in and completely out of place.
This game offers the default cover-based third-person shooter experience with a bit of stealth thrown into the mix. The Warden Crossbow with it's 5 types of different bolts was the only truly outstanding weapon in Sebastian's arsenal and is by far my favorite thing to come from this game. There are never too many enemies, but during the lategame they sometimes take a lot of bullets to kill, therefore making fights longer and more annoying than they have to be in a horror-game. Here's a short list covering some of the issues I had during my playthrough.
TEW2 is a good survival horror game with a lot of flaws. Bad animations, questionable hitboxes, inconsistent stealth and a sometimes confusing story drag this game down. The second half of this game also almost completely lacks the atmosphere and sense of dread the first half had. I'd recommend getting this game for 15-20$ if you've already played RE7, Outlast, Alien:Isolation, etc. otherwise you're probably better off getting one of the games I just listed. It's hard for me to not recommend this game because I loved playing the first half of it. Yet the second half lost me, making it impossible for me to say, that this game is worth buying.

In my opinion, this game is nothing short of a masterpiece. The negative reviews tend to be from people who don't seem to understand the concept of survival horror. It's literally everything I've ever wanted out of an Alien game; incredibly detailed "Nostromo" style atmosphere, great pacing, that feeling of helplessness from the first film, and some of the best AI I've ever encountered in a game. The Alien is completely unpredictable. In most games you can figure out the formula behind and enemy or boss, which becomes easily predictable over time. Not this one. No matter where you are, there is always the feeling that the Alien can pop out and kill you at any second. That combined with the motion tracker (so much nostalgia in the game) makes for some pretty intense game play.
Are there a few issues? Sure, but they are minor ones. The game is long and probably has some filler in it. Parts of the story could have been better. A common criticism is that the Alien makes the game infuriating to play at certain points, because of the lack of an autosave feature. Personally, I think this is what makes the game so damn good. You have to be constantly paying attention for a save point, all while you are being hunted by a merciless killing machine. This adds SO much tension and anxiety that if you took it away, the game would be worse. Oh, you have to start a level over again because you died and missed the save point? Sorry, but

Alien Isolation is one of the first mainstream games to come out in quite a while that is actually true survival horror instead of action horror. Crafting items and using distractions and other tactics is key to survival instead of just aiming a gun at  the scary monster and pulling the trigger until it dies (though there is a bit of that.) The game is amazingly optomized and runs well on my low-mid end PC at 60 FPS. The game DOES seem to have a lot of buggy issues with crashing frequently, always during a reload though whether this is on my PCs end or not I don't know. The game is lengthy and that us both a good and bad thing. More gameplay is always good but the games story drags on and on and on much like dead space, making you repair things all the time to keep the story going. By no means am I criticizing the game for too long, I am simply saying the games story wasn't crafted around that length. Instead the game extends its length through many points where you think "This is the end right" often with a new thing on the space station to fix. Be that as it may, the game never feels boring. It's tense and only gets more tense as the game goes on and consistently raises the stakes and danger on you.
Danger is key here: You ALWAYS feel vulnerable, but sometimes it feels as if the game is trying just a bit too hard. There's numerous pointless jump scares involving the androids; there will be a dead one on the floor that grabs you when you walk buy. The game does this multiple times from start to finish and I truly wonder if the developers thought they'd get anyone with this; even I didn't fall for it because all the jumpscare androids have glowing white eyes, the really dead ones don't. Another part where the game tries to hard is that the alien constantly stalks you in somewhat obvious ways to create tension, almost ALWAYS running up to where you're hiding to scare you, even if he was far away when you hid. The game sounds AMAZING, I'd say the sound is more important than the graphics in this and I fully suggest playing this game with all sounds turned up while wearing headphones. I truly cannot gush about the sound enough, the music is terrifying and keeps you on edge and every creak and squeak on the station causes you to feel tense and uneasy, as if death is right behind you. The graphics are also nice, and the station itself looks right out of Alien. However the NPC character faces tend to look really...off and plastic, creepy to look at.
The story is pretty good and though it drags on, is still pretty solid and keeps you pretty invested in the characters. You want to see what happens to Ripley and the other people aboard the sevastapol station. However, without spoiling anything, I feel like the games ending is a depressing letdown and it feels like there's no real closure.
Overall Alien Isolation is a true return to survival horror, and seriously one of the most suspensful and scary games I've played in a long time, and I've played quite a bit of survival horror but Alien Isolation still manages to scare the crap out of me.
8/10 Would recommend. Definently the best Alien franchise game ever released.

So I recently rediscovered Bioshock and after playing through it twice, I felt like going back to the roots as it were.
I'd heard a lot of good stuff about System Shock 2, and I'm surprised to say that every bit of praise is 100% deserved! The game is creepy, exciting and atmospheric, with gameplay systems as deep as the Mariana trench. There is so much to do and so many ways of ding it, that I feel as though I could go back and play it a second time and have a radically different experience, and unlike most RPGs, it's short enough (at about 12-20 hours) that I could actually go and do just that (because lets be real, who's going to go and play a 100-hour RPG monster through a second time, just to see what's different?).
The game absolutely stands the test of time. It feels as fresh and engaging as if it had come out last year (unless you really have a problem with old-looking games). Sure, it's a little clunky, but it's not an action game, so that shouldn't be an issue. There is so much to like here, that I#m sure you'll find it worth a shot.
Unfortunately, not everything is well balanced. Standard weapons are overwhelmingly more powerful that anything else in the game, but with a game this complex, I suppose making every choice of specialisation equally powerful was asking too much. Probably the worst thing about SS2 is the very final cutscene, which is so unbelievably cringy and cheesy, it's as if the game turned into Duke Nukem at the last minute, or as if the Dog Ending was the only ending in Silent Hill 2. It doesn't hurt the excellent experience that comes before it, but it's best if you know it's coming...
Anyway, great game, true classic. I had fun with it and so will you, I hope.

System Shock 2 is an incredible game and experience. Without a doubt the finest first person rpg ever created, easily surpassing its successors.
The game perfectly captures the grim feeling and tenseness of trying to survive aboard a duo of ships populated only by devolved humans and homicidal AI. Every choice in regards to your character has a meaningful impact.
The presentation of the story is without match in the FPS genre, and every level presents a unique challenge, aesthetic, and area to explore. Levels are smaller and more tightly knitted in SS2 than in the Bioshock series, and it serves the game far better.
Created and perfected in this game, the PDA and audio log system is used for far more than simply giving the player a mandatory code to open a door every ten minutes. Hacking is easy, but still feels plausible in the setting- and of course, many things simply require you to improve your skill before you interact with them.
Enemy design is varied and interesting. While there are a handful of shared enemies throughout most of the game, the enemy variety changes from level to level- giving each section of the Von Braun its own colorful cast of cyberpunk horrors that need dispatching.
Finally, and possibly most of all, the game is a better survival horror experience than any dedicated survival horror game. System Shock 2 understands that, what makes an encounter threatening is not how terrible the controls are, but truly how dangerous your enemy is and how desperate the player is to NOT fight that enemy. Ammo is scarce and depletable, weapons are limited and prone to malfunction, and enemies hit hard and unrelentingly.
Rest assured, unlike its descendents, System Shock 2 is a real challenge. It's frequently unforgiving, and its not for the feint of heart. System Shock 2 will test your skills and your decision making.

Dishonered 2 is the sequel to the fantastic Dishonered developed by Arkane Studios and published by Bethesda Game Studios
For lovers of lore and world-buildling like I am, Dishonored 2 is extraordinary. Before, Dishonored meant Dunwall, but the addition of Karnaca in Dishonored 2 has transformed the Isles into a genuine world, and frankly, it's immensely exciting
Karnaca is just as amazing as Dunwall. The colorful, decaying buildings and monolithic trees are a beautiful counterpoint to Dunwall's ashen, once-regal boulevards, towering whale oil refineries, and hagfish murals. Instead of hearing the deep horns of whaling ships on the Wrenhaven River, you'll listen to the insects and wildlife populating Serkonos. And taking the place of the Clocktower of Dunwall are wind tubes soaring over the city
Every mission is just as good as or better than those of Dishonored 1. The impeccable level design we've come to expect from Arkane is here, and the environments of each mission are stunningly beautiful. Aside from virtual tourism, each mission offers intriguing enemies, a variety of choices that will impact the world, and sidequests
Dishonored 2's combat is better than ever. I played Emily Kaldwin with powers on medium. Combat was always intense; enemies were skilled at parrying and working together to surround or corner me, and even encounters with bloodflies and wolfhounds were exhilarating
Dishonored 2 rivals Dishonored in lore. The books scattered across Karnaca are well-written and interesting, and the voice acting in audiologs and NPC conversations is quality work and does establish believability. However, the voice actors behind Corvo and Emily are okay, nothing special and its a shame that characters from Dishonored do not reprise their role in Dishonored 2
The eerie music, signature to the Dishonored series is here, and to be honest, there's nothing like it. It's still subtle and does take a backseat to the environmental storytelling, but I loved every bit of it
The plot is an acceptable continuation of Delilah's quest for power. It's another tale of revenge, of course, and it works well in this sequel
Arkane's Void Engine looks beautiful, but its performance has not met my expectations. My NVIDIA GTX 1080 struggled with the game's object-dense locations, however, after fiddling around with some of the settings, it ran at a steady pace with some framerate dips here and there. I can't really understand why Arkane moved away from Unreal and onto their own engine
I liked Dishonored 2. It's not perfect, and will certainly never beat Dishonored, but it's every bit as enjoyable as Dishonored, and I cannot wait to go back and play with powers. This world that Arkane has created is absolutely incredible, and I hope that the studio fleshes it out even more!

This would be an unpopular opinion, but I don't find this game enjoyable at all, which sucks, because this game has so much potential. The concept is rich and the pixelated cartoony aesthetic is appropirately funny. But the game mechanic made this game, at least until I write this review, unplayable for me. Let me explain.
First, the not-so-intuitive control. You can only shoot forward (right/left), not up or down. You can climb wall in the same manner as Megaman X did, but your shooting direction would be always to the wall, rather than against it (though this destroys the wall and creates new platform/enterance).
Second, the randomly generated player. So, you play as this Rambo-esque guy, but in the middle of the stage you will find a prisoner in a cage, whom of course you would free. This gives you extra life, but also randomly CHANGES THE CHARACTER YOU ARE PLAYING, which completely changes your main and sub-weapon, forcing you to play the game differently. You previous character has a machine gun, now he only throw dynamites, and then you got a melee type character. This lottery mechanics doesn't make any sense gameplay-wise, because this hinders you from mastery and makes the game experience inconsitent.
Third, the awkward speed of the game. For a game which gives you ludicrous amount of explosions, you would expect the game to be fast, full of shooting, throwing grenades, and jumping from platforms to platforms, like Metal Slug. But no, this game actually needs careful planning because one misstep and you would die. This takes away the delicious experience of careless shooting and blowing stuff up.
Fourth, you die easily. You die by almost anything in the most unpredictable way. Your explosions don't harm you, but the enemies' and the environment's do. And there is no way to tell which is which. Sometimes there is a crowd of enemies and one of them is a demolition man who would run to you so fast and blow himself up. You get too close and kill him, you die too. And one of the character fighting style is melee. You do the math. Sometimes when you were busy fighting the enemy and blowing things up, you got hit by a falling rock. There are cues of danger, but you only have a very small window of chance. There is lilttle to no room for escape. Thers is nothing wrong with tough difficulty in a game, but this game is hard the wrong way. It keeps punishing the player for following their intuition.
Maybe I just suck at this game, because apparently many people love it. But this game honestly doesn't met my expectations. I was hoping to play something that resembles Metal Slug in terms of intuitiveness and goofy experience, but I didn't. This game has done many things right, but the unintuitive mechanics and awkward difficulty, in my opinion, break the game.
Try it before you buy.

Full disclosure, I've played close to 5 hours of this game and it's been nothing but frustration. There's the core complaints that it feels nothing like an Elder Scrolls game. It's just another knock off MMO with an Elder Scrolls skin. You can read through a long list of negative reviews to get this info so I'll end my rehashing of that.
Instead let me tell you what my first few hours were like. First off I got the Imperial Edition of the game. NOT WORTH THE EXTRA $10. All you get is a horse. The Imperial Race does nothing special. You get a wedding ring thing you can give to a friend and grants a bonus XP, but it's barely noticeable. You can reskin an item to look "Imperial" but it's just as likely to destroy your item. More on that later.
So I decide to play a "Nightblade" because I normally like to play sneaky rogues, However all three of their skill trees are basically Warlock-like caster skills. Also most MMO's tend to give quest rewards that line up with your class, ESO doesn't do that. The only quest rewards I ever got were staves outside of a ring, heavy armor chest piece and legs, and a great sword. That's it, just staves everywhere. Also good luck finding a bow. So fine whatever I decide to don the heavy armor stuff. At first I thought it was affecting my sneaking ability, but it turns out SNEAKING DOES NOTHING in this game. Sure you can steal stuff, and try not to get caught, but the only lootable things are food crafting materials and drinks. I maybe found some base level ore but honestly I don't recall. If you're in a dungeon and sneak, all it does is drain your stamina. Enemies can still spot you and other players are just jumping around you anyways so that was pointless.
Skills and combat were boring, but that's not new, most MMO's suffer from boring combat. Worse still is the crafting which has a convoluted interface. If you try to upgrade an item, you're going to lose your item. If you research something, you lose the item. As a "bonus" for purchasing the Imperial Edition you can change items to look imperial. I finally got around to crafting a sword and dagger so that I could dual wield (remember the game only offers staves as quest rewards apparently). I enchanted my sword and when I converted the sword to imperial it disappeared. So at level 9 I no longer had any crafting materials, next to no gold, and only a dagger. Anything of value I had was destroyed trying to improve it.
So yeah that was it for me. The first few hours have been such a bad experience for me that I just don't care to play this game anymore. Worst of all, because I played more than 2 hours I can't get a refund from Steam.
This game sucks. Go play a real Elder Scrolls game if you need your fix.

When ESO came out I was put off by the buy + subscription model as I already paid for World of Warcraft, which I have thousands of hours logged with, having been playing it for about 8 years and I put any thought of purchasing ESO out of my mind. It wasn't until recently when ESO appeared in my discovery queue that I even contemplated buying the game.
I'm glad I did.
It's a very different style of MMO to WOW, not better, just different.
some comments I would make with 12 hours played:
+The combat system is excellent, it's more interactive and visceral than WOW or GuildWars 2 - you don't just click on a mob and spam keyboard buttons, waiting for cooldowns to reset - you actually have to move and fight - it's just "realistic" and feels meaningful.
+questing: there's none of this kill 20 murlocs, collect 15 slimy apples business - there's a story... events are happening... you get sent places to discover things or DO things.
+the graphics: gorgeous, immersive, atmospheric, runs smoothly on what you would perhaps call a mid range pc these days. makes you feel part of a world.
+dialogue: practically everything is voice acted and has subtitles. there's not excessive amounts of dialogue but there's sufficient to  get the point across.
+characterisation/customisability - want to be a mage with heavy armour, but focussed extensively on crafting and have a ton of HP? go for it.
I could probably say a lot more but I'm still learning a lot about the game, I'll conclude with the fact that I'm really enjoying playing it, I envisage playing it a lot more. I will definitely be buying all the DLC packs and I would consider the optional monthly subscription with basically just gives you a bunch of perks, nothing critical or game breaking that are losing out on by just buying the game (+/- the DLC packs).
Oh, I do recommend the Imperial edition of the game at the moment as you get a horse with that, saves you spending a ton of gold on one, but there is a Gold edition of the game, with the first four DLC packs due out in a couple of months so that is potentially worth waiting for, but I have no idea on pricing of that.

System Shock 2 is an incredible game and experience. Without a doubt the finest first person rpg ever created, easily surpassing its successors.
The game perfectly captures the grim feeling and tenseness of trying to survive aboard a duo of ships populated only by devolved humans and homicidal AI. Every choice in regards to your character has a meaningful impact.
The presentation of the story is without match in the FPS genre, and every level presents a unique challenge, aesthetic, and area to explore. Levels are smaller and more tightly knitted in SS2 than in the Bioshock series, and it serves the game far better.
Created and perfected in this game, the PDA and audio log system is used for far more than simply giving the player a mandatory code to open a door every ten minutes. Hacking is easy, but still feels plausible in the setting- and of course, many things simply require you to improve your skill before you interact with them.
Enemy design is varied and interesting. While there are a handful of shared enemies throughout most of the game, the enemy variety changes from level to level- giving each section of the Von Braun its own colorful cast of cyberpunk horrors that need dispatching.
Finally, and possibly most of all, the game is a better survival horror experience than any dedicated survival horror game. System Shock 2 understands that, what makes an encounter threatening is not how terrible the controls are, but truly how dangerous your enemy is and how desperate the player is to NOT fight that enemy. Ammo is scarce and depletable, weapons are limited and prone to malfunction, and enemies hit hard and unrelentingly.
Rest assured, unlike its descendents, System Shock 2 is a real challenge. It's frequently unforgiving, and its not for the feint of heart. System Shock 2 will test your skills and your decision making.

This game has a story that is very easy to follow, and it's quite rewarding to immerse yourself in it. Listening to the records that are scattered throughout the levels can reveal rewarding information, but you're never forced to listen to them. That's a major plus from me.
Fast-paced combat where you quickly have to find a way to defeat your opponents. Being resourceful is super-important (I learnt that the hard way) because every fired bullet is a wasted one. You get the amount of resources that you need to complete the game, but no more.
The only negative experience that I had was that some aspects of the game got a bit confusing. I sometimes found myself not really knowing where to go, or where "Place X" was located. Luckily there's a wiki with all the information you'll ever need. I had to google a few things, but I probably could've found out where I was supposed to go if I didn't mind running around for a few minutes.
It DOES has a slight horror-vibe to it, but don't buy this game if you're expecting an increased heart rate or nightmares. It's.. a bit creepy, but that's about it. That isn't necessarily something negative though, obviously.
The controls can be a bit weird at the beginning, but in one or two hours you'll get used to it. You can easily remap the controls and I recommend you do, because in the vanilla version you can't move backwards (atleast I couldn't).
