It's a classic.  Fantastic sci-fi horror atmosphere, good action, an impressive variety of gameplay options.  You will truly feel your character build in this hardcore experience.  Mix chemicals, hack computers and turrets, sneak around, shoot hivemind zombies, and even some psi powers.  Feels very much like a more complex survival horror game as well as a shooter/RPG hybrid.  This game was EXTREMELY innovative when it was released at the end of the 90s!  There was no such thing as a shooter/RPG especially of such quality as this.
A truly amazing story and some co-op multiplayer if you can get it working properly round off this amazing classic.
The only downside I can think of is getting stuck.  I had to use guides to get through the game.  Not to mention it is very much on the HARD side of things in every way.  It's very complicated, you don't know what to expect, and like many adventure games you WILL get stuck with no idea what to do next.  Just look up some guides ONLY if you need to to keep the immersive experience alive and you'll be fine.  Definitely play on the easiest difficulty the 1st time through.

If you have not heard of this game, and you see the date it was created and you are thinking, "There's no way I'm playing a game that's THAT old!", STOP!!!
If you have not heard of this game, then you have been in the proverbial closet of games for far too long!
I cannot express how amazing this game is, even after it's almost 20 years old now.  I first got this game long before it was available on Steam, and for me it's a classic.  For me, this game set the standard for games I like.  This was one of the first games I've ever played on PC, and it is FUN!
And this is a GREAT DEAL for it: The whole game plus its Expansions/DLC's for $5?  But enough of my rambling praise, let get into WHY it is sooo good.
First off, a bit of history: this game made it.  This was the first game to feature the concept of 3D terrain.  It set a precedent for RTS games in that regard.  To this day, even after its creators went out of business (RIP Cavedog), it still has an active community and modding fanbase.
What makes this game so fun for me is, remarkably, its simplicity.  The game is very straight-forward, so there isn't much of a learning curve to worry about.  All you need to learn are some basic tactics, base defense skills, and then watch as your enemy explodes. #NukesForDays
Skirmishes can add new dynamics/entertainment to the game.  The only point of frustration here is that when it comes to their own bases, the AI are not the brightest (but then again, they're pretty good for something from the mid-90's!).
In short, Do you enjoy watching things explode?  Do you enjoy tactically destroying or swarming your opponent?  Do you like building the figurative ultimate-base/fortress?  DO YOU LIKE WATCHING THINGS EXPLODE!?!?!?
Then get this game, Because it has aged well, and it's Awesome!!!!

There's nothing else out there quite like Dishonored. At its heart a stealth game, it has an incredible number of diferent paths and approaches. You can navigate enormous levels, find different paths towards your objectives, or actually MAKE your own path through clever use of the supernatural skills provided to you. The make-your-own path thing is nice because the levels are not exactly trivial to complete.
Teleport around, turn into a living killer shadow, turn into a rat and go through tunnels, turn into some sort of killer wasp and fly around just because you can. It's also nice to create magical doppelgangers to distract (and fight) enemies. The absolutely most rad thing you can do, though, is to stop time and feel like Dio in Jojo's Bizarre Adventure. Go watch that anime if you haven't, by the way, and come back to Dishonored after completing the third season. In short, the superpowers in this game make you feel like you're in one of your favorite japanese cartoons.

This would be an unpopular opinion, but I don't find this game enjoyable at all, which sucks, because this game has so much potential. The concept is rich and the pixelated cartoony aesthetic is appropirately funny. But the game mechanic made this game, at least until I write this review, unplayable for me. Let me explain.
First, the not-so-intuitive control. You can only shoot forward (right/left), not up or down. You can climb wall in the same manner as Megaman X did, but your shooting direction would be always to the wall, rather than against it (though this destroys the wall and creates new platform/enterance).
Second, the randomly generated player. So, you play as this Rambo-esque guy, but in the middle of the stage you will find a prisoner in a cage, whom of course you would free. This gives you extra life, but also randomly CHANGES THE CHARACTER YOU ARE PLAYING, which completely changes your main and sub-weapon, forcing you to play the game differently. You previous character has a machine gun, now he only throw dynamites, and then you got a melee type character. This lottery mechanics doesn't make any sense gameplay-wise, because this hinders you from mastery and makes the game experience inconsitent.
Third, the awkward speed of the game. For a game which gives you ludicrous amount of explosions, you would expect the game to be fast, full of shooting, throwing grenades, and jumping from platforms to platforms, like Metal Slug. But no, this game actually needs careful planning because one misstep and you would die. This takes away the delicious experience of careless shooting and blowing stuff up.
Fourth, you die easily. You die by almost anything in the most unpredictable way. Your explosions don't harm you, but the enemies' and the environment's do. And there is no way to tell which is which. Sometimes there is a crowd of enemies and one of them is a demolition man who would run to you so fast and blow himself up. You get too close and kill him, you die too. And one of the character fighting style is melee. You do the math. Sometimes when you were busy fighting the enemy and blowing things up, you got hit by a falling rock. There are cues of danger, but you only have a very small window of chance. There is lilttle to no room for escape. Thers is nothing wrong with tough difficulty in a game, but this game is hard the wrong way. It keeps punishing the player for following their intuition.
Maybe I just suck at this game, because apparently many people love it. But this game honestly doesn't met my expectations. I was hoping to play something that resembles Metal Slug in terms of intuitiveness and goofy experience, but I didn't. This game has done many things right, but the unintuitive mechanics and awkward difficulty, in my opinion, break the game.
Try it before you buy.

So, you're thinking about becoming a "Slime Rancher"? Well it isn't for the faint of heart...
...Because those adorable Slimes will make it melt! Welp, now that that's out of the way let's get into it!

In 'Slime Rancher' your main objective is to capture slimes and ranch them for their
, which are crystalized slime excrement, or in layman's terms, poop. Now while this concept may sound boring/silly (and it can be at times) it gets interesting when you mix in a whole cast of slimes and a variety of food types, meaning you'll have to try to ranch the slimes that produce the most valuable plorts while feeding them the correct types of food to get the most
!..
...But it doesnt stop there. Now what if I told you that you can combine two types of slimes to get a big one (called a 'Largo') with both of its progenitors characteristics? If this sounds like a direct upgrade you wouldn't be wrong! 'Largos' are not only bigger, they produce plorts of both their component slimes along with having both of their favourite foods and abilities/disabilities; They really are an amalgamation of their parent slimes!... However if you try to combine a Largo with any other slime... You know what, I'll let you figure that one out on your own! But this is not to say that this is the only challenge of ranching 'Largos', as some slimes can already be dangerous to ranch as babies, but just imagine what happens when you combine a explosive slime with a radiocative slime! Taking all of this into account I think that the 'Largos' are one of the main selling points of the game.
As you progress you will start unlocking equipment for purchase at the shop to help you ranch your slimes, things such as extra health, energy, or even a Jetpack! A lot of the game will be focused on upgrading the ranch or your character to get the most profit from your slimes, but if making the rarest and most beautiful slimes is what you strive for (like me) then you can create somewhat of a Zoo, or even if you want to make a vegetable farm for some reason then you absolutely can! The game advances at whatever pace you're ready to advance at, so take your time and smell the plorts!
I give it a 9/10, the cuteness hooked me in and the gameplay is what kept me hooked! Spent way too many hours getting sidetracked because it has so much to offer! My first impressions world I went to collect something like fruit or vegetables and ended up exploring the 'Dry Reef' (starting area of the 'Far Far Range') for 2 hours or so!... Needless to say my slimes were very hungry... Speaking of that, I should go feed them.
This game is a better pain reliever than Ibuprofen.

Out of all the games I own, this is the one to go to when I feel in need of cheering up. The cheery happy bouncy colorful slimes are adorable, the game keeps getting better, and more keeps getting added in. There are far more serious games in other places, this one is just plain fun, and I reccomend it.

Black Mesa is amazing everything is an upgrade obviously, the visuals and sound are a great leap forward from 1998's Half-Life, which over the years has slowly turned from charmingly ugly to mostly just ugly, except for the most nostalgic of gamers. t the same time, the Source Engine itself is getting pretty darn creaky these days, so Black Mesa doesn't look particularly great alongside current releases, especially the models and animations. Other limits of the Source Engine come quickly into focus as well, mostly in the frequent loading points between maps. The famous tram ride that begins the game in is broken into three parts due to pauses for loading, and in some of the faster paced portions of the game, loading screens crop up so quickly it becomes a little irritating. Source's physics, meanwhile, aren't really exploited for much besides a few new puzzles involving carrying a plug to a socket or reattaching a valve wheel.
The main issues with Black Mesa are the issues that come along with Half-Life itself: the over-reliance on platforming puzzles, vent crawling, ladder climbing, and laser beam hopping. Too much time hunting through a massive complex looking for that one door that will actually open or that one switch that can actually be flipped. Too many similar fights against the same small handful of enemy types. Too many long, slow trips down to some water-filled, body-strewn section of the complex to push a button that starts a generator or pump or giant fan, followed by the long slog back through enemies who suddenly teleport into your path. Too many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ barnacle monsters that will never, ever actually kill you but simply force you to sigh and fire a shotgun blast at the ceiling when they snare you.
Never fear, though. In addition to the chaff, Black Mesa rejuvenates the best parts of Half-Life. The wonderful real-time scripted sequences, in which hapless scientists and guards are dragged off into vents, yanked through ceiling tiles, exploded, shredded, burned, and chomped, which still prove entertaining and serve as warnings as to what dangers lie ahead. Those moments when you fight your way to the surface, only to find it crawling with soldiers who are not there to rescue you but permanently silence you, and you're forced back into a new section of the sprawling subterranean complex. The wonderful chaos when soldiers and aliens encounter each other, and for once you're not the only target in the room. The way your name begins to carry heft and meaning as you progress, as awestruck lab techs and increasingly frustrated grunts learn of your exploits ahead of your arrival.
All in all im in love with Half Life all over again this is amazing and worth the money

Whilst there are a few things where I still prefer the original (i.e. the marines' voice acting, the snarks sounds...), in many cases this game, that started as a mod, turned into a full blown improvement of its master. The tightened difficulty, the reworked areas, and the the absolutely stunning graphics make for a familiar, yet surprising experience of an absolute classic. And with some some minor tweaks in the options it even preserves the benefits of the old-school gameplay that HL1 offered. In short terms: Black Mesa is mostly Half-Life as it should always have been.

Great and educational game! Very simple but very fun: it plays a lot more like a "hands-off" strategy game than something like Civilization. You have a number of points that can be spent on using your trusty "Owlbot" to interact directly with a biome of your choice (currently desert, grassland, or rainforest). Adding plants, animals, and detritivores all consume these points. Successfully maintaining your biome unlocks a second currency that allows you to purchase additional plants and creatures to increase your biodiversity (there are NO real money transactions). The goal is to introduce plants and animals that are all in balance and can eventually maintain your ecosystem without your involvement at all.
All in all, I highly recommend it if you're a bit of an amateur naturalist such as myself. The graphics are nothing spectacular but fun and functional, and I really enjoy the gameplay, though someone looking for a more action orientated experience will be quickly bored. The photo mode is also a nice addition.
TL;DR - For the patient crowd interested in biology and ecosystem studies.

After the quite frankly appalling Alien: Colonial Marines I had little hope for this sci-fi horror franchise. However, there is a beacon of light in the dark tunnels of the Nistromo. Alien: Isolation is a survival horror game from Creative Assembly released in 2014. That’s right folks! The people who bought you the Total War franchise now brings you one of the best Alien games of all time. I’m still salivating over the faithful recreation of Ridley Scott’s Sci-Horror and the new and fantastic cannon it brings to the table. Let’s not get to far ahead of ourselves, however, as this is by no means a perfect survival horror game...

-Stunning visuals; this custom engine has produced some of the best graphical fidelity of PC gaming. Fantastic lighting, character animation, textures and particle effects bring the world to life.
-Surprisingly good story; it stays faithful to Alien law whilst providing new characters and cannon that expands Ridley Scott’s original universe.
-Perfect art style; the 1980s futuristic recreation is a labour of love. The attention to detail and entirely accurate environments makes you feel like you've walked onto the set of Alien. The motion tracker itself is a work of art.
-A good horror; this game actually builds suspense and atmosphere with perfect sound and visual cues putting you on edge the whole way through (this certainly isn't no Evil Within).
-Amazing sound design; the Aliens footsteps, the 1980s computer beeps and the pitch perfect score builds suspense whilst remaining faithful to the film.
-Fantastic port; has great performance on all systems, good options including support for Oculus! (If you've got the balls) and responsive control system.
-Good (and fair) DLC; you can actually play the original film! :D That’s almost as good as the game itself and its priced fairly to.
-Smart AI (see negatives also); the alien stalks well and the Working Joes flank and so on. Its not perfect but I could definitely tell the Alien was learning as the game progressed.
-Good world; exceedingly interesting to explore with audio logs and computers littered about the station to get back story when and where you want it.
-Nice end game; the game rounds up pretty nicely and there are time trials and such to do after you've done.
-Inconsistent AI; The Alien and Working Joes work for the most part. They occasionally glitch or spot you when you feel they shouldn't. It’s the human AI that’s the kicker. Glitches, unfair and just down right annoying.
-Game Length; I don’t usually complain about this but the gameplay is quite repetitive. I felt as though it could have be wrapped up more quickly and thus it would have been more satisfying.
-UI; the crafting menu is very clunky. Not to mention the lack of stealth feedback when sneaking around, making damn near impossible to know when you’re seen.
-Punishing save system; there are save points but there few and hard between. Considering how punishing this game can be and its repetitive nature, it would be nice to have some auto/quick save functionality.
If you like horror or Sci-fi I’m sure you’ll love the world and suspense. If you’re a fan of the Alien universe I’d say this game is a must have. It expands on the law so eloquently and is a perfect spoon full of sugar to take with that bitter pill "Alien: Colonial Marines". Its suspense and its world are some of the best I've seen with the latest cutting edge graphic and sound technology. The AI and punishing save system may drive you slightly crazy by the end but if you can drag through this you'll love every second of this scary, tense, Sci-Fi master piece.

Also know as the best Deus Ex Game Ever Made™
Okay, but seriously: people have always overreacted to sequels that try and change the formula, and Invisible War is no exception. People always think of the original Deus Ex as a flawless masterpiece, and not a buggy mess with terrible graphics and a lot of objectively poor game design decisions. The parts of the game design, atmosphere, and story that worked all created something special: but most people remember it for the game it was trying to be, not the game it was.
Consider this situation: a trained super-agent with nano-augmentation technology can't fire a pistol at someone standing 10 metres in front of them. This 'logic' makes sense in an RPG, but not in a game so predominantly in the first person shooter genre. And for a game whose central premise is augmentations, because of it's RPG-style redundancy (i.e. the aqualung augmentation is pointless when you have rebreathers), it makes them basically pointless. The game can be easily beaten on realistic without them, despite them being the crux of the story and why you - JC Denton - are a super agent able to take on squads of people and save the world.
To it's credit this is what Invisible War tried to improve: guns are always effective to improve the combat, which makes shooting people more reasonable. No longer can you empty an asasult rifle clip at someone standing in front of you and miss almost every single shot. The weird and oft-contradictory mixture of skills and augmentations are now just 'augmentations', making them more effective and critical to the game, which makes more sense in both design and narrative. These were all positive steps to streamline the game's core design philosophy, not (only) 'consolisation'. Instead of expressing your character building through systems, you express it through the way you play and decisions you take in the story. Though the developers clearly went too far in some respects; namely, the much derided Universal Ammo. That was just idiotic.
The hardcore PC Gaming clique, especially in the early days of consoles, is well known for it's open-mindedness and reacted to this
by incessently complaining about the consolisation of a beloved classic and refusing to consider the game on it's own merits. While I agree that this is not the great game Deus Ex was, or that a sequel could have been given different design decisions - the hyperbole that this is 'unplayable' is just ridiculous. Invisible War is a great game, on it's own merits and as a sequel, and stands far above what most other games were doing at the time.
Bizzarely, most of the derision in these steam reviews can be applied to the original Deus Ex as well. A linear story with no consequences? You could literally shoot up a bar and kill every civilian you come across in Deus Ex, and UNATCO won't fire you until the story
you to defect. Also, you can make no meaningful impact on the game's story or missions until the last 20 minutes. Invisible War actually fixes this, by having a greater range of optional missions and different objectives for the primary missions, depending on which faction you're trying to align with. It's not perfect, but it was a good direction to go.
Rant aside, if you're a fan of the series and the original, you should play this. It's a neat story set in the Deus Ex universe with similar gameplay mechanics; everything's a little dumbed down, but it's has the same soul. It's definitely not the fantastic sequel Human Revolution was
, but at least it's better than the goddamn mobile game.

Uh. I want to like this game so much. Dues Ex and Halo are my 2 favorite franchies of all time. I beat the first Dues Ex countless times. I beat Human Revolution on ps3, 360, then PC. I have 100+ hours in Mankind Divided, beat the game in perma death mode, masetered Breach mode, crushed all the crappy short DLC. I beat the silly mobile game, The Fall, managed to shove 6 hours into a 2 hour game. Read the Dues Ex books. I LOVE Dues Ex, and I just can't play this game. Its bad, its not Duex Ex. Its a console game in the worst way when console games and PC games stood miles apart and the limitations that seperated them were as wide as the Grand Canyon.
Edit: and I would like to add that I played this game through back on consoles so 1 hour is not indictive of my entire Invisble War experience.

Back when Deus Ex came out, PC games had a reputation for being more complex than their Console bretheren. PC titles tended to be more complex, have a ton of hotkeys that just couldn't be fit onto a controller, and were larger in just about every way owing to the same factors that make PC's technologically superior to consoles to this day. More RAM, more HD space, better graphical capabilities, etc etc etc.
Well into the 2000's this reality was still prevalent, and no game better encapsulates this contrast and mentality turned reality than Deus Ex: Invisible War-a title made with consoles in mind first and foremost.
Whereas Deus Ex had massive maps that are still respectable to this day. Invisible War entraps you in confined rooms and locales seperated by doorways and gates that lead to loading times. Necessary as the XBox hardware wouldn't allow massive areas. Invisible War attempts to create the illusion of being outside when not in a building, but you might as well be since everything is still corridors and rather tight spaces. The only difference is that there is now a skybox (sometimes) when 'outside', but that skybox is hidden by conveniently large buildings that make the difference between being outdoors and indoors a question of how high the ceiling is and if the ceiling is a solid ceiling or a skybox.
I can't fault this too much as it *is* a game of its time, but it's worth noting since Deus Ex 1 didn't suffer these limitations and it's 5 years older than this title at the point of release. It's taking a step back. To its defense its not a massive deal or anything that would deter the creation of just as engaging a game as the first.
But that's where this title fails again.
Continuing its console syndrome, this game eliminates a vital aspect of the first game: the RPG elements. You don't receive differing damage on your various appendages. You don't have as robust or intriguing an upgrade system to your biomodifications. Gone are the various abilities you could level up from the previous game (proficiency in weapons, heavy weapons, computers, etc). There are no more computers where you can read characters' emails that build the lore and world. You don't hack anymore, you don't talk to as many NPC's and engage in the various side quests that have you building lore and the world. I do not understand why they engaged the subtraction game in aspects that made the first title unique. That was basically all of Deus Ex there.
If they focused on the gunplay and enhanced it, that would be fine, but it's the same as before. Meaning, below average, only now all weapons share the same ammo pool which is just confusing. There is no reason to carry anything past a sniper rifle and perhaps an SMG or shotgun since all weapons have the same ammo pool. It completely defeats the purpose of carrying variety, its just....I don't understand it. I'll have to google the logic behind that.
What of the story and side missions? Well, just as with everything else this area has also been downsized....severely. God has it been downsized. As stated, the sidequests and various characters to talk to are gone for the most part. There just isn't as much there, and what is there is typically rather linear. Wheras in Deus Ex you would engage in quests and be able to maneuver the ordeal and side with parties, here you just get quests and do them. Very few of them require siding with any party. It's just quests to do. There are no repricussions, or rewards for that matter.
Surprisingly, the story isn't *that* bad. Deus Ex had three endings, and here we have a sort of mixture of all three. It actually makes sense, and is rather basic. So basic that I can't really poke too many holes in it, only to say that for a franchise of this caliber this is really....tiny. Deus Ex built on the underlying concepts of the plot through character conversations, books, and logs. You'd delve into the nature of Democracy, Governance, and Free Will which underlied a game about massive institutions lead by a few governing the many. It was a philisophical work.
Invisible War, on the other hand, gives you character dialogue and....that's it. Rather short discussions with no explenation or delving into the underlying concepts. It's rather sad; when they got rid of the RPG elements they *really* did a disservice to the plot. It's as if they had a general outline for the plot....and shipped the game out like that.
And the plot is alright. Some character motives and elements are just left at simple, "it is what it is" explanations. *Slight spoiler warning* the Illuminati is involved once more, and when told that they control factions, including oppositional factions, not much is said as to how contradictory and braindead that is other than, "yeah, its weird right? You gotta build and control" or some other such nonsense. It's a GLARING PLOTHOLE THAT REQUIRED A LOT MORE EXPLENATION
A LOT MORE.
But you know, for convenience sake and to have you follow a linear route lets just say the factions were one in the same. It's such a cop out.
Speaking of which, its difficult to take this game seriously when you can kill faction leaders and...just really disgrace a faction but the ability to still partner with it is available and they merely chastise you over the radio for not following orders. "Well, anyway, please do follow this next order...."
I understand its so that the player can still make his choice in endings, and its much appreaciated. At the same time, it deligitimizes your plot points; you can allow options in endings without disrespecting your world and characters within it.
All in all I'd say its rather mediocre. Wiki the plot or something; its actually decent even if barebones. It follows logically from the first title and makes some familiar faces into villains if you view their actions as villanous...which you totally can. Otherwise, as its own title it really is bad. Only the most dedicated of Deus Ex fans will play it, and only for the plot...and this is assuming they don't just retcon the hell out of this.

System Shock, the original, is a game that has forever impacted the gaming landscape whether or not you have played the original as its influences have expanded beyond its spiritual successor, Bio Shock, or other games that have taken its core ideas of immersive sims such as the Deus Ex games as well as PREY (2017). Exploration-based storytelling through interactable objects such as emails, audio-logs and mixed in with heavy RPG elements that impact the player’s navigation through non-linear environments with multiple entrances and exits are all the cornerstone of System Shock, and unlike the original System Shock 2 is still as playable today as it was when first released—if you are willing to put up with a mechanically dated, though functional, system.
In my previous review of the original System Shock, my main issue was not that it didn’t hold up to modern standards as those aspects remained timeless but that the enemy behaviors/difficulty and narrative had issues as a result of designing its gameplay around its convoluted interface. These aspects are the main sources of improvement of System Shock 2 as it’s not so much of a sequel as it is a reboot with all the same core ideas.
For starters, the interface is much less complicated by making an entire FPS with an inventory button that doesn’t pause the game but allows players to use items, repair weapons or exchange different sorts of ammo that is more intuitive than Ultima Underworld-inspired periscope view with tabs of the original. This design has largely stayed the same for these types of games as PREY (2017) incorporates the same general idea with a pause menu instead/quick-wheel rather than an overlay. As a result, the gameplay holds up to standardized controls which is a godsend because the game is difficult.
Unlike contemporary games that have taken the spliced the DNA of System Shock this game is heavily influenced by its RPG mechanics on the core gunplay that will make for an experience that becomes better the more player is familiar with it. While cyber-modules are plentiful as well as the resources in every level, the scarcity between levels as well as the high damage outputs keeps players from ever feeling safe or over-powered unless they know how to create builds to make them feel godlike.Maintence of the player's tools is one additional means of balancing out the destructive capabilities of the player while also adding tension that a gun may jam or degrade with every confrontation that could be avoided. All these aspects of fighting and of evading are core to what makes System Shock 2 the defintive immersive sim experience.
This is similar to Deus Ex, yet even the worthless skills like Research yield far more usefulness for the player than the useless skills like Swimming. The new additions of ammo types as well as implant-boosts helps make an RPG/FPS that isn’t about looting or the numbers themselves but how the player uses their tools to create their own solutions in a given situation.
Tell me if you have heard this one before: The player wakes up in the aftermath of a mass catastrophe in an isolated area full of madmen and security threats while also following multiple voices telling the player where to go and what to do along with confronting the player with extremes of an ideology that has led to the devastation in the first place. This set-up has been codified into these types of immersive sim experiences that always use the 0451-callback reference as a reference to the original System Shock, yet this standard was solidified more so in the second game than the first.
In the original, the Hacker was the avatar of the player as they navigated Citadel station against the taunts of an unshackled AI, SHODAN, who modified the technology to secure the station as her home as well as create cybernetic minions to do her bidding. The TriOptimum corporation was simply a research megacorporation that while nefarious in their influence of Earth’s government never truly made them into an opposing viewpoint on the benefits of AI whereas SHODAN was an extreme with no remorse. The result was a storyline that favored one side greatly as the other side was monstrously malicious to the player.
System Shock 2 improves upon this issue by putting the player play a soldier in the power-grab between two destructive influences on the experimental vessel, Von Braun, between the returning egotistical AI within the mainframe of the ship and the influence of an alien threat with mental omnipresence referred to as The Many. The way in which both sides are presented are one as a  technologically based egocentric tyrant and the other as a hive-mind collective consciousness that seeks the destruction of the individual for the will of the many. Both threats retain their influence on the player by having total control of the station as they seek the destruction of one another with the player serving as the ethical, human intermediator of their demise. The result creates an uneasy alliance between the enemy of the player with a far greater threat much like how the Vox Populi are as bad, if not worse, than Father Comstock, and the experience of that truce creates some basis of understanding with an opposing viewpoint as the player plays as a cyborg; one part man, another machine.
The narrative within System Shock 2 is far richer as a result of this minor, important change even though the narrative tricks used from the first game (audio/email logs, environmental storytelling, etc.) are retained in their entirety in the sequel with a little more polish. What wasn’t improved, and perhaps is more jarring here than the original because of its darker themes, is the ending as it is mechanically and narratively at odds with the whole game. In System Shock 2, the cybernetic deconstruction of reality leads to a final showdown with SHODAN that is only difficult because of how long of a fight it can be for players who do not expect it. This issue with the finale is not limited to the Shock games but also with immersive sims as a whole as the only games where the ending felt tailored to the gameplay was Deus Ex: Mankind Divided and PREY (2017).
Similar to how Deus Ex’s themes remain timeless such as individual liberties at the risk of ever encroaching national security concerns promoted by the advancement of technology, System Shock 2’s themes will make the game ever more relevant to modern times.  Not only is the conflict of individualism versus collectivism an eons old human struggle but the advancement of our own technology questions the responsibilities as well as the barriers of how far humanity will have to go to prevent our extinction by our own artificial creations or by our discoveries into the unknown of the universe that can only be stopped through our technology. What do we gain? What do we lose in the process? In the aftermath, will we remain human, cybernetic creations manipulated by one construct’s will or the domination of an alien organism that controls our thoughts to rob our own identity?
Whereas Deus Ex explores its questions in the limited scope of a mass conspiracy with as many philosophical quandaries as technological problems, the questions for System Shock 2 are not something the game ever attempts to provide all the answers. Instead, players are placed into these conflicts at the tipping point where humanity must decide how it must survive, and it’s through the player’s own resolve that he or she can surmount the menacing loneliness of space surrounded by as many machinations of life as of death, taunted by their voices seeking to rob the player of his or her humanity through the subjugation of the flesh or through the domination of our technology.

It's in hundreds of top ten lists for a reason.
"There’s an incredible amount of complexity... The full RPG system, the modifiable, configurable weapons, the differing ammo types (and the accompanying differing vulnerabilities of monsters), the psionic disciplines, the research component, the character growth, the traits and every other of the dozens of systems in Shock 2 had to be built, balanced and tuned... upon the core first person gameplay."
-- Quoting from the game manual found amongst the installation files.
System Shock 2 features an immense array of FPS/RPG mechanics, enough to mock modern FPS/RPGs (even the platforming!). Rather than run through them all, I'll let you discover them as you play.
As you'd expect, you can invest in a few skills to match your play style, and accordingly be uniquely rewarded; this allows for superb replayability.
The story/lore is fascinating, a continuous discovery that unfolds right to the end.
Though old, the horror aspect is still present and powerful, with tangible atmosphere and audio design of highest quality, sporting exceptional voice acting, too.
Furthermore, this is no linear game. The spacial progress can be considered fairly basic, but the variety and complexity of objectives is substantial. Mindlessly running and gunning may get you the distance, but won't find you any hidden codes, remove the radiation, or conduct research into alien biology. The combat may be the core of the game, but your smart thinking is what's going to see the ship fixed and the enemy infestation uprooted.
The developers had incredible foresight to make System Shock 2 moddable and put in a cooperative multiplayer option, among other things.
The variety of mechanics, balance between them, the satisfying FPS centre, and the immersive setting all come together to form a unique and incredible game experience, making System Shock 2 stand out from the time of its release to the present - enough to rival Half-Life, Deus Ex, and even modern Fallout games. Personally, System Shock 2 is my favourite of all those.
The gameplay fits the usual 1999 level of challenge, and reward. The initial learning curve can be rather difficult. I recommend you take it slow, refer to the map and objectives ("notes") often, and perhaps even immerse yourself and pretend it is a real experience. If you need more help, there's a perfect, (mostly) spoiler-free guide

This game is meant for people who are willing to come back a couple times a day and check on their biodome(s). If you don't like that, this game may be tough to find fun. However, if you are willing to check back every so often, the game has incredibly well designed ecosystem development and many options for flora and fauna for each of its (currently?) three biome types (in vanilla). The gameplay is mostly placing animals and plants in a custom ecosystem you create from scratch. The longer it works and the more diverse you make your miniature worlds, the more the game rewards you with coins, which let you unlock new animals, plants, etc. Be careful though, as fast breeding grasses and rabbits can overrun the entire environmental plan you thought you had set up, or the extra foxes you put in ate all the herbivores and starved. The only constant is that no plan ever works out perfectly, as the interactions always tend to surprise you each time you log back in. The camera feature gives you extra oppertunities to do some non-ecological work, such as taking snapshots of a bunch of baby hares roaming around in your custom made desert bush garden, or peeking at a sleeping turtle.
The devs are wonderful, active, and more friendly than every other early access devs I have ever talked to. A simple email or a forum post will get their attention, and they will contact you in a timely manner with support and/or response to your feedback.
At this time, however, there are certain things that I found midly troublesome (not to say they ruined my experience, but these small things could greatly improve my gameplay). Listed below:
-clipping (animals can go inside of large trees, making it hard to spot them as well as slightly damaging the realism the game is going for)
-swimming for animals. Not just for realism (which would be amazing in its own right), but because like the tree clipping, it can be hard to spot animals "buried" beneah water. Again with both issues (this and tree clipping) it isn't a huge concern, due to the fact that the need to see individual animals is somewhat small, but it would be nice to keep track of certain smaller populations (such as bobcats or foxes) on a more precise and individual scale without having to look inside of large trees (such as kapok).
-not being able to pan the strategic camera (the top down view) while trying to place animals or plants (this is now possible! thanks againt devs!)
-not being able to see which population I'm being alerted about (a snap to function would be amazing)
Again, this game is lots of fun and functions as a good creative outlet, and for 7$ it is easily worth the cost. Please support these wonderful devs!
(please remember this review was written in later summer of 2016, and despite my efforts to update this review I will not always be on top of any fixes that the dev team makes)

This game surprised me. I expected a kind of boring edutainment game about ecology and instead got a fun and fascinating look into how biomes work and have learned a surprising amount. It's really a lot of fun and dragged me in almost immediately. I'm constantly wondering how my biome is doing and if I put down too many things the last time I was on. The devs also are very active on the forums and open to feedback and suggestions.
This isn't really a game that you sit down for hours and hours and play. You can and I've seen myself playing longer than expected but it doesn't really seem intended for that sort of play. Time passes while you don't play and so you hop on to check on how things are going and if your latest additions screwed up your balance or not. The best thing is that you can adjust the maximum amount of time that will pass while you're away. It defaults to a week but you can set it to a month or 3 months. I've found that 3 months actually isn't that bad but it's a great setting that more games that do this kind of thing need to implement. It's nice to know that my going to sleep/work won't cause a year+ of in game time to pass.
I highly recommend this huge surprise of a game if you want something that is engaging and completely open ended. It's difficult but that's really just because biomes are complicated and it's a lot of trial and error. Definitely expect to restart your biomes a couple times simply because your experiment failed. It's a fantastic game and it's way more engaging and interesting than I expected.
I will definitely buy any and all DLC that might be released (The devs haven't said anything about DLC, just me hoping/speculating).

The release of Rome Total War 2 was one of the worst in gaming history (In my experience only Assassin's Creed Unitys launch was worse), creating a huge outrage even outside the Total War community (and also some pretty funny memes).
The questions is: Is it playable after more than a year? Yes it is. Is it as good as its predecessors? Sadly, no. And while I can recommend it to you, if you're looking for a good casual strategy game, its still a huge step backwards for the franchise, And like after playing Mass Effect 3, I am afraid of what the developers are doing to my beloved franchises next.
So while it has its good aspects, I will focus mainly on the flaws of this game in this review.
The Total War series is my favorite strategy franchise, and maybe my favorite game series in general. You've got a turn based campaign map where you capture and hold cities, build up diplomatic relationships with other nations, recruit armies and so on and so forth. When it comes to battle, the game changes from the campaign to a randomly created battlefield map, where you command your troops in real time. Total War connects the "just-one-more-turn" mentality from games like Civilization with intense real time battles like in World in Conflict for instance. This formula works every time, regardless of the given time period or setting. Creative Assembly added features until 2009s Empire Total War, and with Shogun 2 they've streamlined it back to bare bones to get rid of the problematic AI, which was all over the place in Empire and Napoleon.
Rome 2 promised us an overhaul of the traditional Total War concept while bringing back the diversity of factions (Shoguns Clans all had the same units due to the Japan setting) and adding new features. They have lied to us. I still remember the moment when my legions first encountered the Scythians and their mounted archers in Rome 1. What I'm trying to say is that you had to adapt your tactics to the foe you were fighting back in the day. Now, although the skins and names are different, every nation still seems to have nearly the same roster. Barbarian swordmasters really play like a legionary cohort, they even throw javelins like them.
The biggest two problems I have with Rome 2 is that its a) even more streamlined than Shogun 2 (they've even cut out building and upgrading streets. What the ♥♥♥♥, so you're telling me that some barbarians could march as fast through their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ woods as the mighty legions of rome on their high-tech streets?) And b), the features they've added don't work.
The best example for this problem is how they've "improved" armies and recruitment. Previously you've recruited your troops in your cities and gathered them to army stacks. Now you have a limited amount of stacks, which gets increased by your "empire level" (so even if I have the economic capability to recruit more troops, I can't do that, because my "empire level" isn't high enough? What the flying ♥♥♥♥). Those serve under a general, who materializes the troops out of thin air apparently, as  long as he is marching through friendly territory. And while the RPG elements they've added to the stacks are interesting, not being able to move single or small amounts of units independent from a general breaks your strategy big time. If you want to capture a small city, you used to be able to dispatch a small force to get the job done. Here you have to use one of your huge, bigass Armies to conquer a tiny village. Or imagine a rebellion at the heart of you empire, while all your armies are fighting thousands of miles away. Normally you would recruit some units near the troublespot and eradicate the filthy rebel scum, but now you have to remove one of your armies from the front, leaving your cities near the enemy undefended cause once again, you can't recruit units in your cities, just to march all the way back and crush the rebellion. And if you want to exchange the units beetween your stacks, you have to move your entire stack to the other just to exchange one unit. I don't have to explain why this can be infuriating at times.
Now lets get to the building and campaign map. Cities are now organized in provinces with 2 to 4 of them. This really helps to overwatch and upgrade entire regions but also comes with some problems. Those are the culture spread (Syracuse for instance has a cultural impact on southern Italy because they're in a province together) that creates public discontent, and the public discontent after capturing a city in a province. For instance the people of rome get angry at you when you take a city in northern italy, because they're in the same province. Why does this happen? Why does local discontent have to have an impact on your already captured and secured cities and lead them to rebel? What the ♥♥♥♥ CA.
I could ramble on about the hundreds of minor issues and odd design decisions of Rome 2, like the train wreck politic system, the faceless randomly generated Generals that are just weak compared to the family tree system of Medieval 2 for instance, which created interesting characters that you really cared about. I could talk about how you can't even see the fight animations because battles are huge moshpits with no order or discipline whatsoever (although CA managed to patch the worst parts of these) or how it just fails to get you immersed in the time period. Or that the repeated one-line general "speeches" are a shameful display compared to the long, randomly created ones of the previous games.
But what breaks the game at the end of the day is the bare bones A.I. Total War is a single player game, period. And when you ♥♥♥♥ up the A.I. in a game that is designed for daylong sessions in front of your computer, you're doing something wrong. The A.I. was never CAs strenght, I admit that, but compared to the budget RTW2 had, the A.I. was never this incompetent. And while they fixed the worst insults displayed in the real time battles, it still seems you're playing against a brain dead infant on the campaign map. Giant enemy forces ignoring defenseless cities (garrisons are a joke), the A.I. randomly trying to form contracts with you even if they are completely useless, almost never declaring war on you (except you're playing the Seleucids, where its you against every eastern faction) and army stacks made half out of peasant slingers. And when you want to auto resolve those battles because 2000 slingers aren't worth your time, guess what. the auto resolve system is completely ♥♥♥♥ed, so you either lose or get unacceptable losses with your heavily armored legionaries accompanied by elite cavalry.
But you've gotta give it to Creative Assembly. They know they've ♥♥♥♥ed up and they've patched big times. And while everything I've mentioned is still an issue (bad design decisions can't get patched), this is pure gold compared to the release state of Rome 2. With the release of the emperor edition, this game became something worth your money.
But at the end of the day, looking at all the flaws this game has, you're better off with Medieval 2 or Rome 1.
Speaking of money, my biggest concern about Creative Assembly isn't Rome Total War 2 anymore, its their DLC ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. We're getting stoned to death by unit packs, faction DLC and additional mini campaigns, which are all right to ask money for, but please dont display a ♥♥♥♥ing button in the main menu that tells me to pay 15 ♥♥♥♥ING BUCKS for three uninteresting factions from the black sea. Again, the units are all reskins of the same 10 or so unit types, so why even bother when there are mods that make ALL FACTIONS AVAILABLE. I understand you don't have to buy these DLCs, but they lack quality and are way way overpriced. If they released a single, huge faction pack with 40 or 50 completely new units for 30 bugs, I would buy it. But the bombardment with lazy♥♥♥♥♥pay 15-bucks-for-three-more-dull-factions "expansions" is unacceptable and infuriating.

Tyto Ecology has some room to grow, as an education game it does its job very well. My children love the game and have both managed to create seemingly stable eco systems (They don't play on hard like I do and so far I've had trouble creating a truely stable eco system so at least the game is challenging for parents and children) I would like to see the creatures interact, like a coyote taking down a rabbit or cougar taking down a mule deer for the most part animals just seem to ignore each other.
From a gameplay point of view the game does not offer enough information that actually applies to the game. The biodex offers real life information and often includes items that aren't even in the game as predator/prey relationships. I would love to see a biodex that actually comes out and says exactly what each animal eats and gives more game realted detail as far as how they impact the game world . So far we're left guessing exactly how many of each thing we need, will this animal eat this plant and if so will it actually like it? It seems like when I place down anything it literally interacts with everything else but that doesn't really tell me HOW they interact, is it going to eat it or is it going to hide in it or is it going to trip over it what is going on? How does a tourtise interact with a coyote are they going to fight or what? This has lead to me just putting down everything plant and animal wise and seeing what survives in a survival of the fittest sort of scenario which I guess is true to life : P
One other thing I'd really love to see is some sort of history as to what happened while you were away 3 months. I come back and all animals in my biome are dead other than insects it would be nice to see how or why certain creatures are no longer around. I'm left guesing, did the carinvores eat all the herbivores then starve or did the herbivores survive then over populate and starve death or what? There are no bodies, no evidence, but surely a research assistant was around watching this happen can't I get some kind of report on what is going on while I'm away?
I think the game has a lot of room to improve and I hope the developers continue to do so, as it stands it seems more like an early access game than a full title. Perhaps developers can open up the game to modding and allow them to be hosted on Steam, then players can add their own animals and improve sound effects and graphics, works for Skyrim why not Tyto Ecology  ? :  )

At first I hated the unlock system, because I just wanted to play around with all the things. Coming back the next day to 100 coins per dome (a massive amount) and a completly dead animal population I am very happy with the unlock system, as it lets you learn the basics of how an ecosystem runs before creating anything massive. Hopefully I have adjusted and learned from my mistakes. The only improvments I would ask for in this game is even more biomes, and animal/plant choices (some actuall species instead of common names such as frog would be nice). The base game is good enough though that I would happy to have these options either as mods or payed DLC.

1200 hours... I think I've spent enough time in the world to give my thoughts.
I am NOT a hardcore player. I don't want to be max level. Min/Maxing takes a backseat to fun. I don't enjoy rushing through content. I want a living, breathing world that makes me feel like I am a part of it. To it's credit, Elder Scrolls Online does this very well. The world is immersive, interactive and even slightly dynamic (as in it changes in response to player action). ESO also boasts one of the most robust and diverse roleplay scene I have ever come across in a video game to date.
The hardest part about the game is the first few hours, when you are thrown into the world with only a minimal tutorial to guide you along. I didn't REALLY figure out how to pick locks in the world until I was well past the 30th level on my first character... and I didn't explore crafting until even after that... but I wasn't at a loss for it. There always seems to be just a little bit more to explore and do on your first character, so much so that it can seem almost overwhelming, as at first glance it looks like a pretty simple game. Therein is the beauty of the game, in my opinion. It has depth without being unnecessarily complex or obtuse. It balances those factors very well, for my tastes, and most people I introduce the game to find the combat enjoyable and the world fun to run around in, if nothing else.
The combat is gonna be the thing that either makes or breaks a game, and ESO has hit the balance just right. The action elements are there, but not so twitchy that I feel like I need to be a professional gamer to handle em, the Min/Max elements are there for people who wanna try and come up with "the perfect build" and all of it can be tossed out the window if you want to build a crafting character that can't be much more than middling in a fight.
Leveling is handled slightly differently than in most other games. The main source of EXP won't come from killing monsters outright, but doing quests and exploring. It's not uncommon for me to gain a full pair of levels in a new area, simply by exploring and gathering resources I find while doing it. Of course, there are "world bosses" that spawn at designated locations, and downing them will net you a decent EXP reward and some good loot. What I am saying here only begins to scratch the surface of what the game offers, but either this sounds interesting or dull, depending on the type of gamer you are.
What the game does not do is spawn a lit path for you to follow. Of course, you are free to zoom from quest to quest without stopping, but that misses the point of the world. This is a game for meandering. This is a game that WANTS you to ask, "Huh, what's over there?" only to find some previously unknown quest line or even just a chest you would have missed had you not been willing to wander. If you play for the destination, another game would likely suit you better... but if you play for the journey, ESO is a very decent game and one I recommend more than just about any MMORPG out there to date. It's gettin a little old, but it's still got lots of years left in it!

Warning: I'm about to say a bad thing about a video game. If you are not personally a video game, consider not taking it personally, you weird brand-obsessed jackals.
Nostalgia is clouding a lot of peoples' judgments, but there's some things that not even that can excuse. Half-Life was important and groundbreaking but a lot has changed since its debut and we've come to expect better than its meandering backtracking and strangely unsatisfying gunplay.
Meanwhile, playing the "remade" content is a pretty good picture of why vaporware exists. By the time it came out, Black Mesa had been in development so long that the Source engine and HL2 assets became not all that impressive. It's certainly a cut above the original in terms of graphics, but if the goal was to play Half-Life to something approximating the full ability of modern machines, Black Mesa is much too old to get anywhere near that. And this is with the final section of the game still missing, two years after getting that fatal "soon."
And without cutting-edge graphics, there's not a lot to recommend the remake by. There isn't tighter, more visceral gunplay, map designs retain that uncanny linear feel while simultaneously signposting the linear paths poorly, and it just feels like nothing was really learned from the decade of intervening shooters to improve upon the product.
It's a sad irony that the people most seeking a nostalgic trip through Half-Life are going to be the ones to play this, because they're the ones with the most to lose as they poison those fond memories with a lackluster remake.

It's a game Alien universe always needed. Despite some notable shortcomings.
Pros:
+ Initial missions where you are getting acquainted with the station and Alien missions are the highlight of the game.
+ Alien is very unpredictable and cannot be killed, so you have to use tools you craft or find to distract it. Or better yet - try to sneak around without making any noise. The sense of dread is ever present. Its AI however is nothing innovative despite what reviews tell you, however it works.
+ No autosave, no save-anytime. There are emergency phone stations, that are admittedly well spread across Sevastopol - and that's the only way it happens. DO NOT ignore ANY possibility to save the game!
+ Retrofuturistic art is outstanding. Most of the decorations are direct copies from the Alien movie and the station crafted with them is very memorable. The well done lighting only adds to the atmosphere.
+ Sound is great. Motion tracker (which is the most important tool in the game and looking canonically badass at that) provides only vague clues to where enemies are, so you have to use your own ears too. Besides enemies hear noise too - which itself can be used as a tool. Even hitting the wall with a maintenance jack can work as a distraction.
+ Alien is not the only enemy, initial human/android sections are pretty creepy too. But only at first (see below).
+ Very adequately administered backtracking which I like since it always comes with some new stuff accessible here and there and adds to the sense that you indeed move around the station, instead of following a straight pass like other Alien-universe games.
Cons:
- Lategame missions that serve little purpose but to artificially extend the gametime. They are filled with androids and humans and some parts of them force you into a dull shooty combat. This alone delivers a huge hit to an otherwise interesting and fun game.
- Last missions are extremely scripted and linear, but despite that the game ends abruptly (still worth completing it however).
- Plot is rather weak and is full of cliches and predictable twists collected from across Alien movies.
- Being multiplatform for PS3/X360 forces the game to have small areas and makes loading screens another enemy.
Also to me it's better at being Bioshock (which it clearly tried to copy) in many ways than Bioshock itself.

This is a tough one.  When the game came out it worked great for me!  It ran smooth and I had zero crashes.  The game itself was fun to play and it looks great.  The story, as expected, was pretty terrible, but Just Cause has never been about the story, it's about blowing things up!  The weapons and destruction is super fun!  Destroying the big sphere fuel tanks and watching them roll down a hill on fire never gets old.  The different jets and helicopters are awesome too.  The cars though, kind of suck.  Some are better than others, but a lot of them control strangely.  It's almost as if your controller input has big lag.  I don't know why they chose to do this.  But it can be frustrating.  Especially with motorcycles.  Don't even bother with them.  Compared to Just Cause 2, where the heck are all the civilian airplanes!?  No big passenger planes?  No passenger airports to fool around at?  I was very surprised by this as it was one of the most fun things in Just Cause 2.  Also there is barely any air traffic.  In JC2 you would often see other planes flying about and you could hijack them, but here it is extremely rare.  The wingsuit is amazing!  It's my favorite thing in the game.  It takes a little bit to get used to the controls, but man, gliding just a few feet off the ground is such a great feeling. I'll also say that about half way through the game things started getting pretty boring and repetitive.  Yeah, kind of expected with this type of game, but I think they could have livened it up with better missions.  I mean, GTAV is open world and some of their late game missions are awesome.  Variety is the spice of life I suppose.

Undo whatever you did Avalanche!  I still want to play more of it (but not the DLC, it looks a bit lame).
And bring back the tiny jet from Just Cause 2!  That things was awesome!  Why isn't it in this??
**update august 12th 2016: After installing windows 10 the game finally runs again, but man it runs like garbage.  It ran buttery smooth when it first came out, now, with the same settings, it runs choppy and is basically unplayable.  Really dissapointing...  Sadly, still can't recommend it.

It's the best game I've ever played. No game has provided me with so much fun and excitement in my entire life for as long as
has.
takes everything that was good in
and perfects it for
, removing everything I didn't like from the first game and improving upon the things I did like. I highly recommend buying  this game.
- Story writing and pacing is done incredibly well, it was difficult for me to find stopping points as I became greatly invested in the characters and the story.
- Tons of new enemies/bosses. Almost every chapter introduces some form of new enemy type, and they each come with their own challenges and tactics players require to take them down. Each new boss is brilliantly designed and keeps players engaged and on their toes consistently during battle.
- Tons of new weapons to find. New weapons are placed perfectly and satisfyingly throughout gameplay; I never felt like I possessed too many or too few. Weapons also carry over player upgrades for shotguns, pistols, etc, so leveling up a gun early is at no expense when a new gun of the same type is found.
- Beautifully composed music. I completely fell in love with
's soundtrack. Every track perfectly fits the situation and keeps players engaged and immersed.
- Dialogue system and side quests. Players can engage in dialogue and complete side quests for AI characters throughout the game, and it brings so much more to the table in terms of progression and new content. If a player feels bored with the main storyline, or wants to slow down the pace of their progression, they can go complete a side quest for a new weapon, or additional supplies, but can also learn more about the story as you complete the task. In terms of the dialogue system, talking to someone in the complete hellscape of the STEM system brings the player back down from being too overwhelmed with action and horror, and learning more  about the characters in the game was interesting for me.
- Enormous maps and towns for players to explore and adventure around in free roam.
- The randomness of enemy pathing. It can be the biggest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the entire game when you sneak up to an enemy and they turn around spontanously out of pure randomness, and your stealth situation is compromised. You can always reload the checkpoint, or run away,  hide, and do it again, but it's still one of the most obnoxious things in the entire game.
- The detection meter. Sometimes enemies can see you through barriers of concrete because the tip of your boot was sticking out, and it's ♥♥♥♥ing frustrating as hell, but from a realistic standpoint, it's perfect to a tee.
Overall,
pulled me out of my critical slump for games. I had trouble finding a game that would make me excited, or let me have real, genuine fun, and
was the answer to my prayers. There's so few problems with it and so many things it did right that it made a lasting and unforgettable impression on me. It's the best game I've played of this year, and probably the best game I'll ever play for a long time.

Okay, before I review the aptly named Emperor's Edition of Rome 2 Total War, (for I am clearly the slap-♥♥♥♥♥ apocalyptic Emperor of the entire universe) I feel like I should slip into the RTS (Realistically Titled Smack-addiction) that is the Total War series. Now truth be told, I've never been able to look at the series properly since the flop that was Rome 2 flopped so hard onto the floppy release date that it flopped numerous times in the press before taking a flop at the flop Olympics where it took the gold in flopping. It was bad. The AI was dead, the graphics were a downgrade and I feel like SEGA held a vacuum cleaner to the series' ear and slurped the soul out of the game. So imagine my surprise when I found an Emperor's Edition for the game! The greatest Emperor's Edition in the world! Midst all the others this one is a real stand out!
So! What have they changed for the new revival of this pathetic excuse for a game? A new campaign? Thank you very much. Cinematics? Thanks a bunch! Extras that turn the game into what it should've been in the first place? Okay, now you've officially sold me. Now the Total War series shan't be flopping! Nay! Instead it will be riding backwards on a Harley Davidson, waving the bird at corporate BS and beating up floppy pretenders with their floppy hair. It's a shame it's all a bit too little too late really, especially for the die hard fans of the series who, since Empire and Napoleon, have long fled the nest in the most 'shamefur display' after Rome 2. Creative Assembly have at least shown their aptitude for change and have recognized their mistakes, however it's really not enough to just release a whole update in a feeble attempt to appease us. I'd say I like Rome 2 Emperor's Edition, but then I'd feel like an abused spouse! Demanding a divorce and standing my ground but eventually caving in to my inner fan-boy, who comes back for another right hook in the face just because Creative Assembly brandishes chocolate and alcohol. To be honest that was my only pathetic nit pick kind of like a mother baboon with OCD picking the fleas of her offspring whilst wearing a 40s housewife dress and hoping to get dinner done by the time my husband comes home. Sorry where was I? Oh yeah, the good stuff. Well, upon loading the game up and diving into the new campaign centered around the Roman Civil War (history being an obsessive hobby of mine) I decided to play as Briton because I'm proud of my homeland even though I'm ironically not from Britain at all, and because... Well... Chariots man! If you turn down riding a chariot and instead throwing a sling at the filthy Roman invaders then you clearly shouldn't be allowed near anything sharper than sling ammunition because you clearly don't know that a combination of iron, wood with two spikes lead by two to four heavy horses and archers in the back can be considered the ancient equivalent of a M1A1 Abrams. But imagine my surprise when I launched into my woad-wearing, atavistic campaign when I got an intro cutscene that thrusted the Romans into the spotlight. Oh I see now game. You want me to play as the Romans in this new campaign? Maybe because the whole focus of the Roman Civil War is actually the Romans and not the♥♥♥♥♥♥naked warriors sitting comfortably hundreds of miles and an English Channel away.
Truth be told however, I actually rather enjoyed the campaign even if I was enjoying it for all the wrong reasons. For a game in a series known as Total War I was certainly doing less of the War part. Solving political issues in my tribe and constructing the ever-famous and envied iron mines that Briton was known for at that time could occupy me for hours on end to be perfectly honest. Even if the historical accuracy and peaceful management received a bit of a chip in the windscreen when I conquered Gaul and Germany as the Romans went to war with Egypt and Greece. But that's the beauty of the game. Creating alternate history will make nerds like myself giggle with glee as they play as Athens and slaughter 10,000 prisoners of war and revert back to tribal dancing and pagan worship. And as far as the battles go (and God knows they come and go quicker than a brothel patron for sloppy seconds) they'll take your breath away with sheer size alone.
Graphical fidelity can also be invited to a sophisticated dinner party, even if I am still raising a doubtful eyebrow in the direction of the E3 demo that I'm sure was just a clip from some film that no one has ever heard of. The combat style is a bit more hectic and meat grinder style than the elegant sword play from master samurai in Shogun 2, but for understandable reasons. I doubt there were many Roman generals that adopted the style of the Red Bear whilst he drew his tempered katana. No. They were more in for kicking the opponent in the balls whilst thrusting forward with a rusty gladius. The combat and animations suit the time period, even if the larger battles tend to look like mosh pits in a time period that was all about formations. Another thing though; there are still some questionable frame rate drops and whenever I feel like I'm getting somewhere with the case I keep getting ripped into by his lawyer, good old Mr Dumbass AI, that occasionally has the common courtesy of standing ram-rod stiff in the docks of their city, whilst I  run amok with legions of dudes with swords in the rest of the city. 'Sir what are we doing?' one seemed to ask. 'Well if you must know Tripoli, we are on the look out for a naval assault.' Says his general with a stern face out to sea. 'But sir,' says Tripoli with increasing concern, 'Lenny commands a tribe of blue faced warriors who haven't discovered clothes yet, why are we expecting ships?' To which the general replies 'we discovered ships nearly thirty years ago, but we haven't discovered fire yet... Two words my boy. Research tree.

I want to point 2 things, though.
1) Let's not judge a game according to our expectations from it. Some people expected a R:TW with better graphics, some expected a super game of the century. I say let's judge each of its parameters seperately. The graphics are very good, even at the lowest options, music could be better but it's OK, gameplay is fun and interesting and, for the most part, it contains things that R:TW didn't have, like civil wars and politics for all factions, much more interesting diplomatic options, technology trees, improved ambushes and battlefields etc.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Tyto Ecology is an educational life simulation.
You control an 'owlbot' (I have no idea ...) with which you're able to move around inside your chosen biodome (or 'biome'), interacting simply by placing habitat markers for various insects, plants, and animals. Then you sit back and watch the artificial life unfold, placing more objects as desired in an effort to help, or hinder, your biodome's life.
Graphics - Graphics are okay, leaning towards poor. Stiffly animated and seemingly low-poly models combine with very flat-looking textures to create scenery like that seen in a 15-20-year-old RPG, where nothing really seems to interact with the world. Some of the individual models look okay by themselves, particularly the plants, but taken together they just don't seem to fit right. Water doesn't look anything like water -- it's a solid blue polygon upon which animals can walk -- and there are no fancy graphical effects, except for some shadows. Even with settings turned all the way up the graphics are fairly unimpressive.
There is a certain charm to the creatures, though, and some of the plants individually are quite nice, but placement of them invariably leaves them looking stuck on to the very flat-looking ground surface. You're also unable to overlap different vegetation on the ground, leading to an extremely sparse rainforest environment, for example.
Sound - Sound is minimal. There's some weird music that is hard to hear, interrupted sporadically by piercingly loud noises from some of the mammals. I think a bit of volume normalisation may be in order.
Gameplay - The gameplay itself is very simple. You move your weird owlbot thingy about with WASD, and use the mouse to look around, zoom in and out, and interact with your biodome.
The biodome itself starts out empty; you populate it with various producers (plants), consumers (animals), and decomposers (mushrooms, insects). You don't control any of these yourself, though. Instead you spend some of one or the other of the two in-game currencies (both earned over time, and also through reaching achievements) to purchase a marker for your desired object, which you then place in the world. Some of these (e.g. trees) simply allow you to place the one object and be done with it. Others (e.g. tortoises) allow you to place the marker, from which a host of creatures then spawns within the designated territory.
The key to what Tyto offers is what happens next: the interaction between the game objects you've placed. Consumers require something to survive: either producers or other consumers. They then produce detritus, which builds up in the biodome unless you add decomposers to process it, thus providing extra food for the producers. It's a simple cycle, but given that you don't have any direct control over any of the creatures in your biodome, the interactions between all of the components is quite interesting.
Tyto offers three biodome habitat types, with some overlapping flora and fauna between them: tropical rainforest, grasslands, and desert. It also offers between 2 and 20 of each of the producers, consumers, and decomposers per biodome type, but most of these overlap across two or three of the habitats, so the range of choices isn't as large as it first sounds. You can create multiple biodomes of each type and experiment as you desire; other than the tutorial and achievements, goals are only what you make them.
The game also provides an in-game encyclopaedia of sorts, called the 'biodex'. This is both useful for the game itself, and also an educational resource for someone interested in learning more about some of the insects, plants, and animals featured in Tyto.
Pros:
+ Mostly very well written text; the 'biodex' encyclopaedia thingy is fantastic!
+ Educational
+ Achievements to promote some goals and replayability
+ Developers are very active in the Community Hub and are willing to participate in useful discussions
+ Simple ideas lead to interesting and complex interactions; it's easy to play, but hard to 'master'
+ It's great to see another artificial life simulator on the market; I haven't played one for ages
Cons:
- Graphics are relatively poor
- Sounds and music are minimal, and very out-of-balance as far as volume levels are concerned
- A very limited range of plants and creatures means that it all gets a bit boring after a while
- Some of the achievements are just silly (200 years!)
- No flying or swimming creatures, even though birds and bats are mentioned in a few places in the biodex
- No overlapping plants, and no way to delete or move them after you've placed them, leading to the least forest-like rainforest I've ever seen
- Movement controls stop working when you're placing objects, leading to some annoying place-cancel-rotate-cancel-rotate-place type scenarios (coupled with the above for extra frustration!)
- Sometimes creatures just seem to die off, even when you've accounted for all of their needs
- No simulation of weather, seasons, wind, etc. (I know, it's a biodome simulation, but even a simple biodome would at least have some rain from the watering systems!)
Tyto Ecology is certainly not for everyone. It's an artificial life simulation that is very slow, and sometimes even boring. The graphics are disappointing, and the sound is probably better left off. And the developers made some weird decisions that make your biodomes look very sparsely populated even when they're 'full'. But it's also interesting, and fun at times, and even a little bit rewarding sometimes.
For what it tries to be, Tyto does a reasonable job. I hope the developers stick with it and address some of the problems, and also release more content.
