I recommend this game and indicate below flaws I perceived.
Guards and scientists are distinguished by unique faces but participate in the game ordinarily - guards discharge ammnition and scientists morphine. In Half-Life 2 NPCs were comfortaly generic, their role clear in the efficacy with which they provided cover or healing. Here in Black Mesa every generic NPC is given a fresh face but does not seem authentic. For their scripted lines and operations they do not appear to have come to whatever part of Black Mesa except by being loaded. I suspect that were they dressed in unfamiliar clothes or uncommon in their behaviour I would believe them to be escaping the facility as I am. Freeman doesn't have to be the only protagonist except to the extent that he is the only available rubric through which to experience the resonance cascade. If and when an NPC talks to me I would like to feel as though their agenda is parallel to mine but not in aid of mine. Varied voice acting or more dynamic interractions might help this, but I think the deeper problem is with the puzzles.
Gordon Freeman studied at MIT and so has some understanding that when machinery of the kind in the Black Mesa Research facility is physically damaged it cannot readily be fixed. The nature of the damage was such that simply turning on a switch should not restore functionality. The bounty of red and green lights is confusing and ultimately disappointing. Solve enough problems that rely on pushing a switch and you learn to seek out the amber bulb whenever a door is closed. In Half-Life it was satisfying to do so because the level designers omitted every button that the player had no interest in pressing. There is no challenge in turning off the switch for the auto-turret, but it is no less the reason to evade its fire. I think in Half-Life the "puzzles" are really ways of attaching the combat to the surroundings and enhancing the threat presented by the enemies. Puzzles being secondary to combat by some distance the game should not invite a search for the "on" button. Were all buttons pressable and of some function then this would be good design, but in Black Mesa you can only press the right button. The point of the buttons in, say, Blast Pit, is to convince you of your power in commanding the facility to defeat foes, but before that FIRE button is depressed you have probably pressed E a couple of times without result and felt, in fact, that you had no real idea what anything did until it did it. Naturally machines of this complexity are beyond understanding through observation, unlike the puzzles in Riven. The remaining experts inside the Black Mesa research facility might indicate what apparati do, or be shown looking at information pertaining to a system on a computer. Even knowing how to solve a problem, is it relevant? In Black Mesa, I never know.
Half-Life motivates with violence and fear from Unforseen Consequences to sometime shortly after Office Complex, at which you are told to go to the Lambda complex and launch a rocket to close the portal. WIthout visual proof that the aliens are getting in through a whole in the sky it's hard to feel anything like the urgency conveyed by the panicked scientist at the radio, particularly since the aliens appear to have materialised within an underground bunker, and by all accounts you are a theoretical physicist. Sure, you've come this far, but my prowess needn't be diverted from getting out of New Mexico ASAP. For all the computer terminals and specialised intstruments, for all of Gordon's knowledge of the facility, and for the threat of death I expected the game's providing me a discrete objective facile. No maps or schematics suggest an escape route, the only way available being the only way to wherever. Half-Life is famously dated for being linear in a direction acute with a player's ordinary desires. The remake was an opportunity to make the player want to go to the Lambda Complex, or to otherwise allow Gordon to fire up a Jeep and book it out of there, or get lost five miles outside of Alberquerque.
The project is a little frustratingly so-close-yet-so-far. It is a gorgeous rendering of what most people wanted but for me the game itself is a little messy. I have many nice things to say about it, but the most I'll do is recommend it subject to my criticisms.

I have a degree in Conservation Biology, so I felt compelled to try this game out. It operates on a "high school" model of ecology, but it would be damn near impossible for a game like this to get any more complex than that. I'm glad to see that the developers seem to actually care, and listen to their community. If this game were to be built upon for the foreseeable future, I could see it becoming something really special!
Here are my first impressions and review of the game

(Because of Steam limiting the amount of text for a review I was unable to post the full review here, please see the comments for more information...sorry for how confusing it looks, you have to read the comments from the oldest to the newest for it to be coherent, my apologies).
[04/18/2016] – Final Review
Tyto Ecology is a very intriguing idea where your role is that of god-like being able to place plants, animals, and decomposers as you see fit. However, you are limited in how much you can do with the creatures and biomes; like you cannot shape the terrain nor can you give commands to anything to do something. You are just trying to maintain a balanced eco-system as you fill up the map. That is, if you were able to do that…at all.
The game has a cool idea, but it is hard for me to even call it a game at all. With about 19 hours of gameplay, I was only involved with maybe 5 hours; a few of which I forced myself to play just for this review. The first few hours are fun to mess around with stuff and watch your biome burn from a lack of understanding, but even after reading through the only information given in a form of an index (which I assume is accurate scientific data for the biomes and etc.) you will still be scratching your head wondering why your biome cannot maintain itself except past a certain point. Which becomes a common theme. And it doesn't help that the majority of your time in Tyto Ecology will be spent just waiting…and waiting…and waiting….and waiting…for something to happen.
The game is still un-optimized and contains bugs that will lower your framerate to a slug’s pace (even on my $5000.00 pc), making it un-playable. It has many of the drawbacks of a mobile game where you feel like a lot of decisions for the pace and mechanics of the game were made in the thought of micro-transactions (there are not micro-transactions on PC).
There also isn’t enough information for the player, like given in Sim City or City Skylines, for you to digest or to understand (mechanical information) and even when your waiting for “x” to happen, there is nothing for the player to do (besides reading all the scientific facts of the creatures and plants).
There is also a lot of annoying features and tools that should be in the game, but are missing; like being able to rotate and move the camera while placing objects or being able to rotate larger objects, like trees, a certain way.  It just isn’t fun to play after the initial look, you will find yourself doing other things the majority of the time while this is alt+tabbed in the background.
The developers have been extremely active which is great and makes it more painful for me to say, but this game is not worth $5.00 and you should only really play Tyto Ecology if you’re the type of person who enjoys playing a game, or multiple games, periodically throughout your day.
[04/16/2016] - Initial Entry
Before I give the game a proper review, I currently cannot recommend this title as there are some game breaking bugs that either make it unplayable or very frustrating to play. I will revise this review as updates come out.

First (Sort of, I'd played a bit before) Impressions Video:
Tyto Ecology is a simulation game about building a sustainable ecosystem. It also happens to be rather enjoyable.
The players job is to place plants and animals so that they don't all die a terrible death. This happens to be more complex then you would think (unless you happen to be an ecologist. Then it's about as complex as you would think). It's all about getting the right ratios. As you build your ecosystem you get coins that allow you to purchase new types of plants and animals to add (i.e. use to destroy) to your ecosystem.
The gameplay takes a while to play out. An in game day is maybe (educated guess) ten minutes sped up. However, the game does continue when you turn the game off. your ecosystem will continue to flourish (fat chance) when you leave. You can set the maximum amount of time that is allowed to pass between play sessions, and that acts to decide the difficulty of the game.
Overall, I've really enjoyed Tyto Ecology so far. I've slaughtered healthy Jackrabbit populations with Bobcats and then slaughtered the Bobcats in the name of balancing the ecosystem. For some reason I feel rather evil... well, it's all in the name of progress. If you like slow paced simulations, or enjoy watching ant farms (this game is like a massive, far more interesting ant farm), then check this game out. It'll be right up your alley.

Simple in every aspect. Don´t expect a complex simulation sandbox.
A simple calculation of the food chain and it´s balance graphicly presented. Placing territorys in reach of needed foodsources, maintain a certain balance, unlock species through achievement coins.. beside the simple animations nothing really happens you could watch, while you wait for passing time. Controls are awful. Interface is sufficient. The educational content is the better part of this software, though no mechanic guides you through or links you to, and it is relatively basic as well.
So, i would like to recommend this software, because i appreciate the genre and would like to see more, better and complex kind of this. But i barely would call this either simulation, game or well made. ..for me.

So, i find it still not so well executed, yet.
I would be fine with the progress of the game, if it wouldn´t be released as final game. Though, this might be due to ressource reasons.. So, i quarrel with myself, whether i should recommend and promote or rate and demand. :/

Oh gosh, where to begin . . . being 34 years old, and a fan of the "Alien" franchise for about 10 years or so (didn't watch the first film until I bought the quadrilogy back in 2004 I think), I was hooked on the classical sense of the buildup in suspense.  Alien:  Isolation has done exactly what the original movie couldn't do:  turn suspense into outright fear.  In the movie, you didn't know if the beast was around the corner or hiding in some crevasse, so it had to rely on outright surprise to get you to jump (much like Doom 3).  This game, however . . . you're in tight corridors, few places to hide, but your hear the creature . . . it's hissing, roaring, footfalls, and calmbering through the ventillation shafts.  That's fear on a completely different level.  You know it's near . . . it's hunting  you . . . it knows  you likely don't have anything to stop it . . . and it's trying to get you to poke your head out and look around.  As stated by it's developers, this thing relies on it's own intelligence programming and acts completely independent of all other entities in the game.  Which makes it even scarier in the sense that you could accidently "call" it into your area, or intentionally if you want it to take out something nearby (not recommended if possible).  As for visuals, the game maintains it's homage to the late 70's interpretation of the future (monochromatic CRT computer consoles, blocky tan colored walls, technologically spartan, etc).  YOu can't help but appreciate the level of detail the developers put into this horrific black diamond, and you love them for using it in such a clever fashion.  I'll admit to not having finished the game at this time (and am admittedly too terrified at the moment to continue, even on easy mode).  If anything, I'd recommend this game to those who are fear junkies, who also happen to appreciate classical movie horror . . . if you are skittish . . . well . . . thankfully, this is only a game.

The biggest problem I have right off the bat is how completely underpowered you start. I understand that as the game progresses, you get more powerful, but even at the highest upgrade point in the second you feel so weak compared to Corvo in the first. Here are a few examples:
-I have no proof but I feel so much slower in this game. Even with weapons sheathed sprinting feels like a light jog, and even WITH the bonecharms I feel slow.
-Speaking of bonecharms, this time around they feel so pathetic, especially since you can craft them to be four times as potent. However, with that in mind, I feel as if the developers purposefully made them suck so you don't get too powerful. I'd understand if this was a multiplayer game, but since it's solo why SHOULDN'T I be overpowered? Even with all upgrades and useful bonecharms, compared to the first I feel weak. Blink, again no proof, but to me felt as if it has less range, especially Emily's tentacle. Also after 15 years Corvo has essentially the same powers with no upgrades? Did the outsider take them away from him?
-On a slight tangent, in the first Dishonored, all you really needed to find the charms and bones was the heart, since they were placed in logical places. This time, they're so obnoxiously hidden I needed a guide because I felt so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, which completely breaks the little immersion left, since they won't. stop. narrating. I enjoy reading because it's MY voice, thus making me feel as if I'M the one playing.
-What the everloving F*** was the team thinking with this absolutely abysmal dark vision? First of all, EVERYTHING is yellow, the world is a dark yellow and EVERY item is a slightly lighter yellow, whereas in the first game different types of items had different colors, thus making the power actually useful. Not only is dark vision pointless since everything is F***ing dark, but they also had the genius idea of making it work as a radar with an effective radius of 5 feet, and of course the items don't STAY lit. F*** dark vision it's literally pointless, whereas in the first game I always used it, especially as a tool to lay the foundation of a building. This dark vision DOESN'T EVEN WORK THROUGH WALLS!!! (I think haven't played in a while since I beat it once and felt no desire to run through it again)
-The story is so bland and literally offers no suspense as YOU KNOW how it ends, Corvo/Emily kill the bad witch and all is well in dunwall, whereas the first one had a story that a first time player wouldn't easily guess, nor is it so rushed. Initially Corvo returns unsuccessfully, plays with his daughter, talks to the empress, witnesses her murder, and goes to jail. This feels organic and realistic. In the second, you see Emily, bored of being a ruler and wishing she wasn't, and then BAM guess what your wish came true, some lady who offers no real proof that she is a Kaldwin points a finger at you and says you're guilty, and Emily's "loyal" subjects literally shrug their shoulders and say sure why not. Dishonored 2 Review
I don’t think I’ve ever been as hyped as I had been for a game as I was with Dishonored 2. The amount of variation to each time you play the game from the game’s bewildering mechanics cannot do anything but leave me in awe. The almost unlimited ways you can use the special powers keeps the game fun for dozens of hours.
Dishonored 2 is a first person, stealth video game that takes place in a reimagined world of the Victorian era, one that also offers elements of supernatural magic. Dishonored 2 takes place in a southern European island known as Karnaca, infamous for their blood fly plague, dust storms, clashing factions, and the dreaded Crowned Killer.
One area where Dishonored 2 excels in is its stellar level design. One of the great things about their levels is they all are surrounded by a special theme. One mission you are sneaking through a mansion that changes its layout as you progress through it to another mission where you are teleporting between current day and 1849 version of a house to unreachable locations. And the other great thing about their levels is that there are so many different ways to progress through them. You can play through the same mission more than once and never go through the same area.
One place where you can take away from the game is its somewhat lackluster and predictable story. It is nothing to praise, but one thing you can praise is their attention to smaller stories outside of the realm of the main character that can be picked up through notes and the people around the missions.
Additional Notes:
So some other things I didn't get to mention was the poor performance of some PCs which sure sucks, but I believe that as long as you follow their recommendations you should be fine. I mean you can't really expect to run a brand new 2016 game on PC with 2010 hardware or ect. And if you want my specs I have a FX 8350 and GTX 1080 and got a solid 70fps on Ultra settings. Some people complain that the fps sucks but thats just because they aren't used to playing at < 100 fps.
And to further elaborate on CONS of the game besides performance:
I'd say the story kinda sucks in this game. They kinda just shoved a familiar face into the main antagonist just because and I honestly probably would've prefered otherwise, but I guess they can't really have witches in the game without her so it ended up being okay. And as a counterarguement to the claim the story sucks, I'd say that the lore in this game is great. I love the world that Dishonored has built up from all of the books or abandoned houses or through almost anything, the world and backstory of the Dishonored universe has a great feel.
And another thing is that there is only 9 missions. Granted each mission is about 2-3 hours long per but it definitely does end up feeling like a short game even though a playthrough is around 20 hours. Still though if I were to go in again blind, I would still pay $60 for this game because this leads me into my next part.
A final thing to touch on is that why I would recommend this game is because ARKANE LOVES DISHONORED AND ITS FANBASE! I'm sure you've seen that they have given out TWO FREE UPDATES since it's original release adding in more awesome ways to play. Heck they've even been giving out free PS4s, Collectors Editions of the game, and even awesome artwork from the game on their Twitter! I know they get crap for releasing the PC version unoptimised, but they should get the credit they deserve for working as hard as possible right after and also apologizing by giving out free content. They basically gave up their Thanksgiving break to fix the game so others could enjoy their breaks. I feel so bad when I see how little of my friends own this game and probably how poorly its done on the Steam market. They've poored their hearts out onto this game I wish they were rewarded greater for their efforts. I'm just afraid that if this game did poor, what is to say for the rest of the franchise? I don't want this amazing of a series to end right here. So I'll end on this...
BUY DISHONORED 2 AND SUPPORT THE DEVELOPERS IF YOU WANT TO SEE MORE FROM DISHONORED IN THE FUTURE!

I wanted to like this game. I'm a fan of many survival horror series, and this seemed to have a lot of potential. I can't even put my finger on why I didn't enjoy this. From moment one it seemed like a slog. I played through the first few chapters hoping that it would somehow grab my attention, but it never did.
The concept is good, but the implementation is lacking. The 3rd person view is part of the issue, making aiming more difficult than it should be. I felt like instead of feeling dread or suspense it was frustration and forced horror which ended up meaning that I die, restart, die again, then get it right. By the time you fight your way (or sneak your way) past an enemy it's lost its suspense.
In the end I decided it wasn't worth my time and I decided to move on to something else.

The Story:
The Evil Within 2 is the sequal to the surival horror game The Evil WIthin, unlike the linear hospital setting of the last instalment of the series, this game now takes place in the open world of union, a town which happens to be located inside STEM. The premise of the game this time around happens to be Sebastian Castellanos going back into STEM, trying to find his daughter which was presumed to be dead(but was really didnt). This game is one that made a bland main character in the first one into a character that i personally began to love and feel for. This is a game which isn't only good on its own, but makes its predecessor a greater experience as well.
Combat:
The combat in this game hasn't gotten old at all for me yet, seeing as you can choose to either silently take down your enemies or go in guns blazing(Which isn't recommended most of the time). i haven't completely completed the game yet but the weapons range from pistols, shotguns, and even crossbows! Did i mention that the badass crossbow from the last game is like the second weapon you get in this one? it's pretty great. Moving away from just the crossbow and on to general gameplay, this game gives you a sense of acomplishment for every headshot you get, as not only is your ammo probably going to be very low, but enemies are always twitching and moving around, making it harder to land a accurate shot.The only complaint i have is that some normal enemies take two headshots to kill from a pistol with one more damage upgrade left. This is more of a me thing, as i'm a pretty terrible aim.
Stealth:
it has the same principles as the last game, or for context, stealth from the last of us without the wallhacks. Instead of enemies being complete dumbasses like in the last game, letting you normally walk right behind them without being detected, you actually have to be carefull as there's a system in which you have to make sure your crouched, as you will be heard, you can be seen if you poke your head out from around cover, and a few other improvements to make the game more fun to stealth, which is what you will be doing a lot of.

When people say that games are controversial, that usually involves two sides screaming at each other, saying their opinion is the correct one.
Deus Ex: Invisible War is controversial in the sense that you have the majority of people saying that it's a hyper-streamlined mess, and a smaller, more demure audience saying that "Well, I mean, it's an okay game, just not a great Deus Ex game".
That second audience has a point. Or would, if I could fit the rest of the sentence in without a 15-second long loadpoint inbetween.
Here's Invisible War in a nutshell; Remember Liberty Island from the first game? Nice place, good view.
Now remove everything in the middle, the statue and complex, and quite a bit off the sides. Remove the bunker, that's a loading zone. Remove all the objects, all those walls and suchlike, replace them with some scattered crates. Split what's remaining into 2 different loading zones that you can and will have to repeatedly travel back and forth between. Because that's the final level.
Kneecaps the game straight off the bat. 15 seconds of loading every two minutes. Even less downtime if you're trying to complete a sidequest.
Real shame. Mechanically it's not even bad. Probably enjoyed running a Terminator build better than the first game, energy cells are liberally thrown at you along with unlimited recharge points, and it wants you to use augments whenever you feel like it.
Augments themselves are fun to play it, and weapon mods actually have a couple of interesting effects over just damage and range. Only real issue itself is that your character progression caps out almost immediately if you don't decide to respec with the amount of initial biomods and weapons thrown at you.
Also hacking is an augment now because reasons.
Gameplay itself is standard console FPS stuff. Nothing broken, nothing to write home about.
Unless you're packing the speed augment, movement is slow and enemies, apart from one lategame enemy type, are fairly stationary. There's multiple enemy types to incentivize carrying both EMP and ballistics weapon types, but the universal ammo system, the fairly small ammo cap and that enemies will never really hit you when you're sprinting with the speed augment on, means you can probably just run past them.
Universal ammo and the ammo cap being so small does make it a weird balancing act of strafing and concentrating on actually hitting people in the head. Stop n start pacing. If that sounds strategic, it's not. It's generally pretty good about "refunding" your ammo loss through ammo drops and the environment but there's a lategame enemy type the game loves to spam that doesn't drop ammo and explodes immediately when it dies, making melee a no-go.
There's presumably some stealth stuff, I didn't bother with it.
With your choice of either teen dream pop star with gelled hair, or girl with her eyes textured directly onto her face and looking in slightly different directions, you solve the rather rushed mystery of why your secret biomod academy was raided.
Let's stop this review to say that you don't get to say it's an Invisible War when your main enemy has recruitment booths in the mall.
Invisible War does have the distinction of being the one Deus Ex with decent endings, but the writing does have some anti-climactic pacing issues. It's pretty underwritten and doubles as a tumble of reveals and plot twists without buildup. Ends up feeling floaty.
The best paced reveal in the game is about two competing coffee shops.
So the only real, crippling problem with Invisible War is the tiny levels and constant, unending load times. And that's a very real, crippling problem. So crippling it's booted to the footnotes of history, despite the very real care and effort that went into the game proper.
If you're playing this, you're playing it to see just exactly what happened for this game to end up so ignored. An archaeological dig more than a functioning tour. If you're here for that, it's playable.
Otherwise I'd recommend moving on, like everyone else.

This is a very relaxing game. There is a puzzle element because you have to balance plants and animals, predators and prey. But the pace of events is slow enough that you can think through your changes. It is quite rewarding to play a biome for an hour and watch it fill up with plants and animals. On the down side, the graphics and animations are very basic. The slow evolution of the ecosystem is relaxing, but if you are the type person who likes lots of action it can become boring because there are long stretches when you just watch the animals move about.

All in all, I'd definitely recommend this for the price.

CON

Don't expect to spend longer than four or five hours on this, even if some of that time is devoted to grinding. The controller mapping is in serious need of change. I used an Xbox controller for windows and was confused the whole time as to why certain decisions were made. For instance, there are four special moves in the game, yet none of those were mapped to the main A, B, X and Y buttons. Two were mapped to the Start and Back buttons, and two weren't mapped to any button on the controller at all, which made for awkward combat encounters at some stages.
Having said that, Eternal Senia is an endearing little game about the love between two sisters, a relationship not often explored in video games. There were emotional moments and three considerably different endings, a feat many AAA games can't even achieve. Considering the game is free, it's certainly worthwhile for a short weekend diversion.

First, let's get the negatives out of the way.  Compared to the original, the story and lore's a bit lackluster.  The Soul Memory system makes PVP more of a hassle than it needs to be.  The devs' attempts to "amp up" the difficulty primarily consist of absurd ambushes and damage sponge tank enemies.  The geography of Drangleic is nonsensical (there's a wharf at the bottom of a sunken tower?  Huh?)
However, it gets a LOT right.  Leveling and improving yourself is MUCH easier.  There's a greater variety of enemies and the bosses still manage to keep you on your toes.  I've died to the Ruin Sentinels and Belfry Gargoyles at LEAST three times each, and the latter I still have yet to beat.  The Covenants are pretty decent, with the Bellkeeper Covenant being a good source of PVP and Titanite.  The music is top notch, and in my personal opinion is MUCH better than the original.  The combat is just as fluid and amazing as the original, if not more so, and the NPCs are MUCH more interesting and colorful (though none of them come close to Seigmeyer and Solaire, but then again, what could?)
All in all, while it does have some jagged edges, Dark Souls 2 is a pretty damn good game.

Dark Souls 2 sets out to be a sequel to Dark Souls 1. It aspires to expand upon the game mechanics in Dark Souls 1 and provide more content.
Dark Souls 2 ends up with a few horrible issues which plague gameplay and make it almost painful to see compared to Dark Souls 1.
Firstly, enemy tracking. In DS1 if an enemy is doing the windup to an attack they're
stuck to the direction they face, they can re-position their angle very slightly. In DS2 not only can they move during attacks but they can pretty much always turn, and they do
turn.
. In DS1 those lizards would've been vulnerable during the animation for their fire breathing or during the wind-down. As it is they can literally turn like a record on a player throughout the entire animation.
Moving on, world design. DS1 had a well connected world where often it was possible to shortcut through areas and get to others faster (a good example would be skipping through New Londo into the valley of the drakes to go into Blighttown to buy from Shiva). In Dark Souls 2 you can get to any location 2 ways. Either walk there from Majula, or warp to a nearby bonfire. That's it. The world seems huge and sometimes you can see other locations but you can't get to them without either warping or going back to majula first.
The world design is pretty bland but the level design in some places is even worse. Iron Keep doesn't appear anywhere near Earthen Peak despite being a short distance to travel. Earthen Peak appears to be surrounded by barren rocky land, go up an elevator into the sky and somehow you're now in the middle of a volcano? In addition Yet-Another-Valley-Of-Defilement kicks in and it's a shame because somehow The pit/black gulch manages to be an even less interesting than the previous two given that it's just platforms in the dark with pretty much nothing to explore.
Boss variation is also harmed. In previous games we had some really nice quite unique bosses, Old Hero from DeS who's blind and requires you to be quiet during the fight, False Idol who requires her assistant to be killed before you can kill her, Priscilla who can become invisible and you have to track her footprints etc. In DS2 there are some interesting and original bosses like Demon of Song. The vast majority of the bosses in the game are oversized humanoids, which is both quite boring and incredibly repetitive. Even worse is the addiction to multi-boss fights, these all end up being a game of patience where you just walk around with your shield up and wait for both of the bosses to use their full combo at the same time in order to get a fight in. It's not hard, it's just dull. The only real threat during the duo/trio/multi boss fights is the player becoming frustrated and trying to get two hits in rather than one and subsequently being stunlocked to death by multiple enemies.
A small aside, why does every humanoid enemy have exactly the same moveset? Left sweep, right sweep, overhead slow swing. The complete lack of variation seriously makes it difficult to become interested in fighting generic humanoid enemy #55.
A more widespread issue is the seemingly missing aspect of challenge -> reward. In DS1 the game leads you into challenges and then rewards you with a feeling of achievement for overcoming the obstacle. Somehow the developers thought they could accomplish this by just "making the game hard". In Dark Souls 2 there's multiple sections purposefully designed to be difficult or irritating. One example of this that really stands out would be the double-ogre section of Aldia's Keep, one ogre is defending a doorway into a small room. Once you kill the first ogre and walk into the room, the only point of interest is the doorway and a small item to the side. If you go straight for the door an ogre will break through the wall and do a grab attack, if you go for the item and then go to the door without stopping it breaks through the wall and does a grab attack. Grab attacks are particularly problematic in this game due to the fact that unless you pump stats and defenses they're pretty much always a death sentence. This isn't a challenge that you overcome, it's a trap specifically put there to kill the player so they think "wow this game is hard."
The previous points really harm the game's ability to last but it was the lack of care that From Software put into the online play that really kills this game for me. Every time you absorb souls it keeps a count, people who have too disparate Soul Memory levels cannot play together. This has a noble intention (stop people who have farmed to get strong equipment but stayed low level from invading other low level players) but what it ends up doing is placing an expiry date on every co-op or PvP character. If you co-op a lot, eventually you fall out of the acceptable soul memory range and no one can see your soul sign anymore. If you pvp and win too much eventually you can't invade that area anymore since no one will be within your soul memory.
Even worse, if you DO get people you're matched via soul memory so there's literally no incentive to not pump all of your souls into stats and equips as soon as possible to continue doing well in PVP. This has lead to incredibly homogenised builds where people just wear full havels and then shove on the highest DPS most maxed out build they can. (Notice, not minmax, just max. You don't need to minmax, you can put 99 in every stat and you'll get matched with people who are SL120 who have been PVPing a lot).
There's been cases of characters that have been deleted at early levels (15-30) purely because someone invaded them, died somewhere in their world and it turns out it's a hacked character with a low soul memory but a high SL, so they drop 800K souls and pretty much deem that character PVP/Co-op useless.
Not that it's actually easy to pvp anyway, somewhere along the line a decision was made to ensure that people who want to pvp would have to grind for the item to pvp first because in the previous game the reusable orb was apparently a bad idea. In DS2 you have to continually farm and grind to get the red eye orbs to invade, if not farming to get them you have to fight in the arena for them.
With all the imbalances around, colour me surprised to hear the From Software are released not 1 but
DLC expansions for Dark Souls 2, and strangely releasing all of them within one month. They're even selling a season pass, for 3 DLC being released in one month. This is ridiculous. The former claim "we aim to release the game as a complete experience" suddenly seems quite a hollow promise.
Dark Souls 2 is not a terrible game, but it is a bad game and given the lineage it comes from it feels terrible. If I were to review it based on its own merits I would probably give it a 6/10. Given the game it attempts to follow, somewhere around 4/10 seems appropriate.
If you enjoyed Dark Souls 1, I wouldn't recommend this. I suggest trying out Demon's Souls or waiting for From Software to take some time to pay attention to the glaring flaws already present in the game they're attempting to bleed more money out of.
If you have never played a Souls series game, I suggest Demon's Souls first, then play Dark Souls 1. Skip DS2.

Alien Isolation squanders so much potential it's annoying.
The main problem is that the missions are incredibly tedious because they're all the same: go to this part of the ship, pull that lever to restore/disable the power, make sure you avoid the alien/androids/humans along the way. This monotony dragged on for so long I actually started to wonder if the game had an ending.
Eventually I discovered that it did, and that it involved hacking two computers, pulling a lever, pulling two more levers, then inserting two keycards next to those levers, then pulling up four tubes, then pushing the buttons on the tubes, then completing a series of quick time events, before, finally, you guessed it... pushing one final damn button.
Yup, that's right. There's no tense one-on-one finale with the alien. You don't have to use your flamethrower and your wits to try and coerce the alien into the airlock before blasting it of into space. Nope. You just press another sodding button. The end. Roll credits.
The game does have some redeeming features though (honestly). It looks and sounds truly stunning, and captures the feel of the original Alien movie perfectly, which is a testament to the game engine Creative Assembly have built. It also has some really neat gameplay mechanics and ideas. In the end, though, it fails to convert them into something that's cohesive and fun to play.

This is a very short review of the superb “Alien: Isolation.” I have logged 21 hours with this thriller but I have not finished the PC version of the game. And I don’t think I will. This is because I have reached a point in the game that is just too scary. I know what follows because I accompanied my youngest son as he played through it on the PlayStation when it first came out. In fact, he required me to be there, in the family room, as he/we navigated the horrifying Sevastopol Station. So, I know where I am and I know what happens next. Perhaps I am spoiling it a bit just by making this declaration. So, yea, the game makes a surprising turn and that is when I run away, too ascared to face the frightening later segments of this outstanding game.
The Alien story is one of my favorites in science fiction. Before the movie, “Alien,” came out in 1979, I read with great excitement about the efforts by consulting scientists to create a creature that was formidable and scary, but also possessed a sensible, if unconventional, biology. My first viewing of the movie shortly thereafter would be followed over time with many more, on VHS, DVD, Blu Ray and last fall, a theatrical showing at the Regency Theater in Costa Mesa, CA. Alien is one of those stories and one of those movies that cannot be improved in any way. Like Casablanca, with Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman, It is perfect. Before the game, Alien: Isolation, was released, I worried that it might try too hard to be too fresh and 21st centuryish. But not to worry. The developer, Creative Assembly, captured the spirit and essence of the Alien adventure with stunning fidelity and detail.
While on Sevastopol Station, I was swept back in time to the futuristic Nostromo, as its high tech was imagined in the late 1970s. The monochrome CRTs, and icon-encoded keyboards are there. The lighting and sound effects are so true that often I felt as if I was reliving those classic moments as Dallas or Ripley, hustling through menacing corridors at the behest of alarm claxons and rotating amber emergency lights. The map design is so exquisite and true that I normally would be delighted if I wasn’t so distracted by the rumbling ruckus in the air vents above.
I normally do not play modern horror games because I dislike the notion that I cannot defeat the creatures that trouble me. Still, I had to experience the aesthetic richness of Alien: Isolation in order to have more time observing and hiding from this creature whose “structural perfection is matched only by its hostility.” As I said above, I played much of it but had to stop because I am too chicken to finish it. Nonetheless, I got what I wanted out of it. If you enjoyed the movie, “Alien,” and want to get a sense of what it would be like to be trapped with it on an isolated space station, “Alien: Isolation” is a must... But don’t play it alone.

I'm not a fan of horror games. I don't like being scared. I especially don't like games or movies that rely heavily on jump scares or excessive gore in order brand themselves as horror. This is why I have a lot of respect for this game. It relies on a tense atmosphere to create tension and fear.
It was very clever to make the Alien a free roaming AI controlled enemy, normally in horror games you start walking to what looks like a suspicious area and you brace yourself because you know walking past a certain point will trigger some kind of scare. In Alien: Isolation, when you know the alien is in the vicinity, you are always on edge because there is no predictability.
To make the game more atmospheric I recommend playing this game with a set of headphones, with Razer Surround software installed to emulate surround sound. In my playthrough I also turned the music setting to 0, I did this because the ship generally makes a of noise and I wanted to be able to distinguish environmental noise from the noise the alien makes, and I felt adding music to the mix would make it more complicated. Another reason why I turned the music down is because I didn't want to feel like I was playing a movie, I wanted to feel like the main character.
The only big complaint I have with this game is that the ending dragged out a little too much. The last hour of gameplay felt unnecessary. The ending itself felt unsatisfying.
Minor complaints:
The game should tell you to hold F to put new batteries in your torch when you run out.
When holding your breath for too long in a locker you gradually lose life, but the game doesn't tell you this. Running out of life while holding your breath causes you to reveal your hiding spot.
The map should show different kinds of icons for locked doors. Like a door that needs a keycard should have a different symbol from a door that needs a plasma torch.

6/10

To put it in short, absolutely-fricken-amazing. I bought it on sale a week ago and have been playing it for a few hours each night since then, took me 22.7 hours to complete, while playing it at a casual pace.
Fear/Horror: This game is definately scary up to a certain point, if you die a lot (like I) you will learn when the alien is coming and how it attacks you, so the scares go away from that, but I still jump whenever an android rips me out of a closet or grabs me from behind. Amazing atmoshpere for horror, it isn't a game that scares you using jumps, it uses an amazing mixture of intense sounds, lighting, map layout, etc. to scare you. It's hard to explain. Walk down into your basement in the middle of the night and turn all the nights off, it's that sort of feeling.
Graphics/Performance: I don't have a massive ultra high-spec gaming machine that can power the Large Hadron Collider, so I had to run at near minimum-spec graphics, but they were still pretty good, it doesn't feel like there that low. I'm using a Thinkpad E545 with the AMD A10 processor (Yes, it's a laptop, some people don't have enough money for a desktop), but even on a laptop, it performed pretty well, just make sure that you're plugged into an outlet, because you're going to be using a lot of power.
Overall Plot: I can't say much without ruining the game, but it manages to capture the feel and intensity of the Alien movies, exactly. There are elements in the game which were featured in the movies and it follows a spin-off plot. If you're a fan of the movies, you'll really love this game. When you finish this game, you'll become slightly disheartened that it's over, and the ending is one of those endings you just aren't OK with, it's amazing.
Definately would play again (in fact, I already am), I wouldn't put the idea of a sequel to this down, if done right.

Now with the 2nd Edition Review!
(you can find the old, edited review at the bottom)
-So, what is (T)ESO?-
(T)ESO is a MMO based on the Elder Scrolls Series.
You can find all the gods, races and the "whole" Tamriel along the lines which gives it a slight touch of Skyrim (or any other elder scrolls game) feeling.
There are lots of quests and even more places to explore in the huge world of Tamriel but a lot of the sidequests are very repetitive and get boring very fast.
Sadly, its not more than a generic MMO with Skyrim coat and Elderscrolls story.
-The game and its gods-(Molag Bal is the smallest threat)-
The games is full of bugs, even the launcher can break your neck if you dont know what to do against some of the meanest error codes (while support takes literally ages)
-Gameplay & Graphics-
Its just like any generic MMO with a skyrim cloak on, the only difference so far is that you can only use 5 abilities + one ultimate at a time
The only graphical improvement i've seen so far affected some of the races, the rest of the world seems a bit worse than Skyrim (both on highest settings)
Not gonna lie, some of the races look really great now, especially Khajiit.
-DLC's and new content-
After you have bought the game for the price of a farily new AAA game (imperial edition costs even more) you get a nice and greedy slap in the face:
New content such as the only(!) dedicated pvp map and other stuff like the thiefs guild, dark brotherhood and more come as DLC's.
While all the DLC's can be played for free as ESO Plus member(monthly subscription), you can also buy them through the ingame-crown shop at a price of 2000 crowns (dark brotherhood)(thats about 15 euros for one DLC and the others cost even more)
I wouldn't care if it was just bonus stuff, but the only way to get the new abilities, more land to explore and new high power gear is to buy those DLC's (massive paywalls)
-Things that haven't been said already-
- Dev's cant balance the game properly (some classes are extremely op)
- Even the launcher has more bugs and error codes than 70% of the "alpha access" games out on steam
- Only 2 megaservers (NA and EU) with massive lags at peak times but maintenance every week (up to 10 hour maintenance)

Hoo boy, Invisible War. Where do I begin? Well, first off, no, I don't think it's the worst Deus Ex game (that unfortunate honor goes to The Fall, and don't even get me started on GO), but that doesn't mean I think it's the best, either. There are some things I even believe go above and beyond what Deus Ex 1 did, like the fact that you can choose which faction you can side with, and it actually has consequences for who you decide to help. Granted, you can change sides at a whim, but it was much better than having the game say "nope, you're on this side now because your brother told you so" like the first game, and definitely miles above the later games in the franchise, which have no excuse for how linear they are. Hell, I'd even go as far to say that I prefer IW to the Squeenix DX titles in a good amount of ways.
But, of course, as you've probably all heard, there are some issues with the game. Glaring issues, at that, the largest and most pervasive of which is the dumbing down of the systems relative to Deus Ex 1 in order to get the game running (and selling) on the original Xbox. Skill points are gone, with the skills they represented either gone completely or implemented into augmentations. Individual weapon ammunition gets the boot as well, with a universal ammo system that sounds good on paper but fails in implementation in their place. Independent limb damage also gets the boot, meaning that you can't blow your arms and legs off and crawl around using your nipples anymore. The levels have been shrunk in order to fit into the Xbox's 64 MB of RAM (a limitation that the PC port is also upheld to), which means more loading times as well. And, to top it all off, the script complexity got chopped down heavily in order to get it to look good at 480i on a CRT television.
Unfortunately, on top of that, the game has not aged well in the slightest. Without a patch, it wigs out whenever it's played on a multi-core processor, it crashes frequently, and sometimes even refuses to boot for no discernable reason until you reboot your system. It also doesn't support widescreen displays without hex editing or special tools, and even then, it looks absolutely awful. The visuals (which I'm led to believe were a major cause for the levels being so small) are absolutely horrid by today's standards, even when compared to Deus Ex 1. This mainly comes down to the fact that all the humans rest firmly in the uncanny valley. The DX1 characters were awkward, blocky, and all looked the same, but it worked in their favor because the animation matched that. DX2 characters look realistic in comparison, but... Jesus, they're all grotesque. This falls on the animation, mainly. They animate almost exactly like the DX1 characters, and if you've ever seen DX1 with the HDTP models, you know how bad decent models look with that.
But, overall, I enjoyed Invisible War in spite of its flaws. It's the last game made by the original DX crew, and it's definitely got the same spirit as the first, and is quite fun even if it was cut down. You can do much worse for games, hell, you can do much worse for Deus Ex games than Invisible War, and I'd say it's at least worth one go through for you to decide for yourself if this really is the worst DX game like everyone says it is.

The invisible game that some people insist doesn't exist, despite it being better than some of the major titles released in the past year or so. As others have stated, this game would probably have a much bigger fanbase if it simply didn't have "Deus Ex" in the title.
Deus Ex: Invisible War is a sequel to the original Deus Ex, taking place 20 years after a combination of all three of the original game's endings. The world has suffered from "The Collapse", where all global communication was shut down due to what happened in Area 51 at the end of Deus Ex. In the aftermath, the WTO and the Order helped the world recover. But the conspiracies of those who would control the fate of the world--and humanity--didn't end at Area 51. After a terrorist attack that destroys Chicago, the player is put into the shoes of a biomodified agent-in-training that discovers the truth behind the governments and organizations that run the world in 2072.
As one might expect from how many Deus Ex fans pretend the game doesn't exist, there are a few flaws with Invisible War. Said flaws are important to know in advance to give a proper framework for enjoying the game. One of the big ones is that the game was designed specifically to run on the original Xbox as well as the PC, which means that it doesn't always play nice with modern (Windows 7 and onward) PCs and doesn't make use of multiple CPU cores. This also reflects in the level design, which cuts up some areas into smaller sub-areas with loading screens. The Xbox platform also ended up causing a simplification of the interface, which can go a little too far in some cases (such as the low number of potential keybinds).
Another issue with the game, which it shares with the original game, is the blandness of the voice acting. Aside from the voice-modulated Omar cyborgs, a lot of characters sound more like students reading lines from a textbook than characters in a conspiracy thriller. Sometimes it was intentional or justified (such as JC's monotone in both games, which has reasons that the developers have stated), but most of the time you'll have to add inflection mentally to really get into the story.
On the good side of things, Invisible War allows the same kind of emergent solution-finding as any other Deus Ex game. If you really try, you can play the game in almost any way you want. With the right gear and biomods, you'll almost always have at least two ways to accomplish an objective (and you'll probably have an alternate objective that still continues the story). Stealth, combat (lethal or non-lethal), diplomacy, hacking, lockpicking, and vent-crawling are all encouraged. There are a few overpowered builds (such as melee strength + stealth + baton for near-instant KOs of unarmored human enemies), but almost every option has at least some use. And unlike some games, you'll get more than enough upgrade points to upgrade every biomod, and you have the ability to swap out biomods if you don't like them (at the cost of losing the spent points in the rejected mod). So if you regret your choice in biomods, you don't always have to start over to try again.
The story is much shorter than the original game and Human Revolution, clocking in at about 10 hours if you do ~90% of the content. However, there are enough alternate scenes and objectives that it can be worth replaying if a single playthrough isn't enough. The story itself is decent as a more sci-fi followup to the ending of Deus Ex, but there are some important characters that don't get enough development or screentime and the pacing ramps up a bit too quickly near the end (and leads to an area with so many enemies that some playstyles will be extra difficult at the end). The final choices in the last location are interesting from a philosophical standpoint, but the endings don't seem to fully develop these ideas (many of which were better handled in the ending monologues of Human Revolution).
All in all, it is a good game that gets more bad press than it deserves. It won't ever be able to step out of the shadow of the original Deus Ex or the more recent revival prequels, but it's still a good diversion for those who enjoy cyberpunk games that allow for the freedom of problem-solving that Deus Ex is known for.

Wow, I don't get all the negative reviews about this game.  Although, I agree with the general consensus that this is not on the level of the first Deus Ex in terms of overall game mechanics, depth of story, and function; I still think this game in and of itself is worthy of at least a decent rating to say the least.
What I liked:
I personally liked how the game integrated weapon upgrades and I liked how the weapons themselves functioned, although I do agree that the biomods and overall mechanics are more deeper in Deus Ex 1, this games mechanics while not as intricate are still good in their own right, and you have to remember this was made for both PC and consoles simultaneously so naturally there are going to be some hardware limitations both in function and overall game layout (now weither that is the way it should or was intended to have been is up for debate).
I also liked the very deep explanation and reasoning that JC Denton gave for his world plan, I thought some of the end game speeches were very emotional in terms of philosphy and relatability to the current state of affairs in our world and evolution.  I also liked how alot of the side quests had some end-ties that made you think about people and morality (like the 'coffee wars' and the 'real' NG resonance).
What I disliked:
What I disliked about the game were its minor bugs and quirky mechanics (like the jumping sometimes was springy and ascending and descending ladders sometimes was glitchy as well).  I also disliked the loading screens and I think the devs should have addressed this for the PC release, but as for a console the loading screens are justified due to obvious hardware constraints.
I also disliked the random crashes when simultaneously alt-tabbing and using google chrome, as well as some very rare crash(es) that only happened 1 or 2 times out of 30+ hours of gameplay.  I also thought the keymapping wasn't very well implemented and the fact the steam overlay didn't work due to some .exe anomoly was kinda lazy to not be addressed for the steam release in my opinion. And lastly I thought some of the dialogue was dry and uneventful during some parts of the game.
What is up for debate:
The universal ammo system could be a tossup in terms of it being good or bad as well as how the limited augmentations are implemented, althought the limited augs/biomods and the ability to interchange them mid-game somewhat makes sense in terms of form and function.  As well as how the devs decided to merge all three past endings to be the cannon for this game is all up for debate and is not either good or bad in my opinion.
Pros:
+Very good mid-game and end-game story dialogue that really has some deep morality and philsophical messages.
+Good weapon mechanics and entertaining ragdoll physics.
+Stylish weapons and atmosphere that really capture the futuristic cyberpunk lore.
+Game title that really fits the layout of the game (the wars really are invisible as they are mostly all internal).  As well as some good cannonical endings and happenings that mostly tie in well with the first deus ex (although the implementation of all 3 endings of Deus Ex 1 is debatable in terms of how it was implemented).
+Good music/ambiance and implementation of throwback remixes from Deus Ex 1
Cons:
-Load times that should have been addressed for the PC port.
-Poorly implemented steam interface in terms of in-game functionality of the overlay that should have been addressed pre-release in steam.
-some minor mechanic bugs that seem obvious (namely the jump mechanic and ladder climbing seemed like it had clippng issues at times).
-debatable mechanics in terms of form and function (namely universal ammo and a debatable sneak detection mechanic)
Overall I give this game a strong 7.5/10

However, I find that the first game had a better narrative with a better "villain".  The gameplay mechanics have been tweaked and improved and feel far better than the previous title.
I truly recommend this game for those of you who are looking for a Resident Evil 4 kind of game, or if you like creative and disturbing monster designs from Silent Hill with great boss battles. This is by far one of the best games of 2017 and it deserves far more attention than it is getting.

Honesly with the amount of hype I had for this game, it doesn't surprise me that I was dissapointed. Whenever I get excited for a game it never delivers the promises it makes.
The biggest problem I have right off the bat is how completely underpowered you start. I understand that as the game progresses, you get more powerful, but even at the highest upgrade point in the second you feel so weak compared to Corvo in the first. Here are a few examples:
-I have no proof but I feel so much slower in this game. Even with weapons sheathed sprinting feels like a light jog, and even WITH the bonecharms I feel slow.
-Speaking of bonecharms, this time around they feel so pathetic, especially since you can craft them to be four times as potent. However, with that in mind, I feel as if the developers purposefully made them suck so you don't get too powerful. I'd understand if this was a multiplayer game, but since it's solo why SHOULDN'T I be overpowered? Even with all upgrades and useful bonecharms, compared to the first I feel weak. Blink, again no proof, but to me felt as if it has less range, especially Emily's tentacle. Also after 15 years Corvo has essentially the same powers with no upgrades? Did the outsider take them away from him?
-On a slight tangent, in the first Dishonored, all you really needed to find the charms and bones was the heart, since they were placed in logical places. This time, they're so obnoxiously hidden I needed a guide because I felt so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, which completely breaks the little immersion left, since they won't. stop. narrating. I enjoy reading because it's MY voice, thus making me feel as if I'M the one playing.
-What the everloving F*** was the team thinking with this absolutely abysmal dark vision? First of all, EVERYTHING is yellow, the world is a dark yellow and EVERY item is a slightly lighter yellow, whereas in the first game different types of items had different colors, thus making the power actually useful. Not only is dark vision pointless since everything is F***ing dark, but they also had the genius idea of making it work as a radar with an effective radius of 5 feet, and of course the items don't STAY lit. F*** dark vision it's literally pointless, whereas in the first game I always used it, especially as a tool to lay the foundation of a building. This dark vision DOESN'T EVEN WORK THROUGH WALLS!!! (I think haven't played in a while since I beat it once and felt no desire to run through it again)
-The story is so bland and literally offers no suspense as YOU KNOW how it ends, Corvo/Emily kill the bad witch and all is well in dunwall, whereas the first one had a story that a first time player wouldn't easily guess, nor is it so rushed. Initially Corvo returns unsuccessfully, plays with his daughter, talks to the empress, witnesses her murder, and goes to jail. This feels organic and realistic. In the second, you see Emily, bored of being a ruler and wishing she wasn't, and then BAM guess what your wish came true, some lady who offers no real proof that she is a Kaldwin points a finger at you and says you're guilty, and Emily's "loyal" subjects literally shrug their shoulders and say sure why not. Then, for whatever reason, even though Delilah could easily kill them both, she instead lets one live, for some reason, and orders the other one to be captured, again for some reason (so the game can progress stfu hater=lazy writing). It makes no sense and rushes the game along to start.
-The only level I actually remember playing was Jindosh's level. One giant nagging question, in a city that is plagued by bloodflies, who feast on the deceased and drink blood, why, dear god WHY doesn't the city clean the streets that are literally littered with rivers of blood and piles of dead whales? The fist one made sense as the plague was a thing you could catch but this time they're just carnivorous flies. Why wouldn't the city at least attempt to mitigate the problem?
All in all this game felt rushed out and because of that the feel of the world is slowed in order to pad the runtime. I thoroughly enjoyed playing the first one, I initially had it for the xbox, and out of love I purchased it again. This game? I've played 26 hours. I don't see myself going past 30. Is it a bad game? No. Is it good? Again, no. It's ok, Initially I was going to type that it doesn't desrve its spot on the top 10 of 2016 but considering the other releases I can't confidently say that. I entered hopeful and left dissapointed.

Dishonored 2 Review
I don’t think I’ve ever been as hyped as I had been for a game as I was with Dishonored 2. The amount of variation to each time you play the game from the game’s bewildering mechanics cannot do anything but leave me in awe. The almost unlimited ways you can use the special powers keeps the game fun for dozens of hours.
Dishonored 2 is a first person, stealth video game that takes place in a reimagined world of the Victorian era, one that also offers elements of supernatural magic. Dishonored 2 takes place in a southern European island known as Karnaca, infamous for their blood fly plague, dust storms, clashing factions, and the dreaded Crowned Killer.
One area where Dishonored 2 excels in is its stellar level design. One of the great things about their levels is they all are surrounded by a special theme. One mission you are sneaking through a mansion that changes its layout as you progress through it to another mission where you are teleporting between current day and 1849 version of a house to unreachable locations. And the other great thing about their levels is that there are so many different ways to progress through them. You can play through the same mission more than once and never go through the same area.
One place where you can take away from the game is its somewhat lackluster and predictable story. It is nothing to praise, but one thing you can praise is their attention to smaller stories outside of the realm of the main character that can be picked up through notes and the people around the missions.
Additional Notes:
So some other things I didn't get to mention was the poor performance of some PCs which sure sucks, but I believe that as long as you follow their recommendations you should be fine. I mean you can't really expect to run a brand new 2016 game on PC with 2010 hardware or ect. And if you want my specs I have a FX 8350 and GTX 1080 and got a solid 70fps on Ultra settings. Some people complain that the fps sucks but thats just because they aren't used to playing at < 100 fps.
And to further elaborate on CONS of the game besides performance:
I'd say the story kinda sucks in this game. They kinda just shoved a familiar face into the main antagonist just because and I honestly probably would've prefered otherwise, but I guess they can't really have witches in the game without her so it ended up being okay. And as a counterarguement to the claim the story sucks, I'd say that the lore in this game is great. I love the world that Dishonored has built up from all of the books or abandoned houses or through almost anything, the world and backstory of the Dishonored universe has a great feel.
And another thing is that there is only 9 missions. Granted each mission is about 2-3 hours long per but it definitely does end up feeling like a short game even though a playthrough is around 20 hours. Still though if I were to go in again blind, I would still pay $60 for this game because this leads me into my next part.
A final thing to touch on is that why I would recommend this game is because ARKANE LOVES DISHONORED AND ITS FANBASE! I'm sure you've seen that they have given out TWO FREE UPDATES since it's original release adding in more awesome ways to play. Heck they've even been giving out free PS4s, Collectors Editions of the game, and even awesome artwork from the game on their Twitter! I know they get crap for releasing the PC version unoptimised, but they should get the credit they deserve for working as hard as possible right after and also apologizing by giving out free content. They basically gave up their Thanksgiving break to fix the game so others could enjoy their breaks. I feel so bad when I see how little of my friends own this game and probably how poorly its done on the Steam market. They've poored their hearts out onto this game I wish they were rewarded greater for their efforts. I'm just afraid that if this game did poor, what is to say for the rest of the franchise? I don't want this amazing of a series to end right here. So I'll end on this...
BUY DISHONORED 2 AND SUPPORT THE DEVELOPERS IF YOU WANT TO SEE MORE FROM DISHONORED IN THE FUTURE!
And PS... ITS NOT A PORT BOI IF I HEAR THAT ONE MORE TIMEEEEEEEEE

In this review I'll describe how the game feels to play, some of the features and upcoming features, how the bots are, what I hope to see for the future of this game, and maybe some more. It's a little lengthy but feel free to read if you would like a longer form review for this game.
----
It's too bad Steam has the simplified Y/N Recommendation system, especially for games like Ravenfield. If you're spending $15 on this game now, you'll probably find that the game doesn't quite meet the content you'd excpect at that price, though it does have enough to dig your feet in -- 3 maps and a preview of a 4th, a handful of weapon choices, two game modes (which don't really play that much differently from each other), and a few customization options like how many bots you want added, how you want the teams balanced (bot distribution), a respawn timer, and an option to reverse the teams' starting points or switch your own team. There's also a Day/Night option (with night-vision goggles) which makes for a fun variation to play with.
What you are getting for you money however, and you'll see this right away -- is a game with absolutely massive potential for fun and replayability. When you open the game, you'll be met with a very pleasant sight -- a grayed-out "Coming Soon!" button for a Mods section. When you get yourself into this game you'll see quickly why this button will potentially unlock a huge world of various time settings, landscapes, game types, and more if a community grows from this game.
The game is simplistic, easy and quick to jump into, and all-around perfectly made for a game you can throw on and start playing in 30 seconds. By far, my favorite feature in the game is the Slow Motion feature. This is so cool when you are playing some great music in the background, it looks GREAT and it can be like controlling your own frag movie in real time with how you switch back and forth from slow motion and regular.
What I love about this game so far also is that you can tell the single player only feature is actually what will make a lot of things about the game shine and give it potential for features that simply would not work in a multiplayer setting. The slow motion is an example of this, there is no timer or powerup needed, you can use it for any duration and there's no cooldown, which is exactly how I want it. You don't have to worry about any of that stuff and you can control everything yourself -- if you want to only allow yourself to use it for 3 seconds, use it for 3 seconds! If you want to use it for 5 minutes straight, go for it! All the choices are yours and you can make the game as easy as you want or as difficult.
The bots on Challenging are good enough. They're decently quick and if they run in a group it's easy to get overrun. They're pretty accurate from far distances too. You can use Slow Motion to dodge bullets, as the bullets in this game are not instant point-click-laserbeam, they have velocity and move (what looks to me) almost slightly slower than regular bullets. This means you have to lead shots from far away which adds an extra challenge to keep you wanting to improve your game. Alot of the bots get stuck in places and will repeatedly get stuck in those places after dying, so that will have to get fixed.
The vehicles are pretty good, a little bit plain though and they feel more like World War II era vehicles (next to modern guns which is weird). The mechanics of them are really good, I think I might just suck♥♥♥♥♥with the helicopter but it does feel a little bit unstable, I can't seem to get it to hover, but that might definitely just be me.
I love the guns. It's a great start, not sure if they plan to make more (it'd be cool if they did!) but it gives you a basic multiplayer FPS layout of guns with a variety ranging between shotguns and revolvers to snipers and assault rifles. The explosives are a lot of fun and were a great addition. The scalpel is really cool, especially in Slow Motion!
It didn't take very long at all for me to eat through most of the content this game offers, but it has enough for me to have gotten enough playtime and enough enjoyment to definitely make the $15 worth it, and I am REALLY looking forward to seeing where this game's future is. If more and more content, maps, weapons, game modes, and mods come into the picture -- this could very easily be a game I continue to play for years to come.
P.S. I recommend turning on the "beta branch" for the time being -- Right click in Library --> Properties --> Beta. This will get you a head start on the new features the developer is working on. For example, right now there is a newer version of the Archipelago level that really opens things up, one new gun, a whole new awesome type of vehicle (a warship with a beastly mortar that is a ton of fun to play), and some mechanics updates. If you want to get extra/newer features and don't mind a rougher edge on some of them (which doesn't seem noticeable) this option is for you.

NOW, this game is a masterfully crafted love letter to fans of the orginal Half-Life. Every detail is captured flawlessly in this HD remake. For the asking price, it's very much worth it. And on sale, it's an absolute STEAL.
If what you're looking for is a modern, remastered version of the orginal Half-Life, then I strongly recommend you do.

To put it in short, absolutely-fricken-amazing. I bought it on sale a week ago and have been playing it for a few hours each night since then, took me 22.7 hours to complete, while playing it at a casual pace.
Fear/Horror: This game is definately scary up to a certain point, if you die a lot (like I) you will learn when the alien is coming and how it attacks you, so the scares go away from that, but I still jump whenever an android rips me out of a closet or grabs me from behind. Amazing atmoshpere for horror, it isn't a game that scares you using jumps, it uses an amazing mixture of intense sounds, lighting, map layout, etc. to scare you. It's hard to explain. Walk down into your basement in the middle of the night and turn all the nights off, it's that sort of feeling.
Graphics/Performance: I don't have a massive ultra high-spec gaming machine that can power the Large Hadron Collider, so I had to run at near minimum-spec graphics, but they were still pretty good, it doesn't feel like there that low. I'm using a Thinkpad E545 with the AMD A10 processor (Yes, it's a laptop, some people don't have enough money for a desktop), but even on a laptop, it performed pretty well, just make sure that you're plugged into an outlet, because you're going to be using a lot of power.
Overall Plot: I can't say much without ruining the game, but it manages to capture the feel and intensity of the Alien movies, exactly. There are elements in the game which were featured in the movies and it follows a spin-off plot. If you're a fan of the movies, you'll really love this game. When you finish this game, you'll become slightly disheartened that it's over, and the ending is one of those endings you just aren't OK with, it's amazing.
Definately would play again (in fact, I already am), I wouldn't put the idea of a sequel to this down, if done right.
