Before I start, I have to note that from the ground up, when it comes to character and world design, music, and writing I have nothing negative to say. This is a solid addition to the canon Alien mythos with some interesting twists on old ideas and some of the same familiar themes. So, off the top, this is going to be a slight recommendation for Alien fans and a slight recommendation for buying the game at a discount, which I did (about $14-$20).
Now, as for the nuts and bolts. If you judge a game solely by dollar value per hour of gameplay, you're good to go with this one. You will spend a lot of time trying to get to the end. The problem is that, unfortunately, much of that time is spent backtracking. You will backtrack a lot. It will be by design. In one mission, I found myself criss-crossing a 600 square foot stretch of white padded real estate at least four times and found myself wondering if I had actually gone insane and was really locked in an asylum.
The backtracking isn't so much of a problem itself, except that the hook is an unstoppable murder-machine who will kill you on sight. Imagine playing a game of musical chairs and when the music stops a guy in black leather screeches and punches you in the face. That will happen more than once. You will become familiar with the same territory and you might get bored and irritated.
As for the freaky violent leather monster, the star of this game is a wonderfully-recreated xenomorph/alien whose job it is to hunt you down and kill you. And if I seem to be exaggerating, rest assured  -- this creature exists to kill YOU. The conceit is that you, Amanda Ripley (estranged daughter of Ellen Ripley), are trapped on a failing space station with this monster and have to survive rampaging androids, paranoid humans, and a killer monster picking people off.
This is not actually true. Yes, while the xenomorph will occasionally get pissy if humans start firing guns and kill one or two, it exists solely to eat YOU, the player. And that's when the AI starts to fall apart and all of the seams in this game show.
As a survival horror fan, I'm used to unforgiving monsters tearing me to shreds for making the wrong move. In Alien: Isolation, you will be filled with a constant sense of dread. Not because you never know when the alien will appear but because the alien is ALWAYS THERE. No matter how silent you are, no matter how long you hide, the alien KNOWS you are there and will make it its personal hobby to run around like an idiot for five minutes at 30 miles an hour, jump out of a random ceiling vent, walk in aimless circles for another two or three minutes and then jump back in the vent to repeat the process.
OCCASIONALLY, the alien will get bored and disappear altogether -- for about one minute -- before returning to desperately hunt you down and eat you. It makes one wonder, "Why is everyone so afraid of this thing? It obviously just wants to eat me."
If the alien had been a punishment for engaging in combat or running down halls or getting in a fight. If the sense of dread at the pervasive, ever-present existence of a referee stepping in to say, "Just checking to make sure you know I exist. Feel free to hang out in that locker for the length of a movie trailer while I stretch my legs or you'll have to replay 15 minutes of the game."
No, but seriously, this alien is really obnoxious and not scary at all. But let's continue...
Androids. No complaints with them, since they're scary because aliens suck and androids distract you from aliens. Also, the cut scenes are really great.
Humans. Now, the devs keep stating that the human dialogue determines how they respond to you. Except I've had humans tell me to back away and then FOLLOW ME when I left only to shoot me in the back and tell me they didn't want to do that. But their AI is ridiculous anyway. I've thrown flares right into the middle of crowds and had them not even notice. I've thrown noisemakers and have them comment that there's a really strange sound and then start walking in the other direction. This AI is really bad.
Other highlights:
You draw attention to a group of armed human survivors who seem to not care one bit about the alien...you throw a noisemaker...the alien drops out of a vent, eats two of them, then proceeds to spend the rest of its time running around desperately trying to find YOU, the player, who it DOESN'T EVEN KNOW IS IN THE ROOM.
God help you if it sees you. While a half dozen humans are firing wildly at it, the alien will chase you in circles around a table in a desperate attempt to get the one unarmed person in the room minding its own business.
Like an albatross punishing you for bothering to spend money on this game, the alien is on your motion detector. You sneaking through an empty hallway? Alien is there. You creeping under the table of an abandoned office? The alien is on your motion detector. While at one point I was under the impression that the alien's arrival would be punishment for picking fights, starting generators without a backup plan, or throwing a flashbang, I quickly learned that the alien's arrival was punishment for playing the game.
I could see the devs sitting in front of a white board asking themselves what they needed. "You know what this conversation about rigging electrical backups and rebooting computer systems needs? More alien."
After the second death, the shine wears off. Instead of worrying about screwing up and incurring the wrath of the monster you understand that the monster is just there, like sparking wires or moody music, a way to establish the setting. It's not even scary anymore, just this irritating thing forcing you to constantly keep one eye on the lockers you probably won't even use that much because hiding in them doesn't actually make the alien leave, it just makes it not kill you when it randomly decides to jump out of the ceiling and take a stroll...maybe grab a cup of coffee.
And after 20 hours (oh, my, GOD, you will feel that time...) of watching it move you realize, "This is a stupid robot running on RNG values waiting for me to do something arbitrarily stupid so I can think I screwed up." The AI is really bad.
Also (SLIGHT SPOILERS AFTER THIS)...
Fire. This is supposed to scare the alien off, and while I understand that it eventually loses its efficacy, you've got to be kidding me. In one mission I won't name, the alien drops out of a vent (obviously scripted) and starts desperately running around the room looking for you. The easy way around is to throw a flare in advance and it will stare at it hypnotized, but come on...seriously? There's no way to avoid this alien, unless you know it's going to be there, without firebombing her in the face and it's SCRIPTED.
As for how effective the fire is, in that same mission I lit the alien up, it jumped in a vent, I turned around and TWO SECONDS LATER it jumped out of the vent behind me and ate me. COME ON! And this was one of several missions where you're not really hiding from the alien, you're just waiting for it to jump out of a vent and make a mad charge at you like a bull waiting for you to burn its face and jump out of the way (seriously, jump out of the way if you don't want to get smacked).
...............
That said, it controls well, it plays well, it looks well, and if you turn the music down all of the way the really great soundtrack doesn't make it impossible to hear people sneaking up on you while it blasts heavy techno drowning everything out.
...A slight recommendation.

This game is all about balancing an ecosystem, which sounds easy in theory, but can be much more challenging than you'd actually think. There are three different kinds of ecosystems you can work with: desert, plains, and rainforest. Each one has its own challenges to overcome and its own flora and fauna to interact with each other.
There are three kinds of living things that you can place in your biodome: consumers, producers, and decomposers; within the consumer category, there are four kinds: herbivore, carnivore, insectivore, and omnivore.
Balancing an ecosystem can be challenging as you need to place each of those previous mentioned living entities in such a way that they interact in a positive and beneficial way, not only to themselves, but to the flora and fauna around them.
All-in-all, this game is very well-done. It's simple, yet full of so much thought and preparation. If you're getting this game for an educational purpose, I don't think you will be disappointed.
If you are getting this game in order to mess around and try to break the ecosystem, have fun. During my gameplay, I intentionally starved several carnivores just to see what would happen. The poor things dropped like a bad habit.
In any case, I highly recommend this game. The price is reasonable for what you're getting and if you balance your biodomes properly, you can have several long hours observing the impact of your decisions over the course of in-game weeks, months, and years.

What a refreshing MMO-experience!
The whole world of TESO is such a coherent, vivid and story-rich environment I've never seen before. The lore of the classic single player series (Morrwind - Oblivion - Skyrim) is seriously embroidered into this MMO and there are not much compromises.
PROS:
- hugely immersive world and storyline. It's not easy to wrap the classic structural MMO-quest features into something exciting (fetch this, kill X of that, etc.) but here the intensive and brilliantly composed storyline dresses everything up so nicely that I see epicness having a feast in this game.
- great roleplay. The lore of the game world is huge and extensive and the characters have a strong connection to the overall flow. Countless books to find and read to enhance the immersion further and create a depth no other MMO I've played could deliver.
- simple and yet overly flexible character building. There are no rigid classes and skill trees, anyone can build literally anything from the available races and classes because there's a great freedom in spending the skill points earned by the level ups. Want a sorcerer who can wield a two handed sword? Do it. Want an archer who does magic too? Go for it. Creativity has a great chance here to join the game.
- crafting, enchanting. The system allows a great deal of possibilities in a very sensible structure: constructing, deconstructing, upgrading, researching. Clear as the mountain stream and simple enough not to push players to grind mindlessly. Even those tiny details: getting raw materials take only a few seconds at the source without wasting a lot of time watching a repetitive animation every time.
- combat system. It's just a perfect balance of the classic button pressing parade and the skill based moves: it does matter here to manage the distance (no automation!) and to choose what moves to execute and from what angle. Defending properly also requires personal skill and quick decisions rather than fully relying on the level of the character or the triggered actions learned.
- HUD. It was strange first to have so little information on the screen but after a few hours I started to consider this as a fresh air of added realism. I like to "learn" my way around rather than having a mini map blocking a big ching of my view on the screen: a single line compass on the top does a great job and serves very well. There are only 5 slots on the quick bar which again may sound like a harsh limitation but it does make the game much better in my eyes - it's actually a great part of building my character on a certain way around a few skills and combos and it certainly boosts the strategy value of the game to select "that five" skills to express the best of the character.
- character creation and build. Again, it's simple and yet very deep: only a handful of attributes, all customaizable by the player and not engraved by the race or class, works like a charm. The skill tree also eliminated a lot of classic but unused elements and what's left of it blends into the game world perfectly and offers a great deal of variation and strategic planning. Everything is connected, reading in-game script and books can affect the skill development not just adding a whole lot to the game lore. It's not the character's level at first what improves the skill but the usage rate of that skill - want to have a good two handed weapon skill on a higher level? Stop firing arrows and bring that axe on to battle!
- graphics, music, sounds. All wonderful, seriously immersive and I still have a hard time to belive that it's possible on this level. The world is simply the most attractive and enchanting one I've ever played as an MMO. All dialogs are in excellent quality, famous actors as well involved so it's not just reading masses of tiny letters in a text box. The world is widely interactive, it's possible to talk to literally everyone. Every NPC comes alive with a sentence or two further detailing the whole game world with charm.
- Pricing. This is - for me at least - a very important positive experience: there's an entry price and from that it's free. Really. No pay to win, the game store is there for those willing to pay some extra for a cosmetic or vanity game element or would like to get some extra features earlier than those play for it rather than pay for it.
CONS:
- can't really list anything here so far, however I barely scratched the surface of the game until this point - steam's measurement on my hours spent in the game however is totally inaccurate, possibly because I always start the game from its own launcher rather than through steam.
I can't refer to PVP yet as I have to dig myself into it more, so as guild play is an unknown area for me so far.
Soloing in this game is such a great fun! :)
Will come back to update this review when I feel I have enough experince on the missing topics.

Please take this thumbs up with a serious grain of salt, because I may recommend The Evil Within 2... but
to people who played the first game and got really attached to the characters & universe and want more. Or people who really enjoy games with the words survival/open world/crafting attached to them. I've never met anyone like that but they're probably out there somewhere, considering how many new games fall into all three of those categories these days.
Now, I absolutely adore the first Evil Within game. It is one of my absolute favorites, and the perfect kind of survival horror for me (I prefer games like Dead Space and Alan Wake to things like Amnesia or Outlast). But this sequel just... doesn't sit right. Was it bad? No. But it really wasn't good either. It's like... the Dead Space 3 of The Evil Within series. It's alright but it doesn't feel right in the context of the series.
- The narrative felt very disjointed. It's like someone couldn't decide which villain would be better, so they threw all three options in one after another. Because of this, the buildup that I loved so much in the first game (beginning confusion, revealing the Big Bad, slowly delving into their past and motivations, and eventually confronting them for a final boss fight) isn't there.
It's hard to even care about defeating them.
- The goals just... become repetitive, far worse than the first game was. Instead of the sequence of "get through this dungeon for one or two plot-related cutscenes, rinse and repeat for 15 extremely long chapters" it's now
It's just... not engaging. Emotional, yes, but not engaging.
- People criticize the first Evil Within for having a confusing narrative, various plot holes, and not giving enough information, but this game is far, far worse. While in the first games most things were explained through research notes or characters speculation, that's not done here. The notes in this game were largely useless and unimportant, offering almost nothing to your understanding of STEM and what was happening. Even if you put in the time to find every note, unlike the first game, you won't learn much of anything... and as someone who did put in that effort in the first game, this disappoints me a lot. It's like.. the first game was largely told through background info, and not the characters spelling it out for you... and then this game is the exact opposite. Instead of evening it out they tipped the scale too far over.
- Cutscenes have amazing, gorgeous shots. However, most the conversations you have with others will only have two awkward camera angles, one looking at Sebastian and the other at whoever you're talking to. The movements during these conversations are also extremely awkward. Think Dragon Age: Origins meets Fallout 4, but a thousand times stiffer. This would be fine if it wasn't any important conversations, but.. it isn't just done for sidequests, there are conversations in the main plot that look like this. The difference between cutscenes and coversations is... jarring.
- New characters
You're given little to no background for each of them, and none of them are shown to have any kind of relationship which each other or anyone else. They feel extremely static, and it's hard to become attached to them.
- Side missions only reward supplies. They don't effect anything else, and it kind of feels pointless to have them at all.
- Old characters feel a bit ignored, particulary
- While the original had a few moments of awkward, heavy handed dialogue, this game is full of it. I love this series so much, and usually I can handle weird dialogue in games, but even I couldn't keep myself from cringing during many of the conversations... and all of Sebastian's character growth in the game felt very, very forced.
- The areas just weren't scary or interesting, and there was no real atmosphere to this game. Empty streets, some of the Haunted/Lost (the "zombies" in the game) roaming around, and some supplies... that's really all there is for 90% of the game, and you revisit the same locations many times. The areas just felt like a lot of nothing.
- If you're playing with a controller, the aim assist isn't an assist. It's basically just an aimbot. You just have to scope and immediately pull the trigger for an instant headshot. Personally I don't really mind, I play more for story than gameplay, but that will likely bother some people.
Basically if you want this for the gameplay, go ahead. But if you're looking to get invested in The Evil Within series here, please don't. Save some money and buy the first game instead. The plot is a bit vague and the gameplay sometimes tedious but it has a lot of charm, a well done atmosphere, and the original characters were all very interesting and memorable and I adore them to this day. It's true I did like a few parts of this game, but not enough to honestly recommend it to newcomers. It's emotional, but not interesting or engaging like the first one was.

This is a great game for those left with an itch unscratched after Resident Evil threw its third person horror into the ground. The Evil Within was a great game, but left an odd feeling in my mouth. It felt that there was a lot of wasted potential in the first game. The story was great, the gameplay was alright, the horror was amazing, but there was something missing.
Polish.
Polish was missing. While The Evil Within was a great game in its own right, it lacked smoothness in its stride. The controls and gameplay were lunky but enjoyable, the story was all over the place and at many times incoherent, and the enemies were clunky and easily exploitable. It was clear that all the parts for a great game were there, but it just wasn't ready yet.
Enter The Evil Within 2.
The Evil Within 2 is a perfect sequel to an already great game. They fixed a lot of complaints people had about the first, (namely the story) by making it more easy to follow yet on top of an already mysterious and powerful antagonist organization. This review won't contain any story spoilers, so rest easy if you get upset at that sort of thing. Let's start with the gameplay first.
The gameplay was fixed and served to us with extra polish. The shooting feels nice and has a lot of meat in every shot regardless of the weapon. Speaking of weapons, we're treated to quite a few new weapons as well as refurbished old ones. Players of the original game might remember the Agony Crossbow, which is making its return in the form of the Warden Crossbow. It plays virtually the same but with one or two new bolts to use. Stealth was fixed from the first game by making it a viable strategy in many areas of the game rather than an afterthought in a few places like the first game. Unfortunately, the easily exploitable "stun then stealth stab" mechanic still exists, so try not to break the game doing it, even if it is fun. Enemies have new AI, but despite this are also extremely exploitable. In many of the open areas (I'll get to that in a minute), enemies called The Lost (The Haunted from the previous game, just looks less deformed and more detailed) patrol around. Due to this, they have a very tight "leash" and will lose you very easily if you just sprint away from them. This leads to making virtually every mistake you could make in one of these sub-open world areas inconsequential.
One complaint I don't think anyone had about The Evil Within was that it was too linear. However, Tango Gameworks took strides to fix this "issue" anyways. Now, in addition to your linear story missions, you complete these missions in a somewhat open world environment. There are a few areas that are open with all of them connected to eachother via a "tunnel" system called The Marrow, another sub-open world environment that you unlock portions of as you progress through the game. To fill up this "open world", there are a handful of side quests as well as mini-encounters, secrets to uncover, and a hidden series of quests that ends with a not-so-hidden quest near the end of the game. While almost no one complained about The Evil Within's lack of non-linear action, the way they handled a slightly open world area is actually quite nice. It makes sense and fits thematically with the story and the action of the game.
Due to its baby steps into open world mechanics, The Evil Within 2 has a small crafting system. This system allows you to craft ammo for your guns, bolts for your crossbow, and medical syringes/kits. On lower difficulties, this system almost completely breaks the game, as you will receive more than enough resources to craft yourself a quasi-infinite amount of ammo, bolts, and medical supplies without sprinting off the beaten path all too often. On the other hand, on the harder difficulties, the crafting system does a very good job of forcing you to allocate your resources wisely. Do you need an extra couple of Sniper Rifle bullets or a few Shotgun shells?
The upgrade system didn't escape rennovation either. While the basics from the first game are there, there are also quite a few new and unique upgrades, such as the ability to completely avoid some attacks, slowing down time to concentrate on your shots better, or "Bullet Cascade," which increases your gun damage with every shot you hit an enemy with. The fan-favorite Green Gel returns, with his twin sister, Red Gel. Red Gels is rare in the town of Union, but thankfully, not a lot is needed. Some upgrade nodes are locked to the player until they unlock it using Red Gel. Weapon upgrades are no longer done using Green Gel, but instead with Weapon Parts, a resource commonly found in crates or just randomly lying around. You can upgrade your weapon's damage, reload speed, etc. All the basics are there. Nothing much changed besides the amount of upgrades and the method of obtaining them. Still, credit where credit is due, upgrades feel a lot more organic (no pun intended).
The musical scores and the art direction of the game are amazing, as always. I don't want to give it away, but a certain struggling artist has both the best levels in the game and the best soundtrack.
TL;DR This game is very good. If you're a completionist with a third person shooter itch, this game will scratch it. If you're a horror game enthusiast that Resident Evil 4 left a gaping black hole in, this game will fill it. If you really liked the first game but noticed a few of its more glaring flaws, you'll love this game.

After having the game for years (hence my 30+ hours) and having tried to like it for so long, I thought it finally clicked for me once I gave it a proper shot with the new unofficial patch. I managed to overlook its technically shoddy
gameplay and have a great time in the games first hub. I enjoyed it so much it joined my list of favourite games ever. After that first hub (which lasted roughly 3 hours) however, I hit my first real main objective of infiltrating a
weapons manufacturer's facility in order to accomplish one of two goals given to me by opposing factions both willing to have me join their agenda. Things started to fall apart here. The level was linear and uninteresting and it just wasn't
as fun as the previous hours. I was hardly willing to let that stop me enjoying the whole game though so I continued. When I hit the second hub world this is where I knew that even overlooking the technical failings of this game that were
an issue for so many years (and still are to some extent, despite the patch), the game still sucked. It's a shame. Maybe this hub world just sucks as well, I don't know, but I was unwilling to go on.
The first hub felt like the original and was thoroughly interesting in its world and vast amount of sidequests but the setting, story, characters, writing and most importantly; level design, all failed to impress during the second hub
world. It got a bit strange, too. I was investigating kids, led by a headmaster, who had been missing and in doing so I found that some were in way of 'termination'. I don't know, everything was a bit off. Even if you love Thief Deadly
Shadows (like I absolutely do) and don't mind the engine or think the patch will fix it totally, there's no assurance you'll like this even if you like Deus Ex. It's inferior in every concievable way, even at its best moments.

++The endings are a big improvement over the original
++Augmentations are far better done in this than the original
++You can kill stuck-up, bratty academic kids
+It looks pretty damn impressive for 2003, even despite its shortcomings in its real technicality
+The music is actually really good, if lacking in comparison to the originals more in your face soundtrack
+Passive augmentations are a big yes
+Weapon mods have been improved
+Different ways around enivronments is cool
+Weapons feel very impactful
+Sound design is of a higher quality
+-Loading screens every two seconds is frustrating, but if Half-Life can get away as a masterpiece with having one down every corridor then so can this in every bit of its hubs
-+The faction system is interesting in concept but the lack of consequences for siding on each is disappointing
+-Does universal ammo suck? Absolutely. In terms of gameplay though it didn't bother me nearly as much as I expected. It just means you're always 100% stocked up in this case even if you play it like an FPS.

If ever there was a game that was judged by association, this it it.
More than anything, Invisible War is judged by the Deus Ex in it's name. Before it is even installed, it is expected to be at least as good and preferably better than one of the greatest games of all time. Hardly fair odds.
As a result many people don't see anything other than the fact that Invisible War is not the same as the original Deus Ex. It doen't get a chance to stand on it's own and be judged on merit.
It's like starting a music career by being told that if you don't do better than The Beatles, you are a complete failure.
IMO Invisible War should be seen not as the sequel to Deus Ex, but as a different game in the same universe. The was Thor is not a sequel to Iron Man, but simply a different film set in the same universe.
While there are many of the same themes and elements, the end products are not the same.
If judged on it's own merit, Invisible War is a pretty great game. Sure, the levels are small, but they are well designed and offer many gameplay options.
The shooting is competent. Much better than it ever was in Deus Ex. Controls are well above most games of it's time.
It's no secret that many things were dumbed down from Deus Ex. While I do prefer the old, more advanced system which gave more player options, the new, simpler system is perfectly functional. And given the in-game time gap between the two games, such changes can easily be explained by technological development. Just look at the difference in weapons from WW1 to WW2.
One major point that divides people is the universal ammo. Personally, I think it's interesting. While it doesn't make much logical sense that all types of weapons would use the same ammo, it does bring something new to the game.
Since different weapons use different amounts of ammo with each shot, inventory management becomes more important. Especially for people like me who in most games are used to just using the pistol 95% of the time and therefore always having plenty of ammo for the big guns. In Invisible War you can't just squirrel away lots of ammo for the big guns and save it for the big enemies. Now you actually have to plan ahead from time to time.
While it's not a system I would like to see widely used in games, I do find it interesting.
Bottom line:
I personally think Invisible War is a very solid game. It is unfairly judged by it's association with a game it could never live up to.
Take it as a single game and judge it on it's own merit. Do that and you will likely find that it is much better than people give it credit for. In fact, it is very good game.

***KEEP IN MIND, THIS IS MORE OF A COMPARISON BETWEEN HURTWORLD AND RUST. I AM WRITING THIS TO NOTE MY OPINIONS ON BOTH GAMES AND ON MY OPINIONS OF HOW THEY ARE MOSTLY DIFFERENT***
I play Rust and Hurtworld. If you invest time into both games, you will know they are different; although the concept and start both games are similar. I think you should try the game again once the next major update or alpha build comes out, and try it again. I think you will realise that hurtworld is more farfetched than Rust in some areas. Hurtworld is also for the more invested player than rust; it takes more time to make a base, get geared and in my opinion, maintain a base or compound. So if fast-paced gameplay and quick starts are your thing and your pc will handle it, Rust is nice. Rust also has very PvP orientated gameplay, while Hurtworld is more PvE. Skill in PvP will play a decent role in which game you like more. Rust also benefits clan/group play, as you will have advantages in both fights and raids, with more manpower. More people also means you will likely have people online protecting your base for longer periods of time, as one person may leave and another join, or vice versa. Base expansion and farming also benefits from this, and while clan/group play is also an advantage in Hurtworld, it seems to be less 'satisfying' in my opinion.
Summary:
Rust is more fast-paced
Hurtworld requires more grinding.
Hurtworld is less taxing on your system
Hurtworld is still being updated, a beta build is available.
Rust is also being updated, but it is more finished than Hurtworld

System Shock 2 is a game about a man that wakes up on a ship under siege by zombies and a rampant AI. The only way to survive is to wrest control from the rogue AI with the help of another rogue AI. If you perform well, you get good boy points to spend on
powerups, skills and statboosts.
The game is pretty challenging, you need to play very safely and careful. Conserving your ammunition, healing items and everything else is absolutely vital. You need to watch where you're going and make sure you don't trigger the security.
The game is pretty scary and incredibly atmospheric. You will find cryptic audio logs made by your other crew members, some of which were recorded moments before their death. Its really cool because there's plenty of intertwining and individual stories told by the audio logs as you progress through the game, all of which eventually come to a tragic conclusion.
There's plenty of different playstyles, there's melee weapons, PSI abilities (basically magic), explosive weapons, energy weapons and "exotic" weapons.
Word of advice: Make sure you level up Hacking, I think you literally can't beat the game unless its at least 2.

Finally finished my 1st playthrough, and it did not disappoint why it's the Game of the Year of 2016.
If you were a fan of the first Dishonored, loves stealth games, first person games, or even who loves steampunk/medieval/dark fantasy setting, chances are you'll also love this sequel. Almost every part of the first title were improved, almost.
PROS
- Pick your playstyle. Take either the stealthy superpowered assassin, or the inhuman warrior of the Outsider. Kill or assassinate your foes, or just incapacitate them, or even finish the game without killing anyone, or even anyone noticing you. EVER. The sky's the limit. Hell even you can reject the offer to have superpowers.
- Replayability. Since the playstyle has multiple approach, you can do your first playthrough on one playstyle and then replay with the other one. In addition to that you get to pick two characters now, Corvo, the main protagonist of the first game, and Emily, the new character. The two characters have different powers. Adding to that, there are also multiple endings, so it's absolutely not enough for a single playthrough to experience everything the game offers.
- The level design is EPIC. I have to give Bethesda and Arkane studios a thumbs up for this. At one point you may be exploring the castle sewers for secrets, and at the other you may find yourself in a house with moving rooms, or maybe time travelling in a mansion's past, causing your actions to take effect in the present.
- Solid playtime. A normal playthrough may get you 15 hours or so, which is pretty decent considering the price.
CONS
- AI is not that advanced, sometimes dumb. Sometimes the guards won't spot you even if you're close enough to be spotted.
- Linearity and repetitiveness. Not sure if it's just me but there were points where I felt were kind of repetitive, like finding a locked door at the start of a mission, then finding its key at somewhere in the middle then going back for that door.
-
This is now resolved on my end. Playing on GTX980ti with I7 6700K and 32GB RAM.
When you see this on a discount, consider buying it.
Overall I'd rate it 9/10

Good idea, good intent, poor execution. That's Black Mesa in a nutshell.
Black Mesa is, unfortunately, NOT a worthy reimagining of the source material. Even when viewed as an "alternate" take, it cannot stand. And since the majority of reviews I'm seeing here would suggest that Black Mesa is essentially Half-Life: Remastered, I feel there's a strong need for someone to step up and say "Whoa, Nelly. Let's back up, here." Because this is certainly not the case. Let me explain why (I'll try to be brief).
First, I hate to knock these guys' work. This all began as a fan project - a labor of love, if you will, of an unusual quality. And I mean that. There's some seriously great work in here. There are some admirable sound-alike voice actors (though this itself is an issue, which I hope to have space to touch on ahead), the maps are fantastically well-designed and evocative of the original game without being straight copy-pastes, and some aspects of the game have been remixed just enough for things to feel fresh.
What really lets it down is the just horrible lack of nuance. Everything is in-your-face and over-the-top, *especially* the awkward, flailing attempts at nu-Valvian "humor." There's a scene early in the game where three scientists prattle in metaphor about Half-Life inspiring them to want to make games, how their vision is similar but different, they can bring things up to snuff with the power of modern technology, etc. etc. - and it's positively dreadful. Just straight-up face-wrenching cringe material. Honestly, they could have even done this the correct way. There's room for it in the game, surely. They just lacked the skills to get that statement in the game without completely shattering the mood and sounding terrible. But it doesn't end with this. Every other line of dialogue is some smarmy reference to the original game that makes the whole thing feel hokey.
Black Mesa is *constantly* trying to be funny, and constantly sabotaging its own mood in the process. It's a real shame, because the excellent environmental design tends to do a fantastic job building up ambience - only to have some dumb sign, poster, or quip from a character bring the whole house of cards down on a whim. Yes, it's that much of an issue. It's not nearly rare enough to ignore. While a little bit of levity can serve even in an otherwise straight-laced experience, a lot can be ruining. Especially of that humor is particularly juvenile - which is the case here.
But that's not all. It's not just the humor. The overall design is compromised by a general lack of restraint. Eli and Kleiner are shoehorned into the game, and very, very awkwardly at that. They don't fit in at all, and their appearance is just one more drop of cringe-fuel - just a name drop for the sake of having one, as though they wanted to get the characters in there, but they had no idea where to do it.
Music cues are placed in tremendously galling places, such as the return trip to the rocket test chamber. It's awful. In the original, you had the by-then familiar sound of the monsters hammering on the walkways, and your own silent determination to finish one last step and do what you have to do to win. In Black Mesa, you have godawfully generic electronic music hammering in your ears just screaming "yes, yes, you're about to do the THING!" and completely ruining the moment. Does that sound nit-picky? It ISN'T. The first game was *defined* by everything having been done for a reason. Everything was handcrafted to provide a mood, and every music cue was very, very decisive and meaningful. There was no room for "bum-chicka bum-chicka bum-chicka" just for the sake of it.
And then there's the sound-alike voice actors. They're fine. In fact, in a lot of ways, they emulate the original *two* voice actors (scientists and security guards) pretty much perfectly. But *why* emulate them at all? Why make the entire voice cast one scientist voice and one security guard voice? Surely, with where we are with technology today (I mention this only because the developers did, with their characters' cheeky treatise on their design philosophy near the beginning of the game), they could have gotten away with using bit lines from multiple contributors? Why does every security guard and every scientist have to sound the same, especially when the scientists all sound like silly cartoon chariactures (that voice actor was definitely trying too hard at times)?
The dedication to sound-aliking the characters also comes off as hokey and pointless, even if the actors themselves did a good job. And the idle chatter? Every other line is a silly, goofy "joke" that just torpedoes that mood. "Do I look cool when I hold my gun like this?" Right, right. I know that the original game had humor in their dialogue. The difference is that it wasn't juvenile. Big, big difference.
Compounding the issues are actual technical shortcomings. The Source engine is surprisingly inept at the task of recreating Half-Life, strange as it is to say. I'm talking about the fundamental feel. Gordon doesn't so much as walk as he floats through the air. Guns feel more like airsoft props than firearms. Jumping is unreliable and feels physically wrong.
Worst of all, fights against enemy AI feel like matches against multiplayer bots - and I don't mean that as a compliment. I mean, the most generic, mindless multiplayer bots. Human soldiers shuffle back and forth while hip-firing rifles with near perfect accuracy at any distance. This particular flaw is familiar to anyone who's played through Half-Life 2. The AI is pretty much the same flawed AI of the Combine troops. And there are TONS of human opponents. To make up for their lack of intelligence, the devs placed HECU Marines in massive numbers. The result of this is maddening death by hitscan out in the open with next to no cover in maps like Surface Tension. Fighting the soldiers - a highlight of the original game - is without joy or thrills here. Just disappointment.
Capping off this whole affair is the fact that the game remains unfinished, many, many years later. Half-Life is a game that most gamers should experience at least once. It really *is* worth all the praise. Start with it, come back to this after. If you're undecided, try the mod version. It's free, without risk. It should give you some idea of what to expect, but be warned - the mod was from a time before the team jettisoned any sense of creative restraint. It's a more favorable projection of their intent than is the final product.

Personally, I think this game's over-rated. I found it long, tedious, boring, and not scary.
For the first hour or two, I found it somewhat intriguing. But afterwards it felt like the same thing over and over again. Hack a computer, pull a few levers, start up a generator. I wasn't even really trying after a while. The only reason I took the effort to actually beat the game is so I could see if it got better. There is SOME scenes where they introduce new things and it's interesting for the next 10 minutes or so, but always reverts back to the same "run here, do this, run over there, do that" feeling. Without any real substance. I honestly maybe only used a locker 2x to hide from the Alien. Other than that, once you learn how close/far you can get and what you can do, he really isn't that much of an obstacle.
I find too that the human AI is somewhat unrealistic. Sure, there's a reason to be on edge, I get that. But more than once have I experience the Alien roaming around killing the AI humans, and the humans continue to try to kill me meanwhile the Alien is right in their line of sight. Wow, what a game.
The main story puts you in Amanda Ripleys shoes and sends you off in search of Ellen Ripley, but what you find is only the Infamous Xenomorph and a lot of really disfunctional Androids and Humans.
The pacing is done in a the most thrilling and immersive way they could possibly think of. Everything from the soundtrack, the ambiance, the beeping and sounds of the devices had me on edge every step of the way, so I felt really pressured into playing it as stealthy as I could.

Counter point to Alien AI: it's not clear what it's supposed to be doing. Spoiler to behavior here:
The story is excellent, in that it both captures the feel from the original Alien, as following the story of the Companys relentless pursuit to capture the creature, and marking all their employees as expendable. After going through the final levels, and having a few moments to think of how it could end to snuggly fit into the beggining of Aliens, where Amanda is first mentioned, I had my own little scenario in mind. I was somewhat dissapointed in the conclusion, as it felt either rushed, or not fully exploited due to the buildup.
Gameplay wise, it forces you to play stealth starting Mission 5 (which was the bane of my existence to get past), and after getting the Flamethrower, you feel empowered since you can repell the Alien for short amounts of time. However, having to play switch this button, go through long narrow corridor with Alien ever looming around, open door, blown generator, go back to restart generator parts felt rather tedious and annoying. Yes, immersion was high, and the stress was on, but I was more annoyed than anything to what felt as an artificial prolonging of the level, when at least I have to re-do a gut crawl all around the hostile area 3 times in a row. Thankfully, these instances aren't that many.
Overall, this game was a blast to play through. Worth every cent to someone who apreciated the Alien lore and feel of the first movie, and a game I wanted to play ever since the original AvP from 2000.

Pros:
+ Manages to avoid today's more common "action-horror" style by taking cues from Amnesia and Outlast
+ Handles the canon very well with nods to the original films, a story that is self-contained but an entirely appropriate follow up to Alien, and avoids trying to puts its own spin on the franchise (like many other games do in such situations)
+ Incredibly atmospheric
+ Hauntingly beautiful visuals, fluid animation, and solid voice acting
Cons:
- Big difficulty shift towards the mid-point when you get the flamethrower (makes things ALOT easier)
- Save system is a little frustrating
- Many of the items/tools aren't needed on the easier difficulties
The Bottom Line
When you consider that Isolation came out of a development studio (Creative Assembly) that's spent the last 15 years making historical strategy games (Total War) it makes the fact that the game is so top notch seem even more impressive. Isolation handles the existing Alien universe well by not stepping on any toes and a creating storyline that's both believable and serves as a good follow up to the events of the first film. Supporting this solid storyline then is survival-horror gameplay that actually lives up to its name - resisting the temptation to throw a pulse rifle in the player's hands and instead forcing them to sneak, hide, and use distrations and tools in order to survive encounters with haywire androids, crazed survivors, and the Alien itself.
Alien: Isolation is the game that fans have asked for for years.

What a refreshing MMO-experience!
The whole world of TESO is such a coherent, vivid and story-rich environment I've never seen before. The lore of the classic single player series (Morrwind - Oblivion - Skyrim) is seriously embroidered into this MMO and there are not much compromises.
PROS:
- hugely immersive world and storyline. It's not easy to wrap the classic structural MMO-quest features into something exciting (fetch this, kill X of that, etc.) but here the intensive and brilliantly composed storyline dresses everything up so nicely that I see epicness having a feast in this game.
- great roleplay. The lore of the game world is huge and extensive and the characters have a strong connection to the overall flow. Countless books to find and read to enhance the immersion further and create a depth no other MMO I've played could deliver.
- simple and yet overly flexible character building. There are no rigid classes and skill trees, anyone can build literally anything from the available races and classes because there's a great freedom in spending the skill points earned by the level ups. Want a sorcerer who can wield a two handed sword? Do it. Want an archer who does magic too? Go for it. Creativity has a great chance here to join the game.
- crafting, enchanting. The system allows a great deal of possibilities in a very sensible structure: constructing, deconstructing, upgrading, researching. Clear as the mountain stream and simple enough not to push players to grind mindlessly. Even those tiny details: getting raw materials take only a few seconds at the source without wasting a lot of time watching a repetitive animation every time.
- combat system. It's just a perfect balance of the classic button pressing parade and the skill based moves: it does matter here to manage the distance (no automation!) and to choose what moves to execute and from what angle. Defending properly also requires personal skill and quick decisions rather than fully relying on the level of the character or the triggered actions learned.
- HUD. It was strange first to have so little information on the screen but after a few hours I started to consider this as a fresh air of added realism. I like to "learn" my way around rather than having a mini map blocking a big ching of my view on the screen: a single line compass on the top does a great job and serves very well. There are only 5 slots on the quick bar which again may sound like a harsh limitation but it does make the game much better in my eyes - it's actually a great part of building my character on a certain way around a few skills and combos and it certainly boosts the strategy value of the game to select "that five" skills to express the best of the character.
- character creation and build. Again, it's simple and yet very deep: only a handful of attributes, all customaizable by the player and not engraved by the race or class, works like a charm. The skill tree also eliminated a lot of classic but unused elements and what's left of it blends into the game world perfectly and offers a great deal of variation and strategic planning. Everything is connected, reading in-game script and books can affect the skill development not just adding a whole lot to the game lore. It's not the character's level at first what improves the skill but the usage rate of that skill - want to have a good two handed weapon skill on a higher level? Stop firing arrows and bring that axe on to battle!
- graphics, music, sounds. All wonderful, seriously immersive and I still have a hard time to belive that it's possible on this level. The world is simply the most attractive and enchanting one I've ever played as an MMO. All dialogs are in excellent quality, famous actors as well involved so it's not just reading masses of tiny letters in a text box. The world is widely interactive, it's possible to talk to literally everyone. Every NPC comes alive with a sentence or two further detailing the whole game world with charm.
- Pricing. This is - for me at least - a very important positive experience: there's an entry price and from that it's free. Really. No pay to win, the game store is there for those willing to pay some extra for a cosmetic or vanity game element or would like to get some extra features earlier than those play for it rather than pay for it.
CONS:
- can't really list anything here so far, however I barely scratched the surface of the game until this point - steam's measurement on my hours spent in the game however is totally inaccurate, possibly because I always start the game from its own launcher rather than through steam.
I can't refer to PVP yet as I have to dig myself into it more, so as guild play is an unknown area for me so far.
Soloing in this game is such a great fun! :)
Will come back to update this review when I feel I have enough experince on the missing topics.
Do I recommend TESO?
Absolutely!
Mind the size it takes on your hard drive though, the base game with no add-ons is nearly 70 GB. A good load of data with all the bits in service of a great game!

As someone who just played it for the first time in 2017, System Shock 2 is a great game that holds up quite well despite a few issues.
While I wouldn't call the game scary, it has strong atmosphere and a constant sense of dread. Navigating menus (inventory, PDA etc) can be a bit clunky, but not so much so that you won't get used to it in a relatively brief period. The various ways you can build your character are neat and allow for a good range of playstyles. And finally combat, while also somewhat clunky and simple, is still satisfying with a good variety of weapons and abilties to use and good feedback for when you're hitting an enemy.
Where the game fumbles is in it's last two hours or so of the 14 hour playtime. The expansive ship location you've been having fun exploring/surviving in is replaced by two linear levels that drain your resources with numerous cheap enemy placements and also include a few forced platforming moments. These final bits go against what the rest of the game was achieving and quickly become frusturating and tedious to get through.
Even with that trip at the finish line, I do very much recommend System Shock 2. I'm glad I finally got to experience what many people call a classic and, for the most part, it didn't disappoint.
**NOTE** If you're playing the game at a modern resolution (which is likely), then I recommend editing the game files to resize the HUD as it is incredibly tiny by default.

Let's get right into it:
PROS:
+ great, great story, memorable lines, not that many memorable characters except SHODAN but she makes up for the rest. One of gaming's most memorable plot twists, this is where BioShock came from (same writer after all).
+ incredible level design, sound design, artstyle and general vibe. Nothing I've played so far comes close to this kind of feel
+ one of the first games to effectively and enjoyably combine FPS and RPG mechanics
+ deep gameplay, practically demands multiple playthroughs
+ rudimentary widescreen support and decent environment graphics (for the time and some lighting effects survive well to this day)
+ totally oldschool and unforgiving. Guns break down, resources (ammo/health etc.) are scarce, some new items have to be researched etc. I love this type of thing. However...
CONS:
- ...this game really is totally oldschool and unforgiving. Meaning it's hard to get into.
- shooting is below average, clunky even for it's time. This ain't Doom, sadly. Can't have everyting.
- vanilla environment graphics are OK but the character models are jarringly awful (there are mods to fix this, however)
- there are occasional (potentially gamebreaking or just annoying) bugs, like cyber modules disappearing and such.
Overall, this is a great game with some shortcomings. One of the biggest ones is the unforgiving nature of the choices that you have to make regarding your character, if you're new to this, skim through a guide or two before delving in. I played this game for 6 hours trying to figure stuff out only to realise I completely effed up my character, investing cyber modules (upgrade points) into useless things. A specialised character is greatly favored, I did Navy (guns/hacking) on my first playthrough; I recommend doing the same because it's the least painful and makes the most sense. Then there are the huge non-linear levels with non-linear objectives that sometimes have you running around scratching your head (there's a level where a keycode you need to progress is hidden in something called "art terminals", LCD screens that display different paintings, that kind of stuff). Lastly, the movement and inventory can take a bit of getting used to, it's not really all that buttery smooth.
This review might look like I have more negative than positive things to say, but it's really more a problem of expressing just how awesome the positive stuff is. If you can survive the quirks I mentioned, the gameplay is deep, rich and satisfying, a lot of ways to play this game, a lot of weapons and PSI powers to research and toy around with, lots of hours spent exploring and figuring out how to best this enemy type, whether or not to use that PSI power and so on. Like I said, replay value all day long. I've just finished one playthrough and I'm already looking forward to the next.
If you're a fan of one or more of these things:
exploration, brilliant sound and level design, decent shooting, amazing story, untouchable atmosphere, unique gameplay
you owe it to yourself to play through it. At least once. Insect.

Ok. As a big fan of horror games I just had to get this as I have been looking at it for months and finally got now when it was on sale. I had not played the first one and did not know what to expect from this one. Ive watched videos and tried the demo.
The story starts with a detective going into some matrix type world to save his daughter who he thought was dead. Once in he gets a sort of walkie talkie that can trace voices and events in the past and this is how he follows the trail of his missing daughter.  Along the way he meets a few others (soilders also in the matrix) whom he can do a few sidequest for to get extra ammo or materials. They dont provide much to the story and feel sort of distant and unemotional.
The world itself is not too big and fairly easy to navigate with a dussin building you can actually enter and explore. The "town" feels a little flat and sort of a made in a computer simulation with some monsters running around. But eventually the pace picks up and that world changes into a psykadelic nightmare.
The setup is pretty basic. Collecting ammo and killing/sneaking past enemies to get from point A to B. The fights were actually highly entertaining and the monsters get pretty scary especcially when they gang up on you. The zombies and other monsters were very well designed and realistic with some pretty disturbing sound effects adding to the scariness. As for a zombie killing game its definetly a lot of fun and the 'bosses' or bigger monster carachters and really well made. There is this medusa monster which is made up from severed limbs sown together and a bunch of female heads that keeps chasing you around.
The antagonists or evil doers in the matrix making these monsters and having them fight you are not introduced properly into the whole story and their motives or where they came from are poorly explained. Other than they are evil and likes evil things. And many times it feels like a poor translation from a strange japanese game from the 90s. But that sort of goes for all characters. They dont feel emotionally bound to the story and that (with long cutscences) sort of makes the game less frightening. The story could have been told more simple.
Having said that, this is a very much a really good game with some really cool environments and effects. You even go to hell at one point. And as a fan of horror games this is defenitly a purchase. As a critic i think the story could have been shorter and less dramatic and I would have liked to see a few more sidequests and a little more exploring but still. Its was a lot of fun and took me around 9 hours to finnish.
If you are looking for an action filled zombie game. This is what you want.

This game is majestic, the engine is so optimized that I'm able to run it at Ultra with a dual-core and 2GB RAM DDR2!
As you play, the suspense is in the air, and will even get you nervous. Is such a great experience that gets hard to explain. So let me say that I highly recommend this game.

Pros:
+ Manages to avoid today's more common "action-horror" style by taking cues from Amnesia and Outlast
+ Handles the canon very well with nods to the original films, a story that is self-contained but an entirely appropriate follow up to Alien, and avoids trying to puts its own spin on the franchise (like many other games do in such situations)
+ Incredibly atmospheric
+ Hauntingly beautiful visuals, fluid animation, and solid voice acting
Cons:
- Big difficulty shift towards the mid-point when you get the flamethrower (makes things ALOT easier)
- Save system is a little frustrating
- Many of the items/tools aren't needed on the easier difficulties
The Bottom Line
When you consider that Isolation came out of a development studio (Creative Assembly) that's spent the last 15 years making historical strategy games (Total War) it makes the fact that the game is so top notch seem even more impressive. Isolation handles the existing Alien universe well by not stepping on any toes and a creating storyline that's both believable and serves as a good follow up to the events of the first film. Supporting this solid storyline then is survival-horror gameplay that actually lives up to its name - resisting the temptation to throw a pulse rifle in the player's hands and instead forcing them to sneak, hide, and use distrations and tools in order to survive encounters with haywire androids, crazed survivors, and the Alien itself.
Alien: Isolation is the game that fans have asked for for years.

For those not in the know, Black Mesa is essentially a remake of the original Half-Life. It improves various things as well as adding some new features here and there, making it stay mostly faithful to its roots while still making pieces of the game differ slightly. Though made by a third-party developer, the game still delivers a quality experience that you'd hope and expect from a Half-Life game.
The story is the same old classic with several additional details and differences added into the mix, though as of this writing, the conclusion is still yet to be finished.
Gameplay is pretty much the same as the original while having some improvements thanks to the good ol' Source engine, ranging from cosmetic details to full on changes in certain parts of the game.
The new soundtrack manages to complement the gameplay well and some of the tracks are good enough that I had to look them up on the internet later. Also, the voice acting was very good, which can often be a very tricky thing to nail down.
The price may feel a bit steep for some people, but I would consider this game worth it, especially if you haven't played the original game.

To start off this review I just want to say that I haven't really played a lot of MMORPG's the last couple of years. I was a big fan of MMORPG's when I was younger, but the last years CSGO has taken my time.
When I first got this game I started downloading it and it was 53 GB on steam and I figured, well, that's not that bad. But when I launched the game, I saw that I had to download all the patches on the launcher, which took me 30 GB more, so if you want this game you'll have to be patient with the downloads.
Pros:
- The gameworld; I really enjoy the gameworld, but I think many people's problem is that they expect this game to look like Skyrim, which in this case it doesn't. It looks more like Oblivion and I'm fine with that.
- Not really P2W. A lot of other MMO's you'll have to buy things in-game to either level up faster or to do different stuff, but you don't necessarily need to buy anything in this game to become good in it.
- Community; maybe the part I like the most. Everyone in the chat is helpful and very nice.
- PvP, some of the best PvP yet, even though I've only played for 21 hours.
- Skills and stats is actually very well made in this game and it's very simple to understand what you would prefer to use your skill points on.
- Character selection; You can plays as Breton, Orc, Redguard, Altmer, Wood Elves, Khajiits, Argonians, Dark Elves and Nords. You can also play as Imperial if you wish to use money on it.
- Faction selection; There are three factions to plas as; Ebonheart Pact (Dark Elves, Nords and Argonians), Aldmeri Dominion (Khajiits, Wood Elves and Altmers) and Daggerfall Covenant (Redguards, Orcs and Bretons). Imperials can freely choose what faction they want to be in.
- The Classes; Templar, Nightblade, Dragon Knight and Sorcerer, which I enjoy because of the wide variety of things you can do in the different classes. You choose how to play for yourself, which I really enjoy.
Cons:
- Crafting; the crafting in this game is in my opinion horrible. Some people may like it, others don't but I think it's to confusing for people to learn quick. I didn't learn how to craft until I reached 15 hours on this game and I still don't like it at all.
- Some of the quests; Some of the quests is just really boring and not playable. I really enjoy doing quests in ESO, but when 30% of all the quests is boring as hell and when you don't gain any real xp from doing it you will just waste your time.
- Enchanting, I really loved enchanting in Skyrim, but in this game both the crafting and the enchanting is horrible. Maybe because there is another developer Zenimax that's created ESO, but still, they should have put way more work into it.
So to finish this off, this game is brilliant but it has flaws. Some things might be changed in the future and some will stay the same, but that's just how it is.

The souls franchise has gained a reputation of being Extremely hard. dark souls 2 extends on this tradition with a more refined combat system and punishing enemies. while the game may be hard it is also very rewarding once learned, it also has some of the best skill based combat i have ever seen in a video game yet due to the massive verity in weapons, spells, shields and armor there is a play style for almost everyone. unlike some other RPG games there is rarely any Unfair or Glitch deaths as all attacks can be avoided with proper timing and technique. the game also treats is PVP and coop in a very unique manner by allowing you invade the games of others at any time if you manage to kill the host of the world you invade you are rewarded however this can also happen to you at any time, on the other end of the spectrum is the Coop gameplay unlike most games you can not simply join a friend and play coop through the whole game you can only play with others if you are around the same level, are not in a "Hollowed" state, and have not defeated the boss for the area you are in, i understand that the developers wanted to make players feel isolated and focus on a single player experience but it would still be nice to see coop and pvp without so many restrictions this would remove a lot of frustration when playing with others being 1-2 lvl's off joining you and having to reuse un hollowing items over and over when you mess up a boss. at least when getting summoned to help someone else you don't need to be unhollowed, but this would still help the game be a lot more welcoming to new players and friends looking for a coop experience

for $5 I'd recommend this to anyone unless you really can't stand RTS games in general.

Configuration and graphics:
The main problem for PC is the graphic card, but having a 3GB 1060 i can tell you that i can run this game smoothly with high details, the recommended graphic cards are either ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, or for 4K 60 FPS ? I can't tell you.

Game:
The story is REALLY good and the ending powerful.
Good characters, good villains, interesting bosses and even the area are good.
Gameplay:
The game relies into a seemingly open world with crafting (for ammo and health) which leads ultimatly to very few drops of ammo. You will come back, if you played the first game, to the same weapons and one of the flaw is the almost inutility of the sniper rifle...
I played this game into the hardest difficulty possible, and i can tell you that you need to manage your ressources well which leads to a very good immersion into the survival horror game. Finally, the game length is pretty high, count over 20 hours (i played in the hardest difficulty) if you want to clear everything. On top of those 20 hours, you have New game Plus available and 2 other game mods. This game can be played easily again, so no sweat about that.
Recommendation:
This game has a really good story as said previously, a really good immersion too. Other thing that is really nice is that you can finish the game by blazing your gun everywhere, so you cannot "run it down". And finally, the first game isn't that expensive and you can always wait sales whiles this game is definitly worth your money.

Prior to playing this game, I never did watch the Alien movies, but I  did play a few other survival horror games before, including Condemned: Criminal Origins and the first two Bioshock games. I then became interested in this game, not just because of the praise it was getting, but because it did look like something among the lines of those Bioshock games. So I went and watched the first two Alien movies to get caught up to watching this game, before purchasing this game during Steam's holiday sale last year.
It took a few months to finally play this game, but I'll get to why later. When I finally did, I was immediately addicted! AI is possibly the most tense of the horror games I played so far--then again, I never played other highly acclaimed horror games like Outlast, Amnesia, and the FEAR series (I want to, though.). Still, what's presented here deserved the praise it got late last year, especially when survival horror's a first for strategy game developer Creative Assembly.
So what's the story? Well if you watched at least the first two Alien films (and shouldn't bother with the other two sequels or the canonical Colonial Marines), the game picks up 15 years after the events of the first movie and 42 years before the second. It was brought up in Aliens that Ellen Ripley is a single mother with her only daughter Amanda. Well, that daughter is the main protagonist of this game, working for Weyland Yutani on a personal goal to find her mother. She gets a tip from a Synthenic employee Samuels that a substation the Sevastopol has recently received on board  a flight recording from the obliterated Nostromo. After a little hesitation, Amanda agrees to go, and the two, along with reporter Taylor, head their way over, via the Torren. But as tradition would have it, Sevastopol has gone to hell, but Amanda doesn't really know until a freak accident sends her, along with Samuels and Taylor on board while trying to dock.
While on board, Amanda realizes she has a lot to deal with on Sevastopol, as it's running rampant with desperately insane humans trying to survive (and are the weakest enemies in the game), brutal Working Joe synthetics programmed to kill upon their core AI the Apollo's command, and a Xenomorph running amok in the station.
That's the gist of the plot. the story overall is good, but if you already watched the Alien movies, it's nothing too special and rather predictable in terms of how the story is played out, but I do like how it sheds light in the Ripley family, and how Amanda becomes more and more like her mother as the game progresses.  While it does end on a cliffhanger, I still think it's a good closure to the game's story.
Trust me, though, if for whatever reason you're not into the story, the game is still worth it, largely due to the sound direction, which to me is the highlight of the game. Much like the Ridley Scott original, it uses an atmospheric tone with suspenseful music and sound effects to immerse you into the game, wanting to keep going to find out what will happen next. Both the sound and art direction are incredible, paying homage to the original 1979 film, and will definitely satisfy the Alien purists.
As for gameplay, it's first-person survival horror fare with a few innovative ideas and mechanics. Right off the bat, the only weapon you'll be picking up early in the game is a revolver, but ammo is scarce to scavenge for, but you will pick up maps and materials to craft new gadgets to divert or weaken your enemies--smoke bombs, noi♥♥♥♥ers, molotov cocktails, EMP mines, and even upgrades to said gadgets and tools including a gas torch and hacking device to help reach new areas in the station. Once you have all these gadgets, along with a motion tracker to tell you if an enemy's close and new weapons you'll get later including a shotgun and a flamethrower, you'll have an incredibly versatile Amanda Ripley. And trust me, you will need most if not all these tools to survive, as this game presents a few, shall we say, traditional mechanics with a health bar requiring medkits to heal (Thank you! That auto-heal mechanic has become one of my most HATED mechanics in modern gaming), and a manual save system in the form of yellow phone booths scattered throughout the station, which heightens the tensity of the game, even when you have enemies tailing behind you half the time.
Let's talk about the enemies here, starting with the Xenomorph. CA felt the need to make sure the perfect organism isn't just some lumbering robot walking down a scripted path, and damn, did they do a good job! The alien is the most unpredictable enemy in the game. Even on Easy mode, the encounters with the alien are nerve-wracking; it'll sometimes turn around and go back the way it came, walk slowly in certain areas looking around, and even play tricks with you to lure you out of your hiding place. You can't outrun or kill it when it finds you either, and the alien will kill you immediately, so it becomes a game of cat-and-mouse. You know it's a tense experience, especially when the game has you holding your breath and leaning back in the locker the alien suspects you're in.
The Working Joes are not on the same level as the alien, but are still creepy, nonetheless. They're competitor Seegon's Big Lots answer to the Weyland synthetics, which are a pain to kill. You can't whack it blindly with your wrench, because he'll block your attack, so you'll need to shock him or find a more powerful weapon to take him down, like a shotgun. The worst part, though, is while electrical attacks are the most effective, they'll later become equipped with rubber suits, making them immune to electricity and more difficult to defeat. (In my case, I became pretty good at capping WJs with a bolt gun, which takes time to build up the shot, so you'll need to be careful when using it.)
Speaking of later in the game, I've heard many critics complain how after the first half when you earn a flamethrower and send the alien flying out of Sevastopol, the game goes downhill, but I think the second half of the game is still great if you give it a chance. For one, not a whole lot was revealed about Seegson or Sevastopol or how Ellen's flight recording was retrieved until then, and while you do some backtracking through areas you've been in before, it's not a whole lot and game is only padded briefly on small occasions. In fact that whole section after defeating the alien becomes a huge buildup to something massive! Without trying to spoil too much, I'll say sh*t really hits the fan after a certain event causing the station to deenergize and crumble, making the last few levels the most captivating (and most difficult) in the game.
So, yeah. While there's so much good I've brought up, I've a few minor problems. For one, I'm not very big on the character models. While the voice acting is great, all the characters look too plastic  and shiny for my taste with puppet-like mouth animations and lip synching. The game still looks great, even on the highest settings, but I think a little more care could've been put into making the characters on the level of everything else. Also I've ran into a few bugs and glitches, which can be avoided. No, the reason it took me so long to finally play was due to the video card I had before: a 2GB DDR3 GT 520. I had to save up to by a better one: a 2GB GDDR5 GT 740, because the game was CHUGGING on my older one. If you intend to play this game, play it on a high-tech PC, as the higher specs are required.
Aside from that, Isolation was a great time, but now I did wish I started on Normal. The game was still fairly challenging, but there were a few times I thought the alien spotted me, and I do still get an occasional braindead WJ and human to work with. I'll give Normal and Hard a run at some point, but for now this game is a must buy!

Although currently my steam ID says I beat this game in 10 hours, according to the save time it was actually 8 hours and 2 minutes. To put that in perspective it took me roughly 25-26 hours to beat the first Deus Ex the first time and around 15-16 to beat Mankind Divided, which almost everyone agrees is too short. This game is very short for a Deus Ex game, so don't expect the same amount of build up and revelation that you might have gotten in other games. For instance, in the first hour you discover that the illuminati still exist and are up to no good in the neighborhood. All of that being said, for the price that you can get this game on sale (around $2.49 I think) it's a solid chunk o' fun. You end up going to like 4 cities, so if you were♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that all of Mankind Divided took place in Prague, then this game might suit you.
The most obvious problem with the game is that it was made for consoles, and by consoles I mean OLD consoles (like the first xbox). Therefore you won't get any large areas or levels. Even when they redo liberty island from the first game it is split into 3 different sections (not including UNATCO headquarters). The game was certainly not optimized for PCs and the game engine will crash if there are too many objects with physics. There were a few times when I was stuck because the game would spawn in enemies right after I had made a save and them spawning would crash the game. The way that I found would fix this was to destroy boxes and such that were using the physics engine, but such a problem shouldn't exist in such a simple (both graphically and mechanically) game. Sometimes it feels like no work went into the areas of the game because you generally run into the same features in each city.
-A bar where you hire a pilot and progress the main objective
-A locked off area where the final objective in that area will end up taking you
-Apartments where you have to kill someone or something
-The same factions and coffee shops (I know that it's important to the narrative for both of these, but seriously)
IF I were to commend the game on one thing, it is that each city has roughly the same amount of secondary objectives. I remember when I played the first Deus Ex that all the side quests were in New York and places like Hong Kong had literally nothing to do but follow the main quest (despite Hong Kong being larger and better designed than New York).
Really the only other reason I would recommend this game besides the fact that I like Deus Ex is that this game has some interesting lore. This game doesn't cling on to companies and characters from the first game (although it does include them) and the developers seem to have taken the time to try to develop new ideas. The most interesting that comes to mind is the Omar, who are like a more extreme version of Helios's final phase.
Whatever. I like the game, it was okay, and most importantly it was cheap. Get it when it goes on sale.

To make the review simple and easy to understand, I shall use a few categories:
Gameplay : 9/10
Combat is simple and easy to learn, with sufficient guides and a unique combat system so that even people who are not used to playing games can still complete the dungeons.
Difficulty for boss can be set to either easy for those having troubles beating it, or hard for those seeking more challenge.
Equipment crafting is simple, and the extra stage in each dungeon for farming materials helps a lot in crafting.
Story : 9.5/10
The story starts out simple, with our protagonist Senia looking for her missing sister. She then ventures into the tower of eternity, hoping to find her sister there. The story then flows along and we see more about their pasts, which provides more background for us to emphatise with the character.
BGM : 9/10
The music is well put, and fits well with the scene/situation.
SFX : 9/10
the sound effects are clean and appropriately used.
Overall : 9.5/10
