To start off this review I just want to say that I haven't really played a lot of MMORPG's the last couple of years. I was a big fan of MMORPG's when I was younger, but the last years CSGO has taken my time.
When I first got this game I started downloading it and it was 53 GB on steam and I figured, well, that's not that bad. But when I launched the game, I saw that I had to download all the patches on the launcher, which took me 30 GB more, so if you want this game you'll have to be patient with the downloads.
Pros:
- The gameworld; I really enjoy the gameworld, but I think many people's problem is that they expect this game to look like Skyrim, which in this case it doesn't. It looks more like Oblivion and I'm fine with that.
- Not really P2W. A lot of other MMO's you'll have to buy things in-game to either level up faster or to do different stuff, but you don't necessarily need to buy anything in this game to become good in it.
- Community; maybe the part I like the most. Everyone in the chat is helpful and very nice.
- PvP, some of the best PvP yet, even though I've only played for 21 hours.
- Skills and stats is actually very well made in this game and it's very simple to understand what you would prefer to use your skill points on.
- Character selection; You can plays as Breton, Orc, Redguard, Altmer, Wood Elves, Khajiits, Argonians, Dark Elves and Nords. You can also play as Imperial if you wish to use money on it.
- Faction selection; There are three factions to plas as; Ebonheart Pact (Dark Elves, Nords and Argonians), Aldmeri Dominion (Khajiits, Wood Elves and Altmers) and Daggerfall Covenant (Redguards, Orcs and Bretons). Imperials can freely choose what faction they want to be in.
- The Classes; Templar, Nightblade, Dragon Knight and Sorcerer, which I enjoy because of the wide variety of things you can do in the different classes. You choose how to play for yourself, which I really enjoy.
Cons:
- Crafting; the crafting in this game is in my opinion horrible. Some people may like it, others don't but I think it's to confusing for people to learn quick. I didn't learn how to craft until I reached 15 hours on this game and I still don't like it at all.
- Some of the quests; Some of the quests is just really boring and not playable. I really enjoy doing quests in ESO, but when 30% of all the quests is boring as hell and when you don't gain any real xp from doing it you will just waste your time.
- Enchanting, I really loved enchanting in Skyrim, but in this game both the crafting and the enchanting is horrible. Maybe because there is another developer Zenimax that's created ESO, but still, they should have put way more work into it.
So to finish this off, this game is brilliant but it has flaws. Some things might be changed in the future and some will stay the same, but that's just how it is.
If I was to rate this game I would give it a 8.5/10.
It's worth a try if you love Elder Scrolls and MMO's.

System Shock 2 is one of my top ten games, and I did not play it back at release. Bioshock and Dead Space were the closest approximations I played as a teen, and they were where I first heard about SS. I picked it up during a sale a few years ago on a whim and I was blown away by what this game has to offer. The graphics engine is substantially outdated, but after adding a few high res mods and new textures it is more than serviceable. What this game absolutely nails is atmosphere. It is one of the most anxiety inducing games I have ever played, the enemy design and lore is revolting and intimidating in the best ways possible. Some people may have burnt out on audio logs (it was huge a few years ago) but the ones in SS are absolutely worth a listen. Voice acting is competent throughout, but its the excellent world building in them that really hooked me. The game does an excellent job of telling a captivating story just through gameplay, but those logs were an added treat since I was so invested in the game's world. I really can't say enough good things about this game, despite the small gametime Steam is showing I've beaten the game 3 times now and would happily run through again.

Truly a timeless masterpiece. I wasn't much of a gamer back when this game was released but I tried it out after playing BioShock, its spiritual successor. This game is extremely similar to BioShock so if you loved it, I recommend System Shock 2 to you highly. If you were scared playing BioShock, this game will blow you away. It doesn't have many jump scares because it doesn't need them. With carefully crafted sci-fi horror atmosphere that pervades the whole 15-20 hrs experience it instills a permanent sense of dread in you. The game has a wonderful soundtrack mainly consisting of fast electronic beats but even many slower atmospheric tracks. The story depicts the downfall of the spaceship Von Braun  that is torn apart by infection brought in from a nearby planet and the connection this infection has with an AI called SHODAN. There are some twists and turns affecting the player but most of the backstory is transmitted to the player through audio diaries just like in BioShock. Compared to the BioShock series it has a much more robust RPG system consisting of skills, traits, stats and even psionic abilities. You can develop your character many ways but I found the standard mix of standard weapons mastery and some tech skills like hacking and weapons maintenance most useful and fun for survival on Von Braun. Some of the skills like repair and research and some of the stats have little to no impact on your survivability. The graphics are not outright ugly and serve its purpose well and the sound design is top notch. Also, the level design in this game surpasses most modern FPSes with just enough alternate pathways and hidden areas/items to keep you interested about this game.

The sequel to 1994's System Shock, SS2 sees itself in the hands of a new development team (Irrational Games). The new dev team keeps the core values of the System Shock franchise while also expanding the series out to include psionic and hacking skills. Many of these traits will continue on in the game series' spiritual successor, Bioshock.
Unlike the original System Shock, SS2 is in full 3D. The results are a much more pleasant to play experience, although the early time period of System Shock 2's development (1999) means that many of the levels suffer from the vagaries of early 3D games, such as sticky environmental seams and fuzzy hit boxes on enemies. System Shock 2 is a much more difficult game than the original. The map is both more useful (it actually labels♥♥♥♥♥♥ and less useful (you can't zoom in or go full screen), which can make navigation a pain at times. Players are encouraged to be smart with how they upgrade their characters and with what tools they should keep in their inventory. Not having the right item in one's inventory can mean the difference between a quick battle and a Sisyphean challenge.
As mentioned above, the Bioshock series inherited many of the features first found in System Shock 2. This is so much so that SS2 plays a lot like a very early version of Bioshock. This means that many of the features and tweaks in the Bioshock franchise were done in response to problems found in System Shock 2. This makes going back to play SS2 an occasionally frustrating task. For instance, weapon damage is a big component of System Shock 2, and without the appropriate level of repair and maintenance skills, broken weapons will either stay broken or stay nearly broken for much of the game. The original concept was to force players to be frugal with how they use their weapons, but after the umpteenth time having a gun suddenly jam on you in the middle of a room full of enemies, this gameplay addition quickly wore out its welcome. In the same vein, the games reliance on upgrade trees to build your character up can become a royal pain when you find something like a new, powerful weapon only to discover that it requires a wheelbarrow's worth of cyber modules to build up a skill that you had, until that moment, not thought to be bothered with. The concept of using the skill trees to make your character customizable, as well as encourage multiple playthroughs is laudable, but the limited ways in which one can solve problems in the game (especially the boss battles) essentially forces one down the same, or mostly the same path regardless.
Nonetheless, the story and interplay with the game's main villain, SHODAN, makes these frustrations well worth it. Whereas Portal's GLaDOS was a psychotic, but entertaining AI, SHODAN is pure malevolence. She never misses an opportunity to talk down to you even as she asks for your help in certain tasks. Everthing you do for her gets you closer to your own destruction, and yet it is a necessary evil if you are to ever escape from her clutches. This paradoxical situation makes for a very compelling game experience.
On a side note, I found it interesting that SHODAN went from having a male gender in the first game, to having a female gender in System Shock 2. Given the voice in both games, one would think the female gender would always have been the case, but if one plays the original System Shock, one finds that SHODAN was always referrred to as "he". Making a game of this caliber is truly a labor of love, and when taking into account the fact that it’s based on one of the most beloved franchises of our time – with the added pressure of not ‘screwing it up’ like Gear Box did with the last entry in the Aliens saga (Aliens: Colonial Marines) – that only makes the task the developers have set before them all the more challenging.
But Creative Assembly pulled it off to monumental effect, giving us what is easily the best ‘Alien(s)’ game to date, and more to the point, what is easily one of the most heart-stopping, tension-filled horror gaming experiences in recent memory.  Everything CA put into this game was painstakingly recreated from the movies – the design of the environments and objects therein, the sound design, and that feeling of loneliness (or ‘Isolation’ in this case) that only the vast, cold desolation of space can evoke.  Alien: Isolation all too often makes you feel completely and utterly helpless.  What little weaponry you do get, such as the shotgun, revolver and bolt gun, are effective against humans and androids, but as for the xenos, forget it!  Your only ‘true’ ally in that battle is the flamethrower,  molotovs (and even then the flamethrower runs out of fuel extremely fast, whereas it’s far easier killing yourself with the molotov than it is scaring off the xeno) and stealth………..lots and lots and LOTS OF STEALTH!.
That makes sense when considering that the basis of the ‘horror’ element in this game stems from stealth gameplay mechanics.  No joke, I easily spent 16 hrs of my 18+ hr run cowering in fear under desks, in lockers, behind crates, etc.  and it didn’t help matters that I went through the game on the ‘Nightmare’ difficulty setting (for a first run I highly recommend the higher difficulty settings, but be warned: you generally die with a single hit, at least on ‘Nightmare’).
I can’t recall any game that I’ve ever spent so much time crouching and hiding in.  I would have run when I had the chance but that’s generally useless against the xeno whenever it rears it’s beautiful, elongated, exo-skeletal head.  And trust me, that’s often!!  At least in the parts of the game (the missions) that the xeno influence factors into, it will literally stalk you non-stop for multiple missions – even when you don’t see it, it’s still there….up in the vents…creeping around the next corner….motion tracker is tripping out with signal overload….*whimpers and crouches under desk from the memory*
Yeah, that about sizes up my experience with this game – so much tension and dread that I’ll probably die of old age soon (though I’m presently only in my mid-30’s) because of how much this game has shortened my lifespan.  Seriously, I was terrified to even save at times for fear that I would get killed despite the fact that I was within 5 feet of a save device, or to attempt a hack, input a code, or use a cutter due to how long doing so would take/how much noise I’d make in the process --- I highly recommend this game!!!!
Alien: Isolation is truly a masterwork of suspense set in a beautifully realized/rendered sci-fi environment that won’t soon be forgotten.
Thank you CA for making it necessary for me to wear adult diapers for the duration of this game : ) … but ultimately in staying so true to the vision of Ridley Scott and the ‘Alien(s)’ saga in general.  And thank you SEGA for still believing in this franchise and not letting it die out like so many others have in the past.

So having played this game for about 86 hours, finishing it once and almost finishing it in NG+ before trying out different builds, I feel as though I can finally sit down and write a review of this game.
So the best way I can think of to sum this up, before we begin, is to say it's more Dark Souls but not as good. This isn't to say it's bad, because it's still a good game, but I do feel it lacks the same sort of impact the first game had, which is understandable as this is a sequel and that's a common problem with those. The problem I wouldn't say is understandable is that it's just not as creative.
Bosses tend to play out the same way and are fought the same way, more or less, and while I forget the exact number of them that are like this, there's at least one optional boss that's flat out recycled from Dark Souls 1. The storyline, without spoiling anything, is vague in ways that sometimes don't even work. There's this sudden shift of objective mid-way through that pretty much makes zero sense due to it not really being explained, as far as I recall, and essentially having nothing to do with your objective starting the game out, which seems to be "break the undead curse". Also, again, without spoiling anything, if you remember the final boss of Dark Souls 1? The final boss in this game doesn't compare. It just lacks the same punch the first game had. The environments also feel inconsistent, ranging from ugly texture dumps to actually cool and fun areas to explore.
As far as gameplay, they clearly wanted to improve on Dark Souls 1 but just wound up missing the mark. PvP for instance is still a laggy, broken mess, arguably moreso now that hex spamming is a thing people do. The covenants aren't really as cool or fun and some of the changes feel forced. Why do I need to visit the main hub of the game- something I can do at any point from a bonfire- to level up? What was wrong with just levelling at the bonfire if I can teleport back to where I CAN level from any other bonfire? For that matter, while I can't quite figure out why, the healing system feels worse. Maybe it's the way Estus now works, maybe the fact it's all HoT now, or maybe I just hate that, unless you raise Agility, it feels sluggish in a very frustrating way. Also, the torches are woefully underused as a mechanic, with there being maybe one or two areas they're even useful in.
The port is also not the greatest thing still. While it runs a lot smoother than Dark Souls 1, keyboard and mouse controls are still bad, and probably actually worse due to how the mouse now works. I'll phrase it this way, binding something to a single left click and clicking repeatedly, for instance, won't register due to it counting it as a double click- for which there's also a binding- instead. I also have to wonder how much of the lag from Dark Souls 1 was actually GFWL or if it was simply From being terrible with netcode. From what I hear, it's always been an issue for them, even going back to Demon's Souls.
Overall, though, it's still Dark Souls and it's still fun. I just wish it had more ideas, more spark to it, I suppose. It just isn't as fun to me, though.

At the moment of writing this review I have over 90 hours of played time, I have completed all the achievements and beaten the game three times.
The first playthrough was as Corvo, Low Chaos, no kills and ghost (undetected throughout the whole game). Playing on hard, it was a challenge that made me love the game -even more- than I love the original Dishonored.
Eveything you know from Dishonroed is here - and it's either preserved or improved.
Honestly, unless one expects a gripping Pulitzer-level narrative and numerous plot twists, then Dishonored 2 simply can't disappoint. Everything that we loved from the first part is here, but done better. The AI is (exept a few bugs) better, the enemies have a better spotting algorithm, Clockwork Soldiers are harder to kill than Tallboys, but you can kill them during the Clean Hands run (so the fun intensifies!).
For those who look at all the new powers and think: "They are for the weak!", there is the real Steel and Blood mode, where you can flat out refuse to accept the Mark. If you want to have a real challenge, then aim for Clean Hands/Ghost playthrough without the powers (yes, even without basic blink).
If you succeed, my hat is off to you.
I didn't try it (yet), but the High Chaos playthrough on Corvo was grim and fun, sword and pistol style.
Emily... Corvo's daughter is THE star of Dishonored 2.
Don't get me wrong, Corvo did not disappoint. Both playthroughs I have had on him were marvelous. The character is simply too iconic to just let him go.
Nevertheless, the young Empress is simply insanely fun.
Suited for both stealth and carnage, Emily does everything that Corvo could - but in a different way.
What else can I say?
If you weren't a fan of Dishonored 1, but you enjoy Thief-like games, this version may be up to your liking.
If you like carnage... trust me, Dishonored 2 allows for wicked creativity with wrecking havoc.
If you are a fan of the original... Get the game.
If runs stable 30+ fps on my old-ish gaming laptop (GTX 860, quad core i7 CPU (2.5Ghz each), 16 GB RAM, installed on an SSD drive).
Yes, I'm talking about 1920x1080, Ultra Details (with absolutely everything set on maximum).
On our gaming PC it runs even better, never going below 60fps (and I assume it could do that in 4k).
If optimisation is your concern, judging on some of the reviews, don't fret.
After the first update, the game runs smooth like the Knife of Dunwall through Deliliah's throat.
At the very least, 9/10 (personally, 10/10)

Waited a while to play this game due to the frame issue talk. When I started playing it it played fine. While I noticed some miniscular frame-dips in specific areas, the majority of the game played smoothly. I was playing on the bes♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ settings with a GTX 1060 and an i5-6500 CPU, 16GB RAM.
As for the actual gameplay I loved it. I was already a fan of how Dishonored (1) played. The puzzles were good, the fact that you have all these choices in terms of how you want to complete the mission is great. The atmosphere is fitting, soundtrack makes it quite immersive. Graphics and meshes look good, even when I could notice some clipping here and there when characters were moving.
Something odd I noticed was that you would occasionally just randomly be spotted, even when you shouldn't have been spotted. Another thing is that characters will occasionally start dialogue with you when you are (for example) one level underneath them in a building.
Occasionally I would get to places where I suppose I "shouldn't" have gone, making me unable to progress in that direction, even when I should have been able to in terms of in-game ability.
Overall I found this game to be very enjoyable. You have a great amount of space to be sneaky up high and get past enemies. You have a nice variety of enemies; the game also doesn't hold your hand to explain to you what each enemy's abilities are (which I personally think is very good, you just figure it out on your own). The objectives are interesting. The maps themselves hide a bunch of interesting things and for those who go out of their way to find everything this is really great.
Another cool thing is that you have two characters to choose from in the beginning, which adds some re-playability in addition to the different chaos-level completions. So needless to say I will be replaying this game at least once. Possibly twice down the line. I wonder what sort of DLC will be made for this game. <3

Whatever graphical settings you're able to achieve, the visual design is stunning. The enemies are varied and challenging, and the range of powers gives you many options in every situation.
It's not perfect. The story sometimes feels like it's a step behind the action, and a couple of sections where major characters interupt proceedings to explain their origins rather spoil the pacing. And the needlessly exagerated stakes slightly detracts from the more personal feel of the original. But the characters are interesting and well realised, and the overall theme exploring the long term consequences of individual actions unites narrative and gameplay in a way that is immensely satisfying.
This is a game bursting with ideas, expertly crafted and realised. Equal parts clever and imagintaive, a standout in the stealth action genre, and a unique experience in gaming.

If you're looking for a less overwhelming version of Rust that rewards friendly players, Hurtworld is definitely a game to purchase.

Slime Rancher is one of my favourite games of the year, and I love it for the same reasons I loved Stardew Valley. Slime Rancher is a cute, fun, and relaxing game: in a world of ultra-competitive online games and high-stakes singleplayer RPGs, it's nice to have a game that you can just relax with and just enjoy playing the game.
In Slime Rancher, you're an ambitious rancher who takes care of many cute slimes, by providing them with food, shelter, and unconditional love. You'll encouter beautiful environments, widly different (but all equally cute) types of slimes, and pimp out your farm in the process. Throughout your slime adventures, you'll learn more about where you are, and about your (and a previous rancher's) life.
From a gameplay perspective, Slime Rancher is very simple but addictively fun. Mechanics are really simple, and the game emphasizes player happiness over all else in its design. In fact, there's even a game mode where some of the barriers in gameplay (such as Tarr slimes, the only non-cute slime) are removed - it's really easy to have fun.
I think Slime Rancher is a great game, and I encourage you to give it a shot. While it isn't an inherently complex or competitive game, it's one of the most relaxing and fun experiences I've had from a video game in a long time. Everybody needs at least a little bit of Slime Rancher in their life!

I'm going to be honest. I bought the game because I heard a great song in the trailer. I now have the song in an online playlist of music. I don't have the game anymore.
The game is locked at 30 fps and it honestly makes me sick during some sections. VVVVVV did fine since the screen never scrolls and the only thing that moves is the character, but the whole screen moves in LOVE and it looks and feels terrible.
Also, the reason I bought the game was mainly to listen to music like the one in the trailer. Turns out the rest of the music is nothing like the one in the trailer. Every time you beat a level, the music abruptly stops and switches to another song instead of fading into the next one.
One irksome thing that this game makes you do is set your own checkpoints. In VVVVVV there were checkpoints everywhere. Every time you did a jump or challenge, there was a checkpoint standing there waiting for you to save your progress. In this game, you "get" to set it yourself. This could make the game easier in some cases. However, it was mainly a bother to me. At some points I'd make tremendous progress throughout the level. Then I'd die, feel a slow sinking in my stomach as I remember that I hadn't saved my progress at all and am promptly respawned at my last checkpoint way, way back in the level. Leaving the checkpoints to be set by the player and not designing them around the levels seems like lazy development to me.
It wouldn't be a huge problem if you could set the checkpoints
the checkpoints that are already there, but it's a mechanic that just sucks.
I had to refund the game because the reasons above made the game incredibly unenjoyable for me. I played it and beat it twice as well as playing all the extra levels in search of the fun I so wanted to have in the game, but I just couldn't enjoy it because the music was bad, the fps was too low, the checkpoint system was a pain. Controlling the character also felt less responsive than VVVVVV, but that could be a combination of the 30 fps and the whole screen moving at the same time.
I don't recommend buying this game, but you should definitely check out the song from the trailer.

The biggest flaw I hit in this game: it's possible to make the game unwinnable by placing a respawn point on one of the moving platforms on that "snow" level such that the vehicle then respawns in its default position and the respawn point is left floating in mid-air, and you are repeatedly dropped in the instant-kill snow.  I also kind of would have liked if there was some way to ask the game "what level number is this?".
Contrasted with VVVVVV's patented "ice-level style" slippery controls, which (a) are just mean, (b) are confirmed intentional and (c) [presumably] follow you through all of VVVVVV, LOVE comes out as a definite "CHALLENGING BUT FAIR".

As downloaded from Steam, the game defaults to 250 units and there is no TotalA.ini file, so you'd have to make (or DL) one before you could change to the OTA supported max unit cap of 500 units. However, if this was all you did, then more often than not, the game will crash when both sides are at max units and the fur is starting to fly, and this will happen regardless of whether you have max cap setting of 250 or 500.
As soon as I replaced the default version of TotalA.exe with the version of TotalA.exe included in the 1500 unit patch from TA Universe, the game consistently crashed at random times. This happened several times, even though I was within 500 total units at the time. I tried disabling Direct Sound and used Windows sound instead, but the result was exactly the same. Sound isn't the issue.
My system is Windows 7 x64bit with a relatively old Nvidia GeForce GTX 750Ti graphics card. I have the latest patch from TA Universe installed and three mods installed. No problems. If you loved TA back in the day, and want it back again, you absolutely can. I also highly recommend using TA Universe as your map and mod source for the game. They've come a long way since the old days, and their site is extensive.

This game is one of the most nitpick-able games out there, but not even the mightiest nitpickers can deny this game's utter brilliance. Making clever use of 3D space to create a horrifying FPS/ARPG experience, System Shock 2 is a major precedent when it comes to depth in storytelling and gameplay systems. The role-playing and combat aspects of the game, though unbalanced, manage to add an extra layer of tension and uncertainty to the experience that few other games can claim to have achieved.

Oh, System Shock 2..... the nostalgia. System Shock 2 is an amazing and immersive game. It has a high replayability rate (especially with all the psionic abilities one can invest in) and amazing gameplay mechanics. The atmosphere is gripping and definitely keeps you on your toes with the environment and enemies on the prowl. The plot is superb and throws the player through a loop. The game can be difficult, but is definitely worth it. Also, the ending is worth every penny and minute spent into this game.

I was asked again and again to play this game by a family member, on the grounds that this is a gaming experience not to be missed. They were right. System Shock 2 is a tense, sometimes frenetic first-person action game which expertly incorporates RPG-elements that enable the player to level up to meet the demands of the difficulty curve without ever allowing the player to feel too powerful. The system is fantastic: you "receive" levelling-up points as rewards for completing certain tasks, but are also rewarded for thorough exploration of the large, non-linear levels by finding them in unexpected places. You can then select which areas to improve your character at certain points in the game - you can't just level-up anywhere without finding them first. This provides a unique tension and real incentive to spend a lot of time with the game.
The story is told brilliantly through the use of audio logs - a method that has influenced many games such as BioShock and Doom 3. Like Thief's documents and readable books, this creates not just a game level but a real sense of place. The gunplay becomes more satisfying as you progress through the game, but you can save a lot of ammo with melee combat - but you need to be careful doing this as many enemies are either too tough or too fast for you to catch them. There is also a fantastic research function - where you can improve your chances of killing enemies by analysing their body parts. It's surprisingly fun and is a clear predecessor to BioShock's research camera feature. You are also incentivised to be careful with your weapons and use them sparingly as they don't last forever without a bit of TLC!
There is only one notable problem I thought (be warned): this game has respawning enemies! And it's not just easy enemies that respawn too - sometimes the big, tough ones come back too. This wouldn't be worth mentioning if it sometimes wasn't blatantly obvious that they didn't pop up out of nowhere!
But that said, this is still a fantastic game some years after being released - the levels are all interconnected so you can go back anywhere if you want to, and it's a challenging but fun and immersive experience. It's amazing that this was made using the same engine and level editor as Thief: the games share a DNA but are delightfully different in terms of environment and story. Play this game if you're into FPSes or horror or role-players, or anything else really!

TL DR: System Shock 2 is really great. The RPG systems are broken and the game does drop in quality towards the later third, but the game has very good level design, allows several playstyles despite its systems being broken, and it's a really terrifying game at times. If you've played Bioshock, this is an insanely similar game (especially in terms of story structure) but in space, more atmospheric and with less consolisation.
System Shock 2 is an FPS-RPG made by Looking Glass and Irrational Games in 1999. The game starts of with a pretty immersive character creation sequence, and something that I don't think I've seen in any other game: This sequence never goes through a menu to create your character. You basically enter through one of 3 doors each time, the first selecting your base "class" from Marines/Navy/OSA aka "Pure FPS"/"Hacking FPS"/"Space Magic", and then the following 4 sets of doors are presented as your training before the beginning of the game, each door giving you different stats, skills and Psi powers.
This way of presenting character creation choices to the player is not without its issues. You can't check what stats do and guiding yourself through their names might end up on a crap character, since the game does have some trap options and it's going to be a bit before you can actually level up more skills. Apart from that, where the first System Shock allowed you to use any weapon as long as you had the ammo for it, the sequel restricts the use of every weapon except the wrench to a cretain level in a weapon skill. I mean, even though not any idiot can fire a weapon well, anyone can equip a shotgun. Overall, playing in Normal ended up in having my main stats maxed out (hacking/standard weapons/maintenance) fairly early on and dumping cyber modules (the game's version of skill points which are found throughout levels and given to you for completing objectives) into random stuff just for the heck of it.
The game starts after this sequence with you waking up from cryosleep in the Von Braun, one of the first two ships outifitted with FTL tech, owned by TriOptimum (the same company who owned the Citadel Station and SHODAN in SS1.) The game starts on the Medical-Science Bay with no people alive, Hybrids and Monkeys. Hybrids are pretty creepy and will even shout at you and beg for you to kill them, and Monkeys are plain weird monkeys wiht the ability to shoot psi projectiles. You'll mostly use a wrench or maybe Psi powers for the first few levels, since weapons don't have a lot of ammo and are overall crap to maintain since they last about 100 shots before they break. Using maintenance kits can keep them working but these are expensive at the beginning and low maintenance skill means that you can only increase 1 or 2 points of durability every time you use them in a weapon, resulting in 10-20 more shots. This weapon degradation system is also a bit too much. This is overall a game where you should really hoard resources for the first few levels in order to handle to make the final parts easier, especially since enemies do respawn and using finite resources such as ammo so early can be a waste. Since after you find the appropriate medical station you can respawn for a small fee, it's mostly better to use your wrench to stagger most enemies to death and sometimes die while doing it.
As this is a Shock game, you get the main objectives told to you with mostly minimal story exposition, and this exposition is of course given by audio logs. The voice acting in these can range from pretty good to pretty bad, since part seems to have been done from people who were just around the office. The main antagonists are superbly voice acted though, and one of them is of course iconic. They both have a similar characteristic where their voices are comprised of several different voices which can say a sentence in different tones and tempos, and this cacophony of voice is insane and overwhelmingly creepy. The game reaches a plot twist where one of these antagonists is revealed, but you can see it coming from a mile away, especially if you've played the first game and listened to some audio logs in the second. This doesn't mean that moment isn't one of my favourites in gaming!
Levels in the Von Braun are well-designed, with fairly logical arrangement of space in a spaceship, though different from the first game's circular station. The game doesn't end at the Von Braun, and after that there's a drop in quality. Fortunately the game ends fairly quickly after that (1-2 hours). Not so fortunately is the ending, which feels like a blooper joke ending and was only there because there was no time/money to do a better cutscene. The game also baits a sequel which is only coming now, as the sales in 1999 were terrible (60k units sold) despite glowing praise from critics.
Overall System Shock 2 was a fairly flawed but still great experience. I don't think I'll forget some of the voices from different enemies, and exploring the Von Braun was amazing. Definitely recommended.

Making a game of this caliber is truly a labor of love, and when taking into account the fact that it’s based on one of the most beloved franchises of our time – with the added pressure of not ‘screwing it up’ like Gear Box did with the last entry in the Aliens saga (Aliens: Colonial Marines) – that only makes the task the developers have set before them all the more challenging.
But Creative Assembly pulled it off to monumental effect, giving us what is easily the best ‘Alien(s)’ game to date, and more to the point, what is easily one of the most heart-stopping, tension-filled horror gaming experiences in recent memory.  Everything CA put into this game was painstakingly recreated from the movies – the design of the environments and objects therein, the sound design, and that feeling of loneliness (or ‘Isolation’ in this case) that only the vast, cold desolation of space can evoke.  Alien: Isolation all too often makes you feel completely and utterly helpless.  What little weaponry you do get, such as the shotgun, revolver and bolt gun, are effective against humans and androids, but as for the xenos, forget it!  Your only ‘true’ ally in that battle is the flamethrower,  molotovs (and even then the flamethrower runs out of fuel extremely fast, whereas it’s far easier killing yourself with the molotov than it is scaring off the xeno) and stealth………..lots and lots and LOTS OF STEALTH!.
That makes sense when considering that the basis of the ‘horror’ element in this game stems from stealth gameplay mechanics.  No joke, I easily spent 16 hrs of my 18+ hr run cowering in fear under desks, in lockers, behind crates, etc.  and it didn’t help matters that I went through the game on the ‘Nightmare’ difficulty setting (for a first run I highly recommend the higher difficulty settings, but be warned: you generally die with a single hit, at least on ‘Nightmare’).
I can’t recall any game that I’ve ever spent so much time crouching and hiding in.  I would have run when I had the chance but that’s generally useless against the xeno whenever it rears it’s beautiful, elongated, exo-skeletal head.  And trust me, that’s often!!  At least in the parts of the game (the missions) that the xeno influence factors into, it will literally stalk you non-stop for multiple missions – even when you don’t see it, it’s still there….up in the vents…creeping around the next corner….motion tracker is tripping out with signal overload….*whimpers and crouches under desk from the memory*
Yeah, that about sizes up my experience with this game – so much tension and dread that I’ll probably die of old age soon (though I’m presently only in my mid-30’s) because of how much this game has shortened my lifespan.  Seriously, I was terrified to even save at times for fear that I would get killed despite the fact that I was within 5 feet of a save device, or to attempt a hack, input a code, or use a cutter due to how long doing so would take/how much noise I’d make in the process --- I highly recommend this game!!!!
Alien: Isolation is truly a masterwork of suspense set in a beautifully realized/rendered sci-fi environment that won’t soon be forgotten.
Thank you CA for making it necessary for me to wear adult diapers for the duration of this game : ) … but ultimately in staying so true to the vision of Ridley Scott and the ‘Alien(s)’ saga in general.  And thank you SEGA for still believing in this franchise and not letting it die out like so many others have in the past.

And i have to say something about this cause its something i very, very rarely find in games: first, when you walk around near large servers and computers you hear the spinning fans and hard drive clicking; second, when you run past a power box it hums with electricity. Not only was this another blast of nostalgia (who has an computer that makes the clicking sound anymore?) I dont know how to express in words how much i appreciate these small things added into the same corridors i ran through at 11. Beautiful, i think that sums it up for me.
If you are a fan of half life, immersion, or just a good single player fps; especially someone who played half life back around its release, this is a must have. Its just different enough to give a new take on the game; some weapons pop up at different spots than they did originally, but in the end its half life af. In closing i will say this: i cannot describe to you how awesome it feels to see black mesa as it was meant to be. I want half life 3 more than any other game, but this took the sting away more than anything could.

It still reeks of early access. Netcode is generally functional, but the lobby system is extremely flaky and online play features a LOT of teleporting enemies (particularly the aliens). One or two specific bros are capable of one-shotting bosses for no discernible reason, and the secondary on one of them doesn't seem to be implemented yet. The checkpointing system is all over the place and the difficulty curve is a sine wave. Game frequently hangs for about 20 seconds between levels. The fact that some bros are significantly slower than other bros means that you often wind up with assured death scenarios in multiplayer when facing corridors with timed traps, or rendering a level impassable if you end up as a slow guy and thereby have a gimped jump when forced to confront a 20-tile-wide death pit after half the level exploded. The game in its entirety is a neverending sensory overload, which I guess is more or less the idea, but attempting to have any meaningful engagement with it at times besides flipping a coin and hoping you don't get melted by a random explosion or acid splash seems laughably futile.
That said, it's some good fun if you get it on sale. Don't get me wrong, it's worth the experience, it's just... a very chaotic one, for better and for worse.

A clear improvement over first game:
+ better combat, quite a lot of weapons and ways to deal with enemies
+ stealth is now a valid option (especially with the skill to kill enemies around the corner)
+- an improved skill tree, but some skills are way too expensive for their gain (e.g. stealth sprint and kill ability is quite useless because requires timing, compared to maxed out crouch movement speed and stealth kill)
+ crafting system that allows to basically forget about resource management (especially if playing stealth ammo and health items will never be a problem)
+ a bit more varied types of enemies (many of them can be instantly killed with stealth, while others require two takes)
+- higher grades for weapons and skills need to be unlocked with special items (generally not a problem as on a normal game there will not be enough green gel and parts to get all upgrades)
+ upgrades for caring more ammo/items are now found on bodies and not unlocked with green gel
+ a semi open world for major chapters (good for looting and side quests)
+ a clearer storyline, addition of dialogs with NPCs and even if not played first game a better understanding of what is going on from early chapters
Main things I disliked was the Marrow transition which I generally would prefer to be just a loading screen, less variance in environments and Anima encounters.

This is fantastic. Being a long-time fan of the Battlefield franchise, it's great to see someone working on a game that plays like it, but brings back the much-loved instant action gamemode. Multiplayer support will be appreciated in the future as well as mods. Once this game gets mod support, the doors will blow wide open on this one. I played a bit and while it's bare bones right now, there's so much potential for it to grow and become something fans like me have wanted for a while.
A couple points that would be great to address in the soonest fixes:
1. Add loadouts. Should be pretty basic to program those into the game so you can try multiple different things without having to pick them individually every time you spawn.
2. Work on scaling controls for things like scopes. The AWP in the game basically has a 1:1 ratio for scoped and unscoped which makes the weapon very difficult to handle. I'd advise fixing that up.
3. I can hear audio clips of voices in the background of the menu screens, but nothing, not even grunts of pain, from in-game characters. Stuff like that would be wonderful.
4. I think it goes without saying expanding available gadgets, weapons, maps, vehicles would be a great thing, but opening this up to mod support will pretty much fix that issue.
5. Perhaps at least a guide of some kind to explain the gamemodes and how they work would be appreciated. I like being able to dive-in, but maybe some more in-game explanation as to what the hell is happening would be nice.
6. A mini-map. Please, God, a mini-map. Having to hold M while I'm charging across open territory is a nightmare. At least add the option to have a constant map on the corner of your screen or something.
Overall, the mechanics and what not have been nailed down very nicely for an early access game. It's not pretty, but there are no bugs I've found and that's fantastic for something like this. Keep working on the usual like visuals, audio, and variety of gameplay and you've got a game I'd be willing to pay $40 in stores.

If you're looking at buying this, or already have it, check out the Multiplayer Mod that Nanos Framework is developing, it should be released on Steam sometime in the near future. It's a hell of a lot more stable than the base game (removes NPC traffic and vehicles), custom scripts like infinite boost, Youtube cinemas, bavarium wingsuit modifications and 3D model imports (I have plans for that on Gaveroid's server, come check that out if you're reading this, It's a fun place.)
Overall, I'd say that buying the game is worth it just for the multiplayer mod, but the base game and the DLC are both pretty fun on their own. Before the multiplayer came out, I had around 102 hours or so in the base game.
+ Pros
- Multiplayer
- Explosions
- Various sandbox assets (blowing up bridges, flips and stunts in the air, various mines and ATV tracks)
- Multiplayer (Its free and will be on Steam soon, get it!)
- Cons
- Some vehicle handeling is an issue, JC2 is better if you just like to drive around islands. I beleve that Nanos is also making some sort of modification to improve it and restore it to be better like JC2
- Some various glitches, such as getting thrown under the map (easy way to fix it is to just wingsuit back through). Happens the most, at least for me, in rail tunnels after my car is hit by a train.
Overall, this game is really nice if you want a unique multiplayer experience, I haven't touched the base game for a pretty long time since the multiplayer mod came out. But it's pretty fun overall.

I'll start with a simple statement of opinion: this is an excellent game.
I'll follow with a simple statement of fact: this game is challenging.
While this game is not as hard as its predecessor, it will beat you into the dirt if you're not careful. However, this shouldn't be an immediate turn-off to players who don't like difficulty (more on why later - this paragraph is mostly about how the game will crush your hopes and dreams). It punishes mistakes severely. Enemies do buttloads of damage, and every time you die, you drop all your souls (which function as both the game's money and experience) at the location of your kicked butt, and if you want them back, you have to haul back there and retrieve them before you die again or they're gone forever. You also lose some of your maximum health every time you die until you hit 50% of your initial max health. This can be remedied with items and online play, though (more on that later).
The game does forgive you sometimes - it's very satisfying to somehow be left with a sliver of health to give you a doorway to finally slaying that one guy who keeps killing you. There's also cooperative play if you get stuck, though you need to be human to benefit from it (more on that later, as well).
To top it all off, you eventually get the hang of the game and get to feel awesome as you crush your foes like a boss before moving on and obliterating the actual boss.
The game has excellent combat that favors cautious and thought-out plans of attack rather than Leeroy Jenkins-style assaults. There is a variety of weapons, including four varieties of magic, and there is almost certainly something here to fit your playstyle, whatever it might be. PvP is available (again, more on online play later), and twinking isn't as much of a problem as it was in the first game.
Pro tip: shields are quite possibly the most important item in your arsenal. Make sure you understand what your shield's stats are, what those stats mean, and never go anywhere without one in your inventory (if not equipped, as you probably won't have time to equip it via menu should things go south).
Level design is great, with deadly surprises around every corner and enemies itching to dig their claws, swords, fangs or whatever they might be armed with into you. Exploration is rewarded, but be cautious, as recklessness is met with death. The boss fights are satisfying and memorable (with some exceptions, of course) and the OST is filled with intense boss themes for you to enjoy as you get slaughtered over and over.
The lore is also very rich should you choose to delve into it, and it has plenty of room for speculation if that's your thing (though many questions will likely be answered in the lore of DLC, like with the first game). There are references to the first game left and right, some being more cleverly hidden than others. In fact, in order to fully understand the lore and story of this game, you will likely need to understand (or at least be familiar with) the lore of the first game.
As for the story itself, most of it is contained in the lore, but know this - you are an undead. That's right. You die before the game even starts. But being undead is a curse, so you march off to Drangleic to get souls to avoid going insane. Or do you? Nobody's really sure why they're in Drangleic, and your initial goal may not be what you achieve in the end. The lore contains the answers to most questions you have regarding the story, so it's worth checking out.
Now the multiplayer. Singleplayer and multiplayer are mostly fused in this game. You can summon people into your game to help you out, your game can be invaded by someone intent on killing you, and you can be the person who enters other people's games to assist or slay them. Fear not, all you folks who hate being ganked - 1v1 arenas are available in certain locations if you can't find anybody flying solo in your invasions. Assisting players is very beneficial, though, as fulfilling your duty without perishing results in the restoration of your humanity (your health is restored and you can summon allies again).
Nearly anything is viable in PvP (as long as you've properly upgraded your gear and didn't distribute your stat points like a moron), including cosplays (recreating a character as closely as possible in the game and playing in the manner of that character), which results in some fun builds to both be made and encounter.
Of course, the game is not without flaws - it's not a perfect port, and you'll probably spend a decent chunk of time from the get-go figuring out which buttons do what and then rebinding them to your liking. Getting the hang of the game will take time. Playing the game will also take time, as it takes hard work and dedication to progress. Heck, your first playthrough might last 50+ hours (though that's not necessarily a downside, depending on how you look at it).
New Game+ offers increases in enemy strength, better loot, different enemies (the NG+ welcoming committee is a doozy), and overall decent replayability.
All in all, this game is worth both the time and money. Don't be turned away by that first paragraph or any rumors you may hear of the game's insurmountable difficulty. It's challenging, it's fun, it's rewarding, and it's one of the best games I've ever had the pleasure of playing.

I'm a die-hard fan of this franchise, and after playing Deus Ex and Human Revolution, I decided to give this game a shot.
Storyline wise, I feel like it failed to live up to the complexities of plot associated with the Deus Ex title. When I saw that one of the side quests was about coffee sellers, I was a hightly underwhelmed. Of course, it being Deus Ex, they found a way to make such a trivial thing a part of a more meaningful framework, and that, however, was the impressive part. Such a silly thing was used as an illustrator of the absolute means of control that was in place by the Illuminati.
The numerous options of progressing in the game were a plus, however. Invisible War's faction system that provides you with different groups to give your loyalty to, and the ways that these groups may still ask you to do things that make you uncomfortable are an impressive reflection of the not-so-black-and-white situation of being affiliated with any group. I appreciated the faction system and their contrary objectives in a given stage.
Gameplay was a bit clunky though. That ring-shaped HUD, for one, was a massive, epic fail in my opinion that obscured far too much of the line of sight than I would have liked. Additionally, the limitations on the holding capacity were just silly. Beyond this, the game didn't give you much of an opportunity to stick to a non-lethal approach when it came to the armoured Templars. There was absolutely zero way for you take them down without blowing them up.
There were a few things I really thought were good. I really liked the spiderbombs and the Mag Rail. I really liked the differences in the storyline that you could encounter depending on if you were playing as a female character or male one. I also really, really loved all of the little storyline details that connected the first and second games, such as the Gunther Hermann Skul-Gun request. The reproduction of the original stages and transgenics were also nice to see. I like how those details were reworked into this game.
All in all, if you were a massive fan of the first game, this one might be worth playing if you just want to see what they managed to do with the plot.  It might not be an enjoyable experience, but it might give you a sense of achievement, and might be entertaining to see how they address some of the details that went into the first game.

I love this type of horror (I would assume that all survival horror games ought to scare in a simmilar manner). It's like a big game of hide and seek, with objectives.

-The ship you are on is ♥♥♥♥ing huge and you move around at the pace of a snail...Do the math.

Kind of a weird game. I'm a little dubious about giving it a recommendation, but I'll give it the benefit of the doubt for now.
It's a lot like Battlefield multiplayer. Interestingly, it is single player versus AI modes only -- there is no actual multiplayer of which to speak. I'll do another list, since that allows me to think more clearly:
PROS:
• The basic gameplay is fun. It's basic, but it works. It plays like a standard FPS in terms of controls.
• The damage from player to enemies and vice-versa is effectively the same. Be careful about being shot. I enjoy not being all-powerful in games. You may feel differently.
• The ragdolls are enjoyable, and they have a little bit of animation to them.
• For the most part, all of the current weapons feel somewhat unique and useful in their own ways.
• You can sneak up on enemies and use suppressed weapons on them to remain hidden.
• The scale of the battles can be increased, meaning that if you have a more powerful computer, you can see a lot of units on the map at once.
• Planes and helicopters are fun to pilot, and have satisfying weapons.
• Many of the weapons in general feel satisfying to use.
CONS:
• The AI is often dumb enough to use rocket launchers in CQB and doesn't seem to care about friendly fire at all. This includes vehiclular team killing.
• Explosions affect you through walls. If the terrain was destructible, this would be cooler, but instead you sometimes just get knocked down or killed by an explosion that you couldn't see.
• AI is as often injured as killed. I would prefer this to be less common in favour of outright fatality. It's a nice touch, but I hate always having to stop and finish off enemies.
• Aside from the planes and helicopter, the vehicles feel a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the controls department. The plane/helicopter could use some gauges and additional HUD elements, but they control okay.
• As a suggestion, I'd like the option to set a time for corpse persistence.
• Not a whole lot of content. Only 2/4 maps are interesting IMO.
• The game is kind of expensive for what you get currently, and this is my main point of concern for now. It's 15 US dollars, and I've milked about 2.5 hours out of it. Not a lot, considering.
My suggestion is to maybe wait a while, until more is added, or it goes on special. It's okay, but you might get your money's worth later. I don't think it's there yet.

Okay, first off I very much enjoyed this game. Though I'm not entirely sure about "a focus on a challenging difficulty", the controls were wonderfully consistent and responsive, which I imagine is exactly what you want out of a precision platformer. I never once had a death in this game that I could blame on anything but myself. And that's how it should be, really.
I'm far from an expert on precison platforming, but that feeling of actually being in control is exactly what I'd want out of a skill-based game. The simplicity of the gameplay helps a lot, of course.
Very short, and though the level editor does help, a better level creation interface and/or Steam Workshop support would be nice. However, a game that's short and to the point and doesn't overstay its welcome is better than a long game that gets really redundant and boring after a while.
+very responsive controls
+purely skill-based, no impossible timing or luck or
precise jumps
+reasonable length
+level creation feature (not really a level editor, exactly, you just need to edit a collection of gifs to make a level)
+nice soundtrack
-could have used additional more difficult levels
-visual style is a bit inconsistent (especially the weird backgrouns in the later levels), and "retro" has been done to death
-no Steam Workshop support
(Bought this game on a sale for two bucks, but all in all I'd say it could be worth three.)

My first real time strategy game and the start to one hell of a ride that I have yet to get off from.  If you're looking to experience what is arguably the dawn of modern real time strategy gaming, give this title a spin...  Despite some clunkiness due to age (can't zoom out, for example), it is still a lot of fun and I am glad that it's still playable on modern systems.

Pros:
- Unit variety is great, there is almost a unit for every conceivable role.
- Two resources, metal and energy. Nice and simple, multiple gathering options for each.
- Great base defence options, great variety of turrets.
- Huge variety of maps, covering multiple terrain types.
- Lengthy campaigns, with a great variety of levels.
- Soundtrack is epic, with vibrant orchestral pieces
- Game comes with all expansions and DLC bundled
Cons:
- AI isn't great. Not idiotic, but does occasionally build navies in small lakes
- Battles are often slow-burn affairs as a lot of maps allow for turtling and take time to seize ground, not great for short games.
- AI pathing is capable of spectacular failures, getting units stuck.
- Scenery (specifically trees) make base building awkward on some maps as getting construction units to remove them is time-consuming and they are often hard to click on.

I can recommend Just Cause 3 to others, but just barely because of the poor optimization this game has seen since launch.  I do think some of the patches helped in this area, but it's still incredibly disappointing coming from the same developer of Just Cause 2 and Mad Max, some of the most well-optimized games I've ever played on PC.  I would recommend buying directly through Steam or somewhere else that will issue a refund if this doesn't perform up to your expectations.
Just Cause 3 is one of the few games that I have picked up on launch day, as it was one of the few big releases that I was really looking forward to playing.  This does a great job picking up where Just Cause 2 left off.  Like before, the focus on the game is creating as much destruction and havoc as possible, and this serves as a pretty good way to carry you through the game's story.  I can't speak much on the narrative since it's pretty lackluster in comparison to other AAA titles and some indie offerings, but I do think it's significantly better than what JC2 offered.
Having said that, I'm not here to learn about Rico Rodriguez and his glorious home in Medici.  I want to tether explosives to each other and fly around in a wingsuit all day.  This is where the game can really shine, and if it wasn't for all the issues this game had at launch, it would have been a slam dunk.  At 1080p resolution, I can usually hold a steady 60 frames on very high settings and some AA enabled with an i7-3770, GTX 970, and 16GB of memory.  Sometimes it may drop a bit into the mid-40's if I trigger a chain of explosives that looks like the equivalent of a nuke going off, but there were never any fatal flaws that kept me from enjoying this title.
Bottom line: do be wary if you don't have the latest cutting-edge tech in your machine and keep your refund options available for as long as you can.  Vive Medici!

I don't know what to say without mentioning something which is already said.
So I think I'm gonna tell you my expectations and experiences about the game.
After reading all the praise for Eternal Senia for its storytelling, I decided to play it since I was bored at that time. Easy gameplay, just "died" two times in a fight because I didn't pay attention to my health bar, but if you improve your skills and equipment, it won't take too much effort to beat this game. Therefore it is really relaxing, but also entertaining. I like the artstyle for Senia and Magaleta and I really wish that I could see more "cutscenes".
So I expected a good, fun game to play. However, after finishing the first boss and seeing more and more of Senias background story, I wanted to keep on playing it. Not merely because I wanted to level up, but to experience the story and see how it will end. Will Senia be able to find her sister Magaleta and bring her back home? Or will she forever stay in the Tower of Eternity? And the main reason, why I just have to complete it, is, that I can feel for the characters, thanks to the background stories of Senia and Magaleta.
Eternal Senia is heartwarming and yet sad, with (at least for me 'cause I'm dumb) one unexpected plot twist at the very end. It is a story about the love of two sisters, about loss, and about maturing and resolve.
So yeah, I was kinda overwhelmed to get such a beautiful game experience from a FREE game. I recommend it and if there would be a sequel, I would gladly play it^^

For my part, the game runs beautifully. Despite the shallow story, the environments are gorgeous and immersive. I've played my share of sandbox games but I haven't had this much fun since I first picked up Skyrim. It doesn't hurt that Rico is damn handsome. I saw some of those behind the scenes videos- nice work, ladies of Avalanche!
...Driving down the road I find myself viewing satellite dishes, cell towers and transformer stations a lot differently than I used to. American consumers' access to rocket launchers is woefully inadequate.
I do have a wishlist. Motorcycles that obey the laws of physics in /this/ universe. Rico being voiced by someone that's maybe actually Hispanic or Mediterranean, not a pencil-necked Jersey boy. Local co-op or some form of multiplayer, since you're requiring online access anyway. Marketing to capitalize on Robbaz's "Just Cows" pun...These are but trifles in the face of a game that does such a great job psychologically rewarding me for drop-kicking workers over the side of an aircraft hovering 2 kilometers over the ocean, flinging goat carcasses at the locals and running down tourists on my pimped out pogo stick.
I've had zero stuttering, frame rate, crashing or other accessibility issues. The other gamer in the house, on the other hand, has had a few hangups- mostly graphics bugs like disappearing cars and a memory leak that creeps up if you leave the game running literally all day long. He had some stuttering and frame rate drops that were 100% fixed by disabling Vsync, and rebotting every /four hours/ helps with the rest. We have almost identical high end builds, but he runs dual NVidia cards and I'm using a single AMD card. Still, neither of us have experienced the scale of issues people have been posting. Frankly I'm saddened Avalanche's support is so lacking. I love this game to death and it pains me to think there are people who can't experience it properly because of technical issues. I hope things get resolved for the rest of you because this game deserves far better than the 50-50 rating it's got right now.
Update: Still no graphics issues, and since updating his dual NVidia setup to the most recent drivers the other gamer in the house hasn't had any issues, either. I'd recommend this game to anyone and everyone.

I'm in love with Alien and I'm in love with this game. It is burdened with its share of problems, some of which may understandably be dealbreakers for certain players.
The game is at its best when it's integrating entirely new challenges with its more familiar threats, but that experience is ocassionally undermined when those allegedly 'new' problems can be easily handled with the tactics you've already used many times. It's more interesting when you're forced to tune your strategy to come up with new solutions, and the game doesn't do that nearly enough.
Also, the cutscenes are kind of a drag. I love when the exposition is handled during first-person gameplay, as it really maintains the game's amazing sense of tension. There's a moment in the game where you experience a flashback by playing through a past event, and it's FANTASTIC. It's really telling that this dramatic change in setting and time feels more organic than the blunt transition into a pre-rendered cutscene.
Overall, though, this game is great. I felt the same sense of fear and urgency in the game's final moments as I did during the initial encounter with the alien. The sound design is unparalleled, the art feels innovative and nostalgic at the same time, and playing at the hardest difficulty actually mitigates many of the problems of repetitive gameplay. And if you love Alien as much as I do, you're kind of required to play this game.

You can get dropped off in different places for each new location, you can side with eather faction at any given point in the story and you can actually make meaningful choices at the end as to which faction will rule the world.
Not only that but it digs up the past in the best way possible. It determines that Paul and JC are alive and possibly well if you pick that faction. It boils the game down into a nice package.
In a way I am happy the modern games didn't try to tack onto the series ending that invisible war created because it ended it in a casade of choice.
So for those who value choice and well written narrative the game is worth it.

Recent updates and fixes have now rendered this game PLAYABLE and ENJOYABLE for me, so I will review it now:
==PROS==
+Great gameplay, just as fluid as the first game or more.
+Fun combat (personally I prefer stealth route and avoid combat)
+Replayability factor (Emily loud, Emily stealth, Corvo loud, Corvo stealth) at least 4 different playthoughs there, 50+ hours of content.
+Main characters have outstanding voice acting.
+Great progression and upgrade system.
+Stealth mechanics are improved from the first game, more items and spells are offered if you choose to play stealthy.
+Lore is very complex and interesting, but also completely optional if you don't care about it.
+Good presentation, will keep you invested for hours.
+Free updates
==CONS==
-Massive optimization problems, Void engine is experimental and IT SHOWS. Devs are at least putting some effort in fixing it.
-Jagged edges are a big problem in this game, even with FXAA, TXAA helps somewhat but is demanding on hardware.
-Environment items are harder to see than in the first game, its very easy to miss loot and coins.
-PERSONALLY, the story is meh compared to the first game, and doesn't fit with the Brigmore Witches DLC canon.
(hey, maybe you enjoy it, and good for you)
-Enemy and secondary character voice acting is subpar and unenthusiastic.
-Devs have taken months to fix bugs and optimization problems, and fixes are still ongoing.

I would recommend buying directly through Steam or somewhere else that will issue a refund if this doesn't perform up to your expectations.
Just Cause 3 is one of the few games that I have picked up on launch day, as it was one of the few big releases that I was really looking forward to playing.  This does a great job picking up where Just Cause 2 left off.  Like before, the focus on the game is creating as much destruction and havoc as possible, and this serves as a pretty good way to carry you through the game's story.  I can't speak much on the narrative since it's pretty lackluster in comparison to other AAA titles and some indie offerings, but I do think it's significantly better than what JC2 offered.
Having said that, I'm not here to learn about Rico Rodriguez and his glorious home in Medici.  I want to tether explosives to each other and fly around in a wingsuit all day.  This is where the game can really shine, and if it wasn't for all the issues this game had at launch, it would have been a slam dunk.  At 1080p resolution, I can usually hold a steady 60 frames on very high settings and some AA enabled with an i7-3770, GTX 970, and 16GB of memory.  Sometimes it may drop a bit into the mid-40's if I trigger a chain of explosives that looks like the equivalent of a nuke going off, but there were never any fatal flaws that kept me from enjoying this title.
Bottom line: do be wary if you don't have the latest cutting-edge tech in your machine and keep your refund options available for as long as you can.  Vive Medici!

I love this game. This is one of my favorite games and I have played it dozens of times. It is a richly atmospheric and incredibly detailed world with a great story and amazing art direction that has held up very well over the years. Walking through the corridors of the Von Braun still fills me with the same sense of dread and apprehension that I felt the very first time I played it. The pacing was perfect, the sound design with 3D effects was superb, and the music selection for every deck past the med bay (pounding techno) was excellent. Since 1999, there have been scarier games, there have been homages and spiritual successors, but none have captured all of the elements that make this one of the orignal masterpieces of PC gaming. Even with a third act that drags at times and an ending that is abrupt and out of place, this is still one of the best games I've ever played. Top 5.
Still, there's a caveat when it comes to recommending it. The game is punishingly difficult. I've had to use the ubermensch cheat nearly all of my playthroughs. (Shame!) If you're curious, cheating doesn't ruin the story or break the immersion for me. The lack of quest arrows and handholding tutorials that plague so many modern games are totally absent here. If you liked BIoshock and that's what brought you here, just be aware that this game is way more involved. There's inventory management, weapons stats, char stats, etc. I'm not telling you these things to scare you away -- I just feel that if you're more prepared to deal with them, you'll get past them easier and move onto enjoying the truly excellent core. Be sure to look for mods to improve the textures, sounds, music and animations. There is an amazing online cult community that has created some truly incredible stuff.
Long story short: This is still one of the best games I've ever played. Top 5. It's nearly 20 years old and while many of it's gameplay elements are dated, the storytelling techniques and the immersive sim aspects are features that were ahead of their time and have only recently made their way into the mainstream games.

I think System Shock I---not II---is my favorite game of all time. It was a (nearly!) full-fledged sci-fi horror RPG-FPS hybrid built around story telling and delivering a creepy atmosphere. On top of that, it included finding logs, a lot of backtracking and puzzling too, and making choices what to carry using your clumsy inventory and the worst user-interface since VI. The game has since been updated and is currently in full reboot; I look forward to this game enormously.
System Shock II moves along similar lines, but as you might have guessed, is not my favorite game of all time. But. It is still a great experience and I'd certainly recommend you to try it as it is a stepping stone leading up to other games such as Bioshock, Dead Space, or Alien Isolation. So I know that there are many RPG games such as Dragon Age and Skyrim (actually played the former) and these games are far more elaborate, but for some reason the scifi genre appeals to me much more than the fantasy genre; I like firing lasers and handgrenades more than shooting arrows and casting spells.
The RPG element in Shock II is more a nice attempt than an actual RPG though. From the start of the game you can select three classes but that results in a difference only in the first half hour of the game. The tech-guy with all the hacking is interesting, but after a while you use your PSI skills (i.e., the wizard) to do pretty much anything. I recommend playing as the PSI guy.
System Shock II, like its predecessor, is heavily story driven and the RPG system has matured; slightly. However, there are a few items that, in my opinion, did not make it such a great game to me as Shock I. Mainly, while Shock I would offer you an entire new level to explore, Shock II's level design is much more linear. Like Bioshock most levels are mostly a very long hallway with a few side branches to explore. To me, this resulted in not feeling like you are on a single space ship, rather a collection of levels. There were no new doors or elevators that would transport you to a part of a previous level giving you that "so that is how you get here" feeling. A degree of backtracking was involved though with too many items you could not take with you, in particular the many chemicals you needed to research enemy parts and organs for damage bonuses and advice.
The second main disappointment of the game is that after a while you need to leave all of that behind as you enter the second space ship (the space ship you are in is actually two space ships; perhaps this is why it never felt that you are on a single space ship?) and work your way through lesser level design towards a most unsatisfactory end. But by that time you've experienced several memorable moments and revelations---and admittedly, the kind that were never in Shock I---and that you so liked so much in the Bioshock series.
But what made the game really great (especially compared to Bioshock) is that everything you need is in very, very short supply and the sound design is really wonderful. It's not as if you need to really plan ahead, but it will make you thread more carefully and forces you to use the right type of weapon on the various enemies you encounter. Rome II starts off as a tough cookie. You always lose, even if you've become pretty good at Empire.
With enough experience, you can become good at it. And if you love total strategy and have some patience, it'll work out well for you.
Yes, there's no family tree. Yes, you can only have 16 armies max. Yes, public order seemingly becomes impossible to control if your empire is large enough. But, in all, due to the variety of patches, it's a great game. At around the 200th hour I became a bit sick of it because I'm in a stalemate of sorts with Carthage. But there's always other factions to play as. Replay value is 11/10 with the patches and emperor edition and some mods...
I recommend the 4TPY mod, all factions mod (xcept those that are designated as DLC only - well, I bought Ceasar in Gaul and the Greek States pack at my satisfaction with playing this game)  and the balanced diplomacy mod and the ranged camera mod (so I can see my empire from afar); and finally, the ROME 1 music (it can't be beat) mod.
Also, it looks a bit cartoonish.
Rome II grows on you if you're in to the Total War games. It has become, over more than a year, a stellar game. I think that if it were relaeased today the metacritic score would be more like 85-92.
Battles are great (but make sure you have a decent computer). Loading is kind of long but quotes make it interesting. And of course, decisions decisions decisions. Do you want to upgrade your industry or prepare for a full-on war? It gets very technical so be prepared to lose for 50-200 turns until you master the "glitches" or ways that you can succeed.
Attilla looks more like Rome II should've been. That said, it's still very compelling.
I would give it a solid 9.2/10, and 9.5 if you're into the material surroudning Rome.
Try to get it on sale! I didn't, but that's because I appreciate the work that the developers are doing. I support such cognitively complex games with such replay value.
