I really did not want to give this game and CA this negative review but hopefully after reading it you guys will understand where I am coming from.  I've been a Total war fan since the original Rome was released back in 2004 and I feel like this game has ALMOST ruined the whole franchise for me.  I'm gonna try and make this as short as possibe.
I was one of the "lucky" few to pre-order Rome 2 and I was pumped to get back into my most favorite franchise.  Sadly, when the game finally dropped on September 3rd 2013, I couldnt have been more dissapointed.  For some reason I did not really experience the bugs as much as other people did (the game only crashed once or twice) but what did it for me was the genreal experience of the game.  I couldnt play the main campaign for more than a couple of hours before it became BORING AS HELL!!! Dissapointed, I decided to stop playing the game.  Every couple of months after that I would check back in and see if any of the new patches fixed the mechanics that made the game so unplayable to me.  Sadly month after month I saw no real improvements.  When the Emperor Edition was announced and consequenty released I was excited to dive back into this game, truly hoping that CA had fixed the mess that Rome 2 had become.  After playing the Emperor edition for a couple of hours or so I once again turned the game off dissapointed.  People claim that the Emperor edition is the game that we should have received but I still disagree, the game feels like it's missing many key elements to it that made the previous Total War titles so spectacular.
Pro's:
The graphics are amazing (as they should be)
The Campaign map looks stunning as well as the towns and cities all feel alive on the map
The number of factions is ENORMOUS (even though you cant play them all without mods)
The new vision system added a lot of realism to the game as well as making the game more tactically challenging
The time period the game is set in is fantastic
Diversity of units
(I honestly can't think of anything else.............)
Con's
THE TOTAL WAR WIKI - I hate that thing sooooo much!  The first time it appeared in Shogun 2 it really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.  It was far more complicated than the previous system of just right-clicking on a building or a unit and then it telling you all of the information about said unit/building.  You didn't need to have it LOAD, and the navigation of the wiki pages is soo damn confusing!
TECH/BUILDING TREE - Again, in the previous games everything was easy to find, the building tree was a tab that you could click on that would show you all of the buildings, the buildings you needed to build said buildings and the units/benefits they provided to your city.
GARRISONS - Garrisons were first implemented in Empire (I believe) and they were awesome! They felt realistic, a mob defending their city from massive enemy armies against all odds was fanstastic! In Shogun 2 they expanded this feature and made it even better, you could get more advanced units defending your castles as you leveled them up.  Rome 2 literally broke the whole garrison system.  The armies that the garrison produce are MASSIVE even at the beginning of the campaign, and worst of all THEY ARE IMPOSSIBLE TO SEE ON THE CAMPAIGN MAP!!! You have to scroll over the settlement to see how many units that settlement has garrisoned in it.  And like I mentioned before those garrisons are HUGE, they are almost impossible to defeat especially if the enemy also has a supporting general with an army defending it.  You need massive armies to even challenge minor factions with one or two settlements and worst of all this is in the BEGINNING OF THE CAMPAIGN!!!
ARMIES - WHY DO I NEED TO ALWAYS HAVE A GENERAL TO BE ABLE TO RECRUIT A SINGLE UNIT!!!!?!?!?  If i need units to be recruited in order to support another army closeby in another territory I have to recruit a new general in order to do so and I dont think that should be necessary.  It made the game very restrictive and in turn was a lot less fun to play.  The generals seemed expendable and a lot less important to the whole campaign.
THE FAMILY TREE - Totally missing...................  WHY????? It made the game more engaging.  If one general got killed in battle I made it my goal to go after the murderous army with the dead generals brother/son/father.  I felt more involved with the charachters involved.
BUILDINGS/CITIES - In my opinion Empire had the best building system.  It was easy to understand.  You could build every building you desired (except for Opera Houses) in almost every city and the armies that each city produced were equally as powerful.  There were no "limited building slots". you could build all the buildings that you wanted, provided that they were availabe in that city level.  In Rome 2 AS WELL as Shogun 2, the building system was very restrictive.  I know that they were going for more strategy elements, but that retrictive nature made the game feel more cumbersome.  What I did like in Shogun 2 was the tech tree.  I thought it was the best out of all the total war games.
VIEW CITY ON BATTLEFIELD MAP - Now this is a minor feature that was only present in the first Rome (as far as I know).  You could zoom in to your settlement at any time during your turn and just take a leisurely look around the city and enjoy the epic scale of certain cities as well as the citizens.  Why remove a feature?? Same thing goes for blood in Medieval 2, now it has become a DLC.  WHY TAKE OUT FEATURES FROM OLD GAMES????
Not Pro's and not Con's
The DLC - I dont mind DLC as long as it feels like DLC but not features like blood or more factions!! If the faction is in the game why cant I play with them without using a mod????  In Medieval 2 and Rome 1, you needed to beat the campaign at least once to unlock more factions and I thought that was very interesting as well as engaging.  it forced you to get to know the game and learn the features before you were allowed to play with the harder factions that you UNLOCKED.  DLC should consist of only true expansions, like Caesar in Gaul or Hannibal at the gates.  OR MEDIEVAL KINGDOMS!!!!! (That one was awesome).... They add NEW factions to the game and new events, time periods, units, locations, and bigger and detailed maps to the original game.  You should not have to pay for stuff that was already in the previous games.
THE AI - The AI has always been♥♥♥♥♥♥ and to be honest as long as it puts some sort of effort to fight me I'm happy.  The missing features mentioned above are more important to me personally than the AI.  It would be nice if they improved it.
These are some of the biggest features or lack there of in this game that just ruined this particular title for me.  There are a couple more features that I woul mention but I felt that I was rambling too much already.  I believe in CA and I know that they are a great company because they have made great games in the past and Im sure they'll make some in the future.  The new Atilla game looks like an improvement from this terrible game but as I watch more and more trailers from the upcoming game, I cant help but notice some of the similarities between this trash game and the new up-coming game.  I'm probably gonna have to sit out the next Total War game because I truly feel that they need more time to fix their mistakes, at least to the same state as they were in previous entries.

In one hand I consider this a stronger, more forward game than the first. It gives you an objective out the gate. There are things you must avoid or remove yourself to get there. If you like to explore you will be rewarded, because in context of this game it allows you to do so even if Seabass only wants to save his daughter. Time does not work in STEM like it does in reality.
On the other, I feel like there was some Bethesda meddling. Play the game yourself and see how every encounter with a friendly NPC goes. It's like playing a recent Elder Scrolls/Fallout but in third person and the player character is Seabass himself. There's a crafting system for no reason even though if you're a veteran to older surivial horror it's something out of Resident Evil 3. This also bleeds into a 'leveling' system not just for Seabass himself from the first game concerning green goop but for his weapons too. At level X weapon Y will now have this trait, etc.
I was also seeing more than enough nods to other, previous horror games to boot. Silent Hill, aforementioned Resident Evil. That kind of thing. I mean this game is almost RE4 2.0 to some extent but with strong acknowledgements to earlier horror. The eyeball motiff is very present with Stefano's segments. After that it's like the castle section once you get to Theodore's part but way more 'abstract' in approach.
However I enjoyed playing it. Ran smoothly for most of the time. The combat and stealth was great. All the optional content was satisfying to finish. There is closure and some questions raised about things from the first game. The art direction is more abstract compared to the first that heavily relied on typical horror tropes.
This game also made me cry at one point. I'd rather not say why.
To avoid spoilers I will say the ending leaves a LOT open but you would have to see for yourself if you care about it. Also there's a shooting gallery later on in the game you can unlock but instead of the Merchant it's the Nurse from the first Evil Within. Really worth checking into.

I always thought of the first game as really well-made grindhouse horror movie that was translated into a video game. It had fairly decent scares, but the overall plot and characters were completely over-the-top and and I never took the game too seriously. I enjoyed it for what it was: an action-packed romp through various classic horror tropes.
The second game takes on an ENTIRELY different tone, and I was completely floored. I never cared about Sebastian Castellanos in the first game. He was just a sort of throw-away main character who was there to simply serve as the protagonist. He could have easily had no dialogue and just been called "Player 1" and it would have served the same purpose. Yes, they make reference to the fact that he had suffered a tragedy, but most of that was done through journal entries which easily could have been skipped unless you were a thorough player. Even then, none of his past felt like it had ANY impact on the action or how the story unfolded. It was just there so he could claim to have a "past" and was not simply manifested out of thin air to be in this game (which, he was).
Meanwhile, in the The Evil Within 2, every ounce of his past trauma and psychological torment is felt throughout each moment of the game. And not only is it felt throughout the story, but it is actually manifested in the aesthetics and overall design of the game world. Considering the premise of this game, it completely makes sense why that is, but even still, it's a perfect execution in terms of the art direction. Whether it's a giant camera lens in the sky that replaces the moon, or theater full of people frozen in time as their heads are exploding, the game creates beauty out of the mundane and the grotesque in a way that really blew me away. The tone of the story is deeply somber, but also endearing and hopeful. The game itself is very sobering experience; in fact, if the first Evil Within was the alcohol fueled party the night before, The Evil Within 2 is the hangover the next day, but with more zombies....and you know, fun.
The mind-bendy level design also brilliantly ties into the narrative and everything about this game just ♥♥♥♥ing works! Doors disappear and reappear; you'll walk into a small house, and all of a sudden you're in a decrepit hospital fleeing a singing phantom who can walk through walls. The main over-world section of the game is teeming with hidden nooks and crannies that open up into awesome little side-missions and diversions that make the entire game feel alive and very organic.
I'm really looking forward to more from this franchise, or even an expansion to this story (as long as it's handled with the same attention to detail as this game was).

If like me you are  a fan of the original Alien film, you must play this game! All other Alien fanchiese games I've played try to replicate the fast-pased gun-weilding action of Aliens, but this is the first time something replicating the slow-paced nail-biting  tension of the first film. The design of the ship and the station, all the interfaces and gadgets (notably the terrfying but essential motion sensor) all capture the feel of the original film perfectly. THis is by far the MOST teriffying game I've played. Never have I experienced such intense tension in a game that my hands are shaking when I put down the controller. THe AI of the Alien is very clever and quite sadistiic! Often it makes you think you are safe enough to take a few tentative steps out of your hiding place, only for it come running back and take you down within seconds. You also have rouge androids and angry civilants to deal who are slightly less scary as you at least have a chance ot kill them. If you are after a crazy FPS, this is not for you. You spend much of the game hiding in lockers and under desks becuase because it is always stalking you and you have no way of killing it. This is the games appeal to me. It is a much more realistic response to the scenario, which makes it all the more terrefying.

I waited until I finished the game to write this.  The game is beautiful; the graphics and music are absolutely great.  I felt intense moments of stress and tension at different points in the game and even had to take breaks at some save points because it was too much to bear.  I do recommend checking your map often to always know where your objective is (multiple times I got on the wrong elevator and went to the wrong sections).  It is suggested to play it on "hard" difficulty for the best experience; hard is fine but normal might be more of your flavor.  On hard you are constantly harassed by the alien and it numbs you to its effect.  On normal the alien then is provided a much longer leash and to me that's better because there's more tension from not knowing it's location and when it will be in your direct vicinity.  It is a little pricey (I grabbed it on that flash sale) so if you can wait for the price to lower, the value is worth it.
*Edit-  I retract my earlier preference to play normal vs. hard.  Hard should be your first run and if you want a challenge do nightmare.  I just played through the game again; did a nightmare speedrun and got done in less than 5 1/2 hours.  So people complaining the game is too long; that's on you.  A normal first run should take in the 11-13 hour range; if you take longer it's your fault.  Also never hide in lockers; on that nightmare speedrun I didn't get into a SINGLE locker.

Give it a little patience, download the improved Unified Texture pack made by a fan, patch to 1080 resolution, and this game is quite a good game.
It came from the Eidos era or 2003, which is the same era as Tomb Raider Angel of Darkness,  which could have a great game, but Eidos of this era pushed development teams very hard and had impossibly short deadlines, etc. While AOD wore the brunt of these behind the scenes problems, Deus Ex: Invisible War managed to be at least a coherant complete game. With some problems, sure.
Its biggest problem may be that it has to live up to the incredible success of the first game. A hard task by itself. And does it? Yes and no. While it does not start with the same atmosphere as the first game, after a few levels, and after a few biomod upgrades, it becomes more obvious that it really does exist in the same game world as the opiginal. It is not as long of a game, and its a pity that it ends not very long after reaching its full momentum, but there is enough Role Playing and Action to be fresh and entertaining.
The zones are divided into sections makes it feel less open world in the "safe areas" (i.e. non combat zones where as opposed to zones with 90% combat) that, say, Hong Kong did in the first game. And even on a modern (2016) pc, loading is a bit slow. On Windows 10, you get to see your desktop for at least 10 seconds of loading, and I doubt there will be any patch to fix this in the future. This just means that loading between sub areas can break the momentum and mood slightly. However, there is enough complexity and there are enough missions in the "safe areas". Also each map, while following the city architecture, is different enough to justify it being stored in seperate zones. It would be nice if it was remade in one unified map, but that is unlikely to ever happen. However, it shouldnt ruin the experience.
I've seen many people complain about the UI, which is different to most first person games. I personally liked it. Its circular rather than linear, and that is really the only difference compared to other first person games. Unlike most games, you get to choosethe UI colour. I liked that I could choose a nice subtle red colouor. However, I had some minor issues with the controls. Pressing action on locked objects like doors or chests automatically changed your currently held item to the multi-tool lockpick. Which is fine when you arent in combat, but, if you accidently hit action during combat while beside a locked door or chest, you find yourself trying to defeat the opponent with a lockpick instead of your weapon of choice. The other minor thing, you dont have a "put the item away" button, so its possible to forget you have your weapon out in a non combat zone and accidently shoot an npc. Two minor issues that generally shouldnt be a problem if you are paying attention to what you are doing.
And that is about it. But to summarise:
- It can take some time to setup on a 2016 PC, but there are community guides in the game's section on steam to help with this. Get the improved textures and resolution fixes.
- Its slow to get into the pace of a Deus Ex game, but well worth giving the time to reach its full pace. Sadly I would have liked that pace to have lasted 2-3 additional levels but it is stilla  full complete game that is worth the time.
- There will be many loading screens, but do not let that give you the feeling that the game itself is small.
- There are some minor UI issues but nothing truely problematic.

Approach with managed expectations.

I know this will say I've only put in point-whatever number of hours into this game, but that's somewhat inaccurate. I've been trying to force myself to play through this game since about 2007 on multiple computers and the original Xbox... and I just can't do it.  To me, it looks worse, runs worse, and feels worse than its predecessor.
Yes, I'd rather play through the original Deus Ex with its stiff, robotic character animations and relatively simplistic engine than this bloated, compartmentalized, rushed-out cash-grab of a game.
There is nothing about Invisible War that isn't disappointing.  The HUD is atrocious and obtrusive, the game engine is obviously the same one Ion Storm used for the (equally disappointing) Thief: Deadly Shadows... complete with floppy bodies and almost nonexistant light sources (did it really need to be this dark EVERYWHERE?), there's universal ammo, switching weapons and items is a chore, there's no character customization beyond biomods (of which you can only have up to five TOTAL - yes, you read that right), skills are gone, and with them, any reason to play this game as anything other than an action FPS (non-lethal is pointless, exploration is pointless), your inventory is tiny, the plot is shamefully bad, the NPCs stare at you with these creepy, wide open, unblinking eyes (again, even with worse graphics, the original Deus Ex did it better), a lot of items in the environment lack even basic textures, and then there are the load times... THE LOAD TIMES!
As Invisible War was developed concurrently with the Xbox version, it was built from the ground up with the Xbox in mind... which meant lots of tiny level segments with loads between each.  However, even on current hardware, this game takes forever to load.  I dread level transitions because of this.
This game is pure amateur hour and, as I mentioned, feels rushed and unfinished.  Even for its time, this is just bad.  Thief: Deadly Shadows, which came out about the same time, was made by the same people, and used the same engine, is better and more polished than this (though strangely, it seems Ion Storm had a fixation on forcing the player to choose between multiple, one-dimensional factions during this period, much to the detriment of both games).
So that's it.  I just can't force myself to try to play it anymore.  I'm done.  I'm not going to waste any more time on what will eventually be as much of a disappointment at the end as it was at the beginning.  It will forever be the black sheep of the Deus Ex universe (even with Square Enix at the helm of the series).  This is absolutely not a recommended game.  Play something - anything - else.  Hell, play the IOS games instead.  They can't be any worse than this.

Granted, the maps are small, the UI is odd, and the game does NOT look like the screenshots in the steam store (must be screenshots of a mod or something), but Deus Ex: Invisible war, is overall a good game. The game needed 5 minutes of work after it was installed on my Windows 10, i7, gtx1080, but I solved the problem I had (where game was always in window mode but not filling the whole screen since I kept seeing my desktop which was annoying) by selecting the second highest resolution in the graphics options and that solved the issue for good. Since then I had no issues. Each time the game loads however your screen flickers around as if you would crash back to desktop, but the game each time gets a grip of itself and the map still loads normally, thus, I so far did not even have one game crash, as it runs smooth and stable.
The graphics are very good for a game of that time period, but be aware, this is a much more simplified version from Deus Ex. No more manual input of codes, no more lock picks (multitool does all), no more different ammo types, as MAKO is the only weapons manufacturer which all require the same ammo type (whether a pistol or a rocket launcher). The voice acting also had a bit of a downgrade compared to its predecessor, so let's say the predecessor was a 10, this here would be a 7. For instance, when you traveled to Hong Kong in the predecessor, all NPCs spoke English with a Chinese accent, but this time when you go to Germany or Egypt, most still speak with American accents but there are NPCs that speak English with Arabic or German accents as well. If such minor details do not concern you, you will still love the voice acting. If you play as a male (Alex Denton), your voice seems very tired, which can be a bit frustrating, but then again, the rest of the voice acting is still top notch for today's standards!
Graphics as mentioned before are good. But too bad no more in-game animations like in Deus Ex, where you could see your chopper fly off. Another minor detail but I believe it added a lot of quality to a game for its time, and now it is gone. You just click your aerial transport (Jet or Helicopter, you pick your pilot!) and that is all. Then again, each pilot drops you off in different locations, which was kind of neat, but then again, with the maps so small it won't really matter.
Weapon controls. This is a bit of a disappointment. It is extremely easy to kill now as compared to the predecessor, and another downside is that they completely removed the skill system, so you have the same shooting abilities from the start to the end of the game. Also, you carry much fewer mods than before, and upgrading your mods is extremely easy, so you are already at max strength before even reaching mid-game. If that is good or bad, you tell me, but I liked it better when I used to be JC.
tl;dr:
Pros:
+ Continous great storyline right after where the predecessor ended (Key point in Deus Ex universe!!!)
+ Still pretty good voice acting overall
+ Some nice locations!
+ Fun side quests
+ You can sometimes make some funny choices!!
+ Sound in the night clubs! Real Band known as "Kidney thieves". Good stuff!
+ Plenty hours of gameplay for the price.
Cons:
- Apparently unstable in many systems. Took me 5 mins for it to work well, others apparently need more time.
- Small maps.
- Simplified weapon usage
- no skills, no lockpicks, multi tool does all now.
- Overall simplified game from its predecessor.
- Much more linear gameplay than predecessor.
- Less Augmentations and augmentations very easily upgradeable (simplifying game).
- Less in-game notes (less newspapers, books, texts, logs, screenshots, etc. In Deus Ex you really felt the conspiracy, here not as much).
My advice:
If you just just got into Human Revolutions and then Mankind Divided and find yourself intrigued by the Deus Ex story, then pick up Deus Ex GOTY edition which runs smooth, enjoy that amazing classic, and then afterwards, play through this game as well. Both are worth the money and the first Deus Ex has probably the best replay value for any Single Player game of all time, I play it once a year since 15 years and each time still encounter new hidden areas and locations and outcomes!!! It is incredible!

System Shock 2 is a first person shooter/sci-fi/rpg game, developed by Looking Glass Technologies in 1999. As in the previous game, you follow in the footsteps of an unknown hacker who has to run through a space station and will not only discover lots of new enemies, but also a few new (And unlikely) allies along the way.
Prologue-One of the best first person shooter games I ever played, System Shock 2 offers a little something for everyone (In a high-tech, sci-fi sort-of manner). And in addition to this, System Shock 2 goes at least one step beyond the original System Shock, with new items, a new plot, new characters, and of course, a new RPG element not often seen in first person shooter games.
Gameplay-As in the original System Shock, the gameplay is simple and straightforward: Kill your enemies, don't get killed, kill some more, gather items, learn new skills, and so on. And in addition to everything the original System Shock had, the RPG element allows you to collect nanites and cyber modules, which you can use to buy items and upgrades from certain kiosks found throughout each level. Also, each deck (Numbered 1 through 6) has several sub-levels, with plenty of enemies and puzzles to kill and solve on each sub-level. This time around, you use the left mouse button to attack enemies (And you can move the mouse to look around!) and the right mouse button to pick up items. A single click of these is all you need to engage these actions. Also integral to the gameplay are the two main modes...Shoot Mode and Use Mode. A simple tap of the Tab Key is all you need to do in order to switch between these modes. Your inventory is about the same as it was in the original Shock although it can be expanded by purchasing skill upgrades via cyber modules. Gameplay Score-8 out of 10.
Items-As in the original game, Shock 2 has a wide variety of items (Some more useful than others) to aid you on your endeavors. Such items include your basic healing insurance items (Med Hyops, First Aid Kits), your radiation and toxicity insurance (Yes, Radiation and Toxicity make a huge and scary comeback here), and then you have other such odd items (Like cigarettes, liquor, chips, soda, and juice) which may either help you or hurt you, depending on what you're eating/drinking/smoking. Still, there are other items (Called implants) which you can equip to get a bonus in a certain skill. Furthermore, some items (Like the implants) are in fact rechargeable and can be recharged at a recharge station or by using a portable battery (Yet another useful item). Items Score-9 out of 10.
Weapons-There are a few less weapons in this game than could be found in the original Shock, however, most of these weapons can upgraded, which improves not only their power, but also may reduce their ammo consumption or their kickback (Recoil when fired) or allow more ammo to be loaded into the weapon at a time. In addition to this, some weapons have 2 different modes and some even have 2 or more different kinds of ammo which can be used with it. Unfortunately, some weapons can also degrade over time when used and must be repaired using a Maintenance Tool. Also, a few weapons can only be used against certain kinds of enemies (And there are two kinds of enemies in this game)...Flesh-based enemies and metal-based enemies. You will have to modify your battle tactics throughout the game in order to suit your foes. And if this was not bad enough, some weapons require certain levels in certain skills in order to be used. Weapons Score-6 out of 10.
Ammo-While some weapons do not require ammo, most of the weapons depend on it...Some more heavily than others. Furthermore, as in the original System Shock, some weapons use energy (But this time, their source of energy is through a rechargeable battery attached to the weapon) and like other rechargeable items, they can be recharged at a kiosk or by using a battery. Unfortunately, weapons which use bullets (or in some cases, worms) can be tough to deal with, as contrary to the original game, ammo is quite hard to come by, unless you're willing to spend some nanites to buy a few extra bullets from a nearby replicator. Bearing this in mind, you may want to consider sticking to a melee weapon in order to conserve ammo and pick up every ammo clip you find! Even if you have to unload guns you find along the way and toss them aside. Ammo Score-7 out of 10.
Armor-There are a few different kinds of armor which you can wear. Of course, such armor will offer some protection but certainly will not make you indestructible! Furthermore, most of the armor you find will once again require certain skill levels in order to make use of it. But in exchange for this, wearing such armor will provide you with excellent protection against enemy attacks. In addition to this, there is one very powerful armor which is in fact, rechargeable. Another interesting suit of armor will provide great protection against Radiation and Toxicity. Armor Score-8 out of 10.
Plot-The plot in System Shock 2 is about the same as it was in the original game. There are a few more cut-scenes than there were in the original Shock. Also, the fact that there is more than one enemy and ally present in this game brings the plot up slightly. Be sure to listen to all the audio logs you find. They will not only provide you with some extra story elements, but many of them will reveal access codes to hidden rooms and secret items, although this was also present in the original shock. But now, there are more codes and audio logs to be found. See if you can find them all! They are quite fun to listen to! Plot Score-7 out of 10.
Characters-The presence of characters is a little stronger in this game than in it's prequel. In fact, I can only think of 3 characters in the original System Shock...Rebecca Lansing, Edward Diego, and SHODAN. But in Shock 2, I can think of several, a few of whom you'll meet at certain times during the game. Some of these include: Xerxes, Captain William Diego, Dr. Janice Polito, SHODAN, Sgt. Bronson, and Marie Delacroix. And seeing as how these characters have so many things to say throughout the game, it's no wonder you get to know them so well! Characters Score-7 out of 10.
Sound-The sound effects in System Shock 2 are again slightly better than the original System Shock. Even though they're still fairly quiet, they are considerably louder than in the original Shock. Of interesting note though is the ambient sounds, like some of the computers make when you get near them. Like the graphics of Shock 1, they can be hypnotic to listen to. And the weird sounds the hybrids make are also pretty scary. Sound Score-8 out of 10.
Music-The music in System Shock 2 goes above and beyond the music from the Original System Shock (Which was mediocre at best). In fact, all of the music in Shock 2 not only has a much cooler (And catchy) cyber-punk tune, it also adds to the already suspenseful gameplay, where you must constantly be on your guard since enemies lurk around every corner! So be on your guard, hacker! And don't let the music distract you! Music Score-9 out of 10.
Graphics-Once again, Looking Glass Studios has outdone themselves with state of the art graphics which are once again cutting edge and ahead of most other games from 1999. And even though this is a dark engine game (At least what I heard) I can get it to work just fine on my computer, although at times, it does give me a little trouble. And even though some of these graphics are somewhat simple, they are quite fascinating! In fact, if you throw a container of bullets on top of a fragile computer console, there is a good chance the ammo will break the console! Also, it's really nice to examine all the items you find throughout the game. Snacks, anyone? Graphics Score-9 out of 10.
Final Score-9 out of 10. As I've stated before, there is most likely going to be something for every hard core gaming fan to be had in System Shock 2.

Eternal Senia is a free RPG Maker game that plays more like a classic Legend of Zelda game than a traditional turn-based RPG. You play as Senia - a young adventurer looking for her adoptive sister Magaleta who went missing in the Tower of Eternity. The story and character motivations are told largely through flashbacks and at the end you have a full picture of why our two main characters do what they do - though it is largely a simple story, it is well-executed and easily understood even despite some translation hiccups from the developer's native Mandarin.
The meat of the gameplay is interesting and keeps the player engaged throughout the duration of the story - adding both new skills and new craftable equipment (really, direct upgrades to the player's current gear) as the plot warrants. It is a short game - about three to four hours of dedicated gameplay would be enough to complete and unlock the game's three endings.
For those looking for a good RPG Maker game or a serviceable Legend of Zelda top-down adventure, I would highly recommend Eternal Senia. To everyone else, give it a shot or at least add it to your library - it's free!

If you are getting this game purely for the nostalgia factor for the original Half-Life this might be worth trying. And honestly, I have a huge amount of respect for the team behind this to make something this ambitious.
However, considering the whole point of the game being to remake a game in modern standards, the graphics, gameplay mechanics, physics engine, etc are very subpar. There is a lot of positive feedback about graphics and voice acting in this, but the only way that makes sense is if it is solely being compared to the original Half-Life's capabilities, in 1998. At this point, it seems like it should look like it came out in the 2010's at least, not in 2005.
In the hour I've played this, I clipped into a wall twice trying to crawl through tunnels, fell off of a pipe because I slid off of it while standing still, nearly killed myself when I picked something up and then set it down and it went flying into the opposite direction and hit me, though I literally just set it down. My escort in the first 10 minutes of the gameplay got stuck in a never-ending shoot out with a zombie. Oh, and maybe the biggest annoyance, there is an abrupt, unannounced load every 2 minutes that will freeze the game for a good 10-15 seconds every time. Between a very poor physics engine (which was one of the most marvelous things about Half-Life originally), and iffy AI at best, this just doesn't seem like much more than a slight improvement on the original in some areas, and an actual step back in others.
With a lot of remakes, I feel like I would be impressed with a small studio undertaking something this ambitious and doing a respectable job. But considering the Half-Life franchise more or less set the bar in first person-shooters, this feels underwhelming. Not bad mind you, just very, very underwhelming. If you're looking for a revisit to Half-Life, this might fill that need, but this feels like it came out just a few years after the original, not in 2015.

I never had the chance to play the original Half Life, but after sinking in nearly 20 hours of gameplay, I have to say this is one of the most atmospheric gaming experiences I have ever had. The great pacing, the epic gunplay, and the awesome music prevents me from stopping. Its a shame that Triple A shooters today can't draw you in as magnetically this one can. If you got 25 bucks to spend, this game will give you great experiences for years to come.

Short review: Buy it. Amazing game. My GOTY of 2017.
Long version:
Before I begin, I highly suggest playing on nightmare mode. It never felt too hard for me and it offered a good balance between difficulty and gameplay. Anway, everything about this game, for me, was near perfect and hit all the marks needed for a great survival horror. Although not incredibly scary all the way through, many sequences are quite terrifying. There is also more pshycological horror in this one, and I think the ratio between actual horror and jumpscares is a huge improvement from the first game. The gameplay is spot on, and encourages carefull use of your weapon and management of ammo and other supplies. In the first half of the game, it has it's own miniature open world and I would highly advise you to explore as much as possible, as it is as much fun as it is rewarding. This game is much less linear than the original, however, the game starts to become more linear as your progress further into the game. The story is also pretty good, with a few minor hiccups that can be filled by reading scripts and journals you pick up along your travels. The ending was really impressive, and wrapped up the story very well. The music is also perfect, and added to the immersion of the game. Boss/ enemy design is also great, with alot of variety and a grotesque factor. I cant say much in terms of performance, as I run a stupidly overkill PC that handled the game just fine, so I wont really touch on this.
Overall a solid 9/10, would have liked to have learned a bit more about some of the bosses which the game didnt cover, hopefully we get some sort of DLC to fill this gap.

Rome II starts off as a tough cookie. You always lose, even if you've become pretty good at Empire.
With enough experience, you can become good at it. And if you love total strategy and have some patience, it'll work out well for you.
Yes, there's no family tree. Yes, you can only have 16 armies max. Yes, public order seemingly becomes impossible to control if your empire is large enough. But, in all, due to the variety of patches, it's a great game. At around the 200th hour I became a bit sick of it because I'm in a stalemate of sorts with Carthage. But there's always other factions to play as. Replay value is 11/10 with the patches and emperor edition and some mods...
I recommend the 4TPY mod, all factions mod (xcept those that are designated as DLC only - well, I bought Ceasar in Gaul and the Greek States pack at my satisfaction with playing this game)  and the balanced diplomacy mod and the ranged camera mod (so I can see my empire from afar); and finally, the ROME 1 music (it can't be beat) mod.
Also, it looks a bit cartoonish.
Rome II grows on you if you're in to the Total War games. It has become, over more than a year, a stellar game. I think that if it were relaeased today the metacritic score would be more like 85-92.
Battles are great (but make sure you have a decent computer). Loading is kind of long but quotes make it interesting. And of course, decisions decisions decisions. Do you want to upgrade your industry or prepare for a full-on war? It gets very technical so be prepared to lose for 50-200 turns until you master the "glitches" or ways that you can succeed.
Attilla looks more like Rome II should've been. That said, it's still very compelling.
I would give it a solid 9.2/10, and 9.5 if you're into the material surroudning Rome.
Try to get it on sale! I didn't, but that's because I appreciate the work that the developers are doing. I support such cognitively complex games with such replay value.

I really did not want to give this game and CA this negative review but hopefully after reading it you guys will understand where I am coming from.  I've been a Total war fan since the original Rome was released back in 2004 and I feel like this game has ALMOST ruined the whole franchise for me.  I'm gonna try and make this as short as possibe.
I was one of the "lucky" few to pre-order Rome 2 and I was pumped to get back into my most favorite franchise.  Sadly, when the game finally dropped on September 3rd 2013, I couldnt have been more dissapointed.  For some reason I did not really experience the bugs as much as other people did (the game only crashed once or twice) but what did it for me was the genreal experience of the game.  I couldnt play the main campaign for more than a couple of hours before it became BORING AS HELL!!! Dissapointed, I decided to stop playing the game.  Every couple of months after that I would check back in and see if any of the new patches fixed the mechanics that made the game so unplayable to me.  Sadly month after month I saw no real improvements.  When the Emperor Edition was announced and consequenty released I was excited to dive back into this game, truly hoping that CA had fixed the mess that Rome 2 had become.  After playing the Emperor edition for a couple of hours or so I once again turned the game off dissapointed.  People claim that the Emperor edition is the game that we should have received but I still disagree, the game feels like it's missing many key elements to it that made the previous Total War titles so spectacular.
Pro's:
The graphics are amazing (as they should be)
The Campaign map looks stunning as well as the towns and cities all feel alive on the map
The number of factions is ENORMOUS (even though you cant play them all without mods)
The new vision system added a lot of realism to the game as well as making the game more tactically challenging
The time period the game is set in is fantastic
Diversity of units
(I honestly can't think of anything else.............)
Con's
THE TOTAL WAR WIKI - I hate that thing sooooo much!  The first time it appeared in Shogun 2 it really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.  It was far more complicated than the previous system of just right-clicking on a building or a unit and then it telling you all of the information about said unit/building.  You didn't need to have it LOAD, and the navigation of the wiki pages is soo damn confusing!
TECH/BUILDING TREE - Again, in the previous games everything was easy to find, the building tree was a tab that you could click on that would show you all of the buildings, the buildings you needed to build said buildings and the units/benefits they provided to your city.
GARRISONS - Garrisons were first implemented in Empire (I believe) and they were awesome! They felt realistic, a mob defending their city from massive enemy armies against all odds was fanstastic! In Shogun 2 they expanded this feature and made it even better, you could get more advanced units defending your castles as you leveled them up.  Rome 2 literally broke the whole garrison system.  The armies that the garrison produce are MASSIVE even at the beginning of the campaign, and worst of all THEY ARE IMPOSSIBLE TO SEE ON THE CAMPAIGN MAP!!! You have to scroll over the settlement to see how many units that settlement has garrisoned in it.  And like I mentioned before those garrisons are HUGE, they are almost impossible to defeat especially if the enemy also has a supporting general with an army defending it.  You need massive armies to even challenge minor factions with one or two settlements and worst of all this is in the BEGINNING OF THE CAMPAIGN!!!
ARMIES - WHY DO I NEED TO ALWAYS HAVE A GENERAL TO BE ABLE TO RECRUIT A SINGLE UNIT!!!!?!?!?  If i need units to be recruited in order to support another army closeby in another territory I have to recruit a new general in order to do so and I dont think that should be necessary.  It made the game very restrictive and in turn was a lot less fun to play.  The generals seemed expendable and a lot less important to the whole campaign.
THE FAMILY TREE - Totally missing...................  WHY????? It made the game more engaging.  If one general got killed in battle I made it my goal to go after the murderous army with the dead generals brother/son/father.  I felt more involved with the charachters involved.
BUILDINGS/CITIES - In my opinion Empire had the best building system.  It was easy to understand.  You could build every building you desired (except for Opera Houses) in almost every city and the armies that each city produced were equally as powerful.  There were no "limited building slots". you could build all the buildings that you wanted, provided that they were availabe in that city level.  In Rome 2 AS WELL as Shogun 2, the building system was very restrictive.  I know that they were going for more strategy elements, but that retrictive nature made the game feel more cumbersome.  What I did like in Shogun 2 was the tech tree.  I thought it was the best out of all the total war games.
VIEW CITY ON BATTLEFIELD MAP - Now this is a minor feature that was only present in the first Rome (as far as I know).  You could zoom in to your settlement at any time during your turn and just take a leisurely look around the city and enjoy the epic scale of certain cities as well as the citizens.  Why remove a feature?? Same thing goes for blood in Medieval 2, now it has become a DLC.  WHY TAKE OUT FEATURES FROM OLD GAMES????
Not Pro's and not Con's
The DLC - I dont mind DLC as long as it feels like DLC but not features like blood or more factions!! If the faction is in the game why cant I play with them without using a mod????  In Medieval 2 and Rome 1, you needed to beat the campaign at least once to unlock more factions and I thought that was very interesting as well as engaging.  it forced you to get to know the game and learn the features before you were allowed to play with the harder factions that you UNLOCKED.  DLC should consist of only true expansions, like Caesar in Gaul or Hannibal at the gates.  OR MEDIEVAL KINGDOMS!!!!! (That one was awesome).... They add NEW factions to the game and new events, time periods, units, locations, and bigger and detailed maps to the original game.  You should not have to pay for stuff that was already in the previous games.
THE AI - The AI has always been♥♥♥♥♥♥ and to be honest as long as it puts some sort of effort to fight me I'm happy.  The missing features mentioned above are more important to me personally than the AI.  It would be nice if they improved it.
These are some of the biggest features or lack there of in this game that just ruined this particular title for me.  There are a couple more features that I woul mention but I felt that I was rambling too much already.  I believe in CA and I know that they are a great company because they have made great games in the past and Im sure they'll make some in the future.  The new Atilla game looks like an improvement from this terrible game but as I watch more and more trailers from the upcoming game, I cant help but notice some of the similarities between this trash game and the new up-coming game.  I'm probably gonna have to sit out the next Total War game because I truly feel that they need more time to fix their mistakes, at least to the same state as they were in previous entries.

, at least well above 10. That's not as often as through its predecessor, the original Deus Ex, which must have been well over 20.
I agree that this game is limited in comparison to DX1: The locations are small-scale - Upper Seattle seems like a set of rooms and corridors instead of a city, and the loaded maps themselves are small, so you'll often load a new section, but it's not much higher in frequency than in DX1. There are no skills. There is only one type of ammunition which happily feeds into every weapon. The dialog feels cheaper and rushed (probably to keep the data size small). There's also a lot
dialog/writing. The user interface is simplified, its functionality is limited, and the inventory is small. Quite a few angles from which the console origin shines through. And there must be other reasons that I only played
instead of
.
But I don't agree in the least that the game looks crappy or is considerably worse than DX1. I like the graphics, especially the realtime lighting engine, it's fun to physically toss unconscious/dead people around, and I like exploring / sneaking through the (small) environments. And by the way, the too narrow FOV can be
, apparently the resolution can even be cranked up.
"Invisible War" is a proper entry of the Deus Ex franchise, because it's all there: Lone wolf 1st person superhuman experience, choice of passive/stealthy/aggressive gameplay, alternative routes to objectives (incl. vent crawling), free exploration incl. looting, and a story that starts slow and small, then expands into various factions incl. conspiracy ingredients, then becomes increasingly big just like in DX.
If you think about it, the ending is even done better than in DX1 because while DX1 mostly relied on an end-o-matic solution like DX:HR except the buttons and panels were spread around the map more, DX:IW's ending choices involve battle (incl. all strategic freedom of the franchise except "just sneaking past it"), dialog (Faction relations partially kept open to the very end.), button pushing, and more.
You can even choose whether to play a man or a woman (both conveniently called "Alex").
Deus Ex: Invisible War is a really well done game. It does not live up to the original, but a good part of the reason would be that it follows a template established by DX1 instead of pioneering said template. You play it with expectations instead of not yet knowing what's up and getting your mind blown. Player freedom is also clearly lower.
But it's a firm double-thumbs-up recommendation that, if you haven't played it yet, should be on your list, especially if you love the Deus Ex universe. Just don't forget:

I'm going against recommending LOVE, despite the fact that I did enjoy it. For one, I can appreciate any 2D platformer that has the decency to give you a "save anywhere" feature. Mario and Metroid, while fun can be very tiring after playing the same part of a level over and over and LOVE totally cuts that out. I love it. Thank you.
However, there isn't a whole lot to recommend beyond the save-anywhere feature. You run and jump. You avoid obstacles in well-designed levels. And that's it. Granted, there are changes to gameplay and obstacles but they're so short that you don't get a feeling of actually mastering them, like in Mario or Metroid.
That and the fact that the game has 16 levels (well, technically a lot more with the remix mode), despite the changes in speedrun mode and hard mode... there isn't much to LOVE to really find anything special in. Similar to "You Have to Win the Game", LOVE does has smooth controls, a nice graphical aesthetic, and a great difficulty and save feature, but it's so samey and safe that it's just not something you'll want to go back and play in a while. Or at least I don't.
If you like a fun 2D Platformer, LOVE certainly is that. But beyond the simple mechanics, it's not a particularly memorable experience. I'm giving it a 6/10.

Note: Before I even start, let me mention that if you aren't a fan of the outdated control scheme, then there's an option in the game to rebind the keys to that of a modern fps. You don't even have to rebind them yourself, just check the saved key bindings; there's a layout there already. I hear a lot of complaints about the controls, and frankly they're so easy to change that it really shouldnt be an issue.
Alright, on to the actual review.
System Shock 2 is generally known as an FPS/RPG hybrid, when in reality it's far more Survival/RPG. What few fps elements there are aren't particularly interesting. Headshots and the locations wherein you shoot an enemy make no difference to damage and the enemy placement outside of scripted events is very random, so if you're looking for something akin to Quake or Doom then you'll probably have better luck elsewhere.
What System Shock 2 gets right is the RPG and Survival elements, which complement each other perfectly. You see, you don't get experience via killing enemies in this game, instead the game's equivalent of XP is collected through exploring the environment and searching for pickups called 'cybernetic modules'. Want that extra point in strength?  Well then you're going to have to bite the bullet and search that dark, scary room. Need another point in weapons to wield the assault rifle? Guess you're going to have to poke around that creepy corridor you've been avoiding. It's a great risk/reward   system that makes exploring all the more satisfying. There's nothing like finding a cybernetic module the developers snuck in between a pair of crates or stashed on a corpse. With such an intense atmosphere, everylittle victory feels like a conquest.
And the atmosphere is brilliant, providing you turn off that weird techno soundtrack, of course. The sound design for this game is marvelous. The heavy clank of your footsteps, the far off voices of Hybrids begging for death, the scrambled, mechanial screams of a Cyborg Midwife  as she dies, it's all very immersive stuff. Just do yourself a favour and turn the music off.
The game isn't without its faults, though. For example:
-First time players might make some slip-ups with their levelling and put all the points into something stupid like Research, Agility or repair. There are a lot of skills in System Shock 2 that are sort of useless, so I'd reccomend looking up a few tips before starting.
-Little wizard monkeys are a reccuring enemy in this game. No joke. It's sort of jarring to be fighting some horrific monstrosity one moment only to be going toe-to-toe with a fireball-throwing mokey the next.
-Dying isn't much of an issue, as you just respawn at a reconstruction chamber as soon as you bite the dust. It takes away some of the tension.
-It's ugly. There's no denying it. System Shock 2 is an ugly game. The polygon count is low, all the character models look like origami and looking out of a window into space is like staring at a pixelated screensaver. It's ugly.
-And finally, you might have some trouble running it. I never ran into any issues, but it's an old game and I've heard some complaints. Just a warning.
Overall I'd say that System Shock 2 still holds up today as an impressive RPG, and is worth your time as long as you're okay with resource managment and character development that requires you to have a specific type of character in mind from the start.

Went in with very high expectations, and this game exceeded them.

-Sound design is top-notch.
-Extremely in-depth story with tons of puzzle-peices to put together.
-Graphics are great for the time, and while they aren't the best, the game still retains its ability to be immersive. It feels very isolated and alone.
Do NOT start playing this game co-op. The atmosphere is changed completely and the experience is much scarier and hard-hitting when you are alone; try co-op once you have completed the game solo. You can only play through a game the first time once.
Playing it co-op would be like if your friend told you all of the spoilers to a movie before you saw it- yeah, the movie was probably still amazing, but it probably wasn't nearly as engagin or exciting as it would be had you of gone in without prior knowledge.

Prepare to Die, just not as much as in Demon Souls and Dark Souls.  While I find this game easier, I think many will not.  I have played thousands of hours of the Souls games along with all of the spirtual prequels (King's Field - King's Field: City of Ancients) and while I played this game the least, in many ways it gave me the most enjoyment, only falling short in a few areas.
1. I had to get used to the fast travel, I still think it takes away from the game but I got over it.  I thought Dark Souls had the best world of all 3 souls games due to the pure genius of its interconnected world.  Demon Souls was a bit too seperated for my taste and the world in Dark Souls 2 is diminished by fast travel and corridor design.

The addition of actual dual-wielding was much needed and implemented well.  The strength weapons are much more useful and deadly this time around.  I was dissapointed in the Dex weapons however as they seem underpowered compared to the previous souls games.  I rolled almost exclusively Dex in Demons Souls and Dark Souls but in Dark Souls 2 I usually rolled either Quality or Str/Fth, which in my opionion were both very powerful in this game.  Casting in general is much stronger in PVP in this game, to the point of being a bit OP in some cases, but it IS very fun to use.

4.  Buy this game and remember to PRAISE THE SUN!

As sequels go, this is one that does not disappoint. The Evil Within II manages to improve on gameplay, offers a more expansive world to explore, tells an eerie but riveting story, all while looking great graphically and running smoothly. It isn't quite as frightening as its predecessor, it however nails the psychological aspect and atmosphere of what was introduced previously making it a superb survival horror title.
Story/World
Sebastian Castellanos returns as the main protagonist, but this time around it seems he has fallen on hard times. His family has been missing for a while and all he can do is drown his pain in bottles of liquor. At its core, the story is about a man searching for his family. His search brought on by former colleague Kidman, takes him back to into the otherworldly, mind bending, nightmare that is STEM. STEM is pretty much the horror version of the Matrix. The story though relying on many tropes common to the horror genre still manages to surprise at certain points and keep the attention of the player. The story contains many characters of note, whose intentions range from noble, to misguided, to egotistical, giving the narrative a good amount of variance while remaining dark. The world inside STEM is quite different from the first game, seeing as it has been taken over by the mysterious Mobius Corporation. This time around Sebastian is left to brave the town of Union, created by Mobius. One thing against this sequel is that it is not as horrifying as the first one; it does manage to scare just not as well. The play area is more expanded and open with multiple areas to explore which are quite rewarding seeing as many offer interesting encounters through side stories, and good gear/weapon pickups. Every aspect of the town of Union complements the overall play experience. The areas aren't just there to add fluff but they make exploration meaningful, which is quite important for open world/area games to do nowadays. Additionally there is a sublevel area called the marrow which consists of tunnels leading to the separate areas of Union. As the name suggests it is like the 'skeleton' that holds the ' tissue' of this town together. The monstrosities are for the most part zombie like, with a few more imaginative ones scattered throughout or used as bosses. The story and world go hand in hand almost perfectly.
9.5/10
Gameplay
When playing the game the game there are no complaints. The default controls handle quite well, and on PC the player is allowed to map eight number keys as shortcuts to Sebastian’s ever so large inventory of weapons and healing items. This is definitely a welcome improvement to the previous title's shortcut keys which only allowed the player to map the first four keys. This sequel also involves a light crafting system which allows the player to create ammo and healing items form resources collected in the environment. This addition is most welcome as it feels quite gratifying, especially considering that some achievements are attached to this system. When using the crafting system, one must not stock too much or too little ammo or health items, as they can be found scattered around the different areas of union. This adds another layer of satisfaction to the game when the perfect balance is struck to survive a situation and not have wasted resources doing so. Movement and shooting, both feel very good this time around, with no awkwardly clunky character animations. The same leveling system from the first game is present, as are the loot lockers which need keys that are scattered throughout the various chapters. The weapon upgrade system has been overhauled, adding levels to weapon upgrades that can only be obtained via high grade weapons parts dispersed throughout Union. Many weapons are not just thrust in the player’s path and require exploration to obtain, some even through multi-part scavenger hunts which feel quite fulfilling once completed. On a first play through choose which weapons are most agreeable for a particular play style and focus on maxing those as there are a limited number of high grade parts, making replay via new game plus a must for those who want all the upgrades and the achievement that comes with doing so. A proper cover system is also included in the game which is easy to use and get out of with smooth transitions for stealth takedowns. Use of the crossbow is encouraged more, given the many opportunities to use environmental multi-kills using the likes of fire hydrants and oil barrels placed around the map. The gameplay just seems so perfect.
10/10
Performance/Graphics
Visuals are improved from the previous installment. The character animation and movement don’t feel like they were only made with thirty frames per second in mind and there is a noticeable bump in graphical fidelity and options. There are however noticeable but not inexcusable frame rate dips even with higher end setups such as the 16GB of RAM, i7 6700k, and GTX 1070 used to review this game. Keep in mind that this is the series’ first go at an open world and the engine is quite new. Overall the graphics and performance are great.
8/10
For those who are looking for an amazing recent survival horror game, this is the one to choose. The Evil Within II awes with its world, entrances with its story, and is a sheer joy to play. Although the terrors in this adventure don’t quite reach the same levels as the first game, it is at the end of the day an objectively better videogame and is worth getting even at full price.
Final Score
9.2/10

At this point it seems like a safe bet to consider Total War games as actually being released about a year after they are available to purchase; think of those first 12 months as an early-access beta. After a year the games are generally patched up, cheaper and available with a handful of DLC.
Anyhow, the current incarnation of Rome II seems to have addressed most of the issues which were rampant at release and the game is in a proper and playable state. As Total War games go, Rome II is mostly the expected status quo with a spattering of incremental updates/changes to the game's various systems. For the most part the main changes in Rome II center around streamlining campaign map management. For the most part I've appreciated these changes, myself, but it can sometimes be an irritation that units cannot be moved autonomously in Rome II and must always be part of an army. On the bright side, you are now able to reinforce units directly to your armies rather than having to wait for them to move from city centers. Auto-resolve is also a good deal more usable here though the algorithm will still sometimes give questionable odds for or against you.
Long story short: the game is pretty much fixed and worth buying now so if you enjoy Total War games, don't hesitate to jump in.

This is a game you are free to hate and be right about it.
Customization is very limited, most weapon mods both don't make sense and useless, levels are cramped, game as whole looks bleak, plot is not that bad, but script is like these $2.50 pocketbooks, complete with ugly drawings.
Game can't be even played properly to the end since enemies suddenly become bullet sponges with unresponsive hitboxes. Slap universal ammo on it (Which means once you are out of ammo, you are out of it for EVERY WEAPON YOU HAVE) — and all the talks about ability to choose right tool for the job go down the drain since the only weapon that can manage scarcity of ammo is unique (assassin) pistol with Damage Upgrade and Ammo Scavenger.
But what about good sides? Yep, that's what makes just terrible game PAINFULLY terrible one. It's got good sides!
First, the most responsive climbing mechanic. Ever. No more stupid waist-high walls, you may pull yourself up. You can stack crates high enough for your head to touch the railing at the highest point of jump? You can pull yourself up. And it's not based on some stupid special places to climb - if you can reach it and there is sufficient place to fit while crouched - you'll make it.
Second, EVERY weapon got a secondary mode. SMG with flashbangs? I'll take two. Railgun with alt fire allowing to shoot through walls? Awesome. Flamethrower with alt-fire that allows to bring the flame into mid-range? Neat. Sure, these days everyone and their mothers got weapons with two or more modes, but back in 2003 it was that or Unreal. And Unreal hasn't any RPG elements.
Third, grenade goods. You got regular, flashbangs, smoke, gas, noise (Yep. Extremely rare, and since it's one use…), emp, scramble and… spider grenade. Which spawns actual spider bot, complete with cute zapper and funny turn animation. Same as above, nothing Unreal hadn't, but Unreal is not an RPG in any way.
Fourth, very cool bot hacking mechanic. You stay hidden, then you charge at turret/bot, "tag" him and then you try to hide somewhere waiting for timer to expire. Cha-ching, you are now controlling a piece electronic. Want to shoot the baddies? Not so fast, they don't even know that bot is no longer on their side. Take your time, pick the best position for massacre — fun starts when YOU trigger it.
Fifth, this game got awesome hidden pony — Omars (Appreciating your bussiness, yeah, right), who succesfully achieved hivemind (In other words, creating succesfuly that Helios failed to achieve) and, well, the prosper while rest of the world is crumbling. While they have limited role, they are interesting as concept for post-apocalyptic world. And they got somewhat justified ending should you kill every major faction members in the end (All the wannabe rulers die in a nuclear fire, world is fading out while Omars prosper, later advancing enough to leave the Earth behind).
Conclusion: I wish Steam had ability to be neutral about "Thumbs up" and "Thumbs down".

Much of what this game is and how it plays can be gathered from the video and screenshots on its store page, so I won't bore anyone with too much exposition. Simple platforming.
This is exactly how LOVE shines. Despite garnering somewhat of a reputation for being difficult, it is fair and surprisingly humble. There are no nasty tricks in any of the levels; what you see and anticipate is what you get. The game is minimalistic in its pixel appearance, but quickly apparent that it's not in any cliché sense of retro appeal. It is a subtly stylish game that excels in presenting simple, clean platforming concepts through bite-sized, themed levels. LOVE is even confident enough in its design to allow for manual checkpoint placement in every level, and it works. I have to add that the soundtrack is also pretty fantastic, and helps LOVE maintain a fascinating, enigmatic atmosphere alongside the deliberately minimal visuals.
LOVE is short yet succinct, and a great deal for the price it asks.
Unique and original, while also being familiar and comfortable at the same time with an awesome soundtrack. Great game.

I really liked this one myself, but it's the strange good game that is worse than the sum of its parts. It has amazing craftmanship, both in puzzles, dialogue, and pure technical implementation of a traditional 2d adventure game. This focus on the microdecisions that make each sequence and each puzzle so delightful have a flip side: The overarching story development is closer to those of adventure games of old, instead of the tight, story first, puzzles later designs that you see in games that are closer to walking simulators: The ending and the overall story are afterthoughts, not unlike in a lage majority of old Lucasarts/Sierra adventure games.
When looked through that prism, Thimbleweed Park stands out as a really good old game: If this had been released in 1994, we;d see them as one of the best, if not the best games of the era. It's about as heartefelt a  love letter to the old days as I can think of. An evolutionary dead end, but such an amazing, enjoyable dead end.
I compare it to Mario Odyssey: I can't concieve anything more Mario than Mario Odyssey. So amazing at what it is, that it's almost a genre and formula ending. So good at what they do that the games leave me full. Thimbleweed Park makes me not want another Lucas-style adventure game ever. After this, one has to just aim for something new.
If you were looking for a more modern game, just built by some old masters, you will be sorely disappointed though. This is no Gone Home, no Edith Finch, and no Firewatch.

I was 12 years old when I first played
. I had just received some spending money at Christmas, and decided to go to a local game store to pick up something to play. It was there that I ran across an unassuming box, stamped with an "EA Classics" banner (which I still own) that had what appeared to be a sinister-looking woman hovering over a ship in deep space. Thinking it could be a fun little title, I took it home expecting to be entertained.
It wasn't long until I was reloading a save, practically wetting myself in terror as my character stood outside a cargo bay, listening to ambient chatter from robots that busted out of containers and were trying to hunt me down, and getting instasniped by a turret when I rounded the corner.
is a game that is absolutely dripping in atmosphere and dread. It makes the very act of walking down a hallway an unnerving, terrifying experience. Yet it remains one of my favorite games of all time, and one I've returned to many times over the years. It is an action-RPG that takes everything great about horror games and applies it to the sci-fi/cyberpunk genre.
The game may seem a little dated and archaic now, but back then there was nothing like it. Everything from the interesting set-up (your four-year tour of duty is actually a class/skill selection process), the way the backstory is told through audio logs and final journals, the desolate and unnerving atmosphere and the variety of weapons/armor that could be found (and crafted) added up to a landmark experience.
I have so many fond memories of this game. Seeing my health whittled down to nothing and taking potshots at robots in a desperate attempt to stay alive. Failing to catch an escape pod and walking back through a hallway, only to have to retreat and start firing madly with a shotgun when a horde of techno-zombies appeared in front of me. Crafting a crystal sword and using it to great effect... on dangerous monkeys in a gym that were firing off bolts of energy in my direction.
I couldn't even finish the game the first time I played it, as I crafted a build that was way too reliant on tech skills. I then found myself low on ammo and medicine while trying to sprint through the Body of the Many as a horde of grotesque abominations chased me.
is a game that definitely doesn't hold your hand, but rewards exploration and experimentation.
And that's not even getting into the original queen bee herself, SHODAN. Everything from Terri Brosius' masterful performance to the worst-kept secret (and simultaneous best surprise) in the game oozes villainous appeal. You can be fighting off Machine Mothers while trying to dodge security cameras, and SHODAN will still be pushing you to continue on while simultaneously telling you that you're an "insect" and that you can't comprehend what she's doing. SHODAN is a terrifying but oddly reassuring companion throughout the game and a large part of what has made it so iconic.
This is a title I've carried the torch for over the years, via its CD version, an abandonware copy I turned to because it fixed a major bug and this most recent release from Night Dive Studio, who did a stellar job negotiating the rights to publish both this and the original 1994 title.
There's a reason why this is considered part of the late-90s "holy trinity" alongside
and
. The innovations
pioneered are still being felt in large and small ways in the gaming industry, both in its influences for franchises like
and
and narrative techniques that fully immerse the player into the world without being preachy.
I highly, highly recommend the game. It's one you should play if you haven't done so already.

System Shock 2. A game for people who enjoy playing games without having a tutorial shoved down their throat every 15 seconds.
Firstly, the score that accompanies this game is just amazing (score composed by Eric Brosius), the art design is great and the lighting of all things is still on par with a lot of games today. It runs on the Thief engine and plays flawlessly on today's PC's. No hand holding in this game, just you against the horrific remains of the crew and the morbid voice of Shodan aboard the Von Braun. All of the voice acting in this game is really good, especially the voice of Shodan (Terri Brosius). System Shock is a Sci-Fi, heart attack inducing experience like no other.
The game mechanics can be quite complicating at first (unless you've played SS1) as there are lots of things you must wrap your head around to fully get this game. You have stats for weapons, tech, psi abiltities and overall skills (things like strength and Agility). You have a large grid based inventory that forces you to prioritise certain items over others. you also have a very large range of choice when it comes to weaponry and how you use it. There are multiple ammo types for nearly every weapon and alternate fire modes (obviously not for melee weps).
There are a lot of things that are great in SS2 but there are still many things that hinder it. These hinderences include some horrible level design around 80% into the game's story (the many), shotty hit detection in areas and overlapping dialogue in certain areas of the game. It is also noted that some of the enemies in this game take way too many hits to go down like the rumbler and the psychic floaty squid thingies that dish out insane amounts of damage in return, this wouldn't be so bad if they weren't so frequent in the last portion in the game especially since ammo is very scarce with these guys just eating it for breakfast.
I think SS2 is a game that really benefits from more than one play through as there are many different playstyles and weapons/abilities/skills you can experiment with that will significantly change your experience in sme aspect. Just to warn you, you can seriously ♥♥♥♥ yourself over with your skill points if you use them poorly to the point that it would be better to just start the game again. One thing that I think really holds the game back is that there is only one set ending. Having a set ending isn't such a bad thing but in a game with so much choice in playstyle, it seems sort of like the game is only crippling itself. Multiple endings in my opinion could have made SS2 a much better game with much more replayability and maybe put itself up as high as a game like Deus Ex (which in my opinion is the greatest game ever made on the face of the earth).
I only nitpick because I have now played SS2 multiple times and have had time to analyse it's positives and negatives to further enhance my judgment of the game's quality without too much bias. It is definitely worth buying as it is an extrodinary game overall with great music, dialogue, voice acting and atmosphere. Please, please don't buy the next Call of Duty or Assasins Creed. Buy games that the developers actually gave a♥♥♥♥♥♥about. Buy this and play a real game.
