After completing this game after playing over 13 hours there were some content I did like in the game and some I didn't.
So lets start with the positives, the plot of the game was interesting staring with a drunk Sebastian Castello expressing the guilt and remorse he had not being able to save his daughter from a tragic housefire losing her, his wife and his career in the police force. The story takes an interesting approach with Sebastians Ex partner from the first game Juli Kidmen that his daughter Lilly is alive but captured within the nightmare horror matrix very well known as STEM and thus the nightmare begins searching for his daughters whereabouts to save her and himself from becoming insane from the nightmare and torture sebastian has to face.
So lets talk about characters, the first antagonist in the game that really cpatured my eye (pun intended) was Stefano Valentini. He seemed to be my favorite villian in the game playing the artisitic killer expressing his love for turning his multilated murdered victims into art with photography. The most unique highlight was when he snapped his camera, Stefano seems to freeze the living in little regard, preferring them still and motionless instead, so that he can mold and torment them to his twisted liking. Thus for me he was an interesting character to study throughout the game and he was certainly a challenge to fight.
Another antagonist I really liked also Theodore Wallace a cult leader within the STEM program with the power to progressively manipulate people to follow him and grant powers to them that follow. Thus the torment using hallucinations, emotional stress and guilt towards sebastian taking it's toll throughout the game really making the player having a connection with the protagonist which scores extra points for me.
So onto one particular monster I liked in the game.The Guardian is a towering monstrocity that stands at least the size of an adult grizzly bear, and is made up of the body remains of various women that were murdered. The gurdian has several heads each with different expressions with the central head having red eyes and a sinister grin, this creature also features a long spine connected to the torso which is amazing how she can stay balanced when chasing you with a buzzsaw, thats gaming physics for ya :P. But when I heard the sinister laughing for the first time, first thing I thought was that I was screwed.
There were so many monsters I wanted to talk about in this review so I thought I would keep it as breif as possible to not ruin the game for you of course
So lets move onto the things that I didn't like.
First off I wanted to start with the plot being pretty cliche I found that the whole 'my missing daughter' thing to be used loads in the world of gaming hell Super Mario was one of the first games to do it and it's always a happy ending, I would've thought an unexpected plot twist would've added a better element to the game.
Another thing that I was not too keen on was adding an RPG stealth element to the game which I found pretty dull when all I wanted was to continue the whole story with long hours of intense action gameplay like in the first game which took me a total of around 18 hours to complete. I hated having to constantly hide and play the waiting game when all I wanted to do was  find the parts of a weapon to craft. In addition to this, the side missions were not that long and I felt that this was an add-on for the developers to flash out the game with this unecessary feature.
Unlike the first game the design of the enemy types with interesting features to try and kill sebastian, I found in the game developers were pretty lazy with very few types of enemies that are different looking zombies I mean sure there are like 3 unique types but I felt this ruined the game for me.
The connection with the characters seemed bland with breif interactions with Sebastian and the one highlight I was pretty disapointed with was not seeing much Jodi Kidman throughout the game, she played a hugh part of the first game and I felt her character was wasted in my opinion.
And finally the game could've had the potential to be longer basing the story mainly focusing on the antagonists unlike Ruvik from the first game they seemed to be cut short out of the game and could've scored more points if they were used more to thicken the plot.
In a nutshell I enjoyed the game but again could've been improved with more features, who knows perhaps a DLC may be put into place in which I will most definetly lookut for. :)

The Evil Within 2 is a pretty decent game, taking some of its learnings from the first game and improving on them - mostly.
TEW2 is the follow-up to Shinji Mikami's The Evil Within, which had a very strong cinematic feel. It didn't really work for most players, so this time round he's dropped the cinematic experience (you can still unlock it after finishing the game). Visually, TEW2 is great, it is better optimised than the first game, and it has some visually just brilliant enemies and set pieces.
Aside from the main story, you are able to complete some side missions for either additional weapons, additional (scary) enemies or just plain achievements.  If I am honest, it is worth seeking out some of the radio transmissions!
Sound-wise, the game is good, follows a similar vibe as the previous game, with the soundtrack working really well (particularly in the first half of the game it just "works").
Downsides then: not much to speak of.... I think the only issue (other than some performance dips here and there) is the absolutely cheap acting towards the second half of the game, with the final hours being so poor and cartooney, you'll want to skip some of the cutscenes. But then again, it is a Shinji Mikami game, a bit of cheesy dialogue and acting has to be.
Overall, I really enjoyed the game. If you enjoyed the frist one, get it, you will not be disappointed.

Ravenfield is a simple singleplayer shooter reminiscent of the Star Wars: Battlefront and Battlefield Series. The player sets up a match, chooses the location and circumstances, and charges into the fray. The gunplay is simple yet satisfying, the spawn system is quite nice, and the vehicles are a joy to use (my favorite being the plane.) This is an early access title, yet it has a nice foundation already, which is far more than can be said of other early access games. Low-end machines such as mine will handle this wonderfully, and the game is an excellent means of killing time. While cooperative play is widely requested, the developer has stated that he isn't interested in developing the netcode required; he is, however, planning to add a campaign mode of sorts, as well as official support for modding. Think of it as a hybrid between Unturned and Battlefield. As it stands, I heartily recommend this little gem to anyone that doesn't mind somewhat repetitive play and meathead fps gameplay, or simply to people like myself that enjoy fps games but doesn't want to deal with an obnoxious online community. With any luck, we'll soon see some complex squad command systems (the only area in which I find this game sorely lacking.)

So I initially started this review as a review of another review and I quickly surpassed the character limit. So I will be writing this review in response to common complaints.
"I played the game and felt like the environment was shallow and empty."
I'd give the depth of scene of the game a solid 7.5/10.
I felt that the game was definitely well-rounded. There were so many nooks and crannies with lore, scene development, and character development that I learned something new every time I replayed a mission. Dishonored 2, like it's predecessor, is not a game to be rushed. Take a moment to look at your surroundings. Take a few moments to look at a room. How does that room explain the rest of the house? And what does that house have to say about that particular city? Take a moment to look at the background in the game. I found myself staring at the scenery or watching the whales or gazing at the sunset. Arkane knows how to set the mood.
Why I didn't give it a 10/10: Some areas were designed to be moved through and that's it. Sometimes I would examine a particular path and have to ask why it is there and if it is at all similar to another path I've seen so far. I hate repeated textures/objects that are used to fill up space. Dishonored 2 doesn't have this all the time, but it does some of the time. There are maybe 2 types of writing desks in the whole game and it seemed like every damn house had a writing desk. Maybe that's why I'd find letters or books in every house? Most of the NPCs (excluding the guards who don't know the alphabet) must be literate.
One particular review stated that the character knew information that they should not or could not know.
I'd give the logic of the game a solid 8/10
You weren't paying attention during your playthrough(s) if you couldn't connect lore/information to cause and effect. I was never shocked by the story. If anything, I'd say that it was predictable enough that I was mildly disappointed there wasn't a twist like there was in dishonored 1. I knew why I was where I needed to be at all times in the game. You're an assassin/queen who was just overthrown because you weren't paying enough attention to the political climate. It makes sense that you would have to start from the bottom and build your way up to Delilah who managed to overpower you and politically (and pubicly) shame you in front of your kingdom. You're going to have to take out all of her supporters or she will continue to outplay you.
Why I didn't give it a 10/10:
Some of the events that occur in the game can be so predictable that it hurts. You can literally have a PERFECT game without your character making any mistakes - especially if you save scum. What do I mean by this? Sometimes, events just don't turn out the way you want them to no matter how hard you try. Save one character's life at the cost of another's life. You can literally prevent most (if not all) of the bad events in the game (civilians being murdered, saving shopkeepers from howlers or guards, etc.). The only unpreventable bad events occur at the very beginning of the game.
"The characters are so... blah! They lack substance!"
Character development: 7.5/10
I wrote a list down of all of the targets in the game and was able to jot down a few sentences on their connections to other characters, their personality traits, and their relevance to the plot. I will agree that some of the characters could have been fleshed out more. But I definitely did not kill or neutralize main characters without knowing a lot about them. Remember, you're an assassin. You gather information, sneak in, gather more information, do your bloody business, then sneak out. No assassin in his or her right mind will sit around and talk to the bad guy/girl. That's just plain illogical. You see em' you shoot em' then run for the hills. If you pay attention during the mission you should learn a lot about the targets through their environment, lore, conversations between NPCs, etc.
Why I didn't give it a 10/10:
Delilah was not my favorite. In fact, she was not satisfying at all. I don't like characters that are designed to make you pity them. I enjoy characters that you respect and understand their perspective, THEN kill them. Like Daud. Damn, that was a good character. Dishonored 1 even gave me an existential crisis as I am being attacked my Corvo (the previous 'me') while I am Daud (who totally deserves to be killed) and I'm fighting hard to kick my own♥♥♥♥♥- twice!
"I hate the chaos system!" or "I only killed 'bad' people! Why did I get an evil ending!?"
The chaos system and the endings gets a 9/10.
The complaint regarding using the heart to hear someone's darkest secrets was unfounded as well. You assume that killing a killer makes you a good person. Or maybe you assume it makes you a bad person. These are shallow and abstract concepts. Killing someone BECAUSE they did something evil (what you believe is evil in your culture) doesn't make you a hero or a villain. It means that you decided the fate of others based on your own opinion. The conclusion of the game only has two endings: justice/vindication and despotism/oppression. You kill a bunch of people? Then you are the judge, jury, and executioner. Spare a bunch of people? Then you are probably waiting to dish out the sentences in a public way after the story is completed - or you're a coward. Whichever. Either way it made sense to me.
Why I didn't give it a 10/10:
The only bone I will throw you is that killing people with the shadow kill ability still left me with high chaos and more bloodflies in later missions. However, killing people anywhere will spook a bunch of people and lead to more drastic actions like suicide and murder. So I'd say look at the chaos system as more of a tension system. Kill more people and do a bunch of naughty stuff? The situation becomes drastically more tense and people are more likely to have a fight/flight response. Still... if I kill the random civilian woman at the docks and nobody is around to hear her scream as she turns to ashes, did she make a sound?
Finally, the performance of the game. I played Dishonored 2 on my laptop (on high, not ultra) and had only one instance of performance issues when approaching some of the open areas by boat. It leveled out though. It could definitely be better, but I wouldn't argue that it "destroyed" my experience at all. Not even close. I was at 45 FPS most of the game and my laptop is 2 years old. I'm not going to post my specs because everyone is posting their god-tier PCs and saying that the game runs like trash. Maybe we just define it differently. Maybe you just like to complain because you spent thousands of dollars on a PC and you want the game to look like real life because you don't have one. (Sorry! I had to make one mean comment.) But hey, you're not the only one complaining about this so it is definitely something Arkane should examine.

I loved Dishonored, between the beautiful style, the stealth gameplay, the outsider, loved it all.
That is why after 3 full playthroughs I am terribly dissapointed. The art and enviroment matchs up with Dishonored, but the gameplay was dull at best, and the story was straight disrespectful to it's predecessor. My greatest complaint is the explanatory nature of the game. It feels as if they looked at all the lingering questions from the first game and just answered them all. This was a mistake, part of the fun and intrigue was the mysterious nature of the game. My biggest irritation by far would be the Outsider, It's not the voice, I couldn't care less, it is the bland nature of the new character. I say new because whereas the Outsider used to be mysterious, and poetic. This new Outsider is straight foward, bland, overly gothic. He seems weaker, instead of confusing, he is dumbed down.
This can be said for a lot of the game, instead of puzzles the game makes itself easy and lives in the past, the only new characters play minor roles or are eliminated, in both DLC's and the first game we met new intresting characters who were intregal to the story. This game just rehashed a defeated villain with the same old tricks. Same thing with Lush and Sokolov, our only allies were previous characters? They would be okay for an appearance, but I want characters to rival the first and bringing Lush in ruined her open ended storyline were we were unsure of what happened to her. I didnt feel like I was discovering anything, the bloodflies and the clockwork soilders were perhaps the only intresting new thing.
To summarize, as a loyal fan of the first game I am dissapointed in the simplicity of everythign except the level design, I feel remorse in saying I do not reccomend this game and I weep for the end of Dishonored's legacy. If only more time had been put into characters. I think my only hope for any future dishonored game is to try the Daud storyline because I hated Emily Kaldwin and her simplistic character design.
Sorry Arkane, You'll have to try harder than that to make somethign to match Dishonored, maybe try some ol' fashioned original story?

At this point it seems like a safe bet to consider Total War games as actually being released about a year after they are available to purchase; think of those first 12 months as an early-access beta. After a year the games are generally patched up, cheaper and available with a handful of DLC.
Anyhow, the current incarnation of Rome II seems to have addressed most of the issues which were rampant at release and the game is in a proper and playable state. As Total War games go, Rome II is mostly the expected status quo with a spattering of incremental updates/changes to the game's various systems. For the most part the main changes in Rome II center around streamlining campaign map management. For the most part I've appreciated these changes, myself, but it can sometimes be an irritation that units cannot be moved autonomously in Rome II and must always be part of an army. On the bright side, you are now able to reinforce units directly to your armies rather than having to wait for them to move from city centers. Auto-resolve is also a good deal more usable here though the algorithm will still sometimes give questionable odds for or against you.
Long story short: the game is pretty much fixed and worth buying now so if you enjoy Total War games, don't hesitate to jump in.

I hated this game at first, but with Radious mod package installed it's really growing on me. Lots of changes from previous TW games - city management is less of a chore now as it's handled on a regional level with small settlements behaving more like towns in Empire:TW. The biggest improvements are how garrisons and overseas expeditions are handled. No more squeezing 1200 cavalry onto a trading cog; transport ships are provided automatically when they're required and are usable in sea battles. The old tactic of sinking entire armies with a patrolling trireme no longer works as you'll simply be rammed and boarded. Garrisons are managed automatically, with troop type/numbers dictated by the buildings present in the settlement. This adds a more realistic feel to city defenses.
Combat is ok, but quite fast paced. I'm playing at half-speed to compensate and it's bearable. Abilities have CDs so there's a lot more micromanagement in combat. I disliked this at first, but as with the whole game, it's growing on me.
My only gripe is the lack of historical info on both unit cards and at the start of each year. The UI artwork is equally lacking - I miss the unit portraits from earlier TW games.
It's a good game. Just make sure you download the Radious mod package.

Any serious MMORPG fan should at least give this a try. This Elder Scrolls game falls right in line with the quality of gameplay, lore and graphics as with the older titles. Veterans of this series will be taken down Nostalgia Lane with some of the locations, sounds and music. The MMO aspect is there and it is really awesome to finally see other Heroes in the wilderness and fight monsters together. They really did that aspect well, because you dont have to be grouped to receive loot chance drop and experience. You can also group together, and here is where the main beef of the game really bothers me, since I've been spoiled by other successful MMOs. The group mechanics, in particularly the Tank role, hardly ever holds aggro from pulls (even trash pulls) therefore making the group constantly having to duck and dodge getting hit for simply attacking the monster. This is simply unacceptable in my opinion and should be seriously considered a future patch update to add aggro to the tank's skills. Another problem I have is the constricting number of skills you can have set at a time. You can have countless spells/abilities but you can only bind 5 on your hotbar to use during an encounter. The game is overall enjoyable and I will continue to play even if it will take some getting used to. Seasoned MMO players may experience the same drawbacks as well. The game doesn't require a sub to play but if you do sub you do get quite a bit of perks for doing so. If your interested in purchasing, go to the website to see the difference in no sub/sub.

There are many differences between Deus Ex: Invisible War and the first game, for example:
The maps are fairly smaller.
The skills and augmentations have been combined into biomods.
As the skills have been removed, you are pretty much as proficient with your weapons in the beginning as you are in the end, unless you are using weapon mods or melee biomods.
Despite the skills and augmentations being removed in favor of biomods, there are still many different ways to play the game.
The game didn't allow me to change to windowed mode without manually editing the config, as it was not in the options menu.
As far as I know, by default the game doesn't support aspect ratios outside of 4:3, or changing the resolution to anything besides what the default options menu supports. When I tried either of these, the text in menus often disappeared, and sometimes the game just didn't render at all.
Loading screens often took minutes to load, I believe I fixed this by closing the Logitech Gaming Framework (lcore.exe). Combined with the small areas, which means more minute-long loading screens, it is very annoying to play with this issue.
Like I said, if you don't want to spend time trying to fix it (I almost gave up myself, it took me about an hour before I realized that setting a custom resolution was causing the second problem I stated above), I wouldn't recommend this game. I'd say that it is definitely worth spending some time to get it working though.
If you like the Deus Ex story and world, or you're looking for a fairly simpler version of the first Deus Ex (gameplay-wise) I'd definitely recommend this game, however.

Whether or not I recommend you play this game depends on your answer to one question.
If you really liked it, then I definitely recommend playing this game because I really think that, for all of the game's shortcomings, the story is not one of them- and it carried me through to the end. On the other hand, if you didn't much like the story and universe of the original Deus Ex, then I wouldn't recommend this game- because I found that the story is its one saving grace. Without this factor, you're left with a decidedly subpar game, especially when compared to the original Deus Ex.
Action role-playing game developed by Ion Storm, as a sequel to the hugely successful original Deus Ex on PC. The game was released for PC and the original Xbox- with the developers seeming to focus heavily on optimising the game for the latter.
The game itself plays out as a fairly rudimentary action RPG. It feels like the developers took the in-depth systems of Deus Ex and stripped them down to their bare essentials- probably in order to downsize the game for the benefit of the Xbox. As a consequence, the “skills” system has been completely removed; ammo is universal for all weapons and multitools/lockpicks are now a single item. However, there is one saving grace in the form of the biomodification system. This system plays out in much the same way as the augmentation system from the original Deus Ex, with plenty of scope to craft a character that will cater to your playstyle. The augmentation system was one of the most interesting parts about the original Deus Ex; so I’m glad to see that the developers at least had their priorities in order in this regard when creating Invisible War.
Gameplay itself resembles the original Deus Ex, and the options available to the player in order to achieve certain objectives are much the same. Stealth, combat and hacking are viable options. Similarly you can choose between a non-lethal/lethal playstyle. These options are very rudimentary compared to the original Deus Ex; however their inclusion is appreciated. On the other hand, a major problem of the game is how easy it is. I played on the hardest difficulty (realistic) and didn’t get stuck at all. For the record, I played a stealth character; however I did try out combat as well and wasn’t impressed.
However, hands down the biggest problem for me is the game’s miniscule areas. It’s no secret that the original Deus Ex had massive areas, which you could explore for hours and continue to find new things. The areas in Invisible War are so small that you can finish each in 10 minutes, tops. And after each area you are forced to endure another painfully long loading screen. Any tension or momentum that the game might create is utterly sapped by the repulsively frequent and lengthy loading screens. This is a huge issue, and I would be much more tempted to recommend the game were it not for this problem. Finally, the physics engine is hilariously bad- so be prepared for some unintentionally funny moments if you do decide to play this game!
Adequate. Feels like the developers downsized the original Deus Ex’s systems and were left with incredibly subpar gameplay mechanics and insufferable load times.
It's no embellishment to say that the original Deus Ex had an outstanding soundtrack- with not a single unmemorable tune in the whole repertoire. The sequel to this game, Deus Ex: Human Revolution, also had a great, fitting, memorable soundtrack. Invisible War, once again, falls short of these lofty standards. Tunes aren't particularly memorable, and there aren't too many of them either. Nevertheless, I would say that the soundtrack fits the cyberpunk setting of the game- so it deserves credit in that regard. Similarly, the soundtrack does have SOME particularly good tunes, such as the "Heron's Loft" theme and the title theme.
Adequate. Some standout tracks, but for the most part unmemorable. Nevertheless appropriate for the setting of the game- which is worthy of credit, I think.
Deus Ex: Invisible War, takes place 20 years after the original Deus Ex. An interesting point of note is that the original Deus Ex had multiple endings, so you may be wondering how Invisible War could continue such a story. Interestingly enough, Invisible War does not commit to a single ending- instead melding aspects of each ending into one, and building off of that. I acknowledge that some may not be a fan of this decision- as it essentially invalidates the endgame choices of the original Deus Ex. However, I found this design decision interesting, and was intrigued to see how the game would continue such a story. Overall, I think it did it well. Thematically, Invisible War is extremely similar to the original- tackling the ethics of body modification, as well governments and secret societies and how they influence the world at large. In other words, the game is rich in conspiracy- in true Deus Ex style.
The plot starts out fairly slow- with a tedious tutorial area followed by being ejected into the first “hub area” of the game- Seattle. I found that Seattle was the hub with the most activity; boasting lots of areas and a lot of side missions. However, at the same time I found it to be the least interesting. Instead I think Seattle serves as the area where all of the main factions of the game are introduced, offering the player choice in terms of who to side with at a very early stage. Thankfully you don’t have to commit to a faction for the whole game; you’re given plenty of time to ponder individual ideologies and motivations. In a way, Invisible War trumps even the original Deus Ex in this regard, wherein a lot of the decisions pertaining to “choosing a side” were out of the player’s hands (at least until the end of the game).
Invisible War’s one true claim to fame in my opinion. Not as enthralling as the original Deus Ex’s plot, but it still kept me going until the end. I consider that the plot gains traction when you reach the second hub area, as this is the point where I felt connected to the story, and the compulsion to see it through superseded the subpar gameplay mechanics.
If you’ve stayed with me for this whole review, then I’m sure you’ll have noticed the amount of comparisons to the original Deus Ex. This just goes to show how the odds were stacked against Invisible War from the get-go. It came in with a TON of sequel baggage: the pressure to surpass what many consider to be the greatest game of all time. Couple that with being majorly downsized in order to appeal to the console demographic and it seems that Invisible War was doomed from the start. However, as a huge Deus Ex fan, I find myself recommending this game. Yes all of the gameplay systems are “adequate” instead of “superb”; yes the soundtrack is “okay” instead of “incredible”, but as an entry into the Deus Ex universe of conspiracy and intrigue, it’s just as worthy as Human Revolution in my opinion.
So, if you really want to see where the Deus Ex chronology ends, then I definitely recommend buying this game. On the other hand, if you have absolutely no connection with the story and universe of Deus Ex, then there really is no reason to buy this game- as there are much better alternatives in terms of gameplay. To conclude, I’m perfectly fine with accepting this game into the Deus Ex universe; however it certainly doesn’t hold a candle to the original Deus Ex and Human Revolution. Here’s hoping Mankind Divided will be another worthy addition to the franchise!

Though unfortunatley a product of it's time (janky physics anyone?), Invisible War really does not deserve a lot of the hate it gets. Being given the impossible task to try and stack up against its older brother (which is a MANDATORY play should you want to jump into this), of course it's going to seem mediocre. But when you weigh this game on it's own terms, is when its brilliance shows. Brilliant sound design, an even more dramatic and twisty narrative (actually allowing you to JOIN with specific factions this time around), solid mechanics and overall fun gameplay make for an enjoyable sci-fi/cyberpunk experience.
But again, don't tangle yourself up in comparing it to the original Deus Ex. The mechanics are simplified, to the point to where it really isn't much of an RPG anymore, but they're polished enough to keep things enjoyable. And, unlike the previous game, truly allows you to pursue whatever playstyle you want without any strange setbacks/hiccups.
Overall, great game, not so great sequel. 7/10 would definitley reccomend.

Love is a simple platforming game where you get 100 lives and set your own checkpoints while travelling through 16 different levels. The concept is fine, but it's very flawed when it comes to it's execution.
The look of the game follows this simple aesthetic, and looks a bit like something that would have come out on the Intellivision. However, they don't take the aesthetic far enough so the graphics manage to look more boring and cheaply made instead of retro.
The soundtrack is good, and is likely the best part of the game. However, it's not super mindblowing or anything, just well done.
The part where this game really breaks apart for me is in the level design and the controls. The levels are all really simply designed, with the paths you take through them being really basic without much of anything interesting going on, sometimes simply having them be an excuse to shove some poorly drawn pixel art in your face. All of the levels essentially feel very uninspired.
The controls are really imprecise and don't feel as tight and resonsive as something like a Super Meat Boy or even a VVVVVV. Your jump doesn't really have any weight to it, either. Your character doesn't feel weighty or floaty, there's essentially just no inertia to any of the movement. It just feels like it's moving your character up as you hold the jump button and immediately moving them down as you let go. The controls just feel
and are probably the worst part of the game.
Overall, it's a simple game, and while it's inexpensive, it's also not a great experience. If you're looking for a simple, retro platformer, you could do much better, for not much more money.

If you like retro platforming and short little games, you'll enjoy love.
Pros:
- Very good controls, though the jumping can feel a little floaty until you get used to it
- About the right length
- The Set Respawn Point mechanic, which allows you to set a respawn point anywhere in the level at the cost of some end-of-game points is an interesting way to make the game more challenging the better you get at it--the better you are, the less respawns you use
- Nice soundtrack
Cons:
- I like the game's length but it can be run through in less than an hour the first time if you have any platforming experience. Of course, the real fun is going through it and trying to better your score, so YMMV
- There is one level where it's possible to set a respawn point and make the game unwinnable. It's very close to the end of the game, so that can be frustrating.
Otherwise, I've had a lot of fun with LOVE. The price is right.
Retro platforming done right. Very short and cheap, and easily worth your time. A lot of room for completionists, as well (Trying to finish faster, with less deaths, etc)

Summary: LOVE isn't a bad game exactly, but it's very far from a great one. Mediocre in a lot of ways, LOVE fails to ever exceed expectations, nor does it ever fail to meet them. It's the epitome of generic, and while it is decent, that isn't enough to qualify as a recommendation. LOVE is never great; it's just passable. 
LOVE unfortunately possesses flaws that so many other 8-bit indie platformers have been hampered by. LOVE doesn't really feel like an entirely complete package either, which is a damn shame, because there's obviously a lot of effort and care that's been put into this product. However, it is basically just your run of the mill 8-bit indie platformer. I wouldn't say you shouldn't purchase this, because that's not my decision. Perhaps you will the find the enjoyment in this title that I didn't.

Alien: Isolation's protagonist Amanda Ripley travels to station Sevastapol as she is willing to risk everything to find out what happened to her mother. As she discovers what happened on the station through computer logs she begins to gain a deeper understanding of herself and her own morals. The harsh juxtaposition of action sequences with tranquillity in between them offers a look into the conflicting emotions Ripley is feeling between her mother and her own call of duty. Alistair Hope has carefully crafted these environments and messages throughout the game to give the player a gradual sense of self-discovery.
As Ripley broadens her sense of self, her personality also changes from a strict attitude to a more apathetic outlook on life. When she begins her journey she maintains a sense of duty and professionalism, and operated very much by-the-book and in accordance with the rules. After she encounters the Xenomorph through a series of traumatising events her outlook on life changes. She becomes far colder and more apathetic towards her life, resigned to the fact she had been ruined both professionally and personally by what had happened. Alistair uses emotive and blunt dictation to convey Ripley's feelings in "It's like you feel homesick for a place that doesn't exist". This reflects in the games atmosphere and music, which features less colour and is much calmer than the first sequence. This change also teaches Ripley to break away from the rules, as shown when she fearlessly volunteered to trap the Xenomorph in a remote section of the station. She was able to break away from the conventions of her personality and embrace the unknown through journey.

This is a great game, and one of the trickiest and most satisfying stealth games that I have played for a long time. Throw in the survival-horror factor, which is very psychological, and you have a game which is true to the
film from which it stems. There is a lot going for this perilous cat-and-mouse space adventure, where weapons are mostly ineffective and fighting is futile. In terms of presentation, the graphics are really nice, especially the ambient lighting; the sound effects are excellent, and the music really adds to the creepy atmosphere, where all manner of threats lurk.
As Amanda Ripley, the game's female protagonist, you have to rely on your wits and trusty motion tracker to guide your way through the vast station, utilising blueprints and tools to achieve the ultimate objective of getting off
alive. The alien moves swiftly, responding with lightning reactions to the sounds of running feet and discharged weapons, attacking without fear or remorse; it is convincingly unpredictable in its cunning. Hiding in lockers and beneath desks may seem wise, but don't rely on such tactics to save you indefinitely. You must keep moving, stay low, and always remain alert!

At the moment of writing this, the original Half-Life came out over 18 years ago.
Specifically, 18 years, 4 months, 17 days, 12 hours, and 35 minutes, to be precise.
The original Half-Life was an absolutely revolutionary game that combined FPS elements, a fantastic and gripping storyline, and mild puzzle-solving, with absolutely minimal hand-holding.
Half-Life had its controversy and complaints, too. Xen was certainly... Strange? And "On a Rail" was just absurdly long.
But this isn't Half-Life. This is Black Mesa.
Black Mesa is a fan-made graphical update for Half-Life that brings the 90's straight into.... Well, the... the '10s?
Anyhows, Black Mesa is largely identical to Half Life, with some minor tweaks that feel like huge improvements. "On a Rail" is no longer a slog that just won't end. Xen isn't even in the game yet, that's a pro and a con. We're not quite sure when it will be, and frankly, I don't like the look so far. Looks too much like a cave, and less... Alien?
You don't need another review recommending Half-Life, or by extension, Black Mesa. You already know you should play it. It's an icon for a reason, Those awful, "Half-Life 3 confirmed???" jokes exist for a reason.
Show the devs some support. Nab it now, or on sale. But don't be a tool and wait for Xen to come out. The game is extremely polished. The graphics look fantastic. Sound quality could use an improvement, but it still sounds better than Half-Life.

Looking Glass performs their usual alchemy by providing a unique blend of fps,rpg and survival horror adventure with System Shock 2. Where most modern devs would juggle these aspects by making one or more of the additional mechanics a novel add on, such as the rpg mechanics usually, SS2 is as much a cohesive rpg as it is a first person adventure. The rpg mechanics can be cumbersome to learn for first time players, but allow for the ability to have unique playthroughs which add replay value to the game, and players who come into possession of a decent weapon and with the properly leveled skill level for it will quickly go from prey to hunter on the Von Braun. This combined with the expansive levels will provide players with a Deus Ex level of exploration and multi-approach gameplay within a surivival horror setting.
Credit should be given for SS2's sound, level and game design for effecitvely communicating the experience of a sci-fi horror experience, overcoming the primitive graphics of its time to deliver a game experience which is authentically immersive despite its age. Anyone playing on the higher difficulties will be too occupied with their ammo count, condition of their gun, their immediate surroundings or what they would like to spend their cyber modules on next to be worried about how old the game looks. Immersion through game mechanics is always what made Looking Glass stand out from their peers and it is what makes them stand out to this very day.
For those who enjoyed the Bioshock games and would like to know its spirtual ancestor, System Shock 2 is a worthy game to experience. However, I would like to add that it is not just worth knowing Bioshock's spirtual ancestor, but to know System Shock 2's own ancestor, System Shock 1. The original System Shock is worth playing because not only is it an ancestor to System Shock 2 and Looking Glass' other games, but because it is a relative to nearly every modern first person game in some regard and a worthy experience by its own merit. All of Looking Glass' games should be experienced, because they're more than video game history, they're some of the best experiences that video games has to offer to this very day, System Shock 2 included.

It is now almost 18 years old, and yet, after replaying it a few times over the years - it still has it.  By 'it' I mean the immersive story and atmosphere.  Few games achieve that, but the Half Life series as well as the Bioshock series had it. The sound effects, lighting, music, and the intricate story means it is instantly recognisable from just a few seconds of audio.
Yes, its old, and the graphics looked 'dated' well over a decade ago, but few single players can keep one interested throughout the entire game - and then leave wanting to replay it with a different class.  It is only with more recent games with large maps that I realised just how enjoyable 'exploring' (as in, sticking to objectives, but going off for side missions) is; I think this is the earliest game that had it nailed.
Whilst perhaps not strictly horror when compared to the likes of Amnesia or Soma, it remains unsettling as you find corpses with audio recordings in rooms where clearly something 'dodgy' happened, and the little touches like locked doors (with someone long departed in the room clutching a broken pistol) all add up so I always wanted to know 'more'.  It can be terrifying in places.
It was only after the latest replay (first time on steam) that I realised just how much I enjoyed it - why else would someone replay a game from 1999 unless it has a quality that no other game has?
I don't think any future sequels can really top it, but I'm sure a complete revamp of the graphics would be welcome to bring it to a younger generation. Even so, if you're after a great story, combat that give you brown trousers when your weapons need repairing, and moments where a vague sense of dread has you hiding in a room wondering what to do - this is your game.

I played The Evil Within [TEW] and while I wanted to like it based on the reviews, etc, I basically thought it was a totally mediocre incoherent waste of time, and I only played it through to the end because Im that "driven, completionist" kind of gamer.
The reviews of The Evil Within 2 said its way better than TEW and Bethesda ran their "save single player games" campaign (and I want to save Bethesda, they publish awesome games like  Prey, Skyrim, Fallout4, Doom2016, the recent Wolfensteins, the Dishonoured series, etc and have been doing so back as far as I can remember, eg Arena and Terminator: Future Shock) so I bought and played TEW2 too.
And in playing it, I think Ive finally understood "The Evil Within" games. The horror presented is not that presented *by* the games as you play, the horror lies *within* the playing of the games. What do I mean by that?
"Theres something bad happening in here Kidman". Yeah, no sheet Sherlock.
The writing is abominably bad, I mean really truly awful, everything is hyperdramatic and overacted, the dialogue and plot are fully nonsensical, all characters are caricatures, the whole script a constant litany of stupid that my mind rails against with futility. But surely I exaggerate you say?
"Tell that to my brain". Yes, a character literally says this. Awful writing.
The models and textures are quite basic for a "AAA" game in 2017. The animations, textures, shaders, lighting model, etc are incredibly basic like they have been phoned in, this looks nothing like other contemporary idTech games such as Wolfenstein2 Doom2016, Dishonoured DOTO.
The level design is insipid (all right angles), with nonsensical boundaries (eg cant walk up this very shallow hill, but I can walk on that very shallow hill, cant hop on this blue crate but can hop on this blue crate?!?!), etc etc etc. The art direction, well the game puts it best: "seems content to merely revel in grotesquery for the sake of titillation"
This looks and feels more like a 2008 title*, but right now it just feels tired and mediocre.
(*for example, TEW2 really reminds me of Alone in the Dark 2008, but I kind of think I liked that game more... and its metacritic rating is 55%!)
"What did I do to deserve this?"
The gameplay is very basic 3rd person shooting, some basic sneakery, with a bit of survival horror, evoking memories of countless previous games where any particular aspect you care to think about has already been done better (I'll be helpful to potential players and list them below). In particular, I hate the melee combat, Sebastian flailing away with his knife like a completely inept moron who deserves to have his guts ripped out by a helpful zombie.
Its not all bad though, eg I thought Chapters9, 10 were quite good, the setting and art style, level design, puzzles, combat all gelled within the design of the game, and it made for quite competent sections of gameplay.
Its these observations above that brings me to my understanding of the Evil Within 2. It is a survival horror right? But here's the beautiful thing. The "survival horror" is the horror of playing such a medicore game after paying good money for it, the struggle of retaining your sanity while being besieged by nonsensical writing, surviving its constant onslaught of tedium and mediocrity.

This is either actually astoundingly clever on the part of the developers, very meta and truly artistic, finally putting not the game character (Sebastian), but the player (you and me!) in a survival horror situation. Wow. Incredible. And effective, I dont like being *in* a survival horror situation, so the game is definitely stimulating the desired result.
Or else these are truly medicore games. I think its the latter.
All in all "Its like some kind of sick joke".
Better games list:
Alan Wake: For essentially everything TEW2 tries to do.
Dead Space 1-2: For survival horror
FEAR: for Japanese scary stuff and gunplay
Witcher 3: for open world RPG stuff
Psychonauts: for crazy world design
Outlast: for scares and thrills
Splinter Cell (any): for 3rd person sneakery

Broforce is an extremely wacky, explosive, fun action-platformer with a 4-5 hour campaign, Steam Workshop support (lots o' maps), and tons of different characters that have unique weapons, specials, and movesets.
Uh... You're on the side of freedom and shoot terrorists while causing explosions, but who is that red guy at the end? Mystery, intrigue, Bros!
The game provides a fun experience with some situations that can lead to temporary frustration due to the random nature of what Bro is assigned to you. You start off a level as a single, random Bro and can rescue prisoners to add to your remaining lives. Every time you die, the game reverts back to the last checkpoint you grabbed and gives you another Bro to deal death and freedom. You beat stages by reaching the last checkpoint/flag and escaping via chopper
by winning a boss fight. I have jumped onto the helicopter's blades and shot it down so uh... be careful.
The different Bros make the game handle very differently depending on whom you're controlling. Some of the melee characters have a boosted movespeed, dashes, and bullet deflection. The ranged characters might have you throwing spears, unleashing a spray of bullets, or tossing dynamite (or slapping dynamite on close enemies that then panic). The variety keeps you on your toes and encourages learning how to play with each Bro, but sometimes that variety can impede progress for a bit (usually on a very tough boss) until you receive the right line-up to wreck face. I definitely like Brominator for some bosses since he can turn into the skeleton for invincibility and unleash justice with his minigun. I've ran into this situation around 2-3 times in the campaign, going through Bros until I found the one that fit the situation for me. Overall, the variety keeps the game from becoming stale, and you're not forced to rescue prisoners if you're feeling confident and really like the Bro you're using.
The stages are fully destructible for the most part with ladders and checkpoints being the only things able to survive gunfire and explosions. This allows for paths to be carved with gunfire to avoid enemies, traps, man-made pits, and unintended deaths. It's a fun part of the game and I enjoy being able to wipe out enemies by removing the platform they were standing on so confidently.
Lastly, I didn't play co-op for very long as I don't wish to play with strangers. As a group though, you can completely demolish the stages with all that firepower which can lead to some fantastic deaths and Bro combinations. This game seems like a solid choice for co-op mayhem.
After beating the game on offline mode solo, I tried to join a multiplayer session once which ended up wiping my campaign progress. The unlocked Bros remained persistent and were available to me without an issue. I checked that by going into Arcade mode and by playing in Steam Workshop levels. I even unlocked the next Bro in Arcade mode. Make sure to be careful if you're not hosting and care about your campaign progress.
Also, some levels (near the end of the game) with the sandy type of dirt that crumbles might bug out on a checkpoint loading and crumble without you even touching it leading to death since you can't bridge the gap or you just fall into it. Watch out!
Alright, go have fun. Use the Workshop to play even more levels after beating the campaign.

The game looks and sounds great, and the puzzles are challenging. It feels as if years of developing point-and-click adventure games has culminated in a truly polished product. However, the ending was godawful. It's as if every single popular game since Drawn to Life has pulled a cop-out fourth-wall breaker. One Shot, Undertale, and similar games all have the presumption to try and become a personal investment on the players' part, yet there's no justifiable reciprocation for this, since the game developer doesn't actually know you. They haven't built a personal relationship with you. They're merely infringing on your personal space with this creepy metaphorical feel-copping. Harry Potter readers will probably remember a line the deceased Dumbledore gives toward the end of the series, something along the paraphrased lines of "Just because it's in your head doesn't mean it's not real." Solipsism. It's actually not quite so bad with Thimbleweed Park, but it is a trend that tired rapidly and feeds on the sad cult of celebrity people still shamelessly buy into. It's a fun game to play, it's just that the pay off is as worthless as watching through Lost. Rebuttals will likely quote that it's about the journey, but as I've just stated, the journey through the game is enjoyable. It's just, you really end up only spinning your wheels the whole time.
The call-ins and books from the Kickstarter backers were pretty sad, although a much-needed break from sitting through eleven-hour credits sequences crediting every sap who paid a dollar before any work was put into a product. Still, the content these complete strangers provided ranged from shameless self-advertisement to squalid, out-of-context and outdated memes that dishonor the integrity of adventure gaming. It lends itself to strict criticism on account of the disclaimer provided in-game that the providers are responsible for their own content.
Fun game. The self-references became ham-fisted after a while. We should be pretty tired of Ron Gilbert's opinions and incessant rebuttals by now. I'd rather pay for a game, not every Steam developer's blog entries regarding the latest hashtags.

So I finally got round to playing Dishonored 2, and though it adds a lot more features, as the powers are integrated even more into combat and exploration, the game overall still falls short in terms of making the same impact, or even a remotely similar impact to the first game. The aesthetics of the game and the overall artistic style don't seem to carry on from the first game. It seems as if they forgot what made Dishonoreds world probably one of the most aesthetically pleasing, and just generally cool to play in. Characters fail to make any kind of memorable impression on the players, especially Delilah and Co. From the first game, after fighting Daud, you'd remember him, as possibly one of the greatest badass villain/anti-heroes you'd ever seen, especially after Knife of Dunwall DLC. Though Delilah and Daud are completely different, it's the same thing with Meagan/the former Billie Lurk. I've got to say though, Emily's character in the game is incredible, it's just too bad her powers kind of suck, compared to Corvos.
But is the game necessarily bad to play? OF COURSE NOT! I bought this game since I played the first Dishonored when it came out and that game blew my mind! The mere thought of playing as an Assasin in first person, with Teleportating abilities, jumping from one Victorian Rooftop to another, in a Whale-Punk, Alternative Industrial Revolution was enough to send my then 15-year old self's mind abolutely teeming with the crazy possibilties. Though the level designs weren't too complex, the game had a beautifully cool Aesthetic, with Memorable Characters such as Daud, Slackjaw, Granny Rags, Admiral Havelock, etc. Though Dishonored 2 is not as Aeshtetically pleasing as the first, nor anywhere near the same character impact on the player, it expands on level design, creating much more complex level designs involving backtracking a fair amout for extra loot and much more exploration possibilities. Depending on which difficulty you play the game, (I played it on hard) the enemies actually prove to be much more of a challenge from the first game, posing a threat. The crossbow is significantly downgraded in terms of fire power, range and accuracy, rather than from the first game. I liked how the game allowed you to knock out enemies during combat, if you didnt want to kill anyone too. But the game fails to emphasise the impact of the players chosen ending as much as the first. Though I'm only speaking on a personal level, I feel as if the game/The Outsiders narration at the end failed to make me feel bad for my actions. In fact, in a way, it made me feel some sort of accomplishment. Also, what the heck is with the change in The Outsiders character? Considering everything I've said the game is nowhere near as dark and gloomy as the first Dishonored was. If they make a third Dishonored (which I pray to god they dont do so and ruin this now average franchise), they should bring it back to how the first Dishonored was, just with the combat, gameplay and level exploration of Dishonored 2.
Also, please bear in mind, that the game is still relatively new and lacks optimised drivers for the game. I have a 3gb 1060, and though the game is much optimised a step up from day one release date, expect frame rate drops and a downgrade in graphics, for the time being, unless you've got a £1k beast of a PC. The game has framerate drops and does not play at a solid 60fps at this moment in time.

As a fan of strategy it is only natural that I am a fan of the Total War series, that said I was hesitent to get Rome II at first for reasons that many of us are aware of, at launch it was a buggy nightmare that will cause people to doubt Creative Assembly for quite a while, that and Shogun 2 was excellent enough to not need to move on. Many months later combined with a sale day I was tempted, but first consulted a friend about it. He assured me the game was now very much fixed so I decided to go for it. Put simply I was not dissapointed.
One thing I liked right from the get go was the fact that for the main campaign, known as the Grand Campaign, the map is huge and whether your commanding the Roman war machine or fighting against it you will be there a while and there will be many battles to be had. Most of the series signature features are there, the map, agents that serve various purposes, huge epic battles. That said the family tree is gone sadly, and I do mis it quite a bit as it made me feel even more invested in my game, families still exist but in a somewhat different form that instead plays a part in your chosen culture's internal politics which you are tasked with balancing rather than straight up dominating due to the risk of civil wars that can arise because of the internal factions within your government. Building on this is a system where events will happen and you will have to decide how to deal with them, with the outcome having effect of the political situation within your culture. Mileage will vary on whether or not this a good replacement for the Family Tree but it is a good system nonetheless.
Overall I enjoyed Rome II just like I enjoyed Shogun II, that said many will argue that Shogun II is the smarter buy right now due to be noticably cheaper and I am inclined to agree. That said if you are itching for more total war on an even bigger scale and you spot it on sale go for it, and happy conquering!

-The loading times are much more severe
-The levels are less open and feel more like a series of long hallways than an open map
-Important statistics for various items and abilities that used to be displayed in the menus are no longer viewable, which harms the RPG aspect of the game significantly
-The upgrade systems for weapons, biomods, and your character in general have been harshly simplified and minimalized so that they now lack many of what I considered to be essential aspects of the first Deus Ex
-The game has a lot of bugs that make it difficult to play, whereas the first Deus Ex game was relatively glitch free
-The game no longer features equipment (which, granted, felt relatively useless for most play-styles)
-The notes and various acquired data is less detailed and less diverse; I frequently come across duplicate datapads and books, whereas every datapad and book in the original Deus Ex was unique
-You can no longer assign custom keys for biomods or quick save/load, which is surprisingly tedious in the middle of combat when I have to hit “fn + f6” just to activate my enhanced speed mod, when I’d much rather hit “v” like I could in the first Deus Ex game
-Acquired data, passwords, and passcodes are no longer saved and viewable at any time. Additionally, passwords and passcodes are no longer managed by a player, and the player never has to enter or remember passwords or passcodes in the game. This especially bothers me, because having to manage passwords on your own made hacking feel more like actual hacking, like an achievement of the player. I’d always find myself searching a room for clues as to what a password might be, which felt cool, but I never do that in Deus Ex Invisible War.
-You get so much goddamn money within the first 5th of the game that it loses it’s value. Every other mission or “quest” in the game gives you money, and your rarely use it.
There were some improvements, however. that Deus Ex: Invisible War made to the original game:
-The stealth system is more complex and requires more strategy than the first Deus Ex
-There were many new and interesting weapons and biomods, which give the player even more gameplay options, many of which were very fun to play around with
-The game utilizes factions and loyalty systems to add a level of depth to the RPG experience
-The graphics, obviously, are much better
-The ragdoll physics are really cool, and they make moving bodies way more fun
-The game allows you to play as a female, which is nice
-The characters are slightly more developed, though completely static (as in the first game)
-I imagine that for most people, it’s actually very convenient not having to manage passcodes and passwords themselves
-The narrative in Invisible War is a bit better and more central to the game. In the original Deus Ex, I remember the story being very rough, and the characters to flat to care about. The narrative isn’t great in Invisible War, but it is an improvement.
That was, of course, just a brief list of changes made between Deus Ex 1 and Deus Ex: Invisible War. Even that, however, is likely more information than necessary. In all honesty, there are only a few things to consider if you’re thinking about buying this game: did you really enjoy the original Deus Ex? If the answer is yes, than you should buy this game. As a fan of the first Deus Ex, I thoroughly enjoyed Deus Ex: Invisible War. I would say that the original Deus Ex was better, but Invisible War is still a good sequel that does not betray the aspects that made the original so good.
Overal Score = 6.3/10 (Good, but nothing special)

The description of this is what caught me during one of my “scroll through recs/sale items and download what looks interesting and is cheap” runs that I do during Steam and Humble sales.
I believe that gaming should not be anything complicated or diffcult, but a relaxing and pleasure experience. Therefore, I designed this ARPG battle system which requires no attack button to play. The simplicity brings a fluent and interesting gaming experience.
“Fluid” is definitely a good way to describe this game. It moves forward steadily, but still requires thought. The boss battles and puzzles increased in difficultly without ever becoming frustrating, which I thought was a pretty big accomplishment for such a small game. A completionist run is entirely doable without a guide thanks to the logical way in which things such as the locations of hidden chests are designed, which I appreciated. And true to the designer’s intentions, it is indeed a game anyone can play.
The game is also just the right length for what it has to offer. Another dungeon would have been boring, while one less would have been really, really short.
The game follows the titular Senia, who has entered the cursed Tower of Eternity to rescue her sister, Magaleta (I spent a large part of the game wondering if this was a botched translation of “Magdalena,” since it’s such an unnatural name linguistically). As the game progresses, Senia flashes back to the setup of their lives together and why Mag entered the tower in the first place.
The most glaring issue with the game is that the translation is very bad. The dev is Taiwanese, and it looks like he may have tried to translate it into English himself. This was a mistake, as while it’s still understandable, it doesn’t at any point resemble proper sentences. There were a few times I really had to guess at what he was trying to say. And worst of all, it annihilates any atmosphere the dialogue might have built and none of the characters have unique voices.
I also wasn’t a big fan of the true ending, since you basically end up right back where you started having accomplished nothing. It was too much of a sequel hook and not enough an actual conclusion. I’m shocked at the amount of games that have this problem, actually. To me it seems obvious that when writing even a basic story you should also include an ending. I suppose the issue is that inexperienced writers don’t know how to conserve interesting but unnecessary information — they see it as all-or-nothing, where the game either lays bare everything or hold all the cards close to its chest in lieu of an actual conclusion. This is one of the reasons I always tell people who want to write to read ravenously — seeing how sequels are properly set up goes a long way in not botching your own endings so badly.
I also have been led to understand the game uses a lot of basic rpgmaker assets, but that doesn’t really bother me and I’m always confused as to why people get so high and mighty about it. Surely there’s something impressive in and of itself about creating a unique-looking world from the same building blocks everyone else has. The character art, meanwhile, was clean if unremarkable.
“Clean if unremarkable” describes the whole experience pretty well, actually (except for the translation, which is entirely remarkable in how dirty it is). It offers a unique plot and relaxing gameplay, but not much else. I don’t regret playing it, but I won’t be watching for the sequel.

Is this game the best game in existence?  Heck no.  Is it really, really good though?  It is very much so.  System Shock 2 is an action-rpg with an emphasis on the rpg element.  At first, you'll be very weak with nothing but a wrench, maybe two medical hypos, and a acute fear response to every sound that occurs in the game.  However, System Shock 2's greatest strength is it's depth.  There are tons of items, weapons, and psionic abilities for you to choose from.  The rpg element adds greatly to supporting different builds and playstyles.  Numerous audio logs and emails can be found throughout the game allowing you to piece together the story of what happened to the ship and even use the dead's words to progress through the game.  Not to mention, each item has a description you can spend hours reading describing the item or even giving a little corporate humor.  Sure at first the game can be difficult forcing you to save often and carefully plan your moves, but if you play smartly and allocate your upgrade points appropriately, you can literally become an invisible, flaming, inhumanely strong, lightning fast, psionic ninja that can, I kid you not, two hit every single standard enemy in the game with a hunk of crystal.  You see, I made the mistake of picking a psionic character for my first playthrough, cause you know, FREAKING PSIONICS and choosing to play on hard mode.  You can, however, choose the run and gun marine or the sneaky hacking sailor or whatever combination of the three playstyles.  This isn't to say that System Shock 2 is perfect.  Projectile weapons degrade like wet toilet paper (the primary reason why I only used melee weapons which don't degrade), certain items and abilities clearly weren't balanced appropriately (the crystal shard is actually bugged so it does more than double damage with the smasher perk and the regeneration psionic ability basically makes psi hypos far more valuable than medical hypos), the sensual stimulation units later in the game are broken (reeeeal missed opportunity there (by the way if you don't get that that was a joke, please leave now)), and the heavy weapons, besides the fantastic grenade launcher, are useless or underused.  Still, System Shock 2 is an excellent game and I'm honestly suprised I don't see more people playing or discussing it.  Maybe I've just been to the wrong communities or forums or something, but regardless, System Shock 2 is well worth your time.

Everything I wanted a sequel to Dishonored to be. It doesn't change things up too much that it should be a different game, but it expands on the pre-existing story, gameplay, and world enough to make it a great new game.
The elephant in the room I guess is the performance of the game. It even runs bad on the consoles, which is not a good sign for the PC port. My hardware is above average (EVGA GTX 1080 FTW, Intel i7 6800K, 32GB 3200 RAM, on an SSD) and this game had a lot of microstuttering. I have a 1440p/144Hz monitor with G-Sync, so running it at 1440 and getting to 120fps (the highest the game will let you due to issues that may occurr with iffy physics) was actually pretty easy after turning a few setting off of Ultra, but it's the sudden drops down to fps like 40 and 50 that make the performance suck. Here is a list of pro's and con's.
PROS:
+ The game is free
+ You can kill children
+ You can play with friends
+ Zombies ;3
+ Not many characters so you don't spend time who you want to be
+ There's a female character (Although there's only one)
CONS:
- There isn't enough loot around, you can't find any medkits or bandages 90% of the time.
- Guns are bad, they do little damage (Sometimes 3 headshots to kill 1 zombie) and you have to be lucky enough to find bullets (Which you won't)
- Everything you do is very slow, switching weapons, reloading, swinging a melee weapon etc.
- Getting infected is not cool, its annoying and delays the inevitable, pills will only keep you alive for about 7.4 seconds longer.
- If there are multiple people playing, good luck finding a good item.
- Even with 0 ping, melee weapons are very hard to use because you trade hits with zombies most of the time, and you are likely going to get infected.
- You get "tired" very fast, 3 swings with a sledgehammer and you have to wait 10 hours until you can swing it again.
- The melee weapons are better than guns, but still you will miss most of your swings even at point blank range.
- If you shove a zombie back, they can still attack or grab you immediately after.
- When you get surrounded by a horde of zombies you have to spend a LONG time fighting them off if you cannot run, this becomes tedious and boring.
- The voice acting is not good, the characters sound depressed.
- You movement is restricted, (eg - can't jump on top of cars), it's always at "ground level" so it becomes frustrating to move around the map.
- You cannot use a flashlight with a 2 handed weapon, this sucks because most of the maps are very dark and all the rifles are 2 handed and the good melee weapons are also 2 handed.
- There's little replay value because of the repetitiveness of the objectives.
- You can't see your own HP, someone has to tell you the color of your name above your head so you can estimate it.
- You can only carry a limited amount of things due to the weight limit.
- You can't carry 2 of the same thing (eg - can't carry 2 medkits or 2 bandages or 2 pills)
Overall this game is great xd

As a fan of strategy it is only natural that I am a fan of the Total War series, that said I was hesitent to get Rome II at first for reasons that many of us are aware of, at launch it was a buggy nightmare that will cause people to doubt Creative Assembly for quite a while, that and Shogun 2 was excellent enough to not need to move on. Many months later combined with a sale day I was tempted, but first consulted a friend about it. He assured me the game was now very much fixed so I decided to go for it. Put simply I was not dissapointed.
One thing I liked right from the get go was the fact that for the main campaign, known as the Grand Campaign, the map is huge and whether your commanding the Roman war machine or fighting against it you will be there a while and there will be many battles to be had. Most of the series signature features are there, the map, agents that serve various purposes, huge epic battles. That said the family tree is gone sadly, and I do mis it quite a bit as it made me feel even more invested in my game, families still exist but in a somewhat different form that instead plays a part in your chosen culture's internal politics which you are tasked with balancing rather than straight up dominating due to the risk of civil wars that can arise because of the internal factions within your government. Building on this is a system where events will happen and you will have to decide how to deal with them, with the outcome having effect of the political situation within your culture. Mileage will vary on whether or not this a good replacement for the Family Tree but it is a good system nonetheless.
Overall I enjoyed Rome II just like I enjoyed Shogun II, that said many will argue that Shogun II is the smarter buy right now due to be noticably cheaper and I am inclined to agree. That said if you are itching for more total war on an even bigger scale and you spot it on sale go for it, and happy conquering!

Invisible War is a decent game and a great sucessor to Deus Ex. I say that as someone who loves DX (and not Invisible War as much).
I really like all three Deus Ex games. Yet after playing through Human Revolution I don't really appreciate the DX any more than when I started. But, revisiting DX after playing IW really did make me appreciate Deus Ex more, because certain characters, and their motivations, are well fleshed out in IW. And these motivations are closely related to your expereiences from DX.
IW streamlines the DX experience. The original DX had a problem in that the hub worlds were a slog to get through, yet that slog made the exploration more worthwhile. In later stages of DX, the slog was removed but levels were no longer so open, and you weren't as engaged in your exploration.
Invisible War has more clausterphobic levels throughout the course of the game, in part because of all the clunky reloading, but also because the spaces are smaller. Yet, the choices you have, the elements you can interact with, in all levels of IW (save the last, terrible level, which is spatially more open, yet empty as a vacuum), are as dense as the early levels of DX without being a slog.
IW's story is much more focused than DX, because IW really focuses on a single idea (divisive politics). For example, the false struggle between coffee shops subversively highlights a major plot point and theme of the game; the triad war from DX almost serves a similar role, but the fact you clearly side with one "good" side kind of undermines this thematically.

OK, so, yes, as everyone will tell you, this game doesn't live up to the original Deus Ex, a deep creative-powerhouse that managed to not only be a thoroughly enjoyable cyberpunk game (and there are never enough cyberpunk games) but which, for the time, pushed the technology available and crossed the line from being just a fun game to adding to mankind's philosophical body of knowledge about life.  The first Deus Ex was a work on art in every sense.  Now, I'm not saying that Invisible War had nothing to say.  It had numerous useful witicisms and social and political-economic comentary.  But it wasn't quite as refined as Deus Ex the first.  But, honestly, there's a lot in this game to enjoy.  The hacking gameplay is just a blast, as you vicariously mow down enemies with the robot or turret of your choice, though it certainly could have been more.  The graphics is acceptable for the time, if uninspired, and you have a lot of options with how to take your character in terms of both story and gameplay, though you top out way too early, and there's really not much mechanical reason to do everything there is to do other than the fun of doing it.  The character development isn't nearly as involved (or excellent) as the original either.  I mean, you get money, but you won't have much to spend it on.  The game is also pretty short and somewhat lacking in the challenge department, though it does have the admirable quality of awarding intelligent tactics.  This is a good, fun game, just don't expect a great game.  And, if you're a Deus Ex fan, might as well play it...kind of...if you want to.

I really enjoyed this game. The visuals are very faithful to the original movies and there is a tremendous attention to detail with every surface of this immense Sevastapol station that you get to explore. The ambient sounds also add to the immersion and really help with making you feel you are actually there. I am truly impressed! At times I would catch myself enjoying the view from one of the many windows on this ship, staring at space in all its glorious detail.
I played slowly, so it took me about 20 hours to complete the campaign. This is probably the best game in the Alien franchise so far, and it is a must have for any Alien fan out there! I highly recommend it!

I played through the entire campaign with NVIDIA's 3D Vision. I felt like I was actually there the entire time immersed in the entire experience from start to finish. The sounds, atmosphere, and overall feel of the game are really good. Majority of this game is luck. I can be as quiet as I possibly can be and the Alien just comes out of the vent right next to me, I have zero time to react. By the time I right click to use my devices to scare it off, it has already got me. It was fun at first seing all the different ways the Alien could kill me depending on what position I was in and what I was doing, but after a while this game became extremely frustrating and could only advance to my next objective from stupid luck towards the end. This is a great game but it doesn't really matter how loud or stealthy you are. There are a couple glitches where I get stuck here and there and they got me, some scripted gameplay synematics where the Alien was supposed to be present but was invisible. I just laughed.
Is this game worth it? Only on Steam Sale. You will pay a little more than a movie and get way more hours out of it. I got my worth out of it since it was basically a very interactive 3D movie experience for me. I felt the game didn't look all that great playing with 3D Vision off. It also has the classic fuzz quality the Alien/Aliens movies had the entire time but 3D Vision gets rid of it completely.
If you know nothing about 3D Vision the glasses are battery powered and gives you a completely digital more realistic looking, immersive experience. You can set how much depth you want in your games. In practice, 3D Vision is actually 2x 720p because we get two images from different angles, which doubles the resolution. Just looks incredible. FPSs I recommend 15% or less depth. In this game you can have maybe 25% or so comfortably on your eyes.
I played with a GTX 660 non-ti edition with i7-3820, 16GB RAM, Acer GD245HQ 23.6" 3D Vision ready monitor, if you're interested what specs I used for 3D Vision. 1920x1080, Deep Color & V-Sync on, Level of detail: Ultra, Shadow Res 1024, Shadow mapping high. I always turn shadows down in most games. Shadows are usually what kill your FPS.
OMG, the Alien was soo much scarier for me in 3D. When it put its tail through me, I felt like I could actually feel it. I had the most fun finding humans and making noise so the Alien would kill them for me, make it easier to sneak through some parts. So much fun to watch them shoot helplessly at the Alien and it just wipes them all out.
It's a good game but I can't recommend it. I'm a huge Alien fan, and it is well worth playing as a fan. Just too much dumb luck frustration. I give it a 5/10
