I'm gonna completely rewrite this review, because I don't think I gave DkS2 a fair shake last time.  I did finally get around to beating it, and my opinion is a little bit more charitable towards the story, now.  If anything, I think the implications of the lore of this game are way way bleaker than DkS1, which I dig quite a bit.  Like, even after the end of the world, there's nothing you can do and everything you could possibly try has already been done and failed.  That's pretty cool.  Meanwhile, the game is trying to convince you that there's hope, but it's a big middle finger to your intelligence and free will as the "chosen hero".  You're just expected to go along with it and sit on the throne even though it won't help.  You don't even have a choice, not really.  So basically all this is to say that I no longer have gripes with the atmosphere or story.
What I still have gripes about is the gameplay, particularly the PVP and replay value.  Soul Memory was a garbage change, and it's completely destroyed the PVP meta.  Well, combined with the crappier covenants, anyway.  There's really just not much reason to replay the game except to see if I can beat the 1001 "guy in armor" variants of enemies with a different weapon type, and I'm just not that into it.  They also shouldn't have areas where you're basically required to go offline if you want to get through them for the items (bell towers).  The forest was kinda like that in DkS1, but you had a defense in that you can't get invaded if you're Hollow.  No such luck in 2.  The online components of 2 in general are more irritating and bad.  The only only good thing about 2's online stuff is that it's a bit easier to coordinate playing with people you know in co-op.  Not worth the other problems imo.
I still recommend it, if you're into Dark Souls lore and want to see why your choice at the end of DkS1 literally doesn't matter.  The game is still fun once through.

Pros:
- Compelling & emotional story, especially the last chapter. Thankfully the story this time is a lot easier to follow and not as annoyingly ambiguous as it was in the previous game. Sebastian is also a lot more fleshed out and interesting.
- Fluid & fun gameplay. As other reviewers have noted, the game is really simple and easy to get into, while at the same time extremely satisfying.
- Bigger emphasis on exploration. This is a pretty significant step up from the previous Evil Within, which was a very linear experience. Now, there are quite a number of side quests (which are actually pretty interesting for the most part) to do and places to explore, doing either of which will grant you much needed resources and new weapons.
- Surprising amount of weapon variety.
Cons:
- Voice-acting and dialogue are pretty cringeworthy at times. The worst offender is Sebastian himself, who sounds like a mix between Keanu Reeves and Clint Eastwood.
- Other than Sebastian's character model and certain scripted sequences, the game looks noticeably worse than the first Evil Within.
- Framerate issues. This is a big one. Yes, the game is still playable, but the constant stuttering really takes me out of the game. Literally everytime I move my mouse, the game drops like 5-15 frames.
- Tons of glitches. Sometimes I get stuck on nothing, or I climb a tall ladder and some unknown force pushes me off, or I take a look at my collectibles only to not be able to move and having to load my last save. The worst was when I completed the game and it was showing me my stats, it suddenly wouldn't register any keys I was pressing, so I couldn't press E to go to the next screen and save my game, and so I had to reload and play the last 15 minutes again.
- Stealth is extremely basic and there's nothing to really mix it up to make it more challenging.
- Boss fights boil down to 'run away and shoot the crap out of it'. All the time.
- Difficulty is too easy. I played on Survivor, which I assume is the Normal difficulty, and I only died ONCE throughout the entire game, and it happened because of a glitch that made me unable to move while enemies swarmed me.
Verdict:
An excellent game that improves upon the original, delivering a surprisingly stellar and lengthy campaign with satisfying gameplay, BUT is ultimately held back by technical issues. Get on sale.
An actual AAA game that actually ends surprisingly satisfying.

Updating my review to include a few ideas for development...
As far as my review goes, this is an addictive, fast-paced, and entertaining first-person shooter. It reminds me of the original Battlefront games in the sense that, despite playing on the same maps with the same weapons over and over again, each battle is fresh, fun, and unique. The game was built for singleplayer and it shines exactly how it's supposed to. One of the coolest (and by far most unique) aspects of the game is the ability to shift into slow-motion on demand. This is something of a 'Get Out Of Jail Free" card, as it allows you to quite literally kill thirty people with one magazine, as long as your shots are well placed.
Now, my criticisms are more suggestions for development rather than actual criticisms as the game is an Early Access title and we can't demnad ridiculous things from it (though I'm sure the developer and game would happily oblige).
Now, a campaign is on its way, but I'd really like to see a dynamic campaign in the vein of Running With Rifles. One campaign over a massive, open-world map where intense battle is raging on the front lines, troops are plotting assaults while relaxing in their own territory, and tense operations are happening behind enemy lines while soldiers gather intelligence on the enemy. It would also be interesting if we could order the troops immediately around us to do certain things (go there, fight them, protect this, give me ammo/meds, etc.).
I'd like to see deployable cover at some point...the vanilla maps are static and provide many areas for good cover and firing positions, but who wouldn't be happy to have the option to create their own cover and change the flow of a battle?
Destructable environments are a tall order, but I have faith in the developer's passion for this game, as well as their skill in programming (as is evidenced throughout the rest of the game).
A dedicated cover system with automatic crouching, leaning, blind firing, etc. would do a lot to make the game's firefights even more fun than they already are.
Character and weapon customization and leveling would make the game harder to put down and much more engaging to play. The ability to change our armor/clothing, face, weapon colors, mag sizes, optics, and other attachments would simply be cool; everybody loves customization. Levels fall under the same rationale, making the game more rewarding to play. An assortment of perks that can be unlocked at different levels (greater health pool, carrying more ammo, scavenging for ammo, carrying extra grenades, carrying two primary weapons, running faster, etc.) would be fun.
A dedicated stealth system would be good for the campaign and Spec Ops modes, and would also eliminate the issue of enemies locating you at ~500 yards and all opening fire before you can assess the environment and get into cover.
TL;DR This game is spectacular in its current state, but many things can (and probably will) be done to flesh it out and make it the first-person shooter experience we've all wanted for so long.

I bought System Shock 2 a little over a year and a half ago now, when it was on sale for 99 cents (yay Steam). I had heard that it was an incredibly deep RPG, a thinking man's action game, and a classic 90s FPS, and that sounded perfect for me. When I bought it, though, I didn't play for very long. The atmosphere scared me, and I was overwhelmed by all the mechanics. However, a couple weeks back, it had been languishing in my Steam library long enough to finally motivate me to play through the thing. I've just finished it today, and below are my thoughts.
System Shock 2 is a horror game, and the atmosphere is excellent. It's designed to make the player feel vulnerable, unsafe, confused, and exposed at all times, and it does that pretty damn well. However, a lot of this scariness is dependent on the player feeling helpless, and a decent amount of skill at the game more or less undoes that. Once I figured out that I could kill most basic enemies with just the wrench, I was cruising through the game, having plenty of fun and not really being scared at all. Still, the atmosphere's good while it lasts.
System Shock 2 also has infinite enemies and weapon degradation, which are two things that I normally hate in games. However, the game manages them in a way that makes them less frustrating and stupid than they normally are. The infinite enemies are, as previously discussed, mostly killable with just the wrench, and since that doesn't require ammo you have basically infinite resources with which to fight them (the same holds true of the Lego games, which also have non-annoying infinite enemies). Additionally, they drop useful resources when killed, so you can just farm zombies and cyborg midwives for money, ammo and health indefinitely. This also helps counteract the weapon degradation, which only affects the non-melee weapons and can be repaired with items that one can buy with the infinite money. Both of these features also add to the helpless atmosphere, as the player's weapons aren't dependable and nowhere is safe. System Shock 2 has some features that would seem to be terrible, but it manages them expertly by connecting them to other systems to create a wonderfully realized experience.
(It still doesn't make sense how the infinite enemies get to where they are, though.)
There's no shortage of those other systems, by the way. System Shock 2's proponents aren't kidding about its complexity. You have health, psi energy, weapons (each with a degradation level, upgrade level, different ammo types, and different firing modes), a limited inventory, implants granting different buffs, armor, general skills, tech skills, tech skill-boosting software, weapon skills, psi powers, research requiring different chemicals, and probably a few more that I'm forgetting. It's a lot to wrap your head around at first, but after a while it all becomes second nature to manipulate, and you feel smart for figuring out how to manage your character efficiently.
The writing is similarly deep and complex. The story is decent and mostly related through audio logs and emails, but the fun writing is all in the descriptions of the different items and objects that you can collect. A fascinating amount of effort went into building the world, and it adds greatly to immersion.
System Shock 2 is, of course, an FPSRPG, like Deus Ex a year later. It doesn't allow for as many diverse playstyles as Deus Ex does, though. You're pretty much going to always be a competent hacker who knows his way around firearms, and the only real choice is whether you'll go into Psi powers or not (if not, the game will still throw tons of cyber modules for upgrades at you, even if you stop having any use of them fairly quickly).
Actually, around the middle of the game resources become pretty plentiful. You can get by with almost nothing but the wrench for the first three levels, and ammo, money, and health just pile up in that time. The ammo does get used a lot more often starting around the fourth level, when the cyborg assassins are introduced, but I still ended the game with about 3500 nanites (the game's currency), over 100 cyber modules (the game's upgrade points), and more health items than I could possibly use. Maybe I'm just really good (doubtful), but it seems like the survival aspect got kinda forgotten partway though.
Those first three levels are the best ones, by the way. The game takes a noticeable dip in quality after that, and although it's still good, it's not as fun as before. The last few levels also seem to think that a climactic shift in difficulty can be expressed by just taking your map away, which is dumb.
You don't see a lot of games like System Shock 2 any more. There's a lot of understanding of complex mechanics, unguided exploration, and
expected of the player. There's no forgiveness for character-construction mistakes, and the player is expected to make some decisions and work some things out with no help whatsoever. You enter System Shock 2 on System Shock 2's terms,
, and if you don't like it you can f*ck right off . It's kinda refreshing in a weird way, and whenever you make progress you feel like you've really achieved something. If that sounds great to you, then I wholeheartedly recommend System Shock 2. I know I liked it.

I really enjoyed this game. The visuals are very faithful to the original movies and there is a tremendous attention to detail with every surface of this immense Sevastapol station that you get to explore. The ambient sounds also add to the immersion and really help with making you feel you are actually there. I am truly impressed! At times I would catch myself enjoying the view from one of the many windows on this ship, staring at space in all its glorious detail.
I played slowly, so it took me about 20 hours to complete the campaign. This is probably the best game in the Alien franchise so far, and it is a must have for any Alien fan out there! I highly recommend it!

I played through the entire campaign with NVIDIA's 3D Vision. I felt like I was actually there the entire time immersed in the entire experience from start to finish. The sounds, atmosphere, and overall feel of the game are really good. Majority of this game is luck. I can be as quiet as I possibly can be and the Alien just comes out of the vent right next to me, I have zero time to react. By the time I right click to use my devices to scare it off, it has already got me. It was fun at first seing all the different ways the Alien could kill me depending on what position I was in and what I was doing, but after a while this game became extremely frustrating and could only advance to my next objective from stupid luck towards the end. This is a great game but it doesn't really matter how loud or stealthy you are. There are a couple glitches where I get stuck here and there and they got me, some scripted gameplay synematics where the Alien was supposed to be present but was invisible. I just laughed.
Is this game worth it? Only on Steam Sale. You will pay a little more than a movie and get way more hours out of it. I got my worth out of it since it was basically a very interactive 3D movie experience for me. I felt the game didn't look all that great playing with 3D Vision off. It also has the classic fuzz quality the Alien/Aliens movies had the entire time but 3D Vision gets rid of it completely.
If you know nothing about 3D Vision the glasses are battery powered and gives you a completely digital more realistic looking, immersive experience. You can set how much depth you want in your games. In practice, 3D Vision is actually 2x 720p because we get two images from different angles, which doubles the resolution. Just looks incredible. FPSs I recommend 15% or less depth. In this game you can have maybe 25% or so comfortably on your eyes.
I played with a GTX 660 non-ti edition with i7-3820, 16GB RAM, Acer GD245HQ 23.6" 3D Vision ready monitor, if you're interested what specs I used for 3D Vision. 1920x1080, Deep Color & V-Sync on, Level of detail: Ultra, Shadow Res 1024, Shadow mapping high. I always turn shadows down in most games. Shadows are usually what kill your FPS.
OMG, the Alien was soo much scarier for me in 3D. When it put its tail through me, I felt like I could actually feel it. I had the most fun finding humans and making noise so the Alien would kill them for me, make it easier to sneak through some parts. So much fun to watch them shoot helplessly at the Alien and it just wipes them all out.
It's a good game but I can't recommend it. I'm a huge Alien fan, and it is well worth playing as a fan. Just too much dumb luck frustration. I give it a 5/10

The game is very overrated, imo. At some point it's well done, but that's about it.
During first couple hours I was impressed and really enjoying it, yet the further it was going the more 'wtf' it was becoming.
---spoilers---
Storyline: it came out incredibly cheesy, although it was supposed to make you think that it's sort of deep yet in fact it's just a typical 'soap opera' shallow full of clichés 'sad story'. Some of the characters  and their roles in the game just don't make sense. First it was about the Photographer, then when you go further you realize he has nothing to do with the main story, it jumps from this to that constantly, the concept of the game didn't seem smooth at all.
The only thing that was constant - was goddamn zombies. I was playing the game for about 33 hours total, out of those for 32 hours I was farming zombies (cuz that's the only way to actually go further in the game), then the rest of the time I was fighting big and semi-bosses. Now sorry, but that's boring af. Of course it made the game last 3 times longer than if it wasn't 90% about killing zombies, but come on. Oh, and through the game zombies evolve: first 1/3 of the game you kill regular zombies, then zombies that burn, and then the freezing stone zombies. Wow! Now that's an evolution. The thing is - when you get those repeatitive things in games like Far Cry - it still doesn't get you tired somehow, here - it's just a massive turn off. Especially considering that the game isn't made in a 'realism' genre, so basically the story and everything else could take any kind of major crazy twist (as long as it actually works with the main concept), but creators decided to stay in the same plain line for the whole game.
As for the game challenges besides finding out how to kill zombies in a most efficient way (as after one week of doing just that it gets you pretty bored) - EW2 has zero complications and none of your brain cells will need to be making efforts. You get a door made of fire on your way so you can't go through? - just make one shot into the lever that is right above it - problem solved! Now that's challenging!
The pros of the game would be visuals, a few intresting characters (the laughing chainsaw lady, the green acid guy [I felt a strong urge to hug and comfort him the whole time], the flamethrower dude) and the creepy atmosphere.
I also understand why so many people post positive reviews and find the game entertaining.
Now to sum it up:
If you are bored and need to kill your time with something that isn't too bad and keeps you busy and somewhat emotional - go for it.
If you are demanding, if you appreciate an intelligent story and quality not 'quantity' of your game - there are much better ones.

Dishonored 2 is the long awaited sequel to the award wining game named (you guessed it) Dishonored. I loved and still love the original Dishonored. It is a great game with a compelling story, great mechanics and well designed levels. The world had a consistant feeling of being sinister, dark, but somehow comforting.
This game has none of that. The story is "go here do that then kill your sister", a completely new engine that does the same thing the old one did but runs at a square root of the speed, responds slower, and feels worse in general. The levels have little to no cover for you to hide behind, leading to you just blinking across the rooftops and missing all of the actual level, and it makes you feel like you just wanna be done already.
The gameplay itself is alright. Like I said, it's not really fun, but it's not bad either. The engine is slow and unresponsive, so it will take way too long for you to actually do the thing you pressed the button to do, and there isn't much cover, like I said before. Really not that great. And the one puzzle in the game gives you few clues on how to complete it and does a bad job of explaining what it is you are supposed to do in the first place.
The graphics are really good if you have three Titan Xs running in SLI. If you don't have that, then the game will either run at five frames per second, or with worse graphics than the first game. There isn't even a middleground. Even with medium settings the frames drop to about 20. I am using an EVGA GTX 1060 for reference.
The "story" is a bunch of incoherant tasks you have to complete because the boat you randomly got on because it existed had two very important people who know everyone you need to kill to get to Delila. Everyone you kill is just a guy who has something to do with Delila and you kill them because this one armed lady knows they exist, but you don't even know who they are anyways. There are three targets that are actual characters: Jindosh, the guy with the super cool clockwork mansion that isn't actually that cool in the game. He is your average overconfident genious who is super witty with his dialogue and speaks to you through his speakers in his evil lair and knows everything you do all the time, and then you get to his evil lair room and he's like "oh no i didnt expect you to make it this far wut do i do now?" and has his machines fight you. Then theirs the Duke, I can't even remeber his name. You see him once at the beginning of the game and never again until you kill him. His character is comprised of him being alcoholic, liking orgies, and saying "funny" and "quirky" things that really don't add anything to the story at all. And finally Delila. She's just like any other evil witch ever. She doesn't have any character other than "I am bad and magical".

When Corvo and I took to the streets of Dunwall in Dishonored 1, I would read the in-game books describing Tyvia, Morley, Serkonos, and Gristol and marvel at this excellent world of lore that Arkane has created. There was so much I wanted to see, and I could only dream about visiting a city like Karnaca.
For lovers of lore and world-buildling like I am, Dishonored 2 is extraordinary. Before, Dishonored meant Dunwall, but the addition of Karnaca in Dishonored 2 has transformed the Isles into a genuine
, and frankly, it's immensely exciting.
Karnaca is just as amazing as Dunwall. The colorful, decaying buildings and monolithic trees are a beautiful counterpoint to Dunwall's ashen, once-regal boulevards, towering whale oil refineries, and hagfish murals. Instead of hearing the deep horns of whaling ships on the Wrenhaven River, you'll listen to the insects and wildlife populating Serkonos. And taking the place of the Clocktower of Dunwall are wind tubes soaring over the city.
Every mission is just as good as or better than those of Dishonored 1. The impeccable level design we've come to expect from Arkane is here, and the environments of each mission are stunningly beautiful. Aside from virtual tourism, each mission offers intriguing enemies, a variety of choices that will impact the world, and sidequests.
Dishonored 2's combat is better than ever. I played Corvo Attano without powers on hard and ended up spending most of my time in lethal assault combat. If I had wanted to ghost the entire game, however, I'm fully convinced that I could have done so without powers and on hard. Combat was always intense; enemies were skilled at parrying and working together to surround or corner me, and even encounters with bloodflies and wolfhounds were exhilarating.
Dishonored 2 rivals Dishonored 1 in lore. The books scattered across Karnaca are well-written and interesting, and the voice acting in audiologs and NPC conversations is quality work and does establish believability. In addition, the voice actors behind Corvo and Emily are excellent, and their voices fit their characters.
The eerie music-- signature to the Dishonored series-- is here, and to be honest, there's nothing like it. It's still subtle and does take a backseat to the environmental storytelling, but I loved every bit of it.
The plot is an acceptable continuation of Delilah's quest for power. It's another tale of revenge, of course, and it works well in this sequel. However, it is easier to relate to Hiram Burrows, Pendleton, Havelock and Martin in Dishonored 1 than it is to Meagan Foster, Aramis Stilton, and Kirin Jindosh in this iteration, as Dishonored 2's characters are rather one-dimensional.
Arkane's Void Engine looks beautiful, but its performance has not met my expectations. My GTX 970 struggled with the game's object-dense locations (The Royal Conservatory and Kirin Jindosh's laboratory especially) despite running a medley of high and medium settings and having most of the bells and whistles turned off.
I love Dishonored 2. It's not perfect, but it's every bit as amazing as Dishonored 1, and I cannot wait to go back and play with powers. This world that Arkane has created is absolutely incredible, and I hope that the studio fleshes the Isles out even more with a journey to Tyvia or Morley in Dishonored 3. Wherever they decide to go, I'm on board.

Now hold on here. Hold your horses. This game is not as bad as people say. Not by a long shot.
Sure it is nothing like Human Revolution, and sure it was a bit of a departure from the original title. Sure it was made for the xBox and suffered from some small environments, but this was a
, one of the few games I have ever honest-to-god completed (something which, honest to god, doesn't apply to the original, which was just a little too outdated when I came back to it to try and win through where I had lost interest back in the early 00s)
Put in some hours and you might experience some nice surprises! The graphics might improve dramatically as you venture deeper into the experience, the level design too! The alternate routes that are so famous in the series are right there, waiting for you to exploit them, and the combat is satisfying.
A bit of intrigue does exist, and the controls work well. The story is a lot longer than you expect it to be, and the levels really well made.
Honestly, this is a really fun game, even if it is a little previous-previous-gen. Frankly at certain times the graphics are so well handled that you could be forgiven for mistakenly thinking you were playing a much more recent game.
It is a real shame that this game got such a bad wrap. It was never the same as the original in so many ways, but in a lot of unexpected ways it was a little bit better, and it was a really wonderful taster of the potential of the series in a next-gen world, a taster for a the utter banquet that would be Deus Ex: Human Revolution, my favourite game of all time.

Well I didn't end up playing the game for long before I uninstalled it and jumped onto the IW-hate bandwagon. I barely left the academy (first level) before I decided to not play this game again. As subjective as my opinion is, I cannot see any way of recommending people to put money into it; and I would be reluctant to even say 'go for it' if it was a free game out of fear I will create personal vendettas against me by wasting time.
From the intro alone it has no Deus Ex feeling at all in my opinion; it looks less like a dystopian cyberpunk and more like a bad sci-fi that has none of the charm of the original Deus Ex, if you're pondering on trying the game because it has the name in the title, I recommend looking up the intro on youtube and ask yourself if it's still what you're hoping for.
The second thing I noticed was how utterly difficult it was for me to even get the game to run at all because of the outdated engine that is damn near incompatiable with anything that has multi-cores (which is to say every modern computer) that made it a pain requiring me to down a few hours in searching for a fix online in various forums; which is already a major nono for anything that gets put on steam, if it's on a platform like Steam asking for money to play it, it should at the very least work by default.
If anyone is interested, I'll leave the link that finally made the game run for everyone's convenience:
With the game finally running and having recently finished the original Deus Ex (Revision), I was eager to try the game for myself and see the continuation of the previous game and what effects the events of it would have on the world of the sequel. I knew it was widely hated, but somehow the arguments never quite ran. Small levels and clunky UI sounded like something you could overcome if you were interested in the story, and I really wanted to explore Chicago and Seattle of the future.
So the first thing I do is to set the keymapping to be more akin to the original Deus Ex's controls as much as possible for my own comfort and fixing the mouse sensitivity to be lower. Then I start the game.
First I get that intro cutscene and realize that exploring Chicago is not really on the agenda here. Maybe I should've read into it more, but I guess it just gets destroyed in the cutscene and welcome to Seattle. Okay, fair enough I think.
Then there is Seattle where I try to immerse myself and get comfortable with the controls before I get earthquakes shoved in my face; no time to rest there. When I get into my first conversation I experience a rarity for me: graphics cringe. I'm not one to typically care about graphics; I like the old styles such as the original ones over things like Crysis even, but ♥♥♥♥ me they couldn't have made a poorer job with these. This is without mentioning how lackluster and horribly paced the conversations are.
Go to a let's play and check just the first conversation with Billie to determine it for yourself. If it becomes unbearable, save your money to something more productive. Maybe there's a hobo nearby who could use a cup of coffee for the dollar or whatever that Steam wants for the game.
Anyway the next thing I notice is that the criticisms of small levels well, the fans were not exaggerating; imagine UNATCO HQ in the original game from the moment you step into the upper level where Manderley and your office etc is. Know how there is a lower level too? In IW, that lower level would be behind a loading screen; and the upper level doesn't contain the eye scanner or anything of the sort either. That should give an idea of how small the maps are, and I'm even unsure if that's an exaggeration.
What kills it for me though is how a game riddled more loading screens than♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in an elephant's♥♥♥♥♥seem to have an unhealthy obsession with resetting everything upon a new loading screen; it's like the game restarts itself before the loading screen itself appears, and when it's done loading all the key mappings are reset and all the items- including weapons -are gone. This world of item-vaporizing elevators/doorways becomes especially bothersome if you wanna cap some heads, because good luck getting anything done in terms of combat if you don't have any weapons on you; and weapons aren't in a habit of just laying around everywhere either.
At the final bit of the Seattle Tarsus Academy I just gave up and casually ran past everyone in full view, not even caring about getting shot twice or thrice (which took less than half my hp) and just kept going to see if I could at least get value out of seeing Upper Seattle. Some story blocks along the way I didn't care about later and I realized.. Pretty much no.
The environment is stale and uninspired and conversations don't get anymore interesting from the three or so places in the level that had people. You get more character interaction and personality from a Choice of Games than what I got in Upper Seattle. And that's where I finally lost my last interest and justification for having spent any money on this even at a sale. The only thing I got from that money spent is buyer's remorse; but hey, at least the buyer's remorse is consistent unlike the ♥♥♥♥ing keymapping in IW.

If you're looking for a game that is superior in it's way of storytelling (like Half-Life 1) by having no cutscenes but a movie-like experience where you're seeing the movie through the lead actor's eyes, this one is your game.
It combines sci-fi, action, aliens, government conspiracies, mythic stuff, zombies and way more. Of course, the last 20-40% of the game (depending on how large the devs are gonna be building Xen) is missing but even without Xen it's worth the money if you like the above mentioned.
Winter 2016 the devs said for the first time that they hope to be releasing Xen in Summer/Fall of 2017. If Xen is there and they keep the overall quality as high as they did so far, buying this game is 100% a no-brainer.

Most of the voice acting is very good, and results in a convincing sense of urgency and panic. I heard in a different review for this game that a part of the voice acting that makes it so good and adds to the atmosphere is that the characters don't sound dramatic, they only wish to be heard in a hopes that someone will recieve the message. Other parts of the sound design hold up very well. (some of it even sounds still today very disturbing.) Before I go any further, I must mention the writing is also superb. The hybrids sound scary and tortured, begging you the protagonist to put them out of their misery. The humans sound scared and panicked adding more to the loneliness of the atmosphere. And the cyborg midwifes are beyond terrifying, their humanity washed away by mechanical brainwash, and their monotone voices muttering the most unrealistic yet perfectly written dialogue that makes you almost want to avoid them entirely. (This is my personal experience, tell me how you reacted to them when you get to deck three.) I'm not mentioning anything about the rpg mechanics just because I feel like the game is worth playing just for the atmosphere, I am stunned how well this game still terrifies after eighteen years. Play it, it is definitely worth it. This system shock games are terrific, and I feel they should get moer recognition compared to the bioshock games. (While great games as well, I do not feel they hold up nearly as well if you think on a broader spectrum.) Enjoy the game, it is amazing even to this day.

This is one of the most fun games i've ever played. It can also be scary as hell sometimes. And having played through Silent Hill 2, that's saying a lot. But seriously, this game is a masterpiece.
First off, the gameplay is similar to FPSRPGs such as Fallout, though it is much more linear and closed, although, depending on how well you scour certain areas, there can be a lot of backtracking. The best part of this game, however, is the writing. It features one of the coolest villans, and villan related plot-twists that i've ever seen, and it's definately worth playing to the end.
I would go into a 10 hour long summary of the plot of this game, but I don't want to spoil anything, because this is an experience that should never be spoilt. So, if you want to ruin the experience for youself, go ahead and read about it online. If I were you, however, I would open my wallet and pour it's contents into the hands of Ken Levine. He deserves it.
However... this game came out in 1999. And it has not aged too well since then. As far as glitches go, singleplayer is pretty clean, and I haven't really come across any bugs at all. But multiplayer is a whole different story.
The Co-op of this game, despite being incredibly fun, is the buggiest thing i've ever seen. The game-breaking flaws in the Co-op mode are more easily found and exploited than those found in Sonic 06. Just for a few examples:
My friend tried to give me a surgical activation unit, but it dropped onto the floor instead of going into my inventory, and when it dropped, it became a bulkhead switch, a game entity that is never supposed to be an item in the first place, and definately not supposed to be droppable.
Later on this same playthough, when trying to access another deck, my friend hit the elevator button, and appearently, there was a table in the elevator that I could not see. and certainly wasn't supposed to be there.
But this is just the beginning.
There are some even more game-breaking glitches that i experienced.
Every time a non-host tried to access a bulkhead, it would freeze on the "synchronizing" loading screen, forcing me do alt+tab out of the game. this would kill any unsaved progress, which sometimes, in early parts of the game, basically made it neccessary to start over from the very beginning. he were also severaly glitches where enenmies would stop spawning, or only be visible for one player, or would just not move, and they had nothing to do with internet connection.
Basically, the singleplayer and multiplayer of this game are two, totally different experiences. In singleplayer, this game is a solid, solemn-as-hell space horror shooter RPG, and has some of the best writing and general storylines of any game of it's genre. But the multiplayer is perfect for laughing your♥♥♥♥♥off at some of the hilarious and game-breaking glitches this game has to offer.
All sarcasm and humor aside, however, this game is a true masterpiece, at least in singleplayer, and it is still very enjoyable in multiplayer. I love this game, and it sits comfortably on my list top ten favorite games, without fear of falling off.

I got this game on sale for 23 dollars and I gotta say, it was worth every penny. While I'm happy it was such a bargain, I even feel kind of bad that I payed so little for it now, that's how good it was, lol.
The game cribs notes from a lot of other games. At times it's Splinter Cell, at times it's Resident Evil 4/5, at times it's Silent Hills and other times it reminded me of The Last of Us or State of Decay. But it gets away with it because it's a great game and genuine fun to play. Borrowing from all of those different games (as well as bringing in some neat ideas of it's own) also means that there's a fair bit of variety in what you're doing. Trying to avoid the spotlight kill gaze of Stefano's giant camera monster is a different experience than taking out a small group of The Lost (the game's smarter than zombies, zombies), which is a different experience than hiding from Anima (a scary, unkillable ghost lady who *will* kill you if she sees you).
The only real negative point I have about the game is that it's at it's strongest when you're exploring the large, open world areas and towards the end of the game they pare these away. To be fair, at this point they're barreling you towards the conclusion and you do get some cool encounters by way of compensation, but if you liked the freedom you had before you might find the later 25% or so of the game too restrictive. But that's also really me reaching hard to find a point of detraction.
In short this game was excellent and if an action-stealth-semi-open-world-survival-horror game seems like something that would appeal to you then by all means, pick it up. Even if you want to wait for a sale like I did, I'd urge you to buy this at some point and support the creation of BS-free, high quality, Triple A developed single player games. You actually unlock new outfits for Sebastian by beating the game. How cool is that considering how many others would have just made those outfits DLC? There's a demo out now so there's nothing stopping you from trying the game out.
There's a few other notes I'd like to add. If you're not the patient sort you can stop here, you know enough, but if you are the patient sort then nice to meet you, bear with me a bit here. The sound design in this game is excellent. The sound when you hit a monstrosity with a handaxe is uniquely satisfying (and not just because you're saving ammo) and everything about your run ins with Anima (the aforementioned ghost lady who would be scary enough given her propensity to show up when you haven't saved in a while) is amplified by the sound design of those encounters. From the creepy dissonant music to the way she creepily hums Clare de Lune to the creepy static hum that plays when she's about to walk through a door or wall. Did I mention she was creepy? This is to say nothing of the music, which alternates between creepy, jarring, action packed, epic, driven, classy, hopeful and even tear jerkingly sad when the situation calls for it. They use it to good effect to add atmosphere to boss battles and a lot of the characters have their own "themes". (Tchaikovsky's Serenade for Strings Op 48 will forever belong to pretentious artist and serial killer Stefano Vallentini after you've played this game, lol)
The story of the game was also excellent and it's the thing that's stuck with me the most after playing the game. It's good enough that I'd like to see it adapted into a movie or television show so that people who don't normally play video games could enjoy it, buuut given the track record for adaptations they'ed probably screw something up. Lol.
To put it succinctly, there's a system called STEM that's essentially a bunch of computers interfacing with a living person's brain at it's core. This creates a dream world that other people can enter and interact with but also allows the memories of those within it to be modified. STEM is controlled by MOBIUS, a secretive organization that hopes to use the tech to control the world, but before they can do that they have to reach a critical mass of system storage (around 20,000 live people hooked up to the system). Unknown to MOBIUS, they've placed a secret serial killer and high functioning psychopath into the system, and he has transformed STEM into a nightmare that they've lost control over. Unwilling to abandon the progress they've made towards their goal they send in their own security. When that fails they Shanghai Detective Sebastian Castellanos (an unwilling participant and survivor of a previous STEM experiment) to help them. Why would Sebastian help them? Because this system's core is Lilly, his daughter who they kidnapped years ago and who's death they faked in the hopes of utilizing her promising potential as a core candidate. Armed with the promise that he can save and have his daughter back (a promise he never fully believes, mind you) Sebastian delves into STEM and the game begins.
At this point you might be thinking: "Great another father/daughter story" but it's really carried by what a likable guy Sebastian is. His first instinct when he sees people in danger is to want to save them, he overcomes his personal demons, actually forgives some of the MOBIUS members who had a hand in wronging him in the past, doesn't make a lot of stupid mistakes, doesn't take♥♥♥♥♥♥from the antagonists of the game and has a lot of funny quips that show a really amusing amount of self awareness from the developers. There was one part in a church where I approached a Priest who had transformed into one of The Lost when 3 more Lost burst into the church through the windows, drawn in by all of his screaming. Of course I could have fought them all. Surrounded, outnumbered, in a crampt church. But I chose to run the hell outside instead. Where upon Sebastian shouted "♥♥♥♥ THAT." I laughed. More so because he said what I was thinking when I ran outside. So yeah, you come to like the guy and you want him to succeed after all of his suffering.
Some tips I'd give if you play the game:
Explore. If you explore every corner of the map you will be a lot better off than people who don't. You'll find more ammo, you'll find more weapon parts, those parts will parlay into stronger weapons, which will mean less ammo wasted on each encounter, which will parley into more spare ammunition. You'll also kill more enemies, which means more green gel, which means stronger skills, which means you'll have an easier time killing enemies. Both of these things combined mean that when you DO run into boss monster encounters you will be able to take them down instead of just running away. Which means even more green gel.
Stealth will save you so much ammo. If you don't have the patience to stealth kill every enemy at least try to open an encounter by taking out the low hanging fruit. Get the corner kill skill as soon as you can. It will turn so many traps around to your favor if you can quickly dart behind a corner and grab the first schmuck that runs around it.
Use your ears and don't be afraid to run away. You can often hear enemies that are hiding in bushes or rafters before you see them and those bushes also make OP places for you to ditch enemies.
You can upgrade whatever weapons you want but in general I found the best weapons to be the pistol and long barreled shotgun. Most of the Crossbow bolts also do special things when fully upgraded that are worth serious consideration. The assualt rifle is kind of poop. Even with bullet cascade.
You can backtrack to the start of the game at any point before chapter 8. Before you enter the theatre make good and sure you've collected all the locker keys and collectibles you care to because there's no going back after that.
You can actually kill the Obscura in your second encounter with it, provided you have the firepower on hand.
If you want to reduce the number of encounters you have with Anima, don't enter the house at 336 Cedar Avenue in Ch3 until chapter 7.

If you know nothing about 3D Vision the glasses are battery powered and gives you a completely digital more realistic looking, immersive experience. You can set how much depth you want in your games. In practice, 3D Vision is actually 2x 720p because we get two images from different angles, which doubles the resolution. Just looks incredible. FPSs I recommend 15% or less depth. In this game you can have maybe 25% or so comfortably on your eyes.
I played with a GTX 660 non-ti edition with i7-3820, 16GB RAM, Acer GD245HQ 23.6" 3D Vision ready monitor, if you're interested what specs I used for 3D Vision. 1920x1080, Deep Color & V-Sync on, Level of detail: Ultra, Shadow Res 1024, Shadow mapping high. To get this out of the way, yes I do reccomend this game to Alien franchise enthusiast's.  The game has amazing pace and immersion.  To expedite my points I'll just make a good/bad list:
Good:
- Great immersion
- Music from the first Alien movie makes its way back
- Fantastic graphics
-  Really good voice acting
Bad:
- Same tired cliche's of opening doors, activating switches, turning power back on etc etc....
- The save system is draconic.  There is no autosave as many have already said.  That being said, you will be saving ALOT and often.
- Bad lip syncing for actors while not in pre rendered cut scenes.
- Bad xenomorph AI.  It shows up when the script tells it to for the major events in the game simply to block your path.
- Several times I had to backtrack because the game makes a certain door malfunction forcing me to go back and restart something.  This happens regularly.
As of this review, I am still playing Alien isolation and still having fun.  The arcane save feature needs to go though.  There needs to be an autosave after each task is complete.  I have died soooo many times from the alien and lost like 15 minutes of progress because there weren't any save spots around.   If the dev's decide to keep it for the sequel, the save feature needs to not disrupt the gameplay.  It cuts out the audio when it asks you to confirm your save and this breaks immersion.
The alien is another thing entirely.  Sometimes it'll show up in purely scripted sequences and others, it will ignore armed human's just walking around next to you.  It completely baffles me how the dev's could forget the aliens AI in certain levels.
The dev's claim the alien learns from your mistakes.  This is true.  If you hide in a locker too many times it will eventually figure this out and open it up...go figure.  Ripley can only hold her breath for about 5 seconds before passing out (utterly ridiculous) so make sure you craft plenty of medipacks.
In the end, I only paid 12 bucks for Alien Isolation so I don't feel robbed.  Had I paid full ♥♥♥♥ing price ($50) then no, this is NOT worth a buy.  However, if you gnab it at 75% off then definatly pick it up as you will have a semi- fun 20 hour campaign.  I say semi fun because you will die...ALOT, and lose progress many times.  So save often.

Borderlands 2 does everything that was good in the first game better, and it also knows how to tell a joke.  While the previous installment in this series was slow and had not yet found its voice, BL2 really locked in a solid pacing and a solid narrative style.  Unlike the first game, the story felt important and prominent within the game.  It's clear what are main story quests and what are optional side quests, and excellent voice acting really conveys the story better than the hundreds of quest start/end textboxes from the first.  This helps convey the funny and dark story of BL2 in a way that the first game was only starting to get a hang of in its DLCs.  Don't get me wrong, the first game was funny, but even after +500 hours in BL2 (360 & PC), I still laugh at some of the jokes.
Character progression feels very rewarding between the Badass Ranks and interesting skill trees.  With a big "game changer" skill at the end of any skill tree, there's always something to strive for or respec to.  Most of the skills feel interesting, and the rest are usually just practical to have.  Similarly, the loot game is easily one of the main draws for this game with... idk, 9999999 bazillion guns or whatever the trailer said.  Most of that count comes in from the common to rare weapons, but the true wonder and fun comes in with the Legendary rarity and higher loot.  This stuff isn't just top-tier, it also does awesome♥♥♥♥♥♥  I'd try to explain what I mean, but I'd probably just sound silly telling you about a gun that, when you reload it, your character throws it and it'll slowly fly to the nearest enemy whilst continuing to shoot at that enemy.  I did say "and higher" when describing the best loot, because there's even stuff beyond Legendary.  But those ones aren't just normal loot you find from any suitable loot source.  No, those are rewards for running raids.
Now, coming from an FPS background, I don't know much about raids.  I know they're supposed to be cool, have a big boss, and I know they're supposed to be endgame.  Anything past that I can't talk about, but I can say BL2 has those three things for its raids.  These big baddies are best battled with buddies, because obviously.  Unlike the disappointing final boss of the first game, and the basically unkillable without cheating raid boss from one of its DLCs, these guys are satisfying.  An excellent mix of actually being able to take damage and being able to murder even the most solid of tanks in a few seconds makes the battles feasible, yet challenging.  And if/when you manage to take down one of these raid bosses?  Expect to dig through loot for a few minutes at least.
Similar to the improvements to the main bosses, smaller bosses throughout the game are also much more satisfying.  Part of this comes from the voice shift between the first and second game, and now would be a good time to explain that better.  The first game, while being set on an alien planet filled with giant, four-mandible dogs and death worms, felt like it was trying to be too real and dark.  The vast majority of the enemies, and likewise the bosses, were generic bandit characters with a sliver of individual character infused either through the gun they were using, and/or five seconds of dialog.  And those were the main story quest bosses.  In BL2, even the most mundane of side quest bosses actually feel like they have a place in the world and narrative.  Likewise, we're not in a gritty space western anymore.  Sure there's notes of that, but the story is more about gaining hope, overcoming giant monsters, and building a life for people in the face of a corporate entity hell bent on you not doing any of those things.  The alien elements feel more alien and the main downer emotions come from good storytelling, not from shades of brown and warring bandits.
Of course, all is not well on Pandora.  Sometimes quests are turned in unexpectedly, or parts of them are unclear or hard to do for trivial reasons.  While the majority of skills are good, some don't feel like they do enough to be worth taking.  Similarly, some of the "game changer" skills don't feel game changing enough to earn the title.

Warning: The review below is biased with nostoglia
I remember watching a review of Total Annihiliation from one of those 90's "tech" shows on cable in my early teens.  I recall being immediately blown away by how fluid and realistic the action was.  I remember the presenter showed an ingame clip of the action depicting a dozen of infantry bots marching haphazardly through a plain with some trees scattered about.  Meanwhile ovehead, three fighters intercepts an incoming enemy bomber.  The fighters fired a salvo of missiles, and barrel rolls away from the explosion of a downed bomber.  EPIC.
I brought this game more than 20 years ago.  I've recreated that scene on numerous occasions and then some.  I felt the combination of variety in unit behavior, weapon physic, and the rock/paper/scissor approach to balancing was the epitomy of what real time strategy games are.  Twenty years later, I believe this is still the core defintion that only one other RTS IP was able to achieve, and that's Homeworld.
There's Supreme Commander and Planetary Annihiliation, but those are essentially spiritual successors.  Even then, it's still missing something that makes Total Annihilation unique.
Plus you have these things
Carpet bombing
Aircraft carriers
A wall of artillaries shooting
Flak guns
EPIC SOUNDTRACK
I would buy this again many times over if steam goes away.

There are very few examples of a sequel in any medium being better than the original in the series. This is no exception to that.
Now that I've gotten that out of the way, I'm going to do something a little different than what other reviewers do and repeat what I did with the Duke Nukem Forever review. Instead of pointing out the postivies and negatives, I'm going to say that my opinion is more valid than yours and that most of the negatives I see are either non existent or actually positives.
1. The combat is clunky.
I don't understand this complaint. I played it on the XBox and it was terrible on that system, yeah. But on the PC? It really isn't that terrible and it's more than managable. I think maybe the reason for this is people were playing this like they played the original Deus Ex. In the first game when you first started you sucked with every single ranged weapon ever and had to aim your gun for like 30 minutes before you could actually hit somebody. What I assume is happening is people are doing that in this game, and you really don't need to do that because you actually know how to use a firearm. I'd actually go as far as saying that makes the combat in this game better than in the first game. For some reason, in Deus Ex a highly trained cybernetic special forces operative has no idea how to use a basic handgun.
2. It was dumbed down for consoles.
Well, yes and no. First off, the original Deus Ex engine was basically a bunch of PVC pipes and calculators glued together. It was very simple and didn't eat up a lot of hardware so you could put a crapload of♥♥♥♥♥♥in the game and not worry about running out of space on the install disk along with not worrying about overworking the system memory. This game uses a (for the time) modern next gen engine with (for the time) amazing graphics and effects and stuff, not to mention a (for the time) decent physics engine as well. The short length and small size of levels allowed this to be put on XBox, yeah, but it also made it so we wouldn't have to use like 20 discs on PC. Sure, it would have been cool for the game to be the size of the original and use 20 discs, but come on.
3. The story is dumb.
I agree to some extent. The game is short, and since it's a Deus Ex game there's a plot twist like every 10 minutes so I can't really say much without spoiling like 35% of the story. Basically, at one point in the game you get two huge plot twists at the same exact time, and both of them got completely different reactions from me. The first one I saw coming from a mile away and was so obvious I could have sworn was already mentioned like two hours earlier or something. The second one I didn't see coming from a mile away but felt like a total idiot because I didn't in that it was completely logical. Sudden plot twists, especially of this caliber, are rarely done in such a way that it seems like the perfect conclusion to every single event that preceded. While elements of the story are really, REALLY stupid, for the most part it's very well written and worth your time.
4. Too many RPG elements were removed/Character progression is gimped too much.
I disagree here in that I like to play both of these games when I have completely different mindsets. If I want to play System Shock 1 or 2 but without horror elements I'll play the original Deus Ex, and if I want to play Bioshock 1 or 2 without the horror elements I'll play this. In my opinion, just because a sequel is different, doesn't mean it's bad.
5. There's no multiplayer.
Yes. This is a complaint I've seen people actually make. The original Deus Ex actually had deathmatch multiplayer for some really stupid reason that nobody but total nerds actually played. My guess is this was just one more feature they could complain about being removed from the game so they'd have another bullet to put in IW's skull.
Overall, I give this game 8 out of 10, Deus Ex 9 out of 10 and Deus Ex: HR 8.5 out of 10.

Nowadays Half-life 1 looks really outdated and Black Mesa gives us an opportunity to see a more realistic and polished version of our beloved original game. It has a bit of Source elements like physics, but to me it felt quite natural. The only downside to this game, that not always you can find the "right" way to your objective and the doors are quite random. Some red ones are impossible to open, but others you can. But it's still a really small downside for such a nice and faithful game. If you played Half-life 1 a bit and haven't finished it, I would really suggest to finish the game by playing Black Mesa. Upcoming Xen will look magnificiently!

Black Mesa is an incredibly dedicated fan remake of Half-Life that seeks to not only re-create the game with shiny modern technology, but also fix what doesn't work and improve the game overall. Not all of these improvements are worthwhile, but most are, and the final product is comparable to the original in quality. And because Half-Life is an amazing game, that means that Black Mesa is ♥♥♥♥ing awesome.
The main differences between Black Mesa and Half-Life are the changes to the level design and the new graphics. The new graphics look wonderful, and it's fun to just ogle how much better everything looks. The level progression over the course of the game is basically the same, but almost every individual room has been redesigned to be more realistic and interesting, and a few of the puzzles have been overhauled. All the parts of Half-Life you remember are still there, but a lot of the in-between bits are unrecognizable. The result is an experience that feels new, but also strikingly familiar. It's a bit odd at first, but then you slip into a groove where you're going through the same Half-Life motions, but also appreciating all the new additions.
Along with the level design, lots of the enemy and weapon distribution has been redone. The enemies are more sensibly spaced out (Lambda Core isn't swarming with Alien Grunts any more, thank God), and there are more Houndeyes generally. The weapon progression is not as improved; you get the Crowbar way later than in the original, which necesitates having a security guard babysit you for a significant portion of the beginning, and you get the Magnum where you'd usually get the Shotgun. These are both dumb choices for different reasons, but it's a comparatively minor issue over the course of the game.
As well as being redistributed, many weapons and enemies have been rebalanced. Vortigaunts have enough health to survive a single Magnum round, but can't auto-aim their shots; Houndeyes have more health and don't have a visual for their shockwave attack; Bullsquids now fire a shotgun blast of acid that's far harder to avoid; Headcrabs are exactly the same, because their design has always been perfect; Barnacles take an extra Pistol shot to kill; and Soldiers seem to have better aim. The MP5 seems to be more accurate; the Magnum has ironsights; the Shotgun takes longer to fire in the middle of reloading; the Crossbow's scope requires holding down M2, and the mouse is really sensitive when using it; the Hivehand's damage seems to have been buffed; and all ammo caps have been significantly lowered. These changes are a mixed bag overall, but it's nice to see that the game isn't afraid to fix what it thinks needs fixing.
On that note, a lot of Half-Life's more frustrating sections have been improved, but not all of them. There's still that part where you have to crawl up a Snark-infested vent, Residue Processing is still a ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥how, and Xen (which I never actually thought was that bad) hasn't even been put in yet due to the massive amount of redesign they're putting it through. The improvements are nice, though, and certainly make the game a smoother experience.
Black Mesa is a lot like Half-Life 2 in many ways, which isn't surprising considering they're on the same engine. There's an Oxygen meter, a sprint button, plenty of reused assets, some stuff involving physics, and a lot more personality to the characters. Eli Vance and Isaac Kleiner return briefly, which is fun. Also like Half-Life 2, headcrabs are weak to the Crowbar and the default difficulty is Easy.
This is very much a game by fans, for fans. There're lots of in-jokes and little touches that only make sense if you've played Half-Life before, and it's also somewhat harder for those who've been playing Half-Life for a long time and seek a greater challenge. If you've never played any Half-Life before, it probably won't put you off too much, but it will be kinda noticeable.
The NPCs have received extra attention. There's a lot more dialogue for scientists, security guards, and soldiers, and there are female scientists now, which I liked. There's also a greater variety of faces and voices, giving each individual person you come across a different personality, which adds a surprising amount to the game.
The developers have clearly done a lot to improve the game's playability and make it with the wisdom of modern game design in mind, and that is excellent, but in doing so they occasionally lose track of parts of what made Half-Life great. Gordon has more grunts and wheezes (he also did in Half-Life 2, but they're more noticeable here), which goes against the policy of silence that made him so easy to make your own. Doors also have an annoying habit of locking themselves behind you, forcing you to move forward instead of letting you backtrack as much as you want. These are petty issues, yes, but they still bug me.
Half-Life's realistic but irritating blast damage has been toned down.
They put the unimplemented sleeping behavior for Houndeyes back in!
Ladders are even more awkward, somehow.
The gibs and blood effects have been massively improved, which is the best thing you could possibly add to Half-Life.
The load times are annoying (although that may just be my aging PC).
The music's good, but I kept noticing it, so I guess it didn't blend very well with the game.
The flashlight is infinite, which is a good choice.
Overall, Black Mesa is a successful attempt to bring Half-Life into the modern age. It smooths out rough edges and fixes irritating issues, and I really can't overstate how wonderful it is to see Half-Life looking so good. However, because of the few new issues (and because I'm biased towards things I already like), I still prefer the original. Additionally, I recommend that newcomers to the series play the original Half-Life first, if nothing else than as a lesson in game history. However, if you've played Half-Life before, or want to see how to do a remake well, DO NOT MISS THIS. It's a wonderful game, an astounding adaptation, and definitely worth your time.

My first impressions of this game where "wow, this large scale (or small scale) battle is really cool!" Already, we're off to a gooden, but what is it about this game that made me recommend it?

Anyway, back to the gun play. The guns reload unrealisticly i.e. they don't reload in mags, they reload in numbers, which is great here, because its familiar, friendly and stops the game from becoming annoying. The guns all have different stats too and you can see many guns including the AK-47, a silenced WA2000, a generic AWP, a generic scoped modern military shooter gun, a modern shotgun, a silenced SMG with one of those bar magazines that sticks out the side, a standard SMAW clone, standard Javalin clone, a modern instant rocket RPG thingy, a generic pistol, the same generic pistol but silenced and a revolver. I may have said generic more times than whatever the ♥♥♥♥ you'd write here, but the genericness of the weapons is good because you care less about them being right and all that sort of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you get hung up on if you're autistic. The only bad thing about the guns is that they have no mechanic noises including reload noises. I'm sure the dev will add them soon, but it's quite poor considering every other FPS ever has reload sounds. Apart from that though, bang on.
The maps are nice and big and you feel nice and small in them. My favourite one is the Afgan map because you can pretend to assault eyesis (wink wink, nudge nudge) which is always great fun. The snowy map is just like when the commie reds helped kill all the Germans so make sure you pick red and stop being so American and patriotic for once.
The AI is a mixed bag. On challenging, it's challenging when on foot, but in air, you might as well jump out of your vehicle and on easy, you might as well play the campaign on CoD. Another thing I don't like is Unity. Make you're own options for crying out loud. Some of us have GPUs and CPUs that must be catered for. 4GBs of VRAM is great. I can play at max texture settings on almost all games, but since it's an 850M (coupled with a bollerific CPU) I can't play with shadows very high, AA at all, AO and almost all the other PP effects. So let me turn them off. Please...
While the game may look easy to run, if you ever want to have a realistic battle, you're going to want to buy yourself 3 Intel Core i7-6950Xs if you want to get a couple thousand soldiers on-screen. Apart from that, optimisation's pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥ Sorry developer, but add your a real video settings tab and don't rely on Unity's Godawful presets.
The ragdoll physics are great AND you don't die instantly if you're near an explosion (thank God). You also don't take ragdoll fall damage, or if you do, you have to fall pretty damn far. Either way, the ragdoll mechanics are good. (except that somtimes, enemies will "trip up" when your bullet hits their leg, except that they go about 3 ft into the air, which I didn't know a bullet could do)
Finally, we look at the replayability - it depends on how much you like the AI. With games lilke these, the game is only as good as the AI is. If it's quirky, it's enjoyable. Ask about how they plan to develop it and what direction they take the AI in, because in this game, that's its crutch.
My final verdict? Don't get this game - it's in early access. You wouldn't by a magasine or chocolate bar in "early access" so why treat a computer game any differently?

I will be skipping the explanation of how Dark Souls works as a game (I’m assuming if you are reading this review, you’ve already taken an interest in DS and know how the game isn’t for everyone and the basic mechanics of it). I will also be prefacing this review stating that yes, Dark Souls 1 is in my top games ever made list. Everything worked in DS1; the pitch perfect game design, the world, combat, characters, all drenched in depth, it is truly a work of art. Demons Souls on the other hand, well I played that a number of years ago and while I don’t remember the experience quite as well (I was never able to finish it), I remember having a solid, yet disdainful time with it (Over being a game lacking some of the better design it needed). This is where DS2 comes in. A sequel to the greatest game of last generation? How could I not have expectations sky-high? Yet, did it meet them? While not being as finely tuned as the 1st, yes, I believe it met my expectations right where I put them. I went in to DS2 hoping it would be a worthy Souls game, and I got exactly that, and at its core, that’s what it does best. DS2 is more Dark Souls. Like, a lot more. Like, too much for its own good. Let me explain:
DS2 amplifies 1 by, to my estimation after one playthrough, x1.50. There’s a lot more areas, which is really good because it makes the whole game feel much faster paced and varied. You are able to level up more often and can now even respect your character (Thank god) with an item you get multiple times through the game. More covenants is definitely a good thing, considering they seem more practical now. However, there’s more bosses and gear too, which to me, is where the side effects of more content come into play. Bosses were debatably the greatest part of DS1. All bosses were memorable, perfectly placed, interesting and most importantly, challenging. In DS2, boss battles are a big mixed bag. Only around half felt memorable to me, some felt thrown in because of the need to adapt to a larger number of areas, and some felt way too easy to kill or were too big a difficulty spike to really feel fair (I’m looking at you Sentinels). Looking comparatively, the only boss that really required player summons in DS1 in my mind would be Ornstein and Smough, while in 2, there are quite a few that seemed to require more than you to be able to kill. The more items on the other hand, may not be a universal problem people might have, but it’s one I had. By the end of my first run I had: ~70 weapons, ~115 items (including unused soul and boss packets), 50 helmets, 40 chest-pieces, 30 gloves, 30 leggings, 40 rings and ~25 shields(I did not in any way complete a completely comprehensive run of the game, but I feel that I got about as much done as any other normal player would. It should also be noted that this complaint is also embedded in the fact that I never used bonfires to store items, this was my inventory compiled from the whole game. I found myself to be too lazy to use the storage system considering the lack of a backpack limit). Now, Dark Souls is not Borderlands, it lacks a UI (Though improved from DS1) that can give you a real good feel of what weapon or piece of armor is best to use. Simply put, as many weapons and as much armor as you get becomes difficult to manage. There’s a bevy of different weapons, armors, and rings to use to fit different play styles, and it becomes a bit too hard to determine what you’ll use and do best with, considering you have 3 right and left handed weapon slots, 1 slot for each armor type, and 4 ring slots (Appropriately risen from 2 R&L hand slots and 2 ring slots in DS1 at least). Personally, I ended up just upgrading 2 weapons I got in the mid-early game to the max and used them the whole way through (I also kept using them for the simple reason that it is hard to judge what weapons are better than what when one of them is upgraded, as base weapon stats are not show on the upgraded). As for items, outside of health and magic regen items and wayward bones, I found myself ignoring most all of them as it’s just more convenient to use conventional methods of attack, especially when you have to choose the certain items you want queued up and switch between them. Rings and armor make a good transition over at least, though it still gets very tough deciding on what to pick considering the options available. Shields, however, smartly don’t appear nearly as often, as in the 1st, you simply got a shield with 100% physical damage block, and maybe only changed when going against magic users (Until the Grass Crest Shield). Still yet, I’m sure if I took the time to micromanage the details of my character, this complaint may not be here, but I still think regardless that it is overwhelming.
In terms of design, however, DS2 is, in some ways, better designed than both DS1 and Demons Souls, combining elements from both. For example, DS2’s health recovery system takes from both games to create a system that works extremely well in the early to mid-latish game. Starting with one Estus Flask and having to rely on Lifegems early on creates a great sense fear while also teaching you to play smartly. However, in the late game, lifegems feel a bit useless as you have so many Flasks without the need to ever kindle bonfires like in the first.  However, despite the design improvements, DS2 never really feels like the better designed game than the 1st, if that makes sense. Let me explain, lets imagine a line that goes from the worst possible game design to the best with a wall on either side. Let’s now put DS1 at the edge of the best side. Now, DS2 is right next to it, except it tries to run further up the line. By doing this, DS2 runs into the wall and ends up right back where DS1 is. To put it in more practical terms, DS1 already felt so well designed that the changes, even if better, don’t feel as if they make the game better, only different. Warping allowed from the start? Different because it changes the structure and freedom in the early game, but better than before? Allowing invasions while hollowed? It certainly creates a more tense game, that is, if it occurred more than 5 times while I played. Removing kicking from combat? It changes the way combat is structured, but it isn’t really necessarily better. Changing the way durability works is a plus, but it was never a big deal in DS1 to begin with. What to me is non-debatably good is removing the consequential dialogue options from the game. There was nothing like losing a NPC because you said yes to an innocent question.
In the end, DS2 satisfied me. It was more Dark Souls, and that’s all I really needed out of it. It doesn’t deviate from the Souls formula, and if you’ve played the other games, you already know the traps to expect (Still waiting to see a mimic bonfire). My run timed in at 45 hours, and with DLC upcoming, that time should go up a few hours. Will I return for more playthroughs? Personally, I’m more inclined to replay Dark Souls 1 for the fifth time, but it isn’t out of the question. As for the PC port, it’s solid. The GFWL 70% summon failure is gone. It is still good to know that the PC community can get developers to put effort into putting their product on the PC. Anyways, despite the aforementioned shortcomings, Dark Souls 2 is definitely worth playing if you enjoyed Dark Souls 1 or are remotely interested and think you can “take it.” I haven’t looked into the lore of Drangleic, but I’m sure it doesn’t disappoint. What’s next for Souls? Frankly, I have no idea. A fourth Souls game would just start feeling like déjà vu in my opinion. Perhaps From Software's next title Bloodborne will be a worthy Souls spiritual successor or move in a direction away from Souls. However Bloodborne may turn out, From at the least succeeded in keeping Souls one of the most coveted franchises in all of gaming.

System Shock 2 is The first game that has managed to spook me since I was a kid. The influence that the mechanics and atmosphere of this game had on Bioshock is so clear too, to those who have played it. If you enjoyed Bioshock I cannot recommend this game enough.
The sound design is a particular high point, and I can't think of any recent horror or scifi game that got it as spot-on as SS2. The sounds of the enemies combined with the background hum of the Von Braun's engines and electronics make for a very immersive experience. In some places you also have the great trick of either having no music at all or simply a constant, low-pitched dissonant synth chord - awesome for keeping you on the edge! The electronic/drum and bass inspired soundtrack is pretty great too.
Despite it coming out in 1999, the game actually holds up really well and looks good; the art style and lighting choices are perfect for SS2's aims. Only closer inspection of the in-game models and one or two annoying (but rare) bugs betray the game's actual age. Some of the levels can also get quite labyrinthine if you aren't watching where you're going, so I think a bit of patience is required at some points of the game.
Oh and SHODAN is one of the best villains in game history. Her entrance in this game is both sublime and chilling.

The spiritual prequel of Bioshock. 
If you play both games the resemblance becomes very obvious.
This is a role-playing survival-horror game.
 
While by the end of Bioshock your character becomes so strong with so many weapons that the game ceases to be challenging. SystemShock2 on the other hand, if you don't upgrade your stats very carefully and save up on ammo and consumable items you will have a very hard time. 
The game gets harder as it goes, not easier.
Both games have a problem with balancing difficulty. SS2 gets too hard. Bioshock gets too easy.
Combat is hard.
Weapons degrade and jam (weapons dont jam for enemies though which I find to be cheap). Weapons require specific stats to even be able to use them.
Ammo is scarce.
Inventory space is limited.
Enemies seem to respawn (which can be very frustrating because it wastes your already limited resources). It can feel redundant at times since cameras set off alarms that spawn enemies.
You cant sell items until much later in the game if you get a certain item.
Special actions (hacking, repair, etc) uses up currency (aka Nanites). There is even a minigame to repair items. Failing a minigame results in an explosion, breaking or alarm depending on the object.
The game doesn't hold your hands. Consulting the map doesn't help much either. You will have to explore carefully.
Audio logs and objectives arent that well organised in the menu either.
The game has a real sense of accomplishment whenever you complete an area. 
This is a game best played in limited doses. Don't try to complete it in one playthrough. It will exhaust you and stress you out.
I also found that personally disabling the ingame music alows you to better concentrate.
The game has a very interesting villain... The game, in fact, has villains (plural). But one in particular stands out. A villain that is reminiscent of GlaDOS.
The game is a masterpiece.

DISHONORED 2 REVIEW:
Despite the awful performance of the PC port at initial release, the several patches and updates have fixed most performance issues and I am now able to give the game a fair review. It took most of the positives from the first Dishonored game and developed them further. In particular, they improved the gameplay to feel more smooth and responsive than the first game. They dug up some old narrative from the first game and used it to create a new yet strangely familiar and gripping storyline. The new environments made the game feel fresh and more unique compared to the original. Even though the ending was somewhat predictable, I still really enjoyed playing this game. In my opinion, this was 2016's "Game of the year".

Overall: 9.5/10
