Much like with the 1st game, if you loved RE4 then you will most likely enjoy this.
The Game World
The game is far less "open world" than some reviews would have you believe. There are two areas in the game that are fun to "explore", but there is no reason not to explore them and doing so does not take very long. Basically what counts as sidequests in this game are signals you pick up on your communicator, sometimes it's just some more bullets or crafting material but sometimes it's a sidequest. These signals will have you running everywhere exploring everything anyways and there are few enterable buildings that don't tie in to something.
But the sidequests in this game are FUN, there's story that's sometimes more intense than the main objective you currently have. If you are going to play this game then my suggestion is to follow every single signal you pick up. It's more than worth it.
The Combat:-:
The core of the combat mechanics has not changed that much, if you are familiar with RE4 then it's like that with a stealth mechanic tacked on. Stealth is by far superior to guns in my opinion, since you are reliant on ammo in order to actually use your guns, and ammo might be scarce at times. Stealth not only lets you conserve your ammo so you won't ever find yourself in a situation where you don't have a fallback plan but when you put enough "goo" into the stealth tree you become quite the effective killer. I also love the fact that enemies you kill stay dead, meaning you could clear out an entire map and have the run of the place.
The Difficulty
I played on Survival. The bosses are a little easy, a pack of normal enemies pose more threat than some bosses. Because if you mess up with the pack of enemies you get taken out quickly by multiple slaps, they seem to have balanced bossfights in a way so that you can afford to mess up a lot more, they hit as much if not less than a normal enemy does. This is probably because the boss lasts longer but personally i wish it was harder and more punishing. I'd recommend that you choose a higher difficulty if you are familiar with games like these. I died 4-5 times on my entire playtrough, and two of those death were me exploring mechanics, never to a boss. I will try the game on a higher difficulty, i'm not a fan of clever but vague terms for difficulty as i expected more of a struggle to "survive" on "survival". I also ended up rarely having to heal leaving me with a near infinite supply of materials to craft healing items anytime i needed it.
The Story&Characters(Spoiler free)
Keeping this part spoiler free, the story gets a pass from me. It's not the greatest storytelling that really pulls you in and it has a lot of predictable twists and outcomes. It becomes very clear how the story will go at a certain point and can feel messy at times. But i suppose that's what the game is about, the STEM world being a mess. No characters stood out as particularly unique and interesting to me. It's all very standard yet somehow enjoyable.
Minor things
I wish there were more use of introduced mechanics. Like using the shock bolt on broken fuseboxes to open doors, or more hidden items and loot behind puzzles rather than blindly following the points on the map for rewards.
Performance
Some people seem to have issues with performance on this game. I had no issues keeping the FPS over 55 for most of the game. I had to turn down shadows to medium to keep it somewhat stable. But here are some of my specs. This might have been addressed in a recent patch before i bought the game though.
AMD Radeon R9 390 8GB Series
Intel Core i7-4930K
8GB Ram
It's a far cry from the most powerful setup but it gets the job done.
The Verdict
The Evil Within 2 gets a solid 3/5 from me after my first playtrough on the "normal" difficulty. I could have written a lot more but that would have included spoilers. I would wait until it's on sale because the price is just a bit too high to justify the experience of the game. As with any game you will enjoy it if you enjoy these kinds of games. If you liked the first one and can't wait to get into the second one then by all means feel free to pay the full price. It's definetely a good game, it just feels like there is potential for so much more there that can feel a bit frustrating from time to time.

MMORPG’s live and die based on two primary factors: the combat and the quantity of content. It says a lot then as to the quality of the Elder Scrolls Online that it is mediocre in both of those departments while still being an enticing and fun game. Without the customs inherent to many MMOs or the fully immersive and living feeling of a single player Elder Scrolls game, The Elder Scrolls Online delicately balances the systems required in a multiplayer game, while putting a focus on writing, voice acting and open world group content. The Elder Scrolls Online is a mediocre MMO, and a mediocre Elder Scrolls game, but when combined, it triumphs as an engaging, fun and social experience.
Elder Scrolls Online’s combat feels a lot like Skyrim, in that the weapon connections don’t really feel as solid as they should and the skills don’t always have the sense of impact that they ought to. Likewise, it doesn’t have the snappiness of action bar MMO combat. However, after playing for around 30 hours, I began to realize the nuance and skill it required. The dodging and movement actually lend themselves to very important positional play, and when not utilized, make the combat harder than you’d ever imagine. Trying to play ESO in a static way like one would in most MMOs will result in death, and mobility and awareness are very important. It’s hard to notice the skill required to play ESO well until one participates in one of the many group dungeons ESO offers. ESO has hundreds of public dungeons called Delves that can be played with a group or solo, as well as tradition instanced dungeons for 4 players. The dungeons and delves are very good, with varied environments, enemies and encounters. The dungeon content (including the low level dungeons) is significantly harder than most MMOs and require coordination akin to a positional shooter such as Counter Strike. The complexity of the PvE content overshadows the poor combat feel, making ESO feel like a focused strategy and positional game over a visceral 3rd person action game. Much like Guild Wars 1, ESO allows a limited number of skills (5). The skill system is diverse and interesting, allowing any class to use any weapon or armour. Want to play a heavy armour, great sword wielding mage? Well you can. The restricted skill system makes it feel like there are plentiful build possibilities, and in an MMO, feeling like you actually have the potential to create a unique build that is viable without just googling the most optimal way to play is liberating, and extremely fun. The skill system provides the sense of customization and creativity that an MMO should.
The questing in ESO is full voiced. While the writing isn’t as strong as many single player RPGs, the quest writing tends be relatively strong in comparison to most multiplayer games. There are few throw away quests where a villager needs multiples of a mundane item, such as the hides of 10 boars, and the game generally stays away from kill and collect quests. While the gameplay when questing tends not to be very interesting, there is usually enough of a narrative hook to make even the monotonous quest design interesting. As someone who plays a lot of MMOs, this is the first game in years I did not listen to podcasts the entire time while playing, as I actually opted to listen to the voice acting or read the quest text. Unfortunately, the voice acting is weak, with a very small cast and you will notice repeating actors, often even in the same quest chain. The writing is good though, often presenting shades of gray when moral choices are presented, allowing for interesting resolutions to quests, and the characters are a good mix of likeable and hateable. In the base game, the main story quests follow a pretty generic plot, and are predictable and boring, if not fun in a campy way. However, the two Guilds in the base game, the Fighters Guild and the Mages Guild pick up where the main plot fails. With interesting quests and instanced missions, the Guild quests actually allow for unique and interesting gameplay. The nature of ESO as an MMO cause the impacts of the questing on the world to be relegated to voice lines from the villagers, but the instanced Guild missions allow for more feedback from the world and characters as to the actions of the player. The writing in the Guild storylines is also much stronger than both the main quests and the side content. This leads me into another downfall of ESO - The Elder Scrolls universe just isn’t very interesting. Sure, it has a detailed history, and traditionally has character relationships and interactions that are complex and emotional, but it lacks the flash and outlandishness of other MMOs. Warcraft has a cast of ridiculous caricatures that make the world silly, yet fun and charming. Elder Scrolls is high fantasy in the most boring way. The Mages Guild deals with this problem by having frequent interactions with the Daedric Prince of Madness who pranks and jokes with the player, and I think it comes as no surprise that this is easily the best PvE content that the game has to offer. The generic fantasy of the world significantly reduces the amount I could care about the main quest or side content. I know that eventually the baddie will die, somebody important will die, and all of the faction will put aside our differences to take down the monster that is a threat to us all. The side content suffers from boring-universe-itis too, as the world doesn’t really allow for crazy stories to emerge. Sure there is some interesting moral decisions to be made, but still confined within the dull parameters of generic fantasy. All in all, it takes about 100 hours to hit the level cap, and there are not all that many alternate zones per factions, leading to a fun, well developed but relatively short content play through.
Cyrodil, the continent that Oblivion was set in, is currently not controlled by a faction, and as such serves as the 1v1v1 PvP continent of ESO. Despite problems with performance, long travel times, and some issues with the systems of capturing keeps, Cyrodil offers massive, exciting battles while remaining manageable. Despite my limited experience playing PvP in ESO, the massive battles over castles and keeps tend to feel more controlled than similar games such as Guild Wars 2. It felt like the massive swarm of people eventually dissolved into multiple small team fights and 1v1s. As I was engaged in combat in the stairwell, similar fights surrounded me throughout the entire castle, which made it less overwhelming for me to parse what was going on, while maintaining the feeling of a massive battle. The action combat lent itself to making me feel at fault for my deaths, rather than gear/skills/bad luck losing me fights. The siege weapons are fun to use, and have smart and accessible system to acquire, allowing them to feel fair but still powerful. The games strong visuals and soundtrack help to enhance the scale of the battles, making it feel truly heroic. I think that Cyrodil has potential to be the best open world PvP. A means to allow for small group play (with 3-4 friends for example) in a viable way, perhaps by adding small outposts or villages would really escalate the PvP content to greatness.
Modern MMOs have removed so much of the challenge from trading and social interaction, that it feels less significant to succeed. Back in old school Runescape, sitting in a bank for 3 hours trying to buy a piece of gear wasn’t fun, but when you finally got it, it sure was exciting. ESO straddles the line between player to player trading and modern auction houses with Guild Stores. There are just under one hundred player Guild controlled stores that only sell items at the singular location of each unique store. This limits resources in a way that most MMOs don’t, but also provides an outlet for easy trading in large cities. This all said, chat bubbles are TERRIBLE, as is the group finder.

Borderlands 2 does everything that was good in the first game better, and it also knows how to tell a joke.  While the previous installment in this series was slow and had not yet found its voice, BL2 really locked in a solid pacing and a solid narrative style.  Unlike the first game, the story felt important and prominent within the game.  It's clear what are main story quests and what are optional side quests, and excellent voice acting really conveys the story better than the hundreds of quest start/end textboxes from the first.  This helps convey the funny and dark story of BL2 in a way that the first game was only starting to get a hang of in its DLCs.  Don't get me wrong, the first game was funny, but even after +500 hours in BL2 (360 & PC), I still laugh at some of the jokes.
Character progression feels very rewarding between the Badass Ranks and interesting skill trees.  With a big "game changer" skill at the end of any skill tree, there's always something to strive for or respec to.  Most of the skills feel interesting, and the rest are usually just practical to have.  Similarly, the loot game is easily one of the main draws for this game with... idk, 9999999 bazillion guns or whatever the trailer said.  Most of that count comes in from the common to rare weapons, but the true wonder and fun comes in with the Legendary rarity and higher loot.  This stuff isn't just top-tier, it also does awesome♥♥♥♥♥♥  I'd try to explain what I mean, but I'd probably just sound silly telling you about a gun that, when you reload it, your character throws it and it'll slowly fly to the nearest enemy whilst continuing to shoot at that enemy.  I did say "and higher" when describing the best loot, because there's even stuff beyond Legendary.  But those ones aren't just normal loot you find from any suitable loot source.  No, those are rewards for running raids.
Now, coming from an FPS background, I don't know much about raids.  I know they're supposed to be cool, have a big boss, and I know they're supposed to be endgame.  Anything past that I can't talk about, but I can say BL2 has those three things for its raids.  These big baddies are best battled with buddies, because obviously.  Unlike the disappointing final boss of the first game, and the basically unkillable without cheating raid boss from one of its DLCs, these guys are satisfying.  An excellent mix of actually being able to take damage and being able to murder even the most solid of tanks in a few seconds makes the battles feasible, yet challenging.  And if/when you manage to take down one of these raid bosses?  Expect to dig through loot for a few minutes at least.
Similar to the improvements to the main bosses, smaller bosses throughout the game are also much more satisfying.  Part of this comes from the voice shift between the first and second game, and now would be a good time to explain that better.  The first game, while being set on an alien planet filled with giant, four-mandible dogs and death worms, felt like it was trying to be too real and dark.  The vast majority of the enemies, and likewise the bosses, were generic bandit characters with a sliver of individual character infused either through the gun they were using, and/or five seconds of dialog.  And those were the main story quest bosses.  In BL2, even the most mundane of side quest bosses actually feel like they have a place in the world and narrative.  Likewise, we're not in a gritty space western anymore.  Sure there's notes of that, but the story is more about gaining hope, overcoming giant monsters, and building a life for people in the face of a corporate entity hell bent on you not doing any of those things.  The alien elements feel more alien and the main downer emotions come from good storytelling, not from shades of brown and warring bandits.
Of course, all is not well on Pandora.  Sometimes quests are turned in unexpectedly, or parts of them are unclear or hard to do for trivial reasons.  While the majority of skills are good, some don't feel like they do enough to be worth taking.  Similarly, some of the "game changer" skills don't feel game changing enough to earn the title.

Black Mesa stays relatively true to it's source material, Half-Life, but also takes freedom in artistic design, gameplay and level design, which make the game still feel fresh. The enviroments look very pretty and detailed, yet the most iconic maps are still very recognizable.
Big fights were annoying at times. On hard difficulity the game can be outright unfair. The player is often put into impossible situations with little cover and health pickups. Enemies can be bullet sponges, and sometimes have godlike aim. I had to lower the difficulty from hard to normal in order to progress further.
Puzzles are challenging but not too much, their main purpose is to give a certain pace to the game. during puzzles, the player is given some time take a breather and a chance to explore after a gunfight. This technique is used very well and creates a very dynamic flow in progressing through Black Mesa.
The music differs vastly from the original, giving the game a much more serious mood than the original Half-Life. I personally think that this serious mood fits the game much better than the B-movie atmosphere the original Half-Life was going for.
Overall a very good game and good remake. The game does not feel like an exact copy of it's original, and that makes the game worth playing even if you have finished the original Half-Life.

This game suffered because it was the sequel to the absolutely outstanding Deus Ex, and after waiting for a sequel, fans were delivered this disappointment. That said, this was the first Deus Ex game I ever played, and it was good enough to make me want to play the others.  It's a fun game, with fun gameplay and intriguing mechanics.  If I had played the other Deus Ex games first and played this one after, yes, I would have been disappointed.  This is a failed attempt to match the other games' depth and customization.  But it's

It is worth playing, even as a Deus Ex game.  The plot is passable, as are the NPCs.  There is a "true pacifist" route to be taken if you desire, and there are some fun easter egg references to the first game buried in here.  For $6.99, the game is fantastic and fun, just don't expect a Deus Ex level experience.  Go in with that mindset, and you'll probably have a good time.

When it was released in 1997 it quickly became apparent how TA was going to be THE genre defining game of the decade, going on to win Gamespot's Game of the Year award that same year.
Whether you choose to use lowly k-bots to rush their base, prefer a more elegant appraoch using stealth fighters, or prefer to build an entire line of Big Berthas to long range bomb them into submission there are multiple strategies to winning a battle.
Total Annihilation removes the resource gathering, micromanaging aspect of strategy games and instead focuses on combat. War materials are broken into two catagories of either metal or energy, both of which are harvested at a constant rate through each resource generation structure.
All in all, TA is my favorite strategy game of all time and I've played countless hundreds of hours blowing up my enemies and securing map domination.

I was really surprised by this game. Normally, you would get something of this quality from something you paid around $10, $15 for. The grammar isn't the best, but that's easily something to overlook. One of the few things that I wasn't the happiest about was the battle system. You just walk up to the enemy and the you attack. Fans of games like EverQuest and Warframe, that are used to and enjoy the larger amount of variation may not appreciate this as much as they would appreciate previously stated games. But that's not what the developer was aiming for. This isn't a game based on combat. It's very story-rich and full of puzzles. It's not very long, maybe only 6 hours if you want to get all three endings (I was lazy, so I just watched them on Youtube), and the story really does give you the feels. After you get all three endings though, and possibly 100% it (getting all of the armor, weapons, etc.) there isn't really any replayability (is that a word?) Regardless of the battle system and the sometimes monotonous gameplay, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone willing to try it.

It may have been overshadowed by the scope of its contemporary, Deus Ex, and the streamlined accessibility of its spiritual successor, BioShock, but System Shock 2 was unique in its day and still holds its own today as a classic First-Person Action RPG, providing an experience that, unfortunately, still hasn't quite been reproduced in any other game since.
The original System Shock was somewhat ahead of its time (consequently it suffered from questionable execution of some of its ideas such as with its controls) whereas Shock 2 arrived at just the right time to help define the Immersive Sim genre with an arguably more refined take on the cyberpunk horror concept.
Created from a collaboration between Looking Glass Studios and Irrational Games, Shock 2 has many similar traits to other games from the school of immersive sims such as Thief and the aforementioned Deus Ex. Atmosphere, world-building and multi-solution problems - all pillars of the genre - are to be found here in abundance.
With deep customization trees that allow you to use all kinds of weapons and tools and develop exotic powers, Shock 2 allows you to approach the game in a variety of ways, and then return to its creepy hallways with a new character build for a different experience. Enlist with the Marines to wield the heavy-duty military weapons found scattered across the Von Braun; or spend some time in deep space with the Navy and learn to use highly technical engineering tools such as hacking and energy-based weapons; or maybe you'd rather get in touch with your inner zen and gain mastery in the powers of the mind. Shock 2 might make you work to earn each and every skill point, but it rewards investment into specialisations.
Shock 2's story is told through an impressive number of different narrative devices, each serving to slowly reveal the mysterious ship, its previous owners, and its new inhabitants. Clear plot points and objectives keep you moving forward through the numerous decks of the ship. While wireless transmissions, audio logs and emails are the norm in today's games, they were still new and innovative when Shock 2 made use of them. The game steers clear from technical hurdles that would shatter your immersion - there are no awkward NPCs to draw you out of the experience - instead, the game emphasizes isolation and loneliness, and the characters come to life through their voices, whether logging their last moments or speaking into your receiver to instruct you with dubious intent.
In fact, the sound design may be Shock 2’s crowning achievement. The doom-ambiance of the cargo bays will be an enduring memory for those who have gone through that harrowing ordeal. The multitude of enemies identify themselves through their terrifying sounds, such as the tragi-horrific moans from grunts of the Many, urging you to kill them, and the ear-splitting screeches of the psi-enhanced monkeys. The iconic antagonist SHODAN is memorably characterized by her evilly seductive and corrupted speech, echoing throughout the ship and reverberating within your skull.
Shock 2 won’t be considered a looker today - it certainly wasn't at the time either - but there are a few community-built mods available to help make it more palatable to the eye. By and large, you’ll still have to develop a taste for its neon-green cyberpunk aesthetics and hard-hitting techno soundtrack, but if you do, you’ll find plenty of interesting enemies and well-realised locations as you explore. The layout of the ship follows a believable structure, with different decks for different purposes such as the Medical wing that you start out in, and the Recreational deck complete with a swimming pool and basketball court.
The HUD successfully feels like a cool sci-fi neural interface, allowing you to manage your inventory, browse through your logs and emails, upgrade your software and even conduct research on unknown materials. Not to mention the inclusion of a mini game console, complete with game titles to collect like Overworld Zero, a roguelike to help you unwind during your downtime or to kill the minutes as a security alarm ticks down. The combat might feel rather stiff and clumsy owing to the game’s dated engine, but if you approach every scenario with careful preparation and strategic thinking, you’ll overcome the odds without much fumbling.
All of which is to say that there is so much to System Shock 2 that is worth your time. It’s not easy to get into, but it’s almost impossible to let go of.  It rewards exploration of its mechanics, environments and story. It is a classic that endures the test of time and continues to influence games and gamers, a decade on.

Alien: Isolation is a stealth-based horror game.  In trying to work your way through the game's objectives, it forces you to balance running away from enemies with trying not to attract the alien by making so much noise.
From the beginning, this game plays with light and shadow to make the environment very tense.  For HoH gamers, the game adds to tension with sounds designed to make you question how safe you are.
There are slightly creative solutions for getting past evil robots and other challenges, but once they see you, the AI gets a little weird and they just hang out for you to come out of hiding.
Whether deaf, hoh, or hearing, if you are a fan of psychological horror, this game will definitely deliver.
Rated 7 because of occasionally silly AI and occasional lack of clarity of mission objectives.  (This crosses the line a little between "the gamer can figure it out" and "we just won't help you at all")
A:I seems like a relatively scripted game, so it is may be very similar from one play to the next.  Still, it is challenging enough as it is, so may be worth the challenge on a second game at a higher difficulty.
- You CAN edit options before going in to the game.
- Gamers with mobility issues can rebind keys to accomodate needs.  "Peek" and "Reload" must be held rather than toggled, so keep that in mind.
- HoH gamers can change sound effects volume and music volume separately.
Pros:
- Subtitles are easy to read and in good position on the lower part of the screen.
- For HoH gamers, voice memos and tapes have subtitles and a timer to indicate when the recording is done playing.
Cons:
- This game only offers subtitles, NOT captions.
- Subtitles do not indicate who is talking.
Rated 7/10 for lack of captions vs subtitles.  This is significant since game relies on situational awareness.

Total Annihilation was a stand-out release among a successful and populare genre which has simply died off after age. Many of the good titles are off the market, hard to find or on unpreferred platforms. Dark Reign, Red Alert, Command and Conquer, Total Annihilation, Age of Empires, Age of Mythology and of course Warcraft and Starcraft...
It was a much better time for the genre, where the games were of supreme quality and the hours were infinite. LAN parties flocked with custom maps, units, mods of all the popular titles of the time.
Total Annihilation reigned supreme with the greats - Dark Reign, Warcraft 2, Starcraft and Red Alert 2. It's really fun, simple and intense. Cavedog weren't deserving of going under but they will always will be remembered. If you love strategy games, classics, or simply games, this is a game for you.
This game should be in everybody's collection, without a doubt. And for the price it's going for there's no excuse to not own this one.

I could stop the review right there, 'nuff said. Except no, there's so much more to it than that. Broforce is more than just a one-track gag, it's a love letter to 80s and 90s action heroes wrapped in an homage to Contra, Metal Slug, and with a little Worms for good measure.
At first glance, the game may come off as simply a novelty. But they didn't just take a generic character, slap the name Rambro on him, and call it good. Every single character in the cast of over 30 has a great deal of love and detail worked into them. Each character has a unique primary attack, a special attack, and a melee attack. Rambro has a trusty machine gun and versatile grenades, whereas Bro Heart has a claymore and the ability to scare enemies by screaming at the top of his lungs. If a character is played by Van Damme, you better believe he can deliver split kicks to terrorists' faces.
Therein lies Broforce's "gimmick:" You start each level with a single life and a random Bro you've unlocked so far. Freeing a Bro trapped in a cage will grant you another life, while also swapping your character to another random Bro. Thus, you have to decide between keeping your current character, or getting the extra life. It's a simple mechanic when you get down to it, but it adds a huge amount of replay value to the game - You'll rarely beat a given level the same way twice.
Each character, given that they're completely different, has their own upsides and downsides. Brocketeer may lack the raw firepower of the other characters, but his jetpack lets him rocket punch dudes and make crazy jumps. MacBrover's dynamite may be less straightforward than a gun, but timed right can cause absolute carnage. Of the gigantic cast, there are maybe one or two characters I try to avoid, and even they can get the job done.
Part of Broforce's charm is in its sheer hilarity and the number of things you can do. I once threw a guy at another guy, killing them both...The second guy was a suicide bomber, however, so he exploded, sending a dog flying through a door, which killed another guy as it opened. You can kill a guy by hitting him in the head with a flash grenade. You can kill Satan by throwing another Satan at him (the latter Satan also dies). You can throw your claymore, which decapitates everyone in its path. Someone out of range may try to shoot you, but your claymore, now stuck in the ground, will reflect the bullets right back into his evil face.
That's not to say Broforce is completely without faults. In all the carnage and chain-reactions of destruction, it is pretty easy to die, especially when most characters die from a single shot. There are definitely some deaths that feel like they were unavoidable, such as an explosive barrel falling on top of me from offscreen. The reason why I completely forgive this, however, is because of how fun the whole thing is. Death usually has little consequence, so an annoying moment here and there are easily remedied by the barrels of laughs in between. It's definitely a game that's more fun than frustrating. As someone who's not particularly hardcore, the game has never been so frustrating that it made me want to stop playing.
Multiplayer makes the game even more fun and more chaotic. Depending on the level, adding more players can make the game easier (because of the multiplied firepower) or harder (because of the added chaos and thin-spread lives), but almost always makes it more fun. You can high five one another (triggering slow motion), flex together, and if you really want you can drop the rescue chopper on their head. Everyone starts the next level with exactly 1 life anyway, so messing around at the end of the level is surprisingly consequence-free.
Along with the main levels, there are challenge levels, which when completed unlock powerups in the rest of the game. You can call in an "All-American Supply Drop", aka a nearly-invincible mech with the american flag plastered on in place of a windshield, or take some
that let you throw dudes like Superman and scare enemies with your homoerotic grunts.
At the end of the level, after you've shot Satan in the face (or punched him so hard he exploded, or thrown him off a cliff, or beaten him to death with his own minions, or scared him so hard he jumped to his death), you (and your friends, on the rare occasion you coordinate everyone's jumps correctly) board the rescue chopper and fly off into the distance, as a rockin' victory theme plays and the entire level explodes for no discernible reason.
That's a perfect image to sum up Broforce: Over the top, ridiculous, nonsensical
. It would have been very easy for the developers to take the game's concept and turn it into a one-track novelty that doesn't actually amount to much. But Free Lives is the prime example of what a game developer should be. They didn't just put time, money, and effort into this game: They put
into it. They clearly weren't just trying to make a quick buck, they made Broforce because they loved the things they based it off and wanted to share that with other people. Broforce is a game that's a great idea in theory and an even better idea in reality. It is, quite simply, one of the greatest games I've ever played.

Okay, i have played it and i got to say... this game is just... I don't know whether to say whether this is a good game or not. The price is outraging, the enemies barely drp any gold, you need to pay IRL money to play as imperial, the horses cost up to 17K gold, 42K gold for a decent one... Fast traveling no lnoger exists, some call it an upgrade, some call it a downgrade. I
hate that feature. Because it takes so long to get from point A to point B, that it can be called a walking simulator. The storyline is verry tedious and dull. And why it takes forever to finish is because we gotta level up 5 tiems before you can do another quest. The thieves guild, and dark brotherhood have been stripped from the game and we gotta pay IRL money to play as them, we need to pay IRL money for passage to orsinium. Like 1/6th of each province is actually  present in the game. But! There is a good side, the graphics and music are pretty great. (And those who say "It's passable" they fail to realise this game was made in 2014!) The game can be played more or less like skyrim, just don't use the abilities that any standard MMO gives you. Now, the storyline, that is the main storyline, so stopping coldharbor is verry tedious, the actual faction storyline and the side quests are great! I also did say that only a few parts of the place is present in game, that is true yes... but, considering the fact that all of cyrodil, some chunks of the regions are there, which makes it 160+ hours of content. The community is pretty nice, except for the high level people that kill lower level people (quite common in all MMO's really.)  Now, some stuff i could go either way on. You only get 3 races per faction. So for aldmeri dominion, you can only have khajit, wood elf, and high elf. On one side, it limits you to 3 races per faction, on the other side, it's for roleplaying purposes (like i mean, what the hell would an orc be doing in the aldmeri dominion?) And yeah... that's kind of all i can think of... i give it a B-, i recomend this game if it's on sale, and ONLY if you liked skyrim, and all the other previous games, and ONLY if you are a hardcore, die hard, fan of elder scrolls, but deep down, you will feel like it's not an elder scrolls game at all, but if you meet the conditions, you will be able totolerate this game. So yeah, get it ONLY if it's on sale, otherwise, never bother with this game... EVER!

Just finished the game, and I am impressed.
This game was free, and therefore, I did not expcted that much.
This game surely surpassed my expectation and went beyond.
It is a relatively short game, it took me about 3 good hours to finish (If you were to farm to maximum, then maybe +1 hour at most?). Despite being short, the charater development is enough and solid, while story progression is fast enough to give players feeling to rush through the ending.
Also, this game has one of the unique style of game play. When encounter enemy, you dont go into that typical fight GUI or "screen" to engage each and every battle. Rather, you just simply hit them, and you either take damage back or dodge the counter attack. This simple and fast-pased battle system certainly helps players to enjoy the game, even if players are not very experienced compared to others.
There are 3 different endings, and as story progresses, you kind of know what and how would you be able to accomplish all ending. Also, this game has a bit of puzzle aspect to it, which I enjoyed. (they are fairly easy too, including all the boss battles).
If you like RPG maker based game and want to enjoy a small, little story that is carefully packaged with emotions, for FREE, then this game is for you.

Here is my review for The Evil Within 2!

Enter a world of very bad melee mechanics, bugs, getting killed through walls, checkpoints, betrayal, OH GOD I HAVE NO AMMO, and the "AHA YOU DIED!" screen that will all be made up for by the awesome story.
Difficulty:
The game can be very unforgiving and some enemies can do attack cutscenes that will kill you regardless of how much health you had. Stealth is an important part of the game and one hit melee attacks can only be done from the rear except for consumable axes that break after one use. Invisible collision meshes prevent you from going certain places which may be a death sentence if you're being chased by a horde.
Boss fights can be somewhat difficult and I found myself reloading checkpoints multiple times until learning the strategy to beat them. Hit boxes are poorly done for some enemies and you'll find yourself missing their head completely which isn't great for how limited your ammo supply is. The game does not appear to leave you deadlocked and will supply you with necessary resources in order to beat the bosses.
AI:
The AI pathfinding has some annoying issues that will result in enemies getting stuck on objects or locked doors leaving them in a cautious state until you get far enough away or enter a alert level reset area. Enemies will move to your last seen position and search for you but the programming is so linear that you can wait for them to reset and kill them while they're walking back. In fact a good strategy is to get one enemy to see you and then ambush them while they're alone.
The AI sight pattern was very poorly done. I was able to remain completely hidden with just the center origin point of my character behind an object. I was also able to push a cone around and go right past enemies. Basically what this means is you can remain hidden from sight while your arms and legs are sticking out clearly visible. Furthermore some objects such as pipes do not conceal you from being visibly seen but the enemies AI sight will not notice you.
Gameplay:
The overall gameplay is fun with the except of a few bugs and frustrating moments. Weapons can be upgraded using different costs of weapon parts found across the world. Your character can be upgraded using goo picked up around the world, from kitty <3, and RNG/fixed drops from enemies you kill. Simple puzzle elements will be required to proceed with some parts and some more slightly difficult ones will gain access to doors with resources inside. Enemies can be difficult to place accurate headshots with somewhat random head bobbing and using their arms to block your shots from hitting their heads. Some enemies will not allow stealth and will require you to go loud in order to take them down.
A minigame scoring area will unlock later in the game that will let you test your accuracy or refine your shots. It was a welcome break from normal gameplay but sadly its purpose was short lived with no further purpose to continue after I scored high enough to get all the rewards. It would have been nice if you kept getting rewards for playing even at an increasely reduced rate but nope... Highscore.. then... Never go back..
The game has a few side missions to complete but they don't seem to affect the story at all. Maybe I missed something or maybe it was just that badly merged into the story..
So much more could have been done or done better but overall it was acceptable.
Weapons:
The weapons are fun to use but the crossbow will most likely screw you acouple times if you play long enough. You are required to hold right click longer than the left click when firing resulting in quick shots that may screw up and cancel the shot rather than save your life. This can be fatal if you happened to be low health or were stunning an enemy's one hit kill animation. It might also confuse you to think about reasons why a crossbow needs to charge while aiming each time rather than just at reloads.. I get the feeling the devs don't know the difference between a crossbow and a regular bow.
most weapons and weapon pieces need to be found in set positions in the world and some of them are more hidden than others. I never found the sniper rifle but I'm told I needed to get it in a specific chapter so... I never actually got to use it. I recommend you look up the weapon locations before hand so you don't miss out like I did.
This was a poor choice made by the devs and should have given you the weapon later on in your room if you happened to miss it. Every time I picked up sniper ammo I was reminded that I was never going to get to use it on that playthrough. Don't be like me.. Cheat and find out the locations instead.
Graphics and sound:
The graphics and sound were nicely done minus a few parts. The sound was great until I reached somewhat near the end of the game and then it all desynced from the cut scenes. Normally this would result in the video taking longer than the audio but in my case the audio took much longer than the video. The sound of him hitting the ground came about 12 seconds after he faceplanted.
The graphics were somewhat dynamically emersive but most of the time it was set up as triggers in certain areas. Various screen effects and lighting blended nicely with the audio ambience. The only big issue I had was the flashlight's beam effect. The beam effect can completely cover the screen with no transparency at all in certain cinematics. Not sure if this was by design or a bug but it was year 2000 level graphics and nearly ruined the emersiveness of the cutscene.
Overall the graphics and audio were very emersive with well done ambience. Animators did a great job on showing character emotion with facial expressions.
Horror:
What horror? I was highly disappointed in this regard because the game was advertised and reviewed as a horror game.. You may get startled or get an adrenaline rush acouple times but this game is more grotesque than scary.. If that sort of thing scares you then maybe it will have more of an effect on you than it did me. The game did successfully get me to rapidly spin around 180 degrees once using nothing but building suspense music but you never get that horror experience you were promised.. I kept moving on with the hope that this was all just a buildup to the horror portion of the game but it never came.
Story:
The story was very well done. Characters are set up in a way that you begin to feel an emotional attachment for them. Some parts of the story I saw coming from a mile away but I was still immersed in curiousity to find out where it was going next. I really can't say much without spoiling parts of the story but I will say that it is worth the playthrough.
Overall:
The game doesn't have much replayability. It does have a new game plus mode that carries over some things from your old game but the game itself is very linear. Open world but no real choice as to how you want to play it.. You can do the side missions or not do them.. That's about it for choices.. Worth the playthrough but buy it with the understanding you will probably only play through it once.

I'm not sure that Valve imagined the impact that Half Life would have on the gaming world. In terms of single-player, story driven experiences, it was something of a running jump forward. They stuck the landing and nothing would ever be the same again.
Gabe Newell recently said in an interview that Half Life was "a series of compromises", however. It's easy to see why going back and playing that game (which is soon to celebrate it's 20th birthday) Although beautiful, inventive and smart it has lots of rough edges and vaguely dodgy mechanics. Those would be ironed out in the series' next instalment, which I regard as the finest video game ever made.
What Crowbar Collective have done with Black Mesa is take that old game that is so dear to so many of us, and polish it to modern day standards. The effect is profound. Their obsession with detail pays huge dividends to the original game of course, taking it's wonky shell and giving it a new lick of paint in places and completely re-designing it in others. The bits that annoyed you before (like hopping across those crates suspended over the chasm - you know what I'm talking about) have been reworked. That's not to say compromised, but made challenging in a way that is fairer and more enjoyable.
Gordon's trials in the Black Mesa Research facility are shown in exhaustive detail. On my latest run through the game, I took well over an hour before the resonance cascade sequence just listening to conversations between scientists and looking at the layouts of desks. I've never been so entranced by cathode ray tube monitors and security guard work stations. The love with which it's all crafted is evident, and Black Mesa itself feels alive. Once the disaster happens, the increasing levels of entropy that you encounter are also amazingly realised. It really does feel like the whole place is going to♥♥♥♥♥♥
The weapons are of course punchy, loud and feel dangerous. The shotgun is a particular favourite: dropping a mawman or grunt with a face load of buckshot never ceases to raise a malicious smile. The enemies are lethal and varied too, and staying alive on Hard mode is a considerable challenge. Everything fits together like a jigsaw puzzle. You feel dangerous, but you're never in complete control.
The multiplayer is also a real hoot, and although there aren't that many folks around at the moment, jumping into a game is always good, solid deathmatch based fun.
With the release of the final Xen levels on the horizon, it's hard not to be filled with excitement. If they can find some many ways to refresh planet Earth, the mind boggles at what they could do to the bizarre mountain and cave-scapes of the alien dimension.
If you have played the first Half Life, or are completely new to the series, this is a brilliant place to start. It's a perspective altering experience. 100% recommended to everyone.

Precision platformers with a retro aesthetic are very common these days, but Love hits the right notes.
I'm not a fan of the genre, mostly because I'm not good enough, but Love accommodates the players looking for a more casual challenge with its excellent respawn system. Players are able to drop down checkpoints where they please (as long as it's on a stable surface), effectively minimizing the amount of redoing you'll need to do. Higher difficulties limit these checkpoints (or outright forbid them), but I loved (pun not intended) that there was a more friendly mode as well.
There isn't much else to say. The levels are varied and the game in total does not outstay its welcome.
I'd like respawn systems like this to be in more games, especially skill-based ones, it was definitely the highlight of this game for me.
Recommended as long as you don't expect length, a plot or an explanation of the game's title.

Full disclosure I've only played the arcade mode, but that seems to be the main mode. Love felt like it didn't know what it wanted to be between a casual or hard platformer. The art, the length, and the fact that you can place your respawn at will give the feel that this isn't a hardcore platformer. However, the tight controls, level design, life limit, and if you lose the life limit being forced to start over makes this a precision platformer. Had high hopes for this game since I believe I am exactly the target audience, but I feel like there are much better options out there.

SEGA drop the ball again, and they were so close to being forgiven for 'Aliens: Colonial Marines' and that stinker of an AvP reboot. Having the Alien stomp about like an angry bricklayer with a hangover isn't suspenseful, and giving it a ridiculously long tail and velociraptor legs just adds insult to injury. Plus the same canned animations when you die get tiresome very fast. Thinking about this game makes me sad for what it could have been, but I should have learned by now that the ony Alien(s) game that'll be any good is the one in your head.

You can literally punch Satan so hard he explodes.
I could stop the review right there, 'nuff said. Except no, there's so much more to it than that. Broforce is more than just a one-track gag, it's a love letter to 80s and 90s action heroes wrapped in an homage to Contra, Metal Slug, and with a little Worms for good measure.
At first glance, the game may come off as simply a novelty. But they didn't just take a generic character, slap the name Rambro on him, and call it good. Every single character in the cast of over 30 has a great deal of love and detail worked into them. Each character has a unique primary attack, a special attack, and a melee attack. Rambro has a trusty machine gun and versatile grenades, whereas Bro Heart has a claymore and the ability to scare enemies by screaming at the top of his lungs. If a character is played by Van Damme, you better believe he can deliver split kicks to terrorists' faces.
Therein lies Broforce's "gimmick:" You start each level with a single life and a random Bro you've unlocked so far. Freeing a Bro trapped in a cage will grant you another life, while also swapping your character to another random Bro. Thus, you have to decide between keeping your current character, or getting the extra life. It's a simple mechanic when you get down to it, but it adds a huge amount of replay value to the game - You'll rarely beat a given level the same way twice.
Each character, given that they're completely different, has their own upsides and downsides. Brocketeer may lack the raw firepower of the other characters, but his jetpack lets him rocket punch dudes and make crazy jumps. MacBrover's dynamite may be less straightforward than a gun, but timed right can cause absolute carnage. Of the gigantic cast, there are maybe one or two characters I try to avoid, and even they can get the job done.
Part of Broforce's charm is in its sheer hilarity and the number of things you can do. I once threw a guy at another guy, killing them both...The second guy was a suicide bomber, however, so he exploded, sending a dog flying through a door, which killed another guy as it opened. You can kill a guy by hitting him in the head with a flash grenade. You can kill Satan by throwing another Satan at him (the latter Satan also dies). You can throw your claymore, which decapitates everyone in its path. Someone out of range may try to shoot you, but your claymore, now stuck in the ground, will reflect the bullets right back into his evil face.
That's not to say Broforce is completely without faults. In all the carnage and chain-reactions of destruction, it is pretty easy to die, especially when most characters die from a single shot. There are definitely some deaths that feel like they were unavoidable, such as an explosive barrel falling on top of me from offscreen. The reason why I completely forgive this, however, is because of how fun the whole thing is. Death usually has little consequence, so an annoying moment here and there are easily remedied by the barrels of laughs in between. It's definitely a game that's more fun than frustrating. As someone who's not particularly hardcore, the game has never been so frustrating that it made me want to stop playing.
Multiplayer makes the game even more fun and more chaotic. Depending on the level, adding more players can make the game easier (because of the multiplied firepower) or harder (because of the added chaos and thin-spread lives), but almost always makes it more fun. You can high five one another (triggering slow motion), flex together, and if you really want you can drop the rescue chopper on their head. Everyone starts the next level with exactly 1 life anyway, so messing around at the end of the level is surprisingly consequence-free.
Along with the main levels, there are challenge levels, which when completed unlock powerups in the rest of the game. You can call in an "All-American Supply Drop", aka a nearly-invincible mech with the american flag plastered on in place of a windshield, or take some
that let you throw dudes like Superman and scare enemies with your homoerotic grunts.
At the end of the level, after you've shot Satan in the face (or punched him so hard he exploded, or thrown him off a cliff, or beaten him to death with his own minions, or scared him so hard he jumped to his death), you (and your friends, on the rare occasion you coordinate everyone's jumps correctly) board the rescue chopper and fly off into the distance, as a rockin' victory theme plays and the entire level explodes for no discernible reason.
That's a perfect image to sum up Broforce: Over the top, ridiculous, nonsensical
. It would have been very easy for the developers to take the game's concept and turn it into a one-track novelty that doesn't actually amount to much. But Free Lives is the prime example of what a game developer should be. They didn't just put time, money, and effort into this game: They put
into it. They clearly weren't just trying to make a quick buck, they made Broforce because they loved the things they based it off and wanted to share that with other people. Broforce is a game that's a great idea in theory and an even better idea in reality. It is, quite simply, one of the greatest games I've ever played.

The best series ever

I was very skeptical of this series before ever trying it. All I ever heard was: "It's hard, most punishing game" And I decided to let Dark Souls go under my radar for a long time. However, I watched a friend play Dark Souls: Prepare to Die and liked what I saw. It looked like a classic Castlevania game, but in 3D. I decided that I'd deal with the difficulty, and I bought the game for myself. The first game absolutely floored me with it's brilliance. The scenery, the interesting but mysterious lore; and the amazing boss fights. I was hooked instantly. So when I heard a sequel was coming out, I was excited. Dark Souls II was the first game I've ever pre-ordered. Was it worth the wait?
Absolutely.
Granted, I did not get the same wow factor as I did from the first game in the series, but that's because I already had high expectations. The second game however, did offer a new world, fancy looking new armors, some new mechanics, and its PC port ran very smooth. Dark Souls II had everything I loved about the first game, but offered enough new enemies and situations, where it didn't just feel like "more of the same." The AI was smarter about not letting you flank it, and more enemies had attacks that would sweep their own backs to prevent you hiding in a sort of blind spot. A lot of the bosses are also great. I enjoyed fighting the pursuer 1 on 1 without using the ballistas, and feeling like I bested a sword expert. I liked leaving my summon sign in front of the Rotten, and helping newer players kill a tough boss, and get a sunlight medal for my efforts. This game just has a lot of pull to it that keeps me wanting to make new characters, try new things, and learn more about it. I am still just as happy with Dark Souls II as I was with Dark Souls: Prepare to Die. A series that I almost let pass me by, ended up becoming one of my favorite modern games. It gets a solid 9/10. My only gripe, is the game cannot stand well without the multiplayer aspect. Without the fear of invasions, or jolly co-operation with other players, the game feels a little empty. However, it is a small gripe, as the game's multiplayer feels natural, and not shoehorned on.

If you're a fan of survival-horror then you've come to the right place, but beware this isn't your typical "jump-scare game."   The Evil Within has built it's brand, not on jump scares, but feeding off the fear of the mind.  As you delve further and further into STEM you find out that  not only can the mind be a terrifying place, but the control and power it wields is truly frightening.
The Evil Within 2 follows the events of The Evil Wiithin and it's two story driven DLC (these actually provide a lot of insight into the story if you have yet to play them.)  Sebastian Castellanos returns as our protagonist, but this time a little more willingly.  The key changes from TEW come in the form of a less linear gameplay experience.  If you played the original TEW you are familiar with the linear, chapter based story mode.  The chapters remain, but the ability to explore Union and the Marrow provide for a much different experience than the original game.  This allows you to learn about Union and it's citizens as they begin to face the world and what Mobius is doing.  I believe this adds depth and attachment to a world that is stronger than what we were given with Beacon in the original TEW.
Combat and skill building are very similar to the original with a few new nuances (such as locating and building new weapons) that wasn't preseent in the first game.  That being said, the clunkiness of the combat still remains.  I found many instances where I would shoot through enemies or where my hitbox seemed HUGE.  Enemies grappling you from an inch off to your left or right can be extremely frustrating (especially if you're playing on Nightmare difficulty.)
That being said, what drives this game forward and makes it unforgettable in my book, is the story.  From the first second, until the final post credits (yes, you need to wait around) scene you are drawn to Sebastian and his plight.  And in the end, you will have several instances where this game simply tugs at your heart strings.  You've been by Sebastian for two games now and to see what he's been through, what it has caused, and what has happened bring you extremely close to the character.
If you like survival horror and you enjoy a good story driven game then this is for you.  The gameplay as fun and some very interesting puzzles await you within, but the story will make you thoroughly enjoy every hour put in!

This state of combat affairs is certainly a first in my not-insignificant gaming experience, and really mucks up the fun of the whole advernture.

An excellent survival horror game. In my opinion, EW2 improves on the first game in just about every way. The story is much easier to follow while retaining the same amount of mystery and complexity, and I found myself becoming more invested in it than before. I won't spoil anything, but the ending was excellent as well and I feel it wrapped up the game quite nicely.
Gameplay is top notch, both stealth and head-on combat feels tense and satisfying. Two complaints I thought I would have were with the crafting system and the open world level design, but I honestly liked both of these aspects of the game a lot. I thought the open world sections were a great change of pace from the linear sections, and the sidequests were both interesting and worthwhile. One event in particular is extremely plot relevant and has periodic events for about 60% of the game - did not even realize it was a potentially miss-able sidequest at first! The crafting system is much less complicated than it appears at first glance. Gunpowder ends up feeling like a nice little item to give an extra few bullets for your desired weapon type when you can't seem to find any, rather than being a must-have resource you constantly have to scrounge for.
One thing I adored as a big fan of RE4 were the times when the game manages to be both serious and incredibly silly at the same time. If you ran from the church or spent a lot of time in the training room, you know what I mean. This game has a lot of heart and personality, which is something that I don't say often about modern horror games.
In all - I would recommend this game to any fan of the survival horror genre, regardless of whether or not you have played the first game. Maybe go watch a plot summary on youtube if you are thinking about jumping right in here though, as there are lots of references to EW1 events in the story.

This is not as good as The Evil Within 1, coming from the perspective of someone who thinks RE4 is one of the greatest survival horror game made. But it is still a good game.
The open-world nature of certain sequences didn't sit well with me at first, but I grew to enjoy it. After a learning curve, and being a good gamer, the player becomes the hunter. It doesn't help that stealth kills are so powerful. Am I playing Arkham Asylum? The drawbacks of open world are that "becoming the hunter" is actually contrary to survival horror. Because there are places to explore, and because those places are always filled with supplies, you tend to have plenty of firepower at any given time. And additionally because the levels are openly traversed, video game logic always gives you an option to either circumvent monsters or take them on for additional supplies.
A big part of survival horror is that things are spiraling out of your control, and having freedom, I have to admit, detracts from that in a significant way. We're trading that very specific itch for "traditional fun gameplay". I get why the developers made that choice to appeal to a broader audience, and the goal they set out to achieve was a success, but it is a notable yet entirely subjective demerit by my reckoning.
What I loved so much about TEW1 was that you always felt hunted,♥♥♥♥♥♥was going south faster than you could anticipate. Crazy levels, insane situations, dudes with chainsaws. Carefully crafted levels. Gear and supplies delivered just when you were at your limit. A new game + that let you use that knowledge of upcoming challenges to plan your next course of action. That kind of curation is hard in a more open world design. By the end of TEW2 you feel like your guy might become the next neo in the matrix. There's bosses and situations coming up that you know about, but none of them really require any forethought.
Like the sequel to the rebooted tomb raider, TEW2 suffers from some sequel-itis. There's less gore. There's less death traps. There's less really really hard encounters. A modern haunted town is intrinsically less interesting to me than a gritty fever-dream castle filled with sawblades and pits filled with spikes. I managed to beat TEW2 game on nightmare mode my first run and took on most of the bosses in one or three tries, depending on how aggressive I wanted to get with crossbow bolt ammunition. The result is an agreeable game, but it lacks those really jagged and nasty edges that make it memorable.
While TEW1 was one of the few games that I've 100%ed and is one of my favorite games of all time, I'm probably content with letting this stand at a single run. It's a good game, but not a masterpiece.

GAMEPLAY: Simply inspired- this was basically done to make it easy for people not really proficient in playing. I would have liked it if there was a more... immersive gameplay mode for those who wanted it, but what it has is already very good. And to think this was done in RPGMaker... gotta practice my skills there even more. Heck, in the bonus room, we see parts of the creator's process in making this and you can feel the effort, with comments on how he fine-tuned this, and test-played, making changes as needed. Still, I would have liked more detailed equips, more skills, or even a skill tree...
STORY: Story is what you would expect for such a game- short. However, unlike most free rpgs I've seen, the story here is good! No, it's not on the level of the usual RPGs I play. The game's too short, and the cast too small for that. HOWEVER, this would be a very good backstory game for one such character in a larger cast in a bigger RPG. So no complaints here, really. I'd like to see Senia in a party with going back to the tower as her more personal motivation in joining the group.
MUSIC: It was pretty standard, I suppose. Not monotonous, but nothing super amazing either. Few tracks, but the short gameplay makes them stand out a bit without getting repetitive. One thing I would have liked is if the piano cutscene actually played a piano-only mix of the track...
ART: For most of the map sprites, it's the usual run from rpgmaker resources and other peoples stuff. Good enough, especially with the longer height sprites, but nothing much to be said. The conversational 'VN' sprites were somewhat lacking for me. They could have been done better. Plus, it would have been nice if the side characters (chest, slime, sheep, and Nia) would have conversation sprites while they talk. Same for the bosses. Speaking of which, the boss arts were pretty good, and the parallaxed maps were as well. The only thing that could have improved there was perhaps if the boss battles had the arts changing subtly, or moving like a GIF of sorts, but slow enough to keep the art quality.
OTHERS: Nice autosave system. It really takes out the frustration when you accidentally make a big mistake. Especially on the last parts- the game actually let's you save after the final boss for other things!
Overall, I'd give this a solid 9/10 considering the game length and the price. Worth every second I played :)

This might be what we would have gotten if Half-Life was made around the time Half-Life 2 was made. It's a great remake, and it definitely deserves the label 'remastered'. This game... This is a game I like to remember as being one of the best RTS games ever. Being released in the late 90s it came out amongst other great RTS games like, Starcraft, Warcraft 2, Red Alert, Command and Conquer and Age of Empires. Back then the RTS competition was a tough one to beat and Total Annihilation proved it could be on top with the rest of them. Its gameplay is smooth, it works and its easy to learn.
The resources in this game are Energy and Metal, and the resource gathering is different but works in the case of Income and Loss. Your income will be determined by things such as how many solar collectors you have for energy, and how many metal deposits you are collecting from. You always want to aim for your income to higher than your loss at all times even when you're building, this way you can almost avoid any loss in resources all together. The best way to explain this is like this; Max Metal and Energy at the start is 1000 in stores, A barracks could cost 500 metal and 2350 energy, the game will decide how much you will lose per second that its being built, so youre income of metal might be 5.4, and energy is 111 you're loss might then be 6.2 and 120 so you will start to lose these resources over time and could run out of energy before its finished you avoid this by building more energy collectors to make the income of energy much higher and then not run out of energy in the middle of building.
Most of the gameplay exists around your one main builder unit, The Commander, this guy builds all your buildings and gathers temporary resources (of which btw is pretty much everything, you can gather trees and folliage for energy. Rocks and whats left of units are gathered as metal.). That being said however, once your base is built up and your income of resources is good, is where you start to build your massive robotic army of your infantry, vehicles and aircraft. There is no population cap so you build as much as you like. Through reading everything that is said about the units and buildings you'll be able to find a good mix of what you need nice and easy.
Pros: -Quick Gameplay
- Gameplay makes sense and works
- Robot Armies
- A different type of resource collecting not seen often
- A long story driven campaign
- Pretty much everything explodes
Cons: - its from the 90s so graphics will be out dated

Remember Lucas Arts? Do you? Do you really? Are you sure? Because this game reeeeeeaaaally wants you to remember Lucas Arts. And if you don't, or don't like their games, then this probably isn't the game for you. If you like playing time capsules that give you a look into the past then this is an excellent game.
But if you want to play a adventure game that displays any modicum of the progress that's been made in the industry since the early 90's, then this isn't it.
Go play Limbo, it's cheaper and doesn't rely on base level references to get by.

Short version:
First you break the fourth wall. Then you break the third, mistaking it for the fourth, as well. Then, the second and the first. And then you get squashed by the falling roof.
Longer version:
The designers are quite apt at what they attempt to pull off here, and never is there any doubt that they are doing it on purpose. However, it is a completely different question, whether they are doing it for better or worse.
I expected TP to be a retro-styled adventure game, with well-written dialogue, likable characters and clever puzzles. In addition, I was pretty much sure that, coming from the mind of Ron Gilbert, it would feature lots of references, some thinly disguised whining about the genre’s ill fate, and an unhealthy dose of in-jokes.
I sincerely hoped that, having been created by industry veterans, TP would offer a unique view on puzzle design, some fresh intelligent mechanics, and a stellar story I’d remember for the next decade or two.
Well, guess what? Thimbleweed Park is exactly what I expected it to be, and absolutely not what I hoped it would be. An obnoxiously nostalgic, unbearably meta, quite self-indulgent, slightly better-than-mediocre imitation of the graphic adventures of the golden era, laden with mildly amusing writing, some nice puzzles and an ending that is even uglier than Monkey Island 2’s (which is an achievement in itself). Astonishingly, I suspect that it’s just what the community wants right now.

I recommend the game for it's single player, not it's pvp. The game's single player is rewarding and fun to have a good quality challenge. I didn't play the first Dark Souls, but I, from screenshots and videos of the first game, imagined this game would have better graphics than PS2 Dynasty Warriors 2 graphics. It seemed like they have for some reason decided to downgrade the graphics though for what reason I do not know. The story is terribly convoluted to the point where from the start you have no idea what is going on to the point where at the end you have no idea what's going on. As you can probably imagine this detracts from any sort of connection with any of the other characters in the game. Being invaded is a nightmare unless you have played this game already for 100 hours and then you still have nearly no chance if you are new to the series. Boss fights are challenging though a little too unforgiving. There's dieing to a boss and then there's being gibbed by a boss.
My biggest complaint with the game is the balance of the game, namely the way I wanted to play the game. I wanted to play a pure 2h axe weilding heavy warrior that would use a generic greataxe and weilding NO MAGIC or shield at all. I was in for a rude awakening as I began to be 1-2 shot by any random mage that caught a glimpse of me. Another example would be as I hacked away at a massive rotten pile of flesh weilding a cleaver with my mighty 2h greataxe I put 50 points of strength into, a mage would double my damage at the same rate with lightning bolts off safely in the distance. Meanwhile, I'd be running for cover trying to heal up because I missed the dodge barely on that last sweeping attack and come to find out I nearly 1 shot by the down swing from the boss. Guess my heavy armor has no purpose. PvP doesn't let up any later because that 1-3 shotting from mages continues. What's worse, if I do close the distance with the mage he will barely be able to weild a longsword that is buffed with a magic enchantment that will make the whole point of me putting 50 points into strength null and void. The discussion continues to rage but basically in the lvling system a putting points into strength or dexterity stats(the main two weapon stats) will net no where near the bonus than from putting the points to use in a magic hybrid and buffing the weapon. So, a mage that can weild a sword will always out dps a pure warrior so long as he buffs his weapon. The solution? More health or survivability perhaps? It would work until you slip up and get stunlocked to death because poise stat has no meaning either(stat that represents ability to not be stunned by dmging attacks). Another major downfall for the medium-heavy warrior that has the decency to not wear a full set of Havels.
With the way that people dress up their characters in the pvp I'm guessing I'm the only pure warrior in this world. Everyone else is a wizard or strange fellow that wears full havels(basically heaviest armor in game) except the jester chestpiece. This leads me to believe that people aren't actually being creative with their builds or doing what represents them but are simply feeding into popular pvp metas which equates this pvp community to basically Call of Duty status in my disdain for it.
This reminds me a little too much of the flop that Armored Core 5 was. Such bad design choices in some spots, what looks like a lessor product than it's predecessor, and what ultimately lets down its fanbase. Despite all this I still recommend the game for it's single player challenge though after new game+ you will probably simply get tired of it anyhow. Umm 7/10? Maybe? I guess, yeh.

System Shock 2 is a classic game released back in 1999.
Though dont let the old age turn you away. This game was way ahead of its time.
Following the "Immersive sim" genre that had been established with the original system shock (which is currently being remade) it inspired many games in the years after.
Games such as Bioshock, Dishonored and Prey all lend elements from this game or improved upon it.
The game itself is set aboard the Von Braun. A starship capable of faster than light travel for the first time.
It's mission is to explore the galaxy and possibly make alien contact.
You are a nameless person onboard the ship, the only thing that's made known to you is that you volunteered for some experimental cybernetics that have been implanted into you. As such you now wake with a memory loss and a ship that seems completely devoid of human life.
Corpses are everywhere and an alien force has hijacked the ship.
It's up to the player to sneak, shoot, hack, and psi their way through tough situations. All while building your character in a direction using cybernetic module points. Weither you'll become a super hacker, a tough heavy weapons fighter, or a psionic amplified magician the choice comes down to your preferred playstyle.
The story itself is explained with the game's few characters and the bulk of it through audio logs you can find all around the ship.
Aside from this there are several mods made by the community to really improve upon the game.
With HD textures, improved models, weapons, as well as random assets this game is still supported by a modding community.
I would highly recommend getting the graphical upgrades as they do not break away from the original vision of the game.
Enjoy this classic before the remake of SS1 as well the upcoming sequel SS3 :)

Total Annihilation is a ridiculously fun and addictive RTS game that was developed in 1997 by a little company called Cavedog. For an almost 20-year-old game, it's amazing how fun this game is to still play.
The user interface is very user-friendly, and the game itself is simple to learn. Despite the ease of being able to get into the game and just start playing, there is a wide variety of units that allow an incredible level of complex creativity in terms of strategy. Total Annihilation is like eating candy without the calories: it gives you a cool robot army, huge explosions, and probably one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard composed for a game.
Total Annihilation is also very mod-friendly and customizable.
Despite being a great game, there are some pitfalls: Getting a multiplayer game can be tricky if you have no idea what you're doing. You will need to connect to the ip address of the host, which most modern games do for you automatically. Additionally, there is a unit cap of 250 (which includes buildings) that you *can* increase, but you have to manually edit the totala.ini file. This can be a pain in the butt for the computer-challenged, but isn't difficult to actually do.
The main complaint I hear about this game is the pathfinding. And I agree. Sometimes your units will do what seem to be nonsensical things, like trying to drive up a wall instead of going around it. Very large armies also have difficulty moving around, and the units tend to get stuck on each other. Naval units are the best example of this, where they will grind against each other trying to find their way to a destination. There ARE pathfinding patches out there that will significantly help with these difficulties, though.
Overall, this is a great game. I highly recommend it for pretty much anyone ever.
