One of the seminal 3D games of the RTS genre, this game was far ahead of its time when released. Total Annihilation still remains peerless in how well rounded it is, from both sequels and rivals.
The simplicity of the mechanics is the game's strongest point. All aspects of the game are easy to understand and intuitive. From a clean UI, to satisfying movement and speed of vehicles, the game just feels right. Once you've completed the campaign, skirmishes will entertain for a long time.
The visuals still hold up, with solidly modeled machines, angling to accommodate the contours of the landscape - an original feature at release, it still looks convincing to this day. A very complete selection of environment types to choose from, offering varied experiences.
The music of the game is excellent. Sometimes pensively tense, at other times sorrowful, and occasionally stirring with strident pride - but always memorable.
Perhaps one of the most wholesome RTS games of all time, and certainly one of the most technologically innovative of its time. Own a piece of PC gaming history.

some years back I saw a motivational image about deus ex that says "DEUS EX: every time you mention it, someone will reinstall it" something that stupid made me want to play the game, and as outdate as the combat mechanic is, the game catched my heart, and with and the same time I heard the comments of how it's sequel fall short.

the game is way too easy everything is given to you, you will never run out of anything even the upgrades, you will never have to use your brain, you will never have to manage your items like the original, making the different routes pointless, for example:

Being a huge fan of the Deus Ex series, I had high hopes going into Deus Ex: Invisible War. The story starts off with Alex, an Orphan, raised by a couple in Chicago and put into a special schoolfor gifted children, where she eventually found her way into the Taurus program, a human augmentation program. You start off being attacked by religious fanatics and are given both sides point of view, with each side trying to persuade you the other is the real threat. Interesting story, I like the concept and it had be playing for over an hour, when I only intended a short demo for the review. It appears to further the Deus Ex Canon, and while it has all the wonderful potential of a Deus Ex game, I will warn you now there are bugs.
First of all, every time the game wants to load a new area, It jumps back to your desktop for a a few seconds and the resolution change makes your desktop appear to be supersized. It does this a lot. The graphics are not quite up to par for a sequel to Deus Ex, but it is passable. The game almost has a feel as though it were rushed or poorly ported from a handheld or console. I think it would be a prime candidate for a reboot, as it was interesting. All in all I will recommend it, but only to those who are familiar with the Deus Ex series, so as to acquire this piece of Deus Ex Canon for your collection. Otherwise, if you are looking for a quality game, and don't care about the series, the Original is great, and Deus Ex: Human Revolution is fantastic. Either way, the series is solid.

Dark Souls II is a very enjoyable game, there is no denying it. I've spent many an hour gleefully hacking away at various undead types, and will likely spend dozens more doing so.
In certain ways it is an improvement on its predecessor, it runs so much more smoothly on PC, which really helps with combat. The environments still look very impressive, but this is coupled with the slight lack of huge scenic vistas which were hinted at in the background of Dark Souls 1 areas, so it had a bit less of an "epic" feeling to the scale of the world. Pairing up with other players, especially friends, is distinctly easier, with a ring which facilitates grouping with someone also wearing it (upon equiping you choose one of 8 gods). The music is good and the voice acting is quite well done too. The combat feels meaty and is very satisfying.
There are however some major flaws when compared with the first Dark Souls. The first and biggest flaw for me is hard to adequatly describe, but it's just a lack of a feeling of awe, and a sense of mystery when exploring the world. The "story" is more centred upon the chosen undead, and less upon the crumbling world through which you travel. That was a little disappointing, there was much less interesting information about the world found in item descriptions really. The world felt much less interesting in regards to finding out what happened to it, and even when you find it it just feels kinda lazy.
The layout of the world also doesn't make sense. In DS 1, while down at the hydra boss, if you look up you can see the Undead Burg and physically climb up the tower to it, so the world had a consistent and believeable lay out. In DS 2 you reach the top of a tower you can see from a distance while approaching it. You already konw that the tower has an obvious top, yet when you reach the interior of the structure and get to the top, somehow there is a lift which takes you to a castle which lies surrounded by lava. It just chips away from your suspension of disbelief when you have moments like that. Or viewing what looks to be the tower of flame from Majula, but you reach it by walking a relatively much smaller distance. It seems that giving the player the ability to port from bonfire to bonfire, which is a feature I like, removed their sense of responsibility in making the world fit together logically.
A few other annoying points: your weapons break far too quickly, where it becomes nearly essential to carry 2 decent weapons to clear one damn area. The inclusion of auxiliarly healing items removes an interesting mechanic of trading off risk of dying vs not wasting some of an estus flask. The new invasion mechanic in the tomb of pharros bit is absolute pants, getting pulled in to a players world in room with waist deep water, they stand on a rock launching magic or arrows at you while 2 huge NPCs and a dog attack you is hardly fair. You can argue that the Souls games aren't about fairness, and you'd be right, but this isn't hard, or a challenge, it's just completely frustrating because the odds are nearly always insurmountable. I hold my own when I get invaded in a more normal context, killing between 60 - 70% of my invaders, yet this invasion type places you at a severe disadvantage.
The boss fights suffer from similar problems, not being difficult through interesting abilities or mechanics, but just by having multiple enemies to fight. Some of these boss encounters are still very simple, yet are just made awkward by having attacks coming from multiple sides.
Overall though, it is a very fun game, and I would indeed recommend it. But don't buy it on steam, you can get physical copies for a significant discount (counter intuitive, right?). However if you played the original Dark Souls, it's a little bit disappointing and hollow in some respects. It's a solid 7.5/10, but certainly lives in the shadow of its predecessor.

Any time I'm given a choice between stealth and action, I go stealth. I love the hold-your-breath tension of hoping a guard didn't spot you and the hard-earned triumph of executing a perfectly timed plan. Dishonored 2 delivers that sneaky satisfaction, arming you with stealth essentials like hiding bodies, peering through keyholes, and silent takedowns. But it's also an incredible engine for gleeful chaos, one so engrossing and amusing that I kind of accidentally beat the entire campaign raining hilarious, elaborate death on my enemies.
I kicked people through skylights, blasted them off seaside cliffs, lured them into bottlenecks and watched as my carefully placed shrapnel mine shredded them. At one point, I got murdered badly, so I reloaded a recent quicksave, shot a guard with incendiary bolt, and blew up another four with one grenade when they ran to help. Sadistic? Yes. But also incredibly satisfying from a gameplay standpoint. Moments like that happen frequently in Dishonored 2 because it's as much a toy box as it is a game. It's meant to be experimented with. It rewards and even demands creativity.

First the elephant in the room. Dishonored 2 doesn't run very well on the technical end and has some pretty questionable performance overall. I have a PC that was great when I built it in 2014 and three years later is merely probably good but not great. My graphics card is a GTX 750Ti, my processor is an intel quad core i5-4670k and I've got 16 gigs of ram if you're wondering. In order to get Dishonored 2 to run smoothly I had to halve the resolution and crank most of the graphical settings down to either their lowest or second lowest states. Once I did that however it ran just fine and remained pretty enough to look at even still. I should also note that while the game is poorly optimized in those respects it's plenty stable once you get it running smoothly and nor are the graphics or mechanics marred by in-game glitches.
So with that being the case why am I recommending the game then? Well because it's incredibly fun and worthy sequal to one of my all time favorite games. If you've played the original Dishonored you probably know whether you want to play more of it with new mechanics, powers and a myriad of improvments. If you haven't played the original Dishonored then I strongly suggest you go buy it and it's DLCs first for peanuts the next time they go on sale.
Dishonored is a stealth, magic and gadget focused first person slasher/shooter that can be played in many different ways and offers a very strong attention to detail. It takes place in a fantastically creative fantasy world based on various European cultures during the Age of Reason and styles of speculative fiction from around the same time.
Arkane Studios employs some of the same creators who worked on the Thief trilogy and it shows both in the gameplay and in the worldbuilding. This is a series that can appeal to both an audience that really likes to get immersed in a gameworld as well as those who simply prefer using a deep set of gameplay mechanics to enact absolute bloody mayhem. Things both really cool and hilarious are pretty much bound to happen when you play Dishonored, especially if you're quick witted and have a bit of a sadistic bent.

I've never played an old-school adventure game before, but I took to this one right away. It does have some deep nostalgia (one of the characters runs a Commodore 64) as well as a number of 80s pop-culture references. There is plenty for geeks to love, including a classic Con with sexy Riker. The storyline, particularly between Dolores and her father Franklin, is complex and actually quite moving. It was really interesting to see the way these five character's lives came together and how they had to collaborate to achieve individual ends. With only a handful of exceptions, the solutions to the puzzles made a lot of sense (I was particularly proud of figuring out the county map puzzle all on my own.)
Even though I'm new to these kinds of games, I played on Hard mode and made it through okay, in about 22 hours of play time. I did use the HintTron3000 maybe seven times, and in every case I was extremely close to having figured it out on my own. A lot of my errors were stupid ones that were probably more a result of not having played this style of game before. I like that the Hint machine starts out very vague, then slowly gets more specific, so it's not like it just hands you the answer straightaway.
I had so much fun playing this game, but I have to admit, the ending was a letdown. It was clever, unexpected, and a great homage to game development in general, but it was emotionally unsatisfying. After growing attached to the characters and wanting to help them, it felt like an unfair twist. The C64 terminal scene at the very end of the end credits, while also amazingly clever, makes the sense of disillusionment even worse. Still, I would play games by the same developers and hope they come out with something similar soon. It's been a long time since I've enjoyed a game so much.

Move over LOST, we have a new high watermark for an ending so bad that it poisons the entire work. Up until that point the game had mostly good puzzle design, and writing that whiffed more punchlines than it hit, but none of that matters after the malignant cancer of the conclusion. Based on Thimbleweed Park's final revelation I am glad that Ron Gilbert never got a chance to make a sequel to Monkey Island 2, and it hurts me to be able to honestly say that now.

A good adventure game with great visual and sounds and some laugh out loud humor at some points.
Is it as good as or better than classics like Monkey Island or Space Quest? I'd say no. I think it's partially because they try to do too much such as having so many playable characters. The result of this being that some puzzles and story elements just feel really "light" and not fully developed to their full potential. This leads to some things in the game being more complex than they need to be and others feeling like their interaction and/or purpose is so little you can't help but ask "did this really need to be in the game?"
But it's definitely worth picking up if you're a fan of the genre as it packs in a decent amount of hours of gameplay and enough of an enganging story to keep your interest.
The price seems fair for what you get so I'd say it's worth getting even when it's not on sale. It's a good game despite not being quite to the level of the well thought out, executed and polished Sierra adventure games of the 80's/90's.

Well fool me once shame on you, fool me twice shame on me, I guess.  I’ve always have had a problem with Ron Gilbert games.  I feel he tends to go overboard with jokes.  That being said I do love Monkey Island 1 and Maniac Mansion.  However, I always despised the ending of Monkey Island 2.  I loved Monkey Island 1 so much.  I adored the cast of characters and the insane quirky pirate adventure they were on.  I immediately picked up Monkey Island 2 and loved everything about that…until I got to the ending which I found to be horrendous.  Ron Gilbert set up such a great tale and was literally everything I wanted in a Monkey Island sequel…but that ending, my god.  I’m not even sure how it’s possible to blow an ending so bad.  I hated everything about it.
That is until now.  The ending of Thimbleweed Park literally somehow manages to be worse than Monkey Island 2, it’s just garbage and because of that I can’t recommend it and would go so far as to say it’s pointless to ever play a Ron Gilbert game ever again at least for me.  Which is a real shame, because until that ending I would say Thimbleweed Park is one of the best modern day adventure games.
The presentation is gorgeous.  The artwork and individual screens just look stunning.  The puzzles are almost border on that line of impossible and just right.  The biggest stumbling blocks can be figuring out where you are even supposed to go as opposed to figuring out the actual puzzles.  The fact you need to switch between multiple characters does complicate things, but it all works out very well.  The only puzzle that really just completely confused me was the trampoline puzzle, I just could not figure it out.  After looking up the answer I felt real stupid.  Which is basically how you want to feel when playing an adventure game.  What you don’t want is too look up the answer and say, “that is the dumbest solution I ever heard of in my life, the person who made this game is dumb and should never be allowed to ever make a videogame again.”  No puzzle in this game ever made me feel that way, so this game was by far exceeding all my expectations.
I also felt the game was funny, genuinely funny…well for the most part anyway.  I don’t know what they were thinking with the character of Ransome the clown.  I didn’t find it funny at all, all of his scenes were quite arduous to get through.  Maybe someone likes him, but I didn’t find it funny at all and despised his entire character.  I do wish the 2 FBI agents got to interact more together, because I enjoyed their banter immensely.  I also did enjoy all the voice acting a lot.  Everyone just did a stellar job.
With all that being said I got to now start dumping on the game, because the story is what caused me to not recommend the game.  The start is exactly what I want.  It sets up a wonderfully quirky murder mystery with a strong Twin Peaks/Xfiles vibe.  The game starts with 2 FBI agents coming to the small town of Thimbleweed to investigate a murder and then they start digging into the towns dirty laundry.  In my opinion the best adventure games are either straight up murder mysteries or some other type of mystery so I was super on board with this games story. During the game you meet a cast of bizarre/quirky characters that join your party and you can switch back and forth between them.  I guess the rest is spoilers:
Due to that I just can’t recommend this game, no matter how good the rest of it is and the rest of it is very good.
Some of the humor's a little dumb, but it's worthwhile over all.  The puzzles are pretty fair; I don't think I got stuck enough I had to look up a hint more than once.

When I first played The Evil Within, I was torn. I have just started playing The Evil Within 2, and my god, they have completely rewritten this game from the ground up. I played the first Evil Within on PS4 with high hopes for a spiritual successor from the mind that brought us Resident Evil.  I believe starting over with a new team and publisher limited the scope of the first game as evidenced by the limited confines of the game world and stilted animations of the player character.  Much to my surprise a sequel was greenlit which appears to flesh out most of its shortcomings not unlike the way RE gave way to RE2.
While I remain apprehensive about the quality of the narrative which likely has no aspirations to surpass the original I am very impressed with how much better this game controls.  Sebastian feels fluid in motion compared to the first game and the graphics are wonderful to behold.  Union functions as a much more open world survival experience that lets you search nooks and crannies for secrets compared to the claustrophic hallways of the first game.
The upgrade and crafting systems appear to offer plenty of depth to keep you going even through a new game + run.
You are constantly engaged with how to best make use of limited resources to manufacture ammunition optimal to your present situation.
Horror is quite subjective in terms of what it takes to curdle one's blood but the creatures I have encountered thus far offer up a reimagining of zombies that don't fail to make an impression alongside boss monsters that are creative amalgamations of the tropes you'll find in Hollywood.  I would offer an A for effort as all of these creatures are sure to fire up the fight or flight response in any who venture forth.
Overall:
Graphics - 10
Controls - 10
Plot - If the first one didn't make you cringe I doubt this one can do any worse.
Interface - Servicable compared to so many console to PC titles of late.  Button mapping for controller or keyboard play and plenty of graphics/audio options to tweak.
Fun factor - If you love survival horror games this is right up there with RE4 in my book.

Deus Ex: Invisible War is a game that, in my opinion, receives WAY too much flak. Ok, it's not on the EXACT same level as the original, but the game is a must-buy for any true fan of the Deus Ex franchise. The gameplay is fun, challenging on occasion as it should be, and the story is very in-depth, as you would come to expect, with many Datacubes and News Terminals to hear about the world from. Other than the gripes outlined below, I can see no reason that this game gets as much crap as it does.
#1 - The interface. It's just flat-out not as good as the original.
#2 - Stability. I've not technically beaten this game yet. I only just now reached the abandoned VersaLife base near the end of the game, and I've been completely stopped dead in my tracks as far as Progression is concerned. I've been trying for little over 40 minutes now, and I crash almost every 1-2 minutes, or whenever I try to headshot someone with my sniper rifle.
#3 - The Universal Ammo system. I shouldn't need to explain this one, but it essentially makes it very hard to have more than one weapon. I for one carry many different weapons, including a Silenced Pistol/Sniper Rifle, Shotgun, and a SMG. Shared ammo just doesn't work in a game like this.
Although this may not be a worthy sequel to the original game(which is my favorite game of all time), it is still a great game if you don't compare it to the first game.

If you are a fan of the series and you haven't played it, I suggest you do.

The original Deus Ex is one of the best games ever made, so when Invisible War suffers from a bad reputation, I assumed it was undeserved. I assumed that it would at least be "pretty ok", and that its poor ratings were due to people comparing it to the first game. Holy cow, was I wrong.
This game is atrociously bad, and not just compared to its older brother. It's genuinely a waste of time and money completely by itself. In short: Had I known how frustratingly bad Invisible War was, I wouldn't even have picked it up for free.
Some of the bad parts (no real spoilers):
- The writing. While the story builds on Deus Ex, you get no build-up, no twists (excepting a few incredibly obvious attempts), no suspense, no room for wondering or doubting. You're never allowed to be curious about the world, the backstory or the events of the past, as most of this is just dumped bluntly at your feet. At one point you walk into a bunker, find some high-level people, and out of nowhere these complete strangers start telling you about their deepest, darkest secrets.
- The pacing. At times, people will warn you that "someone has a secret agenda for you", and you can be certain that within two minutes that same "someone" will give you a call to explain their agenda for you, right to your face.
- The level design. Pretty much every single level is a tiny, cramped area. For reference, the 'ton Hotel in Deus Ex is one of the smaller levels in that game, but it would easily fit in as one of the larger levels in Invisible War. This means you'll enjoy a lot more loading screens a lot more often, but it also makes the game feel so much more shallow: When security HQ is 15 meters from the doorstep of the terrorists, suspension of disbelief drops like a rock. It also means walking through four levels blasting bad guys, then walking back through four empty levels.
- The loading screens. Loading time is usually not an issue for me, with a fast SSD in a fast PC. Invisible War doesn't care. Every so often it goes through a complicated series of steps to load a new level, which includes shutting down the rendering engine to flash you your desktop for a few seconds, then going all white for a while as it restarts, and then it starts actually loading, which takes another 10-15 seconds.
- The number of loading screens. In one typical part of the game, you go through a door - loading screen - across a square - loading screen - across a room to talk to someone, then back out - loading screen - around a corner and down a street - loading screen - down some stairs, talk to a guy, and then retrace the whole route with all the loading screens all over again. Steam tells me I've had the game running some 12 hours, but my save game clock tells me I have 7,5 hours playtime. Including a little menu browsing, that means I have likely spent a quarter of my ingame time looking at loading screens.
- The AI. It is so bad it can sometimes be an involuntary source of rare fun. At one point, members of two opposing factions are involved in a firefight, while a couple of guards stroll idly through the crossfire, taking no notice. As the fight ends, the same guards suddenly freak out over the bodies at their feet - "Ah! A body! There's been a murder! You won't get away with this", they exclaim, and then just keep walking. On a different occasion, an NPC shoots another NPC, and then freaks out over the body *which he just made*. "There's been a murder!" - no, really? And that's saying nothing of the shoddy combat AI, nor the incredibly poor search AI. You can actually hide from enemies by standing on the other side of a glass door, or by closing an air vent cover, and they will have no idea where you went.
- Graphics – and I don't mean "it's ugly", I mean it's really poorly designed. Most weapons are close to identical both when equipped and as inventory icons. With a few exceptions, it's hard to tell what things you can pick up in the field really is (except blinky and futuristic). Are those credit chips, datacubes, or maybe weapon modifications? Who knows! Better break into this locker to find out.
- User interface. Of all the compromises made to make this game possible to run for its intended Xbox, this is likely the worst. Honestly, the UI of Invisible War is worse than trying to do internet banking with a broken gamepad.
I could go on for a long time - this is in no way a complete list - but honestly, if you still think it "can't be that bad", go right ahead and buy it. Or save your money, go on YouTube and find a "let's play" video. I enjoyed some 25 hours of fun on my last Deus Ex playthrough. In Invisible War, it took me less than 8 hours to reach the 2nd to last level. Then I just decided I couldn't be bothered, uninstalled it, and would rather just read about the ending than suffer through more.

Oh man. This will be part review and part manifesto. Does Steam have a limit to the length of reviews?!
While you may only see a few minutes of me playing this game, I've actually logged hours with The Houchi Play when it was on the XBox 360 Indie Games store. Pretty sure I paid $2 there as well, or whatever the equivelant in Microsoft Points was.
In "The Houchi Play" you play as Taro Heibon, an IT engineer in City X. A family man who secretly desires to be treated like a pig, a dog and otherwise humiliated by girls in cosplay outfits. To accomplish the goal, you engage in a butt-scooting simulator punctuated by brief drinking games (with a boost power-up for perfect chugging). Do so to creep up on the ladies when they're not paying attention.  Different girls have different patterns and behaviors. It's kinda a stripped down sneaking version of Punch-Out. You have to learn the different character's (somewhat limited) tells and sneak around based on that. The pixel graphics a great and harkent back tot he NEC PC titles of the 90's. Solid soundtrack and the controls feel good. The depth and difficulty is on par with an arcade game, replayability only for novelty or highscore hunting purposes.
Kohei Gallery had a few titles on that marketplace and the one thing they all had in common was irreverant charm. There's something about wacky♥♥♥♥♥ Japanese video games that the world is currently lacking. It might just be me on my old man soapbox, but there was a time where a small team or a single person could create a game. That offered unparalelled freedom compared to what you'll find today. Games are big business. When a publisher is spending hundreds of millions of dollars, they're not likely to take a lot of risks. It saddens me that you just don't see bizarre Japanese games like the days of old. Games like The Houchi Play give me hope that the world hasn't given up on making weird video games.
I'm thrilled that Kohei Gallery is now on Steam and can't wait for more.

There were a few glitches I ran into when playing this game but it did not take away from the overall experience. If you enjoyed the first, you should certainly buy this game when it's on sale. I came into Invisible War expecting the hatred to mostly be the result of the high bar set by the first game. Now that I've actually played it, I can safely say that this is a bad game even outside the context of the vastly superiror Deus Ex and Human Revolution. Bugs abound, the story is boring and full of holes, combat is inane, and most of the biomods are completely uninteresting.
(NOTE: My playtime is inaccurate. I had to play offline because of an obnoxious design flaw that has the game start a new process every time you go to a new area - Steam interprets this as restarting the game and sends annoying popups to all your friends every 5 minutes. My actual time with the game was around 12 hours.)
Pros:
- You can throw furniture at people's heads. Everyone has 5-7 lines of dialogue to complain about you doing this and a funny recoil animation. They'll never go hostile despite threatening to attack. It's fun, and I did it to basically everyone in the game once I realized it wasn't any good.
- You can kill everyone. There are only lasting consequneces for killing plot characters, though, and even those are fairly negligible. See cons.
- The voice acting is generally pretty good. A few minor NPCs do their best to ruin that.
Cons:
- Bugs. So many bugs. A few of the ones I encountered: Multitools sometimes won't stack or count correctly because the devs couldn't ID things correctly, autosaves will randomly delete and send you back 30 minutes, one full CTD, ragdolls try to reach the fourth dimension when shot by turrets or patrol bots, and tons of minor inconveniences like small items not being accessible behind useless aesthetics with large hitboxes or the light from lamps not remotely matching where the bulb is pointed.
- The story is terrible. It tries to be deep, but mostly ends up being nonsensical. International air travel hasn't existed for 20 years, supposedly, but there's a private pilot hanging out in a slum bar in the first area you visit. He owns a Harrier and can fly to Cairo from Seattle.
- There's basically no music.
- The AI is incredibly stupid. You can kill people by pushing flaming barrels into them and no one will care. In combat, they'll stand still with their backs to you for no reason and all try to be in exactly the same spot. The only real threat comes the lack of health restoration in the early game.
- Once you get a sniper rifle, there is no reason to use anything else. It can kill any human enemy (with a very late game exception) in one shot from any distance provided you hit them in the head, which isn't challenging since they're so fond of standing still. Pistols do pathetic damage, shotgun damage dropoff is too high, and all other weapons drain ammo too quickly to be worth using.
- Ammo is shared between all weapons and obnoxiously rare. Quite a few enemy types apparently fire using dark magic and will never drop ammo.
- You can kill everyone, but nobody cares. I walked into a nightclub and proceeded to murder everyone, including a security chief and the Culture Minister of Seattle. The police outside didn't care, and no one ever brought it up again.
- Quests that clearly should be mutually exclusive aren't. You can take a quest to become the enemy of the Omar and the ally of the Omar. If you finish the enemy quest first, you'll briefly be penalized, but then can still reach friend status by completing the other quest. Another early quest pair involving rival businesses can also have both halves completely for full reward.
- No meaningful choices until the end.
- Bad level design. Where Human Revolution and Deus Ex have multiple routes into everything and allow for a stealth approach, Invisible War rarely has alternate routes more interesting than air ducts and seemingly goes out of its way to make stealth unviable.
-------

Now just to be up front; this game makes bad sequels look bad.  After the sheer joy of the first Deus Ex, I was very excited to give this one a try; too bad for me.
While you can still find echoes of the open, multi-method gameplay that Deus Ex is known for, the overall experience is dull.  The AI appears less capable, and the voice acting does nothing to make up for the limitations.  The story just feels less compelling, and they even have one massively contradicting feature from the previous narrative (no spoiler here).  The individual maps are tiny and relatively featureless, and lack enough NPCs to give them life (even the night club’s population is a joke).  There are also no transition animations/mini-movies, which is painful given the amount of traveling you do (remember the small maps?).
Moving on from the atmosphere, the gameplay reeks of a bad console port.  Your options for character customization are a far cry from the previous title; there are less augmentations and items to play with, too.  I also found a severe imbalance concerning ammunition.  If you don’t play it safe and stockpile munitions by the time you’ve got heavy hitters coming at you, and you didn’t plan on using stealth the whole way through (kinda go hand-in-hand, right?) then things get painful.  Oh, and all weapons are supplied by one ammo type, and you can only carry so much.  Not to say, however, that this game is overly challenging all the way through (quite the opposite).
Just everything about this game was “less” than its predecessor.  Unless you are planning to purchase just out of dedication to the Deus Ex franchise, don’t waste your time with this one.

It is with some very mixed feelings that I DO recommend this game. I wouldn't call me playing it a waste of time, because I have played plenty of games worse than this one. The game is awash with bugs - but many are in my opinion only aestethic, and does not affect the general gameplay as much. Sure the floating objects, invisible spider-bots and massive amount of clipping (mostly in cinematics) are disturbing - but again, nothing that should deteriorate you from playing this game, because it does function still.
The ragdoll-graphics bring both joy and annoyance - at times they are hilarious (yes, mostly at the beginning of the game), but at other times they are just plainly frustrating. Not to mention even a bit surreal - but extremely surreal. Sure, this ordinary enemy takes 10 shots to his torso and still lives (like what?), but one shot to the head and he's tossed like 30 feet out from a balcony. From a pistol-shot. With a silencer.
The loading-screens are many, and extremely frustrating. My first (and only, thank God) play-through of this game is roughly 18 hours. Not 18 hours that I was tormented non-stop. More like 3 hours of "damn, this is actually a very good game!" and 15 hours of "omg, I just wanna finish this game so I can move on". Point is, without the extreme amount of loading-screens every 5-10 minutes, my play-time could have been shaved down to like 11 hours or something. Not to mention random crashes (five in my play-through), and the fact that every time the game moves on to another loading-screen it minimizes to my desktop - stays that way for about 20 seconds and then resumes to the loading-screen which is another 30-40 seconds of waiting. And it randomize my oh-so-carefully organized desktop each and every ♥♥♥♥ing time, too.
I didn't really have a problem with the HUD, I thought it was aestethically acceptable and easy to learn and understand. What I did have a problem with was the over-simplification of the biomods, and inventory-screen. Only 5 slots to fill with biomods, and none the ordinary biomods (except for the muscle-thing that expand you inventory) are that appealing seeing as you get a hold of your first supposedly illeagal - and almost too helpful - biomod after about 1 hour of play.
The story of the game is good. Not as good as the first Deus Ex, mind you. But it is still good, and frankly was the only thing that kept me going and completing the game. I think the level-design negatively impact the story-line and sort of cramps the ability to go about everything the way you could in the first Deus Ex, but on the other end the level-design did promote a more direct, fast-paced sort of action (seeing as upgrading the speed-biomod to max-level could be done in about 2 hours of game-time, and thus could be activated basically non-stop the rest of the game due to low bioenergy-consumption and a complete overload of energy-cells throughout the game).
To sum it up: Play this game for the story. It will not perform miracles gameplay-wise. The storyline isn't fantastic either, but I can't call it a waste of time because I did enjoy building upon the legacy that JC Denton left in the original game. I think with a bit more effort from the developers, that this game could have been somewhat better and more of a worthy sequel to the 1st Deus Ex, as opposed to the bleak shadow of the 1st game that it is today. The game is worth 7 €, but I got it on a sale, which somehow eased the discomfort I experienced while playing it.
60/100

Alien: Isolation is a stealth-based survival horror game from the Alien franchaise taking place 15 years after the original movie that puts the player in the shoes of Amanda Ripley, Ellen's daughter and also an engineer working for the Weyland-Yutani corporation, as she tries to discover her mother's fate aboard Sevastopol, a derelict space station on a serious crisis.
To begin with, fans of the Alien series will totally be pleased: the general design of the game (on top of displaying nice graphics and level design) heavily borrows is art style from the movies and the sounds departments is particularly rich. The developers have also made their best effort at putting in the videogame that old horror/helplessness feel the first Alien move had, but see below for details.
In true stealth-based fashion, the main objective of Isolation is to follow the directions you are given towards the goal you are currently given till you are directed to another while basically a horde of enemies is after your blood and you don't have enough health or advanced weaponry to defeat them all safely, so you have to resort to sneaking and sitraction tactics. The enemies you'll have to evade are Sevastopol's human survivors (who wield guns and easily dispatched or dodged with stealth), Working Joe androids (which are synthetic enemies incredibly resiliant to damage and better left by themselves) and, of course, the titular alien.
The Alien is the reccuring enemy of Isolation and will stalk every level in an effort to kill you, something it's very adept at doing: it's completely undamaged by all your weapons and devices (althought some can make it retreat for a while), very easy to allert, capable of killing Amanda in one hit, not afraid to use stealth tactics against you and provided by the developers with an adaptive strategy (for instance, a hidden spot will rarely fool the alien twice or thrice, forcing you to change distractions and position frequently). In short, the alien provides the main horror source for the whole game and dealing with it should be your first priority. The beast also interacts with the other enemies and the environment, althought provoking its attention may be fatal to you.
In order to proceed in your mission, Isolation provides you with different tools you can either find lying around in the levels or craft yourself with the components you can find during moments of (relative) peace. Some are proper weapons which, in true survival horror flavor, should be used sparingly and are more or less effective depending on the enemy; other are tools you can use to create a distraction, like flares or noisemakers, althought they could attract unwanted attention; other still are mainly utilities required to survive your journey, like batteries for your flashlight or medikits to recover health. Resources aboard Sevastopol aren't exactly abundant, forcing you to use the items at your disposal only in a pinch or when there aren't other alternatives. Your most important tool remains the motion tracker, which allows you to get a glare of your enemies general location and prepare your next move and also serves as a guide towards your objective (but it should be noted that in some instances it can get painfully inaccurate, which could as well lead to your death while you desperately try to figure out where to go or what to do next). Amanda can also use her engineering talents to activate various devices aboard the station: some are required to progress through the story, while others can sway the alien and the other enemies.
It's also worth mentioning that the difficulty levels in Isolation are rather meaningful and drastically change the whole experience: the easy setting will often make your enemies miss your presence entirely, medium is a rather average stealth fare and hard basically makes the alien susceptible to even the smallest action you can perform and enemy attacks nearly one-hit kills.
Isolation's stealthy and horror-driven gameplay works well in the long run, save for two minor issue. First, the mission introducing the alien as an active threat is arguably the hardest sequence in the entire game: the beast is far more aggressive than anywhere in the later levels and the whole mission happens rather early (around the fourth or fifth mission or so). Second, the game's main story pace starts to really fall apart in the later stages: while the game seems to end for good at two or three points in the narrative, you discover soon enough that there are still filler-ish things to be done for an hour or two longer. At a certain point you'll just try to waltz through the remaining areas hoping to finish the game as soon as possible and be done with it.
Aside from the main campaign, Isolation also offers a Survival Mode, which is about putting up an endurance round against the alien for as long as possible using the tools and environments you are given.
In short, Alien: Isolation is the videogame with an Alien license the fans of the series were waiting for all these years and an excellent stealth horror title for the rest of the world

How to make stir fry;
Ingredients:
-2 tablespoons of vegetable oil
-1 red bell pepper, matchstick style
-2 carrots, sliced thin af
-1 1/2 cups of fresh broccoli
-1 pound of beef sirloin cut into 2" strips
-1 green onion, chop that thing
-1 teaspoon on minced garlic
-2 tablespoons of sesame seeds, toasted
-2 tablespoons of soy sauce
Directions:
Heat vegetable oil in a large skillet over med-high heat; cook and stir the beeg until browned - that takes like 3-4 minutes usually. Move the beef to the side and add the broccoli, bell pepper, carrots, green onion, and garlic into the center of the work station. Cook the vegetables for 2 minutes, then stir the beef into the vegetables and season it with soy sauce and sesame seeds. Cook and stir until the vegetables are tender, should take around 2 mintes.

Fast, easy yet challenging at times with a touching story and great soundtrack, Eternal Senia is without a doubt one of the best RPG Maker games that I have played in a long time. It is also free so this is definitely worth trying.
The only drawback I have in this game is the pre-written spawn time and locations of monsters; if you leave and re-enter the room, monsters will spawn at the exact same positions and move exactly the same. This makes the game feel unnatural and scripted. Grinding is also a main aspect of this game, so be prepared to spend a couple minutes. The combat system is very simple though, so it shouldn't be a bother.
Eternal Senia leaves a great space for plot development so I would be excited to see future installments of the game, hopefully an entire series that will eventually develop into a fully respected title.

The good: The puzzles were relatively well-balanced and reveled in their own absurdity while still providing logical solutions. I was never forced to use the hint line or summon Google to solve a puzzle and doubt many veteran point-and-click players will have to either. Even in the most frustrating situations, the game rewards patience and trial-and-error.
The bad: Many of the side-characters and in-jokes become irritating and prevent the game from succeeding as an oddball dark comedy. The constant breach of the fourth wall never felt clever or interesting and resulted in more than a few cringe moments. The game works far better as a murder mystery than it does as a pseudo-self-aware journey through adventure gaming history. The final act is the most disappointing of all, rushing the characters to a forced conclusion that tried with all its might to be cathartic and just ended up feeling like bad fan fiction.
Thimbleweed Park scratched the my Monkey Island itch that no point-and-click in recent history has been able to, despite many odd plot holes and a painfully underwhelming conclusion. If you can look past the disappointing story, it's definitely a world worth getting lost in.

Thimbleweed Park is a game where to take control of several characters in order to solve, to begin with, the murder of a European businessman (but it soon escalates to a wider mystery). It is set in Thimbleweed Park, a mysterious town where strange things keep happening.
+Thimbleweed Park is full of interesting characters that are brilliantly written and designed.
+There is a sharp sense of humour that remains throughout the game.
+Taken control of many characters is a fun mechanic that is quite well executed.

+It takes a lot of the positive elements from classic adventure games (Monkey Island, The Day of the Tentacle, etc.)
+A really beautiful 8-bit-eque art style.
-While the story does start off could and the mystery is very interesting, I found that towards the end the story became somewhat ridiculous.
-Some threads are left open and there are a few scenes that are just never explained.
-Trying to get all of the characters set up in the right place for one puzzle is occassionally a needlessly difficult task.
Thimbleweed Park is, overall, a fun game. It doesn't take itself to seriously so some of the story problems don't cause massive issues or annoyance through the game. I would've liked it if some of the stranger events could have been tied up though.
7/10

System Shock is the predecessor to BioShock...if you enjoyed BioShock, System Shock 2 is worth playing. Make sure you get the updated models and texture pack as it adds a few years to the game's overall aesthetic. I played this game through in the year 2016 and it was still quite amazing. The atmosphere had me shaking in my skin a couple times -- this game would have scared the crap out of me in earlier years!
SS2 is not great in the realm of combat itself, as long as you use the right tools you can breeze through any encounter (*ahem* invisibility + AoE fire). The game's charm comes from playing through the story and experiencing the world. Just as with BioShock, you find recordings of the ship's inhabitants as you explore, giving you background narrative and sometimes useful information such as combination codes.
Leveling your character is quite enjoyable. Each upgrade makes you feel more powerful -- there are no "micro" upgrades in this game: each one really helps in their respective realms!
Overall I highly enjoyed this game, and with System Shock 3 in development, I now have the background story for when I play that.

Deus Ex: Invisible War is a for the most part linear FPS-RPG in a sinister Sci-Fi setting.
It's graphics pale compared to other titles using the same engine, levels seem a bit confined especially when compared to the first
and the inventory is tiny - design concessions that had to be made in order for a release on the original Xbox console to be possible.
Frequent loading screens in between small level sections can be somewhat annoying and take between 20-30 seconds even on a SSD. (Save regularly to avoid having to replay lenghty sections because very rarely the game did crash on me and even corrupted a save-file once.)
Sounds bad? Nah.
I played through the game close to its release and played through it again just now. Don't be fooled into thinking this is the abysmal game enthusiasts of the first game often make it out to be. It's less complex in just about every aspect, yes, but it still an enjoyable experience for fans of the series and FPS-RPG fans alike. Shooting feels fine, weapons and gadgets/biomods are fun to use, different approaches to enemy encounters / completing objectives are possible and encouraged, even some plot altering decisions can be made.
Overall it was an enjoyable 20 hour experience (if you take your time like me, and try to find up to six special weapons well hidden in the game). A recommendation when on sale, especially for fans of the first game for story reasons and for fans of the cyberpunk/noir/dark Sci-Fi genres.
(Note: I ran this game on Win 8.1 64-Bit using the community texture pack, at 1080p resolution, 120 FOV and reduced HUD size. Using all these tweaks (to be found in the community section here on steam) I even found it visually to be a somewhat pleasing experience.)

If this game has taught me anything, it is to take what others say with a grain of salt. I went into this expecting an experience akin to that of arm wrestling with a chainsaw, but I guess that everyone's talk of this game lowered my expectations to unreasonable depths. Invisible War is, while not as good as its predecessor, a good game.
A big complaint I notice is the "consolization", the clear downgrade in many aspects of the overall design of the first game, including large levels, complex controls, dynamic damage, skills, and swimming. (The multiplayer is gone as well.) There is a lack of control options, which correlated directly to removal of leaning, reduced toolbelt size and biomod (augmentation) slots, and an ugly HUD. As for the size of areas, I would chalk that up to incredibly sloppy coding and graphics that were ahead of their time. One might look at the game's system requirements and then remember that this released in North America in 2003. However, as far as I'm concerned, it is still little excuse; The smaller areas force a different style of gameplay, and the frequency and time of the loading screens is just annoying.
Atmosphere-wise, there is nothing wrong. The graphics are great, and the story, a direct sequel, I would say surpasses that of the original, at least in terms of depth. In terms of how memorable the characters are... eh, I don't really have much to say. Open-ended missions change the flow of the game. Rather than being given one main objective at a time a la the first game, the player is given multiple objectives from warring factions that ultimately branch to the end, and make the ending seem like more of a result of the path taken throughout the game, rather than a rushed decision made at the last minute, though the latter is certainly still possible should you enjoy being chaotic in choosing your allies.
Sadly, if the story is more open than the original, the same cannot be said for weapons and inventory management. Multitools and lockpicks are now one and the same. Items now only take up one slot each, so there is no need for inventory Tetris, but the small size can only be increased by installing and upgrading a specific biomod. Food can be stacked regardless of the type. Firearms have universal ammo, which I saw to be a self-defeating mechanism. In the original Deus Ex, running out of ammo for a weapon forced me to rethink my entire combat strategy and apply it until I could renew my supplies. Here, run out for one gun, you run out for just about everything else. On top of that, weapons can only take two mods at a time, and mods cannot be removed once applied.
Even with a decent variety of weapons, I found little point to using nonlethal tactics. At least during the first few hours of the first game, you would get reprimanded for it. Here, there is almost never a reason to not just kill enemies on the spot. Even when I do use a nonlethal weapon, the game treats the character as having died, and he or she will not appear again. The small area sizes, while not too restrictive, encourage more aggressive gameplay by giving very limited options as to approach.
The player has fewer biomods/augmentations at one time. Luckily, many of the classics are here, as well as some new ones to compensate for the ones which were pulled. The best change here is having three to choose from for any specific slot, and the ability to change between them should you have the materials. It's a fine way to keep the player from restarting when he's realized that the combination he's chosen to go with is ineffective.
I'm certain I've left something out, but this review has to end sometime. Even with all of its simplification problems, it manages to cling enough to the core Deus Ex gameplay. I plan on coming back to this sometime in the future, as I'm certain there's a lot more for me to discover, and the mission structure provides a great deal of replay value. Methinks people would treat this game better were it not called Deus Ex, but as it stands, Invisible War is a fine addition to the series.

Introduction
Generally speaking I have been disappointed with Alien franchise games - The odd notable exception aside (AvP 2) they have all been basically Doom with different guns and monsters - fun but not exactly stress inducing.
Although I love the film Aliens, Alien is one of my all time favourite movies and I had not considered it a possible subject for  a good game. Thankfully A:I has changed all that.
Gameplay
Like the movie it is not about going in all guns blazing, you don't get much in the way of guns and shooting them is typically the equivalent of ringing the dinner bell anyway (I've played through several times now and not killed anything with a gun).  No - this game is all about stealth. You have to spend pretty much the entire game on your knees crawling about in the dark because
running = noise = alien hears you = alien eats you
shooting = noise = alien hears you =  alien eats you
walking = high visibility = alien sees you = alien eats you
torch = high visibility = aliens sees you = alien eats you.
You spend a lot of time hiding in cupboards because you can hear the alien walking about (or worse see it through the slits in the cupboard) and you are too scared to come out. There was many a time I had to leave the game on pause while i went downstairs to watch something funny just to get my nerves back.
Artificial Intelligence
The alien is random in it's movements - you can save a game - hide in the corner of a room, the alien will come in and 4 out of 5 times it will not look in your direction - but on that 5th time - just when you thought it was following a set pattern it happens to glance to the right and see you. The later in the game the better the AI appears to be so the alien starts to be hovering around you - investigating the doors you recently opened and having a stroll right next to the cupboard you are too scared to get out of.
Graphics
Although the facial animations and models are good they are not exactly awe inspiring and are starting to look a bit old.
The alien itself is well realised and the way it walks about is very good.
The shop design is excellent - very nostalgic - lots of nice touches from the movie like that all monitor screens appear to be VHS tapes with bad tracking
Audio
Truly awesome - memories of the movie flood back at regular intervals when you hear certain sound effects and musical cues.
Plot
Not bad - but not that original - feels a bit like System Shock 2 in parts, lots of reading of dead peoples emails to reveal the reason behind the "accident" on the station
Duration
The game itself is very long (20 - 30 hrs) - and while this is refreshing in the modern day where a long game is deemed 5  hours i did feel it stretched some sections out a fraction too long.
Recommend trying to play it on hard difficulty as this gives you the proper sense of fear

I'm a pretty crappy writer so I apologize in advance.
Total Annihilation is an incredibly unique and intense RTS that was light-years ahead of its time and still is today. I still strongly prefer the original over the more spiritual-successor, Planetary Annihilation.
Total Annihilation features so many small features that just make it amazing, the battles can be huge and intense with massive amounts of units having a huge Warhammer 40k esque fight all on one screen, or the games can be slow and brilliantly thought out. This is a strategy game where you can win purely by 'defensive' play at times, something I find to be rather unique among a lot of strategy games that even today have rather narrow methods to win, usually by just having the larger and better offensive force, but not always in Total Annihilation.
A feature that makes Total Annihilation so unique is the true emphasis on a defensive playstyle, if you so desire. There are an impressive amount of options for defensive, slow play styles and faster, more offensive playstyles alike. You can choose to hunker down and improve your economy while building a large amount of turrets and upgrading to better ones over the course of the game, some are even capable of bombarding your opponent from the entire maps length, assuming you reach the demanding level of tech and economy required for them. Even tactical nukes can be constructed and launched over a map away if the game length and level of sustainable economy is reached. This allows for a lot of options for a lot of different types of players. There is also no real super demanding macro-memory required à la StarCraft II, making the game just a bit more accessable to newer players, especially in more team oriented game modes.
The game also features incredible physics for it's more 2.5 dimensional, isometric strategy experience. One of my favourite things about this game is seeing things like unit inaccuracy, especially when on the move or on unstable ground or even when taking pot-shots at something through the fog-of-war. Units will have better vision when on the high ground and worse vision when in a trench, making a lot of areas on maps incredibly strategic locations. There's even bullet physics, units will often adjust their aim higher or lower depending on the target, and when the steel corpses begin to litter the battlefield they will often block incoming rounds harmlessly while your units continue to trudge past the enemy fire. There's a gritty feeling seeing all your units charge an enemy fortified position only to begin seeing the missiles and rounds begin to rain down upon them and seeing a huge chunk of your force get obliterated by a large round, shaking the screen and sending chunks of steel flying in every direction, the steel "gibs" even damaging nearby units who get hit by them.
The game also features an amazing orchestral 'dynamic' music score written and composed by the one and only Jeremy Soule. The music really compliments an already fantastic game nicely, changing to a more brooding tone as you build up your base and switching to a more heart-pounding score as enemy fighters engage your army. It's an incredible soundtrack that you may even consider finding for your own music player. The sound design alone in this game is also very unique and give it a great distinct and 'mechanical' feel.
If there was one strategy that I think is criminally unknown to most people, this would have to be it. It's made an amazingly tight-knit community that continue to play the original and have a huge modding scene. (Seriously, try the Total Annihilation Escalation mod, it's just insanely good.) Some even going as far as recreating the Total Annihilation experience in full 3D via an open source engine called Spring, try Spring Total Annihilation out sometime, it has a great community still supporting it to this day.
Overall it's my favourite RTS game of all time, and I'm not even a huge RTS fan. It's incredibly exciting just to watch with an amazing soundtrack and huge, epic battles.

Highly, highly recommended to anybody who enjoys point & click gaming, and as an excellent introduction to the genre for those who've yet to dip their foot into this type of game.
Definitely go for the "hard" mode, and avoid the "hintline".  Give your brain time to mull over the puzzles, and don't feel rushed.  The satisfaction from eventually figuring it out on your own is what it's all about!

I didn't have a problem with the nature of the ending - just felt it could have been executed in a more interesting fashion.  I *really* hope these guys keep the momentum going with another game in this genre, as this was definitely a labor of love, and it showed, and I want more!

The campaign map is huge with a large variety of playable factions - and the DLCs add extra campaigns and even more factions. There's no hard time limit, and the game doesn't feel as much of a race as previous TW felt. Black Mesa was hyped up as a rework of Half Life 1 with modern technology, made how HL1 could have been done had it had access to more years of game design experience and a niftier engine.
This isn't what it is, though. It's really just a literal copypaste of Half Life 1 into a better graphical engine, with some areas shortened(though this isn't really BAD as such, since a lot of HL1 areas really dragged on) and some good music in places. If you ever played HL1, there's no purpose to playing this, since zero thought or original creativity went into it. If anything, Black Mesa feels like it MISSES opportunities to improve stuff, like removing some of the less well-thought-out sections(or fixing them, as far as is possible), or fixing things like grenades being thrown off-center of the aiming reticle, or the shotgun and SMG being painfully anemic to use.
Also a baffling decision to limit FOV to 90 unless you use console commands to jam it up to something that won't make you feel like you're wearing blinders.
Definitely don't pay a cent for this lazy project, it's impressive that they managed to drag it out for this long, considering how little work they did.

This game is platforming at its most basic.  The controls are exactly what they need to be for making almost but not quite pixel-perfect jumps, and the graphics, while hardly the best, offer a few well-designed visual backgrounds and are always functional enough to let you recognize what will kill you and what dangers are ahead.  The levels are well designed with just enough trickiness to offer potential traps but that the Single Life mode seems (at least to me) very much possible, some day, with enough practice.  And the levels are also fun, which I think is the most important part.  They are all very memorable in at least one way, and offer a variety of challenges.  They are good enough that I feel it is worth playing through the speedrun mode, and playing multiple rounds to attempt to reach A++ scores.
Basically, it is a well-crafted challenge platformer that is beatable by probably most people but also offers enough challenges that people will want to come back to it repeatedly, and is short enough that a full game is not a huge time sink and failing does not prohibit you from coming back and playing again because you felt like you spent too much time on it.  I would rank it better than average, and well worth the very low price of entry.

There is a TL;DR for those who fear the big wall of text.
Before I begin, no, it's not Skyrim with multiplayer. Take it as its' own thing. Also this massive wall of text is basically everything I could think about.
I have played almost every MMO out there. I played World of Warcraft, I played Maplestory, TERA, FFXIV, and I played Runscape for a time. I played the lesser known ones like The Secret World, Rohan, and Wildstar. ESO is the only game I have consistently played throughout the years. On steam I have 500+ hours on it already.
I started playing Elder Scrolls Online since beta, and when it first came out, it was terrible. Nothing was balanced, there was so little content. It lacked basic features that any and all MMOs have standard. Its opening day was really disappointing. Over the last year and a half this game has exploded and every time I read a patch notes I'm always massively impressed on where they are going. Little by little its becoming a true to life Elder Scrolls game. The game today is immensely cool, very balanced and a ton of fun. I don't even recognize it from a year ago. I really am sad that the initial release marked as a bad MMO.
Even from the start though, this game was insanely pretty, the character customization was on point. Orcs look like they should (finally) and Khajiits look proper. They didn't copy the Skyrim model types, this game feels more like Oblivion with updates. My one gripe about the characters is you need to purchase a certain pack in the store in order to make a any race any where. I got mine for free with my beta.
Combats pretty basic. 5 abilities with an "Ult". You don't need some fancy mouse or macros to beat other people in PVP. You can have two weapon sets that you can constantly switch between, but you don't need that to face stomp.
PVP is really fun. Some of the servers leave much to be desired, but the variety of what you can do is endless. The PVP area is quite massive (typical of an Elder Scrolls game) where you can either go blow up enemy factions' castles or you can quest. The Imperial City ( you need the Imperial Edition for this) is a vastly small battle arena. Its both cool and terrifying.
Questing is straight up hit and miss. I like the Aldmeri Dominion line, Daggerfall was OK. The DLCs have really good stories. World quests are just hit and miss. It feels like they started with the intention of having unique stories all over the place but reverted to using the same formulas over and over. No different from WoW I suppose.
Some people will tell you the subscriptions a waste of cash, but if you really can afford it, go for it. Its got some pretty nice perks to it like access to ALL the DLCs and soon you will have some extra customization tools. The EXP boost is nice and the monthly in game store cash is cool too. But the biggest is double bank space and a bottomless crafting bag.
The DLCs in this game barely are worth the $15-$20 they charge for you. They're a good filler if you have nothing better to do.. Orsinium was pretty good. Thieves guild was boring, but has Maw of Lorkhaj, Dark brotherhoods good, Shadow of the hist is aids. Morrowind is ok.
Everything is scaled to your level, so you can go wherever you want, there isn't too much that's impossible to do at low level.
The main sort of collection/farming part of this game is dyes. You can dye your gear with dyes you've collected from achievements. Most of these are easy but time consuming. Others happen by chance, and a few, well, you gotta be Emperor of Tamriel.
Crafting is the main source of gear. Getting armor/weapons to the best quality/level is a pain. It will take you quite literally 6 months to a year before you have the skills and levels it takes to make max level armor. Once you're there your friends can mooch off you.
Guilds feel useless other than grouping people for PVP/Dungeon parties, There really isn't much to them. They are the only source of an "Auction house," as there isn't one in the regular game. Guild stores are the only way to buy from other players at the moment, which is a drag.
Wana be a criminal? Emulate your real life? YOU CAN! You can steal, pick pocket, murder, flee guards etc. Not the best idea, as your bounty racks up quickly and it follows you everywhere. The guards in cities are unkillable, so it will throw a wrench in your ability to travel.
-=TL;DR=-
1. Combat: Easy, don't need no fancy mouse to MLGPRO someone.
2. The PVP: Its amazing. Blowing up castles, with questing on the side.
3. The questing: Hit and miss. Guild quests are cool. World quests sometimes are cookie cutter.
3. The dungeons: Pretty great. Veteran dungeons are insanely hard. Trials you need to be a big♥♥♥♥♥♥slayer.
4. World bosses. I can't solo most of them.
5. The classes. Non-restrictive. I can do what I want.
6. The crafting. Time consuming. Custom gear set ups and dyes are cool.
7. the DLCs: Orsinium was good. Dark Brotherhood was good. Rest are super meh.
8. Raiding is life.
9. You can do bad things. Kill fools.
10. Games fun. Lacks some social stuff. Overall my favorite MMO ever.
This game is still rough around the edges. There still are major problems. If I wanted to, I could pick this game apart. It is in no way perfect, but it is unique. It is ideal. It's exactly what I want. As much wrong as there is with it, there is a lot of right.

Introduction
Generally speaking I have been disappointed with Alien franchise games - The odd notable exception aside (AvP 2) they have all been basically Doom with different guns and monsters - fun but not exactly stress inducing.
Although I love the film Aliens, Alien is one of my all time favourite movies and I had not considered it a possible subject for  a good game. Thankfully A:I has changed all that.
Gameplay
Like the movie it is not about going in all guns blazing, you don't get much in the way of guns and shooting them is typically the equivalent of ringing the dinner bell anyway (I've played through several times now and not killed anything with a gun).  No - this game is all about stealth. You have to spend pretty much the entire game on your knees crawling about in the dark because
running = noise = alien hears you = alien eats you
shooting = noise = alien hears you =  alien eats you
walking = high visibility = alien sees you = alien eats you
torch = high visibility = aliens sees you = alien eats you.
You spend a lot of time hiding in cupboards because you can hear the alien walking about (or worse see it through the slits in the cupboard) and you are too scared to come out. There was many a time I had to leave the game on pause while i went downstairs to watch something funny just to get my nerves back.
Artificial Intelligence
The alien is random in it's movements - you can save a game - hide in the corner of a room, the alien will come in and 4 out of 5 times it will not look in your direction - but on that 5th time - just when you thought it was following a set pattern it happens to glance to the right and see you. The later in the game the better the AI appears to be so the alien starts to be hovering around you - investigating the doors you recently opened and having a stroll right next to the cupboard you are too scared to get out of.
Graphics
Although the facial animations and models are good they are not exactly awe inspiring and are starting to look a bit old.
The alien itself is well realised and the way it walks about is very good.
The shop design is excellent - very nostalgic - lots of nice touches from the movie like that all monitor screens appear to be VHS tapes with bad tracking
Audio
Truly awesome - memories of the movie flood back at regular intervals when you hear certain sound effects and musical cues.
Plot
Not bad - but not that original - feels a bit like System Shock 2 in parts, lots of reading of dead peoples emails to reveal the reason behind the "accident" on the station
Duration
The game itself is very long (20 - 30 hrs) - and while this is refreshing in the modern day where a long game is deemed 5  hours i did feel it stretched some sections out a fraction too long.
Recommend trying to play it on hard difficulty as this gives you the proper sense of fear

Incredible game: one of the three I've 100%-ed (The other two being Arkham Asylum & City)
+ Insane graphics; extremely detailed models, environemtns use great use of steam and smoke, and particles and lighting are top-notch and incredibly realistic. Film grain and chromatic abberations ground it in 70's-style film. Every corner of Sevastopol is polygon-rich and looks incredibly well thought-out.
+ Solid gameplay; stealth, tools, action sequences - it's always paced wonderfully and nothing feels added in as filler. Peeking, hiding and distracting always triumph over guns, which feel great to use but do little against foes. Motion tracker is underliable and loud, giving an interesting dynamic of checking for enemies without alerting them.
+ Well-paced story; You're Ellen Ripley's daughter, aboard the direlect Sevastopol station in search of the Nostromo's black-box flight recorder. Voicing from the original movie and strong acting by the lead characters all add emotion and weight to the story, even if some dialogue is played out hurriedly or feels tacked-on. Overall, the sense of dread and desperation is impeccably spread throughout the meaty campaign.
+ Unscripted Xenomorph; Though a handful of sequences are scripted for cinematic effect, the vast majority of Isolation takes place with a completely AI-driven Alien, which can vary from on-your-tail-constantly to never-shows-up behaviour, dpeending on how much noise you and others around you make. Being about to actually lure the alien away with a noisemaker is great, because you know that it's
at it; it's not just following a scripted pattern. This means that no two encounters are alike, and also that sometimes you feel you die maybe just a little bit unfairly. But it's all worth it for a creature that feels as though it's truly hunting you.
+ Great Score; a mix of the original film's tracks and new composures, the soundtrack to this game only serves to heighten the tension in intense sections, or enhance the sense of wonder with some more peaceful tracks, and by doing so while not getting in the way, it's a perfect way to balance the tone of the games.
- Lip Sync and Facial Animations; jerky and at times almost creepy, the characters in the game all suffer from only vaguely moving thier lips to follow what they're actually saying. Certainly not a deal-breaker, but it's at times almost comical.
Alien: Isolation is an incredible game, smashing all expectations I had for it. It's the first time I've been scared of a Xeno in a while, because it's a genuinely terrifying and at times pants-wetting experience. Nearly free of bugs and a gorgeous PC port (other than some quick-to-get-accustomed-to poor AA), this game is a steal at $50, let alone the current, measly price of $13.

DO NOT BUY THIS GAME AS IT CURRENTLY IS.
Initial writeup (done a couple weeks back): The game itself is great, I played it on the XBox One and wanted to pick it up for the PC. My PC is high-end and should be able to run this game without a problem. Well it turns out this game has a HUGE issue with memory leaks. Now I'm sure you've heard people complain about memory leaks for games when it's just a minor issue. But that's not this. This game sucks up RAM like crazy. I couldn't get it to start without freezing my computer at first. When I finally got it to start, it took 10 minutes to get to the main menu. When it was finally usable on the main menu, the game was using 2GB of RAM. I thought ok, that's high but it'll probably stay at that amount. NOPE. I started the game and at the initial airplane scene, memory usage was at 3GB. I played for a few more minutes and memory usage was at 4GB and climbing. About 10MB/sec is just eaten up.
Until there is a fix for this issue, stay away or get the console version.
My specs:
i5-4570S
8GB RAM (now 24GB)
7970 GPU
Update: I bought 16 GB of additonal RAM to bring my system total to 24GB. I can run the game fine now and it settles around 4.5GB of RAM. Definitely do not buy this game if you have less than 16GB of RAM. I could not get it to run stably on 8GB of RAM. With nothing open and 6GB+ free, the game still locked up my entire computer, to the point where I had to reboot. Clearly there's an issue with memory usage.
Tl;dr Stay away if you have less than 16GB of RAM. If you have 16GB or more, then you'll need at least 7GB or more free. Despite using 4.5GB of RAM, it could lock up your machine if you have fewer than 7ish free GB of RAM.

You know what Black Mesa is, its in the title of every other review here.
Its also a  fine example of "how to make a game" without a ramming a storyline/narrative/cutscenes in your face while still retaining a great sense of plot and characterisation, HL 1 sets the bar on how you should run FPS shooters with a story
I first palyed HL back in 1998 and playing this now gives me a great sense of nostalgia. Its great to see the levels remade with even more detail than back almost two decades ago. The puzzles and characters are made better with the help of the physics engine and some of the puzzles improved. There's also been in improvement in the voice acting (or at least better quality audio). Soilder AI is much much better than before. Some of the more annoying gameplay elements such as the tiny worms in the water have been removed and the level "On the Rails" has been improved to make it more streamline. The most obvious change is the flashlight no longer needs to be turned off to recharge. These are of course, only a few things that make for a better game.
There are a few small problems; the physics engine also makes crush damage from some of the task such as crawling between machine parts more cumbersome; and not in a challenging way but in a way that you will likely take unavoidable damage thats difficult to justify.  The music while improved, is incredbily loud when it comes on and will at a few points in the game drown out characters talking.
