System Shock 2... where to begin. Awakening on the medical deck of the derelict spacecraft Von Braun, you, a soldier of  the TriOptimum Corporation, are immediately contacted by Dr. Janice Polito, who seems to be the only other survivor on this ship after some type of cataclysmic event. She guides you through a series of virtous challenges to meetup with her, only for you to find the real threat to not only the Von Braun and your survival, but to humanity as a whole...SHODAN.
System Shock 2 was co-developed by Irrational Games and Looking Glass Studios in 1997, 3 years ater the release of System Shock (Who Looking Glass Studios had developed). Looking Glass is known for their great PC games; like Thief 1, 2,  Ultima Underworld I, II, and the System Shock games. Upon release, SS2 was overlooked; but this game has gathered a huge following since 1999, earning awards and praise from gamers and reviewers alike; and for a good reason.
This is definitely one of the best games I've ever played in my life; at least top 3. This game has it all; atmosphere, story, fantastic gmeplay, and of course the unforgettable and debatably most iconic video game villian of all time: SHODAN. I would also like to say that I never played bioshock enough to compare it to this game, but even if I did, I would refuse to anyways because SS2 came out 8 years before Bioshock. So this will not be another "it's bioshock in space" review.
Pros:
-Fantastic ambient horror, unnerving as hell
-Great interface, inventory system & management
-Interesting story that is expanded via logs found throughout the game
-Hard as nails
-Great cyberpunk theme
-Fit for several diferent playstyles
-About 12-14h long, is much longer if you get all extras; about 20h. Even longer if played with all playstyles, up to 80h.
-Runs perfectly on modern machines
-Comes with bonus fan mission mod, extra couple hours
-SHODAN
Cons:
-Doesn't look amazing (there are patches for you graphic snobs)
-Pretty high learning curve
-Controls take some getting used to
-Can be slow paced
Mixed (Pro/Con):
-Coop (ruins immersion, but is tons of fun)
-Enemies respawn, making the game much harder
-Ending is somewhat...lackluster
-The music. Not a lot of tracks and can ruin immersion, although the tracks are great techno. I recommend turning the music off though.
As you can see, the cons are things that any player who puts time into the game or anyone who has played a game that predates 2000 can easily adjust to. This game is fantastic and is a must play if you like rpg, horror, classic, or fps games. This game is probably one of the best games ever created in the 20th century, up there with Deus Ex and the like. Lets all take a moment and thank Nightdive Studios for bringing this masterpiece to steam.
Do yourself a favor and buy this game. If you like it, go back to SS1 and play it; it's great too, although clunkier and not as good as it's sequel. They don't have to be played in order.

We've all wanted that zombie game. That 'one'. you know what i'm talking about. the one in which the zombies actually shuffle at you because you're gun went off by accident. That one that lets you take the decisions into your own hands, like letting an infected friend live because they gave you the last of the ammo later. then waking away alone because everyone was killed. The guilt. The fear. The excitement of watching a long lived character put a gun in his or her mouth because they know they won't survive seeing another zombie child eating an ally, because they were too scared to blow its brains out.
The wait is over. This game has it all. realism, challenge, and even buttons for suicide, pulling out the magazine to check how many bullets you have left, and even one for shoving those little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s away from you.
But in honesty, what really sold it for me, was the fact that every bite could be your last chance. I play with my sister a lot. we're really into the genre, me especially, and we needed something new since standalones glitches and disappointments. Soon we'll be trying out with the 8 players, but so far wwe're following the advice, and sticking to friends. as an example of the amazing experiences we have had so far.
Chinatown. The streets above us no longer bustle with the busy footsteps of strangers, but with the familiarity of the dead. The End has come. Yet we have just begun. We'd scouted the streets many times before, and had even killed a few of them, with our short notice combination of weapons, ranging from old rusty pipes, to huge Rebars. I could tell you about the many times we'd attempted to reach the gun shop from the subway, but the tries were a many. it was the final time, however, that I have told on many occasions.
Me and my sister had held off enough of the horde to fuel the generator of the door to finally get it open. We'd already raided the gun shop, but with such a little amount of ammo, it was still unclear whether we'd make it. I reached for the door switch, and praised the heavens. the door opened, and we were free. I was the first to duck under it as it rose, my sister the second, just barely making it through. What we didn't expect, that there was another horde waiting on the other side. because of our experience in the risky task, we had to make the decision to run through them. unfortunatley, I'd learned to travle light with small arms, whilst my sister had an experience in rifles. I'd seen the difficulty in loading them, when she covered me in the shop whislt I scrounged and searched for the ammo type for my favourite gun, the .22 pistol. She had favoured the SKS, but was betrayed when her ammo count became nil. whilst she moved backwards deeper into the sanctuary of shelves and bodies, she neglected to watch her back. I had managed to load in time, i aimed the pistol over the shelves that divided us, firing a pellet into the rotting corpse's head.
This moment of heroism was briefly lived. As we avoided the hoard in the second part of the street, we'd spotted an alley. I kept running through and pushed as many as i could, but neglected to note how the dead do not stop their stalkerish ways. I made it through the alley to find a Beretta pistol and more ammo, along with a crowbar. I splattered a zombies head as it closed in on me, but was too late to make it back to save my sister from the horde. As I ran back to save her, she was bitten. A bite means infection, but we would have still find a way to sustain it, until at least we were rescued. But this dream was shattered as i saw her still be surrounded by the rest of them. I quickly had to attend to the danger that i was still presented with, splitting three more heads with the gun. The time was enough for my sister to rise again. I turned back in time, just to shoot my second to last bullet into her head. maybe as a sign of thanks for the times she had led me, or as a way of avoiding the regret of not running in to save her. Not that any of it mattered anyway, as the last bullet was spent on myself.
besides, we could always do it again.

This is one of the best MMO's I've ever encountered. From the visual quality to the vast ammount of different ways to play, quests to follow, and things to experience, it's an utterly beautiful game to pick up and put a lot of time into.
Right away there is lot of customizability to your character to have fun with, with nine different races spanning three possible alliances and four different starting classes with their own set of skills and abilities (not including DLC). There's a good ammount of slide-bars to customizing your character's face and body, hair and markings. Each of the three alliances determine where you start in Tamriel after the tutorial (which is optional after its first completion).
The lore and questlines are very in-depth and interesting to follow, especially having played previous Elder Scrolls games. There are more than enough throughout the game, to the point where plenty of them become irrelevant to your level by the time you get to every one in each area. This can make every playthrough, every character, a new and unique experience to the last.
Skills and Abilities from character to character are extremely well thought out, even though a little vague or difficult to understand in the sense that they seem to have different level-up requirements. There's your class skill tree, determined by the one of four classes you chose in the character creation menus. Also there's several skill trees for weaponry alone, including one weapon and shield (also leveled up without a shield), two handed weapons, duel wielding, destruction staff, restoration staff, bows, etc. Beyond weaponry there are tons of skill trees in crafting (including woodworking, alchemy, enchanting, blacksmithing, clothing, etc) as well as world skills (lockpicking, pickpocketing, sneaking etc) guild skills (fighters guild, mages guild, etc) and even more.
On the topic of guilds: Pretty much every Elder Scrolls game has the fighters guild, the mages guild, the thieves guild, etc. Well ESO has more than any of them. It includes these usual guilds and adds plenty more, each with their own skill tree and abilities as well as questlines.
The crafting is very well done, very in-depth with in-game certifications, tutorials, and even questlines for each and every crafting skill which on top of the quests, guilds, and weaponry on top of classes, really makes every play through and character a new experience.
There's great opportinuty to make a stand-alone character, or a full group of differently-talented characters that work well together. This includes a great system for befriending, locating friends, being in groups with trading, sharing xp, player-to-player guilds, etc.
In terms of mechanics: I love the option of first or third person, the VAST array of emotes, the smooth gameplay in and out of combat, the traveling systems, etc.
Plenty of DLC is available to add onto the game and do even more with each character, including mounts, quests, crafting styles of armors and weapons, pets, guilds (thieves guild and Dark Brotherhood are both DLC) etc.
The map size is incredible. There's not much to say other than that it is probably one of the largest maps in a massively multiplayer game I've seen, however still not too large to the point of difficulty moving from lower-level areas to higher ones.
The very first thing I disklied about the game is the fact that the Thieves Guild and Dark Brotherhood are DLC. It's an understandable choice on Bethesda's part, but not a favorable one.
On that note: The DLC is rather expensive. There is a Crown system in place where players purchase crowns (or are rewarded crowns through membership) to be used in any buying of DLC I've listed in things that I like. ESO does make having a membership, even for a 3-6 month period worth it due to the fact that a decent amount of crowns are given per-month on top of full access to all DLC such as the Thieves Guild, Dark Brotherhood, Imperial Race, dungeons etc. However, crowns on their own are expensive and there is no way to earn them without purchasing, which i wish would be changed.
There currently is an achievemtn system which yes, is fun, but is also just like the xbox achievement system where the score/sum of your achievements is purely for bragging rights. Personally, I wish there was a system in place where crowns were awarded based on achievement score; therefore more play-time and effort into the game, the more crowns rewarded for your choice of DLC.
The next thing is the lack of a mass-trader or auction house. There is no way to be a solo player and sell items in a player-to-player store. There is a guild-store that allows you to sell items to other players of the same player-to-player guild (which has a minimum of a 50 people in your guild to be accessable) but other than that, selling and buying items between players is difficult to non-existant.
The final thing is the CO-OP/PVP system, which is a big thing for an MMO. It's an interesting system with the three alliance options. This makes it so each alliance is at war with one-another. Although I do agree that the ability to change alliances after character creation would not work due to people just switching to the winning alliance, I do wish that your race did not determine your alliance, rather you got to choose it seperately than your race. I understand how it is put in place based around lore and storyline, however with such a world make-up that Tamriel has, a personal backstory to why a character of a certain race is in whatever alliance of their choosing is pretty easily explained. And in addition, I do not like the difficulty of playing with friends in different alliances. Because the early levels 1-20 roughly are seperate based on alliance, though you may be in a group with a friend, you cannot actually play together or fight the same enemies until later in the game when the alliances possibly converge in world-space.

This sequel, despite not being as ginourmous as the first game in the series, it is still definitely a fantastic game on its own and a game not to pass. I give up. I really wanted to give this game a chance, because I love the Deus Ex world. After playing slowly and deliberately for an hour, trying to take in the slightly changed gameplay mechanics and learn about the new world post-Area 51, the game quit to the desktop. Not the standard "restart from desktop" that happens literally every time you enter a new area (3-4 rooms), but "click lift button to enter new area, game quits as usual, desktop appears as usual, game never comes back". I spent hours trying the different hacks and tweaks documented online: changing resolutions, binding the executables to individual CPUs, downloading hacked executables, setting it up in compatibility mode, alt-tabbing at the perfect time, creating junctions for 32-bit C:\Program Files, but nothing worked. It's a shame, because I actually quite liked the "circle interface" and the graphics and enemy AI seemed improved over Deus Ex GOTY, though it's hard to tell since I only got to see 6 bad guys and about 10 rooms in total. Running Windows 8.1 on tablet the in-game performance was great, but troubleshooting a show-stopper bug like this is not worth my time, even if there is a great game hidden in there somewhere.

This is one of those old games that age really really well. like the GOG version it works fine on newer systems. And no need for mods to get 1080p or higher. As the game even back in 1997 did scale to your max windows resolutions, sadly the game UI don't. Nor the radar. So at 2K or 4K they are really tiny. And ofc this has the addon "The Core Contingency" and lots of other old bonus missions. And yes. I use Win10 and it works just fine. At the time of this writing the Arm campaing is done, 11 hours played and not a single crash..
This game is equally great for turtle players and rushers alike. The SP campaign AI can be brutal on the attacks at times. But even a turtle player can focus on defenses and hold up until he is ready. Some of the maps are huge and will need some micro managing to get around well, but take your time and it will work out. There are tons of units to select from. So it will fit any style you have the more you progress in the story. I would recommend to google keyboard shortcuts, as there are a ton of then to make the game easier to handle. As the game set the standard for way point systems, so you can order a unit to move to the enemy base, attack a unit, fall back and patrol the base all in one way point go. Or set the commander to build a few buildings while you attack or scout.
For this price, even not on a discount. You would be foolish to skip this part of RTS history. It set the standards along with C&C for all time to come. Old or new RTS player, it won't take long to get into this gem. Even with the huge unit count. Only downside is that buildings count towards the unit cap at 200. But each unit counts as 1. Not 1 to 8 like in SC.
Highly recommended.

Adorableness distilled.  Piles of happily whooping slimes bouncing everywhere. Neatly slotting corrals and gardens and silos (and maybe even an incinerator??  You ... monster!) into place all over your ranch.  And then suddenly feels as you discover the notes from the ranch's former owner, dovetailing with starmail letters from a special someone back on Earth ... oh yeah and slimes.  Lots of slimes.  Lots of adorable (can I use that word again?  Can I use that word all the time when describing this game?) slimes.  Happy slimes, shy slimes, glowy slimes, bouncy slimes, quantum-teleporting slimes, all the slimes.
Okay, so you can get your tush handed to you if you bonk into rock slimes or crystal spikes a few times too much, or get mobbed by enough cranky Feral Largos, or take a tumble all the way into the Slime Sea itself.  But hey!  This game has a Casual Mode now!  Less aggression from Feral Largos?  No Tarr whatsoever?  Please and thank, I'll be over here watching a cornucopia of wild slimes gleefully frolic in enthusiastic peace across sun-baked coral canyons and abandoned indigo-striated mining quarries and lush jungles covered in blankets upon blankets of moss and ancient, time-forgotten slime-statue-festooned ruins (wait, what?) without having to worry about any of them happy babies turning into hideous Tarr at any given moment while I rest assured I filled all the auto-feeders to capacity just this morning to keep my own ranch slimes happy and content.
Happy, bouncing, cheering blobs of colourful goo.

This game, even in single player mode only, is incredibly fun. I cannot wait too see how it develops and am looking forward to multiplayer! The gameplay feels similar to battlefield in some ways, but is definitely an original game in it's own right.
Things I like:
- I like that the graphics are simplified: it let's make play on a non gaming platform like a mac and runs smooth as butter.
- I love that enemies/players are bright blue or red. In otherwise muted landscapes, they really stick out. Which makes this game more action and less peekaboo compared to battlefield. In other words, more pew pew, less sneak sneak.
- Players are pretty easy to kill. This makes it a bit more realistic and having the element of suprise one could easily dispatch 3-4 enemy players from behind. I think once multiplayer comes out, team strategy and tactics are going to be a as important as raw reflex skills.
- Scoped weapons don't have a large field of view: it makes them harder to use close quarters. So - you may have the advantage at a distance, but not so much when someone armed with iron sights is close by. If you've ever shot a scoped rifle, you know you do NOT want to be using that in close quarters. This adds a nice balance to the game and makes pairing the right weapon with your attack strategy important.
- So far, it's not overly complex. It's just really easy to pick up and play. I hope that as the game develops the developer will be able to maintain that simplicity and intuitiveness whilst adding new features.
10/10 for a preview game. Keep up the good work!

TLDR 10/10, very well executed gameplay and horror elements.
In a weird way, this game has a bit of a "Dead Space" vibe in the way it approaches action/horror games. Although the experience is very horror driven and linear, it really doesn't skimp on the core gameplay and manages to feel open and exploratory. There are side missions, but not enough to detract you from playing the main arc for too long and the environments are similarly expansive-yet-contained in a way that never leaves you meandering.
To be real, the stealth elements of the game are fairly well done, although I'll admit that the AI isn't particularly smart, but it's still fairly effective from a brute force perspective. The reality is that it's easy to evade enemies, however, their attacks are powerful enough so that it doesn't take much for them to overtake you. With that being said, the enemies definitely fit into a "zombie-like" category, so it doesn't really break immersion to balance out the AI woes with sheer strength.
The most "dead spacey" elements of this game actually stem from the crafting  and upgrade systems that almost border on RPG levels of customization. Once again, these systems feel very intentional and unbloated, so they make it a happy middle ground for people who focus on horror narrative and those who are more tuned in to the gameplay mechanics. I'd argue that both Dead Space and this game are the positive examples of Action Horror compared to the Resident Evil games that came after 4 and before 7 (granted, I liked 4 and 7).
I'm giving it a solid 10/10, which may seem like a bit much, but I would very much like to see more games like this in the future.

A great callback to the ps2 era of survival horror, and especially Resident Evil 4 but with some new quality of life improvements. The combat is easy to learn but hard to master, and kept me engaged throughout the entire game.
That feeling you got in Resident Evil 4 where the game really incentivized you to carefully place every single shot, The Evil Within 2 nails that. Every bullet carries so much weight, and there's that satisfying "crunch" when you finally pop a limb off a zombie. Combat stays really tense, because you want to clear out every area for upgrade resources - but you want to invest as little as possible weapon resources in doing so. You always feel like you could've done better and you're constantly trying to re-evaluate your strategies for next time. Combat almost plays out like a puzzle game, and feels incredibly satisfying when you get it right.
The story is really (really) cheesy, but it allows for the designers to implement wacky ideas to shake to gameplay up - so I don't mind it. The combat carried the whole experience for me. The horror elements are cliche, but they work. The game definitely spooked me good a couple times. I picked it up for $30 and save for like 3 specific sequences, the game was a blast the whole way through.
If you liked RE4's combat and don't mind a cheesy story, then I think this game is for you!

In what seems like a common turn of events for the games of this sub-genre, corners have been cut and compromises have been made to make The Evil Within 2 cater to the needs of a larger audience. I picked the game because I wanted a narrative driven survival horror experience. What I got instead was a hybrid of genres mastering none, something the current market doesn’t lack. I can’t say I didn’t enjoy the time spent with the game, some of its gameplay segments were quite savory. But for a title that spends so much time trying to channel a meaningful narrative set in a disturbing setting, The Evil Within 2 falls short at its own game. In the end surprise or disappointment will come based on the expectations. However, I feel that the current price tag makes it hard to overlook the game’s shortcomings or justify gambling with expectations.
Pros:
+ Artistically gruesome
+ Extremely atmospheric at times
+ A good combination of action and stealth gameplay
+ Sound design
+ Segments of great level design
+ A good sense of progression
Cons:
- The story is incapable of triggering the emotions it is so desperately trying to convey
- Average graphics with plenty of visual glitches and performance problems
- The semi open world design breaks the immersion of the horror theme
- Uninspired voice acting
- A limited array of enemies
- Underwhelming production value for the price

CONS
- Mechanics from the first game became overly simplified (Guns/ammo, biomods, keycodes, locks, etc).
- Characters are not interesting.
- Stealth and combat are hit and miss.
- HUD is atrocious.
- Loading screens everywhere.
- Game can be a pain to get running correctly sometimes.
One thing I really want to comment on is the fact that I've had this game crash on me numerous times for the most random of reasons. I still don't know what was causing them or what fixed them, it just happens. It also seems to take up an obscene amount of computer processing power/memory for a game made over a decade ago.
It's not a terrible game per se, it's just not the follow up one would hope for after Deus Ex. I played through this because I was curious of the what the world was like after the events of the first game and that alone was what carried me through it. That and NG Resonance Holo-Sim.

I tried really hard to like this game, I really did. I first came across Deus Ex and fell hopelessly in love with it, played it over ten times in a row; I went as far as turning it into a book for a big school project. The characters of the first game are memorable and lovable. JC Denton is my favorite character of everything, Bob Page is the best villian of all time, and who could forget Jock? They've made big impacts in my memory and I can never stop thinking about it.
I discovered Human Revolution next and fell in love with that one, too. Adam Jensen is a fantastic person with awesome sunglasses, doesn't take crap from anyone, the great Francis Pritchard, and the twisted Hugh Darrow. Between these two games, I sometimes get chills down my spine.
Then I found Invisible War. The first time I played it I liked it, not loved it. The characters didn't make a big impact on me, Alex D just doesn't fit in with the Denton crowd. There isn't one villain to focus my hate on. (Don't get me wrong, I love the villains.) In the other games I was scared, my heart was pounding, I was forcing myself to meet deadlines as fast as I could. In Invisible War it felt like there was something I should be doing. There was no big motivation. The ultimate freedom of this game is a hinderence. This fell way short of my expectations.

Compared to the first title of this series and Human revolution, Invisible War strays away from the normal setup of a Deus Ex game. However, I still found it enjoyable despite the changes. However, that said, the biggest thing this game suffers from is the amount of loading screens between areas, as well as an inventory system with one ammo pool that works for all weapons. That said, I still enjoyed playing the game and thought the story was pretty good.
If this were its own game rather than a sequel it wouldn't have such a negative reputation.

Quick side note before the actual "review": Hey Steam, hopefully Steam Direct won't let garbage like Slaughtering Grounds come onto Steam but let games like this continue to entering Steam's store page.
Tl;dr can be found below.
Gameplay:
Combat -
The gameplay is pretty simple, you just move to the direction of an enemy and you'll automatically(?) hit them when you're touching them. There's nothing too engaging like other games like Cross code. The combat system just dumbs down to, you do damage, you take damage that's really how fights work in the game. In the dev's defense he made this game with the idea that it's meant to be a relaxing game so you don't have to constantly put a lot mind and effort into it.
You unlock 4 different skills as you progress, although they are powerful I've never personally felt like I needed to use them or have been pressured into doing so. This is due to how the game's combat works, the majority of mobs never initiate a combat with you nor do they actually continue them. You can be in a room filled with 5-10 mobs but in the end you really only end up
one at a time. You can however use one of the AOE attacks to attack multiple ones at a time.
RPG -
The RPG aspects are pretty simple and doesn't require any huge inventory management or whatever. This does go into the combat a bit, the combat's difficulty also does dumb down to who has the better stats and equipment. For the most part, the only RPG is grinding for materials which is luckily not that difficult or drawn out. Every piece of equipment is just a direct upgrade of the other, there's nothing like "this weapon has higher crits but lower damage than that one..."
Oddly enough you know how to build all the equipment/equipment upgrades without any problem, you don't have to learn or search for an upgrade for this or how to make that. They're automatically there in your menu.  There's only 1 instance where you could arguably "miss" a recipe for a weapon and armor although you technically can't miss it for any reason.
There's not many actual decisions you make throughout the game outside of the endings so not too much in the story RP aspect.
Difficulty:
Asides from the beginning and some boss fights I never actually felt too pushed or huge difficulty spikes when I was playing it. The game arguably isn't all that grindy, I'm not saying you can skip all the grind and immediately just walk through the game with no difficulty but the grind is pretty abysmal.
There is a certain dungeon the game offers you to grind for levels and materials but I'd argue that you'd only need to run them 4-6 times, (one run being 3 minutes at most) to comfortably be at a decent level to fight the other enemies but the numbers maybe an over exaggeration because that may have caused my overall experience to be too easy? By the time I made it to the 2nd dungeon I've pretty much had no issues one-two shotting all the normal mobs up until the end with my default attacks.
Story:
The story is pretty basic, you seek out your sister that went somewhere dangerous. That's really all that could be explained without much spoilers given. The story isn't really ground breaking or inventive and I personally believe you can see where it's going if you've seen enough anime or entertainment in general. It's good enough.
My only gripe is that the only characters that are developed enough are the main character and the sister you're looking for. There's also a fairy that does join you but she just kinda serves as a information guide for when the MC doesn't understand something. You do meet a certain character but she unfortunately just serves as a plot device to progress through the main story.
The interesting thing is you somewhat feel like the dev really wanted to expand on his world but since this is his first attempt at a game he just limited himself to the main story line. Really hoping that the dev takes the feedback and tries to expand the world in the 2nd game.
Music:
There isn't some huge array of music but there is enough variety for what you would expect from a F2P.
Cons:
The cons here are mostly just small nitpicks but they still somewhat annoyed my experience.
- This is a game made by a Taiwanese(?) so expect a lot of grammatical errors, they never really bothered me up until the end since the ending seemed to have a lot of them.
- Game doesn't scale to well at fullscreen, but this is somewhat expected considering it's using pixel graphics.
- The UI is a bit annoying to handle especially when you're trying to upgrade equipment to its superior version, due to how the UI works you can't equip something or else the menu would assume you don't have the requirements to upgrade it.
For example, if I want to upgrade a sword to a mk II I'd need a Mk I version, the problem here is that if I'm equipping the Mk I version the game would assume I do not have one so I have to unequip, upgrade it than equip it again which kinda gets annoying when you have to do this for a few seperate items.
Those are really my only actual gripes about the games.
Afaik, they are currently working on the 2nd game and I'm really hoping the developer takes in the feedback and greatly improves on what he built in this.
When a game like this is given out for free while a lot of Greenlight trash tries to charge you, this game is really good.

First the elephant in the room. Dishonored 2 doesn't run very well on the technical end and has some pretty questionable performance overall. I have a PC that was great when I built it in 2014 and three years later is merely probably good but not great. My graphics card is a GTX 750Ti, my processor is an intel quad core i5-4670k and I've got 16 gigs of ram if you're wondering. In order to get Dishonored 2 to run smoothly I had to halve the resolution and crank most of the graphical settings down to either their lowest or second lowest states. Once I did that however it ran just fine and remained pretty enough to look at even still. I should also note that while the game is poorly optimized in those respects it's plenty stable once you get it running smoothly and nor are the graphics or mechanics marred by in-game glitches.
So with that being the case why am I recommending the game then? Well because it's incredibly fun and worthy sequal to one of my all time favorite games. If you've played the original Dishonored you probably know whether you want to play more of it with new mechanics, powers and a myriad of improvments. If you haven't played the original Dishonored then I strongly suggest you go buy it and it's DLCs first for peanuts the next time they go on sale.
Dishonored is a stealth, magic and gadget focused first person slasher/shooter that can be played in many different ways and offers a very strong attention to detail. It takes place in a fantastically creative fantasy world based on various European cultures during the Age of Reason and styles of speculative fiction from around the same time.
Arkane Studios employs some of the same creators who worked on the Thief trilogy and it shows both in the gameplay and in the worldbuilding. This is a series that can appeal to both an audience that really likes to get immersed in a gameworld as well as those who simply prefer using a deep set of gameplay mechanics to enact absolute bloody mayhem. Things both really cool and hilarious are pretty much bound to happen when you play Dishonored, especially if you're quick witted and have a bit of a sadistic bent.

I bought a hard copy of this game many years ago at the insistence of friends that game was pure brilliance and wow, they were right. I loved every minute of playing through that game, searching for ammo and audio logs, fighting back the Many while trying to piece together what happened. The atmosphere, the difficulty, the tension, it was all fantastic and it created this visceral, rewarding experience. In a way, this is very much like the original Resident Evil games, only it's approaching survival horror another way and producing it's own unique, rich experience in the process. This game easily fits onto many "must play" lists and it's easy to see why.
When I got a Steam message one day about how this game is now available to purchase on Steam for a small fee and you can bet your backside I snapped it up harder and faster than a crackhead grabbing a baggie of drugs off the floor after it falls out of someone's pocket. I loaded it up and dived into the hell aboard the Von Braun and UNN Rickenbacker once again, my trusty wrench at my side. Naturally, for a game that was about 16 years old (at the time of my playthrough), the graphics were a tad dated compared to more modern offerings, but after 5 minutes I was so hooked on the game that I didn't even notice. The sound design of things like the hybrids begging for you to run so they don't kill you, the everyday musings from the ships inhabitants on the audio logs scattered around the ships and the announcements of Xerxes over the PA system combined with visuals of messages written on the walls in blood, bullet holes stitching the walls and the clash of nice looking ship interiors that have been sullied with violence and gore make for a wonderful inducement of dread as you try to slip through the ship, trying to source more ammunition for your trusty pistol and frantically trying to bash in the skull of a shotgun wielding hybrid with a wrench after it surprises you by coming out of a doorway you didn't expect. This game was a more palpable experience than many games I've played in the last few years, despite the fact that some, myself not included, would argue that this game has aged poorly.
If you're someone that can look past a game being older (I.E. you won't refuse to play a game because it doesn't have the latest in graphics), I urge you to give this game a shot. Look up some videos of the gameplay (speedruns don't count, as they're intentionally skipping a lot of stuff), read some reviews and if you're not sure, just wait for a sale to pick up the game. Sure, you'll have to do a tiny bit of control rebinding (it's not that big of deal) and you *will* die a few times at first, but bear with it and you'll find a very enjoyable gameplay experience waiting for you within. There's a reason people love this game so much and I'd very much like for other people to understand why. Hell, after hearing some of the audio logs from the game on a Youtube video, I'm thinking about playing through this game again myself and after writing all of this, I think I will.

Campaign Beaten - 85 % Through Single Player Levels (There are extra ones) - 7 Hours.
Broforce is Brotastic. It is EASILY one of the best designed action-focused sidescrollers I have EVER played.
Concept / Elevator Pitch - A retro (artisticly) inspired side-scroller whereby you play as one of a HUGE roster of 70's/80's/90's inspired action personas/characters (names changed to be "BRO" themed).  Each character has his/her own weapons/playstyle that you use to get to the end of the level. On the way, you will kill all sorts of bad dudes.  Missions (usually) are in clumps of 4-5 levels.
The twist: So in levels, there are "hostages" that look a LOT like homages to metal slug hostages. Rescue one, and you get one extra life starting from the nearest checkpoint. The twist is you become a different BRO from the varied list of unlocked characters. This also happens when you die.
Furthermore....
-4 player coop
-Basically unlimited levels (community built).
-A level editor
-Harder modes if you ever (how could you) find it too easy.
- Levels are physics-based and are fully destructable. Want to avoid an enemy? Shoot a path under it.
Cons
- Really none. It is damn near perfect.

Deus Ex: Invisible War is infamous for being unusually inferior to its predecessor, but exactly how is a question I decided to answer myself by playing the game. Invisible War is a decent game I must stress this, but decent is simply not good enough if you are the direct followup to what many considered, even at the time, one of the greatest video games ever made. Invisible War has a distinction of taking away far too many of the original game's features and depth and offering very little in return aside from prettier graphics and the option to play as a female.
For starters, this is a port of a console game, while the original Deus Ex was custom built exclusively for the PC platform. This alone is a terrible thing, as the game is inherrently bound to the original Xbox's limitations, and these limitations negatively impact nearly every facet of the game. No environment is even half as big as the first level of the original, load times tend to take more screen time than gameplay, and your key binding options are much more limited. There are even actions that cannot be rebound to a different key!
Second of all, ammo across all weapons is universal, the health system is a standard percentage based system rather than one based of areas of the body inflicted (while Human Revolution also does this, that game allows such a system to be upgraded, thus adding depth), and you CANNOT MANUALLY RELOAD YOUR WEAPON. It stupefies gameplay to such a degree that it insults both console players new to this game as well as existing fans. It's the fisher-price version of Deus Ex, and it stars a protagonist that looks like a long-lost Backstreet Boy. There's a reason why it took so long between this and Human Revolution; the new devs had to figure out a proper way to un♥♥♥♥ this franchise.
Other than all that♥♥♥♥♥♥I just said, it's not a broken game. It can be played and enjoyed, especially as a stealth or action game, but do know ahead of time that this is not the proper Deus Ex experience. Choices matter much less, and at times you simply HAVE to kill someone or HAVE to hack this thing. Player flexibility is discarded when seen useful, and that goes against the design philosophy of both the original and the excellent Human Revolution. Only play this as a history lesson on why this is one of the most disappointing sequels ever made.

Many people will say that this game is the worst.  "It's nothing like the first game!  It blows chunks!"
Well, I'll say you're wrong.
It is DEFINATELY not the best game in the series, like the first one.  Like Deus Ex: The Fall you need to look at the game as what they wanted it to be and how accutare the game got to their target.  As we can see in the ad for it, most of what is shown is firefights and explosions.  Perhaps they wanted a more action-esque game?  Yes and no.
I know it says that I'm played very little of the game here on steam, however I had a CD copy of this recently and decided to play it one day as it had only been opened a few times before.  My older cousins would come once in a while and since we had a desktop, cousin P would come and play his collection of PC games he would leave here.  Recently, within the last few months in the smmer, I found the stash and this was in it.
After 6 hours of playing it off the CD I can say, yes the game IS NOT the first one.  Most scenes are better done by running and gunning rather than slow and comprehensive plans and watching the walking patterns.  And sure, it might crash once in a blue moon; who cares!  This is a windows 2000 game :D
Other than the main RPG flaw being that you need a gun no matter what to go anywhere fast, you can definately play the game the old style if you want to.  This does prove to be tougher over all as the enemies don't USUALLY walk on a path anymore.  Nor do the have a specific walk area.  Enemies tend to explore, and if they find you you're done unless you flatten them ASAP.  Armor is indeed hard to come by as an upgrade so it is worth having health items as often as possible.  You will take a hit, even it a random fire starts.
Different from the first game, where in the beginning you have to collect items from enemy guards and such instead of finding them in random places, in this game it is flipped:  you can just find random whatever anywhere on the map.  As I said earlier the RPG elements are indeed lowered.
So what were they aiming for?  While the first game revolutionized how we think of FPRPG's nowadays, at the time quake was the holyfartcow of the universe just as COD is now.  What was most likely being aimed for was the idea of being more like a shooter than an RPG, even though those elements are still there.  Not helpful in a stealth FPRPG.
Overall score?  7.6 / 10.  Not a bad game, just not as good as the first.

First off, this game gets very boring if none of your friends play it. As a long time MMORPG player I wanted to give this game a try although it had very bad reviews at the time. At first it was fun, going through quests and gaining gear matching playstyle and level. The faction system brought diversity to the game and allowed for a semi- different experience in each playthrough. Once end game was reached, getting through the Veteran ranks was a pain. The game went from questing and semi grind, to full time grind. It lost all its fun whilst grinding and because I wasnt a high enough Vet rank I wasn't able to run dungeons and dalies with other players( this is where friends bring the fun.) But once I was max level and ready to hop into PVP and other things, I realised that I need gear. Gear is a huge part of this game, the design and the unique properties of each piece give this game a unique edge. But unfortunatly you need to have good gear in order to dominate in PVP and other gametypes. The PVP aspect of this game was what stood out to me the most. It wasn't a PVP where you stand there and wait for your spells to be up. This game had unique fighting mechanichs that had a huge learning curve. Another thing to keep in mind when buying this game is Ping. Currently living in SEA the ping with very high all the time, most of the time it didn't affect gameplay but sometimes it was noticeable. So yeah, even though this game has quite a bit of flaws, it's still a good amount of fun. Just make sure that you have friends that play so that you can expirience it to it's full capabilities.

Total Annihilation is the defining game of the RTS genre. Looking back to the late 90s and the technology available then, this game was amazingly advanced and did many things that weren't at all common then. Many common RTS elements that are expected in a game released today can be seen in their youth in TA. The order queuing system, the streaming resource and building systems, the diversity of units and asymmetrical factions are all key features that were later used in practically every RTS since. You can clearly see the foundation of Supreme Commander especially. There are aspects of TA that still haven’t been matched, such as the unit diversity: Air, Land, Sea, Seaplane, Hovercraft, Amphibious.
Like artillery? How about the Intimidator, which can fire halfway across the map? Too slow? Build the Buzzsaw: a giant rotary cannon made up of Intimidators that fires as fast as a machine gun and will drain your energy economy in seconds. Yes, it IS the most entertaining gun ever!
The music of TA is the best orchestral soundtrack ever made for a game. I still sometimes listen to the "battle" tracks in my car. I turn the music off in every other game I’ve played and listen to “real” music instead (I remember listening to Spice Girls on a CD while playing), but TA got to keep its soundtrack.
I think a large part of what made TA such a fun and long lasting experience was the modding community. I remember spending as much time finding, downloading (V.90 modem, yo), and figuring out conflicts between mods as playing the game, but those mods extended the diversity and playability of the game so extensively that there are still active players AND active modders for TA. You don’t see that with too many 19 year-old games.
The chief contender for the RTS throne was Starcraft, which was released right around the same time as TA, and went on to define the "twitch" RTS subgenre. Coming from Warcraft 2, I remember buying both games, and being rather disappointed in Starcraft, since it seemed to me to be "Warcraft in space". TA was something entirely new and captured that certain something that makes it a gaming classic... and I've probably spent more time in this game than any other, ever.

When I first heard that Half Life, one of the greatest video games of all time, was being remade in a mod, I felt that the team behind it were set up to fail from the very beginning. Not only did they lack official funding, they were attempting to recreate one of the most refined and masterful experiences the games industry has ever produced. Not only did they smash my expectations, I feel they smashed everyone's. Not only did they manage to produce a great modern take on a old story, they even exceeded it in gameplay, level design and music. Following the success of the mod, I am not surprised it was released on Steam as a full game, due to the fact it is nothing short of remarkable.
Pro's:
Satisfying and refined shooting mechanics.
An immersive and enthralling soundtrack with some of the greatest music in the First Person Shooter genre since the early Halo games.
An adequate level of challenge.
Impressive graphical fidelity with a wide variety of graphical settings.
Well optimised.
A modern take on Half Life's already industry defining art style.
Level design is top notch with a faithful reworking of Half Life's remarkable original layouts.
Intelligent AI.
Con's:
Surprisingly glitchy, with floating NPC's and Clipping problems being particularly rife, especially near the games conclusion.
No Xen sections, though since they are to be released this summer, this is more of a nitpick than a legitimate con.
Overall, Black Mesa is a successful modern take on what made Half Life so ground breaking upon it's release in 1998. All it's aspects both mechanically and aesthetically compliment each other perfectly and come together to create a truly remarkable experience. If you have any interest in the FPS genre or just have an appreciation for games in general, Black Mesa is arguably the game for you.

You don't even get to go to the alien planet and fight the weird alien monster baby.. But the rest of it is still there. It performs well for the most part. I ran it on a i7-3770 and a gtx 970 but came across a lot of slow down when vsync was on.. even at 720p.  But turning it off fixed everything, your mileage may vary. All in all, it is worth a play when it is on sale, but play the original first. It will let you enjoy and appreciate what the fans were able to do even more.

All sorts of vehicles are on hand to wade into the fray: tanks to helicopters and everything in between make an appearance. Their handling is a bit clumsy but they work.

On the other hand, if you have a few bucks to spare and want some riotous action, then jump right in.

So ESO has gotten some bad reviews in the past, and for the consumer, this can look rather unappealing. Allow me to clear some things up:
The game has been improved upon constantly since it's initial release, and has a much more ES feel than it had at that time. However, it is an ***MMO***RPG, and as such, it has many features that seperate it from the feel of a singleplayer Elder Scrolls title. This includes a less realistic combat system that focuses more on strategy with hotbarred-skill sets than sheer strength through magic and the like. Along with the battle system, The quest system is rather dull at first, with many quests requiring a simple walk across town, but the problem is that some decide to do THEM ALL. The game can be a lot more exciting if you don't side-quest for all of eternity. Lastly, progression is slow, but this should be expected from any MMORPG. It takes time. A LOT OF TIME. So if you don't have the time to spare, save your money, but if you like a true MMORPG, you'll enjoy this game.
Actual downsides:
- Though the crown store is mostly cosmetic, it's basically required to look the way you might want. Cooler mounts, etc.
- If your computer can't run the game, but you download and launch it, the updater itself will keep you from a refund. BE WARNED.
- There is no 1v1 PVP. That part truly sucks, but it very well might be added in the future.
Hope this helps at least a little. I do truly reccomend this game to MMORPG fans.

Loved the first one. This was pretty much the same though. Wall of light, get around it, kill the target.
Luckily it ended at 10 hours because it was a chore to play.

1. I had no technical troubles with a GTX 1060 and a mid-tier CPU.
2. The story is super poor to the point of ruining the entire game. This is an even greater grievance because the original was such a masterpiece. It was an engrossing and evocative story of revenge; the plot really made me care about the person I was protecting; and the villains, both former and latter, had depth. Most importantly, you felt like you knew your enemies (except Boyle) and the reason why they had to die. Contrast with Dishonored 2, in which enemies had to die because the mission marker said so; you had never heard of them or interacted with them. Your allies were kind of boring, too: You just kind of collected them, and the reward was a few lines of voiced dialogue on the boat. It was altogether unsatisfying.
Then there's the worldbuilding and environmental storytelling aspects. It seems that random people know random things, which are oddly applicable to your current task and goal. Like in a dream, the world clearly revolves around you, and like a dream it's not very believable. The claim that the protagonists react to their world is also false. I can't tell you how many times I thought Emily was going to say something interesting about a person, but nothing was said other than the person's name. "Delilah." "Duke Abele." And then silence, with no further revelation of Emily's thoughts. Perhaps I'll write down every failure in this aspect in a year or two, when I feel like doing a second run-through with Corvo. It would be a long list. But, hey, they make up for the fact with
One horrible world-building thing that I want to mention specifically is how they portrayed the Outsider. In the first game, he is a mystery, the embodiment of nothingness and decay, and an inscrutable force that gently nudges the world (usually into chaos) and then watches the ripples, seemingly due to boredom. Spoilers: in Dishonored 2, the Outsider is your chatty buddy; he's watching out for you, he's concerned about the world around you, and he has a mundane origin and weakness that are wholly uncharacteristic of this pseudo-devil demigod. They totally ruined the character!
They didn't even explain why it had been two whole months between beginning and end. There were no reasons given, so we must assume Emily/Corvo just sat in the boat playing cards for weeks between missions. The real reason, of course, is that if the protagonist had gone through the whole game within a week or two, there would have been no time for Dunwall to degenerate like it did, thus robbing the game of a cool set transformation and the sense of urgency to your efforts. In the original game, the requisite long period was explaind by being in prison, but once you were freed, you went on a mission once, sometimes twice per day. It made sense. Emily plaing cards on a boat makes no sense... like the rest of the plot.
Finally, the ending was horrible (unlike the first game, where every level was great and every plot advancement made sense and was interesting). Some Deus Ex Machina BS at the very end. Spolers: The big villain of the game flies through a painting, you touch your dad-statue to rescue him, and the game is over.
The good things are good gameplay and fantastic sets. These are some of the prettiest levels I've ever seen. The Grand Palace is absolutely amazing; I can't get over how much thought and detail went into the creation of that beautiful archtecture. Unfortunately, these are not the things that made the first game so great. Maybe that's why it feels like such a disappointment. Everything that one game is good at, the other is bad at. I'd recommend this game, except that I feel weird recommending something that was so disappointing.It's sad to say that a promising new IP was run aground in only its second installment.

Right off the bat I should point out that this is a review on performance, and not on the game-play itself, as I have not been able to play the game yet in the current state it is in.
I have patiently been waiting for a patch that will fix the poor performance issues that are hindering this game. I had my hopes up for the Jan 18th 2017 patch but unfortunately it did nothing for screen stutter, and frame spikes. For me those 2 things are HUGE as they take me right out of the immersion. I can handle occasional frame drops here and there, but a constant shutter make(for me) an unplayable game.
I think there is some confusion going around when it comes to differences in opinions regarding gaming performance. For 1 person stuttering might not bother them that much, or at all so they report a game as running "fine" or "not too bad", for others(like me) it's the exact opposite. Some people might also have a high tolerance for frame drops/spikes, where they simply don't notice them as much, and for others(like me) it's all we see. People have different tolerances for things, that's why I think when some of the people are reporting the game running flawlessly on their 970's or whatever they are using it's  just that they have a different idea from mine on what flawlessly means. In other words it doesn't bother them the way it bothers others.
When I was a kid these things didn't bother me either, now that I'm older(43) I find them extremely annoying, and they literately wreck a gaming experience for me.
I should point out I have a higher end system - gtx 1080(sli) i7 5930k, 32gb ddr4 ram, win 10 - foolishly I thought that being a beefy system I might be able to negate a lot of the problems people were reporting, and I guess a fool and his money are soon parted, as by the time I was done tinkering around trying to get the game to play better I was already way passed the allotted 2 hour steam return policy point.
So I guess I'm stuck waiting for patches with everyone else that cannot tolerate playing un-optimized games. I would definitely return the game if I could, as I have my doubts that this magic patch is even coming at all!

I really didn't enjoy this game at all. I discovered it accidentally on Steam, and I really love point and click adventure games so I thought this would be right up my alley, but playing it felt like a waste of time. The further I got in the game the less I enjoyed it and just wanted it to end, and boy did the ending suck balls.
It wasn't funny, the voice acting was mediocre, the overall aesthetic was mediocre with its half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt at being retro while not really pulling it off at all, but all of that could be excused it the game was good, but it's not. The game starts off exciting, but it just gets lamer and lamer the further you get. And I really hated the hive mind approach to how you controlled all the characters in that the only way to progress in the game was to treat each character as if they shared the same mind, ie. mine. That completely removed any sense of immersion for me. Having to deal with the quirks of the characters in an adventure game is often one of the best things about them, but here they all share the same goals and objectives and even though none of them know each other they are working together as if they were the same person just because I'm controlling them that way.
And there were so many loose ends and wasted potential in this game. There were interesting characters in this game that weren't used for anything interesting and it makes you wonder if this game was rewritten multiple times before shipping and you're just seeing bits and pieces of different games in the final product. I'm not going to spoil any of the story, but I just finished watching season 1 and 2 of Twin Peaks for the first time ever before I found this game on Steam and I was super excited to play it because it looked sort of inspired by Twin Peaks, but just like Twin Peaks this game plays as if it was cancelled midway through. The game starts off rather mysterious and spooky, but everything about that part of the game is suddenly just forgotten and never mentioned again and everything thay comes after is just worse in every way.

I've been wanting someone to make a new SCUMM-style game for ages, as I've played all the LucasArts ones more times than I can count. Thimbleweed Park is quite possibly the best point and click adventure/mystery that I've played, and I've played many! As a seasonsed mystery/adventure gamer, I played through in hard mode and was not disappointed; it was a challenge! This game has flavors of the X-Files and Twin Peaks but is also very much its own story. Unlike many other games of a similar genre, I spent over 17 hours on the first playthrough, very little of which was time spent stuck. Something is always happening in this game  and with five different playable characters there's always a new perspective that you can use to try to solve a problem. It's story-rich and rather than just watching flashbacks, you play through them. I did use the in-game hints several times, because I'm not a very patient gamer, but when I  did I was almost always already on the right track. To me, that's a great sign that all of the puzzles are logic based. Thimbleweed Park is a phenomenal game, especially for adult fans of classic adventure games. I can already see myself replaying this in the future and would purchase another game by the same creators without hesitation.

There is also an exploration aspect in the secrets hidden throughout the game, whether by hundreds of discoverable symbols placed about the map or by the items that contain little bits and pieces of interesting and humurous side story. The main story line itself is interesting and incredibly hilarious. Once you complete the game once, you have the option to play again with a higher difficulty with the same character, giving you the option to keep upgrading your character and its loadout. This can be done multiple times, each time increasing the difficulty. There is also excellent dlc for the game, each piece well-deserving of its price. There is also dlc that is free albeit smaller. Although a great game alone, playing with friends makes this game the best co-op game I have every played. The co-op function of the game is what made my love this game. I have played this game more than 10 times. Not because of the increasing difficulty, but because each time, I played with a different friend. Every playthrough is different as long as you play with a different person.
I really think Handsome Jack just needed a good friend and big ol' Hug, He ain't that bad.
Seriously always find myself coming back to this game.

This game is my #1 game of all time. It holds up to the test of time. This is one of the first PC games my dad taught em to play (probably not a good idea..it's pretty scary for a small child). I came back to it a year or so ago..and actually played it for real.
There are elements of all the best games in this one.
Storyline:
Want a strong storyline? There you go. The game gives you a decent outline of what's going on in the lore, but all of the really in-depth details are in little PDA things..kinda like audio logs.
Don't care for the story? Don't pick up the audiologs.
Progression System:
Before the game even starts, you can choose from a few different "stat boosts" that can help you in the game. You can bolster these abilities and unlock new ones as the game progresses.
Combat:
Not the best...actually. It's glitchy 1999 hitboxes...but it doesn't affect the game that much. There are three branches you can choose from..or mix n' match. You got the rooty shooty gun branch, the stabby slapper melee branch, and then the spooky magic path. Each one of these trees can help you throughout the game. Each combat branch will allow you to progress in different ways. From using your magic USB-ball to pull *USEFUL* objects that are otherwise unreachable. Use your shooty bullet skills to fix and modify guns you find and make the better so you can shooty the snot out of the weird alien things...or just go melee and use the wrench for the majority of the game and beat the heads in of alien things...then get a magical spikey crystal that is even better and makes more pain for the weird grubby aliens.
Skills:
There are a large number of skills you can upgrade and unlock, from hacking cameras and doors to being a telekenisis weilding wizard. You can upgrade your weapon skills that allow you to fix the broken guns you find (to shoot aliens and robots). You can upgrade your wizardry powers to shoot fire! (I mean there are cool things like levitation and turning bullets into med packs...but fire is pretty cool)
It's literally just a great game in every aspect. I would highly reccomend buying this game... it's back in the good ol' 90's when games were actually made to be good instead of pumping out the same each year to make their money.

A surrealist horror game with third person shooter/survival/rpg mechanics. What's not to like? Play as Sebastian Castellanos, a grim detective searching for his daughter in the bizarre, nightmarish world of STEM, a virtual reality formed by combining human minds via a machine. Originally intended to create a utopia, something has gone terribly, terribly wrong and the STEM world has devolved into a realm populated by grotesque amalgamations of what were once human bodies.
+ The pacing and immersion of this game is incredible. I can't remember the last time I couldn't pull myself away from a single player campaign. The world building both in story and map design constantly whetting your appetite for the truth of what exactly is going on, and just when you feel you've got the hang of things the game throws a complete curveball at you, such as an area where your weapons don't work or a brand new type of enemy. I was literally never bored.
+ The mechanics work really well. There is just enough ammo and pickups to keep you going, but you've got to work for it. The combat feels challenging but fair, whenever I died it felt like I messed up and new why. The process for levelling up is well thought out and encourages finding resource efficient ways of dispatching as many enemies as possible. Weapons feel good, overall the combat and general playing feels good and fun.
+ General polish. There are almost no bugs and the design/bindings are very intuitive and work well.
+ Exploration heavily rewarded. Travelling off the beaten path in this game isn't just optional, it's pretty much mandatory. And if you look hard enough there are some insane secrets to be found. Hidden rooms, levels, weapon caches, potential allies, even minigames. The levels aren't the biggest, but they're all cram packed with things to find and explore. I'm consider myself to be pretty thorough at clearing for loot and I can already tell that I've missed a considerable amount. Fortunately that just means my next playthrough will be all the more fun.
- The game does NOT run very well. On my RX 480 I had to cap it at 60 fps because otherwise it would rapidly fluctuate between 30 and 70 which was exceedingly frustrating. And even then I rarely hit 60, only in small corridors mostly, outdoors im lucky to be in the fifties. That said, the style of this game doesn't really necessitate higher than 60 fps to look really good so it doesn't bother me as much as if CS:GO couldn't top 60 but still, not very well optimized. Also, maybe 10 fps max difference between low settings and ultra.
- Your character doesn't really handle all that well. It's fine for stealth and general walking but in combat the transitions between crouching and standing, walking and running, in and out of cover etc are all very slow and clunky when you're trying to run from being Zerg'd by a horde of zombies.
Overall this might be the best game I've played all year. I had way more fun than I expected, 9/10 IMO.

The Evil Within 2 is, at its core, a fun game. I always try to start with that when it comes to games.
There are plenty of 3rd Person Shooters, Horror Games, and others which are in some ways better or more beautiful, but this was probably the first one I played through to the end in quite a while.
For a comparison, I would say this game is somewhere in between Resident Evil 4 and 5. RE5 wasn't a bad game, but lacked the innovation and fun of RE4. I would say The Evil Within 2 (TEW2) is better than RE5.
The gameplay is satisfying. Each weapon delivers the impact you might like. The story, while somewhat simple, progresses nicely.
I played on normal difficulty, which was fair. Some deaths, but not too many. I look forward to continuing my playthrough on Hard.
The game gets a little repetative towards the end, so my only complaint is not enough variety in enemy types as the game closes.
Nevertheless, the visuals are at times pretty cool and the game itself has a lot going for it.
At 18-22 hours for the main campaign, with good replayability (I think) this is a good game for those who liked the direction RE4 took the series, even if RE7 was good too.
In short, an 8/10. Fun, challenging enough, with some cool set pieces.

Broforce is Brotastic. It is EASILY one of the best designed action-focused sidescrollers I have EVER played.
Concept / Elevator Pitch - A retro (artisticly) inspired side-scroller whereby you play as one of a HUGE roster of 70's/80's/90's inspired action personas/characters (names changed to be "BRO" themed).  Each character has his/her own weapons/playstyle that you use to get to the end of the level. On the way, you will kill all sorts of bad dudes.  Missions (usually) are in clumps of 4-5 levels.
The twist: So in levels, there are "hostages" that look a LOT like homages to metal slug hostages. Rescue one, and you get one extra life starting from the nearest checkpoint. The twist is you become a different BRO from the varied list of unlocked characters. This also happens when you die.
Furthermore....
-4 player coop
-Basically unlimited levels (community built).
-A level editor
-Harder modes if you ever (how could you) find it too easy.
- Levels are physics-based and are fully destructable. Want to avoid an enemy? Shoot a path under it.
Cons
- Really none. It is damn near perfect.

I write this review holding my original copy of Total Annihilation in hand. But I'll just set it down, so I can type better. This game is what many other games have tried to emulate, but have failed in some aspect (looking mainly at YOU, Planetary Annihilation). It really should be able to please just about any RTS fan. Want a quick, in your face battle? You got it. Want a long war of attrition? Done (Play Seven Islands for an epic air/sea/nuke battle royale). The campaign is pretty solid too, from what I remember.
The music is what I remembered the most, I think. It was just so epic, and fit the game so perfectly. And, for a game that's pushing 20 years old, it still has a charming look to it, not too far off from some indie games released much later. Sometimes pathing can be a bit annoying, but when your units get stuck, just blast them with your Commander's D-gun, for instant gratification.
I think really the only negative thing I can say, is that this version includes all the expansion(s). I felt the base game is awesome without the new units and such. Also, I can't help but notice that the AI had to have been tweaked in some ways. It's much more predictable with the xpacs, and dumbed down. It is nice they included the map editor though, sometimes it feels that the provided maps can get stale. That might also be from playing every map many, many times.
Cavedog was a pretty legit developer that just unfortunately got overwhelmed by a small market at that time period. I loved their other release, TA: Kingdoms as well. I've sunk tons and tons of hours into both TA series. And Boneyards (their inhouse online service) was so ahead of its time, as far as matchmaking, community, patch releases, and content updates on the reg, it's a shame nothing else has really come along, at least for me, that made the same impression.
Pro Tip(s): You want more than 4 players/AI in a skirmish? After hitting the 'single' button, press * and the corresponding roman numeral to the amount of players you want. Example: *X would bump the limit to 10. Reap benefits and/or get rekt.
You want to play any campaign mission, any way? From the main menu, click 'Single' then type, drdeath    All one word, no spaces, lowercase. A bone will appear in the gap on the right menu, that once clicked, a campaign master menu opens up, from which you can select any assortment of mission you'd like.

This includes the "The Core Contingency" Addon. It runs without any problems on my machine (1920x1080). i recommend to visit

I've played my fair share of free-to-play games on Steam, and while many were good, not all of them were worth writing home about. Despite the all-too-familar presentation and assets that comes with the RPGMaker engine, Eternal Senia does have some interesting quirks that help it stand out from some other RPGMaker games I've played.
The game follows the story of Senia, a girl who was adopted into the care of a young priestess after her parents and village were destroyed. One day, the priestess (named Magaleta) disappears in search of a mystical force called the Eternity, for reasons unbeknownst to Senia. Unwilling to leave Magaleta's side, Senia takes up arms and follows her into the Eternity Tower, putting herself on a path to discovering the true nature of the Eternity...
Personally, I didn't really care much for the story until the latter half of the game. I understand that the creator of the game is desperate to get this story across, but I fault the presentation more for that issue. I've seen a ton of RPGMaker games already, and the reuse of default assets makes the games reek of laziness. In the case of Eternal Senia, I do applaud the creator for actually trying to make his game not look like every other RPGMaker game out there. Senia and Magaleta's sprite designs look unique, the CGs used in the story are quite nice, and the multiple endings do add some replayability to the game.
Now the combat is an interesting topic. It's very reminiscent of the early Ys games, meaning you run into enemies multiple times until either you kill them or they kill you. Most of the time, you'll kill them, but there are some powerful enemies on the field that will give you trouble if you run into them. Thankfully, the amount of grinding you have to do to get up to that point is cut short by the crafting system. Using materials that you pick up from enemies and chests, you can forge weapons and armor to increase your stats. It's a simple and straightforward system, but it entices you to grind for materials and grow stronger at the very least.
I'm honestly surprised a game like this is free when similar games like Skyborn and Machina of the Planet Tree cost money. It's a fairly good RPGMaker experience for those with sad wallets, and I recommend it to anyone with even a passing interest in what this game's all about.

I'll keep it simple; this game is amazing, but it's got sooo many flaws. I've boiled them down to my main 5 complaints:
1. Very difficult to get into it, the learning curve and random quest spacing makes you feel like you're leveling incredibly slowly, regardless of what you're doing.
2. Forums are impossible to use. If you're like me and were a part of the Beta Testing, you were never given a key to join the forums. You need to physically go through their Customer Support and have them set up a profile for you manually.
3. Customer Support is IMPOSSIBLE to get in touch with. I did everything within my power to try and get in contact with someone, but I was redirected to random unhelpful pages telling me that my only solution was to contact Customer Support.
4. Community is a big part of every MMO. You'll have players that spend their whole life in-game, and you'll have those that really don't play that often, then everything inbetween. This game is kinda empty, given there isn't really a community behind it. The ones that do play are either new, or incredibly hardcore about playing. Make a single mistake when running a dungeon and you'll get the boot, regardless of what it is. Same rule applies for a lot of their other "activites".
5. Paid Expansions.. This always irritates me.. So they advertise "no subsciptions", which sounds great - until you want to actually play some of the expansion content that they are shoveling out by the boat load. Don't get me wrong, it's amazing stuff, but they make it so difficult to access, and then put it up behind a pay-wall. So not only do you have to purchase their expansion content, you have to pay a subscription to access that same content that you just purchased. I don't understand that, especially in a game that is advertised as "no subscription".
Outside of that, the game is pretty great. I'll recommend it to people who want a grind MMO with a good storyline, but if you want a solid all-around MMO.. I don't know if it'll be the one you're after.

Dishonored was one of my favorite games ever, so this was the game I had been most looking forward to in 2016. Unfortunately I have found it to be, overall, a disappointment. First, it's crippled by the performance issues. I have a decent PC (gtx 1070 and overclocked 4670k) and it's stutter city. Compared to, for example, DOOM (not a game I like very much either by the way, but it runs amazing), this port is a joke. The performance issues are real. Second, the story is nowhere near as well crafted or engaging as the first game. There is literally no pacing, no good plot twists -- just one level after the next, with the story feeling like padding the dev team phoned in. the hub area is frankly terrible and feels like an afterthought, with none of the charm of the Hound's Pit Pub. The characters and voice acting are likewise not in the same class. Third, while the levels are large, they lack the immersion and variety of the first game. There is nothing like Lady Boyle's party, nothing like the feeling of being betrayed and fighting your way out of the Flooded District. These problems combine to mean that while each level, taken in itself, may be technically impressive (there are undeniably some great ideas here -- the clockwork mansion and the mansion in the dust district being the highlights), overall the game doesn't draw you in and make you care, make you feel immersed as the character in the situation, in the awesome way the first game did. To me the first game was one of my most memorable gaming experiences that I'll never forget -- this one is impressive at times but overall a frustrating experience that never coalesces to the masterpiece it could have been. It'd be a decent game, a solid but not a top recommendation for the sales, if not for the terrible performance issues. Unless they address those my advice is to avoid this one for now. It's such a disappointment writing this, especially in a year so bereft of strong AAA games -- this one was 2016's chance to redeem itself. Too bad.

It is definitely better than Evil Within mechanically, but it does suffer from lack of immensely memorable moments that the first game had. That is not to say this game has a bad story or that it is boring, oh nononono, that is not the case here. Evil Within 2 has a really cool thing going with it by having explorable sections of the world that you can walk around and actually be able to set up ambushes to take down your demented foes. There are of course narrow, dark hall ways that you come to expect in horror games, with some truly ridiculously nasty things to see.
As for the story, the premise is laid out simply as you playing once again as Sebastion Castiannos and this time, he returns to the world of STEM to locate his missing daughter, but of course, things go horrifically wrong and you are trying to survive in this monstrocity of a world. There are cool side quests you can partake in to learn more about the residents that resided in the STEM world, as well as Sebastion himself! I of course wont spoil any of this, since it is actually really good and had some nice moments that made me smile or jump in fright.
The game play is more tight than before, with a good selection of weapons, but you will most likely utilize only a handful of weapons since ammunition if pretty darn scarce and the stronger weapons of course have the most expensive ammunition, making sticking with your handgun, crossbow, and melees are more viable option most of the time. Of course, everyone can have a different opinion, so I will let you be the judge of what weapons are worth your time. Crafting in general is fairly simple; you need you spare parts to upgrade your guns and you need the green gel to upgrade Sebastion's abilities. You find these materials by exploring the world and killing enemies. Easy right?
If you enjoyed the first Evil Within, horror games, or simply games that Shinji Mikami worked on, then Evil Within 2 is definitely a worthy buy!
