Certainly not a perfect version. It still has issues of disappearing status bar at the bottom of the screen if you actually run AT your resolution (1920x1080 for example), you gotta run at something like 1680x900 in order to actually see the entire UI on screen, which is ridiculous.
And it really is a must, because you NEED that status bar to see build rates, energy and metal rates, etc for selected or hovered-over items and factories.
The great thing however is that this IS the best working version so far. You dont have to edit .ini files or use third party apps to get it running properly in fullscreen without glitches, apart from the above mentioned. For that alone it is worth a rebuy (because we cant really blame the original devs for not considering Windows 8 / 10 compatability, now can we?) :)
That said, I highly recommend people to immediately get some of the convenience mods / balance patches out there.
In some ways they are almost required to enjoy the game in a modern RTS mindset.
Such as being able to select groups with just pressing 1, instead of pressing Alt+1 which was ridiculous at that time, and is still highly user-unfriendly today.
Or being able to hold and drag buildings when holding shift. Makes building walls feasible, which it wasnt in vanilla TA placing one at a time, click click click click.
A great masterpiece of a game that DOES show its age due to some weird control schemes they opted for in the old days.
But with mods to modernize and "logicalize" the controls, it still holds up today, despite the awful pathfinding.
The pure atmosphere and "feel" of the game is still un-rivaled. No other RTS "feels" like TA.
Perhaps it is the music, perhaps it is the graphics, perhaps it is the clunky slow controls.
No matter what it is, it is greater than the sum of its part. A robbery at this price, must-buy.

I'll keep it simple; this game is amazing, but it's got sooo many flaws. I've boiled them down to my main 5 complaints:
1. Very difficult to get into it, the learning curve and random quest spacing makes you feel like you're leveling incredibly slowly, regardless of what you're doing.
2. Forums are impossible to use. If you're like me and were a part of the Beta Testing, you were never given a key to join the forums. You need to physically go through their Customer Support and have them set up a profile for you manually.
3. Customer Support is IMPOSSIBLE to get in touch with. I did everything within my power to try and get in contact with someone, but I was redirected to random unhelpful pages telling me that my only solution was to contact Customer Support.
4. Community is a big part of every MMO. You'll have players that spend their whole life in-game, and you'll have those that really don't play that often, then everything inbetween. This game is kinda empty, given there isn't really a community behind it. The ones that do play are either new, or incredibly hardcore about playing. Make a single mistake when running a dungeon and you'll get the boot, regardless of what it is. Same rule applies for a lot of their other "activites".
5. Paid Expansions.. This always irritates me.. So they advertise "no subsciptions", which sounds great - until you want to actually play some of the expansion content that they are shoveling out by the boat load. Don't get me wrong, it's amazing stuff, but they make it so difficult to access, and then put it up behind a pay-wall. So not only do you have to purchase their expansion content, you have to pay a subscription to access that same content that you just purchased. I don't understand that, especially in a game that is advertised as "no subscription".
Outside of that, the game is pretty great. I'll recommend it to people who want a grind MMO with a good storyline, but if you want a solid all-around MMO.. I don't know if it'll be the one you're after.

Enough people have complained about the technical issues, so I won't bother.  The actual gameplay and some of the new abilities are fun.  The writing and story composition on the other hand, is absolutely terrible.
The main character can't seem to shake the uncontrollable urge to spout endless exposition at every opportunity...this not only destroys immersion(I don't need to hear about how my character feels when killing a guard), but often divulges information that you as the PC couldn't possibly know at that point in the story.
All the characters felt really flat, as if they had no connection to eachother or anything else anywhere in the game.  God help me most of the time they actually sounded bored.
All the individual story elements felt like badly composed episodes of a procedural TV show, w/o even having the benefit of the overall narrative to pull everything together.
Then there's the main city of this installment...Karnaca.  Supposedly being oppressed by the duke, it instead felt like I was visiting a European Villa.  Everything looked way too sunny and bright, and served rather poorly to deliver what I can only assume is the intended theme.  The bloodflies felt really forced, as if they were just thrown in to give the player "fodder" to deal with.
tl;dr--With the exception of the actual gameplay itself, Dishonored 2 is the polar opposite of the first game in almost every way.  Even if you are a die-hard fan of the original I would wait for a sale.

Thimbleweed Park is a special affair, it is full with memories of people who shaped the genre in the late eighties, saw its highlights in the early ninties and had to witness how Adventure games became more and more rare, until you could have thought they are more dead than disco.
If you played Zak McKracken or Maniac Mansion (or any other Lucasfilm/Lucas Arts game) then you will find a lot of cameos of characters, little jokes on the old games and the genre, like the Sierra habit of having the player able to die at any failed puzzle, which they tell you pretty early on that you do not need to be afraid of that.
Thimbleweed Park is like a time traveller from the past, it has the old spirit but cleverly disguised itself so it does blend in more with modern days games. Ron Gilbert and his team did bring the genre softly into shape, without trying to do radical things like 3D graphics, but subtle stuff. For the not so subtle stuff, there are a lot of in-jokes and plays on old days games, which some people will hate and some people (like me) find funny to no end. But these can be turned off (in fact by default they seem to be) in the settings so you can concentrate on the actual story, should you wish to do so. If you loved the old Lucas Arts adventure games, you will love this.

An excellent callback to the point-and-click adventure games of years ago. Thimbleweed Park is an adventure game reminiscent of LucasArts games such as the Monkey Island series (fitting since it was made its creators).
In an age of hand-holding, Thimbleweed Park provides a lengthy adventure where the player is required to think outside the box in order to solve the game's puzzles. The puzzles are never impossible, all the clues are there, you never have to make an impossible jump in logic to solve them. While fans of adventure games may love this, TP caters to newer fans and those who may just love a story by implementing an Easy Mode too.
TP may look like an old school point-and-click, but it doesn't rest on its laurels. It keeps things fresh by weaving a story with 5 playable characters the player can use simultaneously to solve the game's puzzles.
The story is somewhat mature, but has plenty of humour and 4th wall-breaking quips.
Just when you think you have things figured out, Thimbleweed Park changes the questions.
With a good 10-15 hours worth of content, Thimbleweed Park is wholeheartedly recommended to someone looking for an enjoyable, brain-testing adventure.

Thimbleweed Park is an very well polished game. Do not be turned off by the fact it was a Kickstarter game. Ron Gilbert of Monkey Island fame was one of the primary designers of the game. It is clear that while the gameplay style is an older varity his experiences in game design have been advantage of with newer technologies to produce challanging puzzles intergrated well into the games main story.
Often point and click adventure games stuggle with smoothly intergrating story into puzzle design. This has lead to older games having some, odd requirements, to solve puzzles. I did not feel like I encoutered this at all.
That game also has an interesting feature for hints if you are unable to decipher the games clue. The game features an ingame phone system allowing you to call a few different ingame characters and have conversations. They used part of this feature to build an in game "hint line".
You pick up the phone and dial the number for the hint line. The game will then contextually pick up on where you are in the game's story and provide hint options on what you might need help with. The hints start off gradually soft. They dont want to ruin the puzzles for you completely. This is useful so that you know if you are head in the right direction. You can keep pressing for a more detailed hint. The game will break the puzzle down for you more and more making it clear what you need to do.
I recommend that you only do this if you are truly lost however. The hint line was built after the game was completed. You are essitnatlly ruining the game experience if you do.

Anyways, I enjoyed this game very much. If you are looking for more games like Monkey Island or even just to try something new overall. This is a good pick.

I started playing NMRIH in 2015 out of curiosity. I’m a huge fan of old school, hardcore survival-horror and the more hardcore and realistic, the better. So I started playing and the first thing that piqued my interest was the soundtrack. That menu theme definitely brings back memories from Resident Evil safe rooms.
I remember that my first games were mostly big fails, trying to melee a single zed and getting infected, trying to shoot with an empty gun I just picked up and so on. This is what NMRIH is all about: survival.
Pushing the Source Engine to its limits, NMRIH looks rather good and sounds fairly well too - and not just “for a mod”. The environnements are very well crafted and each and every map has a theme and a mood of its own, most of which are very inspired by movies or TV shows like Night of Living Dead, The Walking Dead or 28 Days Later to name a few. Voice acting is fine, pretty immersive, and character are also inspired by movies. There can be A LOT of zeds on screen and overall the game is well optimized. First person and zeds animations are fine, however third person character animations are pretty horrid. Being a 3D artist myself I know how hard it is to animate a human character though… It’s hard AF.
Now about the gameplay… That’s where the game really shines. There’s two game modes: Survival being a wave-based, protect the zone thing. The other, Objective, is more like L4D where you have to achieve some objectives to progress and escape, like getting a key or finding the code to open a door, all of which are randomized making each game unique and tense.
You play as your average guy/girl trapped into a “Romero style” zombie infection. Meaning you won’t see any special infectees. Weapons, ammos, healing items - any ressource actually - are really scarce and you’ll have to manage all of this as a team, barricade yourself, set up traps and so on. As such, any form of combat requires training and planning. Running out of stamina because of a missed crowbar swing or gunshot will get you a nice little bite and once infected, there’s not much you can do: you can take pills that will stop the infection for one or two minutes, or wait for a FEMA drop which might have a Gene Therapy. Of course, when infected nothing forces you to tell it to your teammates… But if you die of infection, you’ll raise up as a runner which are a serious threat for your teammates… Or you can kill yourself.
I really recommend this game. It has a mood that Contagion for instance, doesn’t has. It’s absolutely reckless and if you don’t play as a team, plan your actions and manage your inventory and stamina, you’ll die. Again and again. And this is what I like - NMRIH is the Dark Souls of FPS zed survival games.
There’s a sequel in the making, I’m really looking forward to it!

So much has already been said about Dark Souls II that I'll direct you to the "formal" reviews of IGN, PC Gamer, etc.  I will say, at the end of the day, it's a solid game worth every penny to buy.  I will agree that it's "easier" than previous Souls games in several ways, but it is also still a rewarding and enjoyable gaming experience.  If you are spoiler free and going in completely blind, you will find it an incredible challenge.
Personally, I feel the weightiness of combat is actually improved.  The reduction in iFrames is, for me, a welcomed changed; you need to more legitamately avoid being hit versus rolling magically through a sword (note I said "more" because there is still some of this). The addition of 4 ring slots is a welcome customization change.  While they were not able to deliver fully on the lighting and details they had hoped for (and shown us), it is still a visually stunning game that makes you pause frequently to appreciate the artistry.
I do not want to spoil the story, but suffice it to say, it is not as epic as its predecessor.  In its own way, however, it stands up and delivers a tale that rewards the patient listener and reader as souls games have in the past.  Still, it left me wishing for more.
The only comment I will say about PvP is that I feel it was improved.  There was so much gimmickry with Dark Souls 1 that fighting became more about who knew the tricks or who could create a trolling low SL build to ruin the experience for people legitamately playing through the game.  In DS2, however, I felt I was prepared and capable of fighing anyone who invaded me: it just requred patience and attention which are combat skills that SHOULD be an advantage and not made irrelevant because someone was able to easily make a ninja flipping Havel who was the master of lag stabs and lag parries.
In summary, if you enjoy the Souls experience, buy this.  If you're new and intrigued by the Souls experience, buy this.  Personally, I felt they DID make it more accessible while still showing this veteran a good time.  And that was and continues to be well worth my $60.

Dark Souls 2 is the sequel to one of the most deliciously unforgiving games ever created. Why we love it so much is that it pushes players to their very limit, forcing us to think of ways to progress and to be patient under stress, all the while luring us into a rich story that is admittedly easy to miss if you don't keep digging: but you're sure to find gold if you do.
I could talk about the game forever, but i'll some up this review with some succinct pros and cons compared to Dark Souls 1 and in general.
Cons:
- The story and lore feel a bit shallower
- There are fewer NPCs and it feels like time with them is a bit too brief to care for them as much as we could have (like Solaire of Astora or the emotional tearjerker that is the 'Sif and Artorias' lore , though Lucatiel of Mirrah was pretty amicable. I just don't think it pulled at the heartstrings anywhere near as much as DS1 which was much more subtle and bittersweet.)
(The above cons will probably be a thing of the past with the DLC coming!)
- Soundtrack's great but the themes are a bit short/too few
- Not sure just yet what to think about the ending. What i think the Souls series really needs is more of a player-input driven story with multiple outcomes. In DS1, you at least had a choice of the ending: to burn yourself and continue the age of fire a while longer, or usher in an age of darkness and let the abyss spread. Kaath and Frampt were good 'karma' catalysts: you chose how you wanted to be remembered.
- The change to endurance etc are perhaps not always a good thing, but it did need a little tweaking
Pros:
+ There are some real gems in the story, and true to real life, some very multi-dimensional characters like Pate and Creighton - there is much discussion on who we can really class as the 'good guy' - in the end, they both seem about as bad as each other. After a certain part of the game in Tseldora, you'll walk away doublethinking your allegiances and that a game can still do this is excellent.
+ The game runs as smooth as butter and having come from the PS3 version of DS1, the steam version of DS2 looks beautiful. You lose count at how many levels just look stunning - i know a big favourite will be the Aerie near the end.
+ The soundtrack is once again great - with some real teeth clenchers like "Royal Rat Authority" and true to DS-style "Ruin Sentinels"
+ The magic, pyromancy and hexes are as awesome to use as ever, and with a few returning favourites ;)
In DS1, you fought titans and gods that had gone hollow and the lore was as deep as you kept digging, now instead with the flow of time convoluted as in Lordran, you are following the footsteps of King Vendrick, reaccomplishing his deeds in order to replace him as the next monarch. But essentially, you're fighting much less prominent foes and it does feel a bit less dramatic.
I like that the ending is an expression of the neverending cycle of the Lord Souls simply repiecing themselves together and all of life renewing time and time again, rather than the absolute nothingness of the abyss, but it felt like we were powerless to really make a choice - Vendrick chose to put off burning himself and went hollow, keeping the King's Ring safe from Nashandra, but it does feel like towards the end, we are simply marching onwards with very, very little direction or purpose.
I'd absolutely advise buying this. You can see a lot of time and care went into level design and coding, my only wish is that it'd had a tiny bit more dialogue and longer boss themes because it's too good ;D
There are still many questions left to be answered but i must admit i preferred DS1 and would advise buying that before this, if for no other reason than to get a feel for punishment ;)

You know, I made a review about this game, and I completely focused on the cons. I'll take another shotat making a coherant review and reason why you should or shouldn't buy this game.
Dark Souls 2 is a mixed bag in every possible way. Allow me to explain in every single category. First the combat, Dark Souls 2 actually made its combat slightly different then its previous installment, it feels as if Fromsoft slowed the movement of the character, but sped up the weapon swings. This feels as if they are trying to encourage a more strategic thinking of combat but there's a problem, there's no mid-roll anymore. There's a fast roll, fat roll, and tuba walking. In the process of making combat more strategic From has actually just slowed down combat. In addition, the hitboxes are insanely large, so you'll be getting hit by something that won't even touch a pixel of your character.
Speaking of combat Dark Souls 2 is TOO ♥♥♥♥ING EASY. This games idea of "difficulty" is throwing as many enemies as possible at you. Especially the ones the kamikaze at you and deal insane amounts of damage at you. Speaking of as many as possible there's many more bosses that have more than one entity in it. By many more I mean 11 OUT OF 31. And, there's actually a boss that has 3 HEALTH BARS! ♥♥♥♥ING GENIUS!
There are so many things I could go on about. The fact that everything is humanoid except for about 5 enemies, many bosses are uninspired, the areas are boring in both design and layout and so many others. But despite all these flaws and dissapointments, I don't hate this game. Maybe it's because it's a Souls game I can't help but have fun with it.
I actually recommend Dark Souls not to mainstream audiences but only to a demographic that can enjoy a game despite all of its flaws. Maybe you'll have fun with it, or you'll hate it, but these were my feelings over it.

Don't let the release date fool you. It may be an old game, but imo, still one of a kind. Action packed gameplay mixed in with truckloads of humor from the quaint NPCs you meet in the game, especially Claptrap. As much as you feel your brain cells commit suicide one by one whenever Claptrap speaks, you just want to hear more. Odd, I know.
Similar to your typical FPS, but less reality and more crazy fantasy fun. Singleplayer may be a little boring but playing with a friend or two (or three even) is a whole new dimension of fun.

The variety of different weaponry is really one of my favorite aspects of the game. That, along with the different classes and skill trees give you an opportunity to play the game in a variety of different ways: from sniping someone from halfway across the map to getting up close and personal with a shotgun, to just chucking fully loaded guns at them until they die. I love the storyline which is replayable again and again without getting old, and the plethora of sidequests means there's lots to do. I definitely recommend the game of the year edition, because all the DLC is worth it for the content you get.
The humor of the game is enjoyable, and all around it is just a fun game to play. The only issue I have is that it is a bit slow to start. That doesn't matter for the first play through where you're just getting your bearings, but I really wish there was an option to start a new game in true vault hunter mode (or ultimate) for subsequent playthroughs, if only because that's when you have enough skills unlocked that each class starts to truly shine. It would also give me a bit more incentive to play through with each class if it meant I wouldn't have to start from scratch each time.
All in all, great game though. One of my absolute favorites and I completely recommend it!

Haven't played through much of the game yet so I can't give an evaluation of the story.
This game is definitely the worst pc port I've seen yet, admittedly I steer clear of the really bad ports but this is definitely a red flag. Compared to the original game which actually seems to handle anything I threw at it fine (played the game in a window and used a tool to make it borderless) this game flat out refuses to cooperate.
Max resolution available to me is 1280x1024, you can force change this in the ini but the game automatically re-writes settings when it reloads (which is often, more later) so I had to forcibly deny access via Windows security settings.
Windowed mode is also an option via .ini edit however do not expect borderless, the game flips out and the window simply becomes invisible if you attempt to modify anything about the size of the window while it is open, whether that be borderless using a tool or maximizing it in task manager to get rid of the ugly gap beneath the window.
The game also reloads often, loading in any area seems to do this as do some cutscenes, and believe me this is often. As a result of the console release presumably and the limited hardware of said consoles at the time the actual areas loaded in at once are horrifically small (Funnily enough, a criticism of the newer "The Fall" title too). However, this is not just loading screens, the game actually reloads itself entirely each time it does so, other reviews were certainly not exaggerating when they said you will spend more time watching loading screens than in game.
There are some other minor issues arising already, the controls are certainly not as freely rebindable as the first game and the UI compared to the previous game is clearly console-based though workable on PC. Other issues of varying magnitude by individual preference are a somewhat lacking options menu and more.
Overall, as far as a PC title goes this game has a whole host of issues, this game is certainly not for the impatient and many will find the port frustrating to work with (hopefully some of my points help people get the game working how they like it).
As for the story, o far it seems like it could be promising, seen a few Deus Ex 1 style options, the core mechanics are still there though I'm not well they're handled later down the line. So far the game has been very much like a tutorial (or perhaps the game as a whole is too linear). There is certainly a clear conspiracy style storyline (as you would expect for Deus Ex) though perhaps its a little forced this time, as I mentioned I haven't played much so far, only about to leave the first area and I am already being presented by two very distinct sides and making a major choice between the two.
This review isn't really to cover the storyline though, if you've previously played Deus Ex you already know the reputation of Invisible War and are considering playing it because you want to find out what happens after the 1st game, just keep in mind the hurdles in doing so I mentioned earlier. I do think I will play this to the end regardless, just might be in shorter bursts than HR and DX1.

When I first played this game (as a port to the XBox), I thought this game was amazing.  Then I played Deus Ex 1 and my opinion of Invisible War changed for the worse.  Invisible War offers good game play, a good story, some interesting choice mechanics, and smart writing.  But all of this is not as good as what the first Deus Ex, or many other games for that matter.  The game play often times feels streamlined to the point of being dumbed down.  The way choices are presented to the player feels more overt and clunky than Dues Ex.  While the writing is smarter than many other games, the dialouge too often takes the form of exposition dump or feels out of place.  Deus Ex had a similar problem with out of place philosophic dialogue, but Invisible War did it worse.
If steam offered a mixed choice instead just yes or no in terms of recommendations, I would choose that.  Given the binary nature of recommendations, I have to choose yes.   DE Invisible War is by no means a bad game and is actually very enjoyable.  Due to some unfortunate design choices it is not as good as it could have been.

tl,dr: Beautiful game with some technical problems, just awesome if it works as expected
Dishonored 2 truly is a beautiful game in so many respects. Great art style, wonderful music and intriguing game play are paired with meaningful choices, which change the game-world and the interactions of the player character with this world. These choices are mostly dependent on your actions as a player: Will you dispatch your targets through nonlethal means, will you silently assassinate them (and only them) or do you seek bloody revenge on everyone who happens to cross your path, including innocent bystanders? Either way, you'll do whatever you want: If you ask yourself "Couldn't I just do this to achieve that", you'll find out that indeed you can...  In these moments, Dishonored 2 really shines. But it's not all sunshine, unfortunately, because even after several patches, many technical issues of the game still aren't fixed:
* Glitches: mostly scripts not triggering, often fixed by reloading; "wall elevators" are obviously still a thing though
* Bugs: NPCs will die without proper reason, e.g. in the observatory level, unconscious witches will die (if they weren't pacified using sleep darts specifically), just as you go for the nonlethal option and activate
. The post mission screen after level 2 will report a max of collectible coins based on the amount you could collect during a NG+, and there are several other bugs
* Frame drops and stuttering; often fixed by restarting the game
* Crashes; not much you could do (The game crashed around 10 times in 100h of gaming)
* Character control is not consistent, for instance inputs are randomly dropped, or Emily's momentum is not predictably conserved during far reach and similar stuff, which just doesn't work as intended or expected (throwing bottles is another example)
* Unexpected and inconsistent game mechanics like jumping vs. climbing (same control key), which gets in the way of gameplay, mostly notable in a "Flesh and Steel"-Run
* Sound occlusion isn't working properly, which is really confusing: volume levels and spatial positioning of audio sources are  sometimes ... well, just totally off  >:|
But despite it's technical issues, DH 2 is one of the best stealth games I have ever played. So many cool ways to achieve your goals, to manipulate the game and its NPCs. So many details to discover, books to read, conversations to be overheard, treasures to be looted and a level design which is quite unique and inventive, to say the least. I for one enjoyed solving the Jindosh-Lock-Puzzle immensely, but when I discovered in my second play-through that there's actually a pattern, I noticed just how fast these level design gimmicks could get old and boring... Nevertheless, get this game. Work around its problems, and you'll have lots of fun.

TL;DR: I paid less than $20 USD for this game and definitely got my money's worth. Don't pay more than $30.
I love and have an intimate appreciation for the Alien franchise. This game does an excellent job of returning the gaming avenue of Alien back to its roots with just the right touch to music, theme, and application. Unfortunately, I found myself unable to be enchanted by the suspension of disbelief due to some quirky, some downright gimmicky, elements. Certain sequences felt forced, and the last few hours of the game are bloated with horror genre tropes.
I often joke about beloved Dead Space, saying that a more appropriate title would be "Isaac Has A Bad Day", and it seems that someone at Creative Assembly picked up on a similar notion, borrowing that very feel for the driving plot of Alien: Isolation. In it, we play as Amanda Ripley, daughter of the main character from the first film, but are prevented from really appreciating her talents or backstory because of the good-but-fast introduction. Exposition does little to inform us, with terminal log entries being the only way to dive into the lore. Additionally, these terminals are often placed in harm's way, out of the path of natural plot progression, so that if you ignore terminals, the amount of overall conflict is cut in half. This leads for any bad that would happen to Ripley to seemingly come from nowhere and rely on classic jump-scare tactics once our familiarity with the titular enemy of the game settles in.
As others have pointed out, the AI that was boasted for the Alien was overstated and misrepresented. The creature is only random in the sense that it could fall into one of three different behavior patterns: 1. Stay in the vents and follow you everywhere but never attack. 2. Stay on the ground and follow you everywhere but never attack. 3. Stay on the ground and always know where you are, regardless of tactics used to distract and/or hide, and attacking without a chance to prepare or react. These sound puristic in approach, but as other reviewers have mentioned it causes nothing but sheer annoyance after the first few hide-and-seek sequences. You will end up reloading old saves just for the sake of being able to trick the AI into not doing anything so as to continue the plot.
It may seem as that my recommendation is ironic given my complaints but the game does a lot right by way of esoteric traits such as the retro-future atmosphere, the nostalgia-driven music, and the absolutely stunning amount of attention paid to detail both mechanical and abstract features by the team at Creative Assembly. As indicated earlier, I paid less than $20 USD for this game and got my money's worth. However, the persistent inability to retain my attention and draw me in to the terror of the setting caused me to simply laugh, get annoyed at, and ultimately just toy around at the challenges.

Hello. I wanna share some suggestions which I believe can make Hurtworld more balanced and attractive for agressive players and casual as well:
Iron armors. They don't need to be initially too sofisticated in design and crafting materials needed, like for the new players to have some more defense against late players who already have guns. So, the player could craft iron helmets and plate chest armors for better defense, but, on the other hand, this kind of armor would be very sensitive to cold and warm and also heavy. That would make harder for any player to be walking around wearing them all the time because they would easily feel warm or cold and even tired faster, like hungry. The ammount of iron pieces would also cause the player to walk and run slower. All theses aspects would create the suitable balance for theses items.
Shields. It would be nice to have wooden shields which could be upgraded to iron ones or even better ones at late game. These shields and armors would have a rate of bullet proof system, like, a bullet shot on a naked head is one hit kill, but if the player is wearing an iron helmet, the one hit kill would drop to 70% chance to happen.
Bullet proof rate system. It is a MUST. Like I said above, I really enjoy the headshot one hit kills in this game, because it makes Hurtworld feels more hardcore and balanced, but it would also be GREAT if by wearing some iron armors it would make more uncertain to cause damage or headshot killings, like: using the arrow or the bullet against an unprotected head would cause one hit kill for sure as it is already, but if the player would be wearing an iron helmet, that would change: arrows would have like 45% chance to hit kill and bullets would have 70% chance. So, it would vary depending on the armor material and the weapon used. That would cause a nice balance to the game, because players would stop being like immortals (for wearing an advanced armor) or bullet sponges like happen in Ark or other games.
Structure destructibility resistence rate. Just like in the bullet proof system rate, the walls and any other structures of the houses would have a rate to be damaged no matter the main used by the raider, like: - Wood wall would have 75% chance to be damaged by C4 and would need one successful C4 hit to be destroyed. - Stone wall would have 50% chance to be damaged by C4 and would need three successful C4 hits to be destroyed. - Iron wall would have 35% chance to be damaged by C4 and would need three successful C4 hits to be destroyed.
On the other hand, the C4 detonator cap could be a bit easier to be found, since it's an often complaint of most users.
The raiding drill would have its durability decreased as long as it is used to destroy the walls in this proportion:
Wood wall would require one raiding drill;
Stone wall would take longer than wood walls to be damaged and require two raiding drills to be completely destroyed;
Iron wall would take longer than stone walls to be damaged and require three raiding drills to be completely destroyed.
But take these numbers and rates as suggestions. Ok?
General itens durability. Every survival game has this and sincerely I see no reason for Hurtworld not to have the same. Like, the stone pickaxe could last for some hits and the iron one would last longer. The same for the weapons especially, so that it would again give some more balance, since the players would have to be repairing them or crafting new ones.
Itens repair system. Make it possible to repair the itens partially damaged by usage. The cost for repairing could be like 40% of the materials needed to craft a new one.
Terrain protection time. It's a very interesting feature that could enable the sleepers systems finally in this game without making it unbalanced for casual players neither giving the raiders too much power. The Ownership Stake would confer a temporary protection for the itens placed on the owner's terrain that would not allow other players to open chests or destroy itens neither the foundations of the house. The only destructible things would be walls or roofs, windows, such non essential strutuctures. The protection countdown would start at the moment the player's Ownership Stake is damaged by the other players, so the raiders would have to invade the base using siege weapons (C4, raiding drill) to destroy walls or roofs, but would also have to "guard" that location until the protection time for that terrain expires in order to be allowed to open the chests or even destroy all the structure or take the ownership of it by placing a new Ownership Stake.
The Ownership Stake would confer initially 30 minutes of protection as default, then it could be upgraded to confer 3 hours of protection, then upgraded again to confer 12 hours of protection. Once again, to offer 24 hours of protection. And finally, 72 hours of protection. So this would give the lone wolf players chances to keep some of their effort preserved and also make the raider's lives more challenging since they wouldn't just "breach and clear", but also be guarding that location.
Obviously, the cost for upgrading the Ownership Stake would increase as it levels up.
Random spawn location choice. Give the players the choice to spawn randomly next to their base location. It is a feature that would fit just well with the topic before, because since the player base is raided and has it's Ownership Stake damaged, it would be no help for the owner to be respawing inside his house, since he would be an easy target for the raiders.
That's it!! All these suggestions could give more balance to the game and allow the usage of more siege weapons like C4 and the raiding drill, as the developers could just make the fine adjustments on the drop rate of the items needed to craft the siege weapons.

Like a delicious cake that's been left in the desert to decay and rot.
At launch, this game was a breath of fresh air. Exo movements were passable for it being a first iteration. But it has been a downhill slope since this game ever hit Steam.
The EM1 saga left an incurable bruise on this game's PC reputation, taking 5 months to be addressed. By then, the damage had been done. With assistance from absolutely abysmal optimisation, every map stutters, and three maps in particular are lobby killers in that they cause half the lobby to fail to load in. With each patch the problems have not gone away, and instead maps that I used to be able to reach 90 fps on now stutter horribly and are seemingly capped at 50 fps.
FOV resets have been present since launch, and with a recent patch in April, the glitch has been WORSENED. That is unacceptable for a 'AAA' development team. Wallbreaches still exist in great number, and the recon drone glitch still hasn't been fixed either. Instead of opting to devote time to fix these glitches, we are instead given more premium ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to chow down on, to play Barbie's Amazing Dress-up Adventure instead of Call of Duty.
With 365 hours in the game, those will be all I will put into this tragic story of a game. Never before has a developer made me feel genuine contempt against them for their utter ineptitude and ignorance. At this point in the year, most playlists are totally unpopulated, leaving Domination the only remotely interesting game mode that has a few breaths left in it. It has been conquered by toxic clans which set up meat grinder lobbies where they hold the flags indefinitely, and those that dare try to queue for Domination are thrown into the lobby, with no sane choice but to quit.
Ignoring any technical failures, and there are PLENTY, the game fails from a balance viewpoint. The EM1 went unfixed for five months, becoming such a malignant cancer that some people still don't know it's been rebalanced and have their same kneejerk reaction as always. The idea of giving out game-changing weapon variants on a random system, IN A COMPETITIVE MULTIPLAYER SHOOTER, was defective from inception and should have been aborted immediately in the boardroom.
Scorestreaks are a total joke. Even adjusting the System Hack by 100 points, and further adjusting its time modules by 50 points each, they are still so easy to earn that a co-ordinated party can loop them indefinitely. And due to a major oversight, the default system hack denies streaks, despite the 400 point anti-streak module touting that it denies streaks from being called in as one of its selling points. As such, the aforementioned meat grinder lobbies are impossible to retaliate against, as it is impossible to call in any streak you may earn. The Warbird AI modules are only 50 points, yet amplify its effectiveness by such a large margin that it should cost over 500 points for what it gives you.
Inversely, the Missile Strike is so ineffective that the only times they are used are when they appear in care packages. The Goliath is a mockery of past games' Juggernaut suits for being offensively weak and defensively akin to soggy paper.
This game exemplifies how NOT to create a multiplayer shooter. Players become titans only if they own the best guns. Scorestreaks either too strong and almost impossible to destroy, or too weak and offer the enemy team free points. The appalling player count, lagging behind BO2, MW3, and even WaW at times, is telling of this game's subliminal ♥♥♥♥ you to PC players.

I have never seen a remake better than this. This fanmade game blows any official AAA remake out of the water. It takes everything good from Half Life 1 and Half Life 2 and combines it into an experience that surpasses both of them by a huge amount. The fast paced, uninterrupted action and puzzle solving of the first game combined with the atmosphere, dialogue, music and cinematic aspects of the second one; all enhanced by modern graphics. In addition to that, the developers went up and beyond anything that should be expected from a remake. Instead of simply upscaling old areas to modern graphics, they completely redesigned everything from scratch, immensely enhancing the immersion and game feel; making you feel like you are actually in a gigantic science facility. The added music tracks in certain areas create emotion and drive home the feeling of isolation that the game evokes.
If you like Half Life, get it immediately. If you have never played Half Life, get it immediately. Hell, if you don't like Half Life, get it immediately. It's that amazing and more than worth the 20 quids you spend on it. Upon playing it the first time, it managed to launch itself straight into my top 10 games of all time, despite not liking the original Half Life and having 20 years worth of gaming under my belt.
That being said, easily a 10/10. Valve, hire these guys; they might just be better than you.

I started the game back in the 25th of October 2015, and took long breaks in between each few sessions of gameplay, only finishing it today on the 20th of January 2017. For a 4-6 hour game, it is a great RPG Maker title. I just finished all 3 endings, and wow, what a game. First of all, it's free and it's an RPG Maker game which runs well on pretty much any Windows computer within the last 10 years. There's no reason not to try Eternal Senia if you're interested.
The gameplay is similar to classic Legend of Zelda, which is pretty simple, fun, and doesn't take too much away from the challenge. Just walk up to an enemy and press the direction its in, and you attack while the enemy may counterattacks if it can. Or use skills to avoid losing too much health. A disappointment I had was when fighting large forms of regular enemies, they would just stand there and take attacks, only counter-attacking if you attack, just like every other basic enemy in the game. Skills make it easier, as enemies can't counterattack, and you can just wait for Mana to refill before continuing your attack. Grinding is also pretty much required for this game, but it really isn't too bad with the challenge rooms that make grinding enjoyable. Additionally the mechanics of the items, the crafting of equipment, and the skills of Eternal Senia are pretty basic and simple to understand, which makes it easy for anyone to pick up.
Almost all of the bosses are a still image on the screen, lanching attacks onto your limited movement area at the bottom of the screen. I was unimpressed at first, but it was pretty challenging later on. Moving around, dodging a dozen attacks and summons just to get a few hits on the boss before doing it all over again was really fun. Before most boss rooms, the game offers you a chance to back away if you're not prepared yet, or continue on with a difficulty setting for the boss. I think the only change difficulty makes is the damage you can take. The bosses are pretty fun and often get intense.
When I first started the game, I expected the story to be pretty basic. During the first hour or so, I was only slightly impressed. After the forest, I didn't notice myself getting more interested in the plot until after I finished my third session of gameplay. Early on, the plot is still just alright at most. As the game reached the second half, the story became more intriguing. It's obvious that the author, Holy Priest, of Eternal Senia put a lot of thought into the plot. My only criticism about the story are the endings. I mean, I even shed man-tears at them, so the endings are
lame or horribly written. They're really touching endings. It's just that
In general, for an RPG Maker title, the story of Eternal Senia is great.
Some of the dialogue makes it obvious that the author's first language isn't English, which is completely fine. The mistranslations really do not take away from the game that much. There are some unexpected mentions of their Facebook page in the middle of the game, which I honesly think could have been left out of the dialgoue and put in the title screen or character menu. Other than that, the dialgoue is good.
There are only two main characters in the game, Senia and Magaleta. During the first few moments, the player won't learn too much. As the game progresses, the player will find out more and more about the deep past of both characters, which were definitely very interesting. Again, it's clear that the author put great effort into making Eternal Senia shine.
If you've already played the game far enough, you may notice a "Bonus Room" option when you activate save points. Selecting it will ask for a code to enter. I won't give you the code, as you can find it by completing the survey for beating the game. The link for that is given at the ending or by following a link file in the game's files. Essentially, the bonus room contains the thoughts of Holy Preist while he/she was making Eternal Senia. It's a really nice bonus after the ending. I recommend checking it out afterwards. It really shows the amount of work Holy Priest put into the Eternal Senia.
And last and certainly the best point, the music. The soundtrack for the game is great, especially for the short theme song of Eternal Senia, "The Other Side of Sorrow". As soon as I started the game, the title screen music captivated me. The rest of the music and sounds in this game are good as well, but "The Other Side of Sorrow" is just beautiful. If there's one thing I enjoyed about the game, it's that song.
In conclusion, Eternal Senia features fun and simple gameplay, a good story, interesting characters, and a fantastic song. If you're interested, there's no reason not to check it out if you've got a Windows computer and are interested as it's free and light on system requirements. For anyone who likes a good story or likes games, especially light/casual gamers,

TL;DR: I paid less than $20 USD for this game and definitely got my money's worth. Don't pay more than $30.
I love and have an intimate appreciation for the Alien franchise. This game does an excellent job of returning the gaming avenue of Alien back to its roots with just the right touch to music, theme, and application. Unfortunately, I found myself unable to be enchanted by the suspension of disbelief due to some quirky, some downright gimmicky, elements. Certain sequences felt forced, and the last few hours of the game are bloated with horror genre tropes.
I often joke about beloved Dead Space, saying that a more appropriate title would be "Isaac Has A Bad Day", and it seems that someone at Creative Assembly picked up on a similar notion, borrowing that very feel for the driving plot of Alien: Isolation. In it, we play as Amanda Ripley, daughter of the main character from the first film, but are prevented from really appreciating her talents or backstory because of the good-but-fast introduction. Exposition does little to inform us, with terminal log entries being the only way to dive into the lore. Additionally, these terminals are often placed in harm's way, out of the path of natural plot progression, so that if you ignore terminals, the amount of overall conflict is cut in half. This leads for any bad that would happen to Ripley to seemingly come from nowhere and rely on classic jump-scare tactics once our familiarity with the titular enemy of the game settles in.
As others have pointed out, the AI that was boasted for the Alien was overstated and misrepresented. The creature is only random in the sense that it could fall into one of three different behavior patterns: 1. Stay in the vents and follow you everywhere but never attack. 2. Stay on the ground and follow you everywhere but never attack. 3. Stay on the ground and always know where you are, regardless of tactics used to distract and/or hide, and attacking without a chance to prepare or react. These sound puristic in approach, but as other reviewers have mentioned it causes nothing but sheer annoyance after the first few hide-and-seek sequences. You will end up reloading old saves just for the sake of being able to trick the AI into not doing anything so as to continue the plot.
It may seem as that my recommendation is ironic given my complaints but the game does a lot right by way of esoteric traits such as the retro-future atmosphere, the nostalgia-driven music, and the absolutely stunning amount of attention paid to detail both mechanical and abstract features by the team at Creative Assembly. As indicated earlier, I paid less than $20 USD for this game and got my money's worth. However, the persistent inability to retain my attention and draw me in to the terror of the setting caused me to simply laugh, get annoyed at, and ultimately just toy around at the challenges.

The first Evil Within was, when all is said and done, a mish-mash of just about every "survival horror" cliche under the sun. The game had no compunctions, whatsoever, about proudly flying the influence of every major horror game released since the early Resident Evils and Silent Hills...all the way up to the latest-and-greatest released in the twenty-odd years since, such as Outlast and The Last of Us.
It got away with such brazen plagiarism for one reason and one reason alone: it was good. Real good. Probably as good as the best games which helped spawn it, and better than all the rest. Anyone who enjoyed that first instalment should be pleased to hear that not that much has changed for the sophomore outing.
I mean, sure, no one should be surprised to hear that everything's a wee bit "bigger" this time around. More action, more gore, more stealth, more weapons, more crafting, more "open world"-ish elements, and two - count 'em, TWO - different types of safe/save rooms. We all expected this. The good news is that they haven't gone ape♥♥♥♥♥♥with any of it, and the basic charms of the original game remain intact. It's much the same thing, with just a few more mechanics and options, and an ever-so-slightly darker (and, arguably, superior) storyline.
Heck, I was happy. Extremely happy. As I'm sure most fans of the first will be. Clearly one of the best horror games of the year, in a very, VERY good year for such things.
Verdict: 10/10.
(PS Don't believe this game, kids: coffee isn't actually good for your health. Though come to think of it, neither is pretty much anything else portrayed in the game. As you were.)
(PPS I generally hate "side-missions". I really do. This game has some of the most worthwhile side-missions ever, which not only reward the player with the expected "goodies", but with some genuinely interesting side-plots, backstory, and/or just-plain-creepy ideas. That said, I hope Bethesda don't go getting any grander ideas for Evil Within 3, 'cause I'm really not that interested in playing the horror equivalent of Borderlands...)

If you liked Maniac Mansion or Day of the Tentacle, then Thimbleweed Park will also be up your alley. It has an engaging, exciting story, with many characters who are aware of the absurdities the game has placed upon them. The main downside of the game is that there are many puzzles that are artifically gated on you being in a certain chapter of the game. You'll have all the right pieces to do something, but the game says it just isn't the right time to do so. Thankfully, there's a hint line you can call in-game to get nudges in the right direction, and these types of things only occur a few times, so while it is frustrating, it's sufficiently rare to not get in your way too much. And this is when the game really shines: when you have a ton of items, nothing holding you back from using them, and you "just know" what goes where. That, with some unexpectedly deep twists towards the end of the game, make this game worth experiencing.

- The story if you can understand it links up to something else but its long enough will keep you curious to the end.
- Ron Gilbert made this did i mention it already ? There is a ton of stuff that relates to the awesome backers who made this possible they are fun to read and listen.

The same comes back here some characters are *bleep awesome to play as ...some are annoying and people will get stuck.

This game surpassed my expecations. There is a surprisingly large amount of choices which have a real impact on the story. I found the story and side stories to be interesting and supportive of the gameplay. The gameplay itself is pretty damn fun and comparable to the first game, involving stealth, gunplay, tech equipment, special abilities, etc.
I've beaten both the original Deus Ex and now Invisible War and I must say, besides the changes to streamline certain gameplay aspects, Invisible War is just as high quality as the first. It definitely seemed like a true sequel to me, despite what I've read online. And hell, I'd even say the changes make the game a lot easier to get a handle on, as the first game at times felt a bit overwhelming to deal with. I actually felt a lot more engaged with the biomod system in Invisible War because of the fact that it laid out the details more clearly.
The main issue with this game is the loading screen issue. Levels are HEAVILY segmented into separate areas that must be loaded individually, and every time you enter a new area, the game minimizes for a few seconds, comes back up and then takes another few seconds to load. This process also occurs every time you load a save, meaning that even hitting quickload (F12) will force you to wait 10 seconds. The original game had instant quick loading, as MOST games do.
If you are wondering if you should play this after playing the first game, then the answer is yes. Don't let whiny comments about the game being terrible because it was "consolized" fool you. This is a true, high quality sequel to the original Deus Ex.

I played the first Deus Ex years ago and went back to play the next game in the series. I am sad to report that this game is a total piece of garbage. Overall, it was a very consolized and poorly designed sequel. Here is why I would recommend skipping this game:
You will probably spend more time watching loading screens than actually playing the game. The game is set up so that only tiny pieces of each area are loaded at one time so that you have to watch loading screen after loading screen after loading screen just to move through the game. Even the main menu has a loading screen. It is so oppressive that it ruins the gameplay.
All the maps feel like you're moving through tunnels. Even the outdoor areas seem very close quarters and boxed in with loading barriers every 15 feet.
This is kind of self-expanatory, but I personally had a particularly bad problem with random crashing and then corrupt savegames. There were also the other classic bugs such as stuff getting stuck in walls, NPCs battling each other when they're not supposed to, buggy objects jittering around the levels, etc. The camera angles during cutscenes were a joke. It's kind of hard to take the game seriously when the camera angles switch between close up of the floor and half a character's face during every cutscene.
The game played like one of those choose your own adventure books with a little target shooting thrown in here and there. The designers really got into this 'choose between factions' idea and took it too far. All the interactions and cutscenes were nothing more than each faction trying to persuade you to join their side with very little underlying plot or consequences for your actions. The characters seemed so dull and one dimensional. The designers tried to get all philosophical with many elements of the game but failed to impress me with the depth of their ideas and understanding.
After a while, you start to realize that attached to every room it is a grate leading to a gigantic man-sized ventilation shaft with convenient ladders for all the vertical sections. Not only is this kind of silly, but it becomes annyoing when you spend half the game crawling through these vanilla cloned tunnels. Of course you don't HAVE to go that route, but when the alternative is to waste an item, ammo, or other resource, and vent crawling is free, you are encouraged to spend your time exploring the ducts.
The game essentially gives you every item in the game in the first hour of playing. I had about 10 unused biomod upgrades at the end of the game with all my biomods maxed out. You are loaded up with so much stuff that it destroys all the fun of spontaneously finding a new item or upgrading your skill to a new level.
There are quite a few "secondary" goals that typically result in a small cash reward. However, you are already overstocked and a millionaire with nowhere to go and nothing to buy. They add very little to the gameplay because the story underlying each quest is trivial (e.g. go find someone and talk to them to make sure they're ok) and you're so loaded with cash anyway.

Come on, it's not THAT bad! All the bile spewed about this game is totally unfounded. Sure, it's Deus Ex Lite, but that already means it trumps many games out there. Man i just love this game, one of my favourite survival games to be honest. But its not perfect, not at all infact. But even with all of its problems it still has me addicted.
So ill start by going over the stuff i like and dont like, this will be the short review i suppose.
The good stuff:
-Good art style
-Big map
-Lots biomes to explore
-Some fun survival elements
-Driveable cars and bikes
-Infamous system (this system has its up and downs)
-PvP can be fun (also has its problems)
-Taunts and geastures
-Lots of diffrent ores and items
-Easy game to get into
The not so good stuff:
-Shotguns can be op
-Ownership stakes (spawn points) are awful, if someone gets into your base and gets access the base can be destroyed.
-You spawn within 10 seconds no matter how many deaths
-Momentum is broken
-Bors are annoying, they will rush you and dodge your attacks while hitting you.
-Weather seems to be broken, it will be raining for 2 minutes stop and then start raining again in another 2 minutes.
-RNG loot can also be frustrating when looting rad towns.
-Rain can be a death sentence
But what really makes the game so good in my opinion, is the map itself. It is designed so well, you start in the Desert forest, where you have a good amount of resources for starters and no rain. Eventually you will then move on to the rain forest wich is one of the best places to farm for Wood, iron and titranium and what not. But you will exprience lots of cold and rain, so its good to prepare some clothing before going. This is also where i normally set up my first base. Here you also find a radtown where you find car parts, ammo and dynamite. Wich you will need when moving on to the desert. You have this constant feel of progressing here wich i really like. And then theres the arctic too, where you get ultrarnium and all that good stuff.
Raiding and defending your base from a raid though, not as fun. And this is all because of the ownership stake. It is just completely broken right now, how it works is that if you get access to it you can spawn on it (it only takes 10 seconds after you die) and you can basicaly do whatever you want to the base. But the problem here is that because of the spawn timer and the fact that if you dont have infamous you wont drop you gear and weapons, you can just keep running out there with your shotty ti'll you kill the raiders, or the raiders will just camp your door and wait for you to open it, so they can run in there, get access and destroy the whole base. I find this system to just be broken in every way, i just dont get it. But atleast C4 is really hard to get access to, so aslong as you spend time on the base you are good for the most part.
Theres alot more to discuss about this game but for now heres my rating (ill probably update this review some time.)
Rating: 7/10

Dark Souls II is one of the best sequels to come along in a long time.  In almost every way, it enhances the dark, forboding elements of the first game and adds all new features that push the series into the next plateu.
Dark Souls II makes the port of Dark Souls 1 look like a joke in comparison.  With 60FPS, gorgeous HD texturing, and full support for 4k and other PC-specific setups, the graphics are the best the souls series has seen.  Water looks amazing, and the new lighting engine, particle effects, and cloth effects really draw the player into the world.
The game has been made somewhat more accessible for newcomers.  You are given 4 ring slots instead of 2.  You can carry 3 pieces of equipment between hands, and the equip load to movement speed has been raised signifigantly.  Stats have been changed around so that things like your animation speed and spell casting speed can be raised, and there are more options for healing.
However, this does not mean the game has become easy; far from it in fact.  Dark Souls II has a vast depth of difficulty waiting for you, and the same rule as the first applies where the weakest enemies in the game can easily overwhealm the unwary player.  Enemies are smarter, archers will lead their target, parrying and general combat have been adjusted to feel more 'weighty' and medieval, and many areas of the game are very demanding.  This is definitely a souls game through and through.
Multiplayer has been tweaked using centralized servers.  Summoning other players and being summoned now takes seconds rather than minutes, and invasions don't block you off in an area for minutes while waiting for the other player to connect to your world.  If all feels very seamless and this is how multiplayer in the other Souls games should have been.
The world itself is much larger now, and there are many more bosses than in the first games.  Sure, many of the bosses are a variation of 'a dude in armor', but they all have their own style and features that keep the game fresh.  I haven't had the kind of heart-pumping adreniline rush that this game gives since I started the first Dark Souls a few years ago.
Spells, equipment, weapons, armor, and other features have also been heavily expanded.  Weapons that were somewhat unique in the first game now have entire classes devoted to them.  Hiding behind a shield isn't as effective as it was before, and the list of spells, miracles, hexes, and pyromancy will keep devoted players coming back for more.  This game has the kind of replay value rarely seen.
There are a few problems for the seasoned souls player, one of which is that changing weapons and switching between animations is a lot more time-sensitive and you can't just switch weapons and wait for whatever is happening to finish and then have it happen automatically.  Parrying and backstabs are a lot trickier to pulls off, and you can no longer rely on your knowledge of the game mechanics from the previous games to completely walk through Dark Souls II.  This is really another game in its own rite.  However, these problems are quickly overcome and completely overshadowed by the insane depth of gameplay that awaits.
Prepare to die, again.

I really have no other complains other than the fact that it had a terrible start because of the performance problem and will only recommend it to users with the latest GPU's such as the RX 480 and GTX 1060 up. But even with Mid-end cards you'll still see drops on wide areas.
Don't waste your money in this game if you have a lower-end GPU, even a mid-end if you wanna run it on high-ultra settings. But I do recommend it for the people with the higher tier PC's.
My Specs:
i7-4790k 4.0Ghz
GTX 1070
16gb RAM

Brief PC Specs: AMD Sapphire R9 290x, i5 2500 3.3/3.6ghz, 16GB 1600mhz HyperX ram, Samsung Evo 840 Pro SSD. Playing on 2560x1440 resolution. It's an Okay rig. I've managed to pull smooth 2k ultra for every game up till now. I can understand people's frustrations, especially if you've been playing on ultra till now.
The performance was bad. There's no two ways around that. However, with some effort, I could get it to look decent with a "playable" FPS. For me, that meant setting the graphics to High, then manually adjusting textures and characters to very high, setting the TXAA Sharpness to 10, removing light shafts and lens flares. I also benefitted a little from removing bloom and volumetric lighting, but decided to include those again. All that made it playable around 28-48 FPS on average. The lowest FPS come from scenes with further horizons and moving water.
There are still stutters and random freezes that correct themselves after some seconds, though thus far I haven't had crashes. The low FPS makes it alright to play stealth, but it really does feel much heavier when going for the brutal, combat approach.
Would I recommend the game? Yes. It still has the great gameplay from Dishonored 1, which I absolutely love. However, I really hope that the game will not turn into XCom: The Bureau, where the company decided to say screw it and left the performance issues the way they were.
If they can fix the games problems, and make it a much smoother, and optimised, experience I am certain that we're looking at a strong GOTY candidate.

Funny how the world works sometimes. I remember walking through Sam's Club back in 1997 and seeing the display for this game. A buddy of mine bought the game and told me you gotta see this game. Never before had we seen anything like it and we were instantly hooked as were several other of our friends. Back the, you had to download a program so you play against others, so we opted for Lan parties instead.
Since 1997, I have pulled this game out and played it everyyear since. When I tried to load it up a week ago, it didn't work. Was a little dissappointed and thought it was time to move on and then it popped up on my front page yesterday. I didn't hesitate.
The base game and both expansions are here and there are at least 150 single player missions and more units than you can possibly imagine. Makes for very large scale battles, especially if you are playing on one of the metal maps. The graphics are obviousley lacking and the game isn't as revelutionary as it was then, but this game has great meaning for me and changed the way I viewed gaming. It was the first game that got me really excited and it changed the way games were made.
I remember Chris Taylor saying he wanted to go straight to TA2, but they wanted to make TA:Kingdoms, which was a game I enjoyed, but not even close to as much as TA. And because they didn't go straight to TA2, well, the rest is history. TA:K didn't do so well and the company eventually went under with no sequel ever done. The ownership has changed many times over (last I heard a company in Japan had it and wouldn't part with it) and a sequel does not seem to ever be coming which is a tragedy. It is probably one of the reasons this game is as iconic and beloved as it still is today.
After loading up the game last night, I coudn't beleive that 2 hours had passed so quickly. Still love and cherish this game.
Still loving this game and just played it for the 20th year in a row.
Still waiting after all these years for a sequel. Do I think we will get one: Nope. Game still excites me after all these years.

Don't mistake Steam playing time here:
I was 10 when this came out, playing on our old Amstrad Pentium 100MhZ with 1gb HDD. By 1997 we could only really have one game on the PC to play, and Total Annihilation spent alot of time on there. Coming from C&C and AoE TA just blew them out of the water, two lovingly crafted factions, totally unique units and such a wide array of units it had too! You were never locked down into a play style, you had the tools to do whatever you felt necessary. Maps were varied, from closed corridor battles to open ground which often changed from pristine wildernesses to a decimated hell hole throughout the course of the map.
The amount of content here is vast, it's an old school campaign, so tons of missions with good scaling difficulty, piles of maps for skirmishing and top mods available. Not to mention a top soundtrack by Jeremy Soule (Elder Scrolls, KOTOR etc).
And for the pittance they're asking, this a steal.

If there's ever been a stealth company, it's Looking Glass. While other companies come and go claiming themselves to be this month's master of the first-person shooter, Looking Glass spends their time quietly taking the genre to places it's never been before. Perhaps even more amazing is the fact that they manage to set the industry on its ear again and again with startling consistency. With Ultima Underworld and its sequel Ultima Underworld 2, the company took on the daunting task of infusing the depth of an RPG into a first person engine. With the original System Shock, the team created an action game that actually made you feel like you were in a sci-fi movie. With Terra Nova, the developers tackled squad based combat from a first person point of view and succeeded wildly ¿ years before Tribes was even thought about. More recently, the company offered up Thief: The Dark Project, an amazingly deep title that introduced first-person fans to a world in which each enemy was a potentially lethal threat. Each one of these games took a completely new approach to the shoot-everything-in-sight feel of most first-person shooters and instead created a world in which you actually felt as if you were the protagonist. Now, silently, the company has done it again. Their latest foray into the first-person shooter world, System Shock 2, is an amazingly well crafted example of the genre that combines raw action with horror and suspense to deliver a gameplay experience that is very different from anything else on the shelves.
It's funny, usually with a really good game, it takes an enormous amount of time to explain just what it is about the title that sets it apart. With System Shock 2 it can be summed up in a single word ¿ atmosphere. This game creates an incredibly rich game world for you to explore and conquer by offering up flawless graphics, great voice acting, interesting and frightening enemies, and a powerful storyline that meshes seamlessly with the play experience. All of these factors are important on an individual basis but more importantly, they all contribute to the dark, oppressive and often terrifying feel of the game as well. Because of this, while it's easy to sum up what makes System Shock 2 great, it's still very important to take a closer look at how each piece of the game excels and how it fits into the greater whole.
Let's start with the storyline. System Shock 2 takes place in the same game world as the original title, a universe in which the Earth has already reached out and colonized the solar system. Since the out-of-control AI, SHODAN, has been stopped (in the original System Shock this thinking computer went crazy and killed a large number of people on board a the Citadel Space Station) the governments of Earth have come together in the form of a new entity titled the UNN (United National Nominate) and have lashed out at the megacorporations (specifically the largest, the TriOptimum Corporation who was responsible for SHODAN's creation) that have held power for so long. The power struggle has resulted in an uneasy truce in which the UNN still holds power officially and the corporations still hold a great deal of de facto power through their very own armies and police forces. Into this already dangerous struggle comes a new source of tension. A new ship, the Von Braun, is being built that uses a new engine developed by a Nobel scientist that will make the craft capable of faster than light travel. The new craft, which is being built by TriOptimum (despite all efforts by the UNN to keep the company uninvolved), is scheduled to make a maiden voyage that will take it to a far away solar system. Along with the Von Braun will be a security ship, the Rickenbacker, which is designed to 'piggyback' the larger ship in order to take advantage of its FTL engines.
As with most new technologies, the Von Braun doesn't really work as well as it should. Hackers on board the ship have managed to screw up a lot of little things, but some of the major items don't work simply because they haven't been properly tested. One of the problems of greatest concern is that the ship's central computer, XERXES, seems to be all kinds of buggy. Worst of all, the crew, which is made up of both UNN and TriOptimum appointees, is starting to separate into two factions that mistrust and hate the others. As the game begins, the ship receives fragments of a transmission that originates at the Tau Ceti system, far outside the area of explored space. You are assigned to the ship as it begins its journey to find out what is sending that signal, and if possible to make contact with them.
Once the game starts, things really get cooking. You've been kept in cold storage for the journey and awake to the not so dulcet commands of Dr. Janice Polito, the Senior Systems Analyst onboard the Von Braun. Although she's not very clear, it's obvious that the ship is in some kind of serious trouble and it's up to you to sort out what it is. As you travel around the corridors of the ship, you'll have three ways to learn more about the situation. First, you'll occasionally get messages on your PDA from Dr. Polito telling you about things that have just happened and giving you advice on what you must do next. Second, you'll find small disks scattered around the ship that hold the log messages of the crew. As you pick up and read these logs, the story will slowly unfold in front of you and you'll also get more information on how best to proceed. Finally, and perhaps most disturbingly, the cybernetic system that's been installed in you seems to accidentally pick up strong psychic signals much as a bad portable phone picks up the radio. When your system comes in contact with these emanations it will try and interpret them as light and sound. The end result is that occasionally, as you walk through the ship, you will see 'ghosts' of people who lived on the Von Braun. This is really creepy and may cause you to shoot at the images before you realize exactly what they are. Using these clues, you must figure out what happened to the crew of the Von Braun, who's managed to survive it, and how you're going to go about stopping the menace.
While I'd love to go further into the storyline, there's no way to do so without totally spoiling the game. One thing I can tell you is that whatever has taken over the ship has found a way to infect the crew and turn them into horrible zombies. A lot more resilient and intelligent than your run of the mill 'a comet flew over and I was raised from my grave' undead, these vile creatures are smart enough to use complex weaponry, respond to security alarms, and to, after a fashion, speak. Other creatures you'll run into include giant spiders made up of a weird bio-material, cybernetic nursemaids and stealthy cyber-assassins.
Okay, there's a lot of other things I'd like to say about this game, but I think you've probably got the basic idea by now. The one warning that I would offer up is to hard-core action fans who may be put off by the RPG elements that make this game what it is. In the end though, I would recommend this title for just about anyone who's over the age of 16 (this game is really scary) and who likes deep rich play adventures.

When Ron Gilbert announced his plans for Thimbleweed Park on Kickstarter, he wrote that it will feel like a LucasArts game from the 80's. For those of you who are not familiar with adventure video games from that time: They were awesome. LucasArts produced iconic games like Maniac Mansion, Monkey Island, Day of the Tentacle, Indiana Jones games based on the movies and many more. These games redefined what adventure games were supposed to be and they have a large followership to this day.
The question is of course: Did Ron Gilbert succeed in creating another such game in 2017? The answer is "yes, but". And here comes the even better part: While the old LucasArts games were great, they still had quirks in them and the games industry has learned from it's mistakes in the past 20 years. Therefore Thimbleweed Park is not only a genuine spiritual successor of the old adventure games, but it also implements the current state of the art conventions in the adventure game industry. The puzzles are of good quality and if you are totally stuck, there is even a hint system within the game that you can use to get some pointers.
If you like adventure games then I can wholeheartily recommend this game. If you are familiar with the old LucasArts classics, you will enjoy the game even more because it is full of in-jokes about the old classics and the 80's.
This game is a work of love. Of love for adventure games. This one is special. While I doubt that it will have the same massive impact as the classics from back in the day, this game is certainly something that should be in the collection of a modern day's adventure gamer.
