Invisible War is a decent fps rpg, when you consider how rare those actually are.  It unfortunately distills what made it's predecessor great down into mediocre banality.  Where computer skill would allow you to sift through people's personal emails in it's predecessor, learning important information, here you only need click on the computer with a hologram of a rotating letter above it - an insulting symptom of dumbing down of the core game mechanics into big signs that the dumbest of people can see, understand and use.
In fact, gone are the experience points and skill leveling of the first game entirely.  Instead, the only leveling to be done is by biomod cannisters which add and improve abilities (strength, stealth, hacking, etc.) but is so uninteresting and rote in it's implementation that I wish it didn't even bother.  Any "skill" you choose to apply in excludes some others from consideration, but they max out at 3 cannisters each, leading you with a load of unusable biomod cannisters at the end of the game.  Unless you choose to experiment with another "skill" which you won't, because most of them kinda suck anyway.
Weapon modification is worse, because you can only add 2 mods to any weapon and some weapons can't be modded at all, so again, you'll have plenty of weapon mods you can't use.  It's almost pathetically comical that characters give you biomods and weapon mods as rewards in the last several hours of game when you've already settled into the biomod "skills" and weaponry of choice and have modded them all out already.
The story is mostly a rehash with some of the same characters returning for what amounts to the same end game:  control of a technology for world domination, or freedom, depending on your point of view.  The character conversations are sometimes so insipid I just skipped through them, and most of the choices involve either a "yes" or "no" style answer which has no impact on the actual story, because at the end of the game the ending you get is determined, literally, by which button you decide to press.
I just played through it a second time, completely forgetting I had played through it previously, because the visual tone of the game is so bland, and the endings so bad.  It's 90% values of blue and gray.  Beginning of the game you're in a lab, then you're in a city, then you're in another city, and more labs, and another city, at some point you'll be in antartica and at another on Liberty Island (also looking like antartica).  The palate in this game is severely lacking.  And the 4 different endings are all kind of distasteful.
This game also had performance issues on every system I've ever played it on, except the Xbox.  Certain areas would have profound, inexplicable slowdown.  I've had similar performance issues with Thief 3, which was developed by the same peeps using the same Unreal engine,...  my guess is they optimized the engine for the Xbox at the expense of the PC versions.  Still, it's worth a play.

I'm in for a series marathon, and playing each back-to-back seems like a good way to examine the evolution of the whole. I have to disagree with most of the negative feelings toward this title, because a "bad" connotation or "worst in the series" designation to a Deus Ex game still makes for a really great experience. Why? The vastly improved physics certainly don't hurt. That's fun in its own right. Most of the worst reviews I've ever seen lobbed at this sequel come from long-time fans of the original game, and if I had to choose my own least favorite difference between the two, honestly, it is the loss of the corner-leaning function that felt so good in the first; but to me, that is one of the few reductions where many other gameplay elements are definitely improved upon and streamlined. I know that can be a bad word in gaming. Streamlined can easily mean less. Here, it applies.
One of the most common critiques I've heard, from professional critics and caring fans alike, has to do with Invisible War's level design. This seems hollow, I think, given the way this refers almost exclusively to size and wide-open feeling areas. In fact, the generally smaller levels of this sequel are far more efficient in their use of space -- something that seems to help it run better, actually, apart from some crashing which might be rooted in the series' early, unlucky business choices over bad drivers/graphics support for their engine -- you will quickly find so many tasks to complete that your head will be spinning, each with multiple choices, outcomes, and courses to get there. If you play many angles and think on your feet, trying to outwit what only ~seem~ like restraints on the surface, you will not only feel like an absolute bada$$ very early in the game, but be gratified at what you can do with some good creative planning. This is very much in keeping with the spirit of the Deus Ex name, the first mission areas alone having as many or more different paths to victory as any level in the original (if you only look hard enough), with all the cleverness and depth of story and world as every competent fan has come to expect. It doesn't always look or sound pretty, but in plenty of moments remains reasonably passable. Indeed, the beauty of this one, a learning experience in terms of its basic design aspects, are the ways in which your decisions invariably tie together in an emergent fashion. The greatest showcase of its true depth is probably best explained by pointing out how no two walkthroughs for it seem to contain all of the same information, each being subtly different and personal with an active community of explorers necessary to continually discover new things. You might find something new and unexpected, too. I feel like I do each time I play Invisible War, no different than the original, no less than any other standard of the series.
Heck, to provide one non-spoiling testimony, even the most obscure details such as the names of coffee chains they included as a side-plot/metaphorical example to hint at the greater whole of this mystery, are remarkably witty little nods to our every day real life... though they seem almost laughably dumb if you don't know, I realize, that's exactly the point -- the whole story highlights how ignorance can be taken advantage of and manipulated from above, after all... Pequod and Queequeg were two principle characters in Melville's "MobyDick," and the name of the ship's first mate in that old, famous story just happened to be "Starbuck." See the connection? Did you ever realize? It takes digging, sometimes. This game, like the whole series, is overflowing with little details of that sort, the creators working well with whatever they had at hand, and is no less rooted in literature, history, or the greatest schools of philosophical thought than its counterparts. If you are an avid reader, especially of classics, this will be a fun game for you -- as would any Deus Ex game. It is a title that means your brain will be taxed, you'll go to bed either dreaming about your experiences or lying restlessly awake over its implications, and left saying, "wow," at every new twist. Yes, this one seems smaller, and yes, this might be the easiest of the series if you already have a grasp of how to play from the first, but there is a ton of detail within this title which can turn out to be just as rewarding as any other to carry that glorious logo. It's great. For my own part, today, feeling like a kid again, Invisible War was as equally amazing in its own day as the original had been, before.

Eternal Senia is a very quick, 4 hour RPG that channels Ys while still feeling fresh.
The story follows Senia who follows her adoptive sister in the Entinity Tower in an attempt to find her. The story is quite simple, yet it's refreshing since it's her looking for her sister, not a man. Nor are there any true male characters. A "2nd" party member does join, but she's just there. And then there's the translation. It's crap. There are minor gramatical errors and semantic errors that muck up the emotion of the scene.
Gameplay wise, it is reminiscent of Ys with Senia running into her enemies. Unlike Adol, Senia cannot escape damage.  This can make battling the mini-bosses a pain, yet they won't chase her compared to the regular enemies. And when she does run of HP, she normally retreats to the last save point. It saves a lot of frustration, but it also takes away from the challenge. She can upgrade her equipment with a very basic alchemy / crafting system. This typically makes surviving and slicing monsters even easier. The hardest part is when the game begins in the forest and at it's easiest at the end.
Setting wise, the game gets thing done. While the overall feel of the levels will be remembered, there's nothing about the design that will be remembered. Nothing offensive to be seen. The way things are setup with the different "zones" or areas, the transitions are a little jarring. It's like the developer didn't understand how to properly set up boundaries as it would have felt more cohesive with things being set up in 1 or 2 giant areas.
And yet it's hard not to like this game. Even with the poor translation, the passion the developer put into this game is easily appearant. For a 4 hour game, it refused to let me go until it was done. And not knowing the source material is not a blockage for enjoying the game.  And the price makes the overall package a very easy pill to swallow.

If you've played any of the Bioshock games, you owe it to youself to play the one game that started it all. Yes there's System shock 1 which is also good but is different compared to this game. System Shock 2 is considered to be one of the greatest pc games of all time and I'll have to agree. Not the best but one of the best. Like Bioshock, there's a lot of attention to the atmosphere in this game.
You play as a soldier who chooses to part of the Marines, Navy, or OSA. Marine class makes you use great guns earlier, Navy helps you hack in this game which important, and OSA is mage where you use psi abilities to perform various things like hack turrets.
You sleep in a cryochamber and realise the entire van braun ship has either disappeared or died and you'll have to find out what happened.
The best thing about this game is that it doesn't treat you like you're 10 years old. I understand objective markers weren't a thing back then but the game trusts that you understand what to do. Just use your map if you're stuck.
The game retains elements that were removed from it's 2007 successor (Bioshock) such as a proper inventory system, weapon degradation, and actual consequences. Cybernetic Modules (Adam) are really hard to find so you'll need to keep looking for them in order to upgrade your character.
There's a lot to say about this game so you'll need to see why people believe System Shock 2 is one of those games you'll need to play if you're a PC gamer. Along with many other Looking Glass Studio games.

This game is honestly very enjoyable to play. It is full of jokes and pop culture references that give the game a depth that few other games can achieve. It's always very interesting to see what the flavor text for some of the unique weapons is making reference to. Sometimes it's a movie, sometimes it's a political concept, there are even art references.
In addition, I like that each of the playable characters has skills that make them all vastly different to play. It gives the game replay value that the first one didn't really have. If you want to deal huge amounts of elemental damage, pick Maya; if you want to attack enemy critical hit spots, pick Zer0; if you just want to sit back and watch a turret or a robot fight your battles for you, pick Gaige or Axton. The game can change so much just by the character you pick, and even further by how you pick skills. I was playing this game with a friend of mine (he was playing as Axton and I was playing Maya) and we had quite a bit of fun augmenting our character's action skills. By the time we got our characters to level 50, he could deploy two longbow turrets that maglocked to whatever they hit and caused small nuclear explosions. He more or less had two grenades that combined longbow, bouncing betty, and explosive grenade mod abilities. As for my Siren, I could revive him from a distance by phaselocking him, or cause massive amounts of elemental damage to an entire mod of enemies... and I got my phaselock cooldown down to about 3 seconds.
That brings me to the next point: this game is incredibly fun to play with one or more friends. My friend and I sat down to play this game, and before we knew it we had logged 200 hours. We played through the entire game twice. We did not even intend to play it that much, but we just lost track of time. When played with friends, it is extremely difficult for this game to get boring. New things will always be happening. Case in point, a different friend and I were in a location called Tundra Express, fighting insectoid enemies called Varkids. Periodically while fighting, these enemies will metamorphose into stronger versions, which become harder to kill. We left one of them alone for so long that it eventually evolved into something called a Super Badass Varkid. It broke out of its caccoon and roared in the most terrifying way possible. At this point we were sitting there fairly sure that we were screwed. We braced ourselves for what was to come, and then watched the Varkid immediately get hit by a train as soon as it spread its wings. I literally cannot explain how perfect it was

I'm a huge Dishonored fan, and so for me this game was under a lot of pressure to be good. I was surprised when it met all of my expectations, and went even further. Highly recommend it, this game is worth triple what you pay for it.
Dishonored 2 is an amazing game, plain and simple. It takes everything that was good about the first game, and builds on top of it (as a proper sequel should). It improved gameplay quality and mechanics in big and little ways, adding more abilities and possibilities to the arsenal of powers (just one of many examples, you can perform a non-lethal takedown jumping from high up, leveling the playing field for lethal and non-lethal players). The story FELT like a true Dishonored sequel, will all the unique dialogue and creepy backstory that only Dishonored is known for. The graphics are absolutely GOREGEOUS. The first Dishonored was no graphical marvel, but it did use its art style to its advantage. Dishonored 2 has some very impressive graphics, while at the same time using them well and efficiently. One of the worries for the second Dishonored was that it might be short, like the first one. This was not the case. All the levels are extremely well-designed, and they are designed in such a way that you can't truly play through them without exploring everything. I think it's safe to say this campaign got a solid 20 hours on my first play through. I'm confident it will get another 100 more when I play it through using the other options (You can choose to play at Corvo or Emily, and for both you can choose to either accept or reject the powers).
I was very pleased with this sequel, and I hope everyone who enjoyed the first installment will invest in this one as well.
My only major criticism of the game is that the ending was rather short. Not a bad ending, to be clear, just that I felt like they could have added more detail to the resolution. But thankfully in the true Dishonored style, the outcome is different depending on how you played.

Beautiful and immersive environments, with varied and interesting level design. There's a real freedom of expression as a player, but I found myself playing more lethal than stealthy, as it was just more fun that way. I really feel like the developers put quite a lot of effort into this sequel, and the only bug I encountered was that the game wouldn't start properly sometimes and crashed to desktop, but when I was playing I had very minor performance issues. Not many games I would park to play again sometime, but I'm definitely coming back to this and replaying in a year or so. Worthwhile purchase, and highly recommended.

Alien Isolation (PC): Finished this over the weekend at 17 hours (lots of crouching and moving slowly), any fan of the Alien universe is doing themselves and injustice if you haven’t played this. Absolutely fantastic, everything was spot on, sound effects, music, art work, THE ALIEN. I loved how all the settings/props were taken directly from the first movie. The Alien A.I. was fantastic, it had no patterns to memorize you literally had to outsmart it during each encounter to survive. Sometimes it just baffled me how smart and patient it was looking for me, for instance it had a bead on in one area but I managed to sneak in a little cabinet as soon as it lost sight of me around a corner. It was a battle of wills, it knew I was in the area and just slowly moved and stood waiting for what felt like 10 minutes until finally SLOWLY moving on, a couple minutes later I got the nerve to jump out of the cabinet and I look up to see alien drool slowly pouring out of a vent almost directly above me, sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (I got away). The androids sounded spot on and had their own scare factor to them, lifeless faces with red eyes scared me as much as the ♥♥♥♥ing Alien itself. I died a lot but it was never getting old or annoying to me and I have really low patience for games where you die a lot. The Derelict scene alone is worth the play through, they NAILED that entire scene from the movie. sound, graphics, animation, atmosphere ♥♥♥♥ING AWESOME! We need more space walks in games.
I did have a few weird glitches like NPCs doing and saying the exact same scripted lines more than once, a few crashes (only when loading my game). PC version has all bells and whistles including a FOV slider. My only minor complaint is the voice acting for Ripley was a little weak, could have been better.

Let me get this out of the way, as many have already noted, the game doesn't seem to be well optimized for PC. I'm playing on a RX480/8GB and I get about 20-30 FPS in worst case (40-60 in best case) with ULTRA settings @1920x1200. Framerates fluctuate wildly with seemingly not much reason. Lowering the settings seems to impact image quality more than it improves frame rates on my system. Personally, I find it playable enough on Ultra to not be bothered about it. Hopefully some future patches will improve this further but somehow I'm not feeling very confident about that. My guess is that they overloaded a too old graphics engine to make it look current. And, partly, they succeeded in the looks department. In therms of pure graphical 'WOW'-power, this game falls a bit short compared to some current gen blockbusters. Not that it looks bad, the art style, meticulously designed environments and level design make up for any shortcomings in the 'sheer-graphical-horsepower' department. At times, this game looks absolutely stunning, at other times not so much. All in all, the graphics are great with their own distinct style.
I usually avoid stealth games, I didn't even try the original Dishonored when it came out. Last stealth games I tried were MGS V and Deus Ex Mankind Divided, both didn't manage to pull me in for various reasons. Deus Ex is a game I might try and complete eventually, but I digress.
It's hard to describe, but somehow the game mechanics of this game make me actually want to go the stealth route more and more. I started with killing most guards as I'm a total stealth noob, got detected a lot and generally refuse to reload saves. Once I got some of Emily's powers unlocked, playing non-lethal became a ton of fun. The way you can interact with the environment, how stuff mostly makes sense from a gameplay perspective, the branching vertical level design, the multitude of creative ways to tackle any objective and the 'feel' of the game as a whole are on a whole other level from stealth games I played in the past. Playing with a controller, everything is very well thought out and quick and easy to access. Truly, in therms of gameplay mechanics this game is fantastic and, to me personally, the best stealth game I have ever played. That possibly has much to do with the fact that you don't really always need to be stealthy if I don't feel like it, while the stealth mechanics beg to be experimented with. I never thought I'd write this sentence, but these are stealth mechanics I can actually care about.
I haven't completed the story yet but so far it seems ok. Nothing mind blowing like Witcher 3 quality writing or anything, but it gets the job done to lead you from location to location. The locations so far have been nicely varied with their own style, background stories and fantastic level design. Note that this is mostly a linear game (in therms of objectives), linear with a gazillion branching paths that is.
So yeah, I'm a bit torn about recommending this game. On the one hand it's a poor excuse of a PC port, on the other it's a fantastic game with a decent storyline. If you can look past the frame rates, I'd definitely recommend picking this up. Even for people like me, who aren't big stealth fans.

First up: this is an extraordinary game. If you're a fan of classic point-and-click adventures, you'll love it. If you don't know what "classic point-and-click adventures" are, then this is a fantastic introduction.
Like so many detective stories, it begins with a body.
The player controls five characters (beginning with FBI agents Ray and Reyes) as they explore the strange, surreal backwater town of Thimbleweek Park, and the shadow cast over the town by recently-deceased pillow factory owner Chuck Edmund. For the first two minutes I was worried that this was going to be a rehash of Twin Peaks (a influence cited by co-designer Ron Gilbert), The X-Files and Welcome to Night Vale, but it quickly becomes apparent that this is far more than just a police procedural. Despite the weird setting there's real emotion here too.
There are a few small criticisms: I found the two FBI agents a lot less engaging that the other three playable characters, and at times there is a bit of backtracking involved, which can get slightly repetitive. The size of the game means there's definitely a few plotholes, but what ultimately emerges is far more than the sum of its parts: a panoramic view of a town and it's population. The locations are beautiful, the sound design is en pointe (echoes of the classic scores from Monkey Island) and I loved the way some puzzles required teamwork between multiple characters to successfully complete them.  Without wanting to give away any spoilers, there's even an exploration of the idea of video game characters' free will.
All in all, it's a beautifully realised video game. At times you'll be ripping your hair out in frustratation (BACK AWAY FROM THE ONLINE WALKTHROUGH, CHILDREN), but Thimbleweed Park really is worth investing your time in.

Hurtworld is a perfect mixture of what makes so many other games such as red dead redemption and skyrim great. The Hurtworld has many different types of quests from following the trail of a thief to entering the cave of a beast that has been attacking a village. From following the main story you pick up many side quests that will leave you deciding whether to continue the main quest or take the time to help the farmer who is being annoyed by a ghost. You will have many quests in your quest bar that you can take the time to complete or not. There is also a point of interest system in this game where you can come across many different things around the map such as a monster nest or a bandit camp that can lead you all over the place just going from place to place, finding loot upon loot and killing enemy upon enemy. The environment in this game is one of the most place I have seen as there are so many different types of areas such as the snowy mountains to the green fields. This game also has some of the best graphics I have seen and runs well on my pc on high settings. This game very much deserves all the awards it has won and the developers have done a great job on this masterpiece. Thank you CD Projekt Red for making the Witcher 3.

THE BEST adventure game I've ever played. And I've played my fair share of them - all the classics from Lucas Arts; modern ones like Technobabylon; some Telltale games before they got into their 'interactive movies' thing; lots of Russian adventure games from the 90s; even the old obscure, but still awesome ones, like Blazing Dragons on PS1.
Not a single puzzle in Thimbleweed Park felt like it was a leap in logic - a flaw that every adventure game has. I've never had to consult a walkthrough or even lookup a hint, yet the game never felt easy (I was playing on Hard difficulty). I got stuck a couple of times, but somehow I always came up with a solution, which was very satisfying. And it never felt cheap, or stupid.
And once you get the map you can move around the areas fast, unlike other adventure games. So when you're stuck it doesn't feel like you're spending most of your time watching your characters slowly walking around from area to area, forcing you to lookup a hint.
All the characters were likeable and interesting, jokes were spot on, music was awesome. Bottom line - if you're into adventure games buy this now! Don't wait for sale, it's worth every penny. I really hope they make a second game and it turns into a trend!
P.S. My favorite character, Ransom The Clown, bears a strange resemblance to my favorite stand-up comedian Bill Burr... Hmm, I wonder if he was an inspiration. :)

Definitely worth your time as a game that succeeds on its solid puzzle design, not just pandering to the nostalgia of ye olde adventure games of yore. There's a certain degree of obtuseness that comes with the territory of puzzle games, but nothing feels particularly unfair and the game makes it a point for everything to be discoverable - no pixel hunting (well, except for the joke achievements) or easily overlooked locations. Sequencing can be challenging in one of the later acts as it's not clear ahead of time how the puzzles for some of the characters dovetail into the others, but in general the game does do a clever job easing newer players into puzzles of expanding scope in the early acts with the flashbacks and chapter structure, so folks who are new to the genre should not feel intimidated. Pacing at the end is also helped by tightening the scope and focus of the puzzles again.
Where YMMV is the writing: it banks heavily on referential humor, which can get old, though I got a kick out of it. That choice is somewhat justified by a reveal at the end, but it's also a reveal that trivializes a lot of the story/character setup from the rest of the game. Ultimately, it feels like an excuse not to pay off a lot of threads in more interesting ways (e.g. the sheriff/coroner/manager connection, the signals conspiracy etc.) Even the main characters feel shortchanged because there's no emotional investment in their goals (and in Delores' case, her ending feels particularly Twilight Zone ironic.)
If you came for Day of the Tentacle plot shenanigans, you should instead be prepared for cynical Maniac Mansion by way of David Lynch. It's a fun, weird ride, but may not give you the Saturday morning cartoon closure you expect.

This is for those already familiar with souls. It will not be full on review, rather more of a short rundown of SOME of the game's differences when compared to it's predecessor. In short, Dark souls II is not the next step or evolution within souls, it is for the most part MORE SOULS. And this is not a bad thing.
If you are a fan of the souls series then, while DS II wont set your world on fire, you should still be more than satisfied by simply more Dark souls. This is slightly different souls, better in some instances, worse in others.
I wont go into the nature of souls for those uninitiated. Also, I wont go into detailed or even a rough assesment of the quality compared to DS1 of enemy, difficulty, bosses, and so on. This as while some of it is subjective, if you are interested propper or a already a souls player, then you have already decided to play the game, and thus the differences are of greater concern.
World/Story
This time the story of Dark souls has a larger thematic focus on the role of the player, going hollow/being undead, and sementing the cyclical, ever-reapeating nature of the world. Flippped around from in DS1 this game starts of with multiple paths in the first half before going linear in the second half. The areas are excellent by themselves but are not nearly as interconnected nor vertical as in DS1. While still very good, and arguably mostly just different from in DS1, the world, areas and their connection with lore and plot are simply not at cohesive and tight as in DS1, this is the games greatest weakness. But as said, this is only comparatively. The world contains more space and open-sky as a central reoccuring element. Back on the story end, you will play through most of the game doing stuff "...Without really knowing why..." as is often repeated. Basically, since much of the story and details of the world is gated behind the ending, you have less to work with as try to piece together the lore while playing the first time around. While likely intended and creating of an interesting different experience, it lowers immersion from in Dark Souls. There the prolouge gave you more of the setting to work with, in DSII it is much easier to begin building your lore castle only after your first playthough. Past this point though, the endeavour is for the most part similarly sweet.
Mechanics
Roughly, the combat in DS 2 is diversified but with a somewhat slower, heavier and more deliberate pace. For the most part, there is less stamina and weapons consume more of it. Minutely longer windups and downtime post swing promote strategic play where you to a greater degree have to plan and more importantly commint to your moves. On the flip side, there is now greater room for combining/chaining attacks in the new system, both with and without the new dual-wielding powerstances.
On this note, you can now powerstance two weapons if you have x1.5 the stat requirements, details can be found on the wikis.
There is no humanity (haha), but instead scarce human effigies return you to human form and resets you to max hp. Each time you die or get cursed you loose your human form and one 'tic' of max-hp down to half your maximum. There is a ring in the game that sets your max hp to 75% when below that in hollow-from. Online-play now varies more greatly in it's dependancy on host or phantom being human, explore the nuances.
Shields are weaker and guards more easily broken, if this happens either by stamina depletion or the new guard break move that has replaced the kick, one can preform a critical attack much like when ripost'ing. In essence, fewer shields have 100%physical dmg reduction, and more stamina is consumed while blocking. Shields are still invaluable, but must be used with greater skill, tact and planning.
Poise has changed, now it basically only acts while you are mid-action as a form of stagger preventing/reducing hyper-armor. It is weaker as a result, to the grivance of some people, but with the result of diversifying weapon type viability. There is less emphasis on out tanking your opponent in a trade, nor can you phase-tank for a backstab. I consider this system an improvement.
In the realm of stats, we can find that the dud-stat of resistance has been scrapped. The new stat on the block is adaptability which has utility increases like more i-frames on dodge roll from the sub-stat agility (99 agi=DS1 ish frames, 110=better and is the cap), otherwise it boots estus speed and some resistances. For the other stats, attunement now boosts agility slightly and helps govern the new spell related sub-stat of cast speed. Furthermore, The increase of stamina and equip-load are now on two sepparate stats. Nigh all of the first half of the stats increase hp in small amounts, while Vigour is the true main stat for hp.
In the land of the all important equip-load and rolling, it is now so that 70% is the only 'true' breakpoint. I-frames are governed by the agility stat, any change in equip burden below 70% now mainly affect and allow you to manipulate roll distance. Above 70% one gains the infamous fat-roll while higher values remove the ability to roll. But all throughout increasing equip burden will lower stamina regen and possibly also movement speed.
Boss soul trading has been streamlined and improved from the comparatively cumbersome and time consuming system in DS1. Here you simply hand over the souls in question to one of two NPCs and you get your stuff, no need to pre-upgrade a specific weapon to be transformed.
The upgrade system has been improved and streamlined where there is only one upgrade path, but shields and weapons can be infused, a sort of on-the-top-swappable enchantment, to gain and scale with a different damage type.
Things you ought to know
-There are 4 ring slots
-There are now many new things in the game once new game+ starts.
-Many details have been left aside in this rundown, check the wiki, but beware spoilers.
-The region lock is only for Japanese players, so expect everything from smooth summoning and precision duels to lagstabbs from the other side of the level whilst facing each other. Hitboxes are sadly not as precise accross the board as in DS 1, but in all but pve you can count on lagg being responsible for odd occurances. Freak connections aside, playing pvp while giving space for phantom lag hitboxes will ease your experience.
-Matchmaking now depends on a mechanic called Soul Memory or SM for short. In essence this is all the souls your character has cumulatively obtained. This can be viewed in the menues. What range of SM tiers are available for online play with you varies with the type of online play, but anything past 15million is in one tier. Whether sm is good or bad is up for debate with the community. It counteracts twinking and incentivises leveling as far as one wants while still securing the availability of online play. What sort of players you run into online and any community imposed meta aside, higher levels will reduce the drawbacks of certain buildpaths (but not item choices ofc).
-There was no intentional bait and switch advertising / degrade. The story is such that the game had a different lighting engine in earlier builds, as visible in some e3 trailers for the game. This not only made the game look better, but was to create an entirely different Dark Souls II experience centering on light and darkness. This with the player not being able to see more than a few meters in front of themselves without some form of lighting such as torches. It is lamentable that this had to go, as it would have been a drastically different experience, more tense and more of an evolution from DS1. Sadly the game would not run propperly on consoles and as such From Software had to change the lighting and thus the game to accomodate.
-Much of the creative lead for DS1 were not part of the DSII team, instead Miyazaki & co have been working on Bloodborne.

Word of Warning it is a nostalgic game.
A true RTS Game that could be said to have out lasted Starcraft Brood War and inspired the next generation of Real Time Stratergy games, Remember fondly playing this game as a kid and back in the day it was perhaps one of the first community driven games that boasted thousands of mods and total conversions from Star Wars to the Modern World this game was much like the Skyrim of the 90's with an seemingly endless supply of units, mods, and creativity on the part of the community.
Unsurprisingly this hasn't changed, Total Annihilation still retains a small but solid community of players ranging from Casuals to Professionals all it covers all the basis for a RTS game but not without it's issues.
The base game is known to suffer from pathfinding issues, you'll frequently find that without the use of mods or modified scripts the AI will struggle considerably and will at times do stupid things that might ruin the experiance of players looking for a challenge, if that's you then I'd recommend either playing with friends or joining one of the many communities out their!
Or look into getting one of the many mods the game supports, most if not all improve the AI come to ruthless degrees where you'll hard pressed to both micro and marco manage an entire force of soulless machines. The best way I can descrbe it would be to think of Skyrim without mods, then think of Skyrim with mods that's effectively TA in a nuthshell.
Options:
+ The developers certainly had longevity in mind, you can adjust the resolution up to 1920 x 1080.
+ Provides all the options you might expect from a game of this age, perhaps abit more.
- On/Off only, you can't find a middle ground without adjusting the files directly.
Gameplay
+ A map for everybody! - every map has something for everybody the metal maps provide infinite resources and lead to a fast-paced style game. In contrast low metal maps have you fighting over resources while slowly pushing your way into the enemy base. Maps on distant moons have you transporting units by air over impassable chasms or bombing your opponent into the dust.
+ Play how you want - Many RTS games have a 'defined' stratergy TA has no such definition, you will encounter players who love the good old peepee rush or those whose sole purpose is to watch you squirm as they destroy your outlying extractors. You'll encounter the turtles naturally but the game provides you with all the nessesary tools to enact your stratergy and descimate others.
- AI Pathfinding - As mentioned the pathfinding is horrible and will almost certainly require fixing especially if you want to play Skirmish thankfully their are mods and simple scripts to fix this.
- Performance - Most modern day PC's won't have a problem until like Skyrim you hit a point where your computer begins to chug along. This tends to arise from heavily modded games especially when you start to up the unit cap from 200 to 1000+
Community:
+ Still going strong not much else to say here besides the fact you have over 10 years of mods to discover some of which have been developed over so many years.

Alien Isolation (PC): Finished this over the weekend at 17 hours (lots of crouching and moving slowly), any fan of the Alien universe is doing themselves and injustice if you haven’t played this. Absolutely fantastic, everything was spot on, sound effects, music, art work, THE ALIEN. I loved how all the settings/props were taken directly from the first movie. The Alien A.I. was fantastic, it had no patterns to memorize you literally had to outsmart it during each encounter to survive. Sometimes it just baffled me how smart and patient it was looking for me, for instance it had a bead on in one area but I managed to sneak in a little cabinet as soon as it lost sight of me around a corner. It was a battle of wills, it knew I was in the area and just slowly moved and stood waiting for what felt like 10 minutes until finally SLOWLY moving on, a couple minutes later I got the nerve to jump out of the cabinet and I look up to see alien drool slowly pouring out of a vent almost directly above me, sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (I got away). The androids sounded spot on and had their own scare factor to them, lifeless faces with red eyes scared me as much as the ♥♥♥♥ing Alien itself. I played it on normal and never really had a hard time getting through areas including the infamous med bay area I read about. I died a lot but it was never getting old or annoying to me and I have really low patience for games where you die a lot. Save points/checkpoints were located around the area perfectly, I never felt I had to replay a really long section all over again. The Derelict scene alone is worth the play through, they NAILED that entire scene from the movie. sound, graphics, animation, atmosphere ♥♥♥♥ING AWESOME! We need more space walks in games.
I did have a few weird glitches like NPCs doing and saying the exact same scripted lines more than once, a few crashes (only when loading my game). PC version has all bells and whistles including a FOV slider. My only minor complaint is the voice acting for Ripley was a little weak, could have been better.
If you need to remove a certain♥♥♥♥♥♥filled aliens game from your mouth (won’t mention it here by title because it doesn’t deserve to be called out with this game) then play this ASAP.

THE BEST adventure game I've ever played. And I've played my fair share of them - all the classics from Lucas Arts; modern ones like Technobabylon; some Telltale games before they got into their 'interactive movies' thing; lots of Russian adventure games from the 90s; even the old obscure, but still awesome ones, like Blazing Dragons on PS1.
Not a single puzzle in Thimbleweed Park felt like it was a leap in logic - a flaw that every adventure game has. I've never had to consult a walkthrough or even lookup a hint, yet the game never felt easy (I was playing on Hard difficulty). I got stuck a couple of times, but somehow I always came up with a solution, which was very satisfying. And it never felt cheap, or stupid.
And once you get the map you can move around the areas fast, unlike other adventure games. So when you're stuck it doesn't feel like you're spending most of your time watching your characters slowly walking around from area to area, forcing you to lookup a hint.
All the characters were likeable and interesting, jokes were spot on, music was awesome. Bottom line - if you're into adventure games buy this now! Don't wait for sale, it's worth every penny. I really hope they make a second game and it turns into a trend!
P.S. My favorite character, Ransom The Clown, bears a strange resemblance to my favorite stand-up comedian Bill Burr... Hmm, I wonder if he was an inspiration. :)

Definitely worth your time as a game that succeeds on its solid puzzle design, not just pandering to the nostalgia of ye olde adventure games of yore. There's a certain degree of obtuseness that comes with the territory of puzzle games, but nothing feels particularly unfair and the game makes it a point for everything to be discoverable - no pixel hunting (well, except for the joke achievements) or easily overlooked locations. Sequencing can be challenging in one of the later acts as it's not clear ahead of time how the puzzles for some of the characters dovetail into the others, but in general the game does do a clever job easing newer players into puzzles of expanding scope in the early acts with the flashbacks and chapter structure, so folks who are new to the genre should not feel intimidated. Pacing at the end is also helped by tightening the scope and focus of the puzzles again.
Where YMMV is the writing: it banks heavily on referential humor, which can get old, though I got a kick out of it. That choice is somewhat justified by a reveal at the end, but it's also a reveal that trivializes a lot of the story/character setup from the rest of the game. Ultimately, it feels like an excuse not to pay off a lot of threads in more interesting ways (e.g. the sheriff/coroner/manager connection, the signals conspiracy etc.) Even the main characters feel shortchanged because there's no emotional investment in their goals (and in Delores' case, her ending feels particularly Twilight Zone ironic.)
If you came for Day of the Tentacle plot shenanigans, you should instead be prepared for cynical Maniac Mansion by way of David Lynch. It's a fun, weird ride, but may not give you the Saturday morning cartoon closure you expect.

Well, well, well, another Zombie Shooter, eh? The answer is yes, but it's not always a bad thing.
Sure, the video game community contains more than a handful of indie games aswell as triple A titles
revolving almost entirely around a zombie infestation of some sort more or less, so we see these little
rotten buggers everywhere and unfortunately not everyone is set out to be as good as let's say..
"Resident Evil" or "Left 4 Dead" or "Project Zomboid" to name a few titles executing this formula
in different ways.
'No More Room in Hell' is, if i'm not mistaken, built on the infamous Source Engine, used in various mods
and other titles and its focus relies on the same old story. An experiment or biological virus goes rampart
across the planet and you have to survive together with a bunch of people in the middle of this disaster,
however, it features interesting elements that have been used before but not always been done well.
For example, the game features plenty of characters and weaponry at your disposal, it also uses a smart
and quick system of carrying weapons & ammo aswell as health packs & other items separately and allows
you to use any of them at any given time. Healing in particular takes a little extra time which adds to the realism
and can create extra suspense during hectic scenarios. This type of game mechanic works very well here
and not so much in "Alone in the Dark" for the PC & Xbox or any other mod that uses this feature, in my opinion.
The in-game experience is very fun, in my opinion the more the merrier as you have to share items, work together,
build barricades, defend said barricades and sometimes it's pure survival horror if you'd either be left behind or
go scout on your own in the dark hallways of an abandoned apartment complex or out in a wheat field.
What also makes it incredibly fun is that the controls, for the most part, feels very responsive and
accurate to what you're doing. I personally haven't had much issue with them, unless the server itself
experienced a high amount of latency.
Lastly is the music and atmosphere. In terms of atmosphere, it sets the tone just right with the particle
effects, attention to detail and the right amount of "grain" and the color "grey". It sets the mood for
a gloomy doom-ridden world infested by deadites (deadites. get that reference? lol.) The music
is very reminiscent to that of "Resident Evil" and once again, does its job. Everything cues in when
it should and everything is just very functional and effective.
So, all in all, i'd say if you want a positive and fun time killer aswell as a great zombie-survival experience,
well, this is one of those 'gems' in the huge library of zombie games we have today. So do yourself a favor
and add this to your Steam Library, son.

This game is so manly everything in my house now sports a full handlebar moustache,
All jokes aside this game is bloody awesome. Paying tribute to the action films of the 80s and 90s Broforce is a high-octane, side-scrolling, bullet-hellesque, kill everything in your path extravaganza.
Taking control of the various "Bros", each a parodied hero of a movie or tv series, you fight your way through terrorists, aliens, and eventually the spawn of hell.
The game is very liberal in how you can approach the game, enviroments are fully destructable and the game doesn't punish you if you find it easier for simply digging a tunnle under your foes. All it cares about is if you get from point A to point B. The game is constantly throwing new things at you. New enem types, enviromental hazaards, new bros to toy around with, and even various special pick-ups that can be unlocked via covert operations.
I should also note that while the game is pretty loose in it's over-the-top approach to combat (oftentimes you'll kill a dozen dudes simply by chain reaction) it can also be rock hard in terms of difficulty with steller boss fights and a last level that made me scream in impotent rage more than a few times. More often then not you'll be killed becasue of poor reaction time or not being aware of your surroundings (I was crushed by falling rocks more than I was ever shot by the baddies), and while at times it may feel like some of the harder levels feel like they're just throwing everything at you unfairly, you eventually adapt and learn from past mistakes to make them a cakewalk. Luckily respawning is fast and doesn't punish you too heavily for dying.
In addition to a lengthy campaign given it's price. There's also arcade mode, Ironbro mode (only one death per bro), and harder difficulties, there's also steam workshop levels that add infinite replayability to the game. Oddly enough I find the game to be very relaxing as the mindless violence on the easier levels is just enough that I can tune out and forget about my worries as I slaughter hordes of goons.
There's also 4 player online, and local multiplayer for both the campaign and various competitive modes. At the max 4 players on the screen the action can get truly hectic and crazy which makes it excellent with a small group of friends.
All in all I thoroughly recommend for any fan of explosive action or games like Metal Slug or Contra. For such people I would dare to say the game is a must own at sale price.

Yes- I’d certainly recommend it. This game is lauded as one of the greatest PC games of yesteryear for a reason- and I can see why it has afforded such lavish praise. So long as you are a fan of first person action RPGs with horror elements, as well as the admittedly familiar setting of “abandoned space ship crawling with monsters”, I would say you only stand to gain from playing this game. However, I found that there was a learning curve to surpass before I was able to fully enjoy the game (although this may differ for other people)- so be aware of that.
First person action/survival horror RPG, developed by Looking Glass Studios and Irrational Games. System Shock 2 is one third of the triumvirate of quintessential PC games from the past, alongside Thief: The Dark Project and Deus Ex. The game was made using the Dark Engine- a fact that I consider important and will address later on.
The game plays out as an action RPG primarily, with the survival horror elements taking a backseat. The game controls very well- not much more to say there. Gameplay-wise, I was expecting the game to play out like Doom 3 (a game similar to SS2 in both genre and premise). I was expecting to be thrown into the game, issued an objective and I would pick up a variety of weapons throughout the game to make killing the denizens of the space ship easier on my way to the end.
I was pleasantly surprised to find that I was mistaken. Instead, SS2 treated me to a huge array of action RPG options, such as a detailed and nuanced skills system, armour and an arsenal of weapons that caters to many playstyles. I was shocked to see how detailed these gameplay systems were when considering the somewhat limited setting of the game. They’re the kind of systems that I would expect to see in an open-world game such as Fallout rather than the confines of SS2’s space ship. Nevertheless, these mechanics give the game huge scope for replayability.
Put briefly, there are four areas that you can spend your upgrade points on: Combat, Tech, Psi, and Stats. There is a lot on offer, especially when you consider that the Psi category has 5 whole categories of skills. This is one of the reasons for the learning curve. There’s such a huge array of choice that I felt overwhelmed at first- as I didn’t know what to upgrade in order to see everything on offer in the game (word to the wise- invest some points in hacking and research: they’re necessary to beat the game). It took me a good few restarts until I had devised a skillset that I was happy with, but when I did reach that point I had a lot of fun afterwards.
Similarly, the skills system isn’t explained very well. Instead of picking your starting skills from a menu and then beginning the game; you are booted into a tutorial wherein starting skill acquisition is linked with ingame lore (Eg. Navy=Tech, Marines=Combat etc.). The whole process is longwinded, boring and individual skills are very poorly explained- which only compounds the issue of a learning curve.
The depth of SS2’s gameplay systems makes them the game’s greatest strength, in my opinion. However, the skill system lacks clarity- establishing a learning curve which could deter new players. I recommend perseverance- it’s worth it.
The soundtrack is fantastic. It matches the game’s cyber, futuristic setting and each tune is memorable. However, while the soundtrack does match the game’s
, it does not match the game’s
quite so much (IE the survival horror aspect). For me, the music didn’t connote an eerie, oppressive atmosphere as much as it did a fast-paced, frantic one. This is one of the reasons why I consider the game more of an action RPG than a survival horror. There is one notable exception near the end of the game though; one level where your only companion is your footsteps and the ambience of the stage.
The OST perfectly matches the setting, but not so much the genre. Whether or not this is a good thing is debatable, but I for one am glad that we got an enjoyable, memorable soundtrack.

Thankfully you don’t need to have played the original System Shock to appreciate this game’s story. The general gist of the story is that the player wakes up from cryosleep aboard the space ship known as the Von Braun to discover that it is overrun with creatures. They are then tasked with escaping by a benefactor at the other end of the communication device.
The rest of the game’s story is mostly left to the player to figure out; namely via acquiring audio logs that shed more light on the events that led up to the ship’s downfall. Thus the main body of the game’s plot is available via optional collectibles. This could have been problematic for players who don’t stray from the beaten path, but thankfully the developers have accounted for this. Specifically, exploration is essential in SS2. It’s not just encouraged- it’s necessary. Some audio logs contain codes for doors, for example. Ergo even if you’re not directly searching for further insight into the plot, you’ll probably end up finding it anyway due to the emphasis on exploration. The plot itself is adequate- not too interesting or unique; however let’s just say that the antagonist of the game is iconic for good reason.
Although the story itself isn’t too special, the way in which it’s presented to the player is well done. In terms of this narrative style, a close comparison would be Dark Souls (although without the ambiguity).
The graphics are acceptable- not very detailed but also not unpleasant to look at. As for the game engine, I find the choice of using the Dark Engine slightly questionable. After all, this engine’s biggest asset is its audio capabilities- as the player’s footsteps change depending on the surface being walked on. Thief played to this strength very well- because it was a stealth game. SS2, on the other hand, does not. You can still hear your footsteps and how they change, but this ability doesn’t factor into gameplay at all. The lack of this strength accentuates the weaknesses of the engine- such as weird character models (which makes the enemies look ridiculous and often funny instead of scary) and some muddy textures.
SS2 could have been more effective in most departments if it had played more to the strengths of its game engine. I question the use of the Dark Engine; however I can understand it given Looking Glass Studios’ involvement in the game (since they designed the engine themselves).
SS2's biggest strength lies in the most important part of any game (in my opinion): the gameplay. The systems are detailed, there’s a myriad of gameplay choices and above all it’s
. This strength supersedes all of the weaknesses for me and I strongly recommend that you play the game if only for this aspect. The soundtrack is excellent as well, and compliments the setting and fast-paced gameplay very well.
The story is adequate, but presented in an interesting way. The biggest weakness for me is the poorly explained skill systems and the choice of game engine; however even these flaws weren’t enough to hinder my enjoyment overall. As soon as I passed the learning curve I enjoyed the game until the very end. Final note: if you are thinking of buying the game only for the fear factor, I wouldn’t recommend it. I wasn’t scared at all, due in most part to the ridiculous-looking enemies and utter lack of a scary atmosphere (although this is a subjective matter). Nevertheless, I whole-heartedly recommend this game and I believe it deserves the lofty praise it receives.

I downloaded this because there was something free in my discovery queue, and as someone who has abandoned at least 3 RPGMaker projects at this point I felt like paying some respect to one that A) made it to an official Steam release and B) was humble enough to be free anyway. Overall, I was pleasantly surprised.
Pros:
-You can tell that a lot of love was put into the project.
-The game is short enough to beat in one sitting; it doesn't end up falling into the eternal Steam backlog.
-The story has a few touching moments.
-A very unique battle system for an RPGMaker(?) (At least it uses several of the included royalty-free assets) game.
-Three different endings.
-While the lead characters are based on Ragnarok Online, the art itself is original and quite pretty.
Cons (these are mostly minor complaints):
-The writer was a native Chinese speaker, and the very small development team did not have a dedicated translator. The meaning isn't lost, but just having a native English speaker touch up the translation would have done wonders.
-Despite being a 3-4 hour adventure, the game still includes grinding. As an emphasized feature, even. It's not enough to be annoying, though, it's just that there are 3 areas that you will have to revisit a second and maybe third/fourth time to upgrade your gear, and doing so is encouraged. Maxing out your equipment does help you speed through for a while afterwards, so at least it's satisfying.
-The true final boss occasionally completely robs you due to the fact that you can't step on the summoning circles for its minions and it has knockback effects; there's a lot going on and you may find yourself unexpectedly standing in a laser because a summoning circle appeared underneath an animation. There is an easy mode, however, if the fight gets to be too much, and a hard mode if you disagree with my assessment and find it too easy.
8/10 would take a laserbeam to the feels again.

Think I might take a leaf from Jim Sterling's book and call this "Babby's First Game". What do we see here? Another JRPG made with RPG Maker. Artwork looks incredibly same-y to all other RPG Maker games. The story (the core component of any JRPG) is terrible and doesn't really make sense. The characters don't make sense. Very little is explained which would work as a storytelling device if like in Dark Souls there were hints hidden around the world. But there ain't any such hints!
This game is incredibly easy. It has a collision based combat system which actually got me into trouble quite a few times. Not too sure on the mechanics of it. It's not terribly difficult to just grind until you can do everything. Hell, there are special maps designed for them (Called "Arcane Realms") which reeks of terrible development. If you design a map with the express purpose of grinding, you completely messed up in your development cycle. Honestly, I don't think there is ever an excuse for grinding to be a necessary component in your game. Grinding serves only to pad out the run-length. And as I went through the later levels I could smell the reeking scent of "padding out the run-time". Pro-tip: If you're going to pad something in your game, pad the bras not the run-length.
The mechanics can be annoying to get used to. Not sure why every attack on a boss has to knock you back. This becomes especially annoying later in the game when spells are directed at where you were and not where you are. So you get targeted, run forward, attack, get knocked into where you were, take the free damage. Many of the game's puzzles (especially in fights) can become annoying because your combat skills are on QWER but sometimes there are elements in the scene you have to interact with using Z. This is annoying because when I was in "Combat mode" I had my left hand at the top of the keyboard, but upon realizing that I needed to use Z, I had to shift my hand awkwardly. Control design IS part of game design and is a criteria that should be considered.
I honestly don't know why this game has so many positive reviews on Steam. The soundtrack is... okay I guess. Nothing memorable. The story looks like it was written by some Tumblr user that wanted a lesbian-not-lesbian romance story between two sisters. I understand that the game is short, but shoot, so is Momodora and I felt a much stronger connection to that game. Took about the same amount of time to beat too.
Do NOT get this on steam their version doesn't work with about half of the current chipsets out right now.

I really tried to like this game, but after numerous playthroughs, I just can't. Not only is the game - by far - not finished, it's almost completely broken. I mean, practically everything that made the first Deus Ex good has disappeared.
The large open levels from the first game were replaced with small, closed levels. A walk from one level-change door to the next takes less than a minute on all levels in the whole game! The only thing that prolongs them are conversations and enemies, of which you can either skip or run past. While load times has been reduced due to the advancement of computers overall, they were a real pain when DXIW was first released.
The story, and/or the world, has been transformed from the cyberpunk future of the previous game to some kind of anachronistic sci-fi future. Explanations are almost nonexistant. For instance, in 20 years since the Collapse (i.e. the end of the previous game), somehow, a weapons manufacturer managed to completely take over the global market AND develop universal ammo for all those weapons. Yet, airports do not exist or have been transformed to garbage dumps, people have stopped driving cars (or bicycles, or any other vehicle except helicopters). How was this possible?
The story isn't all that bad, but the smallness of the game makes it too big. There simply isn't room enough for exploration or any meaningful sidequests. The choices you make are also pointless, since loyalty is changed back and forth at the slightest wrongdoing, and, as another reviewer said, the missions you get are practically all "kill this person or let it live".
The character you play, as well as the game's NPCs, are almost all irritating fools. The voice acting is ridiculous, and the only two characters I liked were JC Denton and Luminon Saman, them also being the only two characters in the game who have anything interesting to say. The player, Alex D., have been made into an idiot, because it seems that he/she accepts anything another character tells him/her. Now, I know this was due to saving space to crunsh it inside an old X-Box console, but at least let the player read a datacube (which can store documents and so on). Parallell this with JC Denton's skepticism in the first game.
Game mechanics are almost completely broken. Characters have to spin their whole body to face you straight on when they talk - even in a conversation between three people, and for EVERY new sentence. Something seems to be wrong with their eyes, because many NPCs look like they're on drugs. Combat is the only way forward. Want to sneak past an enemy or stun him in the back, like the previous game? Forget it. Get the "silent running" biomod if you want any sneaking, otherwise they will hear you miles away. Besides, where are you going to sneak about? The levels are too small for any kind of "Thiefing" around. Civilians become enemies without you ever touching them, even though they don't attack, but still. Why wasn't this refined for final release?
Skill points are gone, and so are the choices of augmentations. Now there are biomods, and they are everywhere. You can also swap biomods at any point in the game, so it's not like your choice really matters. Besides, about halfway through the game, you have to use rocket launchers, sniper rifles or energy weapons to get anywhere, or you won't stand a chance against the enemy.
Miss the techo-esque music from the first game? Too bad, it's now replaced with ambience. Some band, represented by NG Resonanse, also made it to the game, but they failed after like five songs (I think they were called "Three Faced" or some such). Now, I have no quarrel with ambience, or especially ambient game music (just listen to Fallout 1 & 2 soundtracks, for instance, or Mass Effect soundtracks). But imagine The Elder Scrolls soundtrack being replaced with, say, Viking rock or death metal, playing constantly? Not very moody.
So, is it all that bad? Well, the game is certainly playable. The graphics are pretty neat, but that can't be a "positive" aspect of the game, because games do evolve. New engines are developed. It comes "naturally" if you will. It's just like aging, it happens, people grow up, get jobs, whatever. Of course it will have better graphics. The funny thing is, would it be better if they had reused the Unreal 1 graphical engine? I think yes. It would certainly fit more content. It would be "ugly", but hey, Wasteland 1 is "ugly". Fallout 1 & 2 are "ugly". System Shock 2, the Thief series. That doesn't mean they are bad games.
In any case, get Deus Ex: Human Revolution instead. While it is a prequel, it is a good one in my opinion. Is Invisible War the worst game ever created? Of course not. But it certainly is not anything like the first game, or even close to the prequel.
Oh, wait, there is one good thing about this game - how to not make a sequel. Game developers should definitely try this game then, after playing the first one. The sad thing is that if they had just waited for a couple more years, just until X-Box 360, this game could probably have been better.
So; not recommended.

Probably one of the best games of all time. Between console and pc I have over 6,000+ hours and it still finds a way to entertain me even when I have most likely done everything there is to this game. If you love leveling and guns, this is the game for you. Without DLC's you can get to level 50 for free, with 'em 72 + 8 OP levels! There's so much to explore in this game and I highly recommend you try it out. A bonus feature? It's ♥♥♥♥ing hilarious. By far my favorite game. The "classes" consist of 4 non-DLC and 2 DLC. Six in all if you need a lil' help with the math. The non-DLC "classes" contain  The Gunzerker (Salvador), The Siren (Maya), The Assassin (Zer0, personally the most badass and fun one to play), and The Commando (Axton). The DLC "classes" contain The Psycho (Krieg), and The Mechromancer (Gaige). The Gunzerker is all about his main ability. He can duel wield two weapons at a time whilst using it. The Siren is all about her "magic." Her ability puts enemies into the air for a small amount of time, with upgrades it can be even more devastating. The Assassin can be all about his 'Sword" or his sniping abilities. His ability makes him go invisible for five seconds, great for reviving friends. The Commando, is all about his turrets. When you use your ability you can spawn a little turret, with upgrades it can become two turrets or even four! Now onto the DLC characters. The Psycho is mainly about his melee weapon. His ability makes him pull out his melee weapon and slash enemies with it. You can build him around fire or even elements in general. The Mechromancer is about her mech. Her mech can be considered a better turret. With every class there's three skill trees, so tonsss of diversity. Have fun with that. The elements in the game contain Slag (A debuff for enemies, pretty much needed for end game), fire(As plain as it gets, "OH GOD I'M ON FIRE AHHH AHH"), corrosive(Great for robots, kills 'em quickly), Electric(Used to get through enemies shields, and explosive(Great against robots with a slag combo).
There's tons more in the game to explore but I'll let you figure that out ;) Enjoy your endless fun, Vault Hunter wannabe.

I'm not good at reviewing, so don't take my word, but here's my review on TESO: TU.
Pros.
1. It's mostly free to play after you buy the game.
2. It gives a good sense of Skyrim, Morrowind, Oblivion, and all in between, mixed into the MMORPG Genre.
3. It gives hope to those who wanted a multiplayer version of Skyrim, (and some of Oblivion.)
4. It mixes well with the other games in the MMORPG genre, being one of the many open world ones, where you can do what you want.
5. The faction war system. 3 races per faction, and each one battles with players from level 10 and up.
6. The four classes are very fun to play as, decimating your enemies as quick as possible.
Cons.
1. The Crownshop has DLC, but you need to buy crowns to get it, instead of straight up buying the DLC.
2. The Story Quests, go on for a long time, leaving little time for you to do sidequests, and by the time you are able to, you're too overpowered.
3. Some of the dungeons you go to early in the game are way too hard without a friend, especially if you don't have friends.
4. The game has a lacking of weapons that you can use, and some you get that don't fit your class.
5. To play the game in a good way, you have to get a race that prefers to your class, instead of being what you want.
6. There are a lot of mean people in the chat sometimes, so beware.
But all in all, I recommend ESO.

I’m a fan of survival horror games dating back to the original Resident Evil and Silent Hill and I was very excited when the first The Evil Within was announced, however that excitement diminished quickly after playing it for a few hours. I found the game to be gory for the sake of being gory and was quite bored. I also found the unveiling “storyline” to be cliche and just plain stupid. I eventually gave up and never looked back. I played Alien Isolation instead (which came out at the same time) and found it to be the TRUE return to survival horror.
3 years later, instead of an Alien Isolation sequel we get The Evil Within 2 naturally. I ignored it until it was half off on Steam. I bought it with the idea that I could refund it if it sucked. However, unlike the original I was hooked from the start and knew I’d see this game to the end. This is everything the first game should’ve been. This was Resident Evil, Silent Hill, and the Last of Us combined. This was a true return to survival horror. The best part is I was having fun and very scared.
The early parts of the game were very unique and original, but unfortunately, much like RE7, the storyline turns to mush and revolves around a little girl. Is there some law that every horror game has to have do this?
Regardless of the ending, I had an absolute blast and plan to replay it soon. In the meantime I’ve started playing the first one again. While I feel it’s still inferior, it has grown on me, especially with the later chapters. I feel the early ones set the wrong tone. I can now see how TEW2 is a more refined version, removing a lot of the annoyances (matches, really?) and adding a lot of missing elements (stealth for example).
In closing, if you are a fan of survival horror and hated TEW1 or never played it, get this game. You’ll love it!

I played and loved almost all of the old adventure games Thimbleweed Park is based on, and I can confidently tell you to avoid this game. It is meant as a meta-loveletter of sorts to games of this type, like Monkey Island and Maniac Mansion, but unfortunately misses the mark in several key ways.
- PCs who seem to have too much out-of-character knowledge and the player, despite the inclusion of a to-do list, has no clear indication of what they're current goals are.
- Horrible, third-rate voice acting. Seriously, it's so ameteurish that it harkens back to the early CD-ROM days when they would get any old nobody to provide the voices for the characters. The male federal agent in particular is supposed to have some kind of Latino accent but it mostly comes across as a grating lisp performed by someone who watched a telenovella once.
- Several involved, non-sensical puzzles. And not in a "non-sensical in a funny adventure game way" but non-sensical in a "this is unituitive and no player would think in this way" way. There are puzzles you can only solve by going to locations that the character you have selected would have no reason to visit in the narrative.
- All this could be forgiven if the game was funny and/or well-written a la Monkey Island, but it isn't. It is, in fact, unfunny in the most tragic way: it winks at you the whole time as if it's self-awareness is supposed to make up for the fact that the writers can't write funny dialogue.
- Of the 5 different PCs, only one of these characters, the young game-enthusiast, is at all likable, and the female federal agent character stands out as being particularly nasty for no established reason, other than the fact that the writers thought it would be funny to have a "sardonic" character and then wrote no funny lines for her.
I backed this game on Kickstarter because of the genre it pays homage to and pedigree behind it's developers. I'm shocked and dismayed to see the final product faceplant so profoundly.

I have played a lot of the xbox 360/ps3 versions of Just Cause 2 as well as the PC version so the comparisons are well educated.
Ok this game franchise is not known for its deep story and this is no exception. The story is over the top and absurd yet that is also what I like about it. Some of the characters are quite fun and entertaining while others just kind of float into the background. The dialogue and voice acting is over the top and cheesy and some moments in the cutscenes are actually quite funny. However, the story is still pretty half baked and more annoying than intriguing.
I should just re-name this whole section to, '
' as that sums up the gameplay pretty accurately. Following the themes of the JC series, there is a lot of blowing stuff up in this game and I have to admit the in-game explosions and dynamic physics is absolutely stunning and when a bunch chain together I cannot help but marvel at the scope of it! What makes this better is the fact that you can WINGSUIT. THEY ADDED A WINGSUIT. This is probably the most fun I have ever had just traversing the environment in a game and I rarely used fast travel. Along with the wingsuit there is the traditional parachute and grappel hook which have all ben improved massively to increase the fun factor. The grapple hook system has taken a few hints from modders as now you can have multiple tethers and even retract them which combines for some devestating fun! Whether it's tethering cars and people to explosive structures or a helicopter to the ground, it is definately the most fun way to engage enemies in combat. Seeing as the shooting is pretty average with not very many guns and they don't even feel that different from one another. Now one thing that I hated was the gear mod system. To unlock better skills you need to complete challenges (races, shooting galleries, etc) to unlock gear mods. The challenges are frustrating and not fun (most of the time) and I just ended up getting more frustrated than thrilled. However, the speed and exhileration you get from the wingsuit in the challanges meant that I always tried them! The vehicle controls are also absolutely shocking and no fun at all! They handle awkwardly and swerve uncontrollably.
The game looks amazing and I am playing this on ultra and high settings 1080p FXAA at a solid 70-75 fps and the game looks amazing. The lighting and reflections look stunning with brigh colours and stunning country sides. Every area is fantastic to explore and I never tired of these areas and environments. However, the performance significantly drops during explosions to about 45 FPS during the MASSIVE explosions which is quite understandable but also makes me question why they made them so big anyway (it is almost excessive). The character models are quite detailed and well animated too with pretty medicore voice acting.

Immersive and engaging story told in an an excellently ecclectic way, pieced together as the player uncovers more information, understanding the relationships of the (superbly realised) characters, their stories and what they have been doing whilst you have been restlessy in hypersleep. It sets the whole scene so perfectly: and gives it an inherantly creepy edge all the way through, with the *ghosts* of the crew everywhere.
It also still has some of the most genuinley scary and disquieting parts in any game ever, even still, despite the dated graphics; a real testament to it's creative game design.
The diversity of play available to the player is not only in terms of the 3 main branches of service; but also how to mix and match aspects that come from each, with every new decision meaningful as you get more upgrade modules to enhance your particular chosen skills, that will determine how the game unfolds for you. In all areas there will be things you can not do yet, so you are always having to plan ahead strategically as well as thinking of what your immidiate concerns are. It fits perfectly with the open-ended sandbox type of play. You are set objectives, but so often its totally up you how and when you do them, which becomes more diverse the more you open up new areas; and I have always loved the fact that (nearly always) you can re-visit the early areas of the ship.
This is a game that is packed with lovely ideas: the nav beacon system where you can write notes on the map, the inventive way that your character is *stored and retrieved* by the resurrection stations on each level, the degredation (enhanced entropy) of weapons, the scope of different ways to deal with incresingly complex situations that will have you continually juggling with the different game aspects, and the way that the *rules of the game* change as the story descends into a kind of obsessive bio-technological madness.
I have played this through numerous times (still have the original disk and box and played it many MANY times ever before it was on steam), and is still fun+enaging+ scary AF!
