I first saw Alien in the theater when I was 11 years old back in 1979.  Ever since then I was both fascinated by and haunted by nightmares of the creature.  H.R. Giger created the most bizarre and terrifying monster in the sci-fi genre, and to this day nothing has come close to surpassing it.
I was unsure about playing Alien Isolation when I first learned about it.  Coming off the heels of that awful train wreck which was Alien: Colonial Marines, my confidence in Sega producing a quality Alien game was shattered.  I knew it was in the hands of a different development team, but Creative Assembly didn't make survival horror games, they make strategy war games.
My second reason for  almost not playing Isolation was my past experience with Alien games.  I've never finished any previous Alien game except Colonial Marines.  I finished Colonial Marines because it wasn't scary or terrifying, it was verging on laughably bad.  However, in every other AvP game there was always a level that tapped into my 11 year old psyche and awakened my paralyzing fear of the Alien.  This was my fear with Isolation.  I didn't want another Alien game I'd never finish, but at the same time I was yearning for a great Alien game to be made.  A different kind of Alien game.
I was excited that Alien Isolation was going to be Stealth Survival Horror and not another shooter or Action Survival Horror.  In Action Survival Horror games like Dead Space, The Evil Within, or later Resident Evil titles you're usually armed with weapons allowing you to kill the monsters chasing you.  This lessened the fear I felt.  Whereas in Stealth Survival Horror games like Amnesia and Outlast, you couldn't fight back and were forced to run and hide.
Well it so happens those guys that make strategy war games sure know how to make one heck of a survival horror game.  The decision to step away from the shooter genre and put Alien Isolation into stealthy survival horror was brilliant, and what I believe is the perfect fit for conveying the authentic fear of the monster.  The crew of the Nostromo weren't soldiers able to fight back, and that added so much tension to the story.  It's the same tension you feel playing Alien Isolation.
You couldn't capture the essence of the movie Alien properly without the stealth survival game genre.  Creative Assembly couldn't have done a more dedicated detailed tribute to the source material.  This game is simply gorgeous and beautifully optimized.  The lighting, the sounds, the meticulous attention to details of everything shows through.  They are truly fans of Alien that did extensive research to assure this game looked and felt like everything belonged.  As I watched my Alien Anthology BluRay bonus material, I had to smile as I saw so many assets Creative Assembly used to make Isolation as authentic as possible.
People may not enjoy stealth survival horror games because you can't fight back, and it's just a glorified computer version of hide-n-seek.  Alien Isolation won't change their minds.  However, if you are a fan of both Alien and survival horror then you're in for the most enjoyable, terrifying, nerve wracking 20 hours of hide-n-seek you'll ever experience.  Yes, I finished it.  Yes, I was scared.  It was too good to quit.  It was my personal victory.

In May of 1979 I was 13 years old. A science fiction and horror fan from a young age, Alien was something I wanted to see from the moment I saw that original cracking egg trailer. Sitting in that dark theater staring at the screen, I was hooked. I consumed any material I could get my hands on and became a life-long fan of both Ridley Scott and H.R. Giger. I even read the Alan Dean Foster novelization and wrote an over-written essay for my 9th grade English class. (And if you think my writing is long-winded now, it’s nothing compared to my younger, more exuberant work!)
The world of Alien is one that I love to revisit. Whenever a new game in the franchise is announced, I get excited. When it was established that this game would be more survival horror than action and based primarily on the first movie, I got really excited. The bulk of the Aliens-based games so far have been action shooters, which is fine, I have nothing against a fun shooter of any genre. But the idea of going back to the first movie for inspiration, playing as Amanda Ripley on the quest for answers into the disappearance of her mother? I couldn’t wait to see if it would live up to my expectations.
The “Crew Expendable” DLC was a perfect prologue to the main game. Playing through a part of the original story, and getting to wander around a very authentic version of the Nostromo was a great way to get the feel for what was to come. By the time I found myself on Sevastapol Station I was completely there, hanging on every noise and visual cue.
Wandering the barren and riot-damaged station, knowing that at any point the Alien was going to show up but still having to get to where you needed to go was thrilling for me. I completely love what Creative Assembly did here, building an environment that felt so authentic to the 70’s idea of what life in the future would be. This sense of “retro-futurism” held up from start to finish. At one point I marveled at how similar the stairway in a public section of the station was to the then “state of the art” refurbished elevated train stations of my youth. I found myself stopping to check out the posted ads, each one a pastiche of a time when we imagined a life in outer space, where we lived on space stations and listened to recorded messages and music on our reel-to-reel tape players.
Of course there wasn’t as much time for sight seeing as I’d have liked, seeing as at any turn you might be heading into trouble. The balance of threats and the way you encountered things other than the Alien worked well to break what could have been a monotonous “see the alien, run, hide” routine. And of course the Alien itself, who as advertised, forces you to change up your tactics as the game progresses. The claim is that as it's hunting you, it’s learning, and it sure seems that way. It would have been nice to see it closely examine a cabinet or locker where I might have been to really sell it. Maybe it did, though I never saw it. In it's relentless pursuit, I never felt safe unless I was locked into an elevator or transit car for the brief period moving between sections. After my first encounter with the creature, any time I lingered in a place too long it seemed to eventually drop out of a vent and (if I was lucky) send me cowering in a locker holding my breath.
There’s a lot of talk about Alien: Isolation being too long but I’d disagree. We’ve all played games where it feels that the ending should have come a little earlier than it did, or where parts start feeling repetitious. I played this on hard, which meant a LOT of waiting under or in things and dying often (I even earned the “100 Times Too Many” achievement for dying 100 times.) My final play time was 43 hours, though I did do a bit of exploring and taking pictures. Creative Assembly did so much right with Alien: Isolation. The environments… the music… everything about the game felt so authentic to the source material that when the little homages popped up, or the story takes a twist, it never felt forced. And the ending came right when it should have.
My finale with the game came with the “Last Survivor” DLC. Choosing to go out the way I came in, by revisiting a section of the original story. It’s a short piece, simply covering Ellen Ripley’s attempt to blow up the Nostromo while escaping on the life boat. Like “Crew Expendable” was for my start, this was a great way to finish my time in the Alien universe. For now at least.
Alien: Isolation certainly isn’t for everyone. If you don’t like stealth games, aren’t particularly a patient player, or feel that you don’t want a game that might take longer than the average time to finish then by all means, steer clear. You’ll get nothing here but frustration. But if you aren’t afraid of a challenge, and can be patient enough to wait out a massive xenomorph who’s only thought is of killing you… Grab a copy, set the difficulty to hard and enjoy!

This is definitely one of my favourite games of all time. Thank you Creative Assembly and SEGA for this masterpiece.

Was this game rightly panned? Yes. Is the engine terrible? Yes, with maps under half the size of its predecessor, and twice as crude, albeit with some very nice dynamic lights. Is the gameplay horrendously dumbed down and fundamentally broken in ways (in particularly the universal ammo)? Yes. Although despite losing lean keys, Alex gains the elusive ability to mantle, a welcome return from the SysShocks.
Do you, just for a fleeting moment, sometimes get a little whiff of being an augmented agent preying on terrified goons? Yes, but then you hit a map load barrier. Does it undermine JC and sometimes venture too far into "look, look, a person from the previous game, love me!"? Unfortunately.
But does it still have smart dialogue if you poke about? Yes. Does it have allegiances more complicated and subtle than "good" or "evil"? Yes, and more freedom than DX1. If you can get it stupid-cheap in a sale, is it worth putting up with the gameplay to weave yourself a plot?
Probably.

Deus Ex was a groundbreaking entry into the world of FPS and RPG. Some, such as myself, have praised the first installment as PC gaming's finest masterpiece. Needless to say, Invisible War (IW) had a lot to live up to. As a standalone product, IW is no doubt a competent competitor. However, as a sequel to a legendary franchise, it merely captures what made its predecessor remarkable, doing little to improve anything.
Perhaps the most noticeable change in this game is its simplicity. The original Deus Ex offered an overwhelming amount of skills you could invest in, ranging from your weapon proficency to your augmentations. IW kept only the latter. While this made the game easier to comprehend and manage, it also drastically reduced the versatility so proudly flaunted by the first game.
The AI devolved and bugs are aplenty. Fortunately, moral choices and combat approaches are still as open ended as ever and that, at its core, is what makes IW a great game.
Grade: B+

So on starting the game, I found all the different elements confusing at first (as with a lot of games), but immediately started noticing the similarities between bioshock and SS2:

- Cybernetic Modules = ADAM
- Security Codes

And then we have news that System Shock 3 in development and Terri Brosius is again voicing SHODAN which is the best news ever. I feel as if this game was made for me, as do so many others.

This game isn't fun right now, but it might be fun in the future once it's more polished. Here are the top three reasons why I didn't think it was fun:
1) At this stage in development, there are too many hackers/glitches and you won't realize it until it is too late to refund your purchase.
2) The game mechanics are not clearly conveyed to the player.
3) There are too few people who play this game. Even the most popular servers are less than half full most of the time.
If you do decide to gamble your money on this. Here is some advice.
-Play with friends (solo players are easy prey)
-Avoid playing on servers that say "Infini Wipe." These servers never wipe, so you'll be going up against players with stockpiles of resources.
-Start playing on a recently wiped server (you'll have a level playing field at least from a resource standpoint) \
-If you play on the Aztec Warfare server, you need to record every second of your gameplay. The admins only take action against hackers if you have video evidence.

Personally, I found the game already hard on normal, not because of resources, but because of the way the Alien reacts. But that might just be me.

The first thing I noticed when playing this game was the graphics. Good graphics, to be sure. So that's a good start. Let's fire it up...
....And in come the control cues. Ripped straight from the XBox controllers. Oh dear. What's RT/LT, RB/LB on a keyboard? Nope, can't find that. Time to rebind keys to try and make it easier! Nope, can't do that either; your mouse's extra buttons are not counted as keys to rebind to.
Okay. So at least we can bind key-to-key. Barring the basic lack of key placement for ergonomic reasons (who puts Interact With Item on Enter anyway), and heavy attacks/parries bound to doubleclicking on either RMB or LMB, this is a good start. If you're a beginner games designer, that is. It feels even less user-friendly to handle the controls than Dwarf Fortress (!) and that's saying something. This game is not worth purchasing on PC; it is clearly intended for console users only. Use only with a X360 / PS3 controller on PC, or prepare to be disappointed. Better yet, get it on X360 or PS3. Don't waste your money on the PC version.

TL;DR Good story and pseudo open world mechanics reward exploration. It has its flaws, but the good vastly overshadows the bad. Overall, this is a great game to sink 10 to 15 hours on
Pros:
- Story is engaging enough and the ending is satisfying. At the very least, it is better than the "WTF is happening" story telling of the first game
- The "open world" style of instances provides more choices and rewards exploration
- There are now side quests that add flavor to the overall story
- Good voice acting and weapon feedback especially the magnum
- Bosses have interesting backstories
Cons:
- The color palette is too bright and shiny for a horror/survival game. I enjoyed the gritty/dark colors of the first game which really added to the horror atmosphere.
- Higher difficulties will tend to force the player into a stealth build as ammo and health items become scarce
- No new elements are introduced during boss battles which make them predictable i.e. rinse repeat the typical shoot then run away tactic
- Hitboxes when it comes to melee attacks are weird and clunky
I felt compelled to write this review because this is the first ever game that I completed all achievements and had a blast doing it. A full playthrough will probably give you 10 to 15 hours of game time which is pretty good with today's triple A standards. However, if you are only going to play it once or arent that much of a fan of the series, you might want to wait for a sale.
I, myself, did three full playthroughs - suvival, nightmare, classic so it gave me a more than acceptable dollar per ingame hour ratio. I would suggest however, that a new player skip survival and go straight to nightmare for the better starting experience.
I am happy enough that I would gladly pay for DLCs to expand on the story.
Rating 8/10

This review will be slightly long. Just skip it if you don't like it like that.
This game is pretty much what one should get from a Dishonored game. Impressive and devious level design, fun and refreshing gameplay, and stealth so good you'll literally feel like a badass ninja. In comparison to the first dishonored, this one misses out a little on story, in the sense that the first had an aura of mystery to it... Who is this chap, Corvo? WTF is all this crazy, weird and awesome technology around me? What is Sokolov like, really? High Overseer what? The second feels a little empty in this regard. All the story is almost fully explored from the begginning.
Gameplay-Wise, things are good, and definitely feel new and inventive. Everything is more vertical, especially when exploring. Emily has fun powers, and Both Corvo and Emily feel different and suited to different tasks. Now, since there are
two different characters that play differently, the game almost demands two playthroughs. Which is how things should be.
Levels are so damn fun that you'll literally need to play them twice.
Performance-wise, things are not so good. As the joke goes, this game runs like Stephen Hawking. There are frame drops everywhere, in one part of a level I'm at 40 FPs, in another 25. In combat, frames drop faster than the bass drops in Skrillex's pieces, which is to say to -10 FPs. This is all on a GTX 670 on 1080p. I can run Battlefield 1 on full at 50 FPs.
Now, normally, the researched PC gamer would say to me, "Well, turn down those settings." I did that. ONLY an extra 5-10 FPs. THAT was horrible. Where I can triple My performance in Farcry 4 by turning down settings, I can barely add 10 FPs to my performance here. AND the frame drops from from one area to another area in certain levels occur just as much.
In the end, I do recommend this game. Just know that it is tough. If you don't have much patience for games, or get frustrated with them lots, think hard before getting this one. If your PC has a graphics card equivalent, of say, a 750ti at 1080p, don't get this. Ditto for people with less than 8 GB of Ram or most less than a high-range i5. But, in the end, this game is beautiful. Story was fun, and gameplay second-to none.

I haven't tested this on Win10, so these are few thoughts from playing it on my Win7 PC a couple of years ago.
Firstly, there seems to be some weird issue during load screens where the game re-initialises itself and Steam gets confused about whether the game is still running, so this explains why my hours are so low despite making a bit of progress in the game.
The Jetsons-esque visual style was really off-putting for me. One of the great things about the original Deus Ex was that the world and tech felt grounded and relatable. This just feels too far out there. It's a pretty big leap from cyberpunk (high-tech, low life) to full-blown plasma sci-fi.
The city hub sections are extremely claustrophobic, with many corridors and alleys bridging the various points of interest. It's believed this was done deliberately to help optimise the game for the original Xbox, but it comes at the price of feeling very restricted in the open play area.
The combat was okay from memory; the biggest issue with it is the universal ammo system. Every gun in your inventory uses the same pool of ammo. Bleh.
I really wanted to get invested in the story after the brilliant Deus Ex, but it was quite hard to bear through these gameplay and tech issues.
What a shame.
Not as deep as the original, and the graphics haven't aged well at all. I think I spent more time flinging around corpses than being engrossed by the story.

The game is an old deus ex like shooter. It has all the fun stuff like save scumming and an overly complex character customization system. I mean there are like 7 systems in place at the same time to consider when upgrading your character. Psy stuff, stat points, weapon proficiency, etc. All different categories. On top of that there’s weapon durability to consider, (weapons jam and have to be hacked or repaired in a different way when warn down) type of armour that’s best for a situation to consider and the whatever-they’re-called things that give passive bonuses but run out of rechargeable energy things to equip. There’s a whole lot of complicated systems at play in this game. SS2 comes from an era before game systems were dumbed-down for players.
Enemies respawn but supplies don’t meaning that you’re always sort of on a clock until you’re screwed with no ammo. At some points there are ‘hallways of death’ that are over-tuned and spawn too many enemies every time you have to pass through them. The game encourages specializing in one weapon type but is sparse with ammo suggesting the use of multiple weapons be the best course of action.
In the early part of the game character logs that play back audio are great. Latter on in the game enemies are way more powerful and there’s not really a moment of downtime to listen to them. They stack up. This isn’t a big deal.
The whole psy stuff is cumbersome. Basically the game has a system of using things similar to dues ex augments. Stuff like ‘use this much energy to get a 2 minute long damage reduction shield.’ It’s hard to specialize in psy weapon stuff when you don’t know ahead of time if you’ll ever even use half the abilities they provide. Changing abilities in battle is also hazardous.
The game has a great pace. The game introduces new enemies one at a time. It builds up to the moment and the enemies are really hard when first encountered. Then as time goes on and the player becomes more powerful and new enemies are introduced the old enemies become easy to deal with. This is fun and makes you feel powerful despite your power increase coinciding with the increase of power of enemies.
The game can’t be stealth’d. This is no dues ex. If an enemy is close they know where you are.
The game has a fun twist where you were being directed by the evil AI the entire time. Going-in to the game, basically reading any sort of thing such as the description of the game you’d know ahead of time this was going to happen so this isn’t a spoiler. The thing is: since you know it’ll happen you sort of just wait for it and it’s a bit of a let down.
For some reason the main character can just sort of see ghost custseans every so often. The game explains it with some techno mumbo jumbo. It’s as if the game devs wanted to put everything into the game including the kitchen sink. They really packed the game with stuff that seems unnecessary. Remember before when I mentioned the 7 systems at play at once. Same sort of thing here. There’s no need for randomly 5 or so ghost events to happen for no reason.
The game sort of has a pothole where the AI you’re working with takes over all the ship’s systems but security cameras and bots and stuff are still against you. Wtf? By the way the entire game, well most of it is on a super massive space ship. It even has a shopping mall. It feels like a ship that can support having a shopping mall in it. It’s just that big. There’s a bit of backtracking in the game. It’s fun to go back to old areas. The first wing of the game is basically getting access to 5 main floors of the ship. It feels like a cohesive world when all floors are accessible. Then the game’s like whops there’s a new elevator and now the game is a more linier path forward until the end. Then eventually the player gets to a point of no-going-back and it feels bad to never revisit all the areas cleared of alien infection. BTW there’s an alien parasite sort of thing and that’s why everyone’s dead. The AI you work with made it in SS1.
Anyways. Good game over-all. The very end’s trippy. The final cutsean of the game’s hilarious. No spoilers.

TL;DR: My personal game of the year 2017!
Ron Gilbert and his team managed to create an adventure game that is both true to the classics like Maniac Mansion and Monkey Island and yet so fresh and inspiring as you'd expect it from a game released in 2017. While the art style may look dated at first, it is incredible well done and very detailed (and finally we have ladder-climbing animations!). The story itself is hilarious and includes lots of references and homages to older LucasArts classics while the pizzles are nicely woven into the story.
Some people complained about the voice acting, however it was just like I expected it to be. The LucasArts classics which had voice acting always featured some hilarious (not in a bad way though) voices which added a lot to the game - just like in ThimbleWeed Park.
I've just finished the game and will definitely play it again (this time in casual mode, just to see the differences).
I backed this title when the campaign was live at Kickstarter with $30 and it is worth every penny!
A decent adventure game overall but its story is gradually getting more and more silly and incoherent with each chapter.

When Ron Gilbert announced the making of Thimbleweed Park on his blog back in late 2014, I had very high expectations. Now that I finished the game, I can say they were even surpassed. This is easily one of the best adventure games I ever played, up there with the all-time classics; the attention to details they put into it is astounding. The puzzles are brilliantly designed, the characters and dialogues are both amusing and interesting, the retro pixel graphics are incredibly rich in quality.
In short: if you like adventure games, you can't miss this one.  Even if you're not much into adventure games, I think Thimbleweed Park is still worth a try.

If you were a fan of the classic LucasArts adventure games (such as Maniac Mansion and The Secret of Monkey Island), Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick, who created some of those classics, have teamed up to produce a new game in that style: Thimbleweed Park.
I just finished it and I'm impressed; they made a game which appealed to my nostalgia for old-school adventure games, but which felt *new* at the same time. I would love it if they could start making this sort of game as a normal thing again...

Unsurprisingly, Thimbleweed Park is like Maniac Mansion meets Monkey Island... Maniac Island?  Monkey Mansion?? It truly plays like a forgotten LucasArts game... well, other than the METRIC *BEEP*LOADS of shade thrown on practically EVERYTHING, like "the futuristic year of 2017"...
What I like best is how all the puzzles, for the most part, make sense.  Sure there are comical elements (for instance, how to start a fire in the fireplace), but there aren't any "hypnotize a monkey with a banana"-style solutions.
What I dislike--sort of--is how the characters have this bizarre hive mind once they all become active, which I suppose is from how awkward it would be to have them talk to each other for every little thing so that anything any one character does, the rest will know.  There's not really a better solution, and it's only jarring at first (and also sort of explained away at the end anyway).
What bothers me is the dialogue is for the most part unskippable, and all the loose ends don't get tied up because, ultimately, they don't matter.  That's fine, though, because once you get a certain item, you can make a satisfying BOOM whenever you're feeling frustrated.
I heartily recommend a playthrough if you're a fan of adventure games (and who isn't??).  It's fun to play, and you'll feel smart when you don't have to consult a walkthrough because, really, the only hints you'll need is "thoroughly check EVERY ROOM" and "try EVERY ACTION on EVERYTHING." I only got stuck in two places: where to find an object I knew I needed (didn't look closely enough) and how to use an object (didn't try the correct verb).
Also, it's fun reading in the library and calling everyone in the phone book!  If you feel like it, call me: 1640 (I think I set up the voicemail correctly...?)

The first thing I noticed when playing this game was the graphics. Good graphics, to be sure. So that's a good start. Let's fire it up...
....And in come the control cues. Ripped straight from the XBox controllers. Oh dear. What's RT/LT, RB/LB on a keyboard? Nope, can't find that. Time to rebind keys to try and make it easier! Nope, can't do that either; your mouse's extra buttons are not counted as keys to rebind to.
Okay. So at least we can bind key-to-key. Barring the basic lack of key placement for ergonomic reasons (who puts Interact With Item on Enter anyway), and heavy attacks/parries bound to doubleclicking on either RMB or LMB, this is a good start. If you're a beginner games designer, that is. It feels even less user-friendly to handle the controls than Dwarf Fortress (!) and that's saying something. This game is not worth purchasing on PC; it is clearly intended for console users only. Use only with a X360 / PS3 controller on PC, or prepare to be disappointed. Better yet, get it on X360 or PS3. Don't waste your money on the PC version.

Wow. What to say about this game? Basically, if you like Bioshock, you'll almost certainly like this. It has a lot of similarities in mechanics, with hacking, machines to buy ammo and items, big maps, lot of different kinds of quests you're set on, psychic powers plus weapons, recordings to listen to with door codes and hints and things, etc. But System Shock is FAR more brutal, and I was playing on easy. Be prepared to be always out of ammo, currency, health, inventory space and regen points. Yet, it's really, really, really, REALLY good. It's got depth out to wazoo, and tons of cool features and a bajillion ways to play. There's three major "career choices"--either being a skill monkey (hacking, repairing, etc), straight-up shooter (lots of powerful weapons), and psi (basically magic, with fire, invisibility, telekinesis, etc.) You make the choice at the very beginning and there's not a lot of explanation before you pick, so do a little research online first to find the best fit for your playstyle. Let's break it down to the basics:
Pros:
+Great variety of tasks. It's an FPS, but there's lots of "puzzles". Things like "go to this place and turn on this button." But then there's something that's gone wrong, so now you need to go here and find the problem first, then do this other things, and then you can hit the button. You have to deal with radiation and toxins, can hack things, repair your equipment as it wears down, research items you find, etc.
+Tons of upgrades. Four different main upgrade trees: ability stats (strength, agility, etc), psi powers, weapon proficiency (energy, standard, heavy, etc), and skills (hacking, repairing, etc.)
+Never a dull moment.
+Huge map, with tons of different areas and problems to deal with. It really made you feel like you were on a ship, with a medical/science deck, engineering deck, command, recreation, bridge/operations, etc. You could go back to anywhere anytime. There's only one point where you can never completely retrace your steps.
Neutral:
~It's an old game, so it's polygon count is super low. Expect characters with point heads, cloned textures on the wall, and all around poor graphics. I didn't mind it, because I'm a fan of old games, but it shows its age graphically, which might bother some people.
~ There's a research function that's kind of neat, but also frustrating. You can find objects or organs from enemies to research, and they give you bonuses against them or the ability to use those organs as med kits or psi boosters or weapons. However, it's frustrating because most of the research requires chemicals, which you can't just carry arround because space is at a premium and you never know what chemicals you're going to need later. So you end up having to backtrack a loooooong way just to find the storeroom with the chemicals so you can get that ONE chemical you need. Frustrating, but it's really a neat mechanic in general, so I'm putting it as neutral.
Cons:
-The map is crap. There are little icons telling you where things are, like regeneration points, item purchasing, etc, but the icons are the same color as the map lines, so they're unreadable half the time because you can't tell whether it's a C or S or whatever letter you're trying to find. The low res doesn't help, either. Also, each deck of the ship you're on has different sections, which 1) don't show up on the map until you've been there (understandable), and 2) won't be available to look at when you're in a different section of the ship, even if you HAVE already been there. So trying to find that one place you were at two hours ago that you need to find again is really hard. All together, I probably did about 2-3 hours of wandering in about 30 hours of gameplay. I'm not even exaggerating. I could spend 45 minutes just trying to find a storeroom I'd been looking for.
- There's not a lot of handholding or explanation. There's "enough" for most things, but there's no indication of what early play will be like when you're picking your career path. I started off psi because it sounded the most interesting, only to find out it's basically hard mode, since when you run out of psi points (i.e. mana) you have to resort to other weapons or melee, but your physical stats suck. I ended up restarting as the hacker archetype and made sure to up my weapon use and fared much better. Also, I didn't know when I went to a different deck of the ship that I could go back again. It may be that I'm used to modern games that prevent you from returning to earlier maps (sometimes warning you in advance that you're leaving an area in case you wanted to go back for some reason). But you're on a space ship, and you've got full run of the ship. Which meant I was wandering around, desperate for them to give me a vending machine or a heal or something, never knowing I could go back downstairs to the ones I had already been too. I didn't figure that out on my own until about 5 hours in or so.
- The game is extremely stingy when it comes to weapons, ammo, inventory space, etc. Your weapons take up space in your inventory that could be used for other items, so it's not like the typical "carrying around 8 weapons" situation you have in a lot of FPS games. You have to decide very carefully and commit to using certain weapons or be prepared to switch when you run out of ammo.
- The "currency" of the game is used for hacking AND modifying weapons AND buying things at vending machines, so if you're hacking all the time, you might never have enough to buy bullets. The drop rate of currency itself is also pretty stingy. Most enemies drop no money (frequent), ~25 (decent but infrequent), or 5 (common). But it might take anywhere from 1-5 bullets to take down a single enemy to get that 5 money, and a set of 6 bullets can cost 85!!!! You'll burn through bullets (and thus money) faster than you'll ever get it from enemies. Hacking helps a lot, because it can get you into locked boxes with a nice stash of 25-75 money, but you'll probably burn 20 on a tough hack and 3 on an easy hack, so it's a gamble.
- There's a point of no return before the final boss, but I ended up expending all of my ammo trying to beat the mooks before it so I ended up with no health and very little ammo before the big boss with no way to go back and restock because I had been saving my game in the same save slot. My only saving grace was the implant I had found that regenerates 1 point of health at a rate of 1/30 seconds. I had to let the game idle for about an hour while I let my health regen, then had to do the same evil run through the gauntlet of baddies that took all my ammo last time, but I had to do a PERFECT run or I wouldn't have enough ammo to actually kill the final boss. After ALL that, there's a whole other area with ANOTHER boss to beat, and I got ZERO ammo before it. Ick. Not fair. And that was on easy difficulty.
-They give you respawn points, but you have to activate them before you can use them. If you haven't found the one in the new area you've just entered, you don't respawn, you just die. And if you don't have a recent save point, god help you. I was saving after LITERALLY every fight and LITERALLY ever time I found a new item or healed or whatever. It was about every 5 seconds because having to redo even 5 minutes of work is super frustrating. Also, you only come back at 25 health each time, so recovering from death is very, very difficult.
-Healing. Wow. Super inefficient. There are healing beds (that cost money) scattered around, but except for maybe one, you can't just use them right away. You have to find a key that unlocks them. Which means that you might have been at 25 health for a LONG time, and you FINALLY find a healing bed that will get you back up to full health....and you can't use it.
tl;dr Play this game. Be prepared for a lot of hair pulling, lacking everything you need/want, but if you like difficulty, depth and variety, this is your game.

I got interested in SS2 because I am a big fan of the original Deus Ex and have played through that several times.  This is no Deus Ex.  DX has stealth, conversations, and an engaging story.  SS2 seems to be an old-fashioned shooter that may have story elements to it, but I don't have enough peace from being attacked to listen to any of the logs and understand it.  About the only similarities I see to DX are the graphics and the fact that they both start out relatively hard -- but SS2 is MUCH more difficult to start than DX.  I started at "normal" but immediately had to reduce to the "easy" mode and I still die over and over.  The narrator says things, but I have no idea what she's talking about.  "Go to Storage Room Blah-Blah and get a Something-or-Other."  The storage room isn't marked well on the map, which requires you to tab out to see and then needs a magnifying glass to read it.  If you can see what you want, it's at the far side of a maze and you can't find your way there without constantly re-opening the entire map -- which is usually when you get attacked, so you might as well just roam around and hope you come to the right spot.
You can easily understand the advances in gaming since this game was high tech.  There is no tutorial; the map is poorly designed; every alarm you set off brings fresh hordes of attackers; when your inventory is full and you pick up something, the game drops something else for you, which you may not notice; and items on the floor may disappear without notice.  Another thing I've noticed is that the guides for this game are written by experts who assume more knowledge than I have.
One thing I'm not complaining about are the graphics or the sound; there are enough mods out there that these are not a problem for me.  Just the gameplay.  I've had numerous restarts and spent a couple of hours roaming around and trying to figure things out, and it's just not fun, so I'm giving up on it.  Thankfully it was cheap so no great loss there.

It might not be the sequel we were looking for, but it's still a Deus Ex

That IW is a colossal step down I won't deny.  The two biggest pains in the patoot being the tiny-as-fudgeknuckle box-shaped locations to explore providing far too many visits to the often broken loading screen and the writing itself heading into the fantastical, away from the recognizable and richly-detailed world of the first DX (gone are all the e-mails and most literature and admirable characters--& Pacotti/Grossman's high-quality dialogue with Australian-Chinese bartenders and hidden AI prototypes are limited to just a few instances like with the NG Resonance AI).
BUT: The game's still addictive; the story's stil strong enough to draw you in, and some levels, most notably the Egyptian arcology, are top notch (if you look past the loading screens); the goofy physics of objects and ragdolls are fun to mess around with; the graphics have held up well; and it's beyond satisfying to snoop around and knock out 2-dimensional villains with one baton swing to the face.

Despite all of the cool technical improvements to the first game, and some very cool storytelling, and very decent cutscenes, this game will forever be remembered as the Deus Ex game with "one kind of ammo."

IN-PROGRESS REVIEW
PRE TAMRIEL UNLIMITED: Bought the game when it released under a subscription so I've seen a lot of how it's improved since. I didn't like it as much pre-TESO:TU for a lot of reasons: Bugs, PC controls didn't feel very elder scrolls, exploration and fighting were awkward. I was looking for an Online version of Elder Scrolls and I found just an MMO with an Elder Scrolls face. Ended up only spending a few hours before I gave it time to breath and improve.
POST TAMRIEL UNLIMITED: With the introduction of controller support I've been starting over and found a lot of things have been improved to feel a lot more Elder Scrolls but with a live-community.
EXPLORATION has no markers pointing you to everything you need to find so the exploration aspect is really true to the Elder Scrolls console experiences from Skyrim, Morrowind etc. I stumbled upon random places that aren't even marked on the map and so the pacing of it was a lot more leisurely and curious compared to other MMO's like Guild Wars 2 where everything is marked for you at some point or Wild Star Online.
CONTROLLER buttons are mapped out very intuitively and the fact that you can block and attack with different buttons makes the fighting a lot more involved than other MMO's like FF14AAR. Aiming and positioning and timing are all still very important but because the abilities are numbered about the same as the number of buttons, things work out pretty smoothly, even when you get a second weapon to swap into the second set of skills.
VIBRATION inclusion in the controller makes lock picking MUCH less frustrating than it was before because you can feel when the timing is in addition to seeing it. I don't break as many lockpicks anymore.
DIVERSITY is big in the game because classes aren't restricted to weapons or armor. I haven't gotten to end-game content so I can't comment yet.
JUSTICE system implemented allows you to steal from NPCs (not other players....yet) and the penalty is getting chased by guards etc. It adds a layer of pressure and anxiety to being in town that usually isn't present in other MMO's. It actually makes you feel kind of like an outlaw, even to NPC's rather than just being seen as such by other players, etc.
COMMUNITY is lively and friendly and making parties and going on random adventures feels easier to get started and more fluid and natural rather than needing to stick to pre-planned questlines found in town. NPC's with quests are all over the map rather than just certain areas.
STORY is pretty engaging and true to Elder Scrolls lore ^^ Pretty interesting for the most part so far.
PROS: Controller support, Elder Scrolls feel is a lot improved, Pacing feels a lot more natural, Exploration is actually interesting, Story is good thus far, Community is good.
CONS: Playstyle and skills actually requires a bit of foresight and respeccing doesn't seem to be very easy to do. Getting stuck somewhere because you explored costs you X amount of coins to teleport back to a  waypoint which kind of dampens the curiosity to jump to random structures, esp early game when I'm still poor lol.

When Ron Gilbert announced the making of Thimbleweed Park on his blog back in late 2014, I had very high expectations. Now that I finished the game, I can say they were even surpassed. This is easily one of the best adventure games I ever played, up there with the all-time classics; the attention to details they put into it is astounding. The puzzles are brilliantly designed, the characters and dialogues are both amusing and interesting, the retro pixel graphics are incredibly rich in quality.
In short: if you like adventure games, you can't miss this one.  Even if you're not much into adventure games, I think Thimbleweed Park is still worth a try.

If you were a fan of the classic LucasArts adventure games (such as Maniac Mansion and The Secret of Monkey Island), Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick, who created some of those classics, have teamed up to produce a new game in that style: Thimbleweed Park.
I just finished it and I'm impressed; they made a game which appealed to my nostalgia for old-school adventure games, but which felt *new* at the same time. I would love it if they could start making this sort of game as a normal thing again...

Unsurprisingly, Thimbleweed Park is like Maniac Mansion meets Monkey Island... Maniac Island?  Monkey Mansion?? It truly plays like a forgotten LucasArts game... well, other than the METRIC *BEEP*LOADS of shade thrown on practically EVERYTHING, like "the futuristic year of 2017"...
What I like best is how all the puzzles, for the most part, make sense.  Sure there are comical elements (for instance, how to start a fire in the fireplace), but there aren't any "hypnotize a monkey with a banana"-style solutions.
What I dislike--sort of--is how the characters have this bizarre hive mind once they all become active, which I suppose is from how awkward it would be to have them talk to each other for every little thing so that anything any one character does, the rest will know.  There's not really a better solution, and it's only jarring at first (and also sort of explained away at the end anyway).
What bothers me is the dialogue is for the most part unskippable, and all the loose ends don't get tied up because, ultimately, they don't matter.  That's fine, though, because once you get a certain item, you can make a satisfying BOOM whenever you're feeling frustrated.
I heartily recommend a playthrough if you're a fan of adventure games (and who isn't??).  It's fun to play, and you'll feel smart when you don't have to consult a walkthrough because, really, the only hints you'll need is "thoroughly check EVERY ROOM" and "try EVERY ACTION on EVERYTHING." I only got stuck in two places: where to find an object I knew I needed (didn't look closely enough) and how to use an object (didn't try the correct verb).
Also, it's fun reading in the library and calling everyone in the phone book!  If you feel like it, call me: 1640 (I think I set up the voicemail correctly...?)

This is a technically excellent point & click adventure game - the puzzles are hard, yet logical - they flow well together, rarely outstay their welcome and I only found myself reaching for hints once or twice. The pixel graphics are lovely -  the modern touches that they included work really well, without taking away from the aesthetic. And the voice acting is mostly fantastic - although playing with 5.1 surround sound, occasionally the odd line would come through only one rear speaker, very quietly. But withstanding (presumably fixable) audio playback bugs, the game is clearly a labour of love - and I'm very glad I backed it on Kickstarter.
With all that said, I felt the game lacks much of the soul that made a lot of the classic LucasArt point & clicks so endearing. With the exception of one playable character (arguably two I guess), the majority are flat and uninteresting. The dialog spends far too much time on making jokes about old adventure games or "fan service", which although sometimes smile inducing, rarely got any honest laughs. The storyline starts interestingly, but peters out well before the game actually finishes - and I think the actual ending is a lot less clever than they thought it would be.
All in all, I strongly would recommend all point & click adventure game fans play Thimbleweed Park, if just to see what technical excellence in the genre looks like. If you're not already a fan, I'd suggest looking elsewhere first, such as Day of the Tentacle, Grim Fandango or the Monkey Island series - which on the whole I'd say are more compelling games.

Overall: Fun story continuation of the first game with some great expansions on characters both from the main game and from the Knife of Dunwall and Witches of Brigmore DLCs. The world is intoxicating and the gameplay pretty intuitive, so I always find it hard to put down once I get started. I HIGHLY RECOMMEND playing Knife of Dunwall before this game if you are able to, it will give you some insights into
Witches of Brigmore expands even more on the latter but isn't as crucial.
The Good
+ New Game+ feature is done in a way I like, very fun in the second playthrough.
+ Chaos level works similar to last game's morality scale, has great impacts on the world. Love the graph you get.
+ Characters and the world are as immersive as I hoped, love the lore and magic in here. Lived up to the last game.
+ Achievements are well designed and encourage you to find more remote areas that were lovingly designed.
+ Atmosphere! This game has its own mood, and it is intoxicating to me. Music and sounds are wonderful.
+ Who you play as effects neat background details (some audio logs, notes, etc) beyond chaos level and major decisions.
+ Better emphasis than the first game on shadow and sneaking using shading around the edges of the screen that fluctuate as you move around. I found it very helpful.
+ Emily is a badass. This game feels like it was meant for her, in my opinion, and everything felt more natural while playings as her. I feel the story is more centered around her.
+ Way more information about the heart and how ♥♥♥♥ed up it is.
+ You learn the Outsider's back story a bit more.
+ The Timepiece is
and is the most fun I've had playing a game in years.
+ Jindosh is like the 1800s magical world Tony Stark I never even knew I wanted. If you could have him for the night in-game and then throw him out like the garbage he is, I'd be hollering this game's praises from the rooftops. I felt genuinely bad both
+ The Black Markets are a fun touch, and robbing them is even more enjoyable
The Meh
* The ending cutscenes were okay. Not perfect, not bad. I liked them well enough.
* The plot was pretty damn logical and methodological. It's not a bad thing, it was descent; it wasn't as interesting it could have been, and wasn't as engaging as the previous game's. Plot twists? What plot twists? The only genuinely off-guard thing was
but she hints at it
so you get the suspicious deja vu feeling.
* Corvo feels a little tacked-on, but it might just be me. He has plenty of unique details but the real immersion comes when playing as Emily. I really enjoyed this but it might bother some people.
The Bad
- Some of the hitboxes are HORRIBLE. Walls also occasionally stick out ~3 inches more than their textures show you they are, and you have to keep leaning out and wait for your carefully aimed scope shot's reticle to turn red to know that your arrow will
hit that guard's head rather than shattering point blank on an invisible wall right in your face, alerting everyone and ruining your life.
- Although improved, similar to the previous game, you can occasionally approach someone from behind with intent to choke them and for some reason Emily/Corvo will uselessly swing their sword in the parry/block motion. Reattempting the approach if you have time will usually fix it, but sometimes when timing is crucial this causes you to lose precious seconds.
- On Hard, the Clockwork soldier's ability to detect you is legitimately unreasonable IMHO. It has seen me through walls while I was absolutely stationary and making no noise whatsoever. Shenanigans. Fortunately this was rare.
- It's short! Didn't feel as long as the Last Dishonored.
- Absolutely no shortcuts or options given to restart a level (really annoying when playing for Ghost or Clean Hands). I'm baffled by this because I truly thought I recall the first game providing a level restart at the end of each level. Unsure why they took away a standard from the first game. If Dishonored allowed for as many saves as the user desired I would have no issue with this, however I save like a madman and quickly begin overlapping, so I will usually lose the beginning of the level save by the end. In the future I can plan around this and designate saves better, so it's not a deal breaker so much as an annoyance.
- You cannot select individual levels/missions to play through. Wanted to show a friend the Timepiece, but dont have a save from the 8th mission? Too bad! This specifically made me sad, but I can see how the design of the game, with its very strict linear storyline, would necessitate it. Why not unlock it after one playthrough? Or have the levels unlock as you go? That would preserve the storyline integrity while allowing players to better explore individual parts of the world.
- A significant amount of people had compatibility issues. I had none of the compatibility issues discussed by others here, likely thanks to the update. Game crashed twice in all 72 hours or so of gameplay, which for me is pretty average. I'm running Windows 10 in bootcamp on an old Mac Pro, with a Samsung Evo 500gb SSD, Nvidia GTX 970 (Asus Strix version of the card can't remember but believe it's default overclocked) 4GB VRAM. 8 GB normal ram, Intel Xenon 4 core, somewhere around 2.9GHz. Game ran buttery smooth with high textures settings/medium antialiasing/low shadow and sunbeam details.
Best of luck and I hope this game works for you, should you decide to give it a shot.

Evil Within 2 is such an improvement over the original game, its a night and day difference.  EW2 is picking up directly where the first game left off, but with a slightly different tone.  Sebastian isn't a cop anymore, he's a drunk who is scarred from the first game.  This sets up the rest of the story in some really interesting ways.  A lot of the cheese of the first game is gone, instead focusing more on trying to create a darker atmosphere.  It's still over the top and full of body horror, but the pacing is much better.  It really feels like Evil Within was one of those cheesy, mistranslated PS1 games that you would run across. Now EV2 is more akin to a western style game in tone now.  I really dug a little more serious style resident evil game, but it will be up to you. Really this game feels like the true sequel to RE4. The gameplays smoother than the first and the upgrades are really meaningful.  You could probably end up with quite a different first playthrough if you chose to spec a certain way.  One really nice thing about this game is the amount of guns.  It's weird in modern games, I always feel as if there are not enough guns, but with EW2 you are getting them at a steady pace.  It even has a new game plus mode that allows you bring over all of your stuff from the first playthrough so the replayability is through the roof.  I absolutely loved this game, try to go in without spoilers because anything horror related is best seen for the first time by yourself.

If your looking for a spook, and are checking out the Evil Within 2 remember this (tldr at the bottom):

The gameplay is the same as the last with the absence of matches that I will say I do miss but with this much micromanaging I can see why it was thrown out the window. The story is a meh not that bad but definitly not as good as other horror titles. If you look at it all in retrospect it's good but not as good as the previous game so play that first and try this one if you were able to get into.
TLDR:

-Openworld Sections are as good as they will be in a horror game
-Good but not as good as the last game

Was not a fan of the first game, was trying to to hard to be "scary" and be the new RE4 (understandable  due to the director) but was just too frustrating and didn't hold up to the hype. When i saw the announcement for this game I was both excited and instantly concerened. I hoped they fixed the issues from the first on but wasnt sure it was going to be worth jumping into.
After hearing a lot of pople say it fixed some of the major issues and held up to the horror genre, i decided to try it out. To my suprise, turned out it was an exellent game. This really gives me hope that AAA game industry really can make horror games without BS. (looking at you Konami)
As for the game, the biggest welcome change is semi open maps that you get to explore in the game. At first i thought it was going to be unneeded but they did a great job making exploring extra areas worth it. You can see some really cool moments that you don't expect while you were just looking for ammo or health.
I also really liked the story in this game even if it seemed a bit overboard at times. It is a lot more cinimatic than the last game and seems to draw more influences from more games. It is like Silent Hill, The Last of Us, Resident Evil, and Outlast 2 had a baby. That might sound like an odd combo but it worked really well in the games favor.
Gameplay in the game is alos improved and at times is really tense. Not fully fluid as it should be as sometimes combat felt a bit clunky like a headshot with a fully upgraded shotgun pointblank to the head dues half danage at time. Besides a few set backs. Boss fights were much more enjoyable and really liked the monster designs.
Overall i have to say I was really suprised by this game and highly recommend this game to any horror fan. Personally felt like a step forward in the series and now excited to see if they make a third game.

This was an enjoyable game that I played my way through.  The combat was simple but enjoyable, and I enjoyed getting to move around, dodging attacks and throwing out my own in an RPG Maker game, as opposed to the bread and butter turn-based RPGs you almost always get instead.  I found the music to be calming and spirited, though it does loop tirelessly and can get grating over time.  I was disappointed that it didn't vary at all, even when you went into a new location.  The story was nothing special as far as I'm concerned.  Amnesia, reality-warping magic, and contrived heroine attacking the one she loves because story isn't all that compelling to me.  However, despite myself not finding the story that great, others seem to appreciate it, so perhaps that's just me.  I would recommend this game for anyone as there's nothing inherently wrong with it.  I've paid good money for worse, so seeing as this was free, I see no reason for someone to not at least give it 20 minutes to see if they like it or not.  I'd give it about a 5/10, mainly because the music lacks diversity.

Probably one of the best games of all time. Between console and pc I have over 6,000+ hours and it still finds a way to entertain me even when I have most likely done everything there is to this game. If you love leveling and guns, this is the game for you. Without DLC's you can get to level 50 for free, with 'em 72 + 8 OP levels! There's so much to explore in this game and I highly recommend you try it out. A bonus feature? It's ♥♥♥♥ing hilarious. By far my favorite game. The "classes" consist of 4 non-DLC and 2 DLC. Six in all if you need a lil' help with the math. The non-DLC "classes" contain  The Gunzerker (Salvador), The Siren (Maya), The Assassin (Zer0, personally the most badass and fun one to play), and The Commando (Axton). The DLC "classes" contain The Psycho (Krieg), and The Mechromancer (Gaige). The Gunzerker is all about his main ability. He can duel wield two weapons at a time whilst using it. The Siren is all about her "magic." Her ability puts enemies into the air for a small amount of time, with upgrades it can be even more devastating. The Assassin can be all about his 'Sword" or his sniping abilities. His ability makes him go invisible for five seconds, great for reviving friends. The Commando, is all about his turrets. When you use your ability you can spawn a little turret, with upgrades it can become two turrets or even four! Now onto the DLC characters. The Psycho is mainly about his melee weapon. His ability makes him pull out his melee weapon and slash enemies with it. You can build him around fire or even elements in general. The Mechromancer is about her mech. Her mech can be considered a better turret. With every class there's three skill trees, so tonsss of diversity. Have fun with that. The elements in the game contain Slag (A debuff for enemies, pretty much needed for end game), fire(As plain as it gets, "OH GOD I'M ON FIRE AHHH AHH"), corrosive(Great for robots, kills 'em quickly), Electric(Used to get through enemies shields, and explosive(Great against robots with a slag combo).
There's tons more in the game to explore but I'll let you figure that out ;) Enjoy your endless fun, Vault Hunter wannabe.

There are several things that make a horror game trulely great.
-Tension
-Good Storyline
-Detailed Levels
-Unpredictable AI
-Constant feeling of unstability
This game accomplishes all above and much more. Lets put this game to comparison. I was barely scared playing Outlast, Not even as close playing the Amnesia Series, and The Evil Within was just a joke.. I jumped into this and I kissed my♥♥♥♥♥goodbye. When I say this game is scary, its ♥♥♥♥ing terrifying. The alien is absolutely unpredictible. Not only that but the alien itself is very smart and can detect you by making the most simple of movements. Knock over a chair that happens to make a 'thud' with the alien close by? Dead. Try to run while the alien is a couple rooms away? Dead. Get too close to the alien? You got it, Dead. The game got me to points where I had to stop playing due to getting some sort of sensory overload. I'm not kidding, this game has gotten me to the point where I couldn't stop shaking. It finds ways to put you in such bad situations that its just unbelievable. The parts before the ending as well were incredible.
Now the game isn't all about the greats, while the game was insanely fun, there were some problems I had throughout the game. One being is that the alien can be TOO smart, meaning if he goes by you while your under a table, theres a 50% chance he's going to find you. (Yet again I was playing on Medium, not Easy nor Hard). In other points in the game there would be enemies barely noticable that could one hit kill you ruining the tension. Several enemies do this. Lastly, the ending wasn't the best. I definitely hoped for much more, but I dealt with it and in the end it wasn't all so bad, original but it left me hanging.
Pros and Cons
-
Pros:
+Amazing AI
+Good Mapwork/Detail
+Nice Gameplay Elements
+Insanely Scary
+Holds Tension greatly in some parts
+Very Slow Gameplay that leaves you looking into details for clues.
+Another Terrifying Type of Enemy.
+Unsuspecting Jumpscares (Mostly Original).
Cons:
-Dev says some passengers aboard the station are nice.. Thats a lie.
-AI Can be too smart
-Game has around 2-3 points making you think its the end... Nope.
-Some Sections are pretty difficult
-The game requires Extensive thinking, not puzzle thinking, more like survival thinking. Not easy.
-Some parts can kinda drag on and be boring. (But there are very few parts like this, most of the game is awesome).
-Ending could have been better... Wasn't bad but there was plenty of room for improvement.
-Some sections require insanely long walks that get boring quickly - Especially if you mess up.
-A few Cliche Jumpscares.
Storyline - 9/10

Ending - 6/10
Overall - 8.7/10

IN-PROGRESS REVIEW
PRE TAMRIEL UNLIMITED: Bought the game when it released under a subscription so I've seen a lot of how it's improved since. I didn't like it as much pre-TESO:TU for a lot of reasons: Bugs, PC controls didn't feel very elder scrolls, exploration and fighting were awkward. I was looking for an Online version of Elder Scrolls and I found just an MMO with an Elder Scrolls face. Ended up only spending a few hours before I gave it time to breath and improve.
POST TAMRIEL UNLIMITED: With the introduction of controller support I've been starting over and found a lot of things have been improved to feel a lot more Elder Scrolls but with a live-community.
EXPLORATION has no markers pointing you to everything you need to find so the exploration aspect is really true to the Elder Scrolls console experiences from Skyrim, Morrowind etc. I stumbled upon random places that aren't even marked on the map and so the pacing of it was a lot more leisurely and curious compared to other MMO's like Guild Wars 2 where everything is marked for you at some point or Wild Star Online.
CONTROLLER buttons are mapped out very intuitively and the fact that you can block and attack with different buttons makes the fighting a lot more involved than other MMO's like FF14AAR. Aiming and positioning and timing are all still very important but because the abilities are numbered about the same as the number of buttons, things work out pretty smoothly, even when you get a second weapon to swap into the second set of skills.
VIBRATION inclusion in the controller makes lock picking MUCH less frustrating than it was before because you can feel when the timing is in addition to seeing it. I don't break as many lockpicks anymore.
DIVERSITY is big in the game because classes aren't restricted to weapons or armor. I haven't gotten to end-game content so I can't comment yet.
JUSTICE system implemented allows you to steal from NPCs (not other players....yet) and the penalty is getting chased by guards etc. It adds a layer of pressure and anxiety to being in town that usually isn't present in other MMO's. It actually makes you feel kind of like an outlaw, even to NPC's rather than just being seen as such by other players, etc.
COMMUNITY is lively and friendly and making parties and going on random adventures feels easier to get started and more fluid and natural rather than needing to stick to pre-planned questlines found in town. NPC's with quests are all over the map rather than just certain areas.
STORY is pretty engaging and true to Elder Scrolls lore ^^ Pretty interesting for the most part so far.
PROS: Controller support, Elder Scrolls feel is a lot improved, Pacing feels a lot more natural, Exploration is actually interesting, Story is good thus far, Community is good.
CONS: Playstyle and skills actually requires a bit of foresight and respeccing doesn't seem to be very easy to do. Getting stuck somewhere because you explored costs you X amount of coins to teleport back to a  waypoint which kind of dampens the curiosity to jump to random structures, esp early game when I'm still poor lol.

My favourite adventure game is Monkey Island. I never liked the big heads of Zack McKraken and Maniac M. I didn't back it.
And yet, playing it was such a joy, much more fullfilling than playing Broken Age. The game captures the feel and style of the first LucasArts adventures so well. The exploration, the creepiness, the unexpected places, the naivetee (the phonebook is sorting the first names alphabetically - maybe that is common in the States?; all machines have "-Thron 3000" added to them, you catch criminals by feeding evidence to machines,...), all the red herrings and random unnecessary objects (I never knew I missed them so much!).
At the same time it is a much more mature game, the graphics look beautiful, the story itself twists and wriggles in all directions, and yet seems round and even as a whole, unfolding until the very end and offering a cathartic and melancholic end note.
One of the best adventures I've played in recent years.

System Shock 2 is an easy game to describe generally but a hard one to pin down exactly. In simple terms you can say that it's similar to its contemporary Deus Ex or its successor Bioshock, but I'd say that it's an experience entirely of its own. The main reason for this is that it's gosh dang scary. The logs and character writing give the creepiness depth, but I can't give enough credit to how much atmosphere the game derives from enemies and graphics that by today's standards shouldn't be enough for much more than a jump scare. Instead, even when the hybrids become easy to kill (one of the few flaws is the lack of enemy variety), their appearance and quavering sounds as they approach get me paranoid every time. The player progression is also far deeper than that of the Bioshock games even if it lacks the same in-universe hook to its upgrade system that Bioshock had in the Little Sisters. Overall, System Shock 2 holds up incredibly well as a game that makes being deeper than Bioshock and scarier than Dead Space seem completely effortless. 9/10

Ok, meme review aside, this is probably one of the best remakes of all time, and arguably the best indie game ever made.
If you haven't played the original, do yourself a favor and get it right now. It's cheap on steam, it's one of the best GAMEs of all time period, and is still fun regardless of its advanced age. Play it first, then come back and play this because otherwise you're losing out on some serious nostalgia.
Now that's out of the way, let me tell you about Black Mesa.
Basically Valve decided to port over the original Half Life to the source engine, the problem is it was just a straight port, nothing really changed except water mechanics and the skybox. It was really disappointing, and then they ended up breaking it with an update.
So, some valiant modders decided to to take it upon themselves to deliver the source port Half Life deserved, and so began Black Mesa. It took a long time for this thing to come to come out, but it finally happened in 2012, after so many years in development. After the success of the free mod, they decided to port it to a newer source engine and put it on steam, and after a bunch of updates that polish the game and enhance quality, you have Black Mesa.
It's extremely faithful to its roots only making design changes where it makes sense thanks to the new tools of the source engine compared to the old GoldSrc. The level design is largely the same, enemies act the same (mostly), and some great new voice acting comes in to the fill the void and the game even adds some tie ins to the sequel Half Life 2 with some characters in the beginning and a change to a certain enemy. Nearly every sound and visual is extremely high quality, and the crowbar collective should be proud of themselves. The AI is improved even from Half Life 2, where you have to really work hard to defeat your enemies and it is rare that you come out unscathed.
I have a few gripes here and there, such as the Devs decided to cut out On a Rail to a shorter version. Their belief is that it makes it less dragged out, while I believe that the extreme length is what made the level great. It's supposed to drag, because you're slogging through a MASSIVE BASE to get to a rocket area, and the short amount of time it takes to get there in this version is almost immersion breaking. Thankfully, there is a mod that fixes that "OAR Uncut" which is currently broken but will be updated.
I also think that the music in this, while brilliantly designed, relies too hard on nostalgia and doesn't reinforce the true horror of the first game, and feels really different than what Half Life intended.
However, these are minor gripes that are easily solved by mods. You can choose to play the game straight or mod it right away, check out the workshop. There are plenty of classic renditions of models and sounds to whet your nostalgia, and I personally prefer some of them to whats in game. I made some myself that replace some creature and gun sounds with their classic variants, as well as a remix of the soundtrack. Go check it out.
All in all, a fantastic remake that's worthy of your attention. Right now it's not done yet, Xen is still on its way in 2017, and for a long time was a running joke "DERR WHERES XEN", and really I appreciate the fact that the devs are taking their time and wanting to deliver a quality product. The original Xen in Half Life was highly disappointing, got really frustrating and annoying because of the stupid platforming, and was anti-climactic. Instead, Crowbar Collective is redesigning their Xen to be a different presentation, considering they have a new engine to play with.
Go get this game folks, after you play the original this is a great companion. I also recommend playing Half Life 2 and the episodes before this, but it's your call.

I was skeptical when I learned that Mikami wasn't directing and it would be more "open" than the first game, but The Evil Within 2 surprised me with its excellent gameplay variety and constant incentivizing of exploration and resourcefulness.
Despite some occasional control-related jank and a slow opening hour, just about everything else in this game is a delight to interact with - the scavenging, the punchy shooting action, the stealth kills, the environmental traps, the meaningful upgrades, the rewarding sidequests, the creepy and beautifully animated monster designs. All of it is in service of mainlining fun and thrills across the 15-or-so-hour campaign length.
The weakest point of the game is probably the story - it's mostly just "there", kept afloat by some occasionally offbeat humor and a few likeable characters. The climax is actually pretty good, too, with a focus and emotional urgency that would've been welcome in the preceding hours. Everything else about TEW2 is just so darn fun, though, you may not even notice or care.
In a year stuffed to the brim with amazing games across multiple platforms, this deserves to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with them. It may even be my own personal GOTY. I absolutely loved how it pulled me in and continuously surprised me with its layers of risk and reward.

Dark Souls 1 was a major gaming event for me. There are not many games that have ever had that honor, but I anticipated the release of that game heavily after playing through Demon's Souls and being so thoroughly impressed with it. Not only did I have high expectations, but the game itself even managed lived up to most of them on release. There were niggling complaints, sure, but I would wager that I have spent more hours playing Dark Souls 1 than any other video game in my life. It was THE GAME for me.
Since the game was quite well received after release, Dark Souls 2 was something I expected to happen. I had to reign in my hopes for this game, though. I was very skeptical approaching it. "Sequels never live up to their hype," I told myself. I made sure to be cautious. Nevertheless, I knew it would be a game worth losing tons of hours on.
When I first started playing it, the very first thing I attempted to do was fight the troll available at the start. It was tough, but after my first 2 deaths, I had conquered my first Dark Souls 2 enemy. It felt as awesome as it should have, and the item that was given was quite a reward. I felt my expectations met -- I felt satisfied. I knew that this game, despite my fears, would prove to be just as awesome, beautiful, and challenging as the first one.
... fast forward about 30 hours, and the niggling questions began to form. Why is there a limit on enemy spawns? Why does Soul Memory count all souls ever gained, rather than the number of souls spent to level up, buy gear, or upgrade equipment? Why was the humanity system removed, and replaced with a static Estus Flask amount that refills the same at any run-of-the-mill bonfire? Why can't I dismember foes to earn equipment, like the tails in Dark Souls 1?
Some of these questions have simple answers, and some of the answers are more complex, but the key thing is that I felt that some of the changes made between Dark Souls 1 and Dark Souls 2 were the wrong answer to the first game's problems. As an example, Soul Memory took a hammer to the fine-line issue of low-level invasions and twinking, and it did so at the cost of the multiplayer community's meta-game. People can no longer choose a Soul Level to stop at in order to fight people of a similar level, nor can they simply stop gaining Soul Memory. That's not to say that a solution was not found, but the solution is somewhat of a backdoor, and I feel very uncomfortable playing with game files -- even if it is simply a save file.
That's not to say that some changes weren't welcome; I am absolutely thrilled that weapon durability is now an issue players need to be concerned about, because it encourages back-up weapons and alternative rings and therefor increases the number of choices a player must make between equipment. I love that four rings can be worn now, because having only one ring on each hand in Dark Souls 1 was silly from a certain immersive standpoint, and because the variance between rings is so good anyway that the extra slots still beg a question of choice. The new weapon choices are fun, and spells are continuing to get more and more interesting.
The torch mechanic needs mentioning, though, because I really enjoy the times when it proved useful. Unfortunately, those times are too few and too close together in their occurences. The game seems like it was designed to be played with a LOT more uses of the torch in mind, but it did not see such a mechanic reach its full potential on final release. I have heard similar complaints from various other sources and forums, and it concerns me because it reflects a failure without a real method of addressing. The issue is not one that, as far as I know, can simply be patched away or rebalanced, but is inherent in the map design and loot availability of torches themselves.
The graphics are quite gorgeous, though, and I have no complaints on those. Everything moved better, everything sounded better, and the game was simply more aesthetically pleasing in every way it could have been.
These are just a few of the things that have struck me about the game, and I could talk for days about why the lore doesn't completely meet my standards, but then I fear I might give the wrong impression. I think that From Software should be highly proud of their current videogame output -- both of the Dark Souls games are very top tier, and I still look forward to the next game in the Souls franchise. If you want my advice, definitely play this game, but be aware that while it is still vastly superior to most other games available at this moment, it does not surpass Dark Souls 1 in quality. If they are not roughly equal games, then Dark Souls 1 might be called the better.

They changed how fomations are handled, without actually improving on them, and formations are really only useful during deployment. Forget the idea of marching your Roman legions into war, once you start the battle, you're herding cats.
