Ok, meme review aside, this is probably one of the best remakes of all time, and arguably the best indie game ever made.
If you haven't played the original, do yourself a favor and get it right now. It's cheap on steam, it's one of the best GAMEs of all time period, and is still fun regardless of its advanced age. Play it first, then come back and play this because otherwise you're losing out on some serious nostalgia.
Now that's out of the way, let me tell you about Black Mesa.
Basically Valve decided to port over the original Half Life to the source engine, the problem is it was just a straight port, nothing really changed except water mechanics and the skybox. It was really disappointing, and then they ended up breaking it with an update.
So, some valiant modders decided to to take it upon themselves to deliver the source port Half Life deserved, and so began Black Mesa. It took a long time for this thing to come to come out, but it finally happened in 2012, after so many years in development. After the success of the free mod, they decided to port it to a newer source engine and put it on steam, and after a bunch of updates that polish the game and enhance quality, you have Black Mesa.
It's extremely faithful to its roots only making design changes where it makes sense thanks to the new tools of the source engine compared to the old GoldSrc. The level design is largely the same, enemies act the same (mostly), and some great new voice acting comes in to the fill the void and the game even adds some tie ins to the sequel Half Life 2 with some characters in the beginning and a change to a certain enemy. Nearly every sound and visual is extremely high quality, and the crowbar collective should be proud of themselves. The AI is improved even from Half Life 2, where you have to really work hard to defeat your enemies and it is rare that you come out unscathed.
I have a few gripes here and there, such as the Devs decided to cut out On a Rail to a shorter version. Their belief is that it makes it less dragged out, while I believe that the extreme length is what made the level great. It's supposed to drag, because you're slogging through a MASSIVE BASE to get to a rocket area, and the short amount of time it takes to get there in this version is almost immersion breaking. Thankfully, there is a mod that fixes that "OAR Uncut" which is currently broken but will be updated.
I also think that the music in this, while brilliantly designed, relies too hard on nostalgia and doesn't reinforce the true horror of the first game, and feels really different than what Half Life intended.
However, these are minor gripes that are easily solved by mods. You can choose to play the game straight or mod it right away, check out the workshop. There are plenty of classic renditions of models and sounds to whet your nostalgia, and I personally prefer some of them to whats in game. I made some myself that replace some creature and gun sounds with their classic variants, as well as a remix of the soundtrack. Go check it out.
All in all, a fantastic remake that's worthy of your attention. Right now it's not done yet, Xen is still on its way in 2017, and for a long time was a running joke "DERR WHERES XEN", and really I appreciate the fact that the devs are taking their time and wanting to deliver a quality product. The original Xen in Half Life was highly disappointing, got really frustrating and annoying because of the stupid platforming, and was anti-climactic. Instead, Crowbar Collective is redesigning their Xen to be a different presentation, considering they have a new engine to play with.
Go get this game folks, after you play the original this is a great companion. I also recommend playing Half Life 2 and the episodes before this, but it's your call.

Summary of the review: This game is a must buy for anyone out there who still love single-player story driven 3rd person action games.
Honestly, when I started the game, my expectations were grounded. I've recently finished the first game, so I was expecting something along the lines of the first game in terms of quality. After finishing EW2 I can say that it is by far a superior game.
I will be very short on my review:
Gameplay - tEW2 gameplay is a mix between tEW and The Last of Us, of all things. You get a mix of detailed hub-like areas with side quests and exploration and linear levels, more akin to those that you saw in the first game. Gunplay has the satisfying oomph to it, with nice juicy sounds pleasing your ears when you land that perfect headshots and the enemy's head explode like a melon with a very cinematic quality to it. Stealth now is more viable than in the first game - I spent quite a chince of time being the stabby-Mc'stabber overlord that Sebastian can be - taking down enemies from the corners and from behind and saving that precious ammo and resources, and the whole process was very reminiscent of the Last of Us. You get your standard level up mechanics and some limited crafting along for the ride - both work well within the game and let me tell you, by the end of the game, perked-out and geared-up Sebastian is like a freight train going on a roll.
Story - the game is very story driven, and imho that's it's biggest strength. Nowadays you get 101 open world AAA games with a disjointed story and a map with over 9000 collectables on it. tEW2 has none of that nonesence. At no point in time did I feel that the story took a back seat so far away that I would loose track of it. At no point in time did exploring the hub areas of the game feel like a mandatory chore. The story here is way more coherent than that of the first game, and as a result very easy to follow. You get some side quest, that feel like a nice little addition rather than an overwhelming distractor, and the antagonists are walking the proper line between "just right" and "over the top". The protagonist has a clear goal, and he reaches that goal in the end. Nothing original, but fits well wit the whole B-movie vibe that Tano Gameworks was clearly going for.
Visuals - the game is suitably stylish and overall looks good. It may not be the technical masterpiece that will put your rig on your knees as your marvel at the greatest graphics you've ever seen in your life, but the presentation is still top notch - solid effects, great atmosphere, solid facial animations, and given that Tango Gameworks did a significant rework of idTech 5 engine, their STEM Engine was free of the texture pop-up plague that was common for idTech 5 based games (hello RAGE and Wolftenstein: TNO, I am looking at you two).
Sound - I am not an audiophile, so I can't really comment much on this aspect - all I will say that I was fully immersed in the atmosphere of the game, and at no point in time did I found sound to be distracting or unsatisfying.
Overall, this is my contender for the best 3rd person action-horror games of the year. Solid visuals, immersive and atmospheric world and predictable, yet still decent story, entertaining gameplay - it's all here. In 2017, a AAA single-player only, story-driven game with no microtranscations, no loot boxes, none of that open world collectathon crap is a miracle on its own. If you like Resident Evil 4, if you like the first Evil Within, if you like 3rd person story-driven action games in general - get this game. It's worth the money, it's worth the time.

What an amazing sequel to the original Evil Within. It really makes me happy to see that an enthralling and exhilarating single player experience is still capable of being made, and the Evil Within 2 nails that aspect, with the best ending I have seen in a video game in a long time. Fear not for this review, as I will not spoil any of the story or new characters you will encounter. Let's get started.
You are Sebastian Castellanos, an old washed up ex-cop who's lost everything: His house, his wife, as well as his own daughter. After the events of the first game, Sebastian has tried to track down the mysterious corporation MOBIUS for 3 years... eventually plunging back into the darkness of STEM. Seb sure has been through hell twice now. Also Sebastian is a certified bad@$$*%.
I've invested over 40 hours into the Evil Within 2 and I'm going to try to break down why I enjoyed the game so much. First off, the story of the game is fantastic; it's easy to get into, even if you haven't played the first game. Tango Gameworks and Bethesda took notes on what people said about the first Evil Within on what they didn't like, and they changed almost every aspect in it's sequel. It's cast is very diverse with both good guys and especially the antagonists and the MAJOR antagonists you eventually go up against. I have to say, it's amazing how much graphics have improved in just 3 years.
This is one of the few horror games I played that freaked me out multiple times through my first playthrough, as the events and other things you see get visually and mentally more disturbing the more you progress. Side missions in this game are actually not something I would call 'padding'. These missions actually tie to the overall story of the game pretty well as you learn more about the characters who issue you these missions and you will be vastly rewarded for completing these side missions. It helps to make you feel like this game has a more open-world aspect, giving you a breather in between the main chapters.
Any gaps you feel like you missed throughout the story can be remedied through talking to specific characters, asking them questions, or even finding and collecting some of the many collectible scattered throughout The Evil Within 2 such as computer files, notes, pamphlets and journals.
The story of the game alone could sell me the game.
the gameplay in The Evil Within 2 is phenomenal. One of the things I loved the most was the combat and movement system the game has; it feels very fluid with Sebastian's movements, especially with the thrid-person genre of a horror game. A new feature to The Evil Within 2 is a cover system with a mechanic that allows you to maneuver around cover without breaking from it, but it seems like false window dressing as I only felt the need to maneuver around cover once in the entire game. But it's there. I never felt like the combat itself took away from the horror aspect of the game because I knew I could at any point die off of just making a wrong move.
You can once again upgrade Sebastian's abilities with the green gel dropped by fallen enemies. The most useful skill trees to me are Stealth and Athleticism. However, there are several upgrades you can buy that are next to useless. In combat skills, most of the abilities you have to buy are 'reduced weapon sway' in order to get to some of the better abilities in that skill tree. Oh and one more thing, Tatiana needs to
lols.
The Evil Within 2 has had it's fair share of dumb, yet hilarious AI and glitches.
This is definitely a game you should consider purchasing. I rate The Evil Within 2 at a 9/10.

Having played through twice, the nature of this game becomes very very clear.  It's established on the first run, but concretely confirmed the second.  This game is about focus.  In EVERY aspect.  From its aethestics, mechanics and design, this is meant to be a pure, singular and distilled form of interaction and when it stays true to its course, it is an examplary experience.
You play as Amanda, the daughter of the movie's only survivor Ellen Ripley, following a lead that may help her figure out what happened to her mother.  It sounds like it has some thematic potential, but the game never takes advantage of it, sticking mostly to a Series of Unfortunate Events that Amanda must deal with.  There's nothing truly emotionally impactful that ever happens beyond a few small moments, however, the plot beats themselves do match the orignal film in their beats, with a slow burn to the alien reveal, a mid section respite dealing with an artificial threat, and a third act esclation.
In fact, the game as a whole is slavishly devoted to the original movie.  It's visual design is ripped almost wholesale to the point where it can feel a bit repetative and you begin wondering if there are only two different kind of hallways that can be made in the Alienverse.  There are also plenty of audio and music cues taken directly from the movie, with the only deviation being the alien itself.  Where as the movie presented the creature as a quiet menace, Isolation's black basterd is a loud, thundering presense constantly growling and hissing as he searches for you, with heavy thudding footsteps .  Purists may cry foul, but its a smart change that effectivly transfers the movie's tension into a realtime experience.
And it is an experience don't get me wrong.  When this game hits, it hits on all cylinders.  The Alien is your most common foe and it is effectively dangerous and terrifying.  You will die at its claws CONSTANTLY, and yet it's menace never fully disipates.  At best, you can merely begin 'coping' with his constant harrassment and reaching one the games manual save points is both intense while saving and relieving when done.  It makes for an exhausting experience, but a more than satisfying one.  Going in cold, this game is absolutely worth the price of purchase.
The problems show up when you try to go off the beaten path and the seems begin to show.  As I said, this is a singular experience.  The mechanics and design are devoted to the singular method of steatlh.  Combat's an option, but a costly one as you are constantly scounging for ammo, the majority of your foes are either bullet sponges or in the case of the alien itself, invulnerable and noise like gunshots brings it running anyway.  No, you're going to be crawling almost at all times, avoiding lines of sight and throwing distractions in the game from beginning to end, puncuated by minor quick time events.  It's an effective experience as I said, however it can get repetative during long play sessions.  Also, this is a game that's as linear as any CoD title.  There is ever only one problem to deal with at a time, only one way to get to it and only one way to solve it.  Sure, you can explore the parts of the station you've opened up to your hearts content, but with the constant threat of death by way of xenomorph, there's little to no reason to do so and this becomes painfully obvious in the design of the game once the audio logs come into play:
The game has two 'collectibles'.  ID tags littered about the station that offer...well, nothing much beyond the ability to collect them, and audio logs from the Nostromo voiced by the cast of the original movie.  These logs are littered throughout the station, but locked off with artificial barriers that can be overcome with items obtained later on in the game Metroidvania style.  The problem is that a good majority of these logs are locked off until late in the game, have a VERY small window of opportunity to collect them, and require you to deviate and backtrack in order to do so as the game never actually sends you anywhere NEAR them ever again.  Attempting to collect them through exploration exposes how haphazard the Savastapol station is designed, where a med bay somehow links to a robot factory with no rhyme or reason.  There's very little sense of place in these levels as they relate to the station as a whole and as long as you stay on the intended path, it's not really noticable.  This makes it clear these issues weren't a real concern for the developer, which begs the question of why include exploratory elements in a game that actively discourages exploration with its mechanics...
Presumption says the logs and additional exploritory areas were last minute additions to the game, but it doesn't really matter in the end.  The game is at its best when you are riding its rails and a confusing slog when you don't, but at the end of the day, its dogged focus on transferring the experience of the original movie to an interactive medium is successful and certainly worth the price of purchase or at least a steam sale.

No More Room in Hell is an interesting concept, and for the niche that it fills, it's polished like a kid on school picture day.
But just what
this niche you might ask? Simple, instead of trying to innovate, it dedicates itself to being the most hardcore, rage inducing, tension-filled zombie survival game I've ever seen. See, what I like so much about NMRIH is that it capitalizes on what should, in my mind, normally be the single greatest threat in any zombie scenario: lack of sustainability. Usually in games, Zombies aren't hard to kill, but that's provided there's always plenty of ammo to stuff your pockets with. This naturally leads to other mechanics needing to be mixed in, as  mowing down mindless undead with magazines to spare quickly devolves into a raw power fantasy more than a game. Special zombies in games such as Killing Floor and Left 4 Dead are designed to fill this need, spitting acid, having 20 times more health etc. At some point, one begins to forget what those "regular zombies" were so threatening for in the first place.
This game will remind you, oh boy, will it remind you.
Get ready for half a mag, weaving nimbly in and out of crowds, and being in generally tough-as-nails situations. Make no mistake, the horde is as frightening as ever, and you'd better be prepared to die over and over to learn from your mistakes.
It's not without it's flaws of course, most notably the god-awful voice acting and lack of direct explanation for all the special key bindings and techniques, but the core game is still real fun.
If you've got some friends who're into close squad tactics, and playing it out slow and serious, you'll not regret picking up this game.
Speaking of which, it's free, so... get excited I guess.

So much damn fun!  If you even remotely enjoyed Just Cause 2's openness and ability to let you create wanton chaos (or you just like sandbox, open-world games), you will ADORE Just Cause 3.
The best part of the game:  the tethering system.  The tethers are the star of the show, allowing you to do ridiculous things like tying people to cars, pulling helicopters into the ground, pulling cars into helicopters, pulling enemies into each other, destroying chaos objects, destroying full bridges, pulling your character to locations or into enemies... there's just so much you can do with them that even after dozens of hours, I was still blown away by how useful and fun they were.  You actually have control of them now, too, so you can connect multiple things and pull them all together with the pull of the left trigger.
The physics are very well done and play a huge role in the game along with adding to the hilarity of whatever chaos you can create.  A lovely addition is the 'satchel charges' which you basically have an infinite supply of but can only have a maximum of 5 out at a time.  These can be modified to have a rocket effect which you can imagine can create some hilarious moments.  They're also very useful if you've run out of ammo and your tether might not be strong enough yet to take down bigger chaos object.  Attach a few charges, activate, and you're set.
Many people gripe about the challenges to unlock mods but honestly, the tethers are what I recommend maxing out (which is easy to do).  The other mods really just give you a few additional grenades or other things that, to me, weren't worth the effort.  Honestly, I think some of the mods were actually worse than the default (I preferred to NOT have homing grenades).
Driving in the game is horrible but I spent about 90% of my time traveling through the air either by helicopter (which control fine) or by tethering and parachuting/wingsuiting.
Map is HUGE but only the towns and bases are interesting.  I would wager that about 80% of the map is just filler with absolutely nothing interesting to do or see.
Despite my gripes, the game is an absolute blast.  If you enjoy physics in your games combined with a buttload of tools to create satisfying, non-stop destruction and explosions, this game was made for you.  The developers succeeded in creating an incredibly fun sandbox that lets the player use their intuition and imagination to create their own fun.

I wanted to like this game. Its a neat little budget FPS with fast action and appealing asthetic. sadly the thing that hurts it the most is also the thing its based around, the AI. right now its a neat little proof of concept that could be fun a year down the line, but even after 30 minutes I quickly got bored of the game in its current state. I could see this being more interesting if it was more tactical, sort of like 'Running with Rifles' which does the whole Team vs Team AI shooter concept incredibly well. but currently this game is basically a twitch shooter with AI. The codifier for the space horror survival shooter genre. The gameplay is a lot better than System Shock 1 and largely feels like a modern shooter, the RPG systems have a lot more depth to them than Bioshock, and the graphics are dated but by no means ugly. The atmosphere still holds up incredibly well and gives you a real sense of desolation. It's just you and a very unlikely ally against XERXES and The Many.
System Shock 2 is unfortunately not flawless. My biggest gripe is with a large part of the RPG system. Simply put, you need to invest big time into standard weapons; all the other weapon types are simply not reliable enough to take you through the later levels of the game and this includes the PSI powers. This is one area which Bioshock does a lot better.
Another gripe is with the endgame. There comes a point late in the game where you notice a sudden drop in the quality and intricacy of the level design. This drop keeps going, with as absolute rock bottom the very final level and last boss battle... And of course the ending cutscene, which has Goggles utter his (legendary) only voice line in the game. The reason for this is rather tragic: the game was running late on its development cycle, and the last few levels had to be rushed.
But everything up to that dip in quality is absolutely magnificent, and by then you'll already be many, many hours into the game. If you enjoy Bioshock, Dead Space or any kind of shooter that emphasizes resource management and atmosphere, play the game that did it all before it was cool.

Similar to the original deus ex in a lot of ways but unlike deus ex where i find certain mechanics like stealth for example a bit dated now, i always found nothing dated about system shock 2 and it still holds up very well today.
It's atmosphere, level design, visual design and level of depth in its rpg mechanics is why i love this game. Great techno music during combat, great writing and a fun and creepy story.
It's still an amazing game i just think that most gamers are spoiled with the hand holding in modern games and they will never be able to get into this kind of game and experience it which is sad. You have to figure out what you have to do and where you have to go by yourself. There is no magic waypoint all the time telling you where you need to go. You have to read logs to find codes for doors to progress and research specific items needed to progress using different chemicals that you have to find in the levels. You have to carefully manage your inventory and supplies throughout the whole game or you won't be able to progress. The game forces you to use your brain and you get a great sense of accomplishment when you complete a stage you have been on for hours (engineering).
This game also rewards you very nicely for exploring every area of the game with items which encourages taking your time and exploring every area of the ship. This game has some of the best sound design of all time with the voice of shodan and the sounds of the ship and the music and sound effects etc. It's still honestly one of the best games ever made i would put it somewhere in my top 20 i can't really think of anything i dislike about it.

So let's start this of with the cons:
-Some Gods are heavily overpowered and uncounterable when played right.

-It's a unique take on a moba and feels really good to play.
-Optimized quite well for MOST operating systems.
-73(and counting) playable gods.
- Mostly balanced gameplay( as I mentioned before there are some really unfair gods in this game)

-Super intense pvp.
-It has voice emotes which are cool.
-Funny noobs xD
-Really cool art style and character design.
-No p2w
-Stuff that you should check out because I forgot the rest.
So my honest opinion of this game is altough it has some issues and has had me rage quit quite a few times, it's still really fun and worth a go if you like moba or just want to try something unique. I would recommend giving this game a go. So download it, start playing, get rekt, look up builds and then rek. Then come back and tell me I was awesome for recommeding this game to you. Alien: Isolation is not a fun game to play. As a game it is an incredibly stressful experience, quite possibly the most nerve-shredding I have ever had. It's also a pure master-class in adrenalin pumping terror that plays its audience like a violin and from the very moment you set foot on the doomed space station, the Sevastopol, you are thrust into a never-ending nightmare that is heightened to a fever pitch thanks to some incredibly polished production values that recreate a visually impressive playground that matches the set design of the original 1979 sci-fi horror classic to the tee, coupled with an equally impressive audio soundtrack that brings the stations every creak and groan to life with a thundering bass. Pure dread will be drilled into your bones turning your blood ice-cold when you finally hear the Xenomorph for the first time using the vents and ducts as her mode of transport and the sounds the Alien emits when nearby is blood-curdling. Alien: Isolation is hands down the most visually and aurally impressive game of 2014.

I never knew how much fun I could have hiding under a table! The level design, lighting and sound are all great and really create a tense and foreboding atmosphere - I love the film so inhabiting this landscape was a joy. I had no problem with the length of the game and could have played longer.
There is a lot of repetition involved, especially with the manual save system, but this is what *all* games used to be like and I very much appreciated it; I prefer being able to practice a section and then repeat as necessary to get through as best as you can without having an autosave forcing you to continue with barely any health or mistakenly wasted resources.
I did find that a lot of the time you can get through a level just by hiding in the shadows, and when I did try out using the items they didn't really lend all that much of an advantage, so it was disappointing to rarely get to use them.
It was fun though, and if you're willing to go along with it, scary as hell. There are great action sequences that are fun to take part in rather than just watch. I'd recommend for fans of the film and stealth games; not really one for running, shooting and getting to the next checkpoint.
Despite it's flaws I absolutely loved playing it.

I'm getting pretty close to finishing this game using the Oculus Rift DK2, and it is absolutely amazing. If you are curious on how to enable rift support just search for DK2 in steam guides and there is a russian guide that is easy to follow (even without a translation). Basically you edit two lines in a text file, use task manager to kill OVRServer_x64, and just run the game before OVRServer_x65 comes back up. There are also good guides on reddit to enable rift support, but I use the steam one since it actually was the simplest and most reliable.
Graphics (9/10): The game engine looks great in the rift (or not in the rift), and is easily one of the best looking games I've played in 2014.The death scenes when the alien kills you are well done and really varied. The special effects are some of the best I've seen esspecially: the sparks, the lighting/shadows, and fire/smoke.  It ran great on one or two 780s in SLI, and it runs great on my upgraded setup of just one 980. Some of the effects aren't made for the DK2 (cryo effects are replicated in both eyes making it look not 3d), but nearly 90% of the game looks amazing in the DK2.  The U/I though and game text can be hard to read in the Rift and some text will require you to close one eye to read.
Controls (7/10): Controls are fine by default, but I did have an issue with the crafting system. Its just way too tidious to craft, and when there is an alien stalking you the last thing you want to do is mess around with the crafting menu. Really though you don't need to craft very much to play through the game.
Game play (9/10): Best alien AI in a game yet. Legitimatly scary experience as this thing stalks you. It can be cheezy sometimes as it spawn or objective camps, but mostly it is reasonable. It can find you in ducts, in lockers, or under desks so be careful. It did bug out once and was unable to get me from under a table, but other than that it was awesome.
DLC (5/10): The DLC, especially the surviver mode DLC that is included in the season pass really isn't worth it. Its just extra maps in the survivor mode which is just more of the main game style gameplay. However, the other DLC that includes real voice overs from the orginal movie is AWESOME but its NOT INCLUDED IN THE SEASON PASS for no good reason. Very misleading "season pass" so buyer beware. It would have been nice to see some co-op in the DLC instead of just rehashing the main game without actually adding any value.
Overall (8/10) buy this game if you have a rift, like the alien franchize, or just want to be scared. Its just well done. CA did a good job overall and I can't wait to see what happens next with this franchize.

I had a Love-Hate relationship with this game. As a big fan of the franchise, I really enjoyed the attention to detail and the multiple nods to the movies. If you're into stealth games, you'll find great mechanics and your heart will be pounding at some points, the developers really put great effort to build a stressful and dangerous environment, I played in medium difficulty and I died quite a few times, and had to elaborate at least some basic strategies by crafting and using items to keep progressing. The audio and the video are probably the best thing about this game, everything looks and sounds polished. If you have the chance, I highly recommend playing this game with a surround system, the feeling of hearing the beast walking behind you and the ambient noises will surely improve your experience. As per the graphics, the game is not really demanding, I was able to play at max settings 1080p with my modest GTX 660.
So where is the hate? I feel the game is too repetitive, I had to cross the same areas multiple times just to activate some device or pull a lever, and then go all the way back dealing with the constant danger of being spotted by the enemies, just to find out that I had to go some other place before I could continue. I think the intention was to add more tension and dramatic ambience, however it only feels as if they were trying too hard and I felt frustrated at some points. This renders the game unnecessarily long, at some point I had to take an elevator after a stressful mission only to appear at some room where the only think I had to do was take some items and then take another elevator to finish the mission, couldn't they just use a single one? Another feature I didn't like was some items which I could have really never use, and at some point I didn't know if this was a shooter, horror, stealth game; I feel as if they were trying to include multiple genres to appeal everyone, but the mechanics don't really work well for all of them, specially against synthetics.
Overall I would say this is a really good game especially if you are fan of the franchise and you have been let down by previous Alien games. Alien Isolation points at the right direction, only with some lack of imaginative "quests" and an unnecessary long campaign.

If I could choose, which monster has scared me most ever since my childhood to this very day, you would probably guess either a vampire, a zombie or a bogeyman. But even combined they're nothing when compared to late Swiss artist H.R. Giger's most popular creation: the Alien. Ever since it was seen for the first time back in 1979, success followed on many fronts for a while. But unfortunately, nothing lasts forever. Rebellion (the very team that created two legendary AvP games back in 90's) tried to give us just as tasteful experience in 2010, but the time seemed to have passed the British team.
Still that wasn't even half bad compared to Aliens: Colonial Marines, the game that still gives me (and surely many other Alien -fans) a painful headache. Almost everything from the very core of the game was just messed up and instead of feeling fear, I just felt a shared sense of shame due to wasted potential. But when every last bit of Marine's equipment - even the iconic pulse rifle - is taken from you, what's going to happen then?
Creative Assembly's - British dev team known from Total War series - Alien: Isolation is anything but the same we've seen so many times: instead of being marine equipped with heavy firepower, you're pitted as a civilian, who lacks combat experience and who can be killed at any time. Literally. In Isolation you fight against your threats (mostly) by good thinking, not by guns. And that's just the beginning.
Isolation takes place 15 years after the events of Alien; commercial starship USCSS Nostromo has disappeared and so has  the game's protagonist's (Amanda Ripley) mother, Ellen Ripley. One day a man named Samuels comes to tell her that Sevastopol Station has acquired Nostromo's flight recorder and it doesn't take too much from him to convince Amanda to join retrieval team. Unfortunately things aboard Sevastopol Station aren't going well: humans turn on each other and shoot each other due to paranoia, mannequinlike Working Joe -androids have lost it and they attack humans at sight and last but not least there's an unstoppable, merciless alien roaming around the station.
Sevastopol Station is plainly put gorgeous and Creative Assembly has put the source material to a good use. Everywhere  you see something that reminds you of that time when the future wasn't so high-tech like it is shown in modern sci-fi series. Just add into this an atmospheric soundtrack, that has taken some notes from Jerry Goldsmith's composition and you're at home, especially if you're a die-hard Alien fan. But moving around Sevastopol isn't just exploring, because at the moment you either hear thumping or hissing nearby, you really wish that you knew the environment well enough to escape from the clutches of your enemies.
The mission pattern however is quite simple: most of the time you pull levers, hack the doors with your hacking tool and search for the component X to make it to the next level. But it's all about that nightmarish hide-and-seek -game between life and death that either encourages or discourages you to play the game through. Word of warning: Isolation is
a fun game, but I still like it very much. Why? Because it actually forces you to think even insignificant things through and through. Even the use of a safe system needs to be timed carefully, because when you're saving your progress, you're leaving yourself open to attack. Thus the fear of death is constantly present, especially in the first half of the game.
You're not completely helpless against the enemies, because with a motion tracker you can see their nearby location. As you progress, you'll find blueprints for different kinds of tools, such as EMP mines, noisemakers, smoke bombs etc. Every tool has its strengths and weaknesses, but you shouldn't rely on them too much, if you want to conserve your resources for real nasty situations. Firearms should be forbidden from use most of the time, because the sound of firing attracts unwanted attention and really, that's the last thing you want to do in this game. You can take down both humans and androids with guns, but stopping the alien itself requires either flamethrower, Molotov or pipe bomb, and even then it disappears only for a while.
Alien: Isolation, however, isn't a perfect game. In addition to monotonic mission pattern environments are recycled, especially on the last third of the game. And even though it took me almost 20 hours to complete the game, it would have actually taken 12(!) hours, showing that seemingly little mistakes have a huge impact on the game's events. To be honest, most of the time the fault was mine, because I either let my guard down or didn't pay enough attention to the environment. When I played this game second time on Nightmare -difficulty, only then I felt that some deaths were unfair, like when the alien jumped on me straight out of the vent without a single warning sign.
The game also has a Survivor mode, where you simply try to reach your destination, either as fast as possible or trying to get a good score by completing side objectives during the run. Alien and other enemies, of course, try to put a stop to your plans and you need to either outsmart or get rid of them faster than in the main game, provided you have enough resources to deal with them. Even though I find this mode interesting, with the main game there's only just ONE map and you're not probably going to spend much time with it, unless... you'll buy the DLC (*sigh*).
Anyways, I can say that Alien has finally got the game it truly deserves. The one that respects its source material and it keeps thrill-seeking players in its tight, even sadistic grip all the way through to the credits. Look out, necromorphs and other monsters from outer space, Daddy's come home!

As a life-long fan of the Aveyond series, I can say with certainty that this is an incredible game. However, it's not an Aveyond game. Yes there are references here and there in conversation, but the only thing that makes this game by definition an Aveyond game is the presence of the holy land of Aveyond itself. You could change the name of that place and erase the 5 or 6 references you get in passing and you wouldn't even know it was part of the series. Like I said before I don't think this is a bad game, but it just doesn't have the feeling of being on a proper quest to save the world. In every Aveyond prior to this, there has been a real threat of an evildoer plotting some grand plan, and you are sent on a quest to stop this from happening, running into all sorts of plot twists, tricky puzzles and difficult enemies along the way. In this game,
the main characters brush it off as a joke, leaving the whole plot lacking to feel of a real, important goal.
Another aspect of the game that I believe sets it aside for the rest of the series is the amount of consistencies of the series that were broken:
I feel like any one of these things could be implemented without alienating the game from the series, but all 3 along with others I might not have said are definitely a rather large shock.
As I have already eluded to, I also believe this game relies too much on it's comedic value to hold the player's interest in the plot (and the game as a whole). I had my fair share of good laughs during the Orbs of Magic series (usually during exchanges between Te'ijal and Galahad), and yes they made the games all the more enjoyable and added a sense of personality to the characters, but what keeps me going back to those games (as well as Aveyond 1 and 2) is the sense of completion I get every time I complete a quest, defeat a difficult enemy or ultimately finish the game. But because of all the satire and lack of suspense as to the final boss' plans, I found myself at the end of this game without even realising it. The feeling of approaching the climax of the story (i.e. the final showdown to stop your enemy's plan once and for all) just wasn't there. The fact that so many quests are left out of your journal for you to figure out on your own (i.e.
) didn't help either, as I went into the final fight fully expecting futher story development involving those side quests that I had assumed would come up later. (Please note that I am not saying the unwritten side quests were a negative addition. They are a great source of replay value and add that extra sense of completion to the game. However they should probably be pushed further to the side so as to not interfere with the apparent progression of the main storyline, or else they may actually withdraw from the sense of completion as it did with me).
Another note that I should make is that the number of highly problematic bugs in the game (at least at the time I played it) is rather alarming. Some characters don't show up during cutscenes, images may be doubled (i.e.
). And even carrying certain items interfered with menu interactions.
I love the Aveyond series dearly, and I did thoroughly enjoy this game. I did get a good sense of completion for all the quests I finished and secrets i found. However, it just doesn't fit the epic fantasy adventure RPG role that the series demands of any addition. I find it to be more of a sort of parody of the series. My overall rating for the game (based on satisfaction) would be about 6/10.

I have played all the Aveyond games and I have loved them all... except for this one. That's not to say it isn't an okay game, but it didn't live up to the expectations I have come to have for an Aveyond game. It was a bit disappointing.
Pros:
- The characters are well done. Boyle makes for a fun and interesting "hero". The side characters are just as interesting and the dialog is well written..
- The art is, as usual, beautiful. Each location has so many little details that make the map come alive.
- The mechanics are great. Each character has their own set of unique skills. Changing one active party member for another can have a real impact in a fight.
- The humor is on point.
- Lots of little easter eggs / throwbacks to previous Aveyond games.
Cons:
- The quests were all over the place, to the point it became confusing in parts. While a game can be boring if it is too linear, this game would have benefitted from more clear direction.
- The story started out strong, but fell apart toward the middle.
- Backtracking. A lot of tedious back and forth, zig zagging all over. It got pretty boring.
- The locations, while beautiful, felt small and cramped. The overall world map felt like each continent / island was stuck together on a too-small map at the end. Where previous games felt open and vast, this one felt small and squished.
- The ending. No spoilers, but it was a letdown. I kept saying to myself "That's it?". Pretty disappointing.
Overall, the game started out strong but seemed to lose it's way around the middle. I enjoyed it for the most part, but I felt as though the game had potential to be better than it was. If you love the Aveyond games, by all means get the game. Maybe wait until it's on sale though.

Wish I could recomend this as the only big issues it has are technical.
Primary Issues:
Only two screen sizes, full screen and tiny. Full screen stretches the game for wide screen.
Slow movement. Several things go into this complaint. I'll detail it in full at the bottom.
Audio slider for sound does not work.
Positives:
Story starts out fun and strong. Loses some focus in the middle but never becomes tedium.
Mechanics are an embaressment of riches. Every character has their own.
The meta dungeon was inventive. Cool idea well executed.
Being able to steal anything on the usuable item table was great.
Item that let's you see goodie rooms. Saves me from looking up (more) spoilers online.
Boyle's starting pokemon is the best pokemon for the whole game.
No random encounters, in spots this lets you run past higher level enemies to loot things.
Slow movement:
Late game there's no teleportation between cities, there is a system to reduce how much walking you need to do to get where you want to go but for this whole game you will be walking from point A to point B. There are several points where the next event isn't obvious, searching for them adds to the travel time.
Movement is handled with either mouse or 'wasd'. This is an issue as clicking on some things is hard due to their size while using pure 'wasd' will end up hurting your hand. And when using 'wasd' the fidelity feels off as when the character rotates direction 180 degrees they rotate in 90 degree chunks adding several frames of lag to the movement.
The walk speed is a fixed rate for the whole game and it's not fast. This makes backtracking through large areas like cities painful. Eventually I settled on using both mouse and 'wasd' to minimize hand pain.

No More Room in Hell is the best free to play game on Steam, so far, in terms of versatility and fun. You can play solo or with others in easy to find servers, you can also host your own servers for friends to join (you might have an easier time just finding an already made server), though I did have some lag problems depending on some servers I joined. Game modes are limited to objective and survival, there are plenty maps to choose from and accompanied by many achievements. The authors are also occasionally releasing new content on top of that, such as new maps, playable characters and new zombie models.
If you are a new player looking for something to play, I highly recommend you give this game a shot.

So much damn fun!  If you even remotely enjoyed Just Cause 2's openness and ability to let you create wanton chaos (or you just like sandbox, open-world games), you will ADORE Just Cause 3.
The best part of the game:  the tethering system.  The tethers are the star of the show, allowing you to do ridiculous things like tying people to cars, pulling helicopters into the ground, pulling cars into helicopters, pulling enemies into each other, destroying chaos objects, destroying full bridges, pulling your character to locations or into enemies... there's just so much you can do with them that even after dozens of hours, I was still blown away by how useful and fun they were.  You actually have control of them now, too, so you can connect multiple things and pull them all together with the pull of the left trigger.
The physics are very well done and play a huge role in the game along with adding to the hilarity of whatever chaos you can create.  A lovely addition is the 'satchel charges' which you basically have an infinite supply of but can only have a maximum of 5 out at a time.  These can be modified to have a rocket effect which you can imagine can create some hilarious moments.  They're also very useful if you've run out of ammo and your tether might not be strong enough yet to take down bigger chaos object.  Attach a few charges, activate, and you're set.
Many people gripe about the challenges to unlock mods but honestly, the tethers are what I recommend maxing out (which is easy to do).  The other mods really just give you a few additional grenades or other things that, to me, weren't worth the effort.  Honestly, I think some of the mods were actually worse than the default (I preferred to NOT have homing grenades).
Driving in the game is horrible but I spent about 90% of my time traveling through the air either by helicopter (which control fine) or by tethering and parachuting/wingsuiting.
Map is HUGE but only the towns and bases are interesting.  I would wager that about 80% of the map is just filler with absolutely nothing interesting to do or see.
Despite my gripes, the game is an absolute blast.  If you enjoy physics in your games combined with a buttload of tools to create satisfying, non-stop destruction and explosions, this game was made for you.  The developers succeeded in creating an incredibly fun sandbox that lets the player use their intuition and imagination to create their own fun.

A year after the shipment of a buggy, unpolished, poorly optimised and embarrassment of a game, Creative Assembly have delivered incessant patches to finally transform this title into what it should have been at launch. Hot off the heels of one of their most refined titles, Shogun 2, the series returns to the captivating period of ancient Europe with the rise of the Romans and their struggles with formidable adversaries across the Mediterranean.
This entry boasts better visuals and bigger battles, although you will certainly need a beast of a machine to get the biggest of battles to run smoothly, which is especially difficult when the technical spectacle is often limited by the CPU, rather than the GPU. Nonetheless there isn’t another franchise out there which accomplishes what this one does in terms of creating epic battles with legions of warriors duking it out, and anyone can get caught up in the thrill of epic ancient warfare. When you’re not commanding your troops on the field, you’ll be strategizing the rise of your empire on the intricate campaign map. Since the original Rome: Total War, the franchise has taken many smart steps to make managing the campaign, and the overall game, a more fun experience. The campaign has streamlined out the boring parts of micromanagement from the franchise’s past, whilst at the same time adding depth and intricacies to more interesting areas, such as intra-faction politics and levelling up your legions and special characters through different skill trees.
Ultimately there is virtually limitless amounts of gameplay in Rome 2, as you can play very different campaigns with numerous different factions, strive for different campaign victory conditions, and expand your campaign in different directions across Europe and parts of Asia. The best part is that no campaign is alike; the AI will undertake their own struggles against each other and randomness can create countless different scenarios – you’ll encounter all sorts of differently evolving adversarial empires as you expand your own through the dynamic potentialities of the campaign. Not to mention you can buy extra campaigns or factions for chump change (and quite a few have been added for free). And unlike in Shogun, all the factions can field wildly varied units, and the auxiliary recruitment system means that any faction can field more exotic units into their ranks to mix things up.
The game still has some quirks that can detract from the experience its trailers portray. On higher difficulties you’ll be too busy flying overheard issuing orders to watch much of the action, and you’ll want to save some of your battle replays and watch them later just so you can. And, despite huge improvements in optimisation since launch, it’s extremely unlikely you’ll have a machine powerful enough to see the game’s biggest potential battles, or finest graphical settings, running smoothly. The cavalry charges don’t have the same umph that they used to either. But all in all, however, the game is overall a hard package not to recommend, and presents insane value for money considering all the possibilities and hours you could pour into it, if you wanted to. Nothing quite captures the fun of world domination quite like the Total War franchise does.

For fans of RPGmaker games you will definitely enjoy this one. Great for new players to the series/RPGmaker as it can be played as a stand alone game, and for players of previous Aveyond games there are a few easter eggs that will make you laugh. The dialouge is unique, humorous and engaging, and the story is rich and well rounded. Plenty of side quests to keep you entertained, and multiple endings. The puzzles are fantastic, not too easy but not impossible. The playable characters each have their unique fighting style and are all equally strong, which makes it a difficult choice to choose which ones to play (which in my opinion, is a good thing because you don't have to play characters that you don't like just because they are stronger). Speaking of characters, all characters gain experience points even when not in play, so if you end up wanting to switch later you don't have to go back and grind to raise the level of the excluded characters. The footsteps get a little annoying but I soon forgot after about 5 minutes of playing. Overall, I really enjoyed this game, the developers  for Aveyond really did a great job with this one.

The best Aveyond I ever done played, and a pretty good RPG. Much, much funnier and original than what I usually see in the way of RPGMaker fare. The inclusion of a "Smooth Mode" finally fixes that choppy camera scrolling, which makes even easier to enjoy the writing and story, since I won't suffer from motion sickness anymore. The plugins all work well, the portraits are clean enough for a comic book, the music and sound effects match the great humor and finely paced cutscenes, and nothing feels like it was forced in. Plus you get to play as monsters, and that's always okay by me. It all comes together for a spooky funny fun time, but no onions. Doesn't need 'em, but it could use 'em.

I have played all the Aveyond games and thoroughly enjoyed the series. I was very excited to find out and actually play Aveyond 4: Shadow of the Mist. I am very particular in what games I choose to play and stick to only certain types of games such as RPG and adventure, for example. The platform for this game is different than the others and I believe it is a good change. The storyline is also unique, the main character is a retired villain who failed in taking over the world. This is a great change from the same old hero versus villain games. It also has different versions depending on which direction you choose to take in the game. It is humorous, which adds more fun to the game, and I think, the dialogue isn't overdone where you are just clicking to get through it. In addition, there are numerous side quests and secret caves. Overall, I really liked this Aveyond and would highly recommend it. I look forward to more games by this developer in the future.

I played the game through one time, on the hard setting and was able to beat it in <18 hours. So it is VERY short and fairly easy.
First, the good. The graphics, sound, emersion, lore, and everything else aesthetic about this game is beautiful, you feel like you are really in the Alien universe. As a "ride" this game is fun.
Now...the bad:
First is the AI, its a joke. The alien is not "Smart" at all. Typical Script like activity, warping around the map, and just general stupid behavior. The Humans are even worse, and the androids pose no threat at all. The only time you die in this game is in annoying "gotcha" moments and unfair glitches. There were plenty of times were I would hide, the alien wouldn’t leave, and I would just have to expose myself to die. Every time you die, the Alien randomly spawns somewhere else, so it's really just a dice roll if you are going to make it or not. Another major annoyance for me was there are also random android bodies on the floor, that you can clearly see are traps (but they contain items), however you can only Kill them if you let them attack you first...
The game is also painfully linear, and you spend most of the time following the waypoint maker on your tracking device...exploration gives little to no reward (in game items or entertainment value). The game is extremely repetitive, and the mechanics stay the same from the start (no evolution at all). I don't see any point in getting the DLC and doing more of the same...
The ending is also abrupt and horrible...adding insult to injury.
Overall, it could be worth playing for the graphics, but don't pay more than 20 dollars for it.

TLDR: Alien Isolation provides a very atmospheric movie-like experience. Definitely recommended to Alien-Fans and survival-horror gamers, others might get frustrated either by repetition or disappointing gaps in the game design.
I do not like survival horror games that much, which is why I might basically not be the right type of gamer to play or review Alien Isolation. I am, nonetheless, a huge fan of the whole Alien franchise ever since I saw the movies and played AVP1 and AVP2, which is the reason why I just had to play this game.
Turns out, it was a good choice to leave my comfort zone to delve into a genre which actually does give you some decent but eventually useless weapons into your hands while forcing you to hinde behind corners, under desks, in lockers and of course the obligatory and plentiful ventilation and maintenance shafts. While I dont like being harrassed by invincible enemies and get bored by the always repetitive hide and seek stuff, this principle makes so much sense applied to a game adaptation of the original Alien movie. In this regard, the game excels remarkably. Everything in this game from soundtrack to visual style feels very familiar from the movie and provides a story which extends the Alien universe in an original but highly respective way. Thumbs up for the design!
The same is true for most of the mechanics. Playing this on hard difficulty, which challenged me pretty much at some points, I was totally annoyed by some of the nothing else than time consuming mini-games and qte-like sequences where you need to push buttons, turn wheels, pull levers and similar stuff. It just feels terrible when hitting keys on some computer while you hear noises of an approaching adversary. The thing is, it just has to feel terrible! Hacking annoying door locks while an Alien croaches up behind you is creating exactly the kind of suspense I felt when I watched the first alien movie. Accepting repeated awful deaths and the general powerlessness will enable you to enjoy this game as a horror-movie like experience, which goes much deeper under the skin than any shocking sequence in AVP1 or AVP2 which eventually could just be blown away with almighty guns and explosives.
Of course, some aspects are frustrating nonetheless. Staying true to the visuals, the movie provided, also means that most parts of Sevastopol station look pretty similar. There is the occasional eyecandy here and there, but eventually the scenic bandwidth remains limited. Also, some game design aspects feel slightly stupid, such as the pointless Ion torch upgrades which just open the next door and maybe one or two at some earlier sections which you return to later anyway. Also, there are points in the game which are designed frustratingly difficult by purpose, while other parts are ridiculously easy even on hard. A bit more reliance on the idea of an actively scouting Alien and the possibility to lure it away from you, setting up traps and applaying ruses could have turned the scope of the game a bit more towards strategic thinking and a more balanced and logical experience.
Nevertheless, I think Alien Isolation provides a very atmospheric movie-like experience. Definitely recommended to Alien-Fans and survival-horror gamers, others might get frustrated either by repetition or disappointing gaps in the game design.
Note: This is only a review of the campaing, there is a "survival" challenge mode which might offer new excitement, but I am not too much interested in that part.

got my expectations through the roof, and despite a weak launch and having to wait until they fixed the performance issues, I got everything I expected (and more) from Dishonored 2.
Dishonored 2 is a stealth/action game where proper stealth is rewarded with fair/good outcomes and going on a killing spree is punished with grim/dark outcomes. What's good about this game is that anybody can play it - do you absolutely suck at stealth? No problem! Abuse your powers and get creative in a high chaos run... however, let's not fool ourselves, the game was especifically crafted as a challenge for stealth lovers, and such players will definitely be satisfied by what Dishonored 2 has to offer.
For first-timers I recommend playing with Corvo - I know Emily is more tempting but her powers are more complex and it might feel overwhelming if you're not familiar with the mechanics of the game.
+ One of the most challenging stealth systems I've ever played
+ Good story
+ Unique stealth mechanics and interactive environment
+ Great replayability
+ Different endings based on your actions
+ No DLC/season pass/microtransaction cancer
- Optimization problems (mid and low end rigs will definitely struggle to run this game)
- Stealth can be outrageously tough at times (plenty of "WHAT? HOW THE **** DID HE SEE ME?!" moments will be had)
Very hard, no powers, no kills, no detections... you know you want to.
I won't say anything about the story - if you've got a bit of hindsight you'll see it coming, but if you're like me it'll still blow your mind. PLAY IT! It doesn't disappoint and it's WAY harder than the first one.
+ More challenging than the first one
+ New enemies and mechanics
+ Great replayability
+ You can play as Emily!
+ New weaponry and upgrades
+ There's no Piero, so upgrading your gear is quite different
- Completionists beware: there's NO way to replay missions after you've finished the game! So you better pay attention to those paintings
- Visuals are better but the engine is crappier, performance proves it
- Somehow, low chaos eliminations don't feel as rewarding and severe (judge by yourself though)
It's a must buy for stealth fans, but the sysreqs are no joke - it requires a beefy PC.

As I am a man who absolutely adored the first Dishonored you may want to take this review with a pinch of salt but I will try to be as objective as I can.
This game is great but it is far from perfect. The mechanics are as solid as the first and the level design is as good or better in some cases. The characters are deep and interesting, Jindosh being one of my favourites. There are a few subtle references to the original game (and a lot of hamfisted "DO YOU REMEMBER HOW GOOD DISHONORED ONE WAS?" moments).
In my opinion, the greatest strength of this game is the freedom it gives you to do what you want. It dumps you in a level with a few vague suggestions/clues and tells you to just go have fun. There are a lot of game that try this but fail epically. Dishonored 2 succeeds at this because of the choice it gives you. Do you want to be stealthy? Do you want to take the high ground or the low? Do you want to pass by without hurting anyone or even being noticed? Or do you want to BECOME DEATH INCARNATE AND TAKE HORRIBLE AND PAINFUL REVENGE ON THOSE THAT HAVE TAKEN WHAT WAS YOURS?!
The choices that you make are made possible by Dishonored 2's movement techniques. The ability to sprint, climb, jump, and blink/far reach your way around make you feel like a god. The blink mechanics are possibly my favourite game mechanics of all time.
Now you might be thinking, "This game sounds amazing, I'm gonna drop €60 on this straight away!" but there is one problem, and it's a leviathan of a problem.
This game runs like your overweight uncle after he's been shot in the leg, and also he's on fire.
My PC has an Intel Core i5-4690 and an nVidia GeForce GTX 970, not a machine worthy of the gods but certainly nothing to sneeze at. To get this game to run at 60 (most of the time) I had to resort to using Medium settings.
"MEDIUM?!" I laughed as it autodetected my settings. "I haven't used anything below High since I upgraded." However, fiddling with the settings only made my fear grow stronger. "The rumours were true, it does run like♥♥♥♥♥"
Ok this I could deal with, it's not ars good as it could be but it is still extremely beautiful. So I played a few levels and was completely immersed until I get to the Clockwork Mansion (no spoilers). The Clockwork Mansion may be the greatest level ever devised in all of gaming but I could only get my framerate above 30 if I stared at a blank wall for a few seconds. The framerate hovered around a cinematic 25fps throughout the level and made me feel as if my eyes would bleed.
The framerate does dip in a few other locations, especially those with moving parts. Some of it is understandable with multiple levels being rendered at the same time at one point (spoiler?) but it is not something I can condone.
In conclusion I would definitely recommened Dishonored 2. Despite its obvious flaws and poor performance it is a testament to how games can be made. Excellent levels, excellent mechanics, terrible optimisation.

Dustbowl: A big desert, it has 6 flags and one of the maps to have planes.
Temple: A map set on a temple in the winter. Medium sized. No planes.

I have, however, done a fair share of the PVE content (all the 1-50 4-man dungeons, most of the delves and dolmens, almost every public dungeon) and find that the game excels here as well. The group finder seems to be lacking still, but I think it's just because most people seem to ignore it and choose to form their own groups in chat. Each bro has a unique blend of weaponry and abilities: From Indiana Brones to Rambro, Double Bro Seven to Bronan the Brobarian... there's something for everybody.
Obviously a game like this is designed for multiplayer, where coop is a word to be used lightly. While there is no direct friendly fire, the destructible nature of levels will have you crushing, detonating and sacrificing your friends again and again. Even the level complete system has you racing to a chopper to escape... if you don't make it... you'll run faster next time.
I played the latter half of the game solo, and whilst it loses some of the frantic appeal, the game remains fun and challenging. The boss encounters are (though sometimes glitchy), a huge amount of fun.
I'm not sure how much replayability there is to be had after completion, but with a campaign that'll last upwards of 5hrs, this is a solid purchase...

Feel those waves of nostalgia wash over you. Thimbleweed Park is everything an old Lucasworks game used to be. Closer in style to Maniac Mansion than Monkey Island, it's full of Easter eggs and other fun throwbacks to its forefathers. I clocked in the game at about 15 hours on difficult mode, and I only had to look up three puzzles that absolutely were a leap of logic beyond what I could manage. An extremely colorful and relaxing single-player shooter bursting with cuteness from every corner (with a capital C), Slime Rancher is an adorably surreal bundle of sunshine in a world full of gritty, dark, and usually very drab realism.
You play as Beatrix LeBeau, a spunky girl who lives alone on a ranch in the Far, Far Range. Through her eyes, you explore the world, using your vacpack (a gun that looks very much like it popped straight out of a Jetsons cartoon) all the while to suck things up, such as slimes, food, resources, and other bits and bobs, and shoot them back out as necessary.
Overall, the atmosphere is very cheery. The range is HUGE, and there's always something new to discover and explore around every corner, so playing value (in my opinion) is very high.
The only dangers you ever truly encounter are tarrs (but that's if you don't play casual mode), and some of the range's "natural disasters". Otherwise, with the soft, happy music, the gorgeous graphics, and the focus on making you smile rather than pulling out your hair, Slime Rancher is one of those impeccably beautiful masterpiece games everyone should try at-least once.

The Evil Within 2 was a phenomenal game with a shaky start. It looks and sounds great, characters are phenomenal, and the story is told well on top of everything.
The reason I say "a shaky start" is because I wasn't invested in the game until almost halfway into it, at about chapter 7, out of the whole 17. However, once the story elevated and jumped into the conflict with the first antagonist, Stefano, I became invested enough to finish the game very quickly. Another aspect of the game that surprised me was the fact that there are multiple antagonists.
The numerous plot twists kept me invested in the game throughout its 17 chapter story.
Visually, I was surprised to see the game perform at such a high level, and my setup ran it without issue. The perplexing design of the levels, and even the method of travel between one another added a sense of dread and unease that belongs in the best of the best horror survival games.
Mechanically, it felt almost as if it followed the same formula as mainstream horror games such as Resident Evil 7, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. This meant the controls were taught well, were intuitive, and not clunky. The gameplay was nearly seamless, and worked really well to convey the game to the player.
The story was extremely compelling, and was full of well-constructed characters who all had their own unique development arcs. The most noteworthy was O'Neal, who in the beginning is a cowardly technician who
but later in the game
These constant developments and personalities kept the story fresh and made me want to invest my time to unravel its mysteries and save Sebastian's daughter Lily.
Regarding value, I finished my playthrough in about 15 hours, but that will vary for everyone depending on difficulty. The game also has decent replay value, adding more weapons, enemies, and play style options upon completing the game the first time.
All in all, I definitely think this game is a good choice for anyone who is well into this genre, and it is worth looking into if you can get past the few introductory chapters and really get invested in the game.

When it was released last year, Total War: Rome II was a wreck. It was buggy, it felt unfinished, the AI was terrible, I could go on and on and on. But I shan't. Instead, I will say that now, 14 months and 16 (18 really) patches later, Total War: Rome II is much, much improved. It isn't perfect, and I doubt it will ever be as good as long-term Total War fans like myself hoped it would be during the build-up to its release. But there are a lot of mods out there that fix a lot of the game's shortcomings. Here are just a few without which I would find this game a lot less enjoyable:
-Radious Total War
-Traits, Talents and Toadies
-Four Turns Per Year
There are other mods well worth looking at, but those three are the ones which I feel make the difference between Total War: Rome II being an adequate game and it being a great game.

I also liked the basic set-up of the game. There were one of two large quests to work on throughout the game, which were made up of various smaller quests. There were also side quests that there was the option of working on that I had a lot of fun with. I enjoyed them so much that I refused to fight the final battle until I had finished all of them. The one downside of the game for me was that it sucked me in. ;)  I went to work quite a few times with bleary eyes, because I was enjoying myself too much and wanted to do just one more quest. It was hard for me to resist.

I am a full-on Aveyond Kingdom fan. Amaranth/Aveyond Kingdom and John Wizard are my 2 favorite game makers, and they frequently collaborate with each other. Their games are reminiscent of the old Square Soft games, for the Super Nintendo with strong stories and fun sidequests. They are as much fun as The Legend of Zelda or any early Final Fantasy game ever was.
Aveyond Kingdom’s Aveyond 4, Shadow of the Mist is in many ways, a more polished production than their earlier work.  The graphics and backgrounds are the best they have produced by far. The storyline is both deep and hilarious, and the characters are, for the most part, engaging.
This game incorporates the traditional elements of puzzle-solving, action, and adventure into a neat and enjoyable package. There are the usual elements of high fantasy, with the characters ruthlessly poking fun at themselves. The enemies are creative and fun to fight.
Because they are failed villains, Boyle and Ingrid are unhappily in love, and that storyline adds ongoing humorous elements. Myst and Robin are naive and make good foils for Boyle and Ingrid. Hi’beru and Rowen arrive later in the game, and Phye arrives so late I did wonder why he was included at all. As a Draghar, Phye does have some power, but I think like a writer, so in my opinion, all the characters should be in place at the midpoint. Because he arrives so close to the end, we don’t get to know him as well as I would have liked.
I purchased the game the day it was released. I have played the game through to the end four times. The first time through, I had Ingrid join Lorelei’s coven and married her off to Boyle. With that scenario the game played smoothly with no glitches. I was in love with the game!
The second time through I had Ingrid join Jinx’s coven, but when I tried to complete the task of selling the craft in Robin’s store, the game froze and I had to take drastic measures to close the game down. No matter what I did, in this scenario the game froze at that point every time.
So I went to their website and, following the suggestions in their forums, I reinstalled the game. I never got past that point on that particular attempt.
So I started a new game, and that time I had her join the transformations coven. This went well for the most part, but with one major flaw. Ingrid gained the ability to transform into a dragon, but the skill didn’t appear in her menu. When I went out to the forums to see how to solve that, the answer was that it would be resolved in the next build. I was disappointed, as I did want to have the ability to play her as a dragon.
However, that time I married Ingrid off to Hi’beru, which was cute.
The environments that the game is set in are lush and beautiful, dark and moody. The music is amazing and really contributes to the enjoyment of the game.
The game is fun, hilarious, and when it works properly, it’s a great way to spend 25 or so hours.

Much like many others, I originally came here from League of Legends. I was tired of all the kiddy bullcrap every game and sole reliance on others who would much rather spend time trolling than playing, on top of that with new Champion releases it seemed to make it even more fun for trolls.
With that said the biggest difference to me when I started this game was the difficulty of getting used to the 3rd person view. Since you cannot see overhead, you don't know whos hiding behind the next corner waiting to jump out on you.
The God Pack for me was amazing and continues to be amazing. The single price for every God in game was the first thing that got me hooked, not only does it include past God's but all upcoming God's too.
The community here is a lot better than League and DOTA in general but being an online game you still get toxicity at times and trolling but I find a lot lower trolls here than the other two games.
Smite's biggest downfall to me is the fact every skin seems to come up in chests. Very rarely are skins straight up purchasable anymore and it can be frustrating if there is only one skin you want but its in a chest of junk (aka the current Gentlemans Chest).
Game balance can be mixed, some God's are quite obviously broken and remain to be but Hi-Rez does seem to listen to the community on this side occasionally however the game is balanced around Conquest (the standard 5v5 mode) which leaves lots of inbalance in other game modes such as 1v1 (Duel) and 3v3 (Joust). Whilst this is frustrating sometimes, balance in general doesn't bother me that much because the game is just so fun.
Overall this game is great if you are willing to put time into it and give it a chance. Hi-Rez are very generous when it comes to free Gems (the games premium currency) with weekly quests involving just playing the game and even bonuses for just logging in.
Highly recommended, other developers take note.

MASOCHISTIC SURVIVAL MEETS HARDCORE FPS!
With the gaming market being so heavily saturated with the Open World / Survival / Crafting genre - Gamers now demand something ultra unique and special when they make a purchase.
HURTWORLD has taken some of the best elements of previous Survival games and created not only an aesthetically appealing design in - game and User Interface / Inventory System, but also implemented a strong "endgame" element with unlimited customization options thanks to the addition of the Steam Workshop & consistent optimization updates from the developers.
----------
THE MULTIPLAYER EXPERIENCE:
Major elements of the game that demand excellence are obviously well thought out and extremely appealing to the eyes. The accuracy and realism of the weapons will satisfy even the most demanding hardcore FPS players with all the hallmarks of an excellent shooter that include superior bullet drop, solid reload visuals, and for all the audiophiles - outstanding noise mechanics.
In - game voice and player identification are spot on and well optimized, feeling very "New Age Team Fortress 3" in its presentation - however detailed enough to expand the "cartoon" feeling.
Extreme strengths with the ability to host private servers, implement Steam Workshop content - which include a multitude of maps, base items, weapon skins, vehicle add - ons, and various "Quality Of Life" mods, HURTWORLD gives the player the freedom to expand upon the vanilla experience of the game and literally create a deeply customized reality that caters to the casual and competitive gamer. - Deep Vehicle Customization Options & Superior Driving Experience
- Strong Base Building Elements With Deep Customization Options
- First / Third Person Camera View
-----------
WEAK POINTS OF THE GAME:
- Early Access Title (Thus being subjected to possible bugs / glitches in correlation to patches & updates)
- Hardcore Survival element sets the bar high for players that are new to the genre - Thus manifesting a hardcore player base.
- Significant "Grind" requirement to farm the best gear / vehicle components.

This game is basically the same as Dishonored, only with the mechanics slightly polished.  Your powers are now given development trees, usually to streamline them for either a high or low chaos playthrough.  In terms of the powers they also make the game unbelievably easy now, particularly in the case of Emily who gets the ability to link enemies together so dropping one of them can take out a whole room.  But, just in case you're the Dark Souls kind of gamer who isn't having fun unless you're ready to huck your controller out the window, there's also a no powers mode where you turn down the Outsider's offer.
It can be a little more confusing, though.  The graphics are nicer but that means sometimes you can't tell which things are able to be picked up or not, and whether or not 'picked up'' means "item" or "this is the millionth glass bottle you'll accidentally pick up and have to quietly drop".  Similarly, for all its multiple routes, Dishonored could get pretty straightforward in terms of the direction you were supposed to go, but 2 seems to have larger environments from what I've seen of it so far.  Neutral npcs are a welcome change though.  It's nice to have Karnaca actually feel like a living city despite its problems, unlike Dunwall where the only people we ever saw on the streets were guards, Overseers, and Weepers.  Presumably that gets less so when you're High Chaos, over the course of the game.
However, the majority of this game really doesn't bring anything new to the table.  If you wanted more Dishonored, which is fine because I did too, then you'll like this game.  If you didn't like Dishonored or want something fresh, I'd suggest passing on it or waiting until the price drops.
