OK, so I'm a veteran of gaming of the adventure kind. I played pretty much everything LucasArts put out and loved it at the time.
The non-spoiler version, I guess: if you're a die-hard fan of the 1980s/1990s style of games and wish we were back there, this would completely be the game for you. And if I were the me of that time period, I'd love this game and recommend it to everyone that played adventure games because it's a solid game that exemplifies everything we know and love about the genre as it was then.
The problem is, that's exactly what it is: a love letter to that time, unfortunately 20-odd years too late. I'm not the person I was 20 years ago and in fairness, it is exactly what it seems to be. I wasn't missold on it being a retro-themed game. I'm just bitter that it feels like it violates every one of Gilbert's own 'how not to design an adventure game' rules, whilst piling on the nerd/fanboy references.
-----
Now we've got the tl;dr version out of the way and the people who care about being spoiled are also out of the way, I want to look at what is wrong with this game, and why it is not the game I hoped it would be.
Graphically, it's exactly as presented. I'm a huge fan of the pixel aesthetic and this really shines. The fact that they can use the power of modern graphics to do things not doable in the real resolutions of the day is actually cool; the ghost effects when playing as Franklin after his initial flashback works rather well to set the mood. The tilting of Ransome's trailer gives you a sense of immersion not previously really doable in such games.
But from the off, it sets itself up in so many other bad ways.
Firstly, the references. I'm a fan of the old games. Yes, I know Sandy and Dave were in Maniac Mansion. Yes, I know about the 1138 stuff. Yes, I know who Bernard is. I know about the SCUMM engine. The in-jokes asked at one point which profession was involved, be it flooring inspector, pirate, or leather jacket salesman. I got these. I got them all because I remember.
I don't even mind the occasional wink to the audience, but when it's done gratuitously like this, where you can't move for references to things. It stops being an adventure game with a plot and starts being a love letter to times long ago. And if that's what you want in a game, sure, go for it. Unfortunately I wanted a game with a plot, with the occasional nod to the audience for fun.
Speaking of the plot. The plot is a mess. I get the mechanics of the multi-player making it very hard to have, say, cross-person dialogue. I accept the mechanics required everyone to know things that they individually shouldn't be able to know. I even grudgingly accept the additions to each characters' todo lists to reflect things even when sometimes those things didn't actually reflect the individual character's motivations or goals. But at the same time, the plot is paper thin in places, and obtuse throughout pretty much the story's second act onwards where people do things because the game insists they do them, without rhyme or reason behind it other than the player can direct them to do things. Of course, this does make some grudging sense given the climax, but it's such a cop-out to hand-wave everything in this fashion. More, possibly, of a cop-out than any explanation given after the ending of Monkey Island 2. Big Whoop indeed (even referenced in this game)
Though, I'll add, the todo list was a nice quality of life addition, with this many characters and potential lines of inquiry, it was a nice to have rather than expecting the player to track everything.
Then we have the puzzles. Holy monkey bladders. I will admit up front that I'm clearly insane and tried it in hard mode, and that possibly explains why the puzzles are that obtuse but I refuse to believe this was anything other than bad game design - Gilbert's own list and various articles of his outline what good game design should look like, and I see no reason why this should not extend to the 'hard' version.
There are puzzles that are definitely in the 'why didn't I think of that sooner' territory. And there are puzzles that I simply would not have solved without trying every object with every object in every location because it's simply not that obvious. I mean... the location of the secret bunker. There are so many things in that puzzle that just don't fit together as things you'd logically do to solve it. (SPOILERS AHEAD)
Let me break it down. So there is a secret bunker in the forest. I was vaguely aware this was a thing. But to have to take Delores' trophy, collect some radioactive waste, put it in the puddle in the trailhead, wait for someone to walk through it and then follow the footprints. This is something that would have seemed like a "logical" puzzle in the 1980s. Unfortunately it's 2017, as the game helpfully jokes about on multiple occasions about what life might be like.
And the problem with that being, the genre has moved on. What is considered 'acceptable' by players has moved on. Players who thoroughly favour the illogical hoops to jump through are firmly in the minority now - anyone who has played the Wadjet Eye Games will see the difference; none of those have anything like the guess-the-thing-to-use-with-the-thing games going on.
I still remember the Old Man Murray article that Gilbert referenced on occasion, that 'adventure games killed themselves' with the breakdown of a puzzle from Gabriel Knight. This is exactly what this feels like, a series of things that just happen to work together that don't actually connect except laterally. Gilbert himself stated on multiple occasions that he wanted to set up for the style of puzzle where the player has a problem and has to go find the thing to solve it, rather than being expected to collect everything along the way and somehow be expected to know when to use it - but here even tagging everything along didn't help in the slightest. I don't, for example, know if pewter can withstand radioactive waste - it certainly wouldn't have occurred to me as a first, second or even third thought.
Then there's the thimbleberries. I find this particular puzzle annoying for the wrong reason. I haven't tested it but I find it suspicious that the route to the thimbleberry bush is eeriely similar to a certain set of instructions that could be dancing lessons from a map written in 1990... It was the first thing I tried and it led me straight to them. To say that was disappointing...
And this leads me onto the ending. The ending is horrible. Utterly horrible. It undermines everything the game set itself up for. We had a cast of characters that were annoying to various degrees - but I at least cared about the outcome of them. I wanted Reyes to get his closure. I wanted Ransome to get redeemed (hoping that the interview with Natalie would somehow do this). I didn't know until quite late what Ray's real objective was, and finding out actually undermined her, she seemed like a good agent for the most part (though where she said that all she did was as little work as possible didn't help her at all!)
But I had a cast of characters I had some investment in. And then the finale killed whatever investment I had. Closure for Franklin was nice but overshadowed by the Big Reveal. Reyes getting his closure by way of the newspaper was valid, though it irked me that he didn't keep his promise to Willie and that we didn't actually 'solve' Boris' murder as far as the sheriff-a-reno was concerned. (Also, the a-reno, a-who and a-boo thing was stupid. Very stupid. And it didn't really answer the point from the journal that the coroner had been fired and replaced. Though the coronor was even worse at his job than the sheriff, and that irked me too)
Lots of nice ideas and some technically excellent execution but it's the wrong end of a time warp for me. Wrong end of a time warp and in search of a plot. Shame, too. I really wanted it to not be that.

Having grown up playing Monkey Island, I came to Thimbleweed Park hoping for a dose of nostalgia from that classic era of point and click adventure games. Thimbleweed Park certainly delivered that nostalgia, but exceeded my expectations by proving to be an addictive, mysterious, amusing little adventure in it's own right.  On a technical level, the game is a delight, the pixel style being reminiscent of those old adventures but clearly updated in a way that makes it shine and not look dated in the current day. Sound and voice-acting was excellent too.
I loved the atmosphere of this game. Something I've heard Ron Gilbert talk about in interviews is giving the game a sense of "place" and that's something I really felt, the town intrigued me and was a joy to explore. It definitely has that creepy Twin Peaks vibe. I enjoyed meeting all of the odd and zany characters, especially the main ones you can switch between - Ransome and Delores were particular stand-outs, and I found their individual stories contained some touching moments as well as amusing ones.
Puzzle-wise, I am often worried about getting stumped for hours on illogical puzzles in point and click adventures, but I'm happy to say I didn't feel like that with Thimbleweed Park. I played on "hard", though I would describe it more as the normal mode for those familiar with these sorts of games. I found the majority of the puzzles to be at a good level of logic, and I found that a lot could be solved by paying attention to the details of dialogue and conversations. A few got me stumped for a while but mostly in a way where I could go away and ponder on it, then come back with a new idea, and felt satisfied when I figured them out. Nothing seemed too obscure to me, nor too easy, so I felt the puzzles were at a really good level.
There are so many cool little touches in this game too, particularly for fans of Monkey Island and Maniac Mansion, and even the fact that there are 100s of books in the game written by the fans who kickstarted it. Very cool.
Overall my only complaint with the game is that the later parts felt a little rushed in comparison to the first parts, but it still took me 18 hours overall which felt like a decent length for the adventure.
I would give Thimbleweed Park 8.5/10 just because of the latter part feeling slightly rushed, but all in all I loved this game!

One of the best horror games I've played since the days of Dead Space and Dead Space 2. The Evil Within 2 harkens back to the days of old school survival horror games like Resident Evil and Silent Hill; giving you a fighting chance will still making the need to scrounge around for weapons and ammo a must. Where the first in the series played on a linear path with more calls back to Resident Evil, the sequel feels more like Silent Hill, as the protagonist struggles with his own demons and trauma in a twisted landscape filled with equally twisted creatures. The gameplay is tense, terrifying, and most importantly fun. The story I enjoyed as it explored more about Sebastian, while still giving some world-building elements, and incorportating twists that I never saw coming.
In short, if you're as sick as I am of horror games that give you no fighting chance, and seek the days of Resident Evil and Dead Space, then this game is a must have. If you're looking for more intense horror feel, might want to bump up the difficulty as normal difficulty -while challenging at parts- never really leaves you with a lack of ammo and especially no lack of healing items.

This review comes from a survival difficulty standpoint.
Pros: Bar boss fights, this game is all ABOUT stealth! Writing this review after giving this game a second chance...
To begin with, the character has the movement, agility and endurance of a bedridden man. I spent a lot of skill points (green gel) trying to get some decent movement out of the character, maxing out crouching movement speed and endurance...  he now travels quicker crouched than walking upright, amusing indeed. Also I regularly find moving concealed around objects to be unpredictable and unintuitive (in contrast to games like dishonored, old thief games, deus ex etc).
The weapons are dull and a pain to use. Nothing gets working without aiming it first, so basically there is no hip firing ability. Add the clunky UI and that takes the fun away. Weapons and the way  they handle is CRUCIAL about games like this. Its so bad there is no point whining about it. Ammo is scarce though which is actually good.
Now lets come to the enemies, the low to mid level enemies have a very limited IQ and the attention span of a month old baby. They can appear a bit intimidating in the beginning, especially in groups but soon become easier and more manageable as the character levels. And this is the only part of the game where you have some free will.
At regular intervals throughout the game you will suddenly lose hold of the character and the cutscenes begin, heavy visuals and sound effects... a boss fight ensues.. now this game suddenly becomes an all out shooter... no stealth allowed no other options.. And yes the only way forward is to fight. If and when evasion and stealth is allowed, it is a very linear path and any little deviation from the preplanned escape route is either a player death or losing tons of your already scant ammo... After a while the scare element gives way to annoyance and frustration. I have not seen such poorly developed gameplay in a major title in ages.
Finally what is this? a game, a movie or a game -movie. Gameplay style is torn between stealth, survival and a first person shooter, but fails on all those fronts. Graphics, visuals, cutscenes, sound effects have been used to compensate for the lack of good gameplay. A wasted sequel to an originally crap game. I wanted to play a game, not be a part of a pre conceived horror documentary!
Not recommended.

Took about 22 hours to beat my first run.  I did all side missions (there's only like 4 of them) and tried to get as many collectibles etc. without going too crazy about it.
The story is amazing.  The gameplay was excellent from start to finish.  Please don't watch an LP before playing this, you need to experience this game.
I've seen some people complain about the gameplay at the start: how slow and tedious it is, and how difficult it is to fight enemies with limited resources, etc.  All I have to say is that it isn't bad at all so long as you're careful and you sort of know what you're doing (git gud).  It's a Shinji Mikami game so it's to be expected.  Play it like a stealth game and it's a piece of cake.  Conserve ammo as much as you can, until you feel that you are getting enough resources to start using it more.  Just use your brain.  The scarce resources combined with the horror atmosphere also make a very fun combination.  I look back at the beginning of the game with fondness, not contempt.  I also like the symbolic nature of the gameplay progression since it makes you feel very weak and vulnerable in the beginning, but as you progress through the game and see Sebastian develop as a character, you grow stronger with him.  It ties the gameplay in with the story.
I have some minor complaints with glitchiness after a few chapters, though.  After about 6-7 chapters, the game will noticably start to have lower quality collision geometry in a few specific areas, so some animations might act a little bit wonky.  It's nothing too horrible though, it doesn't affect the gameplay.
Another complaint is that the game starts off as a movie, and has quite a bit of cutscene to get through before you get into the actual game.  I loved the story though, so I'll give it a pass for this.  Also, all the characters in the game are very interesting and have unique traits.  The villains were especially interesting, and you could see how their personalities affected the world around you.
Despite some of the quirkiness involving animations later in the game, the gameplay is loads of fun, the horror elements are great, and the story is excellent; it even had me a bit choked up at the end.  I genuinely cared for the characters throughout the game.
I
recommend this game.  If you have the money, I see absolutely no reason not to own/play this.

This particular Total War game had a rough start.  At first I felt disappointed in CA for having released an incomplete product (after having been a TW fan and loyal customer since Rome 1).  Throughout there have been problems fixed, and others arise.  One in particular that come later was a problem with the co-op/multiplayer portion (desyncs - this has since been fixed as of patch 15 - 16 just released today).
Well, here we are a little over a year later.  It's been WELL worth the wait.  The vanilla game is good, but the mods make the game even better for me.  In particular I've been using the Divide et Impera mod (it's on TWCenter).  A great mod, with an active user base on the forums over at TWCenter.  The mod devs are constantly updating the mod to keep it useable with CAs free-lcs and dlcs.
Overall, I'm very happy with what both the vanilla game has become, and the mods that exist for Rome 2.  I think we're very fortunate that so many talented modders are willing to support this game.
One final note.  The ONLY two things I'd like to see changed/enhanced would be the political system, and the lack of a family tree.  The political system is shallow and annoying at best.  The family tree is only an issue because if you're playing as "House Julii", once your original General dies, some randomly named individual is then in charge.  Small things, and to my understanding both are hard coded and therefore unchangeable.  So I've learned to live with them.

Much like many others, I originally came here from League of Legends. I was tired of all the kiddy bullcrap every game and sole reliance on others who would much rather spend time trolling than playing, on top of that with new Champion releases it seemed to make it even more fun for trolls.
With that said the biggest difference to me when I started this game was the difficulty of getting used to the 3rd person view. Since you cannot see overhead, you don't know whos hiding behind the next corner waiting to jump out on you.
The God Pack for me was amazing and continues to be amazing. The single price for every God in game was the first thing that got me hooked, not only does it include past God's but all upcoming God's too.
The community here is a lot better than League and DOTA in general but being an online game you still get toxicity at times and trolling but I find a lot lower trolls here than the other two games.
Smite's biggest downfall to me is the fact every skin seems to come up in chests. Very rarely are skins straight up purchasable anymore and it can be frustrating if there is only one skin you want but its in a chest of junk (aka the current Gentlemans Chest).
Game balance can be mixed, some God's are quite obviously broken and remain to be but Hi-Rez does seem to listen to the community on this side occasionally however the game is balanced around Conquest (the standard 5v5 mode) which leaves lots of inbalance in other game modes such as 1v1 (Duel) and 3v3 (Joust). Whilst this is frustrating sometimes, balance in general doesn't bother me that much because the game is just so fun.
Overall this game is great if you are willing to put time into it and give it a chance. Hi-Rez are very generous when it comes to free Gems (the games premium currency) with weekly quests involving just playing the game and even bonuses for just logging in.
Highly recommended, other developers take note.

Aveyond is a wonderful series of RPG games. It reminds me of those old school games like Pokemon and Zelda, but the storyline is a lot stronger. The characters are likable, the dialogue is actually hilarious, and there's a great balance between quests and battling.
I've played (and loved!) all of the previous Aveyond games, but you could even start with this game if you've never played an Aveyond game before.

As a long time fan of the Aveyond series, I was excited to hear Aveyond 4 finally come out, and purchased it the day of release.  Soon, I got a free key for Steam from the developer and am excited to see this title finally out on Steam!  I completed the game in a blind playthrough in about 26 1/2 hours between Steam and the non-steam installer.
This game has all of the humor of the other games in the series, but has the unique twist of featuring a villain as the protagonist!  Some of the ongoing storylines from previous games find their way into this one as various cameos, which will appeal to fans of the series.
As for the game itself, it's a fairly easy to pick up RPG.  Instead of the archetypical classes you find in other fantasy based games, each character has their own set of skills and abilities, and each character obtains their abilities in different ways.
The story is engaging, and even the side quests are interesting and entertaining.  My only complaint is that the difficulty of the monsters in the last zone of the game is FAR above the difficulty found in the rest of the game... for instance, the monsters in the previous zone would hit my characters for 1, but in the final zone could kill with bad RNG.
Aside from that nitpick, the game feels polished and plays well on an XBox One controller, despite having to use an analog stick instead of a D-pad.  My only suggestions for improvement are the lack of a scaling full screen mode, and the ability to remap controls.
If you like engaging, story-driven RPGs, Aveyond 4 - or any Aveyond game, really - is for you.

A classic game that I enjoyed immensely, but imo, it's not flawless. Your enjoyment of this game all depends on your playstyle.
Though primarily a FPS, System Shock 2 lets you choose what "class" you want to play as. You can be a hacker, a soldier, a psi practioner, or a combination of all. Honestly, if you choose poorly and waste points, you won't fully enjoy this game. I generally play as a soldier class and much prefer to use traditional weapons in most of the games I play. That generally doesn't limit what I can do, but in System Shock 2, it does.
For a long time in this game, you'll have to conserve your ammo and the wrench you get near the beginning will be your best friend. There will however be a point where you'll need to use your weapons and what little ammo you have. Since ammo is scarce, it's very easy to end up wasting your ammo on some enemy that could've been easily avoided or taken out with your wrench. This ended up happening to me numerous times and I'd have to reload to an earlier time in the game to ensure that my ammo was not irresponsibly spent. Bottomline, your playstyle will greatly affect how much you enjoy this game and some abilities are more OP/useful than others.
Though I did greatly enjoy this game, there were moments when I simply wanted to finish playing the game as quickly as possible, or quit playing it. I've played games for most of my life and I consider myself to be a hardcore gamer, but I found this game to be tough for around 50% of the game. Honestly, it's because I mainly stuck to the soldier class instead of branching out and experimenting with the psi or hacking abilities. It was when I started to use a combination of all three that the game was no longer as tough as it previously was. I still wasn't able to run through this game, but it was much more managable.
Besides your playstyle affecting this game, the atmosphere is immense and greatly adds to the experience. As if being surrounded by mutants and killer AI isn't bad enough, it's the lack of knowledge that truly scares you. You'll be low on ammo or psi points numerous times throughout this game, but there'll be moments when that's made even worse by what you hear, not what you see. At times you'll be running along trying to accomplish your current objective when you suddenly hear enemies you've faced before. You won't know how many there are or if they're truly there and that uncertainty is what adds to your fear.
Lastly, some tips to better enjoy this game.
1) Save often and ensure that it's done between every 20-30 minutes.
2) Conserve ammo and psi points
3) Use the wrench
4) Try to research the best of the three playstyles to ensure that you have many options when dealing with obstacles.
Overall, I can see why this game is thought of as influential. Not only did it help contribute to the hugely popular Bioshock series, it also brought forth the Deus Ex series. With the upcoming System Shock 3 and System Shock 1 remake, many gamers will soon come into contact with this classic and will hopefully enjoy it despite its flaws. I recommend this game, but I know it won't be enjoyed by everyone, it's a very niche game. Most will see it as a classic FPS and automatically connect it to Half-Life, but it's not that type of game. This game requires more management and thinking when it comes to overcoming the obstacles that are thrown your way. I give this game a 3.5/5.

I started with System Shock 1 and I going to systematically play through the entire genre that it inspired in order. So here we are with System Shock 2 (with Dues Ex being next game in-line).
System Shock 2 is a fantastic game that builds on what SS1 did. It refines many of the clunkier elements of SS1 for example picking up items and the inventory system.
This game sees the introduction of the PSI system. With the use of an implant you can you can use many different PSI abilties. Much like we would again see in the Bio Shock series. My only complaint here is they are not utilized very well here. For example in Bio Shock, especially starting with BS2 they worked in tandem with your weapons. Power in one hand, gun in the other, and they would compliment each other. In SS2 you almost have to choose either a 'weapons build' or a 'psi build'. You can mix and match, but its not something first time players are going to be able to do very well without knowing exactly what they want to spend their limited upgrade points on. If you know from the very start you absolutely are not going to be touching heavy and exotic weapons, then you could have integrate some PSI abilities into you build. But for first time players, when you see 'exotic' and 'heavy' weapons skills, how can you not want to find out what those even are. That is my biggest gripe with this game: PSI abilties were not implemented as well as we see in the Bioshock games. Which in many ways is why Deus Ex is my favorite out of all these games. Its 100% tech. No silly "bug swarm" powers.
The mod support for this game is nice. Lots of easy to follow guides. This is maybe my 4th attempt to used mods in my entire life and I found the procedures easy and painless. They have graphical upgrades for nearly everything in this game. Even without them, this game is still fantastic. Its atmospheric and moody. More of a horror fps/rpg (much like SS1).
I can highly recommend this classic game.

The Elder Scrolls: Online has come a very long way. In the beginning, the game was plaugued with bugs, balance issues, a broken economy, and stale gameplay. Thus it was recieved very poorly by critics and fans alike. ESO today, however, is very different from ESO then. Zenimax Online Studios, a virgin game devoloper, realized the error of their ways quickly and worked tirelessly to make their project a success. I can say with confidence that ZOS was largely successful in improving their game.
Zenimax was criticized for it's monetization strategy for the game and rightly so. ESO sold for $60 with an additional $15 monthly subscription fee that was required to play the game. Additionally, many parts of Tamriel were locked behind a paywall. This made ESO, a mediocre game at best, very expensive to play. After a while, ZOS realized that their monetization strategy needed to be improved upon. Thus ESO Tamriel Unlimited was born. This change did away with the manditory subscription fee and many of the pay walls, opting for a more "freemium" style of monetization. Though the cost of the various DLC's and other content can still be quite high, none of it is mandatory.
As far as gamplay issues, ESO has made even bigger strides. The game is still subject to the occasional crash or bug, but few are really game breaking. And many of the actual gameplay mechanics are much improved. Combat feels heavier and less "floaty," leveling feels more impactful and is much more natural. Looting dungeons no longer feels pointless and the PVP is better than ever.
ESO has done something no other game has ever done. It has managed to pull itself back from the brink of irrelevence and is now one of the most popular MMORPG's today. It still remains to be seen if ESO will become really successful - as successful as Zenimax had hoped. The player base is steadily increasing and for good reason. In 2017, I can say with confidence that ESO is worth your money.

Rome II has - in general recieved a lot of negative reviews.  But I find it a refreshing game.   It's a step away from the old style of gameplay, which was good as well, and a step in the direction I think Total War should be going towards in the future.  It provides far greater immersion thanks to it's integrated battles, it allows larger armies to take to the field, and it gives you a real sense of the destruction and chaos that held sway in Roman times.
If there's one thing I would like to see make a come-back, it would be the generals' speeches.  They set the tone for the coming battle, and gave you a vigour and purpose in fighting the battle, made you believe that the men could win, even if the odds were stacked against them.
If I could suggest something to change to the general's speeches, it would be a greater integration depending on the General's personality.  A high dread general would tend to deliver speeches that spoke more of what would happen to the soldiers' families if they failed, about how the enemy is weak and to show no mercy... that kind of stuff.  Whilst a general tending towards the paragon side, would deliver speecher geared more on building up his soldiers' moral.  He might talk about how he trusts them,how they are the best in the world, how their families are waiting for them back at home, stuff like that.
It is never a bad idea to improve the campaign AI, but I hardly found it as lacking as most described it, and the latest patches have cleared up most of the kinks still in there.
All-in-all I found Rome II to be a worthy edition to the Total War saga, a game that's immersive and comprehensive.  It has enough detail to make you think, but isn't so complex that you feel overwhelmed, as one sometimes does with games like Civilization.  It's blending of TBS campaign play, and RTS battles, is unique and still ground-breaking, even today.  Total War is a franchise that I admire and the only one that I follow fervently.  The designers, coders, artists etc. that worked on the franchise through the years have my greatest respect and my humblest support.
I can't wait to see where the franchise will go next, but what ever they decide to do, I know it'll be a game worth playing, and an even greater edition to the Total War series.
The Total War franchise is known for it's historical quotes, and so, pray forgive me for ending my review with one of my own favourite quotes.
"Leaders think and talk about the solutions.  Followers think and talk about the porblems." ~ Brian Tracy

DISCLAIMER -This is targeted at players who have played the first game. No spoilers ahead.
FROM Software does it again and this time sends us to the uncaring, cold and unforgiving kingdom of Drangleic. Tasked with ending the curse of undeath which is plaguing our character, we end up fighting our way through forests, crypts, dark caves and many more locations while an assortment of beasts, demons and undead hollows try to bring us to a premature end.
The game boasts improved graphics and an array of new, prettier animations, complimented by much easier to navigate menus and a more clear and focused UI.
The world is divided in several locations, some of which can only be visited after others have been cleared; although physically connected, most zones, given the fact that the player can teleport between discovered bonfires from the beginning of the game, feel like pocket worlds and don't bring the feeling of visiting a vast, cohesive map like Dark Souls did.

The combat system has been tweaked, eliminating the prevalence of backstab-your-way-to-victory kind of style rampant in the previous installment and introducing dual wielding as an alternative to the old ways of sword and board and spellcasting.  Magic has seen changes in regards of making dark sorceries a standalone class of spells aptly named Hexes and splitting them in being cast by staves or by sacred chimes only. Sorceries, miracles and pyromancies do return in great style with a vast assortment of new spells for each class of magic.
Leveling up is not an option at every bonfire anymore and is only done by talking to a specific NPC in the initial village and central hub of the game. The character attributes are more or less the same as in Dark Souls with a notable exception of Endurance not boosting Equipment load anymore, the latter being governed by a new attribute named Vitality. Also Equipment load has been reworked and now it isn't split in fast, medium and slow roll; being under 70% grants the normal roll and everything above the slow roll. Poise has been toned down and is not as deciding in fights anymore.
Another new mechanic is seen in the form of an assortment of new consumables which restore life and are used in conjunction with the old estus flask.
Enemies in every zone have a number of respawns, usually between 10-12, after which they disapper until new game + or until the players uses a new item called Bonfire Ascetic which resets the zone and respanws every enemy, including bosses, making them stronger.
Covenants are still present, some of them dedicated to PvE and other to PvP. The latter has been revamped and now player are matched based on their Soul Memory which represents the total amount of souls acquired up to that point, even counting souls not spent and souls that have been lost upon double death. Players can invade, participate in duels or assist other players in taking down bosses or killing invaders.
All been said, I do recommend this game to everyone who has enjoyed Dark Souls; while it's inferior to its predecessor regarding some aspects, Dark Souls 2 offers a great experience that no Souls fan should pass.

If you’re a Lucasarts adventure game fan, this game is a must-buy. If you are into 80s pop culture in general, this game is a must-buy. For everyone else, if you’re looking for a humourous trip back to 1987 along with a mystery to solve, I don’t think Thimbleweed Park will disappoint; as Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick put it on their Kickstarter page: “It’s like opening a dusty old drawer and finding an undiscovered Lucasarts adventure game you’ve never played before.” That’s Thimbleweed Park in a nutshell.
The world needs more of this. Too many decades playing murder simulators have left humanity dumb.

Thimbleweed park is an excellent old school graphic adventure by Ron Gilbert, who back in the day helped create some of Lucasarts most memorable adventures including Monkey Island and Maniac Mansion.
As you can tell by the screenshots the game goes for a very retro feel graphically. The scenes and animations are quite well done and are full of life and detail. So long as you dig the kind of retro aesthetic the game is going for, it's a title that really nails what it's aiming at and I enjoyed it a lot.
The sound is a little up and down, music and sound effects are great, but some of the voice work is a little dodgy. I should be clear, there is nothing game breaking here, just some of the characters sound off. For the most part the cast is well voiced though.
As to the gameplay, it's classic old school fare, requiring you to examine things carefully and talk to all the characters to get clues. Most problems are of the use item on item variety and for the vast majority of them, they are very logical. Some of the old school games required great leaps in logic (Or a total absense of logic), Thimbleweed park is a game where in nearly every case, the solution makes sense. There are two difficulty modes, hard for those who prefer more challenging puzzles, and casual for those who would rather just persue the story.
I'm not going to say too much about the story actually, as it's best experienced. It begins with a murder and two FBI agents investigating it. Both characters are playable and as the game goes on, 3 more will be added to the roster. Having 5 different characters makes for some interesting puzzles and you will need your team to work together to finish some of them. If you ever get stuck there is always something to be doing with another character, and its possible that furthering another characters path could open up the solution that was stumping you. Overall I found the story to be quite engaging and it gets deeper as the game unfolds.
My only minor complaints for this one are some patchy voice acting and the inability to skip dialogue you have already heard.
A really solid adventure. 8/10

This is my first review so go easy on me.
Borderlands 2 is a pinnacle of co-op and story and I will explain both. Borderlands 2 utilizes an amazing art style which continues to blow me away.
The co-op in Borderlands 2 is phenomenal. I love playing with friends and nowadays there aren't so many co-op games. Borderlands 2 provides a solution with it's high replayability. The dlc in this gameadds another 20 hours at least and provides a fun new experience in co-op and some light hearted story. The reason I am so critical on co-op is because when I was young, my dad bought Halo Reach for the both of us to play. That was my first truly co-op game and I have loved playing co-op ever since. The problem is, with games like Halo Reach, once you complete it, you already know what happens and there is a small level of replayability. Borderlands 2 solves this problem more than completely and has deep gameplay.
The story in Borderlands 2 is really fun and and exciting at every turn. The one problem is that the story is very predictable and at some points easy. Although the predictability is high, there are still a couple heart wrenching and even "cry your eyeballs out" moments, especially if you have played Borderlands. Altogether, the story is a beautiful symphony of booms, crudeness and overall funnyness!
I would reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys some great gameplay, story, and co-op who would also like to be sincerely touched by the detail and characters.
Thank you Gearbox for creating an amazing and fun driven game!

Gameplay:

I have been a long-time fan of all the Aveyond games--they've followed me through childhood--and playing Aveyond 4 as an adult has been a great way to come back to the series. Each of the games is their own experience, and while in certain narrative ways Aveyond 4 feels like a regression, as far as gameplay goes, the series has grown in some fantastic ways. Though I feel as though the protagonist was the wrong choice for this game, the game maps are extensive and rewarding, and the arc of the game is smooth and fulfilling. The way the game plays is excellent, and the narrative aspect mostly provides context for how to view it, so although I was largely disappointed in the story of the game, I loved Aveyond 4 as a whole.
Overall, I had a great experience and would wholly recommend it. That said, this review is largely narrative critique.
THE NARRATIVE:
Narratively, Boyle felt like the wrong choice for the protagonist. He is not engaging as a main character--the humor regarding 'retired villains' and 'heroes' fell flat, and it felt reductive. The best part about him was his relationship with his dog, but that dedication is not enough to make a protagonist. An attempt at humor regarding evildoing in a comical tone is not enough to make a protagonist, either. While the backstory about how he found his dog as a pup was touching, it does not offer strong enough motive for him to be the main character of this story. He is mostly a static character. While he does admit that doing good is pretty good, it is dulled by the joke of it all, and the retired supervillain aspect diminishes the entire relationship of good and evil. Basically, it seems as though he was truly good all along, and the only amount of growth is in his awareness of this, and it is not enough to drive an entire game. His personal stake in this journey is not, narratively, the strongest one.
Boyle is looking for his dog; Myst is looking for her brother. In order to find his dog, Boyle must find Myst's brother, who was snatched by a demon. Even the game's title, "Shadow Of The Mist", suggests that Myst is the one with more to lose, here. Boyle plays the reluctant hero, but it is irritating to have what feels so much like Myst's story filtered through this flat, reductive joke of a retired supervillain. Myst has never been away from the mountain, and while she also needs to find her little brother, she longs to see the sights outside of The Mist. She has so much to learn, so far to go. She has the most reason to go on this journey to defeat the demon and save her brother, and she has the farthest to grow. She is the most dynamic character, at a tipping point of her life.
If Myst were the main character, the framing of this game would've been much more powerful--and it would've offered a kind of serious beauty to it, too. In that way, it would mirror Aveyond 2, which was personally an extremely successful, gorgeous game with a very gentle, fairy-tale like story. This still would've been light-hearted in (many ways, and a grand heartfelt adventure, but it would've also had the background context of a fairy-tale. This game could've so easily been absolutely incredible, beautiful, had Myst been the protagonist. She has every reason to be. Also, her background as a Myst Wraith is so much more compelling than the dull, simplifying joke of the Retired Supervillain.
THE GAMEPLAY:
The maps are beautiful. They are detailed, extensive, and so very rewarding. The chests are set up so that they can be seen when strolling on the most obvious paths, and while it does take some challenge to look for them, it is not to the point of frustration. Taking the effort to go the long way around for a chest that was seen ten minutes earlier is always worth the effort. The color schemes of the maps are brilliant, well-thought, and the layouts of all the buildings are varied, textured, not tired and reused. Each part of the journey has its own distinctive map which feels like its own little area within a larger world, which helps create a better idea of this lush, full world of Aveyond. The only complaint here is that some of the maps are so ambitious that they lag on soe systems. I also loved how purposeful all the sidequests were; everything was important.
The battle system is set up in a spin of the traditional turn-based system. It makes battles so much less tedious. Each character has a different role in battle, with their own pros and cons, and it is very fun to think about how best to use each character. Myst has a few different abilities, including a healing and shapeshifting one, and using these abilities does not require a cost of mana or skill point, although it does mean that these abilities aren't as powerful as ones that would have a cost. Boyle's darkness points are replenished with physical attacks, and he uses these same points to cast magic, and it is very fun to have a wizard type who is also a formidable physical attacker--in addition to his minion, whose attacks add additional damage at every turn. Those are only two of the characters, but all of them have roles that aren't so simple as deducting a mana / skill point cost. The character battle roles are fun, and the battles demand a measure of attention that makes it so they aren't a matter of grinding through the same predictable battle rhythm again and again. It's more fluid than that.
The only thing I would say is that there are many characters who get introduced too late in the game to really develop an affection for them, or a feel for their role in battle, so they don't get the opportunity to shine. It's more difficult to care about them, when there is so little time to get familiar with them.
LASTLY:
In a lot of ways, I do not think Aveyond is the right arena to even attempt deconstructing Heroes or Villains--that seems more the space of cape comics and games inspired by those. It felt odd and uncomfortable to reference that type of Hero vs. Villain relationship in a largely original, fantastical world such as Aveyond. Also uncomfortable in the game was the way sprites from popular anime series appeared in prominent side quest characters, as if, no one would notice Hetalia sprites or Chi from Chobits acting in ways that seemed to serve no purpose, no reference, to their original series at all. It was not right to include representations of those licensed designs in this original game being sold for its own profit. Original sprites should have been made by the Aveyond team. Both of these aspects broke immersion of Aveyond as the world of Aveyond, an original fantasy world with, largely, its own mythos which does at times reference outside ones, like Aveyond 2 and the Snow Queen, and moments like referencing the Fruit of the (Greek) Gods (a pomegranate) in Aveyond 1.
In terms of media representation, the Aveyond series made such an impact on me as a kid realizing that girls and women were powerful, complex characters, and to see them in positions of power, as heroes unqualified by the acts of men, it was incredible. And honestly, if I wanted to play a game about a man, I'd look literally anywhere else. That was one of the first reasons why Boyle failed as a protagonist for me. He has nothing to add to the conversation. He is not refreshing in any way. There are countless characters like him, and there are so few respectful representations of women in games, especially Fantasy ones known for their trope of women as reward for the (male) hero's triumphs, damsels in distress, or as vile and petty temptations of evil.
All this said: I loved this game. It may be because I played it most recently, but it was my favorite game to play. But, narratively, it doesn't compare with Aveyond 1 or Aveyond 2 and the way those games stayed in my heart. I still had a blast, though, and am looking forward to replaying it

I started with System Shock 1 and I going to systematically play through the entire genre that it inspired in order. So here we are with System Shock 2 (with Dues Ex being next game in-line).
System Shock 2 is a fantastic game that builds on what SS1 did. It refines many of the clunkier elements of SS1 for example picking up items and the inventory system.
This game sees the introduction of the PSI system. With the use of an implant you can you can use many different PSI abilties. Much like we would again see in the Bio Shock series. My only complaint here is they are not utilized very well here. For example in Bio Shock, especially starting with BS2 they worked in tandem with your weapons. Power in one hand, gun in the other, and they would compliment each other. In SS2 you almost have to choose either a 'weapons build' or a 'psi build'. You can mix and match, but its not something first time players are going to be able to do very well without knowing exactly what they want to spend their limited upgrade points on. If you know from the very start you absolutely are not going to be touching heavy and exotic weapons, then you could have integrate some PSI abilities into you build. But for first time players, when you see 'exotic' and 'heavy' weapons skills, how can you not want to find out what those even are. That is my biggest gripe with this game: PSI abilties were not implemented as well as we see in the Bioshock games. Which in many ways is why Deus Ex is my favorite out of all these games. Its 100% tech. No silly "bug swarm" powers.
The mod support for this game is nice. Lots of easy to follow guides. This is maybe my 4th attempt to used mods in my entire life and I found the procedures easy and painless. They have graphical upgrades for nearly everything in this game. Even without them, this game is still fantastic. Its atmospheric and moody. More of a horror fps/rpg (much like SS1).
I can highly recommend this classic game.

Still a classic after all these years.  A complex and wide-ranging RP experience with enough choices to make it worth playing through again and again.  (I've just played through 3 times in a row, once as each class.)  For those who haven't played it, it's sort of a combination of survival horror (you have to use your ammo carefully, especially early in the game) and RPG.
I love the way the plot strings you along, often throwing a curve ball at you just when you think you've reached the goal.
Also enjoyed the semi-open-world design.  While there's a clear sequence of 'chapters' to follow, on each play-through I had many instances where I had to decide what to do next.  Do I go on to the next goal I've been given, do I go back to the chemical store room to finish researching this item, or do I head back to that locked room now that I have a code?
I like the fact that in a recent interview about his joining the group making System Shock 3, Warren Spector said the first thing he was going to do was play through SS1 & SS2.  I hope that helps them recapture the feel of these games.  There's something this series had that just seems to be lacking in modern games, though I can't quite put my finger on it.
P.S. When you finish the official story, check out the fan-made missions
.  I had no idea these existed till I decided to investigate the option that comes up when you start the game.  Having just finished the Ponterbee scenario, I have to say I'm very impressed.

First of all let me be clear on something. Yes, Dishonored 2 had a rocky launch for the first two weeks, but with all the recent patches, Arkane has finally smoothed the game out, at least for me.
My system is an intel i5 and gtx 970; completely capable at running this game with a solid 60fps at High-Medium (shadows on med).
Anyways, with that all aside lets talk about how the game play is.
You play as either Emily or Corvo, you choose either character, and he or she sticks with you until the end of the game.
Dishonored 2 is all about finding a play style that fits you; stealthy, low or high chaos, all out combat low or high chaos. You can mix it up from time to time, or go full on stealth and pacifist for the achievements.
If you love STEALTH games this is for you, if you've played games like Thief before, this is also for you (Voice actor who plays Garrett voices Corvo), but does not utilize a shadow mechanic in the previous Thief games, it just plays very similar to Thief.
Also in Dishonored 2 you get the option of having powers, powers where they aid in your game-play and bring a lot of options and combinations to your play style.

All in all, this game is worth getting, around maybe 30-40 hours of play time if you don't literally rush things like a maniac and enjoy your time exploring the game and what not.

The narrative of the story is intersting.
THE BAD: While I understand that English is not the develper's first language, the fact remains that the writing in this game is horrible. There are a lot of grammatical errors, but those do not  bother me as much. The problem is that most of the sentences feel like a 3rd grader wrote them. I really think that the overall narrative of the story is interesting, to the point where if we could get the game re-written by a native English speaker, this game would become a classic.
SLIGHT SPOILERS: Most people are apparently frusturated with there being no happy ending in this game, but that did not bother me. Unfortunately though, we live in a Disney era where everyone wants the conflict to be resolved in a happy go lucky prince-charming-and-the-princess-get-married way. If you can get past that, there are some potentially (with better writing) deep characters in this game.
CONCLUSION: If you have 4 hours and enjoy eastern-style rpgs, give this game a go.

Improves on the original and some good fun.
To put it bluntly from the get go - If you did not like the first game, then chances are you will probably not like this one.
However, if you did enjoy the first game then I'm sure you will also enjoy this one too.
From a story point of view the game is good, not great, but good. And doesn't break any new ground for the genre when it comes to story telling. But having said that, the execution of mind altering effects and warped realities is fantastic. There were times that I just stood and looked at the messed up world Tango Gameworks had created because it was probably the best videogame representation of these things that I've seen.
The game isn't a standard horror game either. It's more akin to Resident Evil 4 - Horror elements, gruesome and creepy enemies, combined with some good action, tense moments, puzzles and even stealth combat which is quite strong if you choose to play that style.
The Evil Within 2 gives you the freedom to choose how you want to approach a situation which is always a nice thing. But unless you play on the easiest difficulty then ammo will be an issue if you choose to shoot everything in front of you. So it's not completely abandoning its survival horror roots. And while the game is much more open world than the first one, it doesn't feel like it detracts from the game itself. Because of the setting of the story in this sequel, having a semi-open world actually makes sense.
Gameplay is good, guns can be a bit derpy to aim at times. And patience is recommended before taking a shot if you don't have aim assist because of the way the enemies twitch and move. The movement and interaction with the world is pretty smooth and trouble free except for the few bugs I mention below. Otherwise it responds and behaves more or less as you would expect from a 3rd person game.
But the technical execution does leave a bit to be desired sadly. The game on PC at least, suffers from random frame drops at times (GTX 1080) And I encountered about half a dozen bugs or glitches - most were insignificant and only served to ruin the immersion of the game. But unfortunately I did enounter one or two bugs that forced me to quit the game because I was stuck in a chair.
Most of the bugs revolve around clipping issues, pathing issues, hit boxes, and some really horrible textures (not bugs I know but worth mentioning) Now I'm no graphics snob, but there were a few occasions where I was looking at a brick wall from 10 feet away for example, and it was so ugly and distorted that you'd think I was right up against it.
The actual clipping and pathing issues were semi-frequent but ultimately these didnt stop me enjoying the game, they just took away from the experience as they are so noticeable when they happen - which is a dam shame because otherwise the game looks and runs really nice.
My first play-through clocked in at about 20 hours, and that was me completing all of the optional content and collecting most of the collectables.
I would recommend this game, but perhaps wait for it to be maybe 1/3 of the release price or on special first. As it could have honestly done with another month or two of polish and isn't quite worth a full "AAA game" price tag.

Don't believe the metascore. From software very cleverly hid all of the problems in the game in the later parts so as to avoid them being reviewed (as reviews are usually based on a few hours of play).
Firstly: They literally false advertised the matchmaking features of the game, "Soul memory will match players based on a lot of complex factors including character level, areas visited, and gear being used." This is a blataint lie, the soul memory system merely counts the total number of souls you have obtained in the game and places players into extremely wide brackets based on this total. They completely ignore character level, gear, and everything else they stated but very cleverly made it so the lower brackets (the ones you spend the first 10-20 hours in) are so narrow you can't be matched with a player massively overleveld on you. after you break through the roughly 30 hour barrier tho you are guaranteed to be paired with players who massively outlevel you (200-300 levels higher than you if you are lucky.)
Secondly: The netcode is atrocious in this game. google "dark souls 2 phantom hits" and have your self a laugh. Certain weapons are particularly poorly coded. Players like to say "if you swing a katana in new york, you'll hit everyone in california".

There are a lot of other issues having to do with balance but those are minor gripes and could easily be overlooked if the core of the game was even half as solid as it's predecessor.

Disclosure: I purchased this game when it originally came out, and received a free Steam key when it was released on Steam.

THIS MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS!!!
For my review, I'd give it 4/5 (but totally recommend it!). Mainly because I kinda didn't like the art. It really could have been better.
The music on the other hand was (and I quote Sid!) grandiose! Music (for me) is the most important thing in a video game lacking voice over. aveyond 4 blew my mind with its music. My favorite tracks were the ones playing in Ulrock, Delamere and Halaina.
The story was really fun; I enjoyed every bit of it. And I loved how every party member had their own little endings and the consequences of the sidequest we played too!
My favorites were Myst and Hi'beru. Really loved it when Myst angered Boyle. And how Hi'beru always came to rescue when dreams were involved.. and that ending with the gladiator? Priceless!!!
I had Ingrid paired with Phye in my game just because I didn't like her with Boyle. Call me silly, but I think he and Myst have much more chemistry :P
Besides, Ingrid deserves a strong man and Phye was prefect.
Hinting that Boyle has some connections with the Pendragons was interested. I'd love to see this idea being expand on in the future. It really sets the bases for a new game *wink wink*

Regarding the curse; my theory is that Boyle did break it. Remember that moment when he was like "Fang is my true love"? this is a type of unconditional love. Because as far as I know, love extends beyond romance type. So, I think Ingrid knows that too but didn't tell Boyle else her plan will fail. Anyone else thinking the same thing?

A side note; mentioning the suggested subtitles for the game which was posted originally on Facebook dring the ending scene actually made me scream because I was one of the peeps who suggested a subtitle for Aveyond and my submission was considered (albeit for a book about Boyle but anyway)! It made me really, really,really,really,REALLY HAPPY to see it in-game. Thanks so much Aveyond Dev team!

Oh and since I also got the strategy guide, I'd like to point out that it's not as helpful as I expected. I found myself surfing the forums more than reading the guide.
For example, it only mentioned that Myst can get a bear amulet but doesn't mention how to get it and from where. Also that part about Rowen's sword singing skill was not written. I accidentally stumbled upon a topic on the forum discussing it.
However, it came handy when I was looking for the goodie caves before solving Sid's puzzle.
Finally; I'd like to metin that I got this game when it was first released in December from aveyond Kingdom sit, and as soon as the game was released on Steam,  I got a free Steam key, so, I would like to thank Amanda and the team for this. Thimbleweed park is an excellent old school graphic adventure by Ron Gilbert, who back in the day helped create some of Lucasarts most memorable adventures including Monkey Island and Maniac Mansion.
As you can tell by the screenshots the game goes for a very retro feel graphically. The scenes and animations are quite well done and are full of life and detail. So long as you dig the kind of retro aesthetic the game is going for, it's a title that really nails what it's aiming at and I enjoyed it a lot.
The sound is a little up and down, music and sound effects are great, but some of the voice work is a little dodgy. I should be clear, there is nothing game breaking here, just some of the characters sound off. For the most part the cast is well voiced though.
As to the gameplay, it's classic old school fare, requiring you to examine things carefully and talk to all the characters to get clues. Most problems are of the use item on item variety and for the vast majority of them, they are very logical. Some of the old school games required great leaps in logic (Or a total absense of logic), Thimbleweed park is a game where in nearly every case, the solution makes sense. There are two difficulty modes, hard for those who prefer more challenging puzzles, and casual for those who would rather just persue the story.
I'm not going to say too much about the story actually, as it's best experienced. It begins with a murder and two FBI agents investigating it. Both characters are playable and as the game goes on, 3 more will be added to the roster. Having 5 different characters makes for some interesting puzzles and you will need your team to work together to finish some of them. If you ever get stuck there is always something to be doing with another character, and its possible that furthering another characters path could open up the solution that was stumping you. Overall I found the story to be quite engaging and it gets deeper as the game unfolds.
My only minor complaints for this one are some patchy voice acting and the inability to skip dialogue you have already heard.
A really solid adventure. 8/10

What a wonderful and charming game! Thimbleweed Park kept me engaged from start to finish, with colourful characters, well-crafted puzzles, and a meaty mystery to get invested in. It's a classic adventure game where you play as multiple characters that initially set out to solve a murder, but as the story progresses the focus shifts much more onto the main characters and their (sometimes!) dark histories.
The art and sound are top notch, and in classic adventure game fashion reward you with beautiful new locations whenever you solve a new puzzle. Steve Kirk's soundtrack also adds a subtle level of atmosphere to the whole experience, invoking old television series themes and weaving them with tunes that feel right out of the LucasArts (Mmucusphlegm?) games of yore.
The puzzles themselves are very well designed and generally logical. I got stuck a couple of times, but there is so much content that it was never boring to revisit previous locations looking for missed items or dialogue choices. It never took long to find a clue to help point me in the right direction, and each character having a journal always gave me a sense of what I was trying to accomplish.
Don't let the retro style and pixel art fool you! There are a lot of refinements to the general adventure game formula, with fast travel, dialogue and cutscene skipping, quest logs (in a sense), and other clever little quality of life improvements that make the whole experience smoother. The game is designed in such a way as to avoid the old adventure game trap of getting stuck on a single puzzle. With a multitude of player characters each with their own goals, if you ever get stuck you can just switch to another character and start trying to solve a different set of puzzles. You can also tackle many puzzles in whatever order you choose, and as a result there were very few of the bottlenecks that have so often made me turn off the game in the past.
This game is a MUST for adventure game fans, and will delight and amuse you with all the nods and winks to the mighty and venerable genre we know and love. It's also a great game to sit and play through with friends, since the story hooks you in and keeps you guessing right to the incredibly satisifying end. Some of the references might go over the heads of the uninitiated, but that just made the game feel that much more special to me. So go and get a copy of Thimbleweed Park right away, you won't regret it!

Just like I wouldn't normally pick up specks of dust whenever I see them. But that's the thing about this game; you have to do things you wouldn't normally think to do.
Overall, this game is creative, has a wonderful storyline, and requires some out of the box thinking. Half Life was one of my childhood defining games (which is probably a terrible thing, but I digress). I thought, that even with a remake, I would always prefer the original. For example, Pokemon Red/Blue could never truely be replaced by Pokemon FireRed/LeafGreen. The graphics were improved but the feel was just different.
Black Mesa is better.
It captures the EXACT mood and feeling the originals evoked while improving and giving character to the small nooks and crannies that the average player probably wouldn't even think would need touching up. Additionally, I actually really appreciate the game being made in the original Source engine as it, as well as including characters like Kleiner and Eli, really helps glue HL1 and HL2 together, something which I always thought was a bit of a problem storywise. It'd also be awkward to have the first game look better than the second (ala the Star Wars prequels).
The tedium and confusion of some of the original levels has been straightened out and just overall, Black Mesa IS Half Life just better, plain and simple.
Can't wait for the Xen levels! Xen was a complete mess (imho) in the original, especially against the Nihilanth. Really hoping for some fantastic overhauling and a wonferful finish that does Half Life justice.
(P.S. Half Life 3 confirmed.)

System Shock 2 is a mix of FPS, RPG and even survival horror, Irrational Games's sequel to the the Looking Glass's classic using their Dark Engine, released in 1999. You probably know this game as "that some random game that every classic gamer is required to be bonkers about". It also was supposed to come out for Sega Dreamcast but didn't. Shame.
Then in 2013 this game got rereleased digitally thanks to Night Dive studios. Who are quire a heroes, managing to bring this IP out of legal hell, as it was owned by three companies. With some insurance company being one. Now they own it and thus were able to re-release System Shock games so we can all buy it legally and digitally. They also updated the game to work on modern system.
Technically, this game should work pretty nicely on modern systems. It supports widescreen too.
However I had a strange glitch where cutscene movies will not play if I had Firefox Internet browser running. No idea what was conflicting there. But I guess it's just your everyday PC Oh-So-Master Race thing. HA!
This game also includes coop multiplayer. Not sure about multiplayer community, after all it doesn't use server browser, you have to connect directly to IP. So don't expect to just play with random, gotta nag friends up.
And from what I heard multiplayer is there because EA, the original publisher, demanded it. It really is single-player experience. So I guess it's something just-for-funz, not designed for. I just know that they would put game on Hard difficulty. But I didn't yet play it.
Plotwise the game is a direct continuation of the first System Shock, a cyberpunk setting. Or sci-fi. SHODAN's returns once again, as spoiled by cover art. But there is a new horror you must defeat as well on Von Braun ship, the first ever Faster Than Light ship with unknown side effects, accomplished by the Rivenbark ship for security. Or rather, because PsiOptimum and UNN don't trust each other.
Game itself is often called a father of Bioshock games, as well as infulencing other FPS games. There are similar things to it indeed. There is a wrench, there is magical PSI powers, there are logs to learn stories and codes.
You will explore the ship, trying to survive and often backtracking. Ammo is rare and you often will have to use wrench. While also having RPG system that will decide what you can do and what you currently can't equip.
And when compared to System Shock 1 it pretty much adds two things heavily: RPG elements and Survival Horror.
Yet I can't help but to feel dissapointment in this mix of FPS and RPG. Probably because I loved the first one more. The first game was about world immersion, it was about combining all the elements into one belivable game. It had RPG elements, but cleverly implented. You was growing in power, but you did it not with some stats management but by finding new weapons and new hardware, which gave you new powers that you also had to use wisely.
It also gave you full feeling that it was YOU who was taking on SHODAN. No pointers, no objective clearly written, you had to figure it all out by yourself from logs.
The sequel hovewer decided to add much more videogamey RPG elements to it, that it pretty much screws the original ideology of System Shock. The stats building ones, yep. And yea, it's one of those cases where the abstraction of RPG elements doesn't fit perfectly with FPS immersion. Like, for example, you need to have at least 3 points in "standard" weapons category to equip shotgun. Like, we aren't talking about shooting horribly, it's about not knowing how to pull the trigger, it seems.
It also isn't well balanced either. There are options that are much more efficient than others. And some options are so unefficient in how much precious points they require, it's hard for me to say that this game is designed for variety of playstyle. More like for punishing for not knowing what's ahead. It's a linear game after all, with 10+ hours requirement, so it's not sliding. Like, here high investments into hacking, mantaintance and standart weapons are requirements, but no one will tell you so.
Ok, I just did. Welp, at least was lucky that my build was using those so I didn't screw myself.
That, and it feels a bit more dumbened down as well. Ok, more specific, in the name of RPGness, the hacking mini-games were changed from the proper puzzles into just stat-checking RNG thing. And lots of PSI magic weren't so useful.
SHODAN also felt less signifant here, strange that she gained any reputation of character and made every second person on retro forum have her as avatar because of this sequel. That, and I felt much less like I was the one who was moving on storyline, instead being felt like an errand boy. With all objectives clearly being told to you in PDA notes, along with all codes that you have ever saw, so there is only a single time you have to kinda remember and analyse it yourself ("art" part).
I mean, it's not exactly what I would usually complain much. I don't hate what people call "casualized" fun. Like it, even. But we are talking about sequel to System Shock 1. And not just sequel, but the one which is called hardcore old classic and has 96 metacritic score and just gets praised as best game ever. And I came in with my body and mind ready for such thing. But oh well.
Not to say that this sequel is a lost cause. After all it adds more of survival horror to it and some of it is awesome! Thanks to technology of 1999 too. It feels even less abstract and more like real ship. And with such technology, it can show horror much more effective. Mind it, there are no jumpscares. Just twisted, trippy things going on, especially as the end comes closer. It really is quite experience. With nice ambient music occasionally. And action ones too.
Heck, it even makes you often feel unsafe. There is nothing like being busy reading a newly acquired log only to notice a mutant walking into the room where you are hiding.
I also liked the fact that it was taking itself more like survival horror gameplay-wise too, where your ammo and recources are scarse. And everything costs nanities (money thing) now. Well, they kept respawning chamber thing which may not fit with survival, but at least it costs nanities too, even if very very cheap.
It even makes ammo scarse and all guns are easily breakable. Which sounds like survival horror thing. Almost. Because they didn't manage to balance it right, as early in game guns break so much that they are more scarse than ammo. And later in game the whole survival horror feels to go away and instead replaced by just hard corridor shooter. And hard corridor shooter isn't same as hard survival horror.
Not to mention that while other Survival Horror have "shoot or run" thing, this one has "WRENCH THEM ALL and sometimes shoot". No, seriously, melee there is pretty much for everything aside from worms because they are too tiny. Annoying thing. System Shock 1 also had you using melee a lot, but that was because it was very effective and thus mixing of melee/ranged was fun. In SS2, I dunno, it just isn't. You use unfun melee because game doesn't want you to have fun.
Okay, I actually had a fun. And as said, I got lucky with my build. Just a shame that in beggining it will not be much fun for most with those gun breakage while at end it deflates. Then again, later levels, after Von Braun ship, are quite generic and mediocre, really.
Also, research mechanic was interesting. Real-time slow process which also requires visiting chemistry rooms for some chemistry, as there are too many to carry.
But you know, it's quite a goody adventure otherwise. Albeit not the best game ever, sure thing it's not. Quite overrated. But hey, that happens sometimes. Hopefully System Shock 3 will be more in line of what System Shock 1 was standing for.
That, and I want to take one of those maintaince bots to my house. Too cute.

A wonderful, challenging game. Continues the same flavor of gameplay as the rest of the Souls series, with a few new alterations. If you have played and enjoyed Demons' Souls or Dark souls before it, you should enjoy the game just fine. If you didn't like them, well, this game wont likely change that.
The gameplay is just solid and works great for the often slower pace the game encourages. The tone of the game is one of exploration and also apprehension, and the gameplay still stresses that perfectly. If you try to rush ahead, charge into the fray or just underestimate your foes, you WILL die. If you accept the slower pace though, understand the game wants you to learn through trial and error and can accept the deaths you take as steps in that journey, you will be alright.
For those familiar with the series, here's a quick rundown of some changes.
The Good.
Game mechanics. In a number of ways, things have been improved game mechanic wise as well. Dodging and rolling is tied in part to a stat, in part to equipment and is a little more natural in scaling instead of just equipment load tiers. While the equip load tiers still exist, there is more variation between higher and lower end of them. Backstabs and parries have been made much harder to pull off as well, helping people rely more on the mastery of them then circle straff and spam.
Upgrading. While many may dislike the infusion system, the separation of item quality (the +10) from elemental property makes it a lot easier to make the weapon you seek and even keep a weapon you were fond of while still upgrading it without worry of branching convoluted crafting paths.
The Bad.
Soul memory. Every soul you pick up adds to this and based on what your memory is, determines who you run across in multiplayer matches. Initially meant as a way to prevent people from twinking out and killing new players, it instead seems to do little to stop this, but while also punishing those who are still learning by forcing them into higher groups because they gained the memory when they picked up souls but not the benefit of those souls if they died or lost them.
Poise. Quite simply, it is broken. Poise being the stat determines how much you can take a beating before you get stunned, it would seem very important, especially in pvp where stun-locking is abused. Unfortunately, even with the highest poise possible in game, it seems to matter little and stunlocking is rediculously easy. Something about it just seems broken, and as a result when it comes to pvp, player tactics have shifted to take advantage of it.
Covenants. If you played the first game, you know covenants are fun, but in Souls 2, they forgot that part. The invasion mechanic has been nerfed to near worthlessness outside of select areas, and with it several covenants built around making use of invasions. The two blue covenants and the blood one are vastly underused in this aspect. Beyond this, there are still the co op covenants and the dueling ones, which function the same as always. One new, good addition is a reverse invasion covenant through trap filled areas where the pulled spirit has to make it through to win.
Artifical Difficulty. There are a few places in the game, and a few bosses that feel less like a Soul's game and more like the developers wanted you to die just because. Rarely would I use the term "cheap" in the first Dark Souls game, as all deaths were avoidable for the most part even on first playthrough if you paid attention. Not so here. From invisible enemies you have no way to know exist til you are backstabed to death, to a boss fight that requires you know in advance to burn a windmill with a torch, a mechanic never before and never again used, to a boss that will 1-shot you every time (unless you knew beforehand to have the right gear ready), defeating the idea of learning a little at a time from playing before deaths. There are a couple places that would feel right at home in an arcade meant to mill you for quarters here, and while certainly possible to beat, feel far more cheap then usual for a Soul's game, one that usually regardless how often you die, never makes you feel it was anything beside your own fault.

With this much of an improvement, I don't think Black Mesa is left far apart from the modern games that most gamers play nowadays thus making Half Life an unforgetful FPS experience.
The gameplay is very clean, I haven't found even a single bug or problem during my playthrough from the first chapter until the last one (excluding Xen, which isn't released yet). Unlike ubisoft's failed remaster of Assasin Creed 2, this one is a lot different than that, majorly improved yet with bugs free and smooth gameplay.
The surround sounds are really great (better than csgo I'd say), the voices quality has improved, the soundtracks are better, so I'd say I have no objection to the sounds remaster of this game, congrats developer for achieving this up.

I like the game. It is the 4th in a series set in the same universe. All games are independent from each other and can be played independently.
Aveyond 4: Shadow Of The Mist is a classic RPG game that follows a story line, but allows to create your own fighting team from a group of characters that can join you. It involves monster fighting and puzzle solving.
The graphics are old school.
The story line traditional, but the dialogue funny and tongue in cheek.
