The heroes found your evil lair, made it past traps, minions, even a dragon, and now you are utterly defeated.  So what's a villain to do?  Retire.  That is until your dog goes missing after a mysterious fog settles over town.  And now you must go back out into the world to rescue him.
And so the game begins.  Full of wit, well designed gameplay and surprising endearing ex-villains, Aveyond 4 has lived up to all my expectations.  I especially love that this is a full length game, not somethng that is over in the first few hours.  After 17+ hours of game time I'm still discovering new areas of the map, unlocking new side quests, and making progress on the main storyline.  There's still plenty of game ahead and I'm excited to see where it goes.
I originally purchased this game on the Aveyond website when it was first released.  I have been a fan of Amaranth Games since Aveyond 1 and I'm thrilled to see this latest installment with its twist on the classic hero's journey.  I received a free key to download the game here on Steam so that I could share my impressions of the game with the Steam community.  I fully recommend Aveyond 4 to anyone who likes good humor and great RPGs.

Hurtwold is a survival game similar to Ark and Rust.  It has a superior building system to Ark's horribly broken one, but a very similarly flawed overall gameplay philosophy involving hours of grinding that can all be wiped out if you step away from the game too long or if people with enough resources simply decide to do it.
Ultimately, the entire concept of "what do you do in this game" is ill-thought out as it's mostly an exercise in grinding to get a pvp advantage while other people try and rob you while you do so.  Success mostly boils down to gathering as many people with as much free time onto your team as possible, and constantly grouping up in-game.
There is no winning, only temporarily and precariously not losing.
Pros:
Where Ark has super-cool dinosaurs with flawed buggy horrible physics, this has lame vehicles with smoother but still buggy physics.
The building system is quite good.  It yields predictable results and you can make large complex structures without too much difficulty.  It's based on a universal snap point grid which makes it relatively easy to line structures up.
They have also introduced a novel concept to survival where the key items for progression stay with you when you die.  This works well and provides much smoother, less jarring gameplay where you can take more risks and have more fun.
Cons:
There is no way to walk away from the game for a week without losing everything.
The PVP system favors those who ambush people while they are minding their own business.
Battling against "the elements" mostly boils down to being able to survive through the cold caused by rain, which they have it do ridiculously often to the point where the server all collectively groans each time.
Most of the real PVP that happens is actually PVO, where people steal from those who are offline.  That used to have a bit of balance in that things in your inventory where protected when you logged off, but this is being removed.
The UI is complete trash, full of long-standing sizing glitches, broken chat scrolling and no quality of life improving functionality.  The devs need to take a serious look at InventoryTweaks for minecraft and make note of how a survival UI can be not tediously bad.
I think this game suffers from the same problems that have plagued every game in the survival genre, from multiplayer minecraft to rust and ark.  Persistent worlds and PVP are strange companions, and mating them together into something that feels more like a game you can pick up and play when you want to and less like a harmful addiction that punishes you if you ever dare do anything else is difficult, and the Hurtworld devs have definitely failed.
Summary:
If you want to waste a bunch of time in a pointless barely enjoyable struggle against ill-conceived gameplay elements, this game is for you, but trust me, you don't.
If you decide to subject yourself to this game, be prepared for an exercise in futility as the game is not designed to work well without constantly wiping the servers removing all your progress, so they do that and it's not handled in a player-friendly way.

This game is a refreshing take on the stereotypical sword and sorcery rpg storyline.  What happens to villains after they are defeated?  Do they retire?  Is there anything that could cause them to turn a new leaf, and become "heroic"?  The storyline is clever and character interactions are always amusing.  All six playable characters have their own unique gameplay and skills and the ability to freely switch combat members allow you to customize your party for specific encounters.  Gear upgrades are significant enough to feel worthwhile, and while you can finish the main storyline without completely exploring the world, the most powerful armors require full exploration of bonus areas.  Side quests for each area are easy to find or ignore as you see fit, and are generally found in the area where they are completed to cut down on unnecessary backtracking.
The game is challenging enough to need to use your brains, while being balanced around not needing to grind levels to be able to survive the next quest area.  You can save at any time outside of battle, which makes Aveyond 4 perfect for casual gamers or adult gamers who may never know when playtime will be interrupted.  Hidden quests (not listed in your journal), hidden treasures and a hidden class skill for one of the playable characters reward players who take the time to fully explore and pay careful attention to npc conversations.
I have a hard time thinking of cons for this game, but the one annoying thing I have found is that sometimes the mob grouping pulls in enemies from off screen when initiating combat.  When I touch an enemy sprite to initiate combat and I only see two sprites on the screen, I shouldn't pop a battle with 4 mobs.  When the battle is over I see that extra two were around a corner and blocked by trees.  In the same vein, sometimes enemy sprite loot marks are difficult/impossible to find.  This does not happen enough to be more than a temporary irritation though.
Overall it has been a great game, and I highly recommend it both as an introduction to the Aveyond series and for those who played Aveyonds 1-3.

Date: 2/18/16
Review Number: 20
Game: System Shock 2
From (Creator Publisher): Irrational Games/Looking Glass Studios
Played On: Steambox (w/ Controller)
Steam Price as of Review: $9.99
Total Time played: 35 minutes
Review:
Time to take another trip down gaming lane, picking out a random door to knock on and run away giggling while the owner comes to the door with a shotgun to chase me away.  This time the random house happens to belong to System Shock 2, the critical darling of 1999 and FPS RPG of legend.  This one had already seen a good number of hours of playtime both in and out of my Steam collection, however they had long since been removed, so I was working with a new install and a new game, which was just as good, because it appears that I have completely forgotten how to play.
Now, I will say that I do remember why I really enjoyed this game after playing for the thirty five minutes I moved through for this review.  The gameplay is unique, implementing both standard first person shooter elements and RPG elements seamlessly, the storyline is fantastic and complements the story perfectly without becoming too intrusive, and the controls somehow manage to incorporate a lot of technical data in as direct a way as possible (though I will say a lot of button remapping needed to be done to the steam controller before all the possible combinations were covered.  This one may be a mouse and keyboard only sort of game for any long term playing).  The graphics, especially in the character models are significantly dated, but it doesnt vastly interfere with the game, and after some digging I believe improved models have been released, which should mitigate some of that.  But really what makes this game so worth playing is that the whole thing is tied together in a cohesive way that is missed in a lot of games that have been released since.  Many games focus on a single point or two and focus on them often to the exclusion of everything else (see most of the AAA titles that focus so much on graphics that they ignore everything else) but this game takes the entire experience of playing as a cohesive whole, and brings together all the pieces to make a story, writing, sound, graphics, gameplay, and everything else.  In the end, any trip to nostalgia FPS lane would be incomplete if this game was missing.  Definite buy!
Game’s Fate: Uninstalled, really just because I’ve played it enough times to not want to get into it again.
Buy/No Buy: Totally worth buying.  A game that takes some of the best aspects of FPS games and RPGs and puts them together.

Review for those that don't read past the first few line:
I found more joy in uninstalling this game repeatedly for hours than I did in 30+ hours of gameplay.
Review:
I have always been a fan of the Call of Duty franchise.  I've owned most of their titles, but gave up on the franchise after ghosts.  However, the introduction of the exo suit seemed to be the beginning of a reinvigorated franchise that had grown stale.  As a result, I forked over $25, and...regretted it immediately.  I thought my expectations were low because of ghosts, so pretty much anything could have been positive, but somehow, they lowered my expectations further.
Campaign:
So its basically the same plot and iconic scenes from past games reimagined and reskinned for the future.  That being said, the story is alright, but it is linear, rather easy even on the harder difficulties, it is really short (about 7-9 hours), and has significant plot holes.  The graphics are the best COD has offered so far, but frankly that's not saying much.  The one redeeming aspect was Kevin Spacey, but his performance just made the problems with the campaing more glaring.
Pros:
+
+ Kevin Spacey
Cons:
- Reused story (seriously look it up)
- Linear
- Short
Multiplayer:
The introduction of the exosuit was nice becaue it added a new dynamic to the game, making it even more fast pace.  There is a lot of customization to your character and weapons because of the Pick 13 system.  I also like that you can customize killstreaks.  Unfortunately, the good does not outweigh the bad.  First off, there is no weapon balance.  Second, we were promised dedicated servers, but that was a bold faced lie.  Furthermore, the problems most people are having aren't even being addressed.  Instead, they role out DLC that divides the limited playerbase and add DLC weapons that essentially make the game pay to win.
Pros:
+ Exo-suit
+ Graphics (for a COD game)
+ Pick 13 system
+ Customization
Cons:
- Terrible post-launch support
- No weapo balance
- No dedicated servers (host advantage ruins the game )
- Sync issues / connections mean certain maps are essentially unavailable
- Cutting the game through DLC
- No one plays
- The cheat-detection is a joke
- Hackers
- DLC is op
Overall:
I have to ask myself, did anyone actually test the PC version before release, or is it like Paradox's release of Sword of the Stars II?  At this point, it would almost be better to delay COD on pc for a year and have a good port than attempting to play it while it is broken.  At this point, the updates have brought a shattered game to a damaged game, and to me, there is no difference, there is no value in either case, just one looks more presentable than the other.  At this point, all I can do is hope that Treyarch pulls off another Black Ops with Black Ops III.

This is an excellent game. That said, the game is not "fun" in the traditional sense. Rather this game is engaging. The way it builds tension in the early hours of the campaign through carefully crafted world building, and the way it effectively uses sound, gameplay, and graphics to continually reinforce the sense of foreboding throughout the game is terrific. Creative Assembly clearly has a great deal of love of the source material, as the world meshes perfectly with the Alien Films that came before. In some respects, the game is even more effective than the first Alien film in building a palpable sense of dread because you the player actually have to confront the Alien!
I can't think of another game in recent memory that I feared to play each time I booted it up (in a good way!). The Alien has exceptional AI that forces the player to carefully plan their movements and think strategically about how to survive for the next encounter. My only real gripe is that at times, I found myself turned around having some difficulty pinpointing exactly where I was supposed to be going and what my objective was. When this occurred it pulled me out of an otherwise brilliant experience. This was a rare occurrence however, perhaps happening only two or three times during the duration of the fourteen hour campaign.
You do not need to be an Alien fan to appreciate this game. The gameplay is a perfect fit for the world the developers created. It take a little bit of getting used to, but once you adjust to this game’s rhythm and learn to play it on its terms you’ll hooked – otherwise it will drag you through a vent kicking and screaming. As a fan of the franchise, I can say this is the first Alien game that felt true to the source material. Also, it's nice to see a big budget game like this take chances and deliver an experience entirely different from its Triple A brethren. It boggles the mind that it took a strategy game developer to deliver a game worthy of this classic franchise. Hats off to you Creative Assembly!

I am not a big gamer.  I'm old.  Over 50.  When I purchased a new computer recently, wanting to take it for a spin, I asked my son what to do and he told me about Steam.  As an ancient history buff (I'm also a writer and have written a novel about the ancient Spartans), I did searches on Greece and Rome and eventurally found Rome 2.
I read all the negative reviews about the launch.  Things haven't changed much in the gaming industry.  Companies have always rushed their product to market.  I imagine after spending years developing a game they end up deep in the hole and pressured by corporations like Sega to push it out - no matter how many problems exist.  That's been going on for years.  The wise thing to do is to wait.  You know there is going to be a patch.  Why not let someone else trip over all the bugs?  From what I gather, a lot of gamers just can't wait today.
Anyway, I love Rome 2.  When I read about the Emperor's Edition having worked out most of the problems, I dove in.  It's been a delight.  What a great game.  It's more addicting that crack.  Being able to play so many different factions gives it limitless re-playability.  Thus far I've played as the Romans, Spartans, Athenians and Epirus, and have had a blast with each.  There is a huge amount of strategy and tactics available on both the campaign map and the battle maps.  Placing your armies at choke points in the mountains or at river crossings... putting them in ambush mode... slaughtering 2x or 3x your number of units without getting your hands dirty... it's all so gratifying.
One of the things I've noticed is that I usually end up winning by gaining a technological edge over the computer AI factions.  If I can survive the early stages of play, eventually I'll start kicking out armies composed of better units than my opponents.  When the autoresolve gives me results I don't like, saying I'm going to lose, or take unexceptable losses, it's fun to take control of your army and lead them on to victory when the odd♥♥♥♥ers are betting against you.  Of course, often times you're leading superior units against hordes of untrained spearmen or levies, but occasionally the computer gives you a run for your money and there's nothing like destroyng your opponents Praetorian guard or Oathsworn unit that fights to last man.
Big kudos to the modding community.  After playing vanilla R2, I found the Workshop and have been in pure amazement at the products the community has added to the game.  The 4x moves per year mod, agent color coding, the new unit mods, and many others deserve effusive praise.  I feel like a kid on Christmas morning every time I look in the Workshop, wondering what new toy I'll find under the tree today.
The Bad.  I have none.  Okay, okay, there are some, but I'm like a newlywed on his honeymoon right now.  I don't care if she leaves her panties on the bathroom floor or that the 4x calendar year mod makes agents overpowered.  For right now, I'm enjoying the game far too much to complain about a thing.

It's a sad, sad day for video games.
The game feels off. The overworld doesn't fit the scale it's meant to portray. Mountains look like hills, valleys look like ripples in dirt, it looks like the textures were made for a human-scale game that they just inflated. The 3D graphics is exaggerated, bump-mapped, and specular-lightinged to death. They focused on giving everything that "crisp look", but in the process everything was left looking artificial and sterile.
They removed most of the features that made you INVESTED in the game. Family trees are gone. Unique heroes are gone (seriously, why?). Upgrading towns stops because the negative effects you get from upgrading aren't worth it. Battles are always pre-determined, there's little you can do to turn a losing army into a winning battle. The game is slow paced, and the loading times are ridiculous. In the end, you're left with a gameplay that feels like the developers are playing the game for you, and treating you like a 13-year old FPS-addicted idiot.
In short, they goofed up. Don't buy it.

Everything you might hear about this sequel to a serious that started out with it's handful of fan—myself included—is true. THIS IS THE WAY SEQUELS SHOULD BE MADE. IT'S THE WAY ALL GAMES SHOULD BE MADE, OPTIMIZED, AND IMPROVED UPON. It's such a delicious treat for horror fans [balanced well with the intense and vastly improved gameplay], for those more action-oriented [balanced well with the game's dark atmosphere and environments, and for anyone who doesn't have a very healthy taste for creepy enemy design choices and such. They're all really really cool, though.
If you're not familiar with the first game, then the first thing you may hear of when asking a friend is either the somewhat clunky and not-so-tight controls, or the intricate—and convoluted as hell—story. Questions and complaints for both of these things have been both adressed and acknowledged, But if you are familiar, then you'll also be thrilled to know that you can do much, much more this time around, as I also mentioned.
The very basic premise of The Evil Within 2 is that you're taking the plunge back into an intricate system known as 'STEM'. After events from the first game, STEM has been vastly improved upon, and a new 'core' candidate has been found, and is being used as the literal 'core' of it, meaning that the inner world of STEM is founded upon the stability of said core. However, this 'core' is your daughter, who was presumed to be dead. The organization who developed STEM, Mobius, stole her from you right under your nose, and now that you know she's alive, you delve into a new STEM world in hot pursuit of other individuals inside STEM who want to use your daughter for many purposes, including their own. A twisted and utterly disturbed photogapher, a selfish pastor guy who has his own flamethrower-wielding following [not quite a cult. . .yet], and one very special thing that feels the need to heep her within STEM. It's another mind trip to save not only your daughter, but yourself as the world within STEM begins to collape and dismantle. It's a harrowing journey, but also very emotional, too. I was left in tears multiple times. I've spent too many hours than I should have in the first game [but I love it, so yeah], and the final callbacks to it were so powerful that I found myself squealing into my microphone. And oddly enough, there's a great story here in itself; much more immersive than the story present in the first game, I feel.
The gameplay, again, is so imporved upon and evolved from the first game. It's not quite an open-world game, but the areas are huge for a game of this genre: spawling open environments are the main attraction of the game, the part that encourages exploration and scavenging. It is a survival-horror game, after all, and even if you're careful about that sort of thing, you'll surely still have tough times if you're on one of the harder difficulties, or not accustomed to these kinds of games. There are many contextual actions you can take, to interact with not just doors and other simple things, like the first [though it did have many other ways to do so] But this time, you can climb obstacles and debris, vault over fences, unscrew fire hydrants, kick over cans of oil, ACTUALLY HIDE IN BUSHES [you'll need to aim your weapon if you want to see outwards], smash the windows of cars, and also honk their horns. And the enemies actually react to nearly all of this. And of course, sneaking is present here, but it's so much better. You can huddle up against walls and under certain terrain, either crouched or standing, and you could silently run up to another piece of terrain, like if you're in pursuit to sneak kill an enemy, or to quickly get out of one's line of sights.
If you must, wait for a sale on this, but it's definitely worth the full price, especially if you're a fan of true survival horror. Though, buying it on a sale never hurts: again, it's such an astonishing thing they've turned The Evil Within into.

I have to say that I expected TP to be good, considerig who was behind it, but I never thought I would enjoy it just as thoroughly as I did. Much like Ron Gilbert himself proclaimed in pre-release interviews, TP isn't a new point-and-click adventure game trying to replicate the exact formula of 80's/90's adventure games as much as it is a new game that plays out like your *memory* of those games. And most of all, it's a *deconstruction* of the classic adventure game, more than it is a reproduction of it.
And it actually works absolutely marvellously. The quirky, funny and also slightly eerie tone of the game is complimented by some of the best adventure game puzzle design I have seen in years. Playing in hard mode, the challenge was at a perfect level of difficulty almost throughout the the whole game. For once, I found myself truly transported back to my childhood, with puzzles and obstacles lingering in my mind throught the workdays and nights, but never stumping me or forcing me to give in to hints in pure frustration, as is so often the case. Instead, I only felt joy and pure fun from the challenge of thinking out different solutions in my head.
Towards the final couple of chapters, though, the puzzles starts to lose some of their brilliance, and the fun somewhat dries up. Sadly, the story also sort of loses a bit of its charm in time for the last act, with the story taking a meta-turn that is funny in a way, but also sort of dampens the previously built-up tension and engagement in the story.
As a whole, though, TP is a glorious return to form for Ron Gilbert, and a superbly entertaining 80's romp that hopefully makes way for more Ron Gilbert adventure games to come.
Must-play for adventure game fans.

Don't be fooled by my low play time; I bought it from their website originally and just got the key. This is my first ever review, too! Mostly because I'm super lazy. Now here you go: 10/10
This is a great game. I've been a follower of the Aveyond series since it first came out years ago, and (unlike many series), the quality has only gone up with each game.
Story and writing: The story is amazing. Aveyond is what got me into RPGs in the first place, and I've yet to come across another that has such well-written characters and a cohesive plot. It's made me laugh from the get-go and has a bit of a different spin from the other games; this time, you're playing from the perspective of a retired villian who's sort of forced into the role of hero. It's original and well-done, without gramatical or spelling errors.
Music: The soundtrack is, as always, incredible. Aaron Walz has really outdone himself with this one.
Gameplay and controls: There are both keyboard and mouse functions, for whichever you prefer, and everything is really easy to figure out without being annoying. It's pretty stnadard, but in a good way.
Art: Aveyond has given me extemely high standards for art, and is the sole reason why I'm hesitant to play many other RPGs that aren't quite up to par. SotM very much keeps with this standard. The art is beautiful and expressive, and unlike many other games that have decent art to provide nothing more than a visual, the art in this game really adds something. The expressions are hilarious and personal, and you can really tell that a lot of effort was put in.
Combat: Simple without being boring. It's turn-based and the abilities of each character are truly well thought-out.
My impression as a whole: Play the damn game. It's very much worth the price (and to be honest, one of the only games that I'm willing to spend more than $10 on), and the more people who play, the easier it is for the series to continue on and flourish. If you're new to the series, absolutely give it a shot. Hell, give all of them a shot. They're all great. If you're a veteran, well, you probably already own it. 10/10

Ravenfeild is a fun, easy to pick up and play game, with its fair share of bugs.
Graphics: 7/10
Despite the seemingly bland and simple graphics, ravenfeild has a uniqe graphics style. Sadly, the low poly models, and the high poly assets are somewhat clashing.
Gameplay: 9/10
The gameplay is fast, and addicting. The battles take place on 4 different maps, between a red and a blue team. The gunplay is easy to learn, hard to master, with complex mechanics such as bullet drop, and mastering the different guns. The gamemodes are varied, spanning from point match (earn points by capturing bases, and scoring kills), to battalions (something about draining respawns by capturing flags, dont know much about this one) and spec ops (a close quaters stealth-like scenario where you and your small team go in with silenced weapons, trying to take out the reds with no respawns) A negative about the gameplay, though, is that a lot of games result in stalemates, with you desperately trying to take over the final flag, with the entirety of the red team guarding it.
Variety: 9/10
The game currently has 4 maps, and a pool of varied weapons, each with different playstyles in mind. The maps are: island (a close-mid range map, set on an island. the map is the smallest of the lot, but one of the best), dustbowl (a mid-long range map, set in a desert, with canyons, desert town and planes!), temple (a mid-close quaters map, set in a snowy landscape.) and arcipelego (a WIP map, set on an aircraft carrier. this map has only 3 flags, and most of the combat takes place trying to take the deck of the carrier, or in the air, with planes!).
Bugs: 10/10
As with all early access games, it it littered with bugs. Sometimes i sink through the floor, sometimes i get stuck in the ground, sometimes i die on a machine gun emplacement and the skybox is replaced with the scenery, and i sometimes turn upside down. It's a generaly buggy game, but the same can be said for all early access games. I also noticed my framerate signifigantly decrease from the previous betas.
TL;DR
Ravenfeild is a fun, easy to pick up and play game, with addicting and varied gameplay, but a handfull of bugs, and annoying stalemates. 9.5/10 too much of the coulor green.

I loved the old LucasFilm adventure games. I grew up with Monkey Island, Indiana Jones and Loom... Ron Gilbert was a name that got engraved in my memory. So I was quite excited when I heard they were launching a Kickstarter for a new game in the style of their old adventures.
In the meantime, I tried some other, modern adventures and was somehow disappointed. Although they were funny and engaging, I just didn't enjoy them that much. I thought that maybe I just "grew out of it".
That is, until Thimbleweed Park got released.
After some friends of mine totally freaking out about it, I thought "oh well, let's give it one last shot".
And wow, I wasn't disappointed.
I would wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone wo likes a good point & click adventure game.
I found out, I certainly didn't grow out of these :)

I actually made a paper machet model of the Maniac Mansion for when I was in grade school, complete with little figurines of all the Edisons and the main protagonists, all the furniture... even the Edsel! Got away with an A-plus, too. Wish I still had the pictures of that....

This game is really fantastic. I am really very positivly surprised by this because some other adventure games I have played recently didn't really were that good after all.
But Thimbleweed Park has amazing writing, awesome art, good voice acting and amazing music. It really is fantastic, and the length is also perfect. Not too short, but not too long to feel overly drawn out.
In general the jokes are good, but sometimes they might be a bit too much inside gags that a lot of people will not understand.
And here is the only negative thing, people like me, who played all the old LucasArts adventure games will love this game and get all the jokes. But people who haven't or are younger, they will not get them and might rather think they are stupid or not funny at all.
But besides this, if you loved the old Adventure games, this game is a must buy. A real must.

I am an Aveyond fan . . . . This is a new twist of the Aveyond games with a new Darkthrope.  Even if he is "evil" and cursed to marry a witch - he is a very likable character.  You have a great quest to complete and a new group of heros - along with a few favorites from previous games.  Of course you can have a marriage at the end . . . . if you get enough attaction points.  I personally loved the game and will play more than once.

Once in a great while you find a series of games that become milemarkers through the changes and phases of your life.  When I first began playing Ahriman's Prophecy, my daughter was just beginning high school.  I was excited, as our new computer had a brand new operating system called Windows XP.
Fastforward to last summer.  My granddaughter came to stay with my husband and I for the summer.  She played through Aveyond, Aveyond 2 and the various chapters of Aveyond 3.  She quickly fell in love with the games, as had her mother and I years before.  When I told her that the release of Aveyond 4 was on the horizon, she became at least as excited as many fans of the Fallout series, awaiting Fallout 4.
Aveyond is a familiar place, and has seen at least as many changes as the lives of the wonderful people who make up the fanbase. If you're looking for an intense, fast paced game with gore and violence aplenty, move along.  If you'd like to recover some of the innocent wonder and happiness the world so callously tries to strip away, welcome to The Kingdom. Relax, sit back and just...play.
If you've ever had a beloved pet go missing, you'll know very well the depths of despair and challenges of finding them  and bringing them safely home again. In Aveyond 4 you'll revisit this issue, but with a wonderful twist.  There are riddles to be solved, mountains to climb, tournaments to win, and a narcissistic king who simply will not take no for an answer.   Aveyond 4 is packed with various  quests.  There are old friends, new heroes, dragons, elves and wicked witches. Have you ever pondered the meaning of a particularly disturbing nightmare?  Someone in this game might have the answer. Love, betrayal and wonder await you.
If you've ever enjoyed wandering around town and country with a good friend while the rest of the world is quietly slumbering, aiding a hilarious faction that desires to rule the world (a top secret faction that might actually do a better job than the figurehead in place), give this game a try!
This game is not a race, it's a meandering walk throught he woods, exploring every leaf, feeling the wind in your hair and the warmth of the summer sun on your face.  Slow down, lock your inner critic in the dungeon buy this game and just enjoy.

I have long been a fan of the Aveyond games.  However, you do *not* need to have played any of the others to enjoy or understand this game.  There are a couple of long-lived recurring non-playable minor characters from earlier series, but they do not play major roles in this game. You can play this with either a keyboard or a mouse.  I generally prefer the keyboard unless I am trying to navigate tricky terrain or avoid a bad guy without a fight.
This is a long, detailed, well-imagined fantasy game.  There are battles, and you can have up to four fighters (plus one minion) from amongst your seven party members (you won't have seven party members the whole game, for most of it you will have fewer than seven).  Each character has different battle skills and strengths, and you may not want the same fighters in every situation.  You will have a chance to experience the battle interface during the demo.
The party does not always remain the same, either.  Although Boyle is the main character, occasionally other playable characters will have quests without him.   All the characters have unique backgrounds, and many are very different characters than we have seen in previous games.
There is a lot of fun, snarky humor in this game, especially with two of the MCs (Boyle and Ingrid) being an ex-villain and a witch.  Possibly reformed characters make great reluctant heroes.   Boyle's primary loyalty is to his dog/wolf Fang.  It takes him a while to get used to being part of a group.
I don't want to give away much of the plot, but there many different locations in this expansive world, allowing for many different creatures and scenery.  (Mountains, forest, farmland, desert, seaside mining town, swamp, dreamscape, etc).  There are a bunch of main quests, and a fair number of optional side-quests with useful rewards.
There are several options for replayability, too, especially involving Ingrid, who can marry one of several men, depending on who she fancies and how much work she puts into it, and also join one of three witches covens, each with its own unique spells.  Eventually I want to try al the options.
So, try the demo and see if this is the sort of game you like.  (Note: the first half-hour is more scripted than the rest of the game, so do not be misled or turned off by the initial nudging).
Also, my tip to you - save early and often, especially before battle.  And talk to everyone you encounter.
I had (and am having) lots of fun with this game and I hope you do too.  In some respects it is like immersing yourself in an interactive book/movie and experiencing a deep and nuanced world.  You might have to put more effort into it that the normal shooter or point-and-click games, but you will be rewarded for your efforts with a unique experience most games do not give you.  Most games are forgettable and interchangeable, but I always remember the Aveyond games and characters long after I am done playing.  Aveyond 4 makes me smile and forget about the real world for a while.
Disclaimer: I bought the PC version of this game when it was first released in December, and received a free Steam key from the developer.

I am so happy to see Aveyond come on to Steam.  The entire series should be on Steam. Aveyond 4 is the newest release in this wonderful series. The first was in 2006- I have been following it for the last 10 years. This is one of the most clever and unique RPG games you will find.  It is intensely story-driven, immersive, and extremely well-written.  The graphics, while not your typical Skyrim-ish style, are beautiful and engaging. Oh, and the music!! I believe Aaron Walz does the music, and it is just so lovely. I have kept the games on just to play the music for ambience.
Aveyond 4 is about Boyle and his friends- he is a failed villain on a new quest with  some new friends.  It's a funny game.  Very witty. And you get to shapeshift and catch cheekis. And minions!  You can have minions!
DISCLAIMER: I did receive a Steam code for the came in exchange for this review, HOWEVER I did purchase the game from the developer the day it came out, and i would have written the review anyhow. A lot of heart went into this game and the entire series.

I bought this game direct from Amaranth Games when it first came out and received a free Steam key for feedback.
I have enjoyed all of the Aveyond games, but this may be my favorite.  The characters are well developed and the humor is great.
Battles are challenging without being a chore, but certain enemies are tough even on the easy setting.  I found very little grinding to be necessary on the normal setting - usually just needing to switch my party around to suit certain enemies.  Every character is useful at some point.
There are plenty of sidequests with great rewards and some puzzles that are fun to work through.  I have played completely through the game three times to try all possible covens and get all the different marriages at the end.
The main con with the game is that there is a lag in certain areas.  Shutting down background programs helps a little, but doesn't really fix it.  Another minor issue is that you have to buy items one at a time which is a bit of a pain when trying to stock up before a boss battle.
While the game does have references to the previous games in the series, it is not necessary to play them first and this game can stand very well on its own.

Aveyond 4  gave me a nice break from Skyrim.   The entire Aveyond series are among my favorite games, right up there with Skyrim, Fable 3, Fable 2, King's Quest and Dawn's Light.   I got this game through Amaranth games first and received a free steam key to review the game here on Steam.
Aveyond 4, so far my favorite of the series, has an excellent storyline that pulls you right in from the start and keeps your interests with plot twists, entertaining characters and npc's.   Some highlights -- militant squirrels, plenty of humor sometimes when you least expect it, simple controls, beautiful artwork, both the characters and the backgrounds.  And the loot, including hidden goodie caves filled with treasure.
I recommend playing the entire Aveyond series.

Played on normal, the mid-game will turn too easy as you will not care anymore about ammos or meds. And all the terrifying pleasure of this game resides in the fact that you are constently in desperate need of something. Anything...
At the very beginning the wrench will be your best companion and you will scarcely use your gun, only to prevent a looming death involving suicidal robots or deadly firing turrets. Each ammo you'll find will be a light in the dark, each med-hypo will shine as a glimpse of salvation, and you will cherish every single cyber-module you'll be granted. Because in this  nightmare of metal and flesh, almost no voice is there to help you, and the only source of informations you'll find will come from beyond the grave, as audio logs recorded by the long dead crew of the Von Braun.
As the game character you will start lost, confused, afraid of what is beyond the corner. You will roam the corridors of the space-ship in fear, holding your breath and carefully listening to each and evey odd sound. As a player you will achieve your journey relieved, but with this gutt feeling that you still have to explore. Because even though the game is linear, you can approach it in different ways. You can specialise yourself in numerous tech, psionic and biological abilities. Every choice will determine how you will be able to make one more step away from the grave. And the possibilites are large enough for you to start again several times. And hopefully you will want to.
System Shock 2 will leave you breathless, but to truly understand why, you will have to fight your way in a place where monsters intend to become gods...

Basically Mikami isn't directing the game, it's instead directed by the man who's behind the DLCs of part 1. That means multitude of things. Chief among which, completely unbalanced mechanics, stealth is incredibly powerful and makes straight up combat totally unviable (that happens to be the best part of the first game, the combat and variety in encounters and environmental hazards). Stealth is powerful also because of AI that is basic and easily exploitable, possible sacrifice for the large open maps, of which there are TWO. Only chapter 3 could be considered somewhat large map.
Greater focus on the narrative experience, which is a term that is starting to bring true horror because it almost always means compromised gameplay, and it's all the more aggravating when the story and plot and characters are nowhere near as compelling as the first game. Characters don't matter, protagonist's motivation is not interesting, the premise unlikely, the story too straightforward with basically zero mysteries and everything is neatly explained by the end.
In the final segment the sheer gall to copy the mood and music of Inception is also quite obvious and what should have been a cool video game narrative sequence ended up falling flat, final cutscenes a farewell with cheap manipulative tricks with characters we don't have any connection with.
And that's not even getting to the lack of enemy variety, poor pacing, geometry and collision detection jank, missing button prompts, auto saves not triggering properly, reused "boss" enemies, terrible script with some truly horrific lines, etc.
There are some very cool things this game does WELL, one thing I would not hestitate to call innovative and that is the seamless switching between planes/realities during the open map exploration. That was easily the most impressive feature of the game, but again, it compromised the gameplay.
I valued the first game for its ability to constantly surprise me and keep me guessing, this game did that too, for the first 6 chapters, but then everything is predictable and generic, that is also when you realize the optimal strategy to deal with encounters and all tension is gone, I didn't have to craft a single healing item, nor did I have to use more than a couple in the rest of the playthrough on Nightmare at that point. Also everybody talks too much, most of it inconsequential.
If you liked heavy rain and JAASON! Then you will enjoy the sequel, this time it's all LILY!!!
I played the game with japanese voice acting and recommend it (unlike the english version, the JP voice actors are the same as the first game), lip syncing is for the english version but by Umbasa, the japanese voices made me care at least for a while and Kidman in JP is actually the same voice as Claire Redfield in Revelations 2... Well, See ya!

Wonderful game. I played for 14 hours without using a guide but in the end hit a brick wall and had to google the solution to a few puzzles in order to make progress.  Those puzzles weren't necessarily more difficult than the puzzles I had already solved, but after 14 hours of puzzle solving...my old brain said "no more". It says something about how much I loved this game that I spent two or three hours trying everything to solve those remaining puzzles (and I solved a lot of puzzles in that time, but not them all).

I've only talked about the puzzles but there are so many other positive aspects to Thimbleweed Park. Not least the ending, which will put a smile on the face of anyone who's been following this game from the beginning. I won't say any more. :)

I've been helping test the earlier beta versions and the the game just keeps on getting better and better. Steelraven (the developer) listens to feedback and interacts with the community a lot.
The game is a simple single player experience that is just great to play if you want to relax after work. The active ragdolls are hilarious and the weapons and vehicles offer enough variety to suit variety of playstyles. The game also runs well on older machines and you can change the amount of bots and the team balance to your liking. Weapons feel powerful and each hit makes enemies flinch a little. Harder hits knock them down and you can finish them off while they are scrambling to get back on their feet. There aren't many vehicles in this first release but more will be added in the future.
I would yet again like to remind people that the game is singleplayer only. No multiplayer planned so please don't ask for that.

RavenField is a goddamn brilliant game which allows you to relive your childhood memories of spawn killing NPCs or killing them in the thousands. It's unending game system is amazing to see and the options in the menu are really neat and customisable compared to most games.
It’s got an amazing AI system, great maps, well thought-out game options and some of the best, intense fps gameplay I’ve ever experienced.
However, it does suffer from a few things; The new map, Archipelago, is awfully unbalanced. Whole most maps have a flag or a side which is only partly unbalanced, Archipelago really takes the cake for the most unbalanced map. Once you have taken the carrier it’s incredibly hard, if not impossible, to take it back. From there, taking the island is a piece of cake.
The game is also lacking a feature I loved from the beta; the ability to set a score. It’s not too much to worry about but in games with large armies it’s incredibly useful to have. Actually, speaking of big armies; THE OPTIMISATION IS THE BEST PART OF THIS GAME! Broforce is not simply another mindless videogame. It handles war more clever than even the Metal Gear games to critique the American military industrial complex in the conflicts of the bleaker moments of US history as well as the politics of today.
Upon first-glances, the game appears as a nonsense-filled American adventure of blinding heroism. Underlying the action-hero storyline and gameplay, there is a self-awareness of the pro-war sentimentality of the U.S and Allied nations from the '60s through '90s.
Through the action-hero icons of your playable cast, the game uses its macho heroes' aesthetic to convey its patriotism. This is a deliberate choice to make the player think what he is doing is ALWAYS right. And the game's narrative reinforces that idea by ignoring the enemies' thoughts and the game always blaiming them for being potential terrorists because they are different.
For example,  the POWs, a horrible memory of history ,is rendered into an action-hero mechanic. They are not beaten, mentally-unstable individuals who at any moment might die in their capter's hands. Instead, they are all potential action-heros to take the spotlight should a "bro" fall in combat.
The geography of the map also emphasizes the severity behind the "in-game" mechanics/enemies like the POWs (taken from Metal Slug and set in not-Vietnam), the nameless, demonized terrorists in the East (Russians, Muslims and the IRA) and aliens (encrouching upon the homeland). Finally coming to a self-awareness that even America, land of freedom, is ultimately plagued by satantists and demons, and they must be purged (atheists and non-Christians).
The message through gameplay is that all conflicts can be resolved with blind heroics just like the Hollywood blockbusters have instilled into the minds of the masses. But what is always there while you play are the real-world conflicts masked by the fantasy of an action-hero movie.
In the end, you perservere any obstacle in your way clinging to a false notion of freedom. At what cost is that freedom worth to corpses? At one point do you consider the ramifications of your heroics? How can you justify your actions?
These are the difficult questions the game leaves you with...
Okay, real-talk. I completely made up that entire interepretation of this game. And yet, after finishing through two runs of the game (12 hours), I cannot but wonder if the game played me like a fool when I first paroided something that always seemed to be aware of the joke too.
The main point I'm trying to say is... Don't take this game too seriously. Have fun!
This game is what it sells itself; cheesy, nonsense American action with all your favorite action heroes. Each character controls similarly (one attack, one special and one melee--or another special--attack) as a basic jump-and-shoot game.
The interesting aspect is each character's unique abilities and quirks. In total, there is a cast of 29/30 to play with, and as you start off with Rambro, the simpliest character, you can get some ludicrous characters that require skill like Cherry Bromb, Indiana Brones and Bronan the Barbarian.
The game keeps a "rogue-lite" feel without making an entirely random experience. This is a statement both to the game's benefit and to its detriment.
Levels are always the same, but how you go through them is based on who you are playing. Every level does not require you to have one specific character, and every level has fully-destructable terrain to make each playthrough (or retry) different from the last. You can carve your own paths, literally, and this mechanic never entirely ruins or breaks the game.
No character is mandatory, but there are some levels better suited towards the level/boss. This wouldn't be a problem if you could select your bro-loadout (maybe as a post-game reward) or know what you will have at any point in the game.
Every time you begin a level you start with a random bro, and whenever you save a Bro on the battlefield you will get another randomized Bro (and an extra life, which is very useful as every Bro takes one hit).
This "rouge-lite" experience doesn't get in your way because the levels are short (2 to 3 mins if you're careful, excluding boss-fights), and if you fail you can retry the same stage without playing it the same way. It's a good solution to make playing the game over again better as well as failing those harder stages multiple times.
But, as I mentioned before, not everything is flawless because of the random nature of the game.
That is my reaction whenever I get the worst character possible for a level, and this is not because one character requires more skill. It's because of balancing issues. Namely the enemy variety towards the end-game.
When fighting from terrorists to aliens to demons, most characters retain a balancing act hampered only by enemy behaviors not compatible with a specific hero. Bosses are the worst at this, which can either be riddiculous challenges with some characters or a breeze with certain characters (Cherry Bomb with the Alien Heart is so simple).
It also doesn't help that some abilities are rendered useless because of the level (Chuck Norris' airstrikes underground) or by the enemies your fighting (Neo's bullettime with Xenomorphs). Thankfully, some characters are compensated for when their abilities are useless (Norris' shotgun is my favorite).
The level-design is never against you, which is good, but I think if they fleshed out some characters' abilities to work on specific enemies or all of them, then the game would be a lot more polished without these unfair difficulty spikes.
Also, one important point: This game is not a game where you need to grab some friends. (Although it makes the game a lot more interesting/chaotic). The game balances its overall difficulty nicely by giving solo players more extra bros to spare, while making extra players more helpful in dealing with bosses and hordes of enemies.
And despite the problems with the game, none of these ruin the game from being enjoyed for what it is and the replay value is high with muliple modes, the rouge-lite elements and the Steam Workshop levels (only the devs can provide more heroes to keep every character interesting and balanced).
Is it worth $15? I would think so, even when playing by yourself for a 4 to 5 hour adventure. There is Ironbro Mode for a Contra-like feel, the Workshop campaigns, and the game itself is a joy. And cooperative play will offer tons of other replay value from the amount of chaos you can unlesh with a group of four.
Just don't take this game seriously. It's not.

The Elder Scrolls Online - Tamriel Unlimited
Introduction
Tamriel. A continent at war. The Dominion, Pact and Covenant fight for supremacy in the Imperial province of Cyrodiil. Meanwhile, Molag Bal has stolen your ♥♥♥♥ing soul.
Review -11/26/15
Graphics
Tamriel Unlimited is pretty. It has a variety of different environments - from the sandy, sunbaked land of Elsweyr, to the frigid, unforgiving land that is Eastmarch. Whilst no, the graphics aren't particularly revolutionary, and definitely not the same quality as Skryim, this is to be expected. For an MMORPG, the Elder Scrolls Online is up there with one of the best looking. Occasionally the world looks a bit 'the same', but usually as you advance to other provinces, the environment and ambience is noticeably different.
EDIT: After a discussion with someone who commented on this review (which you can read below) I'd like to add this:
Skyrim was a very graphically capable game. The base game, on ultra, compared to ESO, on ultra, is more graphically detailed than ESO in my opinion. However, this may depend on different viewpoints and whatnot. The graphics design and feel each game wishes to portray is different, and this may lead to differences in opinion - which is to be expected.
8/10
PvE
Player vs Environment is the part of this game that gets particularly monotonous. It's the easiest way to level up, as you gain a considerable amount of experience for each quest you complete, but it does indeed become a chore. The characters are forgettable, the quests the same. Kill this, gather 'x' amount of this, talk to her/him. In my 145 hours of playtime, only a few quests have got me genuinely interested. You skip dialogue as it does not mean anything or add to the plot. It does, however, reveal some beautiful locations and there are a FEW interesting quests. For the most part, however, PvE in ESO:TU is pretty 'meh'.
4.5/10
PvP
If you're not sure about buying ESO for the PvE aspect, definitely consider buying it for the PvP aspect. It is likely the most fun I've ever had in an MMORPG. Nothing quite compares to standing aside a host of 50+ players as trebuchets pound castle walls, the walls crumble, and hundreds of players clash on the field of battle. If you're an Elder Scrolls fan and have always fantasized about some sort of war in Tamriel - buy this game. You're allowed to enter Tamriel at Lvl 10 (3-4 hours of playtime?). Once you enter, your stats are boosted to Veteran Rank 1(?). This means a Level 10 can still be (relatively) effective fighting higher levels, so it's pretty balanced. The PvP itself takes place in the Imperial Province of Cyrodiil, which has been invaded by three seperate factions-
The Aldmeri Dominion (High Elf, Wood Elf, Khajit)
The Daggerfall Covenant (Breton, Orc, Redguard)
The Ebonheart Pact (Argonian, Nord, Dunmer)
(With Imperial package you can play as an Imperial in any alliance)
There are 15/16 castles around the province, 6 of which surround the Imperial City. There are also various outposts. Around the castles are resources, which, if captured, give benefits to the faction who owns them.
The PvP is what makes this game, and what convinced me to stay for 100+ hours.
9.5/10
UI/Levelling
The UI is well-designed, not too obtrusive. Levelling up is also pretty simple - each time you level up, you get to choose which stat to invest in - stamina, health or magicka.You can then choose a skill which you can plonk in your hotbar and use. Nothing broken or overpowered, though it does take testing to find the most effective skill sets.
8.5/10
Crafting
I'm not going to lie, I've not experimented in crafting at all, so this section is from friends' experiences.
It's good. Dying your items can make your armor very unique, the materials are varied and it does take up time. It's not simple. Which is good.

SS2 is a superb game, even if you slept on it and are new to the series in 2016, like me. The intriciate storytelling, immersive level design, and long length bring back memories from the golden age of PC gaming: late 90s. If you are looking for something on the scale of Half Life, but with a more scifi feel, this is the game for you.
Off the bat I have to say yes, you have to play this game with graphical and gameplay mods. I would recommend installing them right away, because the vanilla game is almost 20 years old. However, the mods are very easy to install using BMM, its about as intuitive as the nexus mod manager. There is a good SS2 community online with a recommended mod setup. I followed their guidelines and the game looked great honestly.
The best parts about the game:
- Wonderful story with great voice acting and music. Once you start you have to finish.
- With graphical overhaul mods the game looks pretty good and (energy) weapons are very stylish
- In this day and age of AAA flops and DLC on disc, this game delivers great value. Grab it on sale and you're set.
Some cons:
- Honestly, I found the game difficult at first coming in with no background. Sometimes I had to use console. However, I was really engrossed by the story and it didn't bother me after a while
- The combat is dated if you're coming from recent PC games. It's still fun but not mindblowing in any way. However it does hold up well, no doubt about it
- Some of the menus have small print
Overall a great game for the price. I think every gamer who appreciates a timeless story and wants to see the critical predecessors to modern RPG games should check this one out.

I beat Thimbleweed Park last night. It requires two play-throughs to 100% achievements.
There are a few places it stumbles but I'm not actually sure if it was *intended* to be "bad" in those particular instances. Without giving out spoilers, I'll give an example that was used in-game.
Very early on in the game, there is a moment where the fourth wall is broken and they reassure the player that Thimbleweed Park is not like Sierra games where the game can suddenly end and you'll need to back track through saves. But there actually *is* one instance where, KABOOM, game over, you shouldn't have done that, reload.
We, the players, are given fourth-wall-breaking information that is purposely false. While at first I thought this was just tongue-in-cheek stuff to laugh at older P&C tropes, instead I'm now thinking that there is an added layer of mystery that we're supposed to figure out?
The first half of the game starts with a Mystery Murder whose protagonists have hidden agendas themselves. During the course of the game as you reveal the plot, I almost feel like the mystery inverts itself. Like the information that we're given as players is, once again, false.
That is to say, I think there are multiple endings, but I've only experienced one. I experienced the one where I thought the fourth wall breaking information was truthful.
Naturally I could be WELL over-thinking things, but having experienced an ending that was kind of lackluster and re-thinking events that happened in the game, I have to wonder if there aren't more layers.
Anyhoo, Thimbleweed Park is solid even if you take everything at face value in the game.
Side-note: the voice actor for Leisure Suit Larry uses the Larry voice in the game. Not sure why that is either. MORE MYSTERIES.

Thimbleweed Park might look gloriously retro, but is actually a ground-breaking adventure game when it comes to puzzle design and utilizing an open world. Excellent puzzles, solid writing, a unique setting, great soundtrack, complex ideas, and some absolutely wonderful visuals. Highly recommended!

TLDR: Get it on sale if you must. If you liked the first game this sequel will make you appreciate the first game even more. The best parts of the first game are gone, replaced with NARRATIVE and EXPLANATIONS (but not the things you want to know from the first game).
Basically Mikami isn't directing the game, it's instead directed by the man who's behind the DLCs of part 1. That means multitude of things. Chief among which, completely unbalanced mechanics, stealth is incredibly powerful and makes straight up combat totally unviable (that happens to be the best part of the first game, the combat and variety in encounters and environmental hazards). Stealth is powerful also because of AI that is basic and easily exploitable, possible sacrifice for the large open maps, of which there are TWO. Only chapter 3 could be considered somewhat large map.
Greater focus on the narrative experience, which is a term that is starting to bring true horror because it almost always means compromised gameplay, and it's all the more aggravating when the story and plot and characters are nowhere near as compelling as the first game. Characters don't matter, protagonist's motivation is not interesting, the premise unlikely, the story too straightforward with basically zero mysteries and everything is neatly explained by the end.
In the final segment the sheer gall to copy the mood and music of Inception is also quite obvious and what should have been a cool video game narrative sequence ended up falling flat, final cutscenes a farewell with cheap manipulative tricks with characters we don't have any connection with.
And that's not even getting to the lack of enemy variety, poor pacing, geometry and collision detection jank, missing button prompts, auto saves not triggering properly, reused "boss" enemies, terrible script with some truly horrific lines, etc.
There are some very cool things this game does WELL, one thing I would not hestitate to call innovative and that is the seamless switching between planes/realities during the open map exploration. That was easily the most impressive feature of the game, but again, it compromised the gameplay.
I valued the first game for its ability to constantly surprise me and keep me guessing, this game did that too, for the first 6 chapters, but then everything is predictable and generic, that is also when you realize the optimal strategy to deal with encounters and all tension is gone, I didn't have to craft a single healing item, nor did I have to use more than a couple in the rest of the playthrough on Nightmare at that point. Also everybody talks too much, most of it inconsequential.

Dishonored 2 feels shorter than the first game, but is still a worthy successor. Now that all the patches have been out for some time, the game seems to run fairly smoothly, although it requires a fairly decent graphics card to play. On a laptop with a GTX 960m I was clocking at about 25-30 FPS, but it didn't detract from the game experience too much. The game looks fine even on very low settings due to the oil pastel style.
Dishonored 2 only took about 10 hours so far on my first run through, but the game has a lot of replayability so I would probably lengthen this to 30ish hours if you're really trying to explore all the options. Dishonored 2 has some of the best animation of any game, and a fairly memorable cast of characters, and set pieces. And the set pieces and levels are what make this game shine. The Clockwork Mansion and a Crack in the Slab are easily some of the most fun levels I've had the privilege of playing through. The game rushes the plot at the beginning and continues to hurtle the plot forward for the first half of the game, only catching its breath in the last few missions.
While the plot is fairly lackluster, the world is far more refined. The world is on par with any of the Bioshock games, and makes you feel completely transported. Conversations between guards, servants, nobles, and civilians bring the world to life. The story telling and secrets in parts of the world are very discreet and you shouldn't expect everything to be presented to you outright.
I'd recommend the game to anyone who was a fan of the original, but to anyone who hasn't played the first, I would advise playing the first Dishonored before starting this up. Play Dishonored, play the Knife of Dunwall, and the Brigmore Witches, and then you'll be more in on what's happening in the plot and the world around you.

While this is by all means a sequel to Just Cause 2, it feels more like a experiment of ideas they couldnt put into JC2 for various reasons. As entertaining as it is, this is one of the situations where i wish there was a "meh" recommendation. If you already own and have played Just Cause 2 extensively, you may likely find this is not worth the purchase. Due to a lack of interest to keep playing after about 15 hours (as seen above) i will not recommend this, however.
Pros:
+Visually its beautiful. Hardly mindblowing, but rather good looking for how well it runs. (i5 4690k, GTX 970, 8gb RAM)
+The Addition of unlimited explosives and extra grapple lines (as well as grapple retractions) makes it clear they understood where Just Cause 2 sat as a sandbox Michael Bay simulator.
+Towns are not copy pasted, unlike a decent few in JC2 which felt the same but altered to fit the terrain around it.
+New and improved cars allows for some amusing and fast travelling chaos to occur in various forms, much like in JC2, but on drugs.
+Upgrade tree which allows you to enable and disable upgrades whenever you want after unlocking allows for an even larger freeform of destruction.
+Addition of the wingsuit means you can travel around the world a bit faster than you could in Just Cause 2, with a little more sensation of the actual speed.
+Introduction of the 'new and improved' vehicle purchase system allows you to access what you want wherever, at a small cost of an item easily replenished at any nearby fuel station.  You can access any weapons and vehicles you have unlocked prior, with the upgrades you have unlocked for them (only accessible on the vehicles you acquire via this supply drop system).
+
Cons:
-The Map and towns in the game are rather uninteresting. While unique to one another they lack pretty much any remarkable features to them, a majority of the objectives being on the rooftops and leaving little reason to explore them other than to pull up the settlement flag (to capture the settlement), and to eliminate the police station there.
-Story is pretty... well... its a story. Thats about all i can say for it. Its hardly remarkable and it doesnt make a whole lot of sense compared to what Just Cause 2 offered (JC2: Cause chaos to unsettle the tyrannical government. JC3: Blow some more stuff up, because thats how you liberate towns apparently). Thats about all i can say for it though, since, as you can see, i had difficulty motivating to finish the game.
-Driving. Its bad. The cars seem to be designed to ♥♥♥♥ the player over with the exception of the high powered cars which seem to be the only ones capable of not spinning out. For instance, when turning, the car barely turns at all until it reaches about 10 degrees of an angle upon which it typically then goes all the way at once and spins out. Drifting is poorly concieved as while its not too hard to slide around a corner, ending the drift typically results in your car attempting to reangle back a huge distance the way you came. Not helpful in the least.
-Driving Pt2. Motorbikes, while previously a menace to use in JC2 due to how often the wheels left the ground, have become even worse somehow. Clearly designed by someone who has never actually ridden a motorbike (i do, before anyone calls me out), the damn things tend to barely turn, or not even turn at all, until Ricos knees are just about touching the road. Which of course makes driving a huge pain since it basically means you have a 100ms latency on turning. Plus going over a bump means hell for you.
-Flying (or Driving Pt3) has been... more or less untouched. Its still the most efficient means of getting around should you find yourself in easy reach of a jet or plane. However, its slightly ruined by them using the same button for Accelerate as Turbo. For anyone who hasnt played the game yet, what this means is that NORMALLY, you have a 'flight speed' which for this example shall be 200km/h. Its about the area your speed 'maxes' out at if you arent accelerating constantly, and slowly drops from if you arent. Pressing the accelerate button boosts your speed past that max about 10% (so, lets say to 220km/h) but letting go off accelerate quickly dips it back to 200 again (much faster than your speed drops below 200). This is alright, allowing you to accelerate out of curves, and stop during them to make tighter turns. All good. All fun.
And then theres the turbo. Bound to the same button as accelerate (which you CANNOT unbind when i last played it, due to switching one button automatically switching the other) it basically replaces your accelerate. You dont accelerate up the runway, you turbo up the runway. You dont regenerate turbo while accelerating either, so if you want to regenerate turbo you have to let your speed dip again down to 200 (which ends up at about 180 or so by the time turbo has fully recharged). Ive said it before, and ill say it again, if you have to screw up one mechanic to make the new mechanic have a purpose, maybe the new mechanic isnt worth it. The chute was inconic to Just Cause, and this game doesnt do it justice at all.
-You actually have to do a fair amount before you unlock most of the more entertaining mods, but due to the map haveing an obscenely small amount of settlements (compared to Just Cause 2) its unlikely youll have too many left to do by the time you acquire them. SS2 is a superb game, even if you slept on it and are new to the series in 2016, like me. The intriciate storytelling, immersive level design, and long length bring back memories from the golden age of PC gaming: late 90s. If you are looking for something on the scale of Half Life, but with a more scifi feel, this is the game for you.
Off the bat I have to say yes, you have to play this game with graphical and gameplay mods. I would recommend installing them right away, because the vanilla game is almost 20 years old. However, the mods are very easy to install using BMM, its about as intuitive as the nexus mod manager. There is a good SS2 community online with a recommended mod setup. I followed their guidelines and the game looked great honestly.
The best parts about the game:
- Wonderful story with great voice acting and music. Once you start you have to finish.
- With graphical overhaul mods the game looks pretty good and (energy) weapons are very stylish
- In this day and age of AAA flops and DLC on disc, this game delivers great value. Grab it on sale and you're set.
Some cons:
- Honestly, I found the game difficult at first coming in with no background. Sometimes I had to use console. However, I was really engrossed by the story and it didn't bother me after a while
- The combat is dated if you're coming from recent PC games. It's still fun but not mindblowing in any way. However it does hold up well, no doubt about it
- Some of the menus have small print
Overall a great game for the price. I think every gamer who appreciates a timeless story and wants to see the critical predecessors to modern RPG games should check this one out.

The problem with System Shock 2 like in it's weapon systems, overly complex RPG elements and its GOD AWFUL wrench combat.
In Bioshock it's not always a big deal to be left with only your wrench to use. In System Shock 2 it's a much different story. The attack animation is ridiculously dated and there isn't even a mod to improve it.
This wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for the aforementioned problems with the weapons and RPG elements were better.
Ammo is way too scarce and powerful weapons like the shotgun and grenade launcher for example require you to level up certain skills before you can even use them even after you've found them. So, for a nice few hours of backtracking and getting enough cyber modules just to use ONE WEAPON(that still may only last you for so long due to scarce ammo), you'll be using the wrench.

I just played this game for the first time 2 years ago (in 2013) not having played it back in the day, so this review comes from someone who was used to the modern shooter before having tried this.  System Shock 2 quickly became not only one of my favorite shooters of all time, but one of my favorite games of all time.  Between the atmosphere, the challenge, the creepy graphics and sounds, and especially the character building, it is just an absolute delight from beginning to end.  I recommend this game for people who like haunted environments, isolation, and people who enjoy using limited resources and character points to create a powerful character capable of rising to the increasing challenges the game throws at you.
I also highly recommend NOT installing the graphics mod that everyone swears by.  Yes, it makes the graphics look a little sleeker, but the new enemy models simply don't have the same impact as the old ones.  I've tried both, and it wasn't long before I switched back to the unmodded version.
One last thing:  Key binding.  If you are used to the controls of a modern shooter, you will want to rebind the keys.  I've seen a lot of negative reviews stating the controls are too hard to use.  I agree.  That is easily remedied.  Just go into the options, and in game controls you can rebind the keys so that W,A,S,D move you in the way you are used to.  It's the first thing I did when I bought the game.  To me this is obvious, but I supposed people without previous experience might not know this is possible and easy to do.

First, a disclaimer: I am one of the original Kickstarter backers, so I could be biased towards wanting to like the game in a less objective way than as a mere customer. On the other hand, the expectation for the game's qualities was also very high.
To me, Thimbleweed Park(TM) has ticks in all the boxes: it presents a rich and colourful world, an intriguing plot and many interesting characters. It builds on the reputation of the adventure game classics and pioneers, but the execution works well  for the modern desktop, and I can imagine it fits into living room or mobile platform just as well.
The designers' choice was to go for a pixelated 16-bit-like graphics. This is in no way a downside, because it manages to pull off many beautiful screens and backgrounds. It also adds to the visuals features like dynamic character lighting and shading, which would not be doable 30 years ago.
The puzzles are all solvable as long as you pay attention, remember the places and characters and apply logical thinking. I got stuck only a handful of times, but to my own oversight. The player does need to apply some sense to the game, so I would not call the game trivial and easy, at least not on the hardcore mode.
I did find it a bit annoying at the beginning that the game seemed to have been stealing control over the current character in the many of the introductory flashbacks. But in the long run (and by that I mean 15 hours gameplay and more), these introductions were well worth it, because we do get to meet and know these characters better. I particularly liked being able to revisit the town and its inhabitants with the newcomers, getting fresh perspectives on their own background and the backround of the locals.
I think we have come a long way with the adventure games. Thimbleweed Park(TM) works so much better than just the parts from Maniac Mansion and Monkey Island combined. It delivers a rich and entertaining package well worth the price tag.
Easily the best point and click adventure game made in the past decade.

Instead, I have been so engrossed by this game that I only went to the walkthroughs once (I don't WANT to go to the walkthroughs, it ruins my experience almost every time)... I thought I was totally stuck in the sewer, but the answer was right in front of me. If you love point and clicks like Monkey Island and the other LucasArts games, etc then PLAY THIS GAME! Just do it! This is the first Steam game I have ever paid full price for, and not only dont I regret it... I probably would've paid more. Mark my words, this game will go down in history as one of the best point-n-click adventure games EVER. It has just the right level of difficulty, is so entertaining, and the characters are fantastic (especially Ransome). I just started Chapter 4, and I have to stop playing and go to bed now because I work tonight. I will be dreaming of Thimbleweed Park.
