I played the original Evil Within game when it came out a few years ago, soley on the pure fact that it was a survival horror game made by some of the people that worked on Resident Evil 4.  However, I was not pleased with the first game to the point I wasn't able to complete the game.
With that being said, the EVIL WITHIN 2 IS A COMPLETELY DIFFERENT EXPERIENCE.  This sequel has met and surpassed my expectations for a survival horror game.  I am a person who favors survival horror games and understand that not many get made now a days or are simply just poorly made.  If you are a person who likes to be put on the edge of your seat in tense and horrifying moments, you're not going to be disappointed at all with this game.  Below are points that I feel are important for anyone who is interested in this game to know and understand.
I'd first like to start off with what I don't think is a strong point in the game, and quite frankly, this is the only weakness of the game in my opinon.  The story of the game is nothing unique or extraordinary.  It's a simple story of unraveling a mystery behind the abduction of your daughter and show casing what your willing to do as the protagonist to save her.  So if your looking for a game where the story is out of this world or completely special, this might not be the game for you.  If you don't mind a typical Father/Detective saving loved ones, this will be a story that's good enough to easily keep you going.
NOW THE AWESOME POINTS:
Graphics of the game have been greatly improved since the original game and for the version I have (PC) I haven't had any glitches or problems.  The game runs very smooth and the controls are comfortable to utilize.
The atmosphere of this game is completely incredible, it's creepy, engaging, and most importantly diverse.  The area in which you play in is creative which allows exploring to be fun and exciting while also staying spooky.
With the world of the Evil Within 2 being so open world like, it's easy to find your self spending hours in completeing "Side Quests" and obtaining new gear and weapons.  This aspect alone increased the survival horror experience by a lot and also adds many exhilerating hours to the game.  These can also expand your knowledge of the story and give you better insight, so it's completely worth it, but again optional.
Combat in the game is very fun and well balanced between having to shoot your way out of situations or deciding that the theme of a fight is best done stealthy.  In the end result, 90% of the situations you encounter can be altered to your play style.  If you want to reserve ammo and become the Solid Snake/Sam Fisher of a horror genre, nothings stopping you.  On the other end of the spectrum, if you have been lucky or strategic enough to have maxed out ammo pouches you can go full Leon S. Kennedy style on some enemies and head shot your way through until it's safe.
A unique and well put together aspect of the game is the leveling up system.  Like the first game, there is a leveling up system that you can utilize from collecting Green Gel and improve your characters personal abilities and skills.  Nothing seems over priced and over powerful to the point where the game becomes a walk through the park.  In addition, the leveling up tree for your weapons is just as easy to use and fun.  So if character growth in the sense of skills and abilities is something you're looking for, this game nails it perfectly.
Lastly, the horror in this game is top notch.  I say this because more than often a game is titled as a horror game but in reality it's just jump scares and loud noises.  To me horror has to be greatly more than just something popping up on screen with a screech followed after it.  This game creates good old psychological/paranoid style horror.  Through out the game I played with the emotion of feeling nervous, tense, worried, hesistant, and scared.  Where there are good jump scares, there is still a sense of urgency and just wanting things to end soon type horror feel to the game which I haven't seen or felt in a long time.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game to anyone that wants a fun and different style of a survival horror game.  It has all the right elements to make this game easily worth it's price.  The time and experience put into the game can become a simple basic play it and beat it, explore and expand the game, or play it and beat it just to play it all over again with a different style.  It has great controls and graphics for all systems.  Becoming involved and immersed is fun and easily achievable.  Hope this review helps anyone who is hesitant on buying the game, especially for those who lost faith in this game because of the poor performance and rating of the first game.

While I really liked the first one, the 2nd is not as good in my opinion.  Given, it has a few artfully done levels, but they mostly gave up with the interesting new stuff after chapter 5 (of 15). There were a couple high points along the way, but not enough to keep me happy about the general gameplay, and mostly it was a grind.  They also don't build up the suspense like they did in the first.  This one was heavy on a contrived back story to fit this sequel and not a lot of mystery.  This one is more of a point to point, methodical progression than an adventurous dark thriller like the first.
I seriously hate the wonky character controls, ambulation, and animations that seem to take over the character, and generally do their own thing regardless of your input.  It really got on my nerves during critical fight scenes. There is serious mouse lag as well.  Rediculous for a shooter.  You can switch to first person but you can't look down more than about 30 degrees, and if so you can forget about picking things up at your feet unless you back up a lot.
The difficulty setting in this game does not correspond to better AI or more/harder enemies.  It only has to do with how many supplies you get to kill said enemies.  Unless you like foraging for supplies for hours to kill one zombie, I'm not sure you'll like this game.  Some enemies cannot be killed without bullets, so you jut have to avoid them (no choice if you don't have the ammo).  That does not equate to extra difficulty, its just a boring choice.  Do I save ammo for this guy, or the next?
Much worse is the fact that mini-bosses do not have unlimitted ammo spawns around them (unlike bosses).  If you are out of ammo at a mini-boss area you can literally be SOL and have to go back to an old save where you had ammo.  Then you have to play all the way back to the mini-boss conserving your ammo.  You cannot stab a mini-boss to death, or boss for that matter.
I wanted to give this game a thumbs up, but the game mechanics and lack of ammo/supplies really got in my way of having much fun.  If this review has you dithering on whether to buy it or not, I'd say its worth the $29 I payed for it on cdkeys with a coupon, but no more.  Its also not a sequel I'm going to remember in 6 months.
The combat is super streamlined, possibly to enhance the horror experience, but I find it to be extremely annoying. It's nearly impossible to kill anything early-game on normal or hard difficulty.

Pretty much everything decent about this game stops halfway through.  You like the open world part?  Gone, replaced with some very tedious corridor crawling.  Like the big bad guy?  Gone, replaced with a really tedious and cliche one.  All those skills and upgrades you were looking at in the first half of the game?  The game completely changes and makes a lot of them pointless, so hopefully you weren't investing in the wrong ones.
I really have no idea how this got reviewed so positively, other than maybe reviewers didn't play more than the first 4-5 hours.  I clocked in at 18 hours and felt like the last 8 were a total waste of time, so I felt pretty ripped off.  Save your money for something that doesn't feel like a mediocre PS2-era game with modern graphics.

My declining love for the game reached bottom in the final "interactive" cutscene in which you have two options: a) urinate on the headstone of the fallen final boss or b) ALT-F4 the game.  I just don't enjoy the direction the Broforce devs took, and for that reason, I can't recommend it.

Playing this game for the first time 17 years after its prime definitely gives me some mixed feelings. On the one hand, Teenage Me might have thought this was amazing, and similar to playing through Front Mission 3 for the first, it brought me back to that era of gaming and reminded me of some of the tropes that I wish were still around. On the other hand, I've played Kevin Lavine's latest works - seen the evolution of his directing - and while it's interesting to see the progenitor of not just the cliches found in his future games, but the industry as a whole, I feel like we could do, and have done, a lot better than what System Shock 2 has to offer.
The Gameplay
Gradually the "Shock" games evolved into strictly FPS affairs, capstoning with Infinite being the worst offender in terms of streamlining to the detriment of the gameplay, it was refreshing to see the series' earlier attempt at making itself into something unique. The first person perspective being sort of incidental, System Shock 2 feels like a Survival horror game with RPG elements. There is a lot of flavor that got mixed into Bioshock, but crucial elements such as managing your resources and constantly being hungry for ever-consuming energy helps keep the tension at a level that I don't think its spiritual successor managed to achieve. Without the hand holding of objectives being marked visibly on your map, or the railroading of cinematic breakages in Rapture, the focus here feels entirely on the exploration of the Ship where the game takes place, rather than the slightly more combat oriented Bioshock.
Remember how I said the combat was the weakest part about the first Bioshock? Some of my thoughts about how to make it better would be to slow down the pace of the enemies to make it more cerebral rather than feeling too much like an arcade shooting gallery. Well, System Shock 2 has lumbering slow enemies, that gradually lift their weapons up, giving you plenty of time to react - most of the time anyway. It just feels better for the setting - especially considering how wonky the inventory controls are. If you're not equipped with the right ammo, rather than auto-loading it in with the flick of a switch, you almost have to find a safe corner to open the menu and get it set right. It gives it a better feel of realism - in a gamey sense. In speaking of special ammo, because ammo is in such short supply the armor piercing and flesh tearing types actually surve a purpose than just fodder to take over when you run out of the standard stuff. Making every shot count will make or break your game, especially considering your guns wear down toward breaking when you fire them.
It's fun. It's unique. I miss this kind of thing. Bioshock 1 is close, so very close, but I think in terms of gameplay tying in with the atmosphere, System Shock 2 is the superior game.
Is it perfect? Heck no. It could use another sequel. They just didn't change the right things when they made Bioshock. Only time will tell if System Shock 3 really gets it.
The Story
The strongest point of Bioshock 1... is sadly System Shock 2's weak point for me. I'll start off by saying that there is nothing wrong with System Shock 2's story. It just feels like a classic archetypical villain vs. protagonist story - now predictable plot twists aside. There are some interesting things to see, and it's still fun to find all the journal tapes to hear about the plight of the ship's crew, but as a jaded gamer who's been through two other titles by the same director, as well as several other games that I clearly see were ripping System Shock 2 off, I'm afraid there wasn't much that surprised me.
The villain feels like a great demon from a typical mythology, and their treachery runs no deeper than the shallow pool their personality is written from. I never felt like I understood the villain, it was more of a man vs. nature type conflict. The idea of the many is admittedly much more interesting (and more realistic) than pheromone controlled crazies that still apparently have their basic personalities. But overall it feels like a dungeon crawl - our hero going to face Diablo - and then making a 90s action movie style final quip in the story's climax. The villain was scary, but I think a little more character development at least on the part of the victims would have made it all powerful.
So which game do I like more? I'm going to have to give it to Bioshock.
I do think System Shock 2 is great, and I'd recommend it, especially if you want to check out some late 90s game design that really needs to be revisited.

This is a wonderful program, especially for the price, that fills an important need. The reviewers complaining about the lack of fine details are missing the point: textbooks contain as much fine detail as anybody could want, and physiology too, but they are relatively poor at showing overall anatomical context, and how everything relates to each other and the body as a whole. That's exactly where this program comes in and shines. It provides a wealth of tools to visualize the systems you're interested in, including the ability to hide or shade elements so as to be be able to hone in (or out) to see exactly what you want. Being able to move the model around brings those spacial relations to life. It's excellent as a study aid or as an educational tool for basic anatomy. There are tools supporting all of these purposes too: including basic but accurate descriptions for all of the parts, the ability take notes on things, draw on the image, and save it for later. This makes it useful for a wide range of people, from the curious 12 (or 40) year old, to educators, to students wanting to supplement their textbooks.
At the time of this writing, it does have a few rough edges, but nothing show stopping at all (not staying in fullscreen mode is the most frustrating thing to me). Some additional things would be nice, like being able to shade whole systems at once, or especially having a proper female model. But those are minor complaints given how much functionality is already in place, and this program accomplishes it's core goal of anatomy visualization quite well.
If you or somebody you know is actively interested in anatomy, i would recommend just getting it. The price is worth it (would you spend as much or more on a book?) Otherwise wait for a sale perhaps, but definitely consider supporting this project. It's pretty cool stuff.
Honestly, my biggest complaint is that this didn't exist 20 years ago. Medis Media really dropped the ball on that one ;-) (Seriously, y'all are awesome, thank you!)

This is probably some of the best money I've ever spent. I'm an EMT and have been trying to brush up on my anatomical knowledge, and this app has helped me learn more in two hours than countless hours of textbook and classroom-based rote-memorization ever could. Being a kinesthetic learner, I can't speak highly enough about the ability to isolate various bodily tissues and organ systems and study their relationships with each another.
Also, being able to physically manipulate an accurately scaled and fully interactive anatomical model has helped me considerably with learning the true size and orientation of various body parts and organs, which has always been difficult since my spatial reasoning is generally pretty poor.
For general study and academic pursuits this app is a quite literally a life-saver. I purchased this app while it was on sale but even at full price it's practically theft. Definitely cannot recommend this highly enough for anybody in the medical field.
TL;DR 10/10, probably the best 3D anatomy sim currently on the market.

TL;DR: I love this game but it has horribly unbalanced characters, bosses that require specific characters to do well, "difficulty" that makes it stupid and ruins the fun, and certain things that can kill you through your 'spawn-in invincibility', which is either lazy programming or a terrible idea.
I'd like the start off this review by saying most of the game is AWESOME. I really really love this game, or at least I would like to. See, this game suffers from two problems: horribly unbalanced characters/bosses, and a badly done "difficulty" increase. So, most characters are great, some are amazing, and I'd bet that each boss has one character that does really well against it. Then there are the other characters, the horribly ♥♥♥♥♥♥, nigh unusable characters that make you hate whatever RNG god had a beef with you on that run. Anyways, the game is supposed to be hard, but as it stands the harder levels are not harder in a fun way, they are harder in a way that you can be instantly killed by any one of the swarms of enemies that attack you, in a manner that just makes you want to stop playing. There's no dodging or smart plays involved, in the later levels you usually end up dying via cheap gimmicks. The last levels also feel unpolsihed, I've had static blocks of the bosses appear where they're supposed to spawn in later, parts of the background disappear, and just in general it feels less interesting than the original levels. The early-to-midgame bosses are made so that pretty much every class can beat them if you play it right. The late bosses are made so that certain characters deal insane amounts of damage and are literally the only way to win. The entire Satan boss fight is dumb, from start to finish. The way the level is desgined compared to how he plays makes it seem like it could be fun, but stupid mistakes related to how your character moves nad how he attacks end up with yet another restart. The second level of the Satan boss fight (and many other lategame bosses) involves him firing a wall of fireballs that are impassable and irritating to dodge. Then he summons giant fire snakes moving at high sped with little warning that can kill you regardless of whether you have that 'spawn invincibility' thing. You heard that right, there are things in the game that can bipass your only way to get back into the fight, with no ability to doge it because you jsut spawned in. Also, you have to get more lives by waiting for them to spawn in, but most of the time they just get killed by the boss' attacks and you end up dying and losing yet another life for trying. This is not how difficulty works, this is not how bosses work, this is not fun. I would actually love it if their next update brought in more maps and bosses like the original, because that was actually fun. The aliens and the hellscape were cool looking and intersting in theory, but instead were sometimes just painful to go through. So here's my lengthy thoughts, if anyone bothers to read it all. I really like this game and the kind of difficulty it starts out with, as well as the abiltiy to either play it really smart and tactical or just hold down the fire button the whole time. It's just got some bad features that break the entire experience for me, and did so every time I redid the campaign (I completed it every once in a while, and did a full playthrough on full realease, and now I'm stuck on the Satan fight in Hard mode, a mode which relaly has no effect on a lot of the gameplay, only giving the mooks slightly enhanced attacks).

It's honestly not horrible. The game however doesn't hold up to Skyrim, the system of spells and quests is a little wonky. The graphics aren't really any better than Skyrim, and ontop of all that there are minor things that just kill it.
-Armor no matter the kind slows you down in no way.
-The combat is repetetive and very lacking
-Enemies have the most limited AI I've seen for a while.
Those are just a few pet peeves of mine but they're very noticeable. The things that also get on my nerves they almost got right.
-Weapons and armor take damage only when you die, it should be hard work to keep your gear in good shape.
-Spells and skills, it's not a horrible system but it needs work.
Apart from those few things I only have good things to say.
*Character creation, it's by far one of most expansive-evening allowing you to adjust height.
*Story line, while I'm not very far in the story I've enjoyed it so far.
*Dialogue is clear and immersive for the most part, there are a few occasions where it's not.
That's my personal take on the game. It's not for everyone and honestly I haven't played in a while and it's failed to draw me back. I am a die hard bethesda fan and I understand that online games like ESO are hard to get right, but they could improve if they listened to their fans. So I recommend the game, but keep in mind it may not be for you.

I give this game a big thumbs up and a nomination for the "Wow, dude!" category, because it simply deserves it!
First of, we need to take into account that the first Half-Life game get released back in 1998, running on a heavily modded Quake engine, which Valve named the "GoldSRC/GoldSource" engine.
Half-Life was a great success for it's long playing time without losing your attention, intricate puzzles and for that time something that was quite radical: no cutscenes.
Now, we can relive the game that we might call the blueprint of modern FPS games in a quality that makes it interesting for newcomers to play
You have to take into account that the Source Engine was first released back in 2004, and even though it got some updates, it's still an old engine. Yet this game delivers a graphics quality of which I thought the Source Engine could never deliver, but it does! And the best of it is that you don't even need a killer of a pc for pretty decent graphics!
Back in 1998 when basically everything in a computer was limited, maps couldn't get as big and advanced as what's possible now. Thanks to the Source Engine, maps now look much nicer and puzzled could be recycled in a much better way as the Havok Physics engine allows you to do much more.
I also love the swing of what the developers gave to some of the maps to make them more exciting.
Joel, you're a genius. The soundtrack is just perfect and suits the entire game well. Especially Blast Pit 3 and Forget About Freeman, which foreshadows what's about to come if you listen closely to them.

I'm a latecomer to the System Shock 2 party, only just recently playing and finishing it 16 years after it's original release. Despite it's old age, I can confidently say that SS2 holds up extremely well, like many other Looking Glass classics. It's a phenominal cyberpunk RPG adventure that presents a wonderful and perilous world for players to get lost in. I'm a sucker for games that reward thorough exploration, and System Shock 2 is pretty much the perfect game for just that.
But be forewarned, newcomers, as parts of SS2 may feel antiquated in today's gaming climate: dated graphics, clunky combat, complex inventory management and item maintenance, and a generally brutal difficulty. If your willing to give the game a chance, however, you'll find that those complexities and old school quirks are exactly what make System Shock 2 such a terrifying and awesome experience.

The game holds up great with some graphical mods installed but still impressing in the gameplay department, while the game may be hard to get into if you don't read into the stats and info kiosks than the game can be really hard to get into for first timers, other than that the game is still miles ahead of modern gaming, please buy this and be patient if you are a new comer beacause once it clicks...... There is nothing else quite like it

Excellent. While this was made for those who always loved the classic LucasArts adventure games, it really should appeal to anyone who wants a game that truly feels like soulful art coming from an individual/small team. This game has personality. It's akin to an interactive book from your favorite author VS a mainstream Hollywood production that's passed through 1000 hands.
It 100% captures the spirit of an old LucasArts adventure game, in the best way possible, and I am honestly more drawn to it than many of my AAA games I still haven't finished. It's hard to put down, because it's just so enjoyable to experience the world, characters, and story. This game is pure joy, and while it will absolutely appeal to any and every old school adventure game player I can't imagine it wouldn't appeal to anyone open to a good, unique game. It's not for the ADD inclined fancy graphics, shooter crowd. And while I love those too, this sort of game is an absolute lost art and I'm convinced if more people experienced it, the genre would make a resurgence. It's funny, it's witty, it's entertaining, it's smart, and THANK GOD - the return of the LucasArt's adventure game is back.
Everything I had hoped it would turn out to be, and honestly, I think a bit more. Big thumbs up.

Just finished the game. I liked it.
One of the first video games that I ever played was Monkey Island 1 and I was hooked on LucasArt's point and clicks after that. I've ultimately played the entire adventure game catalog from LucasArts.
This game is like the old LucasArts never went away and kept the SCUMM engine alive. The puzzles in this game are a lot more logical than the older games and the overall game sees the benefit of having veteren adventure game developers make the game.
The story is overall pretty interesting though maybe some weak parts at the end. The interesting story and puzzles carry the game. The humor isn't quite as strong when compared to the older, more cartoony point and clicks. It's got the same kind of quirky and tongue-in-cheek absurdity of Full Throttle I'd say. The story this time is a mystery and that's probably what dicated the feel of the game. The older games were never shy about referencing other games, but this game definitely pushes the references harder; maybe a bit too much. Still, if you like the LucasArt's point and clicks, this is a no-brainer recommendation.
p.s. For those that might not know or remember, the "." button lets you fast forward through text in the game, like the old LucasArts stuff. I wish they let us map this to a different keyboard button though, since it's a bit awkward with it being away from the other shortcut keys (i.e. q, w, e, a, s, d, z, x, c)

I know you probaby heard terrible things about this game and about how awful the AI is and how terrible the textures were. But have you ever thought why the game has the words 'Emperor Edition' at the end of it now almost a year after being released simply as Total War Rome II?
The words 'Emperor Edition' denote to the player that Creative Assembly have patched the game to the state that they want us to experience the game. This is clear given that CA have been patching the game weekly for several months since its release. I will be frank with you, reader. When I first got this game I was excited, very excited. Sadly, the AI was dumb and the game was near broken. I gave up on it. I recently picked it up again, questioning what 'Emperor Edition' meant, and now I know that the game, without mods mind you, is coherent, and not only playable but enjoyable.
If you enjoy strategy games, if you are fascinated by history, I recomend that you play this game at once.
Be warned, however, the game is not perfect. It does feature its fair share of glitches, loading time extensions, AI foolishness, historical inaccuracy, and HUD annyoance. But the majority of these problems are solved through the harmless instalation of mods such as 'Radious' from the steam workshop.
Happy conquering, and as always, ROMA VICTOR!

-Weapons and armor take damage only when you die, it should be hard work to keep your gear in good shape.

Apart from those few things I only have good things to say.

The Evil Within 2: an incredibly enjoyable horror game that suffers from all of the same issues the original had - and more.
The Evil WIthin 1 was an amalgamation of many other horror games all brought together in a janky mess with crazy pacing issues, a ridiculous story, constant gameplay shifts, and not a single likable character. That being said, I still absolutely adored the mess that it was. It was up there with RE4 for me in terms of the action-horror genre.
The Evil Within 2 follows all of the exact same trends the first game has, but now throws smaller "open-world" segments in, more characters that are still not written well enough to enjoy, even more awkward character animations, a more simplified and understandable narrative (for better or worse), even worse writing than the first, and they doubled down on the upgrade system making weapon crafting a large mechanic.
Most of those seem like cons, right? Well, much like the first, I still inexplicable loved almost every second of the game. Yes, the antagonist's plans are all poorly thought out and pretty stupid. Yes, STEM should have been dropped by the "big bad" the second it all went to♥♥♥♥♥♥in the first game. Yes, "THEY'RE ALL STILL ALIVE" is a dumb excuse to bring us back in. Yes, the character interactions are all absolutely hilarious to listen/watch with how fake and cliched it all is. And, yes the Open-World elements definitely hurt the game more than help push it along, but all of those negatives I can't help enjoy. It's a really rough game with lots of ideas borrowed from other properties and thrown together in a melting pot of horror B-Movie cliche's that I can't help cheering on.
Where this game, and the first, truly shine are in the really cool use of the environment and set piece moments during the heavily linear segments of the game. Tight quarters, low ammo reserves, lots of enemies everywhere, crazy psychological mind-♥♥♥♥ery going on to skew your perspective around. It's all really cool and comes together to create an incredible mixture of Silent Hill-esque environments with the action gameplay of the later Resident Evil games. The best of both horror genre worlds.
This isn't to say I love everything about the game, mind you. The enemy AI is abosolutely garbage and that shows more than ever in the open-world sections. Crouching in a bush is instant invisibility, most enemies leash after barely walking 20 feet away, entering any door drops all enemies from following and makes them turn around.
The writing, even though I did enjoy it for how bad it is, is equally horribly frustrating with how good it *could* be. There's a lot of really awesome set pieces and moments that could be a lot more enjoyable with better narrative moments and character interactions to invest in you what's going on. As it stands, at least it is all still great to laugh at.
The bosses in this one were almost all a letdown. While the first one had a lot of *VERY* memorable enemies that all were really cool physical manifestaions of Ruvik's psyche, this one only had a small handful of memorable boss fights. On top of that this game, as a whole, was a much easier romp through the game. While maybe not a con for some I would have enjoyed being tested as a player a bit more during boss fights.
Going back to Ruvik, the main antagonists in this game are pretty much all "Evil for the sake of evil". While Ruvik himself was definitely evil, he had a ton of build up and explanation throughout the entire game as you wandered further and further into his mind. Seeing Ruvik's life unfold over the course of the original game providing answers as to why the envoronment looks/behaves was really damn cool and provided the game with an incredibly interesting character that the player got to understand. This is a game that by rights should never have existed. Most other publishers would have sent their lawyers after it, with a relative few tolerating its existence as a fan work. Valve not only chose to keep the lawyers at bay, but approved the game as a Steam Greenlight title, and ultimately even allowed the developers to license the Source engine and put Black Mesa on the Steam store as a purchasable produce. So as far as getting a legal release, the game beat the odds, but was it all worth it?
Absolutely!
Despite the ambitious scale of the task for a group of hobbyists spread around the globe, Black Mesa did not end up being a vaporware failure or a disappointment. The efforts of the dedicated team resulted in a reimagining of Half-Life that rivals Valve's own quality standards for their games. They pushed the limits of the Source SDK as far as they could, creating visuals that are comparable to recent Source engine titles. Scripted sequences are further fleshed out, giving the various scientists and security staff far more personality and dialogue than they ever had in the original game. Levels were reworked to provide more sensible layouts, while still maintaining the feel of the original environments.
There are some flaws--or at least there were in the free mod version I played. A couple of areas were cut short--a little too short in at least one section. Combined with a balance issue in which human enemies were tougher than the alien invaders were, some of the in-game action was inconsistent with the narrative. Some of these issues may have been fixed. I was so happy with the free version, that I purchased Black Mesa as soon as it became available for sale, but am waiting for the eventual release of Xen before fully replaying it. In the meantime, my understanding is that the developers have restored some cut content, and have been continuing to improve visuals as they continue to work toward the final release. If they also rework some of the AI to make the aliens a more credible threat to the human soldiers, then even the few flaws I found with the game will be a thing of the past. But even with the flaws I experienced in the free version, and even with the absence of the Xen portion of the game, it's absolutely worth the price. Despite the game not technically being complete, it ends at a very good point for a natural cliffhanger, so it's a satisfying narrative even in the absence of Xen.
For anyone who is interested in Half-Life but has trouble dealing with the dated visuals and '90s style gameplay, Black Mesa will allow you to experience a greatly enhanced version of the original Half-Life that treats the source material (pardon the pun) with the utmost respect. And for those who played and loved the original Half-Life, Black Mesa is a great way to revisit the Half-Life universe. The experience is so lovingly crafted, it's easy to forget it wasn't made by Valve. Even without the inclusion of Xen, the Crowbar Collective made a game that's worth every penny and more. And with the eventual release of Xen on the horizon, Black Mesa promised to get even better.

First off I am not a fan of horror survival games but since this was Alien i had to try it out.  And i must say I am glad I did.  If i had not gotten this game on sale I would have gladly paid the full price for it.  The game is great looking, attention to detail is fantastic, sounds are key in this game and they feel true to the senario and also source material.
I don't agree with the one negative comment alot of people say about having to backtrack too much.  Yes you do go back through certain areas a few times (not ALOT) but its different on your way back things are usually different and also it makes it easier because you know the area a bit, you know there is a hiding spot there or a vent over there so it makes traversing these areas a bit easier especially when your tense and wondering why that Alien just seems to love you so much and wont leave you alone.  The backtracking felt needed also due to the objectives and the layout of the station.  Its a space station without backtracking through it and going through the same areas the game would feel WAY too linear.  There is a good amount of extra exploration but thats not needed unless you feel the need to do so.  The save system is nice I think the save points are well spaced.  And yes you can die while saving...takes 3 seconds to save during which you are a sitting duck but luckily the save device does give a warning to nearby hostiles.  I only died once during a save and that was cuz i got freaked out and the save spot was right next to me...i thought i could make it....
The interaction is great, specially if your using a keyboard, pressing the buttons on the security scanner really brought me into the game, along with other things like having to hold down mouse buttons to grab a lever and actually pull it myself, not just "press interaction key"  and watch an animation.  The game is very tense, makes you feel very vulnerable even when you are armed to the teeth.  Also the story is more indepth then I thought at first, its not just you on a station with an Alien and I will just leave it at that.
Again another complaint people had was that the game turns into a FPS at one point.... I think they are stretching this idea ALOT.  Yes you do have to kill a few androids and such but its not that bad and it makes sense in the game.  Personally I think it would be stupid to not have you use the weapons you have for something like this.  You spent all this time running in the shadows now you have a nice change of pace where you are still in danger but you can atleast take on a few androids. Honestly the way some people worded this part of the game I was expecting a massive shoot out or something.  Its NOTHING like that, its not even that big of an area  It works for the game, its probably not in line with a strict survival horror game, but for this game I think this mechanic works well.  The entire game is about you being in a situation your trying to survive....well  this fits the bill in my opinion.
To sum up its a great game, great story, great length,tense, perfect for an Alien fan even if you dont like this genre of game.  Highly recommend checking it out at some point.  Is it actually one of the best Alien games I have played.

The game crashed every time I ran it and froze my computer completely (Win 7 sp2). I got a new computer (not to play the game) with Win 8.1 and now it runs fine. The game is an odd mixture of good and bad characteristics. It has high quality graphics, sound and music, but some of the movement options one normally expects with a game of this sort just aren't there-- for instance, Ripley can't jump or climb, and her running speed is pedestrian. There is no "quick save" feature either, so one is constantly replaying segments that ended in untimely death.
After one gets through the first 3 or so introductory segments one meets the alien. From then on the alien is always nearby. No matter how far Ripley travels by transport or how stealthily she moves, the alien magically knows where she is, and frequently appears just on the other side of a door in the opposite direction from where it was headed (according to the motion tracker).  When one finally succeeds in eluding the alien long enough to make it to the mission destination, the reason for moving there is not easily found, again allowing Mr. Alien to show up and end any search activities.
The other issue is that the game is clearly based on the movies, and in the movies the basic hunter-killer alien isn't impregnable. Their power came through numbers and stealth. In this game the alien tromps around openly and noisily and Ripley seems powerless to hurt it even though she appears to have a .357 magnum revolver.  The other jarring note is that 1970's technology shows up all over this futuristic space station. At first it just seems odd, but then it becomes irritating. It is currently 2015 and nobody uses cassette tape recorders anymore, so why would they figure prominently in the future?
I found the game to be tense and exciting the first few times I had to elude the alien, but then it just became tedious and unrewarding.

System Shock 2 is a classic and still holds up today despite dated graphics (the game is good enough that you don't even care about the graphics though). But it's not for the faint of heart.
Considered one of the games that spawned the FPS/RPG genre, although it's more survival-horror based than trigger-happy shoot-em up FPS. Weapons literally break down after extended use and bullets are not easy to come by (unless you saved your "money" and can buy a ton). The gameplay is more complex than modern shooters which requires you to manage your limited inventory, research your enemies, maintain weapons, engage fight or flight mode, strategically plan out your character build, and so on.
As said, it's not for the faint of heart. The atmosphere is dark and monstrosities randomly respawn to keep you paranoid and on your toes. Add to that a storyline and a twist that provides even more creepiness to the surrounding context as you courageously progress.
I recommend System Shock 2 to those who like to be emotionally challenged or want gameplay that's more involved than what is found in most games today. Also recommended to those who enjoy survival horror elements in a game.

It's absurdly difficult for me to review Dishonored 2 such that I can pick Recommend: Yes or No, but the current
average on Steam I think isn't far off. There are so many good points to the game, offset by some significant bad points. It's such a huge pity that the game wasn't given longer in post-production polish. Where to begin...
The performance issues have been done to death by many reviewers both user & critic, but suffice it to say that at time of writing, the 1.1 patch and associated driver updates have helped, but the game still struggles on a reasonable PC. Even the credits stuttered, which is a sign something just isn't quite right with the engine. For a full price AAA title this is unacceptable. Since I got the game in a 50% sale, I can justify it to myself, but still, it's irritating to deal with the performance troubles throughout what is otherwise a gorgeous fun game. Throw in a fair number of bugs, some subtle and some more obvious, and the experience is like someone whispering all throughout a movie; one never quite gets to stop noticing the technical difficulties and just enjoy the game.
I truly wanted to love Dishonored 2, and the game has been mostly fun to play. When you play the few fascinating levels, or try out new combinations of powers, or just listen to Emily's story unfold, it's clear that the developers tried to put their heart and souls into the game as much as the first time around. It's a game that might miss the mark in places, but tries so hard to win you back any time you feel disappointed, you can't help but smile and give it another chance. I can imagine that I'll play it again, exploring alternative levels of chaos, playing as Corvo or the New Game+ with both sets of abilities, and just enjoying romping through levels experimenting. The world built is a delight, one that I'm glad to return to after Dishonored, and I hope to see more of it in future; even if a Dishonored 3 might be pushing things for the same protagonists, I probably wouldn't care and just be happy to get more of the same.
The game experience itself is well structured, with good level design, interesting mechanics, and a variety of choices in how to approach & disrupt the world. Two levels in particular stood out as really cleverly put together; it's therefore unfortunate that other levels are just... mundane when contrasted with the incredible variety the original Dishonored provided. There's nothing akin to Lady Boyle's party or the assassins of the flooded district; the protagonist is almost always initially confronted with guards, a checkpoint, a black market shop, and some ways around the checkpoint, as just one example of the design's predictability. The feel of Dunwall in chaos, the depth of the Rat Plague, the loudspeaker announcements, the backstory of random citizens, the amusing banter of guards - it's all missing - Karnaca in the sequel struggles to feel alive, as though a few NPCs saying 'things are bad' makes you empathise with them. There's no end of notes and newspapers and lore to discover; the world is still
to get you to connect with it, and if you let your imagination run free, you can find yourself drifting into it; it's just not as polished an effort.
Gone too are the relatively exciting side characters. Dishonored provided an interesting cast in the Loyalists, with different viewpoints, conversations, and interactions, as well as Slackjaw & Granny Rags. The sequel provides just two characters that have very little depth; even as the meager backstory of Meagan unfolds, it feels like so much more could have been made of it. The main plot itself is a thrilling ride of a revenge tale, and I'd personally recommend playing Emily as it feels much more personal an experience as a result - the lack of the surrounding backstories and rather less exposition of the world runs the risk that the story feels flat against a two-dimensional painting, rather than the full world that Dishonored managed to convey.
The targets, our rogues gallery to eliminate, similarly lack depth; they are mostly caged in small areas of their level, interacting with nobody, evoking little in the way of emotions (themselves or in the player). Kirin Jindosh's taunting genius goes some way to salvaging this, but when compared to the likes of the despicable Pendleton twins of the original, there's rather less satisfaction in their removal. It's barely clear who they are beyond that they helped to really inconvenience you during the lacklustre intro of 'surprise, coup!' at the start of the game (which cried out for far more foreshadowing opportunity). One key area I was disappointed to see lacking investment was disposing of them - the non-lethal approaches are simple & handed to you, and though the game offers many interesting weapons with which to kill, there's no nod towards even a chance to make their deaths seem like accidents. For a game invested heavily in offering stealth, none of these individuals even stray near a convenient third-floor balcony, let alone the original's moments such as a karmic use of a target's poisoned drink.
Despite lacking as many interesting characters, the voice acting for them is mostly top notch. I'm so glad to hear Stephen Russell & Terri Brosius in a game which is practically an homage to
, and Erica Luttrell really brings Emily to life; it was a bit of a disappointment that they couldn't get Billy Lush for the Outsider, as the difference is rather noticeable. Audio can behave a little strangely, with characters sounding like they're behind you when they're in front, but for the most part the sounds are very good. The music seems lacking in some way compared to the original; it's closer to background ambience than the more interesting scores present and used to highlight events in the original, and the game doesn't feel as alive as a result.
Where Dishonored 2 exceeds its predecessor is in the gameplay itself. Stealth is dramatically improved, taking into account lighting, broken objects, open doors, as well as line of sight & sound playing more of a role. The mixture of weapons, upgrades and powers has been expanded & varies nicely depending on whether you play Emily or Corvo, and all the same fun interactions remain feasible as in the original. The AI is smarter, with more varied opponents, and if you play as a stealth or ghost game with all the easy-mode markers & Dark Vision turned off, you can really crank the difficulty up while still seeming believable. The replayability offered is definitely higher with a range of consequences for your major choices through the levels (not just high and low chaos), though the endings leave a little to be desired, with twenty seconds of flat, oddly ordered, exposition being all you get before credits roll. Contrast with the original touching credits as 'Honor For All' starts to play, and the sequel's approach feels tacked together, like a producer said 'oh, don't forget the ending slides, say some blah blah about what happened'.
To bring this review to a conclusion, the harshness of my critique stems from how great the game feels like it
have been. Dishonored was a superb title worthy of Game Of The Year, one that I played a second time
, and twice more since, building a world I fell in love with. Dishonored 2 is a pedestrian sequel, plagued by technical difficulties, with less polished an experience. The game's problems smack of rushed deadlines & lower production values, and yet, the world within the game is struggling so hard to come out, to show what it can be, to give the player a superb and immersive time. I'd be doing a disservice to the great game beneath the technical difficulties if I didn't say Yes, give it a go, even if you wait for a discount.

After about 100 hours on this game I would definitely suggest it to everyone is looking for a hardcore game.
I also played Dark Souls 1, and, compared to the first episode, I found this one a little easier on the first steps, with difficulty raising smoothly without big hard points (Sen's Fortress anyone?). If Dark Souls was defined "Hard" I would define Dark Souls 2 "Challenging", it's different, because there is less frunstration and more challenge, naturally. I am not a fan of fantasy games, with mages, dragons, spells and stuff, but Dark Souls 2 allows you to develop your character the way you want it, and if you want to try a different build, there is the option to reallocate your skill points. I am talking about skill points like every other RPG, sure, but in Dark Souls 2 your success on the field is not dependent only on your stats, but also on your skills. you could have 99 of every point, but if you don't know, for example, when to dodge a sword thrust from an enemy, you will die anyways, naked or with a stainless steel armor +5. And the only way to raise your skill is practising, trying new combat styles until you find the one that fits you them most. But remember, maybe the next boss requires a completely different style. So don't fear death, and keep trying until you see the health bar of the boss reaching 0, and then, before any kind of reward, like souls (currency) or items, you will feel great, powerful, because you finally slain that damned boss. This is My favourite aspect of Dark Souls, 1 and 2. I would definitely give it a 10/10

Oh and they reused a lot of voices, for the same kinds of personalities of characters from Dark Souls 1, but for characters who aren't the same ones in DS1. RavenField while being a single player-only Early Access game, it doesen't fail to impress but nor is it perfect.
Despite the game currently having only four maps, 3 game modes and some weapons RavenField is a fun casual game to play when you're bored or just wanting to make things explode and shoot ragdol enemies.
What I enjoy about playing the game is the large-scale battles. both teams attempts to rush ahead and capture as many objectives as possible to win against the other team and this usualy turns into a large open conflict with tanks, infanty and even aircraft, mix this in with the challanging AI difficulty and you have quite a brutal combat game where just a few bullets will kill you dead.
While only being a single-player game the AI isnt stupid like the AI in games like fallout, call of duty or some other games. The AI will drop Ammunition and medications for their teammates (And you)  in the heat of battle, they'll take cover and even flank enemy objectives. The AI knows how to use vehicles but i wouldn't say they're the smartest as i will commonly see a enemy tank , jeep or quad drive directly into my team's obejctive which involves them getting easily surrounded and blown to bits with Anti-Tank Equipment. The AI in the air is slightly diffrent as they actually do bombing runs against the enemy's objectives and positions but air units can always be brought down very quickly using missiles or a flak turret. Hell, sometimes Anti-Tank units are smart enough to fire an unguided rocket at you if you're flying low enough in an aircraft.
Currently there are 3 game modes, two are very simular and can be described as conquest from the Battlefield Series, Capture the objectives and eliminate the other team's "Battalions" until they have no soldiers left. the last game mode is currently a "preview" but it seems to put you in command of 3 soldiers who follow you and i believe you have to attack an enemy objective and if you or you're soldiers die then they're dead.
There's a decent ammount of diffrent weapons and some equipment which offers a versitile selection of gear to choose from, whether you want to be a sniper or a close up and personal maniac with a shotgun or a mix between the two.
Map selection feels limited at the moment as there's only four maps (two small, two large) but this may not be an issue if/when Custom Map Support is released in the future.
For being a somewhat non-expencive early-access game RavenField is a quite an enjoyable game to play, even casualy. The game shows alot of promise and I hope the developer continues adding new features into the game in the future.
Should you get it? If you have the money and looking for a casual game like this, give it a try.

Wow, I just finished the game, and all of the alternate endings as well.  What a great, bittersweet ride!
I read many of the reviews of this game, and most of them were very positive.  Still, many were really picky and negative as well.
Let me start by saying I've been playing RPG's since the beginning (the Ultima series on C-64 type of beginning - yes, they were on Apple first... blah blah..).
While those games were groundbreaking, they also involved quite a bit of 'grinding'.  It appears to be the norm from then until now.
There is a decent bit of grinding to be done to get your armor and weapons up to spec for the battle, but it's nothing like WoW grinding.  All of the rooms appear to refresh after you leave and come back, so it's pretty easy to find a room that has several monsters in it, and not too many obstacles, and just go in, knock them out, leave, and repeat.  What's worse, grinding to get up to spec, or getting trashed by the boss?  ;)
Yes, there are grammatical errors throughout the game.  Let's just say that Holy Priest speaks (or writes) better English than most of us can speak (or write) his/her language.  If you're a nitpicky person that is deeply disturbed by grammatical errors, then just move along, after all, you wouldn't want to experience a fun and not too deep RPG with a nice story and great artwork that's also free, right?
I thought the story line, cut scenes, and overall gameplay were superb!  It's meant to be simple, and even the toughest boss (for me, anyway) only took 3 tries to kill.  There's enough armor and weapon crafting to make it interesting, but not overboard.  Again, all pretty simple, and very entertaining.  There are plenty of save spots, and other than not being able to make it to the 'exit' screen from in the game, I think it all went pretty well.  I ended up hitting the windows key and ending the game once it was minimized by right clicking on the icon on the windows bar and selecting close.  All of my saves worked fine, etc.
The music was nice, and it didn't get in the way, or get annoying, and the sound effects were simple and effective.  The artwork was top notch, and the graphics are reminders of RPG days gone by, and I mean that in a good way!
If you're looking to play some RPG's, but don't have a lot of time to invest, then this game is a must.  You can simply save in the save areas (which are pretty common), or you can do a couple of red-eye's like I did and finish it in 2 sittings.
I also appreciated that you can get to the other endings without replaying the entire game!
There is always room for improvement, and that's with all games.  To think that this much work was put into a game and then offered for free - it's a really nice thing to happen for gamers.  It's not ALWAYS about the money, and that's refreshing.
Big thanks to Holy Priest for taking the time, and making this little gem.  I'd love to find a place where you could contact the author and send suggestions, alternate phrasing and words, etc. if only to keep the nitpicker's happy, or at least quieter...
I have not played Ragnarok Online, which this game is influenced by / based on, but I'm interested in trying it out now.
Anyway, this game was very fun to play, the grinding wasn't insane, (and it was pretty simple), and the storyline is happy and sad.  Bittersweet.  I enjoyed it thorougly!

After just under an hour of playing, I'm afraid I couldn't take 'Eternal Senia' any more.
An interesting, yet incomprehensible game with characters and plot that feel like they were cut out from cardboard, game design more backhanded than a Rakshasa and all put to the most baffling musical scoring I have ever encountered.
The game's writing is full of contrivances, grammatical errors and scenes that are either unneccessary or perhaps just a little bit too long.
I remember a key instance where an elf showed up in my path, armed with a bow and arrow. Immediately I saw that the bridge I was stood on was wide enough to sidestep their attack, and that they had a missile nocked and ready to fire, but the game decided that Senia hadn't fulfilled her moping quota yet and needed to strain out a tutorial disguised as poor character development, instead of me just knocking the forest dweller onto his silken britches.
The gameplay is fundementally flawed, if at times entirely broken. The key to interaction here seems to be a unique, action-oriented combat system in which mobile foes wander around aimlessly on a grid, until you walk up to them in order to initiate an auto-attack, slicing them to peices with your sword. However, attacking has a high chance to knock you back one space (Though not into hazards like trips and traps, because that would be engaging), and very quickly it devolves into 'Butt Heads with Creepy Mc. Crawly #394 encounting'.
Bosses tend to shake things up a bit more than regular grunts, with actual attack patterns that force you to move around the arena instead of just bumping into them repeatedly, but they're all far too easy and exploitable to see the full potential of this system. The first boss in particular, was a dragon with a mighty breath weapon... and an arthritic neck. I slew him easily by moving up to his left flank and carving it into wyrm-burgers.
There are also puzzles - which are nearly all beatable from brute force - traps that pose little to no threat when your Hit Points regenerates faster than lightning and a crafting system that aims to releive frustration, but this is mitigated by the overly fast pace and the fact that a girl I found in a magical forest, deep within a ethereal kingdom of swords and sorcery knows what 'Facebook' is.

JumpBall took the indie dev scene by storm. With exciting, innovative mechanics and a colorful design, it was an impressive and enduring experience for gamers of all ages and backgrounds.
With the announcement of JumpBall 2, many fans were skeptical as to how the original could possibly be improved upon. As a die-hard JumpBall fan myself, I admit I was unsure alongside them.
Then I played the game.
JumpBall 2 has done it again, folks. The same characters we've come to know and love take on a brand new challenge, and with new ways to play. The addition of the midair jump added an entirely new dimension to the gameplay, making levels that are as challenging as they are fun to play. The level design is polished and robust, mirroring the likes of its predecessors while acheiving a new flair only this studio could imagine. The black ninja adversaries gave more depth to the characters and lore of the world, making me want to learn more about the ninja history.
Earning my diploma was no small feat. Life after life was lost completing each and every level of the game, yet every time I felt like I was at fault for dying, and in no way felt like the game cheated me out of a finish. I fought through exciting levels featuring astounding backgrounds and a soundtrack that parallels the original. Each new challenge felt fresh, with combinations of jumping and ball jumping giving me six whole combinations of movement. The game is forgiving, because it allows you to lose all 100 lives and have 0 score, but the game is not forgiving, because when I completed this challenge, I was met with words that will ring in my head "you were terrible, do it again." Thus, I will continue to challenge myself as a gamer and a person to master the skills needed to beat JumpBall 2 like a professional.
As a speedrunner, there are mechanics and secrets that I discovered while trying to beat each level as fast as possible. Jumping accelerates your ninjas, which mirrors sprinting or dashing in other popular speedruns. But there is also an invisible hitbox at the start of each level that requires frame-perfect jumping to miss and still get the jump boost. Jump boosting against the final boss in particular rewards you with single-ninja mode, making the level faster and easier than before. This is quite an impressive secret, and I feel lucky to have discovered it. I hope to work on my time so this game makes it to the next AGDQ.
All in all, JumpBall 2 is not "more of the same" like a lot of AAA titles these days. Unlike Pokemon, Call of Duty, or even Star Wars Battlefront, this game delivers on a visual and gameplay level that is only rivaled by its value. The dev team should be proud of thier work, and I hope this game breathes more life into a prosperous community of ninjas.

In the midst of thousands of titles released onto steam on a daily basis, one shines above all others today. Was it fate that this game be released? It most certainly was. With the resounding success of Jumpball, Andre Bertaglia's first smash hit, there was no question that the sequel was coming. I, as a fan, was nervous that it would not live up to the standards of the first game. However, I was pleasantly surprised that this game has surpassed my every expectation of what a game should be! The character development, the story, the punishment and reward system, and the music and graphics that appropriately call back to the days when the only jumping balls we were getting were in "Jumpball". Everything about this game just adds up to be the PERFECT package of challenge, reward, and just good quality fun! If you don't already own this game, BUY IT NOW! You won't regret it. Thank you Andre for another incredible gaming masterpiece. I CAN'T WAIT FOR JUMPBALL 3!!!

Easily one of the best games I have ever had the privilege of playing. It is truly a masterful work that really gets inside your head and endlessly messes with you. It's probably the only video game I have ever played that was able to retain its degree of horror despite how dated it looks, as your mind seems to fill in whatever blanks are created from the lack of graphical quality. Its atmosphere and dark themes end up seriously getting to you, and you'll find yourself anxiously checking every corner at the sound of an enemy or freaking out whenever a security camera goes off.
The only real low points of the game (aside from how dated it may seem to some) are the controls. They're somewhat convoluted and take some getting used to. There is also much rebinding to do upon first launch (A and D are bound to turn instead of strafe and X is bound to backing up instead of S). But despite this, the controls are totally possible (and totally worth) getting used to.
All in all, this is a game that I recommend to absolutely everyone. Even if you are not a fan of retro PC gaming or find yourself cringing at anything that seems too outdated, this game is easily worth getting.

People often compare Bioshock with System Shock, calling Bioshock the predecessor of System Shock, but that's just bs. Maybe story wise the original Bioshock is on par, but gameplay wise System Shock 2 is far superior. Bioshock is more of a shooter while System Shock 2 is an RPG, there is so much more content in System Shock2 for you to explore, and the atmosphere so cold, making the title a combination of almost perfect story and gameplay. To be frank, the graphics of SyS2 might be a lil bit out dated but a real hardcore gamer shouldn't judge a game by its graphics, but its gameplay.
Overall, the game was way ahead of its time and gameplay wise the depth it offers has surpassed even most, if not all of the modern titles. Bioshock Infinite is a joke when compared with SyS2, the only selling point of the former is that the plot is 'deep', but to me that's just artificial mind♥♥♥♥ery that appears to be deep, I have no idea why such a mediocre shooter could be so overhyped. tis really a shame that most modern gamers have never even heard of System Shock, and no more titles like this can be produced today even though the budgets of modern video games are much much larger.
In short, ditch Bioshock Infinite and buy System Shock 2, try it and see for youself, you'll never want to go back, and become as cynical about the Bioshock series as I am.
